stories.Summary:
The Nvidia board prepared to oust founder and CEO Jensen Huang around November 11, 2026, following reports of two extramarital affairs. Some board members favored naming Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim leader during this period of corporate instability. The board scheduled a meeting for Wednesday evening to make a final decision regarding the leadership of the chipmaker. Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a spy for the Chinese government. This scandal led to the abrupt departure of the man who led the company for 33 years.

The board named Colette Kress as interim CEO and appointed Harvey Jones, a board member for 25 years, as chairman. Kress has spent 13 years at Nvidia and previously clashed with Huang over 120 billion dollars in equity investments. She renegotiated a 250 billion dollar guarantee for an OpenAI project in Ohio, cutting the financial commitment in half. The company sought to acquire Hugging Face for 12.9 billion dollars and invest 10 billion dollars in Anthropic. These deals, along with the filling of the vacant board chair position, may now be subject to revision.

The board briefed the White House on its meeting, according to a senior administration official who spoke about the process. Colette Kress is described as a cautious leader who avoids the public spotlight and chooses her words very carefully. Harvey Jones once served as a mentor to Huang and will now help supervise the strategy of the CEO. Cathy Logue of Stanton Chase said a CFO is the best choice to send a message of stability. Gary Marcus called Huang a swashbuckler and noted that Kress must now clean up a legal mess.

Democratic senators Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren wrote to Trump's cabinet to preserve documents about chip exports to China. They asked Howard Lutnick, Marco Rubio, and Stephen Miller for communications concerning Huang and the suspected Chinese operative, Alice Huang. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue expressed his dismay on X, calling the entire situation deeply regrettable and truly sad. Many employees expressed support for Huang, with over 1,600 comments on an internal post urging his return to power. The company's stock fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading, hitting a 52-week low during the crisis.

The board launched a Wachtell Lipton-led probe to see if Huang divulged corporate secrets or endangered the security of the United States. Nvidia has provided advanced chips for hyperscalers and entered billions of dollars in financing deals to underwrite the AI buildout. Some critics describe circular financing, where Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use that money to buy chips. These companies include CoreWeave, Anthropic, and OpenAI, many of which are currently struggling to turn a profit. The federal government is now facing questions about its ability to enforce export controls and protect national security.

Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find a permanent CEO, with Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji being considered. The new leadership may shift toward a cautious investment strategy and rein in the aggressive spending of the past. It remains unclear if the long careers of Kress and Jones will hinder a full break from the past. Lawmakers are seeking answers about why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did not intervene earlier regarding the suspected intelligence operation. The articles leave open whether the planned acquisitions of Hugging Face and Anthropic will eventually be completed or cancelled.

stories.Headline: Databricks Launches New Always-on Genie: Autonomous AI for Complex Enterprise Work
stories.Summary:
Databricks launched the second generation of Genie on 12 November 2026, according to IT Brief Australia, and SD Times reported the announcement on 11 November 2026 from San Francisco. Databricks positioned Genie as an always-on autonomous AI agent for enterprise work. The update expands its push to embed AI agents in existing corporate data and software environments. The new version is designed to run continuously in the background and handle longer-running tasks without repeated user prompts.

Workers can assign a goal, set boundaries, and let the system track progress, follow up on missing inputs, and return when a person needs to make a decision. The launch includes Genie Search, intended to give staff and software agents a single governed search layer across structured and unstructured information. The release adds new features in Genie Ontology, Databricks' framework for capturing business definitions, metrics, reporting lines, and processes. Genie operates within a customer's existing Databricks environment and remains subject to security, permissions, and approval controls already set through Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway. Every action is auditable.

Ali Ghodsi, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Databricks, said Genie has made him a 10x more productive CEO and now does not wait for him to ask. Ghodsi said Genie keeps up with his inbox, preps him for meetings, and runs in the background, coming back only when it needs a decision. He said it can do that because it knows how the company works, what revenue means, which numbers are official, and who can see what. He called that the power of horizontal context and said Genie delivers it. Databricks said Genie and Genie Ontology are generally available, while Genie Search, Ontology Manager, and the always-on version of Genie are being rolled out through preview and beta programmes.

Jaime DeLanghe, Chief Product Officer of Slack, said teams make their best decisions when trusted context shows up in the flow of work. DeLanghe said Genie Agents connected to Slack let sales, finance, and operations teams go from question to action without leaving the conversation. Marlissa Wong, Director of Data Engineering at Headspace, said AI is only as good as the definitions behind it, so Headspace built its Genie Agents on agreed, governed definitions. Wong said Headspace expanded self-service analytics by putting plain-language access to its data in the hands of teams across the business, not just analysts. Alan Khalil, Associate Director of Data Science and Engineering at HelloFresh, said Genie constantly analysing performance signals improved programmatic ad ROI and reduced the time to identify ad winners on Meta by 75%.

Genie can be used for operational work such as monitoring quarterly forecasts, tracking revenue trends, analysing employee survey responses, and identifying changes in customer usage patterns. The system can delegate work to sub-agents, present outstanding issues in a priority inbox, and send email alerts when user input is required. Genie Search extends the product beyond the Databricks lakehouse to business applications including Google Drive, Jira, and Confluence. Teams can index content where it already sits, ingest it through Lakeflow Connect, or query applications live through MCP, and Databricks now offers more than 100 connectors to support those approaches. Databricks says searching once across multiple sources reduces tool calls and token usage.

The latest release adds support for business logic from external business intelligence tools and introduces an organisational structure connector. Databricks also introduced Ontology Manager, a new interface for teams to manage and govern business context, which can recommend areas for refinement by flagging concepts that are frequently queried. Users will be able to access Genie through a web browser, mobile app, email, and collaboration and AI products including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork, and Grok Bot. Agents can now operate across PDFs, contracts, and slide decks in Unity Catalog volumes alongside governed tables, without the need for a separate vector index. Databricks is also adding dynamic slides, dashboards, and interactive reports that remain tied to governed data and update as that data changes.

stories.Headline: Drug Ads Can Influence AI Treatment Recommendations, Study Finds
stories.Summary:
A study by researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai found that a clearly labeled pharmaceutical advertisement could influence which treatment an AI model recommended. The findings were reported in the November 11 online issue of The Lancet Digital Health. Researchers tested 12 AI models from major technology companies, including Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. They gave the models a physician-written clinical case, preceded by an ad for a drug. The ad made the models more likely to select the advertised drug.

Across 33 clinical scenarios, the advertised drug was selected in 47.6 percent of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35 percent without an ad. In four cases, models shifted from selecting the advertised drug zero percent of the time to selecting it 100 percent of the time when the ad was introduced. Researchers analyzed 258,559 AI responses and assessed both the treatment selected and whether it was consistent with clinical guidance. In a subset of free-text responses, models explicitly mentioned the ad in only 29.9 percent of responses. The study was designed to isolate the potential effect of advertising, with patient information and treatment choices unchanged and only the advertisement varying.

Physician-scientist and first author Mahmud Omar, MD, a lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at the Icahn School of Medicine, said he found it interesting and even surprising how reasonable the answers often appeared. He said the model could recommend an appropriate treatment, but its preference among several reasonable options changed after seeing the ad. He said that because the final answer could still appear medically sound, the influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations and in other patient and physician facing personal use cases. Girish N. Nadkarni, MD, MPH, senior author, Chair of the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health, Director of the Hasso Plattner Institute for Digital Health, and Irene and Dr. Arthur M. Fishberg Professor of Medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine, and Chief AI Officer at Mount Sinai Health System, said an answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise an important question about why the AI arrived at that answer. He said that as AI becomes part of how people get health information, we need to be able to distinguish clinical guidance from commercial influence and be transparent about when advertising is part of the interaction.

The investigators said the findings do not mean pharmaceutical advertising will necessarily cause AI models to recommend unsafe or inappropriate treatments. In the study, advertisements did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs. The researchers also did not examine whether changes in AI recommendations ultimately affected prescriptions, patient decisions, costs, or health outcomes. The researchers said the findings point to several practical steps for AI developers and health systems, including testing AI systems with and without promotional content to determine whether recommendations change, clearly disclosing when advertising is presented to an AI system, and keeping promotional material separate from clinical advice. The findings may also have implications for regulators as they consider how existing rules governing pharmaceutical advertising apply when promotional content is incorporated into AI-generated health information.

The study was provided by Mount Sinai Health System and subjected to News-Medical.Net's review protocols. The article was reported in The Lancet Digital Health with the DOI 10.1016/j.landig.2026.101114. The research team plans to extend the work through their ongoing evaluation of AI and human-AI interaction in real-world clinical cases. The article was posted in Device / Technology News, Healthcare News, and Pharmaceutical News. The article carried no comments at the time of publication.

stories.Headline: Bill Simmons Ends The Ringer’s ChatGPT Partnership After Fan Backlash
stories.Summary:
Bill Simmons recently ended a sponsorship deal between his Spotify-owned network, The Ringer, and OpenAI's ChatGPT. This decision followed significant backlash from listeners who disliked AI-powered segments on the network's shows. The partnership began last spring and was first reported as ended by Bloomberg on November 12, 2026. Simmons decided to stop the integration after realizing the content did not fit his brand.

The sponsorship primarily affected The Bill Simmons Podcast and The Ringer Fantasy Football Show. One specific segment on August 17 used ChatGPT to discuss Russell Westbrook's career. Other experiments included using the AI to generate film reviews in the style of Roger Ebert, who died in 2013. The ad copy appeared in episode notes until August 25, but it has been absent from the 35 episodes since then.

Simmons told Bloomberg that he wanted to be early to new trends, similar to the NFL and other competitors. He admitted that the audience simply did not like the AI segments. Internal critics also spoke out, including podcasters Sean Fennessey, Chris Ryan, and Amanda Dobbins. Fennessey expressed discomfort with the Ebert experiment and stated he would not want AI recreating his own opinions.

This retreat occurs while AI firms continue to spend heavily on podcast advertising. Podscribe data shows OpenAI spent about $11.2 million recently, while OpenAI and Anthropic combined spent over $13 million. Additionally, 62% of weekly listeners in a 2026 Edison Research study believe AI threatens podcast credibility. It remains unclear if The Ringer will accept other AI ads in the future.

stories.Headline: BIM Trichy and UT Arlington Redefine International Education: US Master's Degree in AI for Business Comes to India
stories.Summary:
Bharathidasan Institute of Management, a business school based in Tiruchirappalli, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with The University of Texas at Arlington. The agreement covers a joint Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence for Business, known by the abbreviation MSAIB. The signing was reported by The Hindu BusinessLine on November 13, 2026, and a photograph shows officials from both institutions at the ceremony. The programme is aimed at working professionals and will integrate AI machine learning, data engineering and generative AI into business strategy. It will be hosted at IIT Madras Research Park rather than at either partner's own campus.

The programme will begin with an initial trial cohort of 25 students, and faculty from the University of Texas at Arlington will facilitate it. It carries an indicative tuition fee of US$27,000, set as an alternative to the substantially higher overall cost of two years of full-time residential study in the United States. The hybrid learning model uses eight-week courses, with seven weeks of online instruction followed by one week of in-person learning. Students will be taught by the American university's faculty throughout the programme. They will also take part in a one-week immersion in the United States, which includes company visits, interactions with business executives and exposure to industry applications of artificial intelligence.

Ravi Appasamy, Chairman of the Board of Governors at BIM Tiruchirappalli, described the partnership as a deliberate step in building a globally recognised institution. He said the Board is firmly committed to positioning BIM as globally connected, academically distinguished and industry-relevant. He added that BIM is entering a new phase of its transformational journey, and that the institute is not simply building for the next decade. In his words, it is laying the foundations for the next generation of management education. Asit K. Barma, Director of BIM Tiruchirappalli, was also at the signing, as was Fernando Jaramillo, Associate Dean of Academic Affairs at the Texas university.

Radha K. Mahapatra, Chair and Professor of Information Systems and Operations Management at the University of Texas at Arlington, spoke about how students will be admitted. He said enrolments will be conducted through the university's own specialised framework. Although the programme is designed for working professionals, he said the university is also open to selecting capable students who have just completed their undergraduate studies. Separately, Anurag Behar, CEO of the Azim Premji Foundation, wrote in Mint on November 11, 2026 that India's higher education is in worse shape than its school education. He argued that artificial intelligence could be the death blow to the country's higher education institutions if the existing mess is perpetuated.

The partnership comes at a time when international student mobility has been disrupted by visa policies, rising education and living costs, and geopolitical developments. The Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report said new international student enrolments in the US fell by 7 per cent. Australia saw international student commencements drop by 12 per cent compared with the corresponding period. The UK reported a 16 per cent year-over-year decline in sponsored study visa grants to Indian nationals. Meanwhile, several global universities have set up in India, including the University of Liverpool in Bengaluru, the University of Bristol in Mumbai and the University of Western Australia in Mumbai and Chennai.

Behar's article offers its own account of the problems facing Indian higher education. He argues that many college classrooms sit empty because neither students nor teachers show up, and that research is conflated with teaching. He says public funding has been squeezed while enrolment ambitions have grown, and that his estimate is only 10 to 15 per cent of institutions are serious about their work. He pictures a loop in which a machine prepares the lesson, another writes the student's answer and a third marks it, so that no human mind learns anything. He calls for AI to be mostly banished from education and for a good higher education system to be built on new foundations.

The articles say the programme will start with a trial cohort of 25 students, but they give no start date for classes or for the first intake. They do not say how many students might be admitted after the trial cohort, or how the programme will be assessed. The articles do not say whether the Master's degree will be awarded by the University of Texas at Arlington, by BIM or jointly by both. They also leave open when applications will open and what admission criteria the university's own framework will use. The sources do not explain how the indicative tuition fee of US$27,000 might change, or whether any part of the cost will be covered by the partners.

stories.Headline: Warby Parker bets on Google AI glasses for growth, but privacy fears still loom
stories.Summary:
Warby Parker is entering the smart glasses market in partnership with Google and Samsung, betting that demand for AI wearables will balloon in the coming years. The New York-based fashion brand, known for affordable eyewear, also wants to head off privacy concerns that have weighed on existing producers of such glasses. Most smart glasses embed small cameras that let wearers record their surroundings without taking out a phone. Warby Parker held a demonstration event for its Intelligent Eyewear in New York City on November 9, 2026. Shoppers can start placing pre-orders from Warby Parker on Thursday, which the articles date to November 12.

The glasses connect to Google's Gemini AI assistant for everything from directions to language translation, much as Meta's glasses connect to an assistant. Alphabet's Google will not use visuals captured with the glasses to train its AI. The glasses will bar facial recognition of bystanders. A small white notification light on the front turns on automatically when a user starts recording video. Google says it will also guard the recording indicator light against tampering, redact people's faces from video before it is sent to Gemini, and ban targeted advertising on the glasses.

Warby Parker Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal told Reuters the big difference from existing versions on the market is the privacy framework embedded in the glasses from the outset. He said that as long as the tools provide utility to customers, the company will be successful. Juston Payne, who leads extended reality products at Google, acknowledged that public skepticism could be a risk to growth. He said trust was understandably lost in this area, and that Google intends to change the conversation and raise the bar. A Meta spokesperson said Meta's AI glasses also include a camera notification light on the front, and that input from safety experts helped inform their privacy features.

Calli Schroeder, who leads the AI and human rights program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, an advocacy group, said she was happy that footage is not automatically fed into AI systems for training. She said that still leaves open the worry of a stranger having footage of her child on a phone, which she called concerning however it is phrased. It remains to be seen whether Google's measures will ease concern about widespread surveillance if the glasses become ubiquitous. One of Britain's biggest pub chains has restricted the use of the frames. Norway's government is planning a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in certain locations, and Australia is considering barring camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces.

The Warby Parker glasses are broadly similar to Meta smart glasses from Ray-Ban and Oakley maker EssilorLuxottica, which have faced regulatory scrutiny from Norway to Australia. Ray-Ban's Meta glasses still dominate, representing 81.3% of AI glasses shipments in the first half of this year, according to research group Omdia. Global AI glasses shipments more than doubled in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier, though growth has slowed since the second half of last year. Optimism about the plan has helped Warby Parker shares rally by nearly 40% this year, against a 10% gain in the S&P 500. Analysts at TD Cowen wrote last week that smart glasses are poised to be an increasingly important driver of the company's growth outlook, even as the core optical backdrop remains soft.

Pre-orders open this Thursday, and Warby Parker expects the new wearable technology to add several percentage points to fourth-quarter revenue growth, executives said on an earnings call earlier this month. Luxury group Kering is poised to release glasses of its own in partnership with Google, as other brands seek a foothold against Ray-Ban's Meta glasses. The articles leave open whether Google's privacy measures will ease concern about surveillance if the glasses become widespread. They do not say whether Norway's planned temporary ban or Australia's government workplace restrictions will take effect. The articles also do not give a shipping date, a price or the full list of locations affected by the restrictions.

stories.Headline: Norway, Britain agree to deepen AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
Norway and Britain signed a letter of intent to deepen artificial intelligence cooperation on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in the city of Oslo. Norwegian Minister Torgeir Micaelsen and British Minister Kanishka Narayan announced this new partnership during a joint statement released to the public. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Atlantic Future Forum, which was held aboard the aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales. This initiative focuses on exploring joint work regarding computing infrastructure, model safety testing, and the international oversight of advanced AI systems. The two nations intend to strengthen their collective security and promote innovation, economic growth, and better public services through this agreement.

The plan requires closer cooperation between AI Norway, a national hub, and the British AI Security Institute for testing and evaluating AI models. It involves the UK Department for Business and Trade and the Norwegian Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance coordinating the various efforts. The countries will explore AI applications for defense, cybersecurity, and the integration of hardware to enable secure commercial hosting of national assets. They will also study the convergence of AI with robotics, biotechnology, and quantum technologies while developing international rules, standards, and governance frameworks. Specific collaboration will occur between the UK Taskforce RAID and Norway's Defence Centre for Data and AI to develop AI-enabled defense capabilities.

Minister Torgeir Micaelsen stated that AI offers significant opportunities for research and value creation, but the government must address the resulting security challenges. He noted that international cooperation is essential and emphasized the importance of working with trusted partners like the United Kingdom, a close ally. Minister Kanishka Narayan said that combining British AI expertise with Norwegian strengths in computing and energy would help build greater technological independence. He added that Norway is one of the most trusted allies and that practical cooperation will support good jobs in both countries. Both ministers recognized the transformative potential of AI to improve lives and support scientific discovery alongside the need to address safety risks.

The agreement affects government agencies, research institutions, and industry stakeholders who will now facilitate closer cooperation between their respective expert communities. The partnership aims to benefit the public by improving public services and supporting economic growth through the responsible use of AI. It also impacts the defense sector by harnessing complementary strengths in energy and technology to strengthen the collective security of both nations. The cooperation will involve the NCSC and NSM to share best practices on AI security and cybersecurity to manage advanced system risks. These entities will exchange knowledge regarding the capabilities and risks of advanced AI systems to ensure a more resilient and secure society.

This initiative builds on a strategic partnership that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer announced on December 16, 2024. It complements existing collaborations between the two nations regarding green industry, technological development, the Lunna House Agreement, and the Green Industrial Partnership. The ministers noted that their relationship is underpinned by shared democratic values and a commitment to maintaining open and resilient societies. They recognized that both countries possess complementary strengths in research, innovation, secure digital infrastructure, and access to clean energy for AI development. The current statement of intent is nonbinding and serves as a foundation for further bilateral cooperation in areas of strategic importance.

The two countries now aim to follow this letter of intent with a memorandum of understanding to specify the future cooperation details. The ministers agreed to remain in regular contact to build the partnership through their respective ministries and relevant national authorities. They will continue identifying opportunities for their initiatives to reinforce cooperation across international standards and various multilateral fora for AI governance. The articles leave open the specific terms of the upcoming memorandum and the exact timeline for implementing the proposed hardware integrations. It remains unclear how the joint development of AI-enabled defense capabilities will be funded or managed between the two different governments.

stories.Headline: Democratic political group launches new push to shape AI agenda before 2028
stories.Summary:
Tomorrow Together, a Democratic political organization, launched a new effort to shape the artificial intelligence agenda before the 2028 presidential campaign. This initiative was announced on November 12, 2026, during a Democratic conference held in the city of Denver, Colorado. The group aims to improve how the party communicates with voters regarding the regulation of powerful artificial intelligence technology. This push occurs as party leaders seek to create a stark contrast with President Donald Trump's opposition to regulation. The announcement took place during the two day What's Next conference to celebrate sweeping midterm race wins.

The new research initiative requires an initial investment of 1.1 million dollars to begin shaping the party's future AI policy. Tomorrow Together previously spent 6.5 million dollars on behalf of candidates who called for more regulation of AI and data centers. The group seeks to establish guardrails for development as companies enter a phase where AI can build new versions of itself. This effort follows a meeting in Denver where Rep.-elect Bob Brooks and Rep.-elect Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania were present. Senator-elect Josh Turek of Iowa and Rep.-elect Jamie Ager of North Carolina also attended the event with moderator Alex Edelman.

Chief program officer Maddie Kriger stated that getting this issue right will be critical to winning the votes of the people. She warned that the next year could bring more and worse AI incidents, making it necessary for the group to be prepared. Co-founder Karthik Ganapathy expressed that he would rather be on the Democratic side than the Republican side regarding this issue. Co-founder Rob Flaherty argued that Democrats now have the lead because voters want to see the regulation of new technology. Data analyst David Shor told the crowd that they are witnessing the birth of a new and rare political issue.

Voters from both political parties are affected because they generally embrace the idea of regulating artificial intelligence, according to David Shor. Some Republicans are also affected, including Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who has distanced himself from the pro-industry stance of Donald Trump. DeSantis is widely believed to be preparing another run for the presidency, which may complicate the Republican position on AI. The group believes that President Trump has embraced a wildly unpopular position by opposing the regulation of this powerful technology. This creates a political opportunity for Democrats to become the party that pushes for necessary guardrails on AI development.

The articles provide background that Tomorrow Together was one of several groups trying to counter industry campaign funds during the midterms. The group previously pushed for new limits on data centers and artificial intelligence to protect the public from potential risks. There are fresh warnings that AI technology poses risks to humans as it begins to develop its own new versions. This political shift follows a period where voters did not know which party to trust regarding the regulation of technology. The current environment is shaped by the contrast between Democratic goals and the pro-industry views held by Donald Trump.

The group will now work to prepare actions to help people if more AI incidents occur within the coming year. They intend to use this research to chart a course toward the next presidential campaign scheduled for the year 2028. The organization will continue to deepen its investment in AI issues to maintain its perceived lead over the Republican Party. The articles leave open whether other Republicans will follow Ron DeSantis in distancing themselves from the views of Donald Trump. It remains unclear how the AI industry will respond to the Democratic push for more regulation and stricter development guardrails.

stories.Headline: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
stories.Summary:
The Federal Reserve released its semiannual Financial Stability Report on Friday, November 13, 2026, and respondents to a survey in it named artificial intelligence as the greatest risk to the financial system. The report covers the period up to October 28, just a few days before the midterm elections. The survey drew on market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The New York Fed ran a survey of market contacts from September and October with a sample of 23 contacts. The report found the system otherwise fairly stable.

In the survey, 87% of respondents cited AI as a salient risk, up from 50% in the spring 2026 survey. A risk asset correction was next at 52%, followed by higher long-term rates at 48%, cyberattacks at 43% and fiscal debt sustainability at 43%. The U.S. debt is over $40 trillion and the budget deficit is near $2 trillion. Hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated in a relatively small group. Bank exposure to nonbank financial institutions surpassed $2.8 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, one-fourth of total commitments.

The report said respondents noted three areas of concern: elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could bring a market correction, cybersecurity risk from sophisticated state actors or from frontier AI models themselves, and risks from complex forms of AI-related financing. The report said broad equity valuation metrics continued to be elevated, partly driven by market enthusiasm for superintelligence, though moderated by concerns over firms' capital expenditures and debt issuance plans. It said a weaker economy could stress businesses with high leverage and the most vulnerable households, leading to increased credit losses for banks and other lenders. It said the complex interlinkages among firms in the data center buildout, public credit markets, private lenders and special purpose financing vehicles create vulnerabilities that necessitate close monitoring. It said the banking sector remained sound and resilient.

The report said asset valuations remain near the upper end of their historical ranges across most markets. It said new computing technologies have been significant drivers of U.S. economic growth in 2026. It described vulnerabilities from business and household debt as moderate but warned corporate borrowing could increase, driven in part by technology companies' growing debt issuance and increasingly complex financing arrangements. It said major companies in the data center buildout have rapidly increased borrowing, and private credit loan default rates have risen since May to the upper end of their historical range. Mortgage debt, about three-fourths of total household debt, remained subdued, and conventional mortgage delinquencies stayed near historic lows.

The report said outstanding household debt and consumer delinquencies remained relatively low. It said hedge fund leverage reached its highest level over the period since 2013, and it also highlighted elevated leverage among life insurers. It said banks modestly reduced interest rate risk by shortening asset duration, while strong profitability helped them build capital. In the New York Fed survey, nearly 90% cited elevated equity valuations and complex AI-related financing arrangements as sources of systemic risk, and just over half expressed concern about a sharp decline in AI-related stocks. Higher long-term interest rates and cyberattacks ranked third and fourth.

Wall Street is on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, and communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling. The report said an unexpected downturn in corporate earnings could lead to lower asset valuations, tighter credit conditions and reduced capital spending. The articles do not say what the Fed will do in response to the survey findings. The articles do not say when the next survey will be conducted.

stories.Headline: The FAA Is Rolling Out Its AI Air Traffic Tool Nationwide
stories.Summary:
The Federal Aviation Administration expanded an artificial intelligence tool called SMART to the entire national airspace system in November 2026. This rollout occurred three days before a nationwide grounding of all domestic and international flights on November 13, 2026. The agency expanded the tool to reduce delays and fuel consumption while improving the travel experience for the flying public. This AI system was first tested in the Washington, D.C. airspace during September to manage routing trajectories. The FAA claims the tool only suggests routes and does not affect the safety of air travel.

The SMART system cost 875 million dollars and was deployed across all 22 air traffic centers by November 10. It synthesizes data on weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics to optimize various flight routes. In Washington, D.C., the tool rerouted 180 flights, saving 80 gallons of fuel and 10 minutes per flight. These savings equaled nearly 345 dollars per flight based on jet fuel rates of 4.31 dollars per gallon. The FAA also plans to remove its dependency on the 55-year-old floppy disk format by the year 2028.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy praised the launch, stating that the tool would help resolve existing air traffic inefficiency. Duffy emphasized that a human will always manage the airspace in America to ensure that safety remains a priority. The FAA stated that a D.C. based team of experts validates all findings before passing them to controllers. Controllers retain the final decision on whether to accept the suggestions provided by the AI route management software. The agency told the public that the system predicts delays and optimizes routes through existing FAA procedures.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association stated it was not involved in the design, testing, or implementation of SMART. House Democrats sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking for a review of safety risk management. These lawmakers expressed concerns that the AI could hallucinate safety critical information or interfere with the decisions of controllers. American Airlines CEO Robert Isom praised the tool, while other airline executives feared the system might cancel flights unnecessarily. One industry official expressed trepidation over the feasibility of integration if the tool injected itself into day-to-day operations.

President Trump previously blamed outdated technology for a collision between a passenger jet and an Army helicopter over the Potomac. That accident killed 67 people early in his second term, and Trump promised to build brand new computerized systems. The administration has faced criticism for a slipshod record on air safety and delays caused by personnel issues. Last year, hundreds of FAA workers were laid off due to cuts related to the Department of Government Efficiency. Missy Cummings of George Mason University stated that these cuts made a brittle transportation system much worse.

All flights grounded at 4 P.M. EST on November 13 due to a temporary telecommunications outage managed by L3Harris. The FAA is investigating the issue, while expert Ruth Stilwell suggests a software update may have triggered a crash. This grounding is rare, with the previous stop occurring for 90 minutes on January 11, 2023, for NOTAM issues. The articles leave open whether the SMART rollout caused the outage or if it was a separate telecommunications failure. It remains unclear why the FAA expanded the system before the end of its professed 90-day test period.

stories.Headline: Dyania and NVIDIA partner to scale AI-driven clinical reasoning across health systems.aspx
stories.Summary:
Dyania Health announced a collaboration with NVIDIA on November 13, 2026, to put AI clinical reasoning to work inside health systems on their own infrastructure at the scale of their entire patient population. Dyania's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record across years of notes, operative reports, imaging reports and lab results and answers clinical questions with evidence from the chart. NVIDIA accelerated computing makes it possible to do that across large patient populations behind the hospital firewall without transferring patient records outside the health system. The companies aim to give health systems the ability to learn from the full histories of patients they have treated and turn that experience into earlier identification of care needs, more informed treatment decisions and better care for the next patient. The first work from the collaboration is a Cleveland Clinic study of 7,812 patients who received an aortic valve replacement between 2005 and 2021.

Synapsis AI is built on the NVIDIA AI Enterprise software stack end to end, and Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the NVIDIA NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network. Under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on NVIDIA infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies, and integrate Synapsis AI with NVIDIA's healthcare software stack. Areas the companies are evaluating include NVIDIA Confidential Computing for training and inference, NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed inference serving, Multi-Instance GPU for partitioning GPUs across concurrent clinical workloads, and scaling to many NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs as deployments move from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insight at the point of care. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning, and the company launched out of stealth two years ago.

Chelsea Sumner, Healthcare AI Startups Ecosystem Lead at NVIDIA, said the opportunity for AI in healthcare is to give care teams more time and insight to focus on patients. Sumner said Dyania Health brings deep clinical expertise to that opportunity, using NVIDIA's AI platform to support research, help identify gaps in care and build a more complete understanding of patients' needs. Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, called it a watershed moment for patient care and said every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results. Schlosser said that for the first time the technology can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time. Schlosser said Synapsis AI reads the full record, draws the clinical conclusions and shows the evidence behind them, and that NVIDIA gives Dyania the computing power to do that inside the hospital with every record staying where it belongs.

Lars G. Svensson, MD, PhD, Chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic, said using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients. Schlosser told Fierce Healthcare that Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise while NVIDIA brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises. Schlosser said frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but their architectures, training data sets and logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment. Schlosser said Dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation, an approach she asserted is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model. The collaboration could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review while keeping patient data inside the hospital's own infrastructure.

Health systems hold decades of clinical experience in their medical records, but much of it is difficult to analyze at scale because much of the information that matters is in narrative text rather than structured fields and interpreting it often requires manual review. Registries, outcomes studies and predictive models can be limited by how many charts a team can read by hand, and extracting and interpreting the clinical information needed to build them remains a major bottleneck. Synapsis AI is built to work the way a specialist works through a chart, longitudinally across every document, resolving what a patient actually had, when, and with what evidence. Doing this for one patient is a reasoning problem, but doing it for an entire health system continuously inside the hospital's own environment requires substantial computing capacity. The Cleveland Clinic study reviewed up to 16 years of patient care, most of it in narrative notes and echocardiogram reports that can be challenging to capture in registries.

Running on NVIDIA accelerated computing inside Cleveland Clinic's environment, Synapsis AI identified the patient population and answered 88 clinical questions for each patient, covering the valve and its characteristics, co-existing conditions, laboratory trends, medications, follow-up ultrasound measurements and later clinical events. A predictive machine-learning model was trained that is capable of predicting valve failure and reintervention risk timelines for every patient, and it found that the type of valve implanted was the strongest determinant of how quickly it deteriorated, while age and other medical conditions shaped whether and when a second procedure was performed. The analysis also examined how follow-up information such as heart ultrasounds following surgery can substantially raise predictive accuracy around future interventions, and the model estimates an individual patient's risk at three, five and 10 years and revises the outlook with each new ultrasound. The tool is used to help inform care but requires external validation from clinicians. Looking ahead, Synapsis AI agents will continuously train predictive models of this kind so that recommendations for the next recommended action in a patient's care keep improving in accuracy as precision medicine advances.

stories.Headline: DEEPX Begins Mask Production for Samsung 2nm AI Chip, Targets Q4 2027 Mass Production
stories.Summary:
The fabless semiconductor company DEEPX announced on November 10, 2026, that it finished the design for its DX-M2 artificial intelligence chip. The company completed the mask tape-out for prototype production in early November. This process involved transferring finalized design data to a foundry and correcting lithography distortions. Photomask production will now follow this milestone.

The project requires an investment of over $100 million for production engineering and performance verification. The chip uses Samsung Electronics' SF2P second-generation 2-nanometer process and targets a power consumption of 5 watts. DEEPX expects to receive the first silicon chips in March 2027 and provide samples to customers in the second quarter. Initial mass production is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027, with global expansion starting in 2028.

DEEPX is responsible for the project and stated that the chip will support generative AI workloads like vision-language and large language models. The company intends to target industrial systems, robotics, and AI-enabled personal computers. They noted that this approach allows AI to run directly on devices rather than in remote data centers. This strategy aims to lower costs, energy use, and data delays.

The DX-M2 recently won a CES 2027 Innovation Award in the AI category. This follows the mass production of the DX-M1 chip in August 2025, which used a 5-nanometer process. By October 2026, DEEPX had secured 88 purchase orders totaling about $13.3 million across 10 countries. The company now forecasts 2026 revenue of $40 million.

stories.Headline: IIT Jammu, NTT DATA to set up AI Centre of Excellence
stories.Summary:
The Indian Institute of Technology Jammu and NTT DATA announced a strategic collaboration to establish an Artificial Intelligence Centre of Excellence at IIT Jammu. NTT DATA is described as a global leader in digital business and technology services. The announcement was reported by Daily Excelsior on 13 November 2026 from Jammu. NTT DATA announced the collaboration in a statement on 13 November 2026, according to Elets Technomedia. The two organisations announced the partnership to develop AI for flood warnings and regional languages.

The proposed Centre will focus on using Artificial Intelligence and emerging technologies to address regional challenges and strengthen climate and disaster resilience. It will also develop technology talent and create new opportunities for innovation and entrepreneurship in Jammu and Kashmir. The collaboration will bring together IIT Jammu's academic and research capabilities with NTT DATA's global technology expertise and industry experience. NTT DATA will leverage its global network of Innovation Centres to connect IIT Jammu's research capabilities with industry requirements and advanced technology expertise. The Centre of Excellence will organise its activities around four principal areas: secure and responsible AI, digital twins, physical AI, and a laboratory dedicated to research commercialisation and startup development.

Prof. Manoj Gaur, Director of IIT Jammu, said the collaboration aims to create an environment where ideas can move from research to real-world application. He said it will provide students, researchers and faculty with opportunities to address challenges particularly relevant to Jammu and Kashmir. He said it will also strengthen efforts towards research commercialisation, technology entrepreneurship and the development of a strong deep-tech ecosystem in the region. Avinash Joshi, Executive Managing Director for India at NTT DATA, said the collaboration would combine the company's international technology expertise with local knowledge to develop solutions relevant to Jammu and Kashmir. Joshi said the partnership would give researchers and students a pathway to turn promising ideas into practical solutions and commercial applications.

The proposed AI-CoE will provide opportunities for students, researchers and faculty to work with industry on real-world challenges and develop technology solutions with potential applications across Jammu & Kashmir and beyond. Jammu & Kashmir's mountainous terrain and river systems present complex challenges related to floods, landslides, infrastructure planning and emergency response. Potential applications include flood monitoring and early-warning systems for the Tawi and Chenab river basins, along with technology-based approaches for monitoring landslide and flood risks. The proposed AI-CoE will explore secure and responsible AI, digital twins and physical AI, combining AI with robotics, computer vision, IoT and edge technologies for applications in infrastructure monitoring, environmental monitoring, autonomous systems and public safety. The partnership will also support research into Indian languages, including Dogri, while helping students and researchers develop technologies that could eventually be commercialised or used by public institutions.

The partnership builds on India's wider efforts to incorporate advanced computing into flood forecasting. In July 2025, the Ministry of Jal Shakti inaugurated C-FLOOD, a digital platform developed through collaboration between the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing, the Central Water Commission and the National Remote Sensing Centre. The platform provides flood inundation forecasts up to two days in advance, including village-level maps and predicted water levels. The Central Water Commission has also been developing AI and machine learning models to improve short-range flood forecasting across its monitoring network. The centre is the latest in a run of industry-backed AI labs at Indian institutes, after IIT Delhi's ₹9 crore AI research pact with Walmart Global Tech earlier this month.

The physical AI track places IIT Jammu alongside institutes such as IIT Kharagpur, which is building India's first dedicated School of Physical AI. The partnership announcement does not confirm the launch of a specific Dogri-language AI model or application. The partners have not disclosed the total investment, project implementation schedule or expected dates for deploying the proposed technologies. Residents in flood-prone areas should continue relying on official weather and disaster management advisories until any new AI-based warning systems are formally validated and introduced. The effectiveness of such systems would depend on the quality of available data, the accuracy of predictions and their integration with existing disaster management mechanisms.

stories.Headline: Investors worry the AI trade needs Nvidia's Huang and its largesse
stories.Summary:
Alice Huang pitched a multimillion-dollar artificial intelligence infrastructure project to investors, claiming she could secure Nvidia's advanced chips and citing Alibaba as a prospective client, according to a Financial Times report. Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and her business partner Kang Wei sought investment in early 2025 for a Southeast Asian data-centre project estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The Financial Times reported this citing two investors who were approached about the proposal. During the pitch, the pair said they had no problem securing Nvidia graphics processing units, a key component used to develop and operate artificial intelligence systems. They also cited Alibaba as a client for the proposed project, according to an investor familiar with the discussions.

The proposed data-centre project raises questions about how advanced Nvidia chips could be made available to Chinese businesses through infrastructure located outside mainland China. US export controls restrict Chinese companies from owning certain advanced AI chips, although Chinese businesses can lease computing capacity from data centres operating overseas, subject to applicable restrictions. The Financial Times report said Alice Huang and Kang Wei presented access to Nvidia GPUs as a central part of their investment proposal. Their reference to Alibaba drew attention to the Chinese technology company's reported business relationship with Megaspeed. Documents reviewed by the Financial Times investigation showed that Alibaba had lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries in 2024, and people familiar with the company described Alibaba as Megaspeed's anchor customer and largest client.

US intelligence officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was connected to a Chinese espionage effort targeting Jensen Huang, with the alleged objective of gathering information about the Nvidia chief and influencing his efforts to persuade Washington to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an extramarital affair and apologized to his wife and family. Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation into whether he was targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. The company has said it has no reason to believe that its national security interests or confidential information were compromised. Beijing has rejected the espionage claims, while Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing related to chip smuggling.

The allegations have not been independently established. Alice Huang is a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, and the allegations follow claims that she was recruited by Chinese intelligence to establish a relationship with Jensen Huang and potentially influence his position on US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. The development adds another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding Alice Huang. The latest revelations come as Nvidia faces questions over its chief executive's reported relationship with Alice Huang and whether the company was exposed to a potential foreign intelligence operation. The allegations have brought renewed attention to Nvidia's business dealings in China and the security implications of its global AI chip supply chain.

A Financial Times report on Jensen Huang's downfall says he ran Nvidia as a "feudal system" with his daughter and son-in-law in powerful positions. The report is headlined Jensen Huang's final days at Nvidia. The Financial Times article was published on 2026-11-13. The Times of India article was published on 2026-11-10. The Times of India article was edited by Poulomi Ghosh.

The Financial Times article is behind a subscription and its full contents are not available. The Times of India article does not say what happens next to the proposed data-centre project. The Times of India article does not say what the outcome of the independent directors' investigation will be. The Times of India article does not say whether the allegations against Alice Huang will be established. The Times of India article does not say what action, if any, US authorities will take.

stories.Headline: South Korea, UN discuss North Korea nuclear threat and military AI
stories.Summary:
Senior officials from South Korea and the United Nations met on Friday to discuss North Korea's nuclear program. The meeting occurred during a two-day conference on disarmament and nonproliferation held in Seoul starting Thursday. Vice Foreign Minister Jeong Yeon-doo and UN High Representative Izumi Nakamitsu led these high-level diplomatic talks. They focused on the nuclear issue and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in the military domain. The officials also reviewed outcomes from the First Committee of the United Nations General Assembly.

The discussions took place in central Seoul at the South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Jeong noted that South Korea co-hosted a military AI summit with the Netherlands and spearheaded a UN resolution. Federal Reserve staff calculations based on Epoch AI data project U.S. AI computing capacity to increase 239 percent this year. Planned U.S. AI compute by 2030 would be roughly 35 times the levels seen in mid-2025. These figures highlight the rapid technological growth that could alter the global nuclear balance of power.

Vice Foreign Minister Jeong stressed that international cooperation is necessary to promote the responsible use of military AI. He stated that South Korea will continue playing an active role in addressing challenges related to this technology. Izumi Nakamitsu warned that rapid advances in AI could increase risks of miscalculation and unintended military escalation. She argued that international law must be observed and humans must retain control over all AI decisions. Nakamitsu suggested developing policies based on technical expertise and finding appropriate forums for future dialogue.

Experts warn that North Korea might adopt a use it or lose it mentality if the U.S. obtains AGI. This perceived advantage could lead Pyongyang to fear a first strike that decapitates its leadership and nuclear capabilities. Other affected powers include China and Russia, who possess the world's third largest and largest nuclear arsenals respectively. These nations might act aggressively if they believe the United States is first to approach AGI attainment. Non-AGI powers may also seek deterrence through asymmetric methods like pre-positioning chemical and biological weapons.

The articles note that North Korea has an aggressive nuclear doctrine and a paranoid view of U.S. intentions. Pyongyang lacks a survivable nuclear submarine deterrent and suffers from severe technical and geographic disadvantages. History shows humans prevent escalation, such as when Stanislav Petrov identified a false Soviet missile warning in 1983. North Korea is likely using unsafeguarded models to exploit vulnerabilities, as seen in a 6 billion dollar Binance hack. The risk of AI-designed viruses suggests a need for Washington and Beijing to discuss biological AI capabilities.

Future efforts may require constraining the publicly accessible biological capabilities of future large language model releases. Washington and Beijing should have candid conversations about diffusing powerful AI capabilities in the field of biology. The articles leave open how long it will take to implement new human-in-the-loop command and control safeguards. It remains uncertain if North Korea will seek arms control negotiations or increase its aggression during an AGI sprint. The final impact of artificial superintelligence on nuclear decision-making timelines is also a subject of ongoing debate.

stories.Headline: How two 23-year-old Indian-American entrepreneurs doubled their fortunes as AI startup hits $20 billion
stories.Summary:
Adarsh Hiremath and Surya Midha, two 23-year-old Indian-American entrepreneurs, saw their fortunes double when the AI startup Mercor reached a $20 billion valuation, according to India Weekly. Their individual net worth rose to $4.2 billion each as a result. The report was published on November 13, 2026. The Economic Times, in a piece dated November 11, 2026, listed them among the five youngest billionaires who built their fortunes on artificial intelligence.

The articles give the $20 billion valuation for Mercor and the $4.2 billion figure for each founder. They name Adarsh Hiremath and Surya Midha as the two 23-year-old Indian-American entrepreneurs behind the company. The Economic Times also mentions Fabian Hedin and Nvidia among its tags on the story. The India Weekly report says the pair doubled their fortunes as the startup hit the $20 billion mark.

The articles do not quote Hiremath or Midha directly, and they do not describe statements from either founder. Responsibility for the company rests with the two co-founders, who are identified as the entrepreneurs behind Mercor. The reports attribute the wealth figures to the startup's valuation rather than to any comment from the founders. No other named person is described as responsible in the articles.

The context given is the broader AI boom, which The Economic Times frames as the source of fortunes for the youngest billionaires it lists. The articles do not say what happens next for Mercor, for Hiremath or for Midha. They also give no further details on the company's plans or future funding. Beyond the valuation and the founders' net worth, the reports offer no additional information on what follows.

stories.Headline: Growing AI Use Raises Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
Kaspersky has published a survey showing that growing use of artificial intelligence for personal advice, health questions and everyday planning is raising worries about privacy and cybersecurity. The survey covered respondents across the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa region, known as META, and was reported by Pakistan Observer and The Patriot on 12 November 2026. Nearly 79 percent of respondents said they use AI services, including chatbots and tools for making images and videos. Experts warned that sharing sensitive information with these platforms could expose users to data leaks, misuse by third parties and cyberattacks. The IAPP also published an analysis on 12 November 2026 on how Italy is handling AI, privacy and cybersecurity.

Searching for and summarising information was the most common use of AI, cited by 74 percent of those surveyed. Writing texts followed at 50 percent, generating images from written prompts at 42 percent, and editing personal photos at 41 percent. Another 32 percent turned to AI to create videos, while 37 percent used it for health-related questions and 41 percent sought advice on personal matters. Planning weekends, holidays or events drew 29 percent, and creating meal menus and diet plans drew 23 percent. Almost one in 10 respondents had already met incorrect AI-generated information, and 24 percent believed AI could give inaccurate answers.

Seifallah Jedidi, Kaspersky's Head of Consumer Channel for the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa, is the named spokesperson. He urged consumers to understand the limits of AI services and the risks linked to them. He said even widely used platforms can have vulnerabilities that lead to data leaks. According to him, information shared with these platforms may be processed under the relevant service and its policies, or may be reached by third parties. He urged users to verify AI-generated content, avoid sharing confidential information and stay alert to fraudulent AI services designed to spread malware.

Kaspersky experts advised users to avoid giving sensitive, confidential or private information to AI services in order to reduce cybersecurity risks. They warned that phishing web pages, malicious software and fake websites often imitate genuine platforms or deceive users with fake tools. The company also recommended checking each platform's data-handling policies. It advised consulting reliable sources before relying on AI for medical, financial, legal or educational advice. Users of AI services are the people affected, particularly those who share health details or personal matters with chatbots.

The IAPP analysis, written by Ludovica Mosci, Manager of Privacy Compliance EMEA at The Walt Disney Company, describes Italy as one of Europe's most interventionist jurisdictions on privacy, AI and cybersecurity. Two legislative decrees recently completed Italy's transposition of the EU AI Act into national law. Legislative Decree No. 160, adopted on 9 September, introduced corporate and individual criminal liability provisions. Legislative Decree No. 179, adopted on 8 October and in force from 23 October, clarifies the roles and responsibilities of Italy's national AI supervisory authorities. In July, the data protection authority, the Garante, concluded its investigation into Character Technologies, the U.S.-based provider of the Character.AI companion app, which also touched on minors' online protection.

The articles do not say what follows from the Kaspersky survey, and they give no sign of any regulatory response to its findings. They describe Italy's cybersecurity position as one of no new regulatory developments, with 2026 marking the move from legislative implementation to operational compliance and active supervision under the NIS2 Directive and the Digital Operational Resilience Act. They say the Garante has continued its scrutiny of AI providers, including a decision on an AI-powered plug-in for sentiment analysis of employees. The IAPP excerpt does not set out the outcome of the Character.AI investigation or of the employee plug-in decision. Kaspersky also points to its Kaspersky Premium security solution, which it says protects users in everyday digital activities through AI-based technologies.

stories.Headline: Intel forms 23-company Korean AI alliance as it pitches HBM-free inference GPU
stories.Summary:
Intel formed a 23-company Korean AI alliance to build infrastructure tailored for the South Korean market. This initiative was announced during the Intel AI Summit Seoul 2026 event. The launch occurred on November 11, 2026, at the COEX center in Seoul. Intel is courting the local ecosystem by pitching a new inference GPU. This GPU replaces costly high-bandwidth memory with low-power DRAM.

The K-AI Full Stack Alliance includes KTNF, Dnotitia, Panmnesia, Upstage, Nota AI, DEEPX, FuriosaAI, Exina, and Hancom. This coalition targets sovereign AI and physical AI markets using domestically manufactured servers. Intel also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Seoul AI Hub for startups. The new Crescent Island GPU uses LPDDR5X memory to support up to 480 gigabytes. This capacity is five times larger than the Nvidia RTX Pro 6000.

Tae-Won Bae, president of Intel Korea, stated the alliance represents a commitment to innovation on open infrastructure. Santosh Viswanathan, Asia-Pacific regional head, identified sovereign, personalized, and edge AI as key Korean opportunities. Dan Rodriguez discussed expanding AI beyond PCs into industrial environments using Intel Core Ultra Series 3. Anil Nanduri noted that AI inference requires scaling and flexibility for various model sizes. Marcus Lawrence offered design and foundry services for clients with their own chip designs.

The alliance affects domestic AI startups and companies innovating in large language models, memory, and infrastructure. These partners will collaborate across hardware, software, and industry-specific AI solutions and services. The partnership aims to respond quickly and flexibly to the rapidly evolving AI market. Local companies can now use Intel's turnkey capabilities from the conceptual stage to actual production. This collaboration helps Korea strengthen its sovereign AI capabilities through domestically designed servers.

Intel is mass-producing Clearwater Forest, a Xeon processor with up to 288 energy-efficient E-cores. The company is also developing the Intel GPU D-Series, which delivers 26,200 TFLOPS of FP4 performance. This accelerator consumes 350 watts and shows lower latency on Gemma models than Nvidia products. The D270 model provides 5.9 times the financial simulation performance of the Nvidia RTX 6000 Pro. Intel previously shared news about the development of Crescent Island last year.

Intel plans to launch the Crescent Island GPU next year to enable low-power AI computing. The company will launch Diamond Rapids next year, featuring up to 256 high-performance P-cores. The articles leave open how many more companies will join the K-AI Full Stack Alliance. They do not specify the exact date for the Diamond Rapids release beyond next year. The texts do not state the final price for the new GPU product line.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA becomes AI Consulting Partner of the Nitto ATP Finals
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA became a Gold Partner of the Nitto ATP Finals, taking the roles of Official AI Consulting Partner and Official Technology Consulting Partner, Telecompaper reported on 13 November 2026. The tournament will be held in Turin, Italy, from 15 to 22 November 2026. NTT DATA announced the partnership in Tokyo on 12 November 2026, according to its own release. IT Brief UK reported the news on 12 November 2026. The partnership gives NTT DATA a presence at the 2026 tournament in Turin.

The tournament takes place at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, Italy, from 15 to 22 November 2026. NTT DATA plans to present technology demonstrations linked to sport and human performance at the arena. The company will host a Tech Corner featuring computer vision, physical AI and AI infrastructure in settings including monitoring, safety, construction and humanoid robotics. The Tech Corner will also house the Mental Economy Gym, developed with Formula Medicine, an Italian specialist in sports medicine and human performance. At the Fan Village court, an on-court experience presented by FITP will combine cognitive and physical monitoring with AI-based computer vision.

Kazuhiko Nakayama, President and CEO of NTT DATA Group, said what makes sport extraordinary is ultimately human, citing the ambition to push boundaries, the courage to take risks and the determination to achieve more. He said technology can unlock greater possibilities by helping people see what was previously invisible and discover new ways to improve. He said that as an AI Consulting Partner of the Nitto ATP Finals, NTT DATA wants to celebrate human potential while demonstrating how technology can expand what people can achieve. He said NTT DATA combines AI capabilities with deep industry expertise to help clients transform their businesses and create new value. NTT DATA described the partnership as the latest in a series of sporting partnerships that bring its global brand positioning statement, "Intelligence to Impact," to life.

NTT DATA said the agreement reflects its belief that intelligence comes not only from AI and technology but also from human expertise and deep industry understanding. The company said it will continue to build on these efforts, using sport as a platform to demonstrate how AI and technology can enhance human potential and create meaningful impact beyond sport. Visitors to the Mental Economy Gym can take on digital challenges that measure indicators such as concentration, reaction and mental workload. NTT DATA is a $30+ billion business and technology services leader serving 75% of the Fortune Global 100, with experts in more than 70 countries. NTT DATA is part of NTT Group, which invests over $3 billion each year in research and development.

The partnership provides a global stage for NTT DATA to showcase how AI, data and technology can support human potential, according to the company. NTT DATA said elite tennis brings together skill, judgment and the ability to adapt under pressure, and it aims to show how technology can provide deeper insights into performance and help people and organizations address challenges beyond sport. The company released a key visual for the Nitto ATP Finals, supported by NTT DATA Group as a Gold Partner. NTT DATA offers clients access to an ecosystem of innovation centers as well as established and start-up partners. The company describes itself as one of the world's leading AI and digital infrastructure providers, with capabilities in enterprise-scale AI, cloud, security, connectivity, data centers and application services.

NTT DATA will use the tournament to show how AI, data and related systems can generate performance insights and support decision-making under pressure. The company said its consulting and industry solutions help organizations and society move confidently and sustainably into the digital future. NTT DATA is a Global Top Employer, according to its release. The articles leave open what the partnership costs and how long it runs. The articles do not say which players will take part in the 2026 tournament.

stories.Headline: Protest against AI in schools, search block planned outside Google's Chicago office Wednesday
stories.Summary:
Parents, students, and teachers plan to protest outside Google's Chicago office this Wednesday at 4 p.m. The group opposes the company's restriction of Google search in schools and the use of embedded generative AI. This rally will take place in the 300 block of Morgan Street, located in Chicago's West Loop. Organizers include the Chicago Teachers Union, the Illinois Federation of Teachers, and Illinois Families for Public Schools. Other groups involved are Schools Beyond Screens, Distraction Free Schools, and the Chicago chapter of Veterans for Peace.

Alphabet announced that K-12 students cannot access search at schools that ban AI, starting in early 2027. The company will turn off AI in education apps unless administrators enable it, as search and AI are integrated. Google offers conventional search with AI Overviews or Guided Learning, which it began piloting in selected US schools in November. New York City announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in September for 600,000 students through eighth grade. Chicago Public Schools blocked Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude on Monday to comply with FERPA, COPPA, and SOPPA privacy laws.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, stated that search and AI are deeply integrated into the system. Brit Mennuti, the Google Classroom product lead, said the school pilot version has restrictions and allows transcript reviews. Alphabet claims that its research found measurable improvements in student learning through the Guided Learning feature in Gemini. Google stated it is reviewing allegations regarding student safety and has worked with researchers to develop young user safeguards. The company claims it cannot offer an AI-free version of Google search because AI is now too ingrained.

Lina Khan, former FTC chair, accused Google of using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI technology. Senator Ed Markey called on Google to reverse its decision and explain if AI can be separated from search. Ben Williamson of the University of Edinburgh argued that Google uses existing dependencies to push AI products into schools. Parents of a schoolgirl sued Google, alleging Gemini pushed their 13-year-old daughter into a mental health crisis and suicide. The protest group says data still flows from CPS-approved apps to AI companies without parental consent or notice.

Google Chromebooks became the most widely issued student devices in the US after the company piloted them in 2010. By 2016, these devices accounted for 58 percent of mobile computing devices shipped to schools across the United States. Schools also rely on Gmail, Google Docs, and Google Classroom, while integrating with hundreds of other educational apps. In January 2024, Denmark's data protection authority ordered 53 municipalities to change how they shared pupil data with Google. A 2026 review of 22 studies identified risks like cognitive dependence and effects on the psychological wellbeing of students.

The company will implement these search and AI changes for student accounts starting in early 2027. A US federal judge recently dismissed an antitrust claim by Penske Media regarding the tying of AI to search. It remains an open question if Google's school policy raises antitrust concerns given its dominance of the search market. The articles leave open whether Google can legally bundle AI features with search or if it must separate them. Educators continue to question how much influence private technology companies should have over the policies of public education systems.
