stories.Headline: OpenAI launches local API inference for GPT-6 Luna in India
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has launched local processing and inference for its API in India, so eligible organisations can run supported AI workloads without sending any requests outside the country. The announcement was reported by Inc42 on 12 November 2026 and by TechGig on 13 November 2026. The service is limited to the GPT-6 Luna model at launch, and it expands the data residency options OpenAI already offered in India. With the update, both the handling of an API request and the model computation take place on servers located in India. Supported customer content is also kept within the country, which gives businesses greater control over where their data is processed.

The new offering supports GPT-6 Luna input and output through two interfaces, the Responses API and the Chat Completions API. To use it, developers must create a new API project, select India as the region for both storage and processing, and use the India regional endpoint. Local processing applies only to direct API usage, so it does not extend to other ways of reaching the model. Businesses can use it for text-based tasks, including document summaries, drafting replies, and analysing information for employees. With the launch, India joins Australia and Japan as the markets where OpenAI has introduced regional API inference capability.

Nitin Bawankule, who heads enterprise in India at OpenAI, said the need for in-country processing had stopped some Indian businesses from using AI for important work. Local inference is intended to remove that barrier, and he said it could help more organisations move from experimenting with AI to deploying it in everyday operations. He also said it gives businesses greater control over where their data is processed. OpenAI is responsible for building and offering the service, and it has presented the launch as part of its broader push in India. The company has set out specific steps for customers to follow in order to use the new offering.

Reports from Inc42 and TechGig say the feature is aimed at sectors such as financial services, where data handling rules dictate how AI applications are deployed at scale. Inc42 notes that banks, financial institutions and government agencies cannot compromise on how data is stored and processed before a model is deployed. For these clients, data residency and infrastructure requirements can limit the use of international frontier AI models in production environments. Indian businesses that need in-country processing are the main group affected by the change. Inc42 also says the entry of OpenAI and Anthropic into this segment could narrow the advantage that locally hosted inference gave Indian AI startups such as Sarvam AI.

Until now, OpenAI's residency options in India only covered the storage of customer data, which left the processing of requests outside the country. Inc42 says OpenAI is not the first international AI company to address India's data localisation requirements. In August, Anthropic announced plans to bring in-country inference for its Claude models to India through Amazon Bedrock, the managed service from AWS for building generative AI applications. Anthropic has since made similar data residency capabilities available for certain models on AWS Bedrock. The launch also follows the OpenAI for India initiative announced earlier this year, which covers AI infrastructure, enterprise adoption, skills, and local partnerships, including a partnership with Tata Group to build domestic AI data centre capacity.

Inc42 reports that OpenAI has a strong position in the Indian market, where more than 10 Cr people use ChatGPT every week, and that the company is looking to earn revenue from it. Data inference is described as another piece of that India revenue, alongside new business tools such as Businesses in ChatGPT. That beta lets companies claim and manage their profiles through a Business Hub, where eligible businesses in markets including India can claim profiles subject to verification requirements. Business Agents, which let customers ask product questions inside ChatGPT, are initially available only to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the US. The articles do not say when local inference will extend beyond GPT-6 Luna, and they give no timeline for supporting other models or other ways of accessing them.

stories.Headline: S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Nvidia CEO's exit rattles AI stocks
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks ended slightly lower on Thursday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The company named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The news shook confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, and Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14 percent at the open before recovering part of the loss. By the close, the stock was down 4.34 percent at 166.19 dollars.

The three major indexes all finished in the red. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 189.4 points, or 0.36 percent, to 52,297.09. The S&P 500 lost 26.98 points, or 0.35 percent, to 7,592.4, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 100.1 points, or 0.39 percent, to 25,366.09. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next Tuesday.

Not every chip stock followed Nvidia lower, as investors looked for companies that might benefit from the leadership turmoil at the AI industry's biggest supplier. Advanced Micro Devices rose 5.86 percent and Broadcom gained 5.54 percent. Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said the AI revolution is much bigger than any one company. He argued that if Nvidia's chips were no longer the best, buyers would switch to rivals such as AMD or Google, and that demand for the chips is not falling.

Other market moves added to the pressure. Traders kept pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with markets putting the chance of a quarter-point move at about 91 percent. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note rose to 5.1 percent, after closing at 4.98 percent late Tuesday, before the Veterans Day bond market holiday. Oil prices jumped after a social media post from President Trump dampened hopes of a deal with Iran any time soon, with West Texas Intermediate settling at 88.74 dollars a barrel, up 2.55 percent, and Brent crude at 95.82 dollars, up 3.3 percent. AI cloud company Nebius fell 16.84 percent after its quarterly report, even though its revenue rose sharply from a year earlier.

stories.Headline: Surging AI chip revenue and Microsoft deal boost Cerebras Systems stock by 17%
stories.Summary:
Cerebras Systems Inc. reported third quarter revenue that beat expectations on November 12, 2026. The AI chipmaker also announced a new deal with Microsoft Corp. during this report. These combined events caused the company stock to rise almost 18 percent in late trading. The financial results showed strong growth for the company over the most recent quarter. Investors reacted positively to the revenue surge and the new partnership with Microsoft Corp.

Core adjusted revenue reached 230.9 million dollars, which is 70 percent higher than the previous year. This figure surpassed the Wall Street target of 214.7 million dollars for the same period. The company reported a loss of 67 cents per share, missing the guidance of 14 cents. An adjusted operating margin of -14 percent beat the previous guidance of -24 percent from three months ago. The hardware and cloud services backlog grew from 25 billion dollars in August to 26 billion dollars.

Chief Executive Andrew Feldman told analysts that the company has a clear advantage over its current competitors. He stated that long lead times for GPUs and higher expenses create opportunities for Cerebras hardware sales. Feldman explained that the Microsoft agreement was signed and sealed one month before the current announcement. He noted that a large part of the backlog relates to a deal with OpenAI Group PBC. Feldman believes that company revenue will triple by the end of fiscal 2027.

Wall Street analysts are looking for a core gross margin of 42.1 percent on sales of 271 million dollars. Some analysts believe that Nvidia Corp. still dominates the industry by accounting for over 90 percent of sales. Investors expressed concerns that the new deals with Microsoft, Oracle Corp., and Amazon Web Services Inc. are small. Other customers are affected by the backlog, though Feldman suggests they do not wait as long for orders. The company is now evaluating financing options to meet demand and reduce its order backlog.

Nvidia is currently in turmoil following the shocking resignation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang. Reports suggest Huang had affairs with three people, including an executive at a Singapore data center infrastructure firm. That executive is believed to be a spy for Chinese intelligence and a conduit for illegal GPU shipments. Nvidia is seeking stability by appointing longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim CEO. This disruption at the biggest rival may provide a strategic benefit to Cerebras and other chipmakers.

Cerebras anticipates fourth quarter revenue between 310 million and 330 million dollars with a core gross margin of 47 to 49 percent. The company expects revenue from the Microsoft deal to appear in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Full year revenue for fiscal 2027 is estimated at 2.85 billion dollars, slightly below the forecast of 2.92 billion dollars. The articles leave open exactly what the new financing options for the company will look like. It remains unclear how long it will take for Cerebras to fully exploit the disruption at Nvidia.

stories.Headline: AI privacy starts with your data
stories.Summary:
The European Union has fined Match Group, the owner of the dating app Tinder, €11 million for failing to give users proper access to their personal data. The fine was reported by AFP on 13 November 2026, and the penalty was imposed by Ireland's Data Protection Commission. The regulator found that Tinder's "Download My Data" tool left out certain categories of personal information, which broke EU data protection rules. In other cases the tool offered only summaries of the data without clearly telling users that this was all they were receiving. The investigation behind the decision was launched in 2020, so the case has taken roughly six years to reach this outcome.

The decision does more than impose a financial penalty, because it also orders Match Group to change how it handles personal data. Ireland's Data Protection Commission requires the company to bring its data processing practices into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation, known as the GDPR. The deadline set for that compliance is three months, which gives Match Group a short window to correct the problems the regulator identified. The €11 million figure applies to the failures found in the "Download My Data" tool, and the order covers how the company processes personal information more broadly. The articles name Ireland as the country whose regulator led the case, and they identify Tinder as the service whose users were affected.

Responsibility for the violations lies with Match Group, which owns Tinder and operates the "Download My Data" tool at the centre of the case. Match Group rejected the findings of the Irish regulator and said it does not accept that it broke the rules as described. The company announced that it plans to appeal the decision, so the penalty and the order may be challenged rather than simply accepted. It also insisted that Tinder maintains strong privacy protections for its users, offering that as its answer to the regulator's conclusions. Ireland's Data Protection Commission stands behind its findings and is the body that issued both the fine and the order to comply.

The people most directly affected are Tinder's users, who were meant to be able to see their personal data through the "Download My Data" tool but did not always receive all of it. Some of the information they were entitled to was missing from what they could download, and some was provided only as a summary without a clear explanation. Match Group's own response is the main reaction the articles report, since the company disputes the regulator's account and says user privacy is well protected. The AFP report, relayed by BGNES, presents the €11 million fine as an action taken by the European Union as a whole, even though Ireland's regulator carried it out. A separate opinion piece published the same day by TechRadar discusses data privacy in a different setting and does not mention Tinder or Match Group.

The background the articles give begins with the investigation, which was launched in 2020 and examined how Tinder let users reach their own data. Under EU data protection rules, people are entitled to access their personal information, and the regulator judged that the Tinder tool fell short of that standard. The TechRadar opinion piece, written by Adam Mayer, who is Technical Product Marketing Director at Qlik, describes how privacy challenges grow as artificial intelligence gains access to more company data. It reports that 95% of enterprises have delayed or cancelled AI projects because of infrastructure and data governance challenges, a figure it ties to the difficulty of managing privacy. The same piece says personally identifiable information such as names, addresses or financial details should be clearly labelled, and that sensitive information should stay in live systems wherever possible.

The next step in the Tinder case is the appeal that Match Group has said it will bring against the findings of Ireland's Data Protection Commission. The three-month deadline for bringing its data processing practices into line with the GDPR is already running under the regulator's order. The articles do not say where or when the appeal will be filed, nor whether the order and the fine remain in force while it is pending. They also do not say whether the missing categories of personal data will be restored to users or how any changes to the tool would work. Nothing in the articles explains how Match Group will answer the specific omissions the regulator found, or when the dispute might finally be resolved.

stories.Headline: Robin Li: Why Build a New Factory in the AI Era? Insights into Baidu’s AI-Driven Manufacturing Strategy
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, Baidu founder Li Yanhong spoke at the Baidu World conference in Beijing about the AI transformation of enterprises. He discussed the AI-driven manufacturing strategy with his guest, Lenovo Group Chairman Yang Yuanqing, during the event. Li urged companies to reorganize around artificial intelligence to realize true productivity gains. He argued that the current exploration of AI by enterprises is still in the early stage. The two technology leaders agreed that companies must continue exploring in environments that encourage practice.

Li proposed a smart organization, which is an AI-native organizational system that replaces conventional hierarchical structures. This system requires breaking job boundaries, precipitating tacit knowledge, and designing closed process loops to promote evolution. Baidu unveiled Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview with 280 billion parameters, 14 billion active per token, and a 1-million-token context window. The strategy focuses on a full-stack layout involving chips, cloud, models, and agents. Li believes that the downstream of AI technology is organizational capability, which creates new moats.

Li Yanhong stated that AI is the new electric energy and the smart organization is the new factory. He explained that companies have only replaced the motor but have not yet redesigned the factory for the AI era. Li believes traditional organizations are job-centered, while organizations in the AI era must become task-centered to release vitality. He noted that Baidu encountered pitfalls by allowing departments to train models alone or chasing agent application hot spots. He summarized his method for continuous evolution as being measurable and looping.

Many industries face a pain point where personal efficiency improves but overall enterprise profit does not reflect these gains. McKinsey surveyed 1719 respondents from 97 countries, finding 80 percent saw personal productivity gains but only 37 percent saw EBIT contributions. A World Economic Forum report found global AI investment exceeded 2500 billion US dollars in 2025, yet only 25 percent felt disruptive impact. A European energy provider saw its dependence on external providers drop by over 90 percent after reorganizing around AI. This case showed that changing the division of labor is what transforms pilot results into productivity.

The articles mention the Solow Paradox from 1987, where computers were seen everywhere except in the productivity statistics. Overseas views describe the AI industry as a five-layer cake consisting of energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and applications. Baidu Dazi ranked second among domestic AI office-agent applications in September 2026 with 9.8 million monthly active users. Tencent's WorkBuddy led with 32.4 million users, while Alibaba's Qwen Office had 7.9 million users according to QuestMobile data. Baidu's daily active agents grew from 5,000 to 37,000 in a year, with weekly tasks rising to over 1 million.

Baidu will continue to invest in researching and developing more cutting-edge next-generation basic large models for the future. The company will adhere to the parallel evolution of models and agents to optimize large models for specific applications. Baidu has already built 4300 Workspaces and precipitated more than 20,000 organizational skills to share experience across the company. Baidu shares fell 2.3 percent to close at HK$76.8 in Hong Kong on the day of the conference. The articles leave open how other industries will specifically implement the three principles of organizational evolution.

stories.Headline: A Practical Blueprint for an AI-Ready Enterprise
stories.Summary:
Braiin Limited, which trades as NASDAQ: BRAI, announced on Nov. 11, 2026 that its Agentic Real Estate Intelligence and Automation platform, ARIA, won the 2026 Best Enterprise-Ready AI Platform Award from the Polirian Awards. The announcement was issued from New York, NY, through GlobeNewswire. Braiin describes itself as a global AI platform company delivering automation and predictive analytics across precision agriculture, customer experience and property technology. ARIA is described as an AI-native workforce designed for the global real estate industry. Polirian selected Braiin for ARIA's agentic AI approach to planning and coordinating multi-step operational workflows across connected systems.

The award recognizes comprehensive AI platforms built for organizational use and evaluates enterprise readiness, measurable business value, AI relevance, usability and market differentiation. ARIA is designed to understand an operational objective, plan the steps needed to complete it and coordinate execution across property and customer systems. The platform combines agent orchestration, natural-language interaction, document generation and data analysis with human-in-the-loop controls. It is designed to maintain auditable records of actions, approvals and exceptions, and to escalate material decisions and exceptions for human review. Its intended workflows include preparing tenancy documents, identifying potential lease compliance issues, producing comparative market reports and supporting rent reconciliation.

Natraj Balasubramanian, Braiin's Founder and CEO, said real estate teams spend considerable time moving information between systems, following up on documents and coordinating the services people need when they move into a property. He said ARIA was designed to help bring that work together, with agentic AI planning and coordinating the steps while professionals retain control over important decisions. He said the recognition reflects the direction the company is building toward. The platform is designed to keep human review for consequential legal, financial and operational decisions. ARIA moves beyond conventional generative AI assistants that primarily answer questions or produce content.

Its intended workflows also include managing routine tenant and landlord communications, analyzing rent rolls to flag risks and opportunities, coordinating e-signature workflows and building customized workflows from plain-language instructions. The platform's design connects property workflows with residential services such as utility activation, broadband and insurance. It draws on Braiin's broader capabilities across artificial intelligence, customer experience automation and property technology. This approach supports Braiin's broader strategy of connecting property technology with the services residents need throughout the tenancy and when moving between homes. The award evaluates platforms built for organizational use.

Article one reports that Adobe's 2026 State of AI Readiness Report found around 59% of organisations in the region are stuck in the "Frozen Middle," where they are piloting or deploying AI but lack the coordination needed to scale it. For agentic AI, that figure stands at 40%. Neo-cloud provider Neysa observed that enterprise leaders are increasingly comfortable adopting AI but remain significantly less comfortable relinquishing control, with the dominant preference being enterprise-controlled AI rather than vendor-controlled AI. Neysa proposed a shared AI Platform to help enterprises move from experiments to everyday use. Neysa describes a walled garden for AI as a controlled environment in which an enterprise manages the infrastructure supporting its AI applications.

Neysa's proposed architecture divides this environment into three areas: an experimentation environment for innovation teams to test models, fine-tune existing ones, build applications and run POCs; a tightly controlled environment for workloads with strict data privacy, security and compliance requirements; and a general deployment environment for applications without the same level of regulatory oversight or data protection. Adopt AI uses TrueFoundry's AI Gateway to connect applications to models from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock and Groq. Adopt AI's co-founder and CTO Rahul Bhattacharya explains that applications no longer communicate directly with individual model providers, and requests pass through a central gateway. Neysa's approach allows enterprises to retain existing investments, for example continuing to use Azure AI Foundry while directing computing workloads to Neysa infrastructure. The exact implementation would depend on the services involved, the integration available and the enterprise's technical requirements.

Before an AI application moves into everyday use, article one says it needs a named business owner, approved data access, measurable quality targets, a support plan and an operating budget. Enterprises should understand what might make future changes difficult, since an application may depend heavily on one provider's tools or on how a particular model responds. Models, tools and frameworks should be interchangeable within the platform, subject to compatibility, security and performance requirements. Replacing one component with another would not always be straightforward, and enterprises would still need to test compatibility, evaluate performance and ensure changes meet security and governance requirements. Data movement, latency, security responsibilities and the cost of operating across multiple environments would also need to be considered.

Article one says the architecture must account for governance, interoperability and cost economics, and that organisations would still need to implement and monitor policies and controls on a common platform. The cost of running AI depends on factors such as the models selected, computing capacity, workload volumes and the infrastructure required to support applications in production. stories.Headline: New York's AI Safety Law Hits OpenAI, Anthropic Today
stories.Summary:
New York State launched the RAISE Act to regulate frontier AI developers on November 10, 2026. This safety and transparency law targets companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. The state opened a corporate registration portal to begin implementing these new rules. These regulations will fully take effect early next year. The law focuses on the most advanced high performance models.

Frontier AI developers with annual revenues exceeding 500 million dollars must register by January 1, 2027. They must publish safety management policies and model transparency reports on their websites. Major safety incidents must be reported to authorities within 72 hours. The Division of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust, called DIGIT, will enforce these rules. First violations cost 1 million dollars, while repeat violations cost 3 million dollars.

Governor Kathy Hochul launched the New York AI Responsibility and Research Center at Binghamton University. This center received 55 million dollars in donations and capital to independently review safety policies. Hochul criticized tech moguls for justifying harm in the name of the AI development race. She stated that the state is building a sensible regulatory model for the public. She believes people should come before powerful technology and corporations.

Large AI developers face increased cost burdens and must build new internal compliance systems. Companies operating in multiple states must design systems to meet the strictest reporting standards. California's SB 53 requires safety disclosures and incident reporting within 15 days. Illinois's SB 315 requires independent audits and takes effect early next year. These varying state rules affect how frontier AI companies manage their operational staff.

New York has enforced a law requiring AI companion services to identify themselves as non human. This law also requires efforts to detect signs of self harm or suicidal thoughts. A chatbot safety law for minors takes effect on June 1 of next year. This law restricts emotionally manipulative responses and behavior that encourages eating disorders. Anthropic is also planning a record 1.4 trillion dollar initial public offering.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicts agent swarms will patch system flaws within one year. He believes AI will eventually be safer when automated than when humans control it. The company's SEC filings highlight risks that models may outstrip the ability to control them. The articles do not state the specific enforcement methods for unregistered companies. They leave open whether AI can ever be one hundred percent safe.

stories.Headline: Getty Images v Stability AI – Court of Appeal hearing
stories.Summary:
The Court of Appeal held the second day of a landmark hearing on November 12, 2026. Getty Images brought this appeal against Stability AI, the developer of the Stable Diffusion AI image generator. This legal dispute focuses on intellectual property and how copyright law applies to generative AI models. The case follows a mixed High Court judgment delivered in November 2025 that largely favoured Stability AI. Getty won a small part of its trade mark claim, but its copyright claim failed.

The appeal examines section 27(3) of the Copyright, Designs, and Patents Act 1988 regarding infringing copies. Getty argues that making a model includes training it, even if the finished article contains no copies. Stability AI wants to overturn findings that an intangible model is an article and that it distributed it. The High Court previously ruled that Stable Diffusion was not an infringing copy because it stored no images. This specific model was trained outside the United Kingdom, which influenced the original trial's copyright claims.

Getty Images argues that the law does not require a finished model to contain copies of works. They claim that any article whose making in the UK would be infringing is an infringing copy. Stability AI says the court should focus on what was produced rather than how it was developed. Stability AI further argues that extending laws to overseas training is a matter for Parliament, not courts. They believe the High Court was correct in its original ruling regarding the nature of copies.

The British Recorded Music Industry Limited intervened to support Getty and warn of consequences for creative industries. BPI says the High Court approach could let developers train models offshore and bring them back. BPI also cited two Munich Court cases where AI models were found to have memorised copyright works. This intervention highlights that the outcome will affect a wide spectrum of various global creative industries. Rights holders and AI developers are both affected by how these legal protections are eventually applied.

Getty previously dropped primary copyright claims on June 25, 2025, to pursue secondary infringement and passing off. The High Court accepted that intangible models are articles but rejected the secondary infringement claim in 2025. This dispute is part of a wider wave of litigation, including a US lawsuit over 12 million images. The UK government is also considering its approach to copyright and AI after a March 2026 report. Parallel proceedings between Getty and Stability AI are currently ongoing within the United States legal system.

The Court of Appeal will now hand down a judgment that may influence how rights holders protect content. A Getty victory would allow copyright claims against models trained abroad on unlicensed works, regardless of storage. A Stability AI victory would keep the training location and storage of copies as the key factors. The articles leave open whether the court will overturn the findings on intangible articles and distribution. The final ruling will determine if AI models can be infringing copies without containing the original works.

stories.Headline: Meta, TikTok join Google to push back on Indonesia’s planned AI copyright law revisions
stories.Summary:
Meta and TikTok joined Google on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, in pushing back against proposed revisions to Indonesia's copyright law at a parliamentary hearing in Jakarta. The revisions would require digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content, and would also set rules for artificial intelligence. Reuters reported the story from Jakarta in a dispatch dated November 11, reporting by Stanley Widianto and editing by Emelia Sithole-Matarise. The three companies each sent a representative to speak before lawmakers about the proposed changes to the law. Reuters first reported the planned revisions exclusively in July, citing a draft of the bill.

If the bill is passed, Indonesia could become the first country in Southeast Asia to incorporate AI into its copyright law. The proposed revisions would require digital platforms to pay publishers when they display news content, a requirement that is central to the objections raised at the hearing. The bill would also set rules for AI, a field in which governments around the world are grappling with the technology's impact on copyright rules. One open question globally is the use of work created by humans to train AI models. TikTok's objection concerned disclosure requirements, which it argued should not apply where AI is used only in an assistive capacity rather than to fully create content.

Agung Pamungkas, Google's Indonesia government affairs and public policy manager, told the hearing that requiring tech platforms to pay compensation for showing links to news content from publishers would limit Indonesians' access to news. Berni Moestafa, Meta's public policy head in Indonesia, said that requiring platforms to pay compensation meant publishers could lose readership traffic, along with potential advertising and subscription revenue. Berni added that directing readers to an article is different from reproducing or republishing the article itself. Noudhy Valdryno, TikTok's head of public policy in Indonesia, spoke separately and told lawmakers that disclosure requirements should not apply to assistive uses of AI. Noudhy also urged lawmakers to preserve safe-harbour protections, saying platforms cannot reliably determine copyright ownership or licences.

The people and groups affected include digital platforms, which would face the payment and disclosure obligations, and the publishers who would receive payment for news content shown by platforms. Indonesians who read news through these platforms are also affected, since Google argued that the payment requirement would limit their access to news. Meta argued that publishers themselves could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue if the payment rule were adopted. The articles do not report any statement from publishers, from lawmakers, or from the Indonesian government in response to the platforms' testimony. The Reuters report records only the three companies' positions at the hearing, with no reply from those who drafted the bill.

The background the articles give is limited to the bill's origin and its place in a wider global debate. Reuters exclusively reported the planned revisions in July, citing a draft of the bill, which is how the proposal first became public. Governments globally are working out how AI affects copyright rules, including the use of human-created work to train AI models. Indonesia's draft would put it among the first countries to write AI directly into its copyright law, and the first in Southeast Asia. The same week, a separate report from Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications examined how Google, LINE Yahoo, Meta and TikTok handle personal information through conversational AI and advertising, though that report concerns privacy rather than copyright.

The articles do not say when Indonesia's parliament will vote on the bill, so the timetable for any decision remains open. They also do not say whether lawmakers will change the draft in response to the objections from Google, Meta and TikTok. It is not stated whether the payment requirement for news content or the AI disclosure rules will survive in their current form. What compensation publishers would receive, and how it would be calculated, is not set out in the reporting. The Japanese report on privacy risks was not finalised until after deliberations held from October 19 to 21, 2026, and the available text does not say what steps Japan will take next.

stories.Headline: Global AI stocks sink as Nvidia crisis deepens sector selloff - CNA
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, Nov 12, 2026, following a deepening scandal around his affairs, and global AI-linked stocks tumbled as a result. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent successor. Nvidia's shares fell 8.2 per cent to a more than 16-month low in early trading that day. Its market value was on track to close below US$4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. The chip giant has lost more than US$550 billion in market value since its board announced an investigation on Sunday.

The investigation concerns Huang's relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. Chipmakers led the selloff, with the Philadelphia chips index sliding 1.3 per cent, while Marvell Technology slumped 3.8 per cent and Oracle shed 2.6 per cent. Micron Technology fell 2.5 per cent, Sandisk eased 6 per cent and Western Digital 3.7 per cent. Lumentum, Coherent and Dell eased between 3 per cent and 5.1 per cent, while Caterpillar and Vistra slipped about 0.5 per cent each. Japan and South Korea closed nearly 0.7 per cent lower, and tech stocks in Europe were down about 1 per cent.

Nvidia's board announced the investigation on Sunday, and the company said Kress would serve as interim CEO as it searches for a successor. The articles give no comment from Huang himself on his resignation. On Tuesday, Nvidia had already hired lawyers for an internal investigation tied to its CEO. Yahoo Finance's page also carried a banner reporting that Huang had been accused of a second affair. Nvidia's leadership now rests with Kress while the search continues.

Analysts and investors voiced concern about what the turmoil means for the wider sector. Joe Saluzzi of Themis Trading noted that Nvidia has been called the "Bank of AI" and asked whether a step back could cut off funding to smaller companies that need it. Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers said the interlocking deals raise the question of whether they created more stability or more fragility, and that the coming weeks will show. Tim Ghriskey of Ingalls & Snyder said he sees selling in Nvidia and other AI firms as buying opportunities and does not see Nvidia falling apart. Neocloud firms CoreWeave fell 9.1 per cent and Nebius dropped 16.2 per cent after saying its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its forecast, while IREN and Applied Digital also traded lower.

Nvidia finances infrastructure built around its chips, a strategy that has drawn scrutiny over circular funding. CoreWeave, which Nvidia backs, had surged more than 27 per cent in the previous session when its earnings ignited a relief rally in AI stocks. Earlier this month the Nasdaq entered a technical correction after the Democrats swept the midterm elections, including in states opposed to data centres, stoking fears that tighter regulation could slow the AI build-out. On Tuesday, selling was also driven by a hot US inflation report that raised expectations the Federal Reserve will raise rates again next month. Over the past month the Nasdaq Composite has dropped by 1 per cent or more eight times and risen by that much six times.

Short sellers of Nvidia have made US$9.6 billion in on-paper profits so far this week, according to the data firm ORTEX. Nvidia trades at about 12 times its 12-month forward earnings estimates, its lowest since November 2012, according to data compiled by LSEG. AMD and Broadcom rose 3.7 per cent and 5.6 per cent on expectations that the turmoil could create opportunity for rivals, and Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft rose between 0.8 per cent and 2.7 per cent. Analysts have said the scandal could spur tighter US scrutiny of AI cloud providers in Southeast Asia. The articles do not say who will become permanent CEO, how long the investigation will last, or whether the allegations against Alice Huang will be substantiated.

stories.Headline: Google Brings Gemini Live to Apple CarPlay
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Wednesday, Nov. 11, that it is bringing its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant to Apple CarPlay, extending its conversational AI experience to Apple's in-car platform. The global rollout gives iPhone users another way to interact with Google's services hands-free through their vehicle's display. Users can start a new conversation or resume a recent one by tapping the Gemini icon on the CarPlay screen. Google said the integration is designed to let drivers accomplish more during their commutes while minimizing distractions. Users can interrupt Gemini to provide additional information, change subjects or pause conversations when they need to concentrate on driving.

The rollout is available globally to Gemini users on iOS in all languages supported by Gemini Live. To access the feature, users must update the Gemini application on their iPhones, enable microphone permissions and have used Gemini Live on their phones at least once. Through connected Google Workspace applications, including Gmail and Google Calendar, drivers can ask Gemini to summarize unread emails, review long message threads, check upcoming appointments and prepare for meetings. Gemini already supports Android Auto and vehicles equipped with Google built-in, while its earlier CarPlay integration was limited to Google Maps. Gemini's arrival follows the expansion of other AI assistants onto CarPlay, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft's Copilot, Perplexity and xAI's Grok.

Google said the integration is designed to let drivers accomplish more during their commutes while minimizing distractions, and that users can interrupt the assistant as needed. Google said in September that its Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking models were designed to power more capable voice agents, with improvements in real-time reasoning and complex task completion. The Gemini app surpassed 1 billion monthly active users in August, becoming Google's fastest-growing product to reach that milestone, according to the company. The move expands Google's competition in the growing market for conversational AI assistants across mobile and connected devices. The additions give drivers more ways to access conversational AI through their vehicles rather than relying exclusively on traditional voice assistants.

The expansion builds on Google's broader push to make Gemini a conversational interface across consumer and enterprise applications. The integration also extends Gemini's reach into Google's productivity ecosystem through connected Google Workspace applications. The CarPlay feature is available to Gemini users on iOS in all languages supported by Gemini Live. Drivers can ask Gemini to summarize unread emails, review long message threads, check upcoming appointments and prepare for meetings. The earlier CarPlay integration was limited to Google Maps, while Gemini already supports Android Auto and vehicles equipped with Google built-in.

Gemini's arrival on CarPlay follows the expansion of other AI assistants onto the platform, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft's Copilot, Perplexity and xAI's Grok. Google said in September that its Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking models were designed to power more capable voice agents. The Gemini app surpassed 1 billion monthly active users in August, becoming Google's fastest-growing product to reach that milestone, according to the company. The move expands Google's competition in the growing market for conversational AI assistants across mobile and connected devices. The additions give drivers more ways to access conversational AI through their vehicles rather than relying exclusively on traditional voice assistants.

Users must update the Gemini application on their iPhones, enable microphone permissions and have used Gemini Live on their phones at least once to access the feature. The rollout is available globally to Gemini users on iOS in all languages supported by Gemini Live. Google said the integration is designed to let drivers accomplish more during their commutes while minimizing distractions. Users can interrupt Gemini to provide additional information, change subjects or pause conversations when they need to concentrate on driving. The integration also extends Gemini's reach into Google's productivity ecosystem through connected Google Workspace applications, including Gmail and Google Calendar.

stories.Headline: Netflix builds knowledge graph for AI-driven observability
stories.Summary:
Netflix is developing an ontology-driven knowledge graph to accelerate production investigations and give AI agents a shared understanding of its operational environment, TechGig reported on November 13, 2026. The platform connects information about applications, incidents, deployments, alerts, and infrastructure dependencies across Netflix's systems. Engineers investigating a typical application regression can spend around four hours piecing together scattered information. Much of that time goes to reconstructing relationships between systems rather than analysing data. Netflix's solution makes these relationships explicit through an operational ontology and knowledge graph.

The Observability Ontology defines operational entities, their properties, and their relationships, using standards including RDF, OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL. The knowledge graph is stored in QuipuDB, Netflix's distributed RDF database built on Rust's redb storage engine. A pipeline of components called enrichers populates the graph by consuming information from operational systems and transforming it into subject-predicate-object triples. Some enrichment is deterministic, while other stages use LLMs and probabilistic techniques to interpret less structured information. Netflix constrains these outputs through strict validation rules, including consistent entity types, URI naming conventions, and checks against its software catalogue.

Netflix identified a missing capability: a consistent way to describe how components relate to one another, and its Observability Ontology provides that common model. The company also captures information from incident discussions, including hypotheses, rejected explanations, and mitigation decisions, so human reasoning becomes part of the operational knowledge base. Its correlation engine examines 13 types of signals, including log errors, metric anomalies, traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, configuration changes, experiments, and code changes. The engine searches for potential causal relationships and evaluates evidence like temporal proximity and severity, producing ranked hypotheses. The knowledge graph underpins AutoRCA, Netflix's internal agentic AI system for root-cause analysis.

Agents analysing traces, logs, or deployments use the ontology as a common interface, contributing information about operational entities without understanding each other's internal implementations. Netflix already collects metrics, events, logs, and traces across its applications and infrastructure, but these signals are spread across alerting, incident management, deployment tooling, and engineering communication platforms. An application regression might originate from a client release, an experiment, infrastructure load shedding, or a downstream service, and engineers often connect this evidence manually. Netflix intends to use this foundation to produce ranked, evidence-backed explanations for incidents. The system aims to reduce the four-hour investigation times for application regressions and support automated root-cause analysis and self-healing infrastructure.

QCon AI New York 2026 has published its full schedule for December 15, 16, where engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, and other organizations will examine production AI systems. Fan Yang, Staff Software Engineer building Netflix's AI serving platform, and Rajat Shah, who leads technical architecture for ML model serving, explain how Netflix serves ML and GenAI from one platform. That platform handles about 1 million inference requests per second across 300+ models, after five years of consolidation. Ronak Nathani, Principal Staff Software Engineer in Compute Infrastructure at LinkedIn, presents LinkedIn's Kubernetes ops agent, which works across 500,000+ nodes and 5M+ pods. Its guardrails sit on the server, including rate limits, delete protection, and peer approval for production changes.

Pratik Agarwal, Distributed Systems Engineer on Figma's sandbox and caching platforms, explains how Figma provisions and secures production agents, with warm pools cutting provisioning latency by 90% and availability rising from 99% to 99.95%. Fabio Flores, Software Engineer at DoorDash who leads foundation development for its agentic ordering system, explains the eval loop behind it, where every change is checked before launch by an LLM judge calibrated against human reviewers. Min Chen, Principal Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, presents LinkedIn's AI code review system, which reviews tens of thousands of pull requests a week across about 10,000 repositories, with more than 60% of sampled suggestions accepted. Liz Fong-Jones, Technical Fellow at Honeycomb, and Rebecca Murphey, Principal for AI Ops at Honeycomb, reflect on Honeycomb's 2x initiative, where peak weekday PR merges to its main monorepo rose from about 30 to about 74 between early 2025 and April 2026. Group registration for teams of three or more closes on November 27, 2026, with savings of $50 to $125 per ticket, and individual tickets are $1,790 until December 8.

stories.Headline: The Next AI Chip Shortage May Be the Machines That Make HBM
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on November 12, 2026, that it had moved up the planned opening of its new high-bandwidth memory packaging plant in South Korea by one year. The new opening date is June 2028, according to Digitimes, and the company said the change was made to meet rising demand for AI server memory. The announcement came on the same day that ground was broken at the company's Onyang semiconductor campus in Asan. At the groundbreaking, President Lee Jae-myung spoke of a new advanced packaging fab there, followed in sequence by advanced equipment.

The articles give figures for the Onyang campus, which sits in Asan, South Korea. The new advanced packaging fab is put at about 6 trillion won, and the follow-on advanced equipment at about 40 trillion won. Together the fab and equipment come to 46 trillion won, which Aju Business Daily put at about $34.4 billion. At the day's base rate of 1,336.7 won per dollar, the equipment alone is about $29.9 billion, by FourWeekMBA's arithmetic. That equipment is about 6.7 times the fab figure.

President Lee Jae-myung spoke at the groundbreaking of the Chungcheong mega-project, where three investment projects began construction. They are an advanced semiconductor packaging fab and an advanced display line in Asan, plus a plant for high-performance AI server substrates in Sejong. He said companies and the government pledged the investment plan in July, and that the promise was becoming reality just four months later. He said the campus will become a key hub for advanced HBM packaging. Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong, who attended, said the site, which centred on simple assembly and testing of general chips, will become a hub for advanced HBM for AI chips, as Financial News reported.

The articles carry few outside voices on the groundbreaking itself, though SMIC is cited by Digitimes on the wider memory market. Digitimes lists a report that AI memory may balance after mid-2028 while compute and supporting chips stay short, according to SMIC. The speech also named other Chungcheong projects whose groundbreakings are on schedule, including a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data centre in Dangjin and a biopharmaceutical plant in Osong. For HBM buyers, Samsung said on its earnings call that its 2027 HBM supply was already sold out. Samsung's market value rose about $11 billion at the Seoul open on November 12, as FourWeekMBA reported.

The articles give background on Samsung's spending, which FourWeekMBA took from the company's third-quarter release of October 29. Samsung said its capital expenditure reached 29 trillion won in the third quarter, up 19.8 trillion won from a year earlier. It expects about 84.4 trillion won for the full year, including 76.8 trillion won in its Device Solutions chip division. By FourWeekMBA's arithmetic, the 40 trillion won of Onyang equipment equals about 47% of the full-year figure, about 52% of the division's budget and about 1.4 times the third quarter's spending. Samsung also said it significantly scaled up sales of HBM4 in the third quarter, and that it expects AI infrastructure capital expenditure to reach a historic level in 2027.

Samsung has given the new opening date of June 2028 for the packaging plant, but the articles leave much open. President Lee gave no schedule or split by year for the 40 trillion won of equipment, saying only that it follows the fab in sequence. How much of that spending falls inside the 84.4 trillion won 2026 guidance is not stated, according to FourWeekMBA. Samsung's Korean newsroom had not published a release on the groundbreaking when FourWeekMBA checked, and it could not load the presidential office's own transcript. FourWeekMBA also said it did not contact Samsung for its piece, so the figures rest on the president's words as quoted by Korean outlets.

stories.Headline: Fireworks AI Breach Widens to Expose Customer Billing Data and Incomplete Model Weights
stories.Summary:
AI infrastructure company Fireworks AI said hackers stole customer data during two separate breaches in October, according to a notice it updated on Monday, November 9, 2026. Fireworks hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate the first incident, which it discovered on October 6. A well-known, financially motivated cybercriminal group carried out that attack and took account and billing information, plus secrets that grant access to human users or apps. The second breach came through a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks research and development machines, which was attacked on October 23. Fireworks contained the second incident on the same day it occurred, according to SecurityWeek.

On October 24, the unauthorized party used the provider to reach Fireworks development machines and ran an unauthorized workload that affected additional customer data. The exposed data included internal Fireworks data, resource metadata, billing information, invoices, payment history, and datasets and other AI-related data. TechGig reported that some customers also had incomplete model weights exposed. Customer payment card numbers were not accessed, because Fireworks does not store them. Fireworks said it revoked and replaced compromised internal credentials and service accounts, restricted unauthorized network pathways, isolated affected systems, and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems.

Fireworks, a San Mateo company founded in 2022 that has more than 10,000 customers, is the party responsible for notifying those affected. It said the first incident touched only a limited number of customer accounts, and that all of them were notified. The company said the impacted customers from the second incident were also notified, and that it is working with Palo Alto Networks on hardening its security and revoking compromised credentials. Fireworks described its breaches as part of a larger string of attacks recently spotlighted by incident responders at Google. It said it detected the activity on October 24 and began remediation immediately.

Digital workspace company Notion said it was notified of the incident on November 2, disconnected its systems from Fireworks, and deleted all data in the Fireworks system. On November 6, Fireworks told Notion that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data, and Notion began another internal investigation. Notion found that the hackers accessed Notion AI chat transcripts used for its Insights feature, and that fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces were affected. Most transcripts could not be tied to a customer or workspace, though Notion did not say how many customers were affected. Notion told customers to treat the data as exposed and to rotate any credentials, such as passwords or API keys, that they pasted into Notion AI during the incident.

Notion had used Fireworks for classification jobs behind Insights, which helps customers understand their own AI usage, and as a general inference provider serving open-weight models. Fireworks is a cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models. SecurityWeek reported that the second incident was linked to a recent rise in LLMJacking activity, in which hackers hijack an enterprise's access to large language models. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published a blog about the tactic last week and said they have responded to multiple LLMJacking incidents in 2026. Those incidents hit organizations in North America, South America and Asia Pacific, across the financial services, retail, technology and transportation sectors.

Mandiant researchers said LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges within hours, unlike the gradual resource consumption of cryptojacking. Individual incidents showed fraudulent charges above $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reached $1 million before access was revoked. Google's group identified a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions, and some are maturing by handing off initial access to groups that resell it. Multiple investigations showed the groups were mainly trying to steal tokens or credentials that give footholds into target infrastructure. Google said that as enterprises adopt higher-tier models and agentic workflows, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance targeting exposed API tokens and vulnerabilities in model routing middleware.

Fireworks is still working with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 to investigate the full scope and impact of the breaches. Notion has disabled its Insights feature while it investigates, and it no longer serves open-weight models through Fireworks. Notion contacted the affected customers with instructions on how to securely retrieve and review the data in their workspaces. SecurityWeek has emailed Notion for additional information and said it will update its article if the company responds. The articles do not say how many Fireworks customers were affected, or when Insights might return.

stories.Headline: Lee Jae-yong Pledges 46 Trillion Won Investment to Transform Onyang Campus into HBM Hub
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong unveiled plans on Thursday to transform the company's Onyang Campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province, into a major advanced packaging hub for high-bandwidth memory. Samsung Electronics plans to invest a total of 46 trillion won in the campus in phases and build five HBM production lines. Lee attended the groundbreaking ceremony for the Chungcheong Mega Project at the Onyang Campus alongside President Lee Jae-myung, government officials, local government representatives and business leaders. Lee said in his welcoming remarks that with today's groundbreaking ceremony the company promises another leap forward. He added that the Onyang Campus would evolve from a facility primarily focused on semiconductor assembly and testing into a cutting-edge HBM hub.

Samsung plans to invest 6 trillion won in construction and another 40 trillion won in advanced equipment as part of the 46 trillion won investment. The new facility being launched with the groundbreaking ceremony, known as the fifth production line, will feature a cleanroom covering approximately 31,000 square meters in a three-story building. Samsung aims to begin operations in June 2028. Once completed, the total floor area of the Onyang Campus will expand from the current 270,000 square meters to approximately 420,000 square meters, an increase of about 60%. The new facility is expected to create around 700 direct jobs.

Lee recalled that about four decades ago the area consisted largely of barren land and unpaved roads, but has since developed into an advanced semiconductor facility specializing in assembly and testing. He stressed the importance of cooperation between the government, local authorities and businesses in carrying out the large-scale investment. He pledged that Samsung would take greater responsibility in strengthening the country's industrial competitiveness, saying the company will take on an even greater sense of responsibility. President Lee Jae-myung praised Samsung's investment decision at the groundbreaking ceremony. He noted that construction began roughly four months after Samsung announced its Chungcheong investment plan in July, thanking Lee Jae-yong and Samsung employees for making bold investment decisions and implementing them quickly.

The two leaders toured the site together following the ceremony, and Lee Jae-yong introduced the president to Samsung's Test & System Package, one of the main products manufactured at the Onyang Campus. President Lee signed the product during the visit. The president later attended the fourth public-private joint inspection meeting for the Mega Project, where the government discussed measures to proactively address difficulties faced by companies at investment sites and accelerate the realization of investment outcomes. The Onyang Campus has served as one of Samsung Electronics' key semiconductor back-end manufacturing sites since late 1991. The company has accumulated more than three decades of experience in semiconductor assembly and testing at the site.

HBM consists of multiple DRAM chips vertically stacked to deliver high bandwidth and improved data-processing efficiency. As demand for AI accelerators and data centers grows, advanced packaging technologies for connecting, stacking and testing memory chips have become increasingly important to HBM competitiveness. The project is also part of Samsung's broader plan to strengthen the semiconductor ecosystem in the Chungcheong region. By combining the existing semiconductor infrastructure in Cheonan and Asan with new HBM packaging capabilities in Onyang, Samsung aims to establish the region as a major production base for advanced semiconductor packaging. Industry observers say the competition in the HBM market is increasingly extending beyond memory production capacity to advanced packaging technology.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive on November 12, and Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and Harvey Jones as board chair. South Korea's government said on November 13 that Nvidia's commitment to supply more than 260,000 graphics processing units, along with existing technology partnerships, remained unchanged. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix held 50% of the global HBM market by revenue in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung Electronics accounted for 33%, and their combined share reached 83%, far exceeding Micron's reported 18%. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon said on November 13 that approximately 21,000 of the 35,000 Nvidia B200 GPUs targeted for direct government procurement had been secured. The remaining 14,000 are expected to arrive by early 2027, while another 15,000 GPUs are being pursued through the National AI Computing Center.

stories.Headline: HK ranks 11th in digital and AI competitiveness
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong placed 11th in the world and fourth in Asia in the World Digital and AI Ranking 2026, which the Switzerland-based International Institute for Management Development (IMD) published on Wednesday, November 11. The ranking covered 70 economies. It assesses how well an economy can develop, adopt, deploy and govern digital technologies and artificial intelligence in a way that produces lasting economic and social value. Hong Kong's result was announced alongside the rest of the list, which showed several other Asian economies placing in or near the top ten.

The benchmark is built on five factors, and Hong Kong did best in workforce development, where it came second in the world. It ranked fifth for efficiency and 10th for technology and infrastructure. At the sub-factor level, the city came first globally in technological framework, practices, and education and training. It also placed among the world's top ten in talent, societal attitudes and regulatory framework.

The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government responded through a spokesperson, who said the result recognised the city as one of the world's most competitive economies in digital and AI development. The spokesperson said the government is fully committed to turning Hong Kong into an international innovation and technology centre, in line with the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Plans include strengthening the institutional framework for innovation and technology development and speeding up alignment with key national technology strategies. The government also intends to build a new model based on three major innovation and technology parks and five key research and development institutions.

The spokesperson added that the city will create a full industrial ecosystem that covers research and development, commercialisation, pilot production and mass production. It will also push new industrialisation and use AI to empower different parts of the economy. For comparison, South Korea's science ministry said its country climbed eight places to rank tenth, just ahead of Hong Kong. The United States took first place after rising three spots, Singapore was second among Asia-Pacific economies, China was seventh and Japan was 19th, while last year's leader Canada fell to fifth.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Business – What's New?
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Business, a beta product that gives companies a new way to reach the roughly 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. The release was reported by ummid.com, and a second outlet, Smart Company, noted that Australian businesses can now claim themselves in ChatGPT. OpenAI said the first piece, Business Hub, lets companies claim their business, manage their information and see insights on how people engage with them in ChatGPT. The second piece, Business Agents, gives companies a way to talk directly with users.

Under the new setup, any eligible business in a market where ChatGPT is available can claim its profile through Business Hub. Once verified, a company can update key details and add self-service product feeds that carry pricing and availability, so ChatGPT can describe its products and services with current information. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. After claiming a profile, an eligible business can build, test and launch a Business Agent, and a user who finds the business in a ChatGPT answer can open its profile and start a conversation with that agent, if one exists. Customers can ask about products, compare features and work out which option suits them.

Availability differs between the two tools. Business Hub is open to eligible businesses in any market where ChatGPT is available, while Business Agents are limited for now to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Both are free as of now. Businesses can also sponsor their agents and use them as destinations for ChatGPT Ads, and OpenAI says sponsored placements will be clearly labelled and kept separate from regular ChatGPT responses.

OpenAI is the company behind the launch, and it described the move as an early step. It said it plans to expand to more countries and business categories, along with tools for organisations with more complex needs. The company also said users' chats, including conversations with Business Agents, will not be shared with businesses. The launch builds on Sponsored Agents, which OpenAI began testing in September, according to The Next Web.

stories.Headline: What Does CoreWeave (CRWV) Winning A New AI Training Deal Mean?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares jumped 10 per cent on Wednesday, setting off a rally in battered AI cloud stocks, after the company reported strong revenue growth from its heavy spending. The company also signaled a pullback from the borrowing binge that had raised alarms about an AI bubble. The earnings lifted shares of key CoreWeave backer Nvidia by 5 per cent, following a bruising two-day slide. That slide was driven by worries about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the company after his affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Shares of so-called neoclouds including Nebius and Iren also rallied, after weeks of turmoil over fears that debt-fueled data center expansion could backfire if AI demand slows.

CoreWeave raised its annual revenue forecast and said it would not tap unsecured debt markets, following a recent spike in borrowing costs. The company said cash flow from existing contracts would cover both current and future debt repayments. In premarket trading, Nebius, Iren, Oracle and Applied Digital climbed between 4.7 per cent and 11.8 per cent. All of those stocks except Nebius had lost 32 per cent to 48 per cent this year as of Tuesday, while Nebius had surged 60 per cent. Together, the cloud companies including CoreWeave were set to gain more than $25 billion in market value on the day, while Nvidia alone stood to add about $210 billion if the gains hold.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters on Tuesday that greater scrutiny could slow data center construction across the industry. He did not expect it to significantly alter the company's expansion plans or drive up its costs. The company itself said it would avoid unsecured debt markets and rely on cash flow from existing contracts to meet its debt repayments. Intrator's comments came after last week's Democratic midterm sweep, which dealt another blow to the AI industry. The company's raised annual revenue forecast was central to the results that investors cheered on Wednesday.

Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei said CoreWeave delivered about the best quarter they could have asked for. In a client note, they said the stats were good-to-great, funding concerns were addressed and the strategic moves make sense. The analysts also warned that CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the crunch in AI computing capacity eases. Several winning candidates in the Democratic midterm sweep campaigned for tighter regulation and for moratoriums on new data center construction, including in the crucial market of Texas. Investors in AI infrastructure stocks, including the neoclouds and Nvidia, had reason to cheer after the results.

The articles describe how the neocloud stocks had faced weeks of turmoil on fears that their debt-fueled data center expansion could backfire if AI demand slows. CoreWeave's results came after a recent spike in borrowing costs that prompted the company to rule out unsecured debt markets. The risks of mistiming AI investments became evident on Tuesday, when SoftBank took a $3.7 billion writedown on non-refundable payments for equipment to power its US data centers. That writedown pushed the Japanese tech investor to a second-quarter net loss of $7 billion, its first in nearly two years. Nvidia had suffered a two-day slide over worries about Huang's future, tied to his affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nebius is due to report results before Thursday's opening bell, giving investors the next look at the neocloud group. The articles do not say whether the rally across AI cloud stocks will hold, noting only that the market value gains are set if they do. They also leave open how far scrutiny and proposed data center moratoriums, including in Texas, will slow construction across the industry. It remains unclear how Huang's situation will play out at Nvidia, since the articles describe only the worries that drove its two-day slide. The articles give no date for when the crunch in AI computing capacity might ease, which Bernstein says would hit CoreWeave first and hardest.

stories.Headline: As AI stakes its claim in higher education, colleges and universities across Chicago aim to embrace it
stories.Summary:
DePaul University in Chicago recently released a document called "Guiding Principles on Artificial Intelligence," which calls for academic integrity, intellectual honesty, transparency and human-centered use of the technology. The principles were published last month, according to a Chicago Tribune report on how Chicago-area colleges are responding to artificial intelligence. About a dozen students routinely work at the university's Responsible AI Systems and Experiences lab, known as the RAISE Lab, on its Loop campus. They spend hours there exploring how artificial intelligence affects daily life and how much it should influence the human experience. The story, reported by Kate Perez, describes a wider push by Chicago-area schools to embrace the technology.

The principles came out of DePaul's 26-member Provost's Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which worked for more than a year to develop them. That committee meets monthly to discuss policy, practices and how artificial intelligence is used in the classroom. Elsewhere in Chicago, the University of Chicago will launch a new master's degree in applied artificial intelligence in fall 2027. Northwestern University launched an undergraduate major in artificial intelligence this fall, along with a webpage of tools and resources for students, faculty and staff. At Wilbur Wright College, City Colleges of Chicago introduced its first artificial intelligence degree this fall, an Associate of Applied Science in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Development.

John Shanahan, a professor of English, chairs DePaul's advisory committee and brought together faculty who held very different views of the technology. He said the committee gives faculty from acting to computer science a shared space to talk, to hear what is happening in their units and to vet ideas for the future. Jay Cunningham, the RAISE Lab creator and an assistant professor of computing, said the principles go beyond academic integrity. His goal is for students to see artificial intelligence as a tool that attempts to model human behavior, interactions and decision-making. Cunningham, who launched the lab in 2025, said it is the job of humans to wield such tools in ways that serve them best.

At City Colleges of Chicago, Provost and Chief Academic Officer Mark Potter told the Tribune that the new degree applies across all disciplines, from history and law to transportation and distribution. He said the system cannot shy away from the technology or bury its head in the sand, and that students need artificial intelligence competencies, including responsible and ethical use. Ayoka Noelle Mota Samuels, the system's associate vice chancellor of technology sector strategy, said City Colleges should be a trusted and affordable place for people of all backgrounds to learn about artificial intelligence. She warned that without educators in leadership on the subject, some people risk being left out. City Colleges serves more than 73,000 students a year through its network of public community colleges, so its approach reaches a large student body.

Shanahan said DePaul has increasingly recognized over the last two years that artificial intelligence does not have to be feared. He described a mix of enthusiasm, excitement, skepticism and fear, and said the advancements have benefited the university, though he acknowledged that we are at the beginning of this. DePaul had published an earlier statement on artificial intelligence in 2023, which Shanahan said now feels like it came 100 years ago given how fast things are changing. Before launching its degree, City Colleges created a district-wide artificial intelligence steering committee that helped articulate its position on preparing students for an AI-enabled workforce and society. Other Chicago campuses have formed committees, launched classes and majors, and pushed for artificial intelligence literacy among students and faculty, and the University of Chicago's law school prohibits note-taking on electronic devices in some classes.

Over the past half-decade, Cunningham has watched more fields demand that workers understand artificial intelligence, creating a need for students to learn the technology as it progresses. DePaul remains faced with how to manage, embrace and integrate artificial intelligence use while weighing the opinions of faculty, administrators and students. Shanahan said the university is having conversations and being proactive about meeting the challenges of integration. He said there will be times when the technology is useful and times when it is better to think your own thoughts and write your own sentences. The articles do not say what changes the advisory committee will recommend next, or how the many schools' approaches will compare over time.
