stories.Headline: Meta is launching its "smallest and most efficient" AI model: Muse Ember.
stories.Summary:
Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Ember, which it calls its smallest and most efficient model, a hosted multimodal reasoning model built for the repetitive steps inside agents. Meta lists tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long document parsing as its targets. According to MarkTechPost, the model scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort. Meta puts its cost at about $0.14 per index task, or $0.136 on its own chart. The article says Muse Ember is the fourth model under the Muse brand, after Spark, Glimmer and Wonder.

The model has a 1M-token context window and can produce up to 512K output tokens, four times the 128K cap on both rivals. It natively accepts text, images, audio and video, so an agent can read screenshots, charts, scanned pages, voice memos and meeting recordings without a separate model. Muse Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, and cached input costs $0.004 per million. Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna list the same base rates, and Meta lists no long-context tier for Ember. The comparison table gives the release date as Nov 9, 2026, against Oct 7, 2026 for Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sep 22, 2026 for GPT-6 Luna.

Meta Superintelligence Labs is responsible for the release, and Meta describes the model as sitting below its larger ones. According to the company, Muse Wonder handles the hardest problems and Muse Spark covers coding and agentic workflows. Ember takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale, and Meta's own framing is that Wonder plans while Ember handles the volume. The company says Ember is the first model it trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model. Separately, Alexandr Wang, Meta's Chief AI Officer, pitched the Muse agent's new phone-calling feature in a post that asked whether users want help with insurance, cable, the DMV or dinner reservations.

The cost gap comes from tokens used per task, because list prices are identical, and on Meta's chart Ember at max scores 35.8 for $0.136 per task while Haiku 5.5 at max scores 36.2 for $0.411. Artificial Analysis summarised this as matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task. On AutomationBench-AA, 657 Zapier business workflows, Ember completes 37.8% of tasks, against 20.2% for GPT-6 Luna and 13.9% for Claude Haiku 5.5. Ember leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 40.9 versus 39.2 for Haiku and 16.4 for Luna, but it loses FrontierCode 2.0-AA, where Haiku scores 34.9 and Ember 27.2. Developers should note that weights are private, so there is no local GPU, laptop or quantized option, and access runs through the Meta Model API and Muse Code.

The wider Muse agent, which launched on September 8, has passed 10 million users, according to Meta, and TechCrunch and Engadget reported on November 12 that it can now place outbound calls to US businesses for paying subscribers. TechCrunch puts the paid plans at $20 a month for 500 million tokens a week and $100 a month for 3 billion, while Engadget describes only a separate subscription with extra tokens and features. Muse has a free tier, but calling is not included in it. Google's Gemini and the startup Instinct already offer similar calling features, as TechCrunch notes, so Meta is not first. On September 22, Reuters reported that Meta was testing a human concierge option in which a trained human agent could take over a request and make the call.

According to 404 Media, Meta communications expected human-placed calls to succeed 95% to 98% of the time, well above what AI-only calling managed. Reuters said half of Meta's employees had the human option switched on for the test, with the ability to opt out, and some staff warned internally that sensitive details could reach call-center contractors. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reuters the company would roll it out only when it was ready and with the proper disclosures. Later coverage by Cybernews and VKTR reported that a Meta executive conceded that using humans without clear disclosure was a mistake and that the feature was pulled back for now. Muse jumped to No. 2 on the US App Store days after launch and got a Mac app on September 17, but its downloads trail Threads and Meta's own chatbot app.

The articles leave open whether the $20 plan alone unlocks phone calls or whether the feature sits higher up the ladder, and Engadget does not spell out the prices. Neither TechCrunch nor Engadget mentions human callers in their November 12 pieces, so it remains unresolved whether paying customers can be routed to a person today. Meta has said it will roll out the human concierge option only with the proper disclosures, but it has given no date. On the model side, the MarkTechPost article does not say whether Meta will ever release Ember's weights, which are private for now. Reported Android traction for the Muse app is weak, and the articles do not say whether the calling feature will change that or how many users will pay.

stories.Headline: European shares log record close on Siemens, CoreWeave-fuelled AI optimism
stories.Summary:
European shares closed at a record on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, just short of their intraday high, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and CoreWeave lifted investor confidence in artificial intelligence. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 0.72 per cent to 663.05 points, a whisker below the intraday record of 663.41. Germany's DAX also rose 1.2 per cent and hovered near its own all-time high. Siemens Energy led the gains after its shares jumped 10.8 per cent.

The AI equipment maker raised its profit margin expectations for 2027 and said it planned to more than triple its dividend. Peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, while the broader tech sector added 2.5 per cent. Chip-related stocks also rose, with Soitec up 11.9 per cent and Aixtron up 8 per cent. Optimism was further boosted by CoreWeave, a neocloud company, which said it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.

CoreWeave had been at the centre of AI bubble fears that triggered a global market selloff the previous week. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether the large AI investment would prove profitable across the industry, noting that not all AI companies would succeed. Societe Generale analysts said the rally looked somewhat stretched given political and economic risks, and they saw limited further upside for the index by year-end. Investors also watched interest rates closely after hotter-than-expected US inflation data and hawkish Federal Reserve comments pointed to another rate hike next month.

Sectors less exposed to AI, including retail and food and beverage, lagged on the day. Czech ammunition and arms producer CSG fell 21.6 per cent after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast. A rebound in Brent crude after shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz added to inflation concerns in energy-importing Europe. Traders expect at least one quarter-point rate hike by the European Central Bank by February 2027.

stories.Headline: Alibaba chip unit T-Head files for Hong Kong IPO amid China’s AI push
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Group said on Tuesday, Nov 10, that its chip design unit T-Head has confidentially filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong. The company disclosed the move in a stock-exchange filing that evening. T-Head submitted a confidential Form A1 application on Sep 11, after the Hong Kong Stock Exchange cleared Alibaba to go ahead with the proposed spin-off. T-Head is a wholly owned Alibaba subsidiary that provides full-stack data centre chips, and it is expected to stay a subsidiary of Alibaba once the spin-off is complete.

The size of the deal, the offering structure and the stake Alibaba will hold after the listing have not yet been decided. The listing is also subject to regulatory approvals. Founded in 2018, T-Head sits at the centre of Alibaba's push to build its own AI and computing capabilities. In September, the company unveiled the unit's Zhenwu V900 AI processor, which it said delivers three times the performance of its previous-generation chip and will underpin training and inference for next-generation AI models.

Alibaba said the spin-off would let investors value T-Head and its core businesses separately from the rest of the group, while helping the chipmaker raise capital on its own and strengthen ties with customers, suppliers and strategic partners. The exchange filing also said the proposal would allow for a more efficient deployment of Alibaba's financial resources. Analysts at the Chinese financial data provider Wind said in a research note that the chip business was previously hidden inside Alibaba Cloud and hard to price independently. In their view, a separate listing becomes a new yardstick for whether Alibaba is undervalued, and analysts more broadly see the spin-off as a test of whether the sum of Alibaba's parts is worth significantly more than its current market valuation.

The filing comes as Chinese technology firms race to meet rising demand for AI infrastructure and to reduce their reliance on Nvidia's AI processors amid US export restrictions. It also lands amid rising competition between the US and China, as Beijing continues to push for tech self-sufficiency. In January, Baidu's chip unit Kunlunxin also confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing, a sign of growing investor appetite for Chinese semiconductor and AI-linked assets. Alibaba's Hong Kong-listed shares closed 2.9 per cent lower on Tuesday and slipped about 1 per cent to HK$100.60 on Wednesday, and they have fallen nearly 30 per cent so far this year.

stories.Headline: Google’s new AI ‘ultimatum’ sparks concern over tech giant’s power in California schools
stories.Summary:
Google announced this week that starting in January it plans to block K-12 students from using its search engine unless districts opt into the company's AI-generated version of it. The announcement came on a Tuesday, according to KXAN, and Google's Chris Phillips discussed it on Monday during a virtual briefing. Google has long been woven into California students' education through Google search, Chromebooks and Gmail. The decadeslong relationship between the search giant and education turned into the subject of a furor this week. Phillips is Google's vice president and general manager of education.

Google will block K-12 students from Search unless districts opt into its AI version, and early next year Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will automatically be turned off for school districts. Administrators will have to choose to opt into the features, but Google said Search and AI are "deeply integrated" and it will not be possible to turn on Google Search without accepting AI. Google is updating its Search feature so AI Overviews "will offer step-by-step guided learning" instead of instantly giving students the answers. Google said in a blog post on Tuesday that it will update its search function for schools, and it clarified in a post on X on Tuesday that schools can turn off Gemini and Gemini Notebook. About three-quarters of American teens and tweens use or interact with the AI summaries in search results, according to a recent report by Common Sense Media.

Phillips said that if a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then it has the choice to not have Search at all. Google said it has engaged educators in recent months and will continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure it is giving schools more choice, more controls and improved Search for learning. Lila Byock said that "educational value ,  not shareholder value ,  must determine" the technology used by students. Byock said Google forced its AI products into classrooms and parents fought back, and that the company's hostile ultimatum is a desperate attempt to maintain its stranglehold on public education. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into public schools.

In a series of 180 tests, Common Sense Media researchers found that Google's AI Mode completed students' homework for them every time, and the AI feature also invented fake questions and cited unreliable sources such as Reddit and Facebook. Yvette Renteria, chief program officer at Common Sense Media, said Google search, Google Drive and other Google tools support student learning in a myriad of ways. Renteria said media literacy, understanding, evaluating and analyzing resources are crucial to learning, and not having that as an option seems like a missed opportunity. Common Sense Media researchers have not reviewed Google's Guided Learning mode, and many school districts will have to decide to opt into Google's AI-integrated search or find a new search alternative in the middle of the school year. Byock said districts should "reclaim their authority from corporate interests and divest from Google."

Rory Mir, director of community tech engagement at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said "degoogling," or divesting from Google software, may be easier for individuals or smaller organizations than for school districts. Mir said the trick comes with real monetary costs as well as labor costs and disruption. Renteria said school districts with more robust technology departments are more likely to handle the change. Los Angeles Unified, the state's largest district, has already placed restrictions on generative AI, and Google's decision could complicate such efforts, particularly because schools rely on the company's digital tools. L.A. Unified uses a statewide purchasing arrangement for Google Workspace, and a district spokesperson said the district is evaluating the announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators and students.

Some parents of Long Beach Unified students, who are part of a new tech policy group that also includes teachers, students, administrators and industry experts, will "have an opportunity to provide input" into the district's options, a district spokesperson said. The Long Beach Unified spokesperson said the district is in the middle of a student survey about AI use in school. Mir said Google's new policy should involve among schools a "big discussion about Google's role as a monopolist" with "undue power over" schools' decisions. Mir said that short of that, it is important for Google to do the right thing and offer more control over these tools to administrators and users, so they can choose the experience that is right for their students and not get swept up into these suites where it's all or nothing. Mir said he is hoping that folding in a higher bar for students happens.

Districts across California are debating restrictions on artificial intelligence and technology use in the classroom. School officials trying to push back on an encroaching AI are in a bind, because the tech giant dominates search online and it didn't give much time for districts to make their decisions. District leaders say a fight would be a big undertaking, but some may be up to the challenge, especially as public outcry after the announcement grows. For some parents who have been critics of technology use in school, Google's so-called "ultimatum" may be the extra push to get schools to reconsider their reliance on tech. The furor follows Google's Tuesday statement that education leaders need to either accept some AI in classrooms or lose access to its search engine.

Many school districts will have to decide to opt into Google's AI-integrated search or find a new search alternative in the middle of the school year. Some parents of Long Beach Unified students will have an opportunity to provide input into the district's options, and the district is in the middle of a student survey about AI use in school. A district spokesperson said L.A. Unified is evaluating the announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators and students. Common Sense Media researchers have not reviewed Google's Guided Learning mode, and Mir said he is hoping that folding in a higher bar for students happens. Google said it will continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure it is giving schools more choice, more controls and improved Search for learning.

A group of experts and nonprofit organizations filed a lawsuit against five major technology companies on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The legal action was submitted to the Superior Court of the State of California for the County of San Francisco. The plaintiffs include the Heat Initiative, the Alliance for Secure AI, the Irreplaceable Education Fund, and Public Citizen. They are suing Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceXSI.

The lawsuit seeks to address the potential for advanced artificial intelligence systems to cause catastrophic risks to humanity. The plaintiffs argue that these systems must be managed before they can cause severe damage to the world. The legal challenge targets the developers of these advanced technologies to prevent future disasters. This action aims to hold the five named tech giants accountable for the safety of their creations.

The nonprofits and experts responsible for the complaint claim that the defendants cannot control the systems they have built. They believe that the current trajectory of AI development poses a fundamental threat to human existence. By taking this case to court, the organizations hope to force a change in how these companies deploy their technology. They assert that the risks are too great to leave to the companies alone.

stories.Headline: Help wanted: AI firms court ex-spies as Nvidia drama spotlights security risks
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence firms are hiring former spies to protect against blackmail and trade secret theft. This trend gained attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026. His departure followed reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. These companies now face increasing threats from nation-state actors and criminal groups.

The new security roles offer salaries between US$200,000 and US$500,000, while top chiefs can earn up to US$4 million. OpenAI added Paul Nakasone to its board in June 2024 and fired an engineer in October after finding a hidden recording device. Anthropic formed a national security advisory council in August 2025 with David Cohen and Dave Luber. ASML hired Sebastian Reyn in 2024 and created an Intelligence Fusion Centre.

Christopher Falkenberg, a former Secret Service agent, stated that demand for experienced security talent currently exceeds the supply. Catherine Marinis-Yaqub of Control Risks noted that experts help executives avoid traps set by spies in public places. Recruiter Kathy Lavinder explained that high pay reflects the scarcity of these skills. She also mentioned that security teams cannot control the private lives of executives.

The industry is reacting to a global geopolitical race where AI technology is a primary prize. Many firms previously ignored the risk of executives being targeted by foreign agents. ASML continues to expand its defenses, including seeking an officer for Taiwan with 10 years of experience. Companies are now focusing more on insider threats, sabotage, and AI-driven hacking.

stories.Headline: AMA: Physicians need to lead on AI’s use in medicine
stories.Summary:
The American Medical Association says existing regulatory, licensure and liability frameworks were not designed for artificial intelligence and need updating, because patients and medical professionals are adopting AI faster than the health system is adapting. The AMA, which is advancing AI governance, economic sustainability and care transformation, wants physicians to take the leading role in shaping how AI is developed and used in medicine. Its report, "AI and the Practice of Medicine: Examining Accountability and Responsibility in the AI Era," was based on a joint forum held in September in Washington, D.C., with the Federation of State Medical Boards. The AMA and the FSMB released a framework that is a shared foundation for work to be done, including best practices and the evidence needed for AI adoption in clinical settings. The report also clarifies the roles of state medical boards, federal regulators, AI developers, physicians and other stakeholders in oversight and accountability.

The report modernizes oversight, accountability and liability frameworks and establishes how responsibility for AI-related patient harm should be assigned. It calls for clarity on the boundary between clinical technology and the practice of medicine, defining when AI functions as a clinical tool and when it constitutes the practice of medicine. Physicians and the care team need preparation through medical education, clinical training, continuing professional development and care models that support responsible AI use. AI must be integrated into care delivery in ways that are safe, transparent and equitable, strengthening the physician-patient relationship and upholding medical ethics. The AMA's Center for Digital Health and AI and the FSMB Workgroup on the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Medicine will continue working on the identified priorities.

AMA CEO and Executive Vice President Dr. John Whyte said patients and physicians are embracing AI at a remarkable pace, and the questions about responsibility cannot wait. Whyte said there is a difference between automating medical tasks and automating medicine itself, and physicians must help define where that line is drawn. FSMB President and CEO Humayun J. Chaudhry said state medical boards exist to protect patients, and that mission does not change as the tools of medicine change. Chaudhry said patients deserve clarity about who is responsible for their care and who is accountable when something goes wrong. The AMA said AI is already changing how medicine is practiced and will redefine care teams and the physician's role.

Dr. Jason Hill, vice chair for hospital medicine and innovation at Ochsner Health, will speak at Centenary College of Louisiana on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at 11:15 a.m. in the Whited Room of Bynum Commons, in a free, public talk titled "You Are Training for a Job That Doesn't Exist Yet: AI, Clinical Partnership, and the Future of Medicine." Hill, a member of Ochsner's Artificial Intelligence Steering Committee, said the students entering medicine today will spend their careers working alongside AI. Centenary provost Dr. Karen Soul said the college wants students to think critically about AI and weigh the ethical questions it raises. The talk is designed for practicing physicians, nurses, administrators and students in the Shreveport-Bossier medical community.

Hill's talk is the third installment of the AI in the Modern World series, following sessions on AI in everyday life and AI in business. The AMA's report follows its joint forum with the FSMB in September in Washington, D.C., and the framework was released by the two organizations together. Ochsner Health, the largest health system in Louisiana, partners with LSU Health Shreveport to operate Ochsner LSU Health, which includes North Louisiana's only Level I trauma center. Hill is board certified in internal medicine and clinical informatics and earned degrees from Louisiana Tech University, Tulane University and Louisiana State University Medical Center in New Orleans. Hill led system-wide AI projects as one of Ochsner's associate chief medical information officers and now drives adoption of new technologies across hospital medicine.

Reservations for the Centenary talk are made at centenary.edu/speakerseries. The FSMB workgroup plans to release draft guidance and recommendations for public comment in December. The FSMB House of Delegates is scheduled to vote on adoption in April 2027. The articles do not say what the final guidance will require, or how the AMA framework will be enforced.

stories.Headline: AI bots are using credit cards. Banks are racing to keep up.
stories.Summary:
Meta’s Muse, Instinct and other personal AI assistants have been empowered in recent weeks to make purchases on behalf of cardholders, the Journal reported on 13 November 2026. Cards from Bank of America, Capital One and Citigroup are being used by agents when consumers enable them. JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. credit-card issuer by purchase volume, has been blocking agents when consumers give the bots their card information. Amazon in September blocked Meta’s Muse from making purchases. United Airlines said Wednesday it will prevent personal AI assistants from accessing its systems to book tickets.

Stripe is leveraging its Link wallet, which has more than 300 million users, to enable agentic shoppers to execute purchases. Link uses agentic tokens provided by Visa and Mastercard, which hide the card’s number and carry data on what consumers want bought, their purchase limits and whether the bot is trusted. For Chase cards and other issuers, Stripe’s wallet has used one-time virtual cards equal to the purchase amount, then charged the amount to the consumer’s actual card. Merchants complain to Visa and Mastercard that the virtual card, classified as a commercial card, carries higher fees on average than the consumer’s actual card. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency this month gave bank examiners a framework listing “autonomous payment agent[s]” at the highest risk tier.

Farooq Malik, CEO of Rain, an agentic payments and stablecoin infrastructure company, said, “It’s a land grab right now.” A Stripe spokesman said, “Agentic commerce is nascent but promising,” adding that Stripe is working with partners to build the technology. Michael Spelfogel, president of Cardless, said his company is working with network partners to enable agentic spending. Spelfogel said people already want AI agents to shop for them and the technology to do it safely is built. Spelfogel said banks can slow this down for a year or two but can’t stop people from using agents to spend their own money.

Some payment executives say they are already seeing higher returns from agentic shopping than from consumers’ own purchases, as well as elevated fraud cases, such as agents buying from fake online stores that never deliver. Large banks including JPMorgan, Citigroup, Bank of America and Capital One recently moved to restrict AI agents from accessing consumer deposit accounts over the safety of personal information. Economists and analysts have raised fears that AI agents will find higher-yielding deposit accounts elsewhere and transfer deposit holders’ money there. The Treasury Department is asking banks questions related to frameworks around AI and payments. Walmart said it would allow consumers to authorize AI agents and distinguish between purchases they and the agents initiated.

The systems that power payments today are built on byzantine rules, fraud protections, federal laws and network and bank fees that aren’t intended for robots. This ecosystem has long been in constant tension between merchants, networks that set fees and rules, and card issuers that extend credit to consumers. Move one piece or change one fee even by a cent and the impact can quickly ripple into billions of dollars won and lost. It is early days, and the number of consumer card transactions made by AI bots is small, but it is likely to grow materially, according to payments executives. The underlying tension for banks and payments companies is the risk of being left behind if they choose the wrong technology or are too slow to act.

JPMorgan has been at odds with the agentic token technology used by Stripe and has been slow to implement it. Executives at other large banks say they view spotting AI bots and shutting them off as a difficult-to-impossible challenge. Some executives say their banks plan to tell consumers they are treating authorization of an agent to shop with their card as equivalent to giving their cards to relatives or friends. Credit cards come with fraud protection for users, but banks don’t view an authorized charge the same way. Some payment executives are concerned about AI supercharging points gaming, which could make premium cards more expensive for banks.

stories.Headline: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive
stories.Summary:
EU leaders gathered in Dublin on Friday for the bloc's first-ever summit on artificial intelligence, held at the Convention Center where the European Political Community summit had met that same week. The meeting came at a critical moment as the EU sought a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology. French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," addressed the leaders. Mensch urged them to act now to keep pace with the United States and China in AI development.

The articles describe no new law, budget or rule adopted at the summit. Mensch said Europe needs speed, financing and strong coordination between member states to compete. Estonia and Finland wrote a letter before the summit calling for EU-level arrangements to respond to serious AI incidents. That letter also urged developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly. European Council President Antonio Costa said Europe must capture AI's benefits, from higher productivity to better public services, while managing its risks and changes.

Costa's office framed the summit's aim as helping set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI. Costa stated the summit's purpose in a post on X. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she was frustrated with the notion that Europe had somehow lost the AI race. She said the EU has world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI, and that ideas need financing to grow in Europe. Kaja Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, cited drones equipped with artificial intelligence being used to find and kill targets in Ukraine.

The summit came amid growing worries about a technology expected to transform industries, labor markets and societies. It followed a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign this week after it was revealed he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company. Leaders faced questions about how to unlock AI's potential, catch up with China and the United States, and protect individuals and businesses from its risks. The articles also note that weekend protests across Europe were warning of AI's environmental costs and demanding a halt to new data center expansion.

Mensch's company, Mistral, is considered Europe's leading AI model developer. The articles describe the summit as taking place as the bloc sought a common position on a technology it had not yet unified its policy on. Metsola's comments responded directly to the perception that Europe was trailing in the race. Concerns about the risks to individuals and businesses were raised alongside the push for competitiveness. The protests against data centers add the environmental dimension to the debate over AI's costs.

The articles do not say what policies, funding or coordination mechanisms, if any, the leaders agreed to pursue after the summit. They also do not state whether the EU-level incident response arrangements proposed by Estonia and Finland will be adopted. How Europe will catch up with the United States and China, and how it will balance AI ambitions against citizen protection, remain unresolved in the reporting. The articles leave open when, or whether, the bloc will act on Mensch's call to move now.

stories.Headline: Banks Face Agentic AI’s Twin Tests: Customer Authority and Internal Costs
stories.Summary:
Banks are facing two linked pressures as artificial intelligence agents move from answering questions to taking action. On one side, customers may delegate financial decisions to agents, raising legal questions about consent and accountability. On the other, banks deploying their own agents may face runaway computing costs that erode expected savings. A WilmerHale client alert and a Reuters report on McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review describe both problems.

The compliance issue starts with whose instructions a bank is carrying out. WilmerHale's analysis, focused on the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority framework, separates authenticating an agent from establishing its authority. Software may legitimately access an account yet make a transfer or investment beyond the limits the customer intended. Under the U.K. Payment Services Regulations, payment authorization depends on payer consent through an agreed procedure, and strong customer authentication is a separate requirement. Banks therefore need to consider how authority is established, restricted and withdrawn, and when customers must approve further action.

Those concerns help explain the caution across the industry. Reuters reported that most banks currently block external agents from authorizing transactions within their systems. Demand nevertheless appears substantial, since McKinsey surveyed 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide. Among AI users, 72% said they would allow a banking agent to perform one financial task, though they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. The consultancy expects widespread customer use of agents within three years.

Delegation also complicates financial crime monitoring and disputes. WilmerHale describes an agent choosing payment methods, currencies or intermediaries that individually seem reasonable but collectively produce unusual activity. Existing anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations still apply, so banks must separate legitimate automation from fraud or evasion. When a customer disputes a transaction, ordinary records may not show whether the agent followed its instructions, so WilmerHale suggests banks consider what evidence they need, including permissions and action histories.

Banks' own agents raise a separate cost problem. Reuters reported McKinsey's warning that token spending, the units underlying AI processing charges, could easily reach 20% of banks' total labor costs. Some banks have assigned oversight to teams called AI FinOps, and agent-to-agent communication makes earlier usage controls less effective. As a result, banks are becoming more selective, favoring applications with stronger expected returns and asking whether added revenue justifies higher AI spending. The two pressures could compound, since customer agents might shift deposits into higher-yielding alternatives while banks absorb the costs of their own automation.

stories.Headline: Sources: Nvidia faced pressure to boost its 25% residual value support backstop on a planned $500B AI financing vehicle with asset managers before Huang's exit (Bloomberg)
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive, president, and board member of Nvidia on December 12. His departure is now disrupting a massive artificial intelligence financing plan that he had previously championed. This initiative was designed to help various AI companies raise money for expensive chips and computing equipment. Some Wall Street firms that pledged to participate are now considering pulling out of the project. This shift has deepened the uncertainty surrounding the future of the entire financing vehicle.

The plan announced in August aims to supply more than 500 billion dollars for AI computing infrastructure. It involves six firms, including Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs, and KKR. Nvidia planned to provide residual value guarantees covering up to 25 percent of each transaction. However, asset managers pushed for a higher level of coverage before the exit of Jensen Huang. No loans have been made under this specific financing plan as of the current reports.

Jensen Huang personally led the effort by lobbying major Wall Street firms to form a joint consortium. He contacted the heads of these financial firms, including Goldman Sachs Chief Executive David Solomon, to propose lending. Some executives at the participating firms stated they had not been fully briefed on the plan. Negotiations over financial guarantees were already difficult before the former chief executive stepped down from his role. The company faced pressure over the past month to expand the size of its guarantees.

Michael Edwards of Forum Markets compared Nvidia to a central bank of the AI industry without a chairman. Wall Street banks, financial advisers, and asset managers are concerned because they earned billions in transaction fees. At least one of the six participating financial institutions discussed withdrawing from the project on December 12. Other analysts argue that Nvidia's influence will not weaken due to its dominance in AI chips. These observers point to the company's ample cash and a favorable regulatory stance from the Trump administration.

Huang had driven large scale investment and fundraising across the AI industry before his sudden resignation. Nvidia took stakes in data center companies, including IREN, Nebius, and CoreWeave, to expand its reach. The company moved aggressively into acquisitions and investments involving AI chips and other related technology. His departure follows reports of an affair with a woman suspected of spying for the Chinese government. These allegations raised national security concerns that contributed to his exit from the company.

An actual transaction under the financing plan may not be announced until January at the earliest. CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board considers candidates for the role. Harvey C. Jones has been appointed as the first ever chair of the Nvidia board. It remains open whether the exit of Huang will derail individual contracts or the whole program. The board is still searching for a permanent replacement to lead the company forward.

stories.Headline: ASEAN AI Regulation: 49th Summit Puts AI Center Stage
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is set to take center stage at the 49th ASEAN Summit, which leaders will hold in the Philippines this November. ABS-CBN News reported on November 11, 2026, that AI is expected near the top of the summit agenda. The same report said leaders are expected to sign the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, known as DEFA, at the meeting. ABS-CBN News also carried an August report in which a commission warned that unauthorized AI deepfakes of real people may violate data privacy. A trending post also claimed a tech expert urged greater ASEAN action on AI regulation, but the verified ABS-CBN report does not name any such expert.

The verified reporting describes a trade-style framework agreement and a growth-oriented statement, not a binding AI law. Leaders are expected to consider a statement on AI-powered growth for micro, small, and medium enterprises, known as MSMEs. The talks also cover AI in healthcare, including health services and medical diagnosis, and AI's potential role in addressing climate change. The report does not describe a licensing regime for frontier models or a numeric safety threshold. DEFA is the agreement most likely to define the summit's legacy, and the verified reporting says AI cooperation was a negotiation priority.

Dominic Xavier Imperial, Executive Director of the DFA ASEAN Office, described AI as very prominently involved in the ASEAN discussions during the Philippine chairship this year. Imperial also said ASEAN is now more responsive to whatever crisis or emerging threat arises. The Philippines holds the chairship this year and shapes what gets drafted for the summit. ASEAN works by consultation and consensus, so the chair sets the agenda but cannot impose outcomes on member states. Member states will weigh the draft texts before leaders sign anything.

The ASEAN Secretary-General, Kao Kim Hourn, said in 2024 that the bloc had identified cooperation on emerging technologies, including AI, as a key priority in the DEFA negotiations. He also said the bloc was committed to concluding DEFA by 2025 and that it could unlock up to USD2 trillion in digital economic value by 2030. That 2025 target has slipped, since signing is now expected in November 2026. Kao described ASEAN's guidance instruments as proof of the bloc's leadership in setting norms, and those instruments affect organizations across the region's digital economy and its MSMEs.

ASEAN adopted its Guide on AI Governance and Ethics in 2024 as a voluntary baseline for responsible AI governance across the bloc. In 2025 ASEAN approved an expanded guide focused on generative AI risks, along with a Responsible AI Roadmap for member states. At the 47th ASEAN Summit in October 2025, leaders adopted the declaration establishing the ASEAN AI Safety Network, called AI SAFE. The network is described as reflecting a commitment to a human-centered approach to AI development and safety. ASEAN Secretariat materials say officials were developing a Leaders' Declaration on AI-powered growth for MSMEs together with an action plan.

The verified reporting does not say whether the summit will adopt a binding AI law, and no outlet reviewed names one. The articles also leave open whether the final DEFA text contains model-level obligations, since no clause list has been published. It is unclear how far member states will translate the shared principles into domestic rules. The articles do not say whether the MSME statement and action plan will be adopted at the summit. They also do not confirm the identity or remarks of the tech expert named in the trending post.

stories.Headline: AI Is Killing Autonomously. Time for New Rules.
stories.Summary:
Next week, leaders will gather at the United Nations in Geneva to decide whether to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons, according to León Castellanos-Jankiewicz, writing on November 13, 2026. He says machines of this kind have already killed soldiers in eastern Ukraine, and three civilians in Zaporizhzhia last July. The first such incident came two years ago, when a swarm of ten drones struck a field near Bakhmut and killed at least two combatants. In the July case, a Russian drone guided by experimental AI killed three Ukrainians after failing to clear a building and exploding near sheltering civilians. Separately, UVA Darden professors Mike Lenox and Alex Cowan have proposed that AI firms using unlicensed training material release their model weights to the public once a year.

The Geneva meeting is where officials will decide whether to start negotiating a binding treaty, and the report drafted by governmental experts is the latest text on the table. That report covers human control before and during deployment, but once a drone is jammed, only inputs made before launch remain relevant for liability. The Russian drone was programmed by human operators to destroy propane fuel tanks at a gas station, and forensic analysis showed it flew with no link to an operator. It steered itself with a commercially available Nvidia chip, and the writer notes that the operators selected a target category, not a victim. Under the Darden proposal, any firm training models on unlicensed material, or building on a model that did, would release those weights annually, while keeping a lead of six to 18 months, about a year on average.

Castellanos-Jankiewicz is a senior researcher in International Law at the University of Amsterdam Faculty of Law and a non-resident fellow at the UN Institute for Disarmament Research. He argues that the experts' report is a good start but fails to close the enforcement gap for weapons operating in unobserved environments. He says it assigns no responsibility to the tech companies building these systems, which fiercely protect their commercial secrets from public scrutiny. He calls for enforceable obligations on states that field unpredictable killing machines, and for liability on the companies that build them. On the other side, Lenox and Cowan say their annual release rule would advance safety, competition and fairness, and that the time to adopt it is before AI companies go public.

Ukrainian drone maker Alexander Kokhanovskyy said the Bakhmut targets were identified by AI, adding that they simply launch it and know everything in the selected area will be dead. The International Committee of the Red Cross has called for unpredictable autonomous systems to be prohibited outright. Some argue that drone commanders already carry liability under existing laws, but the writer says this is hard to sustain when drones fly in dark mode behind enemy lines with no pilot input. In electronically jammed missions, he says, it becomes impossible to verify what the drones saw or targeted, even after strikes happen. Civilians such as the three killed in Zaporizhzhia are among those affected, while the Darden authors point to a public that is worried, with 55% to 77% in five national polls saying AI is moving too fast or should slow down.

Castellanos-Jankiewicz says international humanitarian law assumes each attack flows from a discrete decision, whereas drone swarms are decentralized by definition. He adds that machine learning systems can show emergent behavior, so their choices cannot be fully predicted or explained ahead of time as the law requires. A 2019 US Army report identified neural, ocular and auditory enhancement as technically feasible by mid-century, which he says further blurs the line between operators and their platforms. The Darden authors note that on October 26 Anthropic filed to go public, with reports putting its valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion. Three days later, Alphabet lost nearly 13% of its value in a single day, about $500 billion, on worries about whether its AI spending will pay off.

The articles do not say whether the Geneva leaders will vote to open treaty negotiations, only that they meet next week to decide. Castellanos-Jankiewicz warns that if diplomats fail to negotiate a new treaty, ever more lives will hang by a line of code. The Darden authors say their proposal could be tried first, and that if it proves insufficient the public could ask for more regulation. They add that under Nasdaq's new fast-entry rules, a newly public company of significant size can join the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days. The articles leave open how states and companies would respond, and whether any treaty or release rule would reach weapons that operate while jammed.

Air Space Intelligence, an AI startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, said its software did not cause the nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026. The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop due to reasons of safety. The FAA later lifted the ground stop as thousands of flights were canceled. NBC News' Brian Cheung and Jared Perlo reported on the AI system and its new implementation by the FAA.

Secretary Mullin said the FAA ground stop was caused by a telecommunication outage. Duffy said data inconsistencies triggered the FAA ground stop. Duffy also detailed a timeline of the ground stop and demanded more FAA funding. He called on Congress to fund improvements to the air system. The Department of Homeland Security said the ground stop was not a cyberattack and said, "We are built to handle crisis like this."

Travelers were stranded at Raleigh-Durham airport and weighed in on the ground stop, saying they were very upset. Frustrated Chicago travelers sought answers on checked bags amid the ground stop. stories.Headline: Judge Says Fake AI Case Citations Warrant Sanctions
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Pennsylvania has recommended dismissing with prejudice a pro se couple's lawsuit over a mortgage foreclosure, and said their continued use of fictitious case citations warrants sanctions. The recommendation came in a November 4 report in Torres v. Freedom Mortgage Corp., issued by U.S. Magistrate Judge Martin C. Carlson of the Middle District of Pennsylvania. Carlson said Hericson and Leigh Torres kept citing cases that do not exist after both a bankruptcy court and the federal court had warned them. The recommendation now goes to Judge Karoline Mehalchick, and the parties have 14 days to file objections.

The Torres filing is a report and recommendation, so the district judge may accept, modify, or reject it. Freedom Mortgage obtained a default judgment against Hericson Torres in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, in December 2023, with damages assessed at $308,604. State courts denied two petitions to open that judgment. On February 26, 2026, the day the sheriff sold the property, Leigh Torres filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. On March 31, the bankruptcy court found that Leigh Torres had cited nonexistent or inaccurate case law and ordered her to certify any future use of generative AI in filings.

Three days later, the couple filed a federal complaint asserting 13 counts, including claims under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, RESPA and the CARES Act. Carlson said the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, claim preclusion, and the Anti-Injunction Act barred the attempt to relitigate the foreclosure. He wrote that there was no bankruptcy stay to violate, because two earlier bankruptcy cases had been dismissed within the previous year. He also found that private lenders are not state actors for constitutional claims, and that the sheriff has quasi-judicial immunity for carrying out a court-ordered sale. Carlson noted that the FDCPA's one-year limitations period bars any claim based on conduct before April 3, 2025.

He wrote that once a foreclosure judgment is entered, the mortgage merges into the judgment and there is no servicer for RESPA purposes. In their opposition brief, the plaintiffs cited Caban v. Caban, 259 A.3d 527, to argue that void judgments are legal nullities. Carlson said that citation points to a criminal case, Commonwealth v. Sanders, that does not address civil judgments, and he could find no Pennsylvania case by that name on the point.

He wrote that the plaintiffs' briefs persisted in citing cases and quotations that do not exist, despite having been admonished. He also noted that Rule 11 applies to unrepresented parties, citing a 2025 Middle District of Pennsylvania decision, Kholod v. Nationstar Mortgage. Carlson concluded the conduct warrants the imposition of sanctions, but his recommendation does not specify a penalty. Attorneys Manny Newburger and Brit Suttell of Barron & Newburger, P.C. noted in a legal alert that pro se litigants are more likely than attorneys to abuse the legal system with generative AI.

According to Damien Charlotin's AI Hallucination Cases database, courts worldwide had documented nearly 2,000 cases of AI-fabricated content in filings as of late August 2026, including more than 1,300 in the U.S. The reasoning gives collection agencies and their counsel a roadmap for the kind of serial, AI-assisted filings they increasingly see. Earlier ACA-tracked rulings include Harris v. Pinnacle Bank in Mississippi and Owens v. Select Portfolio Servicing in New York.

Separately, a federal judge in Mississippi, U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock, issued sanctions on June 8, 2026, in a contract dispute between Louisiana attorney Tom Withers III and the City of Aberdeen. She removed all four attorneys from the case, imposed $8,000 in fines, and barred two lawyers from appearing in the Northern District of Mississippi for two years. Kathleen Wilson, who used the AI program First Drafts, told the judge she had used the software for about six months and was unaware AI could invent authorities. Aycock called that explanation "insufficient and incredulous," and she extended the proceedings' suspension for 60 days, with the parties given until August 7 to secure new representation.

stories.Headline: DUI suspect released after officer used AI in arrest report: Judge
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, an Arizona judge released Anthony Edward Rene Quidera, a DUI suspect, after the arresting officer used artificial intelligence in his arrest report. Maricopa Superior Court Judge Daniel Fenzel ordered the release during Quidera's initial court hearing. The police report about the October 29 arrest ended with a disclaimer that it was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. Quidera, 37, was accused of driving 100 miles per hour on Interstate 10 in Phoenix around 12:33 a.m. The unidentified Arizona Department of Public Safety trooper alleged he smelled an intoxicating beverage and found several open containers in the car.

Quidera was arrested on October 29, 2026, on charges of DUI, exceeding the posted speed limit by more than 20 mph, and possession of an open container in a vehicle. The arrest occurred on eastbound Interstate 10 after a trooper observed a vehicle traveling over 100 mph in a 65 mph zone near 79th Avenue. The trooper alleged Quidera's Dodge Charger failed to maintain its lane and drove on the left median shoulder. The trooper reported bloodshot, red, and watery eyes and six out of six cues on a Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus test. Quidera allegedly declined a preliminary breath test, and several open containers were found on the passenger floorboard.

Fenzel said the use of generative AI affected the case and that the court was unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations were authored in whole or in part by AI. Fenzel said the court was therefore unable to determine probable cause at this time. Fenzel added that his order did not mean the DUI case could not go forward in the future. Raul Garcia, who represents DPS, said the department uses Truleo to help draft reports. Garcia said AI tools may be used only as an aid, the trooper remains the author and is responsible for accuracy, and a supervisor must review reports before they become part of the official record.

Garcia said troopers must review drafts against body-worn camera footage and other evidence, verify times, names, locations, and actions, and correct errors. Garcia said troopers may not use the tool until they complete Department-approved training. Attorney information for Quidera wasn't available, and a spokesman for the Arizona DPS declined to comment. The case comes weeks after the Arizona Court of Appeals ordered Gabriel Paul Horcasitas to be resentenced for his manslaughter conviction. The September 30 appellate ruling found that the judge's consideration of an AI video so prejudiced Horcasitas as to render the sentencing procedure fundamentally unfair.

In October, ABC15 reported on Phoenix PD's trial program with Axon's Draft One AI report writing software. In September, an appeals court threw out a 10-year sentence in a road rage shooting after determining an AI victim impact statement influenced the sentence. The Arizona Supreme Court has declined to ban judges from using AI. The Court asked the Arizona Steering Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts to recommend rules or administrative orders for clear standards on responsible use of emerging AI technologies. The Court asked the Committee to send a status report by March 1, 2027.

An arraignment date was scheduled for Thursday, and Maricopa County Justice Court records show Quidera was eventually charged and scheduled to be arraigned on November 12th. The ruling raises new legal questions about how AI-generated or AI-assisted police reports may hold up in court. The articles do not say what happened at the arraignment or how the case was resolved. The articles do not give the outcome of any further probable cause review. The articles do not identify the trooper or provide Quidera's attorney information.

stories.Headline: Without Huang, Nvidia’s chips hold up. But its AI investment web may not.
stories.Summary:
Nvidia’s board met Wednesday to decide whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported, after he admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, according to The New York Times. The New York Times also reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. The board’s meeting threatened to end 33 years of founder-led management at the company. The JoongAng Ilbo interviewed eight experts about the possible ouster of Huang. Visitors explored booths at Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at Coex in Gangnam District, southern Seoul, on Nov. 10.

The most pressing concern the experts cited is that Nvidia has no obvious successor. Shin Jae-yong, a business administration professor at Seoul National University, said U.S. boards usually review succession planning regularly and manage a pool of candidates, but no one has emerged as a potential successor at Nvidia even though it is the world’s most valuable company. Nvidia prizes “intellectual honesty,” and Huang is known for a hands-on management style with dozens of direct reports whom he often meets as a group. Huang personally reads employees’ “Top 5 Things” emails, in which staff list their five most important tasks, so he can keep track of even small changes across the company. Powell is one of approximately 60 senior executives who report directly to Huang and is considered a key figure at Nvidia.

Kwon Ki-bum, an education professor at Korea University and former associate editor of the academic journal Human Resource Development Quarterly, said Huang could win engineers’ trust and strike a chord with them with a single remark from the stage, calling the situation a major crisis in terms of organizational continuity and culture. Yoo Eung-joon, CEO of JOON AI Consulting and a former head of Nvidia Korea, disagreed, saying Nvidia has encouraged each employee to become a guru. Yoo said that because its people have a high level of expertise and autonomy, the culture won’t be shaken. Kim Joung-ho, a professor of electrical engineering at KAIST, said Huang personally made physical AI the company’s next growth engine and expanded its ecosystem, so if he steps down, cooperation with Korean companies could also slow. Noh Geun-chang, head of Semicon Research Lab, said financial relationships such as investments and payment guarantees are intricately tangled around Nvidia, so if financial companies that place weight on management credibility become cautious about investing, vendor financing will also shrink for the time being.

Jeong Hyung-gon, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy, said that with the U.S.-China tech rivalry having expanded into a race for AI supremacy, the United States cannot stop investing. Jeong added that because Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are among the few suppliers of high-performance memory, the impact on them would be limited. Yoo Hoi-jun, head of KAIST’s Graduate School of AI Semiconductor, said the technology of Nvidia’s GPUs alone creates a barrier to entry so high that competitors find it hard to catch up. Yoo Eung-joon said CUDA, Nvidia’s software ecosystem, is also a strong line of defense. Lee Jae-wook, head of Seoul National University’s AI Institute, said CUDA is built around Nvidia GPUs and Nvidia even controls the tools developers use, known as libraries, so it is not an ecosystem that will collapse overnight.

Nvidia has invested in and guaranteed payments for AI companies that in turn buy its chips, tying the finances of many AI companies to Nvidia. Vendor financing, a related practice, is when a supplier like Nvidia helps its customers raise money to buy its products. The Financial Times reported that Huang’s Nvidia ploughed its vast profits into bankrolling AI startups, suppliers, and chip customers, a web of dependencies that could now unravel. Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported that former Nvidia CEO Huang had a relationship with a second employee after he resigned amid reports of other affairs. Taiwan barred Alice Huang, who has been linked to Jensen Huang in allegations of an extramarital affair, from returning.

A related JoongAng Ilbo article said Huang’s troubles threaten AI alliances built on personal ties with Korean tech titans. Another related article said that with Huang’s leadership on the line, the CFO and chief engineer emerged as favored candidates. A photo reportedly uploaded to Alice Huang’s WeChat account showed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who has been linked to him in allegations of an extramarital affair. A photo showed Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has been named in allegations of an extramarital affair involving Huang, following similar allegations involving Alice Huang, who has been accused of links to Chinese espionage. The JoongAng Ilbo article was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor, and all AI-assisted translations are reviewed and refined by the newsroom.

A related article asked who Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim CEO, is, saying the longtime executive took the top spot after Jensen Huang resigned. That article said veteran CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO as Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis and investor concerns over its financing deals. Another related article said Nvidia’s longtime CEO stepped down after reports linked his personal relationships to scrutiny over China and chip exports. A Korean-language related article said leadership uncertainty and looming U.S. export controls could disrupt Korean chipmakers’ AI partnerships, China operations and broader economy. The Financial Times article was not fully available, with the publication offering subscription access instead of the full text.

stories.Headline: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
stories.Summary:
Researcher Will DePue published a report on November 12, 2026, saying six AI models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry a hardware fingerprint matching NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs. The models include DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3 and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-flash. The report says the models were released between April and October 2026. Blackwell chips are restricted from export to China under U.S. rules, and the report says no export license has been reported for them.

The fingerprint is read from the published weights, the adjustable numbers that determine how a model works. The report describes how those starting values depend on a random seed and on the number of processing units, called streaming multiprocessors, on a chip. The B200 and B300 have 148 of these units, while the GB200 and GB300 have 152. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the B200 or B300, and the other four match the GB200 or GB300. The report says the method was checked against 24 models whose developers had publicly disclosed their hardware, and it agreed in every case.

DePue says the six models were likely trained on Blackwell hardware, and he estimates roughly 12,000 GPUs were used across the five largest training runs. He writes that the cost of those GPUs would be more than half a billion dollars, based on a price of about $70,000 per chip. He says the estimate rests on assumptions the weights cannot confirm, including how efficiently each lab used its GPUs. The report says the fingerprint establishes how the starting weights were created, and that training on Blackwell is a supported inference rather than a proven fact. It adds that the figures cover only final training runs, not experiments or serving.

The report states that it cannot establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. It notes that Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. A companion article from Startup Fortune reports that DePue posted on X that he had "conclusive forensic evidence," and that no lab has responded to the findings. Earlier, U.S. officials and press reports had alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI used Blackwell chips, but without publishing technical evidence.

Several other Chinese labs appear to have stayed on NVIDIA's older Hopper generation. The report says the newest models examined from Alibaba, Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan said its LongCat-2.0 was trained on "AI ASIC superpods," and the report found no NVIDIA fingerprint in that model's weights. The report notes that NVIDIA's own Nemotron-3 Ultra reads as 152 streaming multiprocessors, matching Kimi K3.

Chinese labs began training on Blackwell relatively recently, according to the report. DeepSeek's models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3, released in December 2024, and as Blackwell from V4, released in April 2026. Moonshot's models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 in January 2026 and as Blackwell from K3 in July 2026, while MiniMax's shift came with M3 in June 2026. The report says Ant Group's Ling-3.0-flash in August 2026 read as Hopper, and its Ling-3.1-flash in October 2026 read as Blackwell.

The report leaves several questions open, including where the chips were located and how the labs obtained them. It also does not establish whether export controls were violated. The article from Startup Fortune notes that the claim has not been verified by outside reviewers, and the report names no outside reviewer. The findings are DePue's own, and the article says the report does not mention Singapore or Megaspeed. Whether the labs or U.S. regulators will respond to the report is not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: Cisco forecasts $9 billion in AI infrastructure revenue in FY27
stories.Summary:
Cisco reported record quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion for its fiscal first quarter ended October 24, up 24% year over year, and record non-GAAP earnings per share of $1.40, up 40% year over year. CEO Chuck Robbins said on the vendor's quarterly financial call that these were Cisco's strongest top and bottom-line growth rates in over 15 years. Networking product orders grew 28% in Q1, Cisco's ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, with double-digit growth across every product family. Robbins said the results support Cisco's view that it is in the early stages of a multiyear, multibillion-dollar networking supercycle. Cisco said its AI infrastructure revenue is projected to grow to $9 billion in fiscal year 2027, more than double fiscal year 2026 levels.

Enterprise product orders were up 15% year-over-year, on top of 4% growth a year ago, with double-digit growth across all geographies and in networking and security. Campus networking product orders grew 14% year-over-year, and Robbins said the transition is less than 10% along. Product orders from service provider and cloud customers grew 47% year-over-year. Cisco had 18 AI design wins in the last 5 quarters, and Robbins said hyperscalers are deploying its scale-across networking architecture as they extend coordinated AI workloads across data centers. Core security products aside from Splunk grew 15%, the best in three years, firewall orders grew more than 30% for the third consecutive quarter, and the zero-trust secure access portfolio has 5,400 customers after almost 800 were added in Q1.

Robbins attributed the growth to five technology drivers: hyperscale success, campus refresh, the post-Mythos opportunity, sovereignty, and the hybrid data center. He said Cisco announced Sovereign Critical Infrastructure for Europe a year ago, expanded and launched it for Canada, and recently preannounced it in India. He said work with sovereign cloud providers such as Humai and G42 continues to grow. He said enterprise data center networking orders have seen double-digit growth in 9 of the last 11 quarters as customers run open weight and open-source models and train on their own data in their own data centers. He said Cisco is protecting 2 trillion tokens per month at the AI Defense layer and approaching 500 customers for AI Defense.

Robbins said customers in Europe are attributing orders to early Mythos implications, including service providers upgrading managed services CPE for their customers. He said customers want to move fast but are taking time to plan and design the right architecture. He said Cisco earlier this week announced it is integrating Anthropic's Claude Mythos cybersecurity model into Cisco AI Defense for adaptive AI red teaming, providing automated, continuous testing across enterprise systems. He said Cisco is using Splunk as a platform for AI security and that customers are buying into security and networking coming together on monitoring workloads and east-west traffic segmentation with technologies such as Hypershield and Live Protect. The articles name no other affected parties beyond Cisco, its hyperscaler, service provider, cloud and enterprise customers, and Anthropic.

The article, by Network World senior editor Michael Cooney and dated November 13, 2026, describes Cisco as continuing to benefit from a networking supercycle driven by demand for AI infrastructure, security, and campus refreshes from hyperscalers and enterprise customers. It cites the five drivers Robbins listed as fueling what he called a multiyear, multi-billion-dollar market opportunity. It notes that Cisco's zero-trust secure access portfolio, which includes Duo, Secure Access and Identity Services Engine, did not exist three years ago. It also lists related Network World coverage, including Cisco boosting its AI Defense platform with Anthropic's Claude Mythos on November 11, 2026, and Arista posting record growth as the AI networking supercycle accelerates on November 4, 2026.

The articles do not say when Cisco will report fiscal year 2027 results or how the $9 billion projection compares with any figure other than fiscal year 2026 levels. They do not give the size of Cisco's fiscal year 2026 AI infrastructure revenue, the terms of the Anthropic integration, or the names of the 18 AI design wins. They do not identify the customers behind the 5,400 secure access customers or the roughly 500 AI Defense customers. They do not say which countries beyond Europe, Canada and India will receive Sovereign Critical Infrastructure. They do not give a date for the full rollout of the sovereign offering or further detail on the Mythos orders heard in Europe.

stories.Headline: AI productivity gains need to be shared — but how?
stories.Summary:
The Australian government has released a draft "Best practice guide on the adoption of AI in the workplace," announced by Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth this week. The release comes as AI is already contributing to job losses across the country, including at Qantas, Canva and Australia's big banks. Rishworth discussed the guide with POLITICO's Amanda Copp on the Canberra Playbook Podcast. The guidance is aimed at helping business owners and workers prepare for disruption from AI.

The guide advises employers to involve workers when they deploy AI, to redesign jobs and to build skills among their staff. It also calls for clear accountability and ongoing checks to make sure AI systems are safe and fair. The government's position, as the article reports it, is that AI can benefit both businesses and workers. The guidelines are not enforceable, however, so they set out expectations rather than binding rules. The article's headline frames the central question as how the productivity gains from AI should be shared.

Rishworth's office is responsible for the guide, and the minister spoke about how the government is trying to help the business community and workers adjust. The article paraphrases her approach as one of preparation, not compulsion. The Labor government's view, as relayed in the piece, is that well-managed AI adoption can serve both sides of the workplace. The article gives no timeline for when the draft will be finalised or whether any part of it will become law.

The piece places the guidance within a broader Australian policy debate, noting that Canberra is weighing questions about technology regulation alongside other pressures. The article describes Australia as a middle power with major resources, including a large share of the world's uranium and lithium. It also references the AUKUS defence program and the country's energy transition. The article does not say what steps will follow the draft guide or how employers and unions are expected to respond.

stories.Headline: Inside the algorithms: How artificial intelligence is enhancing traditional pathology practice
stories.Summary:
Lee Cooper, director of computational pathology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, said digital imaging methods are becoming more popular in pathology, as Medill Reports described on November 13, 2026. After a blood or tissue sample is placed on a glass slide, the slide goes into a scanner that produces a digital image that can be shared electronically. Cooper runs a lab where researchers develop artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms that review digitized samples. He said the algorithms will help pathologists make more accurate and detailed diagnoses and help researchers interpret how diseases progressed in past patients. The article said glass slides are often still carried between offices so multiple pathologists can look at them.

Cooper said a computer can analyze a sample in much greater detail than a human can, because each image could contain a million cells or more. Researcher Fattaneh Pourakpour, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, uses digitized tissue data from Northwestern’s Mesulam Institute for Cognitive Neurology and Alzheimer’s Disease brain bank, which accepts brain donations upon death from people who had dementia. Her tissue segmentation algorithms distinguish brain regions such as gray matter and white matter, and her cell classifier algorithms identify and categorize cell types within gray matter. Researcher Ramin Nateghi, a post-doctoral researcher with a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from Shiraz University of Technology in Shiraz, Iran, applies machine learning to prostate cancer detection. Nateghi said biopsies taken over time might show few differences over 25 years, so detecting subtle changes in slides can help doctors make better decisions.

Cooper said digital pathology tools are meant to augment pathologists, not replace them, because the models he works with operate on the basis of correlation and have no causal understanding inside them. He said an algorithm is less helpful on a rare case it has never seen, and that he does not think the models should be trusted implicitly. Researcher Lawrence Chillrud, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, said the United States has a huge shortage of pathologists but heaps of patient biopsy data that needs to be inspected, analyzed and reviewed. Chillrud develops tools that conduct a preliminary screen of pathology data, sort out the most obvious cases and flag others for fast-tracked, specialized review. His models might also count items such as a certain kind of cell, direct a pathologist’s attention to important areas or review a pathologist’s report for potential errors.

Chillrud is also developing uncertainty tools that quantify the likely accuracy of a model’s prediction, because many models are overconfident and give a false picture of how well their predictions can be trusted. He said models inherit the biases of the data sets they are trained on, giving the example of training on mostly white, affluent patients living in a certain part of a city. Artificial intelligence pathology tools can also help address shortages of specialized pathologists, since a general pathologist might not have the training for a detailed read of a prostate cancer biopsy. Specialists are harder to find in smaller, more rural areas, while large, city-based medical systems might have them on staff. According to Cooper, the Northwestern Medicine health care system generates about 2 million glass slides per year.

Cooper is not sure how quickly digital pathology will become commonplace, because the tools must undergo FDA clearance and be validated on very high-quality data that can be hard to access. Not all medical systems have adopted the digitizing tools and technology Northwestern has access to. In the Cooper Lab, glass slides are digitized using the Aperio slide scanner, manufactured by Leica, which takes about 90 seconds per slide and can hold up to 450 glass slides at a time. Cooper said each image typically has several billion pixels, and pathology at Northwestern generates about 3 petabytes, or 3 million gigabytes, per year. Cooper said he is optimistic about adoption after seeing researchers use the tools to measure patterns in tissue and relate them to metrics such as treatment success.

Cooper said the tools are useful and easy to use, and that it is not just tool developers but scientists using them. The article said pathology data is by far the biggest source of data in the medical field. Whether models possess deep understandings of the subjects they are trained in, or only superficial ones, is an unanswered question, though Cooper said he thinks they can deliver accurate and efficient predictions regardless. Cooper said computers can consider many more properties of the samples than a doctor could, which can help generate a fuller prediction of that patient’s future. The article did not say when the algorithms might receive FDA clearance or reach routine clinical use.
