stories.Headline: Governor Hochul Announces Cutting Edge AI Company Aaru Will Expand in New York City, Creating Over 650 New Jobs | Empire State Development
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul announced that Aaru, a Manhattan-based AI company that helps businesses test new products and ideas before bringing them to market, will expand its operations in New York City. The expansion is expected to create more than 650 new jobs over the next five years, and the company plans to make New York the home of its research and development operations. The announcement was made on November 13, 2026. Aaru will lease and build out more than 27,000 square feet of office space near Union Square. The company currently employs about 60 people and expects its workforce to grow to more than 700.

Under the plan, Aaru will invest in the State as it grows, deepening its roots in the city where it was founded just two years ago. The company's workforce is set to grow tenfold, which Governor Hochul pointed to as evidence that New York has overtaken the San Francisco Bay Area as the nation's largest tech talent market. Hochul credited her investments in computing power, research and talent with drawing companies and jobs to the state. She said Aaru started in New York, is growing here, and is creating hundreds of well-paying jobs for New Yorkers. The governor's remarks framed the expansion as a sign that leading AI companies are choosing New York to grow.

Aaru Co-Founder and CEO Cameron Fink said the company deliberately chose to build in New York City. He pointed to the depth and diversity of local talent, the closeness to the world's largest enterprises, and the city's history of innovation as reasons for the decision. Fink also said being a New York company is central to Aaru's identity and thanked Hochul and Empire State Development for their support. Empire State Development President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said the company's growth shows what innovative firms can achieve when they have the talent, resources and support they need. Knight described the expansion as an important investment in Aaru's future and said the state is helping companies scale their operations and build lasting economic opportunities.

stories.Headline: Rajnath Singh calls for stronger defensive capabilities to maintain 'element of surprise' in future warfare; launches UDAAN-developed AI applications
stories.Summary:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh spoke at the Air Force Commanders' Conference in New Delhi on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He called for stronger offensive and defensive capabilities to maintain the element of surprise against various adversaries. The minister launched a suite of artificial intelligence applications developed in-house by the IAF's AI Centre of Excellence. These new tools were created by the Unit for Digitisation, Automation, Artificial Intelligence and Application Networking, known as UDAAN. The event focused on maintaining operational readiness against conventional and emerging threats arising from rapid technological advancements.

The AI applications are deployed on the secure network of the IAF to automate tasks in operations, administration, and aerospace safety. The two-day conference used the theme The Year of Empowerment: Maximising Efficiency Through Decentralisation to guide senior leadership deliberations. Attendees included Raksha Rajya Mantri Sanjay Seth, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, and Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. Secretary of Defence Production Sanjeev Kumar and Secretary of Defence Finance Vishvajit Sahay also attended the inaugural session of the meeting. All Principal Staff Officers, Director Generals, and Air Officers Commanding-in-Chief of all IAF Commands participated in the conference.

Rajnath Singh stated that defence forces must develop methods that leave enemies no time to react or recover from strikes. He said that intelligence and surveillance mechanisms must be strengthened to ensure personnel remain alert, agile, and equipped for challenges. The minister asserted that victory in future conflicts depends on technological sophistication, speed of response, and precision rather than aircraft numbers. He urged commanders to integrate emerging challenges into institutional thinking, planning, and operational processes as a core priority. Singh also noted that the government decided on a second tour of duty for Agniveers based on feedback.

The minister highlighted that drones and air defence systems are now critical components of modern warfare for the armed forces. He specifically mentioned the Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Hamas conflicts as examples of how contemporary conflicts extend beyond traditional battlefields. Commanders were exhorted to prepare for emerging threats such as kamikaze drones, surveillance operations, and various counter-drone operations. The Indian Air Force is affected by the need to develop dedicated doctrines for electronic, cyber, and space domains. Singh emphasized that the technological expertise of young recruits could contribute significantly to stronger decision-making and organisational development.

The articles state that the defence forces are currently undergoing a transformative phase involving reforms in organisational structures and operational concepts. This transformation includes a focus on jointness and integration, which was effectively demonstrated during the execution of Operation Sindoor. The lessons learned from Operation Sindoor are now shaping the pace and direction of changes within the Indian Defence Forces. These lessons specifically increased the emphasis on air defence systems and drones, which the minister called vital to national security. The changing security environment has necessitated a forward-looking approach to military preparedness and continuous adaptation of all military strategies.

The IAF will continue to use the UDAAN applications to expedite administrative functions and improve overall efficiency through technology-driven solutions. Military planning and operational execution will continue to be guided by the principles of jointness and integrated efforts among services. The Air Force will sustain efforts to train air warriors in emerging technologies to keep pace with rapid technological advancements. The articles leave open how the IAF will specifically implement the new doctrines for the cyber, electronic, and space domains. It remains unspecified how the second tour of duty for Agniveers will be structured to bolster the three services.

stories.Headline: Akhilesh Yadav says phones can't be trusted in AI age amid Rahul Gandhi's phone-tapping allegation
stories.Summary:
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Friday backed Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's allegation that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was having his phone tapped. Yadav said phones and modern technology could not be trusted in the age of Artificial Intelligence. He spoke in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, on November 13, 2026, after arriving at the Samajwadi Party's state headquarters. He came to attend an election review meeting with assembly-level presidents of 86 reserved constituencies. Rahul Gandhi made his allegation the same Friday in a video posted by the Congress on X.

Yadav claimed 1.27 crore names had been removed from electoral rolls and that votes belonging to the Samajwadi Party were being deleted. He said the Chief Minister knows that 12.7 million, or 1 crore 27 lakh, voters have been removed from the rolls. He alleged the BJP was preparing to bring people from Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh to register them as voters in Uttar Pradesh. He also named Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand among the places from which people could be brought. He said the BJP was preparing a plan to replace votes deleted due to relocation and fraudulent registrations by bringing in people from outside the state.

Yadav said one should not trust the technology of today and that in the age of AI anything is possible. He added that a leader who was no longer alive had once spoken about their phones being tapped. He said that if it is true that 1.27 crore Hindu voters are missing, that is precisely why the BJP meeting is taking place. He alleged the BJP was preparing regarding those shifting votes, votes deleted due to people relocating to Delhi or elsewhere, and instances where fraudulent names had been added. He said the BJP was orchestrating a plan involving underground or unregistered elements to bring in individuals from Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and potentially other locations to get them registered as voters.

Gandhi said the Prime Minister is aware of the tapping because he has his phone tapped. Gandhi said that the day Modi agrees to a face-to-face debate, everyone will learn who is under the control of foreign powers, who is anti-national, and how long they have been involved in anti-national activities. Gandhi claimed proof of the Prime Minister being under the control of foreign powers was already available on his phone, adding that Modi was aware of the evidence. Congress MP Imran Masood said the PM is scared and the country is listening to Rahul Gandhi. Masood also reacted to the UP CM's claim of 1.27 crore Hindu voters missing, saying what can we say in this fight between the CM and the Deputy CM, and that we know there has been an about the SIR.

Yadav said the Samajwadi Party had raised the voter list issue in Pilibhit, following which action was taken against two Sub-Divisional Magistrates. He alleged a major scheme is underway to manipulate the voter list. He warned that voters might reach polling booths only to be told their votes were not registered there, forcing them to search for their names elsewhere. He called for a durable and secure card linked to Aadhaar and advocated biometric-based voting to ensure greater transparency. He said that if a Samajwadi Party government is formed, they will introduce biometric voter cards.

Yadav said he would say to announce the election dates, and that the very day they are announced, the BJP will be defeated. He made the remarks as the 2027 State Assembly election approaches, with both the BJP and the Samajwadi Party exchanging heated jibes. The articles do not say what the BJP said in response to Yadav's allegations. The articles do not say what action, if any, followed Gandhi's phone-tapping allegation. stories.Headline: AI spending helps lift UK growth to fastest since early 2024
stories.Summary:
Britain’s economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter of 2026, the fastest rate in two-and-a-half years, helped by investment in artificial intelligence. The Office for National Statistics said on Thursday that gross domestic product grew 0.7% in the July-to-September period, up from 0.5% in the second quarter. The expansion was the strongest calendar-quarter growth since the first quarter of 2024 and defied predictions of a slowdown made after the Iran war began. The annual growth rate picked up to 1.9% in the third quarter, the strongest reading since the fourth quarter of 2024. On a rolling three-month basis, growth was the fastest since May, and in September alone output climbed 0.2%, bucking expectations for unchanged output.

The ONS said there was widespread strength in industries which may be related to artificial intelligence, with computer programming, consultancy and related activity making the largest single contribution to growth. Computer manufacturing made the biggest contribution to industrial production, up 4.6% in the three months to September. Business investment grew just 0.4% on the quarter, half economists’ expectations in a Reuters poll and the weakest growth since the start of the year. The Bank of England now expects GDP to expand 1.6% this year, much stronger than the 1.2% forecast by the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility after finance minister John Healey’s October 28 budget. The central bank attributed some of the strength to spending on AI and a small, temporary boost from Healey’s fiscal plan.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said something is stirring, noting that monthly GDP beat consensus for the fifth straight month and the seventh in eight. Wood said the data strengthened the chances of another Bank of England rate hike next month. He said that with growth and inflation both strong, he was comfortable expecting at least two more Monetary Policy Committee hikes, and that the figures made a December hike more likely. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JP Morgan Personal Investing, said that while the UK economy has been relatively resilient since the conflict started, that strength will be tested in the months ahead. Gardner said nervousness in the lead-up to the autumn budget and continued uncertainty from the Middle East war is expected to weigh on confidence and activity over the coming GDP readings.

British growth in the third quarter was the second-fastest in the Group of Seven advanced economies, just behind the US. So far this year, growth has been the strongest since 2017, excluding the post-pandemic rebound. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey welcomed the data, which is likely to increase pressure on the BoE to raise interest rates again. The central bank warned last week that inflation will near 5% in 2027, and investors see a 73% chance of a back-to-back hike in December after November’s increase and two or possibly three more moves next year. Official data showed a fall in retail sales volumes in September and consumer confidence suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since April 2020 before the budget.

Britain’s economy has shown surprising resilience in the first half of 2026 after expanding by 0.6% in the first quarter. While some economists expect slower growth in the final quarter of the year as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on activity, the Bank of England last week upgraded its growth projection for 2026 alongside increasing interest rates. Britain’s government has offered limited support to help families absorb the financial impact of the energy price shock. Although a recent fall in oil prices might lower petrol prices, household gas and electricity bills are still set to rise by about 25% when the country’s energy price cap changes in January. There have been some recent signs of weakening consumer and business demand in the face of prolonged high energy prices and rising interest rates.

The quarterly growth rates were in line with economists’ expectations in a Reuters poll. The BoE’s upgraded projection did not factor in some recent stronger GDP data and upward revisions to past numbers. The articles do not say what the Bank of England will decide at its December meeting. The articles do not give the date of the next GDP release or the size of any expected rate increase. The articles do not say how much of the third-quarter growth came from AI investment.

stories.Headline: Alberta expanding use of AI technology that speeds up MRIs after successful pilot
stories.Summary:
The Alberta government said on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, that it will spend $14 million on artificial intelligence technology that speeds up the MRI testing process. The Canadian Press reported the announcement from Edmonton, and the story appeared in the Brandon Sun and the Winnipeg Free Press that same day. The decision followed a successful pilot program that began last year, according to the government. That pilot led to almost 12,000 more MRIs being done. The government says the technology is installed directly to MRI machines in hospitals.

The technology improves image clarity while also shortening examination times, the government says. The money will increase the province's testing capacity and reduce wait times, according to Hospitals Minister Adriana LaGrange. The government says the technology is expected to be installed provincewide by 2028. It says patient data will remain safe. stories.Headline: China's $3 billion-plus pipeline of Nvidia-powered AI data centres
stories.Summary:
Reuters has identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia's restricted processors, according to a report published on November 13, 2026. The findings came a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive over a scandal. The review found projects ranging from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces. Nvidia has said that US export controls have effectively shut it out of the Chinese AI data-centre market. The report stresses how deeply Nvidia's technology remains embedded in China's AI expansion.

A proposed 6.2 billion yuan, or $873 million, AI computing centre in Xianyou county, Fujian province, specifies Nvidia H100 chips and is seeking commercial partners. In Shaanxi province, Sinomach said a subsidiary won a contract for a 3 billion yuan computing centre specifying H100 and H200 processors. An April government prospectus in Jilin province describes a 2.26 billion yuan project combining H100 processors with Chinese-developed chips, with banks expected to finance about 80% of the investment. In Inner Mongolia, a 1.5 billion yuan development proposes installing 625 Nvidia H200 servers. In Gansu province, a 1.16 billion yuan contract awarded in July covers a centre planning about 3,072 Nvidia processors.

The report suggests these plans depend on US processors that are vulnerable to trade restrictions. Tighter curbs could cause construction delays, higher costs or redesigns around domestic alternatives. Nvidia's chief executive resigned, and Huang's departure could deepen vulnerabilities for Chinese companies exposed to potential delays and supply disruptions. The Reuters review did not establish whether the processors in the Gansu project have been delivered. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, had been a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions.

Other Chinese facilities already use restricted Nvidia hardware, according to the review. The Wuxi municipal government in Jiangsu province said in March 2025 that a computing cluster using H800 processors had entered operation. In June, Shanghai-listed Damingcheng disclosed that a computing venture in Fujian had built an H800 cluster under a computing-services agreement originally worth 759 million yuan, which ended early. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors in September, and US-blacklisted Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips the following month. Demand thus extends to research institutions.

A separate Global Times editorial published on November 8 argued that US technology companies could consider deploying some AI computing capacity in China. The editorial pointed to American constraints such as insufficient electricity supply, grid upgrade delays, high construction costs, lengthy approvals and local opposition to data centres after the midterm elections. It cited China's advantages in electricity, equipment manufacturing and infrastructure planning. Some estimates in a related commentary put US construction costs at $8 million to $12 million per megawatt, against $5.5 million to $6.5 million in China. The editorial acknowledged practical limits involving national security, data protection, latency and regulation.

The Global Times commentary described the idea of "American computing, Chinese data centre" as an online joke that is little more than a joke because of Washington's securitisation of technology. It blamed continued US export controls and investment restrictions for making cooperation harder. The editorial said the two countries should move away from zero-sum competition and expand practical cooperation while jointly advancing AI governance. It also urged the United States to recognise China's strengths rather than pursue technological decoupling. Commentary on the editorial said it should not be mistaken for an official policy proposal.

Background from the articles shows that Nvidia's restricted chips have been used in China despite US curbs, and that several projects and buyers, including state-owned and university entities, rely on them. The Reuters review noted that Nvidia has said export controls effectively shut it out of this market. The Global Times editorial framed the issue around US grid and construction bottlenecks, while the Reuters review focused on the exposure of Chinese projects to trade restrictions. The articles also reference earlier reporting on Chinese purchases of restricted Nvidia chips and on the chief executive's departure.

The articles leave open whether the Gansu processors were delivered and how the Xianyou, Shaanxi and Jilin projects will be financed or completed. They do not establish how tighter US curbs will affect the projects or whether Chinese companies will switch to domestic alternatives. It is unclear whether US companies will take up the offshore data-centre idea, and the Global Times editorial was not an official policy proposal. The articles also leave open how the APEC leaders' meeting may shape these positions, and whether any cooperation on AI governance will follow.

stories.Headline: Global powers head to Asia with trade, AI, security in focus
stories.Summary:
Global leaders will travel to Asia for high stakes meetings starting Sunday in Manila. These events focus on artificial intelligence, trade, and potentially nuclear disarmament during November 2026. Three summits will occur over five days across different Asian cities. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations opens its final leaders summit first. French President Emmanuel Macron will also attend a Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh.

The annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference takes place in Shenzhen, China. US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will attend both APEC and ASEAN. Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected at APEC, while India's Narendra Modi attends ASEAN. A proposed meeting includes Xi Jinping, Trump, and Putin to discuss denuclearisation and Iran. The Philippines chairs ASEAN, seeking a South China Sea Code of Conduct with China.

Siew Mun Tang says the region will not see Trump as a lame duck. Ryan Hass believes the symbolism of the Xi, Trump, and Putin meeting is its substance. Wang Wen says there is a high probability that these talks end without a breakthrough. Stephen Wu suggests a hotline for AI incidents is diplomacy's cheapest possible outcome. Harry Murphy Cruise warns that reversing US trade tariffs would require legislation.

A Southeast Asian diplomat believes no agreement on the South China Sea will be reached. Influencers like Cole Bennett and Kallmekris had their faces stolen by an AI deepfake campaign. Aengus Bridgman says words are being put in people's mouths and shown to millions. TikTok spokesperson Danielle Morgan says the company banned accounts for breaking rules on deceptive behaviours. US officials accused Nvidia boss Jensen Huang of sleeping with a woman working for Beijing.

Xi and Trump agreed in September to set up a communication channel for AI incidents. A US trade war pause was extended through January 10 during Xi's White House visit. McGill University researchers found 3,000 deepfake videos targeting Alberta, British Columbia, Quebec, and US-Canada trade. This network of 293 accounts likely stems from East or Southeast Asia, including China. Some deepfakes falsely claimed Mark Carney cancelled 8 billion dollars in US defence contracts.

APEC talks could build on the previous communication channel agreement between Washington and Beijing. The Philippines' year as ASEAN chair may end without a signed South China Sea Code. Future US trade policy changes remain unlikely for the rest of APEC and ASEAN nations. The source of the AI deepfake campaign remains unidentified by the McGill University researchers. stories.Headline: Chatbot privacy lawsuits: AI wiretapping claims and the legal fight over customer conversations
stories.Summary:
A visitor who opens a retailer’s chat box to ask where an order has gone has the message routed through a software provider’s servers, which generate a transcript, identify the customer and possibly analyze the exchange to improve the product. The visitor may assume the conversation is only between the customer and the retailer, while a plaintiff’s lawyer may see an electronic communication acquired by an undisclosed third party. That difference in perspective has produced years of litigation over website chat, and AI assistants, automated call centers, meeting transcription tools and model-training practices have made the underlying question more complicated. California courts have considered cases involving American Eagle Outfitters, Sephora, Ford and Beyond Yoga, and a federal court ruled on Google’s AI-powered customer-contact system in October 2026. Another federal court allowed an Electronic Communications Privacy Act claim against the AI meeting assistant Otter.ai to move past dismissal in August 2026, and the results differ materially.

Some complaints failed because plaintiffs could not show interception in transit, an independent third-party eavesdropper or legally insufficient consent, while others survived because the allegations described more than a vendor acting as a digital recorder. A chatbot may combine a website widget, customer relationship management system, transcript database, live-agent dashboard, language model, analytics platform and multiple subprocessors, and the legal answer depends on what each component actually does rather than the marketing description. California Penal Code Section 631, part of the California Invasion of Privacy Act, prohibits specified wiretapping and unauthorized attempts to read or learn the contents of communications in transit without the required consent, and it also reaches people who aid or assist conduct prohibited by its operative provisions. Section 632 addresses intentional recording or eavesdropping on a confidential communication without all-party consent, and Section 632.7 applies to recording specified communications involving cellular and cordless telephones. The federal Wiretap Act, 18 U.S.C. Section 2511, prohibits certain intentional interceptions of wire, oral or electronic communications, and a federal civil remedy is available under 18 U.S.C. Section 2520.

Under California Penal Code Section 637.2 as amended in 2026, qualifying civil CIPA claims may seek the greater of $5,000 per violation or three times actual damages, with the relevant exceptions and restrictions. The statute does not mean every message, page visit or transmitted packet automatically produces a separate award, and whether a violation occurred, how it should be counted, standing, class treatment, other defenses and the applicable cause of action are all disputed issues. A plaintiff may nevertheless invoke the statutory figure to frame settlement negotiations, and for a large retailer with substantial chat volume, multiplying a proposed per-violation amount by hypothetical interactions produces an intimidating headline number. That calculation is not an adjudicated exposure estimate and often leaves unanswered whether every class member communicated without consent, which vendor received which data, and whether the same transmission supports separate counts. Companies also incur costs without any judgment: investigating network activity, preserving logs, reviewing contracts, retaining expert witnesses, responding to discovery, and defending a putative class action or individual arbitration.

In Licea v. Cinmar, LLC, plaintiffs challenged the chat function on Frontgate’s website, and on Feb. 13, 2023, a federal district court in California dismissed the Section 631 claim because the allegations did not overcome the party-exemption theory or adequately establish interception in transit. It also dismissed the Section 632.7 claim with prejudice based on the statutory telephone-communication requirement, and counsel’s contemporaneous account of the ruling identifies the distinct grounds. The point was not that outsourced chat platforms enjoy blanket immunity, but that a plaintiff must plead more than the existence of a third-party software vendor. In Martin v.

Sephora USA, Inc., the plaintiff alleged that the retailer used chat software that created transcripts and allowed HubSpot and/or Salesforce to receive the content, and the complaint asserted CIPA claims under Sections 631 and 632.7. A March 2023 findings and recommendations examined the party-exemption and interception issues, and an April 24, 2023 order granted dismissal with leave to amend. A 2023 review of the early live-chat docket by law firm Hogan Lovells Cadwalader described more than 70 putative class actions involving website chat features filed over roughly an 18-month period, a figure that refers to that early period and specific litigation category and should not be treated as a 2026 national chatbot case count. A 2026 Legal 500 analysis cited a Baker Botts review of 284 deployer-facing AI litigation matters and reported that chatbot wiretap matters increased from two in 2021 to 30 in 2025.

That dataset concerns identified AI-deployer litigation, not every chat-widget complaint, private demand letter or arbitration filing, and it is evidence of an expanding theory rather than proof that every chatbot presents a statutory violation. Claims started with an apparently familiar form of consumer interaction, and plaintiffs later focused on session replay, embedded analytics, online forms and pixels. Generative AI has brought the question back to conversations themselves, since a chatbot that merely relays a question raises one set of issues while a provider that independently retains the text, evaluates sentiment, builds user profiles or trains models with it raises another. Pennsylvania’s Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act, Florida’s Security of Communications Act and other state statutes create additional questions about consent, location and the characteristics of covered communications, and some states require all-party consent for particular kinds of recordings.

AI voice systems also create potential biometric issues when they generate or retain voiceprints capable of identifying individuals, and Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act has specific notice, consent and retention provisions. Privacy-notice accuracy, unfair or deceptive practices, children’s data and sector-specific confidentiality obligations can add exposure even when a wiretap theory fails, and a HIPAA-covered entity must separately examine whether its vendor relationship and handling of protected health information meet applicable requirements. Cyber insurers have to distinguish a credible privacy event from a complaint built mainly around a website scan and assumptions about the vendor’s capabilities. The guide from Captain Compliance examines the cases, the law, the firms pursuing digital wiretap claims, the defenses that have worked, and the technical evidence that businesses and insurers should obtain before assessing exposure.

stories.Headline: Gov't vows zero tolerance against cheating with AI glasses
stories.Summary:
The South Korean government has promised zero tolerance for cheating with artificial intelligence glasses in next week's nationwide college entrance exam. The pledge, announced on Friday, followed suspicions raised by an unusually high score in this year's certified tax accountant exam. The Prime Minister's Secretariat and the Office for Government Policy Coordination made the statements, with the Yonhap and KBS reports both covering the announcement. The College Scholastic Ability Test, known as the Suneung, is set for Thursday, November 19, according to the reports' timing.

The suspicions began when the highest scorer in the tax accountant exam's first round earned 397.5 points out of a possible 400. That person missed only one of the 160 questions, a result many test-takers consider unrealistic. Specialized personnel will be deployed to test sites to detect AI glasses during the Suneung. The government said it would dispatch additional staff and coordinate a quick response between the education ministry and regional education offices. Anyone caught faces punishment for interference with business and obstruction of official duties by fraudulent means, and loses eligibility to retake the exam for three years.

The Office for Government Policy Coordination said cheating with AI glasses is a serious issue that infringes on fair opportunities for diligent students. The office said it takes public concerns on the matter very seriously. The Prime Minister's Secretariat said it takes growing public concern about recent fraudulent acts involving AI glasses during state-run exams very seriously. The government said it will make thorough preparations for the Suneung and closely monitor exam operations until the test concludes. Students who have worked hard for the exam are the people the government says these measures are meant to protect.

Public concern has grown after recent fraudulent acts involving AI glasses during various state-run exams. The suspicion over the tax accountant result has raised worries that similar AI-assisted cheating could occur in the Suneung. Students taking the Suneung on Thursday are directly affected by the heightened monitoring at test sites. Test-takers in the tax accountant exam have also voiced doubts about the top score. The government said last month that it would take steps to catch cheaters using AI-equipped smart glasses, which indicates the problem had already been under discussion before the latest announcement.

The government said it will also seek to clear up suspicions raised in the tax accountant exam, including by requesting an investigation. If cheating is confirmed, the government said it will enforce corresponding accountability under relevant laws and regulations. The Prime Minister's Secretariat said it plans to thoroughly review how state-run exams are managed and to roll out measures against cheating with smart devices. The articles do not say when the tax accountant investigation will conclude or who will carry it out. They also do not say how many cheaters, if any, will be detected in the Suneung or how the planned review will be structured.

stories.Headline: Exclusive: US-sanctioned Jinan Supercomputing Center still gets Nvidia AI products
stories.Summary:
Radio Free Asia revealed that sanctioned Chinese entities obtained Nvidia AI chips despite strict United States export restrictions. This discovery happened as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation on a Thursday in November 2026. Huang resigned during a scandal involving an alleged affair that may have been a Chinese spy plot. The United States government is investigating his ties to Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. She is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud data center company suspected of spying.

The Shandong Computing Center, also called the National Supercomputing Center Jinan, listed restricted products in a June 2026 bid. On June 17, 2026, the China Government Procurement Network announced a winning bid for an AI workstation project. Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd. won the bid with a price of RMB 148,500 or US$22,000. The procurement included RTX 5090 graphics cards and DGX Spark systems under the brand name Yixin. The RTX 5090 uses Blackwell architecture, while the DGX Spark uses the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip.

The United States Department of Commerce is responsible for the entity list and the Export Administration Regulations. Officials stated that the Jinan center supported Chinese military units and weapons of mass destruction programs. Chris Tseng said that export controls travel with the item, requiring a license for controlled entities. He noted that current controls rely heavily on corporate self-compliance by Nvidia and various third-country distributors. Sylvia Chen explained that third-party enterprises may bear legal liability for illegally transferring controlled products within China.

The investigation affects Nvidia and the United States government, which must track the flow of advanced AI chips. Other affected parties include the Bureau of Industry and Security, which manages end-user verification for restricted items. A commentator suggested that Qiyuan Jiasu might be a shell company for the sanctioned firm Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology. This suspicion arises because both companies share identical website text, client lists, and offices in Tianjin and Beijing. These similarities suggest one company may be operating under two different banners to bypass United States sanctions.

The Shandong Computing Center was established in 1976 and is affiliated with the Qilu University of Technology. The National Supercomputing Center Jinan was established in 2011 and shares the same institutional framework as Shandong. The United States placed the center on the entity list in April 2021 for national security reasons. Broad export restrictions on advanced computing chips to China began later, starting in the year 2022. Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology was an Nvidia Elite Partner until it was sanctioned on April 11, 2024.

The United States government will continue investigating Alice Huang for collecting intelligence for Beijing and assisting Chinese clients. Nvidia may need to investigate the ultimate flow of products if Qiyuan Jiasu inherited Sitonholy's original business operations. The Bureau of Industry and Security faces staffing constraints, with only fifteen export control officers stationed worldwide. Only one such officer is currently stationed in Beijing to handle end-use and end-user verification tasks. The articles leave open whether the RTX 5090s purchased were original versions or the China special edition.

stories.Headline: Naver clinches $1.5 bil. AI computing deal with US firm
stories.Summary:
Naver, the South Korean internet company, has signed a 2 trillion-won ($1.5 billion) computing services supply contract with a U.S. artificial intelligence inference company, its first customer for its AI infrastructure business. The deal was announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, during the company's third-quarter earnings call, and it comes ahead of a commercial launch planned for the first half of next year. The contract covers computing services using next-generation graphics processing units, with the initial supply scheduled to begin in 2027. Naver's chief executive, Choi Soo-yeon, described the agreement as confirming real market demand and the early commercial viability of the AI factory business. Naver also said it had reported record quarterly revenue alongside weaker operating profit.

The contract covers about 20 megawatts of capacity over four to five years, according to reporting on the deal. Naver plans to expand its AI factory capacity from 55 megawatts next year to 200 megawatts by 2028. The company said its contracted data center capacity already exceeds that 200-megawatt target for 2028. Naver is in talks with more than 10 prospective customers outside Asia, including major AI model developers, for the remaining capacity. Separately, the company plans to set up a dedicated logistics subsidiary and expand its leased fulfillment centers, with investment expected to approach 1 trillion won through 2030.

Choi said the AI factory is being developed in partnership with the Canadian asset manager Brookfield and the U.S. chipmaker Nvidia. Choi said Naver was pursuing long-term contracts with major customers while widening its customer base to include global AI companies with strong growth potential. She said this would reduce reliance on individual clients and help the company seek stable, higher-margin business. Choi also said the company would seek appropriate financing and revenue structures to limit the impact of logistics spending on cash flow and earnings. Naver's chief financial officer, Kim Hee-cheol, spoke about the negotiations with prospective customers.

The company reported third-quarter sales of 3.47 trillion won, up 10.7 percent from a year earlier, marking its sixth consecutive quarterly revenue record. Operating profit fell 20.9 percent to 451.3 billion won, giving an operating margin of 13 percent, as AI-related investment and content spending weighed on earnings. Platform revenue rose 7.3 percent to 1.95 trillion won, while financial platform revenue increased 14.1 percent to 487.7 billion won. Global business revenue climbed 15.9 percent to 1.04 trillion won, driven by consumer-to-consumer businesses including Wallapop and Poshmark. Naver also plans to launch a personal AI agent app by the end of this year that can carry out tasks such as shopping and making reservations.

Naver is also planning robotic delivery services at residential complexes in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in the first half of 2027, combining its digital-twin mapping technology with Naver Labs' Nuri robot. Choi said traffic from the AI Tab to shopping and local services has nearly doubled since its launch, with transaction value also growing. The expansion of AI infrastructure and logistics is aimed at reducing reliance on search and e-commerce as revenue sources. Naver's global business and Saudi digital-twin projects also contributed to the growth in its global ventures revenue. The company's stated plans cover the coming years, but the articles do not say how the logistics investment will be financed.

Naver has not named the U.S. customer, and the articles do not say which specific AI models will run on the capacity. The articles also do not say how much revenue the AI factory will generate once commercial services begin in the first half of next year. Whether Naver will sign contracts with the more than 10 companies it is negotiating with remains unknown from the reporting. The articles also leave open how quickly the logistics subsidiary will be established and how the personal AI agent app will perform once launched.

stories.Headline: Labels required for AI-made dramas
stories.Summary:
China's top broadcast regulator introduced landmark rules for the digital entertainment market to bring AI generated short dramas under unified national oversight. The National Radio and Television Administration enacted these new policy measures on September 1 to manage the booming micro short drama sector. This regulatory crackdown followed an explosive surge in production volume and widespread viewer backlash regarding a market plagued by disorder. These rules now subject AI titles to mandatory pre release filings and strict tiered administrative reviews to improve overall output quality. The move formalizes an ecosystem that previously existed in a regulatory gray zone between casual short videos and full scale series.

The rules require episode by episode AI labels and a three tiered system based on budgets and themes for all productions. High budget works of 800,000 yuan or more, or those covering politics, national security, military, or religion, need NRTA licenses. Mid tier productions between 300,000 and 800,000 yuan are subject to review and registration by provincial level broadcast authorities in China. Low cost productions under 300,000 yuan can be reviewed internally by the hosting platform and assigned a program registration number. This differs from live action dramas, which typically require budgets of 2 million to 3 million yuan to trigger top level licensing.

He Biao, deputy director of the National Radio and Television Administration, stated in early November that standardized governance is essential for quality. He argued that regulating AI short dramas means stabilizing volume and improving quality while holding the copyright and ethical bottom lines. Lin Qiwen, vice president of DataEye, said the measures fill a gap in industry rules and give AI dramas identity. Lin noted that clear labeling protects the right of viewers to know and reduces risks of being misled by false content. He added that these rules provide a foundation for the industry to move toward a more quality driven development model.

Viewers complained of repetitive tropes like domineering executive romances, time travel themes, instant revenge stories, clickbait, copyright theft, and digital clones. Model Qi Hai found the AI serial Taohuazan on the Hongguo app used her likeness without consent, gaining 40 million views. Actor Luo Yunxi had his legal team object to a near identical digital replica of his likeness in another AI production. DataEye reported the user base for AI assisted series grew from 120 million in 2025 to 600 million in 2026. On Douyin, 221,900 AI series were published in early 2026, but only 1,055 exceeded 100 million views per series.

Micro short dramas are ultra concise serials with episodes typically lasting one to two minutes that dominate mobile screens across China. The China Network Audiovisual Association found that platforms released over 367,000 micro short drama series in the first half of 2026. AI generated series accounted for more than 74 percent of that volume, with over 1,500 new AI series published daily. Professor Zhang Lanshan of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications said AI makes narratives more industrialized and standardized for creators. She believes humans must remain responsible for guarding the soul of narrative, including creation values, story themes, and character emotions.

The NRTA launched a two month enforcement campaign on November 6 targeting low brow themes, copyright violations, and various technical loopholes. Regulators are currently working to eliminate the practice of smaller studios shrinking disclaimers into screen corners to maintain viewer immersion. Officials are still refining operational definitions, such as the exact percentage of AI assets that triggers the mandatory labeling requirement. They are also determining how self review standards should be unified across the different competing streaming platforms operating within the market. The articles leave open how these unified standards will be finalized and how the enforcement campaign will specifically penalize violators.

stories.Headline: 5 AI trends CIOs should watch in 2027
stories.Summary:
AI spending is set to get more selective in 2027, according to five trends interviews with technology leaders point to. CIOs plan to concentrate investment on a handful of business processes while competitors push them to rethink customer experience. Other priorities include matching AI models to specific tasks, bringing finance and business leaders into spending decisions, and building networks of AI champions. Those five priorities were drawn from interviews with technology leaders, and the article presents them as the shape of the next year's agenda.

Several CIOs are concentrating AI investment on a few business processes after experimenting across individual tasks. Travelers' Bond & Specialty unit redesigned how it receives submissions, cutting registration time from two hours to two minutes. Vrinda Menon of JPMorganChase urged focus on two or three big bets, noting there are thousands of pilots. Infotech's 2027 Global IT Leadership Survey found only 24% of respondents had the architecture in place to monitor agentic workflows. Deloitte's "Finance Trends 2027" report found 42% of finance leaders said agentic AI ambitions exceeded current capabilities.

Those leaders say the gains come from redesigning work rather than automating old methods, as JPMorganChase CIO Gill Haus put it. stories.Headline: AI coding: Humans remain accountable for generated code
stories.Summary:
Software engineer Hugo Venturini stated that humans should be accountable when artificial intelligence writes code, calling AI a powerful tool whose human operator is ultimately responsible for failures. He made the remarks in an article published by TechGig on November 13, 2026. The same day, 36Kr reported that coding agents collectively failed to write valid test cases. A team led by Professor Liu Jiaheng of Nanjing University proposed a new benchmark called TestPrism. The study found that the pass rate of AI-generated code was overestimated by 100%.

TestPrism contains 300 test tasks and 3000 candidate implementations drawn from 17 sources. Each task carries a verified panel of 1 reference implementation, 4 correct alternative implementations and 5 wrong implementations, hidden from the agent during test generation. The core indicator, the Joint Success Function, requires a test to fail on the original code, accept all correct implementations and reject all wrong implementations. Among 14 Coding Agent configurations, the strongest reached a JSF of only 28.00%, while its success rate under single reference evaluation was 59.67%. The 300 test-set tasks cover six languages including Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C/C++ and Go, come from 67 code repositories and projects, and split into Bug Fix (167), Programs and Algorithms (53), Performance Optimization (28), Feature Expansion (20), Project and Workflow (19) and Refactoring and Migration (13).

Venturini said pull request sizes are increasing, a trend predating AI, and suggested automating boilerplate code verification. He said merging software engineer and tester roles, similar to Microsoft's 2014 approach, could enhance quality by making engineers accountable for the final product. He noted a current absence of quality improvement with AI, possibly because people attribute issues to the AI rather than taking responsibility for the tooling's output. He stressed training engineers to ask effective questions of AI, since asking the right questions is a hallmark of senior-level expertise. He highlighted cultivating transparency and psychological safety so people can take risks without fear of blame, citing weekly transparent Q&A sessions, and said mistakes are acceptable but repeating them is not.

The 36Kr article said mainstream benchmarks use Single Reference Evaluation, counting a test successful if it fails on the original code and passes on a single Gold Solution. The study annotated 286 failure traces, summarized 3 categories and 7 test generation error mechanisms, and proposed the TestHelix framework. TestHelix raised JSF by 11.67 to 12.00 percentage points under the same reasoning budget through heterogeneous synthesis, peer cross-validation and recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks include TestGenEval, CLOVER and MultiFileTest at function, file or multi-file level, and SWT Bench and TDD Bench Verified on real repositories. Works such as OmniCode and SWE Mutation introduced implementation variants but mainly examine rejection of wrong variants.

TestPrism holds 2000 tasks in total, of which 1700 form the training set for TestHelix strategy optimization and 300 form the test set, with no overlap. Tasks were collected from 17 public benchmarks including the SWE-bench series, Terminal-Bench series, SWE PolyBench, SWE rebench, EvoEval, USACO and AlgoTune. Two experts with development experience independently evaluated requirements and verifiers, excluding doubtful tasks (Cohen's κ = 0.68). Candidate implementations came from different Coding Agents and models actually solving the tasks, with labels fixed after running the original verifier in a clean environment. The team required the correct group to meet an average AST distance standard and the wrong group diverse failed check sets or an AST Jaccard distance check.

Venturini also pointed out that managers operate within two teams, their direct reports and a team of managers, requiring them to consider broader organisational growth beyond their immediate team. The 36Kr article described Reference Acceptance Rate, Valid Acceptance Rate, Invalid Rejection Rate, H as the harmonic mean of VAR and IRR, and Change Coverage and Entry Coverage following SWT Bench and TestExplora definitions. It said JSF never exceeds RAR, and the gap between the two is the proportion of tests that pass the reference answer but cannot withstand more implementations. It asked whether tests generated by current Coding Agents can stably distinguish correct and wrong implementations, evaluating 14 configurations from six model families. The main table reports the highest-JSF configuration per family, prioritizing each model's native Coding Agent.

stories.Headline: AI Job Interviews Lead to Better Outcomes - The University of Chicago Booth School of Business
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon’s Brian Jabarian, a former principal researcher at Chicago Booth, and his coauthor partnered with a recruiting firm hiring for customer service positions, and 70,000 candidates were randomly assigned to interview with an AI agent or a human recruiter. Candidates knew when they were speaking with AI, and final hiring decisions were always made by human recruiters reviewing the interview transcripts and audio. The researchers found that candidates who got a job interview with an AI were more likely to receive a job offer, more likely to start the job, and more likely to stay in the position after 30 days and up to four months. The retention rate was much better for the AI-interviewed group, and this retention did not come at the cost of productivity loss. Comparing employees interviewed by an AI and employees interviewed by a human, the researchers saw no difference in productivity metrics and no difference in separation after 30 days.

Both human and AI recruiters were required to cover 14 interview topics, but humans naturally vary in how consistently they conduct interviews, and fatigue, time pressure, and conversational drift can all change how questions are asked. AI is more consistent than human recruiters at covering more topics, with less variation in follow-ups and in the flow of the interview, and it more consistently applies a higher language across interviews. In response to this consistency, candidates are more likely to reveal their true type in a job interview conducted by an AI than in one conducted by a human. Candidates who got a job interview with an AI are more likely to display interactivity as a signal during a job interview and less likely to display other cues. Forty percent of people left voluntarily in both cases, and the researchers saw no deterioration in productivity downstream.

Jabarian said the overall takeaway of the research is not that you should replace all the time humans by AI, calling it more subtle and more complicated. He said AI adoption shouldn’t be seen as a task-by-task decision but more about organizational design as a whole, and about thinking how to combine AI agents working together with human agents in the workplace. He said AI is not so magic, and that it is an interesting tool to more consistently perform different interviewing tasks, such as covering a certain set of topics, having a certain order, and having a certain language. He said that when you are a human interviewer, sometimes you start the job interview in the morning and perform really well at your task, but for reasons of fatigue you might be less consistent. He said that if we were in a world where AI was artificially inflating your value during a job interview, you would see deterioration in terms of productivity downstream, but we don’t see this here.

Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company, said human eyes may not be the first to look at a job application these days. He said most of the companies he deals with run applications through that, and then they have also a human or HR professional. He said the practice picked up in the last two years, with technology scanning resumes for buzzwords pulled from the posted job description. He cautioned against copying a posting outright, saying you want to tailor it to the job description when you are applying, but you don’t want it to read word for word, which indicates a red flag to an employer. He recommends people use AI to help organize and format a resume, and not use it to embellish skills they do not have, and he said Microsoft and Claude work well.

Pasola said he “absolutely” believes some qualified candidates are slipping through the cracks or not getting hired because they are not using AI tools. He said this is because they have skills that they can put to the forefront in front of the employer that they are not showing. As Texas prepares for its first new governor in 12 years, Gina Hinojosa is searching for her team using a digital portal rather than a stack of paper resumes. That mirrors a hiring shift playing out across the job market, according to Pasola. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these accounts.

The articles leave open what happens next, and they do not give further background beyond the experiment and the staffing company’s observations. The Chicago Booth article was published November 13, 2026, and the KSAT article was published November 11, 2026. The KSAT article was reported by Olivia Dague, who joined KSAT 12 in July 2026 after spending three years reporting in Knoxville, Tennessee, at WBIR. Dague is from Arlington, Texas, and is a graduate of the University of Oklahoma. The articles do not state any additional plans or follow-up studies.

The connectivity lets organizations bring enterprise information governed through Arctera into supported Copilot workflows. The capability gives employees access to more of their company's information for AI-assisted work while keeping established governance and compliance controls in place. The new connectivity is part of Arctera AI Converge, which uses MCP to link AI models with enterprise information that Arctera governs. The company said the connectivity is available now.

Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications with external data sources and tools. Through a custom federated connector, Microsoft 365 Copilot can reach Arctera's MCP server and interact with enterprise information governed through the platform. Organizations keep control over who can access the information, how it can be used, and how long it must be kept. The connectivity supports Arctera's Modern Compliance Intelligence strategy and builds on the Arctera Unified Platform's communications governance, compliance, and eDiscovery capabilities. Arctera's platform can capture data from more than 130 content sources and includes more than 280 AI policies.

Irfan Shuttari, product manager at Arctera, said that connecting enterprise information to Copilot requires preserving the governance controls built into that content. He said that pairing MCP connectivity with years of secure collaboration data managed within Arctera can accelerate regulatory inquiries and legal investigations while maintaining full compliance. Soniya Bopache, SVP and GM at Arctera, said that much of an organization's knowledge sits outside the workflows where employees could use it. She said the Copilot connectivity brings that information into work while preserving the governance controls businesses have established. Bopache added that leaders can get more value from information they already manage and from their AI investments.

The articles present the Arctera announcement as aimed at organizations that hold valuable information spread across systems and want their workforce to get more useful output from AI tools. Arctera is described as helping the biggest companies in the world monitor and control how their information is accessed, used and shared. Arctera was created in 2024 from Veritas Technologies. A separate article from ITWeb, dated November 12, 2026 and written by Joanne Carew for CloudZA in Johannesburg, covers AI governance for businesses. It recalls that in April South Africa's Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy was officially withdrawn by Communications and Digital Technologies Minister Solly Malatsi because it contained fake, AI-generated academic references.

Jonathan Oaker, founder and CEO of CloudZA, advises that good AI governance starts with understanding the data a business holds and sorting it into categories. He recommends assessing AI tools by where each model gets its data, how it was trained and what access it has to business information. Oaker suggests weighing return on investment for the next six months or year and embracing Open Telemetry from day one. He says a business that cannot fail and handles identifiable data should consult a service provider or partner, and he warns that retrofitting governance later is complex and costly. Failing to consider governance can expose businesses to data breaches, legal liability and reputational damage.

stories.Headline: The promise and peril of AI in government
stories.Summary:
Taoyuan, Taiwan's industrial hub home to 200 semiconductor facilities, is using AI to manage its fast growth under Mayor San-Cheng Chang. The city runs an AI-powered lung cancer screening program for residents over 40 with risk factors such as occupational exposure or family history. The program began in March 2023 and screened over 400,000 residents within two years. Chang previously served as Taiwan's first nonpartisan premier and held leadership roles at Google and Acer. The Post and Courier separately argues that AI's potential benefits, such as a phone app describing scenes for blind users, deserve attention alongside its risks.

Taoyuan, which is home to Taiwan's international airport and 2.2 million residents, must handle heavy truck traffic, air pollution, population growth and constant construction. The screening program detected 233 lung cancer cases, with 90% at an early stage, and saved NT$500 million, about $17 million, through AI-aided diagnostics. The software predicts cancer risk from a single low-dose CT scan without requiring additional clinical data. The city also built a system that analyzes exhaust pipe images against a database of legal configurations, and complaints about illegal exhausts fell 20% over last year. AI cameras monitor construction sites and factory chimneys, and traffic lights now shave about 10 seconds off each wait.

Mayor Chang is responsible for these projects and has been selective about which AI tools his administration adopts. He has said he will not sanction generative AI chatbots that could hallucinate. He distinguishes between machine learning that detects existing conditions and machine learning that predicts future outcomes, favoring the former. The Taoyuan administration uses AI to locate potholes and to identify wheelchair users at train station elevators so assistance can be ready. The article presents these uses as ones where AI sees what is already present without automating human decisions.

The article's author, Beth Simone Noveck, warns that predictive AI is being relied on for decisions such as sentencing, parole, credit scoring and hiring. Princeton researcher Arvind Narayanan is quoted as warning that predicting job performance or recidivism involves countless unpredictable variables. Fraud-detection systems may misclassify a struggling single parent with irregular gig income as a fraud risk. The Post and Courier editorial, meanwhile, says the public conversation about AI has been largely negative and that Democrats are taking control of Congress partly by pointing to AI's dangers. Students at the College of Charleston, including Saif Chaundry, have built an app that narrates surroundings for visually impaired users.

Narayanan identifies five ways predictive systems break down, including models that miss crucial context, systems that can be gamed, and overreliance on automated outputs. A sepsis prediction system sold by Epic was trained on national data and proved ineffective for local patient populations. The author distinguishes population-level forecasting, such as for forest fires, from judgments about individuals, which she says should be advisory and contestable rather than automated. Labor disputes in Taiwan's semiconductor industry and worries about cost and context for non-English languages also appear in the coverage. The Post and Courier argues that the federal government has declined to restrict AI development or require public disclosure of its use.

The articles leave open how Taoyuan's screening and traffic programs will be evaluated over the long term and whether other governments will adopt similar limits on predictive tools. They do not say whether the federal government will impose the restrictions the Post and Courier calls for once Democrats take control of Congress. The College of Charleston app's release and wider adoption are not described, and the outcomes of the Taiwanese labor disputes are not reported. The articles also do not say whether individual-level predictive systems will be restricted or made contestable in practice.

stories.Headline: Same Prompt, More Complete Prints: Meshy.ai Publishes Printability Benchmark for AI-Generated 3D Models
stories.Summary:
Meshy.ai published the results of a printability benchmark for AI-generated 3D models on November 13, 2026, conducted with the Advanced Digital Design and Fabrication facility at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. In an FDM print test, Meshy.ai's Make Printable feature reduced prints with major missing features or holes from 44% (11 of 25) to 8% (2 of 25). The study, which Meshy.ai commissioned and funded, used six Bambu Lab A1 printers and printed 125 parts from 25 hard-to-print prompts across five workflows. Facility staff prepared and sliced the files, printed the parts, removed supports and graded every part objectively. Facility participation does not constitute endorsement of Meshy.ai products or an audit of its software.

Make Printable repairs mesh defects and reinforces thin features for the selected size and process, and it works on both Meshy.ai-generated models and uploaded models. Three experienced 3D printing users scored each part against a five-criterion rubric, while 17 volunteers ranked the anonymous prints. Across the 100 prompts in a larger geometry assessment, models with complete, connected surfaces rose from 33.4% for raw Meshy 7 output to 98.8% after Make Printable. In the physical test, 23 of 25 Meshy 7 with Make Printable prints (92%) had no major missing features or holes, compared with 56% to 84% for three other AI 3D generators. The full whitepaper is available on the Meshy.ai blog, and Make Printable is available now as part of Print Check in Meshy.ai.

Dave Follette, Director of ADDFab at UMass Amherst, said that the study aimed to evaluate AI platforms by actually 3D printing each part on a consumer FDM printer. Jessie Bergau, 3D Printing Product and Partnerships Manager at Meshy.ai, said that users want to bring ideas to life rather than spend hours repairing models before printing. Two Meshy 7 with Make Printable prints, a six-legged insect and a long-finned tropical fish, still had major missing features or holes. The study's 25 prompts were deliberately chosen to challenge the models, so the findings should not be read as representative of all prompts. The physical test covered only FDM printing, and the company notes that future testing could extend to SLA, SLS and Full-Color printing.

On November 12, 2026, Rapidflare launched Rapidbench, a research benchmark that measures how accurately AI agents answer technical queries about electronics products. Rapidflare CEO Navanee Sundaramoorthy said general-purpose benchmarks do not show how well an agent handles queries across complex electronics catalogs. The first version tests AI agents on 116 technical product queries involving NVIDIA's Jetson and IGX platforms and partner products. The test catalog covers 2,130 products from 212 manufacturers across 54 categories. Rapidflare compared agents without tools, with web search, and with access to its structured catalog through the Model Context Protocol.

Across three runs, the tested models achieved pass rates of about 18% without tools, 49% to 60% with web search, and 88% to 94% with Rapidflare's structured catalog via MCP. Rapidflare generated the query set from its product catalog, guided by real search trends, and validated each query against the catalog. Human reviewers agreed with the automated judge's pass/fail decisions on 98% of the reviewed subset. Rapidflare CTO Vasanth Asokan said the team verified product data against manufacturer sources and reconciled conflicting specifications.

The company is based in San Jose, California, and its platform works with companies including AMD, Qorvo, Amphenol and Taoglas. Rapidflare has published the methodology, limitations and evaluation trajectories on its website so readers can examine how the results were produced. The first version is limited to NVIDIA's Jetson and IGX ecosystem and 116 queries. The articles do not say when a later version of Rapidbench will be released or whether the Meshy.ai study will be extended beyond FDM printing.

stories.Headline: Applied Materials Q3 CY2026 deep dive: AI demand and advanced packaging drive outlook
stories.Summary:
Applied Materials reported results for its calendar third quarter of 2026, which is its fiscal fourth quarter, on November 12, 2026. Sales rose 53.1% from a year earlier to $10.41 billion, above the $10.33 billion analysts expected. Non-GAAP profit was $4.16 per share, 2.6% above the $4.05 consensus. Adjusted operating income was $3.68 billion, a 35.3% margin, and operating margin was 35.1%, up from 25.2% a year earlier. Inventory days outstanding fell to 122 from 132 in the prior quarter, and market capitalization stood at $302.3 billion.

For the next quarter, the company guided revenue to $11.1 billion at the midpoint, above the $10.87 billion analysts estimated, and adjusted earnings per share to $4.35 at the midpoint, above the $4.23 consensus. Advanced packaging revenue grew about 90% for the year, and the eBeam and optical process control businesses grew more than 50%. The connected installed base passed 37,000 chambers, with service and spares revenue up 26% year over year. Customer roadmaps now extend through 2030, and more than 10 new major fab projects were recently added to its tracker.

CEO Gary Dickerson credited leadership in foundry logic, DRAM and advanced packaging, where he said customer demand was strong because of AI computing investments. Management said record revenue and profitability came from operational execution and supply chain collaboration. CFO Brice Hill said the company is investing so it can double systems output by 2028, and he described AI-driven demand as a multi-year opportunity for revenue and margins. The company also cited rolling eight-quarter customer forecasts and earlier orders.

Applied Materials plans to more than double manufacturing and lab capacity by 2030. Management said growth depends on scaling the whole semiconductor ecosystem, including clean room availability and supplier capacity, and that delays there could be headwinds. The stock traded at $383.72, roughly in line with $380.96 just before the earnings. Analysts will watch whether advanced packaging and process control momentum holds, how fast capacity expands, and progress on doubling output and growing service revenue.

stories.Headline: AI Expert, Spelman College President’s New Book Offers a New Vision for the Future of Artificial Intelligence - Carroll County Mirror-Democrat
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Spelman College in Atlanta hosted an event to launch Spelman President Ayanna Howard's new book about the future of artificial intelligence. The book, titled REBOOTING THE MACHINES: A New Human Vision for Artificial Intelligence, was celebrated with a fireside chat, an audience question-and-answer session, and a book signing. All proceeds from the event went toward Spelman scholarships. The press release announcing the event was issued on November 12, 2026, through GlobeNewswire, and the same text appeared in other outlets. Howard's book is presented as a new vision for AI that centers human values, ethics, and diverse perspectives.

Howard draws on her experience as an AI and robotics expert, entrepreneur, and academic leader to examine how human values shape AI's future. In the book she argues that AI, including robotics, is not built with a moral center, so people must supply that moral compass if the technology is to serve all humanity. An excerpt quotes her saying that people must take stock of AI's influence on their lives to thrive in an AI-infused world. She also says society has the power both to build AI that reflects society as it is and to build AI that fosters the society people aspire to have. The book offers a practical roadmap for deciding what to demand from tech companies, what to resist, and how to build ethical human values into machines.

Howard, who became president of Spelman in August 2026, wrote the book as the author and speaker in the launch. The press release attributes the book's message to her and quotes her directly. The release does not describe any other person as responsible for the book's arguments. Its contents are presented as her own views on AI's moral foundations and its social role. The release frames the book as her contribution to the discussion, supported by the launch event.

The release says that students in higher education worry that AI will erase the futures they worked hard to build. Howard's arrival at Spelman comes during this period of anxiety, according to the release. At the launch, engineer and policy scholar Dr. Kamau Bobb and WABE's Rose Scot joined Howard in a conversation about AI's changing effect on the workforce. They also discussed the importance of diversity among AI developers, ways to address bias in new technologies, and shared responsibility for a more equitable AI future. Spelman students and the wider public are the groups the release identifies as affected by these concerns.

Spelman College was founded in 1881 and is located in Atlanta, where it has 2,700 students. The release describes Spelman as a liberal arts college focused on educating women of African descent, and it says the college leads the country in producing Black women who complete Ph.D.s in STEM fields. U.S. News & World Report ranked Spelman No. 34 among liberal arts colleges and No. 1 among historically Black colleges and universities for the 20th year. Recent initiatives include a Department of Defense designation as a Center of Excellence for Minority Women in STEM and collaborations with MIT's Media Lab, the Broad Institute, and the Army Research Lab on AI and machine learning. The release also lists notable alumnae such as Marian Wright Edelman, Rosalind Brewer, Stacey Abrams, and Tayari Jones.

The articles do not say whether a second printing, further events, or policy steps will follow the book's launch. They also do not state the book's sales figures or how much money the scholarships will ultimately receive. Readers can learn more or buy the book at www.broadleafbooks.com, and the release directs media questions to Spelman's public relations office. The articles do not describe any response from tech companies or government bodies to Howard's proposals.

stories.Headline: [INTERVIEW] Ex-vice minister brings Shakespeare to life with AI music
stories.Summary:
Yong Ho-seong, former vice minister of culture, sports and tourism, released his debut full-length album “Fragile Beauty” on Nov. 10 under the stage name Dr. Dragon. The album sets 15 of William Shakespeare’s sonnets to AI-assisted music and vocals. It is the first installment of “DiVerse,” a project to set all 154 of Shakespeare’s sonnets to modern music. Yong gave an interview to The Korea Times at a cafe in Seoul on Thursday, published Nov. 13, 2026. The idea was sparked by a hardcover edition of Shakespeare’s complete sonnets that a British friend gifted him while he was director of the Korean Cultural Centre UK.

The album leans into late-1960s avant-garde folk and chamber folk, using nylon-string guitars, upright contrabass, cellos, violas, flutes, harmoniums and bass clarinets. It features the contralto tones of his AI vocal persona NikkiD. Yong adapted the sonnets’ themes for modern listeners, recasting a verse about passing down family lineage as a message about artists sharing their talents with the world. He said the name DiVerse reflects Shakespeare’s original verse, the newly written lyrics and the diverse genres used to reimagine the classics. In July, Yong won the AI.LOVE.JAZZ.

composition competition in Montreux, Switzerland, with “Frozen Edge,” a vocal jazz piece inspired by Sonnet 97. Yong said he uses AI as a creative assistant rather than a replacement for human artistry. He writes detailed prompts spanning a full page to specify rhythm, instrumentation and musical references, and sometimes regenerates a track 30 or 40 times before editing individual tracks himself. He compared AI to the introduction of digital sampling in popular music in the 1980s, saying it broadens the pool of people who can create music. He said students could turn personal stories and daily emotions into original songs, calling music a powerful tool for self-expression.

He said happiness is not about the high intensity of achievements but the frequency of joyful moments. Yong plans to issue a new sonnet-inspired album every month, spanning jazz, blues, hip-hop, rap-metal and K-pop. He has reached out to Shakespeare-related societies, associations and academic institutions around the world to explore educational and cultural collaborations. He is developing progressive rock operas based on Shakespeare’s tragedies “Hamlet” and “Macbeth,” and a project reinterpreting the poetry of Joseon Dynasty poet Yi Mae-chang (1573-1610).

Before retiring last year, he studied classical music and jazz, collected more than 10,000 records, debuted as a music critic in 1993 and played drums in jazz and rock bands. He composes up to six hours a day and practices drums for two hours, and he recently earned his first musician revenue by composing a theme song for T&C Foundation. In fall 2026, Concord Academy presented Shakespeare’s “Macbeth” in the Hammett Ory Theater, directed by Shelley Bolman P’27. The production used AI-inspired staging to explore the tension between power and technology, with intricate dance and fight choreography.

Bolman said greed for power and artificial intelligence both resonate strongly with the current time. William Jiang-Fogel ’27 played Macbeth, who is consumed by prophecies of his ascent and murders the king to seize the throne. The production retained Shakespeare’s original language and immersed audiences in a world where technology and human behavior are intertwined. Audiences sat on either side of a spare central stage, where a staircase and gate with camouflage paint were entwined with wires and cable extending across archways and pillars.

Live feeds displayed the opposite side of the audience, while screens featured “Heck 8.0,” an AI system that generated prophetic outputs. The production opened in darkness with a flash of lightning illuminating an ensemble in Guy Fawkes masks, and the Weird Sisters were reimagined as analogues for predictive AI. Lady Macbeth, played by Aslan Liu ’27, and Fleance, played by Ren Lipman ’29, were depicted as frequently attached to their phones. Bolman said the play offered an excellent opportunity to bring an over 400-year-old text from the classroom to the stage.
