stories.Headline: Cerebras shares surge as profit surprise, forecast raise ease AI spending worries - CNA
stories.Summary:
Cerebras Systems shares rose more than 14 per cent in early trading on Friday, after the chipmaker raised its annual sales forecast and posted a surprise profit. The company said it now expects 2026 adjusted revenue of $940 million to $960 million, up from its previous forecast of $880 million to $890 million. Analysts had expected sales of $887.04 million for the period, according to LSEG data. If the gains hold, they would add over $3 billion to Cerebras' market value.

The results come as Cerebras challenges Nvidia in the AI chip market. Adjusted cloud and services revenue, which reflects its OpenAI deal, more than tripled to $144.9 million for the third quarter. Adjusted profit was $29.82 million, compared with an adjusted loss of $10.86 million a year earlier, while analysts had expected an adjusted loss of $38.4 million. As of Thursday's close, Cerebras shares were down 47.2 per cent from their May IPO price of $185 apiece.

CEO Andrew Feldman said on the earnings call that delivery delays under Cerebras' $20 billion multi-year OpenAI deal came from industry-wide shortages of land and power, not chip manufacturing constraints. The chipmaker reiterated plans to triple revenue in 2027. It also said it has signed a cloud deal with Microsoft, with details to be shared next year. The upbeat forecast helped offset concerns over heavy AI spending and uncertainty triggered by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation.

stories.Headline: Tougher curbs on AI chip sales to China likely after Nvidia CEO resigns
stories.Summary:
US lawmakers from both parties are pushing for tighter limits on China's access to advanced AI chips after media reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang stepped down on Nov 12, days after the reports surfaced. The reports concerned an executive at a Singapore-based tech company whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia did not address Huang's actions in its statement, and Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair without naming the person.

Congress is weighing several Bills that would give lawmakers more control over chip exports, track advanced chips, and pressure allies to limit help to China. House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Nov 12 that a growing consensus in Congress favours new restrictions. A handful of lawmakers want to attach the proposals to the annual defence authorisation Bill, which typically attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of that legislation already includes several of them, including the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act and Match Act.

The AI Overwatch Act, proposed by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks, would give Congress a larger role in reviewing changes to export rules, which the Commerce Department now controls largely without congressional input. The Chip Security Act would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users. The Match Act would pressure allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to restrict sales and maintenance of chipmaking equipment bound for China. The Remote Access Security Act, which passed the House in January and awaits Senate consideration, would give the Commerce Department authority to regulate Chinese firms renting Nvidia-powered computing power overseas.

Nvidia's revenue from chip sales to Chinese data centres is near zero, according to an August company statement, and the company does not expect that to change in the third quarter. The company said in July that the remote-access measure, if enacted, could have "a material impact on our business." Reuters reported on Nov 12 that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure access to Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China. The Semiconductor Industry Association, whose members include Nvidia, has said mandatory tracking requirements could be costly. The proposals remain under consideration, and the articles do not say when or whether they will pass.

stories.Headline: AI Lab Mirendil Raises $1B Series A: Release Names No Valuation, Cites Only Company Tests
stories.Summary:
AI lab Mirendil announced a one billion dollar Series A funding round on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The funding was led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital. Former Anthropic researchers founded the company to democratize frontier AI research and development. This round follows a two hundred million dollar seed round from June. The seed round occurred at a one billion dollar valuation.

The Series A included Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, Gil and Co, Google, M13, Pear VC, and S32. Mirendil-Base cost less than ten million dollars in compute and has 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Larger models range from 0.5 trillion to 2 trillion and 2 trillion to 10 trillion parameters. Fern claims ten million tokens of context, while Lor is in private beta. The company is based in San Francisco.

Mirendil reports that AI agents wrote over 99 percent of the code for its smallest model. One researcher directed the work, but the company says it has not reached fully autonomous recursive self-improvement. Kleiner Perkins aims for a system that continually improves itself toward any user goal. The CEO told TechCrunch that a Google Cloud deal is worth upward of 100 million dollars. Google is both an investor and a compute supplier.

Matt Bornstein of Andreessen Horowitz told the Wall Street Journal that there must be an independent company. The company's own test ranks Mirendil-Base second to Kimi-K3 on a bits-per-byte comparison. No independent party has reproduced these results or evaluated any Mirendil model. The RULER benchmark authors found that many models claiming long context fail satisfactory performance tests. Users of Lor can stop any agent at any time.

Mirendil launched on June 24 with twenty researchers from Anthropic, xAI, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI. Typical 2024 U.S. medians were 3.1 million dollars for seed and 12.4 million dollars for Series A. Thinking Machines Lab raised two billion dollars at a twelve billion dollar valuation in July 2025. Recursive Superintelligence raised 650 million dollars in May, and Safe Superintelligence was valued at 32 billion dollars. Nvidia invested after the seed round.

Lawmakers are weighing the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act and the Human Control Over AI Act. The former would pause systems trained on 10 to the 25th power or more operations. The Series A release does not state a valuation or describe safety checks for automated retraining. Bloomberg reported talks at a five billion dollar valuation, but no source confirmed final terms. Results for larger models remain undisclosed.

stories.Headline: White House Urges Easing Liability to Encourage AI Disclosure
stories.Summary:
A White House AI task force issued a recommendation on Thursday, November 13, 2026. The group urged federal agencies to stop using regulatory penalties against companies that report cybersecurity incidents in good faith. This proposal aims to encourage firms to disclose vulnerabilities rather than hide them. The task force believes that current enforcement standards may be outdated.

The plan suggests a liability relief window of at least 12 months, which could be extended later. This relief applies only to cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents, not to general AI failures or bad advice. For the plan to work, agencies must write it into formal guidance. Additionally, Congress must renew the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015.

The task force includes National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, Pentagon research chief Emil Michael, and OPM Director Scott Kupor. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also attended the meeting. These officials argued that strict penalties create a chilling effect on information sharing. They noted that organizations are now more vulnerable because attackers use AI tools.

The recommendation is currently voluntary and is not an executive order or a law. Agencies can choose to ignore the advice, and none have promised to follow it yet. The government is also discussing a voluntary process to analyze reports and share defensive data. Future success depends on whether regulators actually offer the promised relief.

stories.Headline: Pentagon rebrands principle AI shop as 'Super Intelligence Office'
stories.Summary:
The Defense Department announced that its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, known as the CDAO, has been redesignated as the Super Intelligence Office, or SIO. The change was reported on November 13, 2026, by Breaking Defense. The department said the new name does not alter the office's mission. It said the change instead lines the office up with a broader push across the federal government to replace references to artificial intelligence with the term "super intelligence."

The department said the transition will roll out across digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters over the coming weeks. Existing operational programs, industry solicitations and defense partnerships will continue without interruption under the new name. The department has also launched SI.mil, which will serve as the renamed office's main digital domain. The office's portfolio includes the Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, a central data hub formerly known as Advana.

Cameron Stanley, the department's top AI official who also leads the office, said in a statement that the rebrand reflects the Pentagon's priorities going forward. He said the department has moved beyond experimental prototypes. Stanley said the office's mission is to harness the full power of sovereign super intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain. The redesignation follows an announcement by President Donald Trump in September that federal agencies should replace AI references with the term super intelligence, which he argued made the technology sound fake.

The article notes that the terminology has drawn questions in the tech community, where superintelligence has traditionally described a hypothetical form of general artificial intelligence that exceeds overall human intelligence. The Pentagon has been among the federal government's most aggressive adopters of AI, with the CDAO leading efforts to expand its use across military operations. Those efforts include making generative AI tools more widely available to personnel through GenAI.mil, an enterprise platform providing access to commercial generative AI models. The article does not say what the rebrand will cost or whether it will affect the office's budget.

stories.Headline: OpenAI joins push to curb China’s access to AI chips and chipmaking tools
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has backed a bipartisan effort in Congress to block China's access to artificial intelligence chips and curb its access to chipmaking equipment. The AI developer confirmed to lawmakers this week that it would support the measures, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be named. The support came as legislation gained momentum after a scandal that led to Jensen Huang's removal as chief executive of Nvidia Corp. on Thursday. Lawmakers have seized on revelations that Huang had an affair with an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed named Alice Huang. OpenAI's backing was reportedly in the works well before the Nvidia scandal erupted.

Congress is weighing three proposals that would restrict future sales of high-end chips, reduce the diversion of Nvidia's AI processors and block China from accessing sophisticated machinery from ASML Holding NV. The Match Act seeks to further restrict the chip tools China may purchase, while the Chip Security Act would direct the administration to require a security mechanism capable of preventing smuggling. The AI Overwatch Act, pushed by Senator Jim Banks and Senator Elizabeth Warren, would freeze existing rules on which chips Nvidia can sell to China for at least 18 months. The measures would be attached to annual defense legislation that must pass before the end of the year. Lawmakers and administration officials are still negotiating the exact terms, and the bills could be scrapped, especially if President Donald Trump threatens a veto.

OpenAI declined to comment on its position, though a policy document published earlier this month said it "continues to support" strengthening export controls. Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, said in a Wednesday X post that Congress has a "generational opportunity" to address pathways China uses to access US chips through the defense bill. Representative John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, said Nvidia "must now change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority." The Justice Department is conducting an espionage probe that includes looking at Alice Huang's relationship with the former Nvidia chief, Bloomberg has reported. Megaspeed is also under US investigation for possible export control violations, and the company has denied wrongdoing.

Nvidia's allies in Washington, including trade groups, have mobilized against the provisions, arguing they would harm the ecosystem of companies tied to Nvidia. Nvidia itself has remained relatively quiet as the defense bill effort gains steam. Lawmakers including outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, expected speaker Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer have voiced support for the measures. Senate Majority Leader John Thune remains publicly undecided. Democratic lawmakers have complained that the administration has failed to enforce existing AI chip export restrictions since Trump returned to office last year.

Nvidia and Huang opposed tighter restrictions, and last year the chipmaker helped kill the Gain AI Act, which would have required chipmakers to ensure no US customers sought a chip before selling it to China. China's Ministry of Commerce vowed in April to "take necessary measures" to safeguard its interests after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced the Match Act. The ministry said the bills would "severely undermine the international economic and trade order." China has previously used rare earth mineral export controls to retaliate against US chip restrictions. The administration has been wary of imperiling a delicate trade truce with China, which is set to expire on Jan. 10.

Huang's departure from Nvidia on Thursday removed a longtime foe of stricter US export controls and diminished the chipmaker's clout on Capitol Hill. Analysts at Bloomberg have noted that his exit increases the chances all three measures pass this year. Moolenaar said Congress should "act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill." Lawmakers must finish the defense bill before the year ends for the provisions to take effect. Whether the measures become law, and how the administration and China respond, remains unresolved in the articles.

stories.Headline: Scale AI Launches Singapore Legal Reasoning Benchmark with IMDA
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, Scale AI and Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) introduced SG-LegalClarify, a benchmark for testing AI on Singapore law. The benchmark tested 19 language models on 1,860 scenarios spanning 10 domains of Singapore law. It assesses both legal accuracy and whether a model asks for missing facts before answering. Scale presents it as the first research initiative under a collaboration that was formalized in April 2026 and publicly described on July 7, 2026. The project is meant to help governments check AI systems against their own laws and institutions, rather than assuming international benchmark results carry over.

The dataset begins with 1,100 English-language source questions, of which 340 are fully specified and 760 are underspecified. Each underspecified question is paired with a fully specified counterpart that contains the hidden facts. Twenty-three verified lawyers wrote the questions, and seven of them also served as reviewers, with legal experience ranging from two to 37 years and a median of six. Each question carries a lawyer-written rubric of 12,546 criteria covering issue identification, rule recall, application and conclusion. Of these criteria, 89.0% are mandatory for a substantively correct answer, and the headline results count only those mandatory items.

The researchers say that a sufficiency gate first requires each model to either answer directly or gather facts. On the fact-gathering path, a simulated user reveals hidden facts only when the model explicitly asks for them. A three-model AI judge panel, chosen by comparison with human lawyer assessments, grades each criterion by majority vote. The benchmark is designed to test a skill separate from accuracy: deciding whether a query contains enough legally material information to be answered at all. Singapore is described as a demanding test because English common law operates alongside local modifications and Singapore-specific statutes.

Scale states that Singapore's legal system draws on English common law while incorporating its own statutes and principles, so a model relying on general common-law concepts may reach the wrong conclusion. The company says governments need ways to independently assess whether AI systems perform reliably against their own laws, institutions and standards. It also notes that many existing legal benchmarks assume all necessary information has already been supplied. Scale describes SG-LegalClarify as a milestone in its collaboration with IMDA, with IMDA contributing expertise in Singapore's regulatory environment and AI governance. Scale says its own contribution is developing rigorous benchmarks and evaluating frontier models.

The results in the paper show that Claude Fable 5 led closed-book testing by satisfying 69.8% of mandatory criteria, against an average of 53.8% across models. With web search, Kimi K3 led at 77.8%, and the average rose to 63.0%, with every model improving to varying degrees. Rule recall was the weakest component, with pass rates of 43.2% without search and 56.5% with it. Without web search, about 39% of closed-book scenarios with missing facts received no clarifying question, while models asked unnecessary questions in about 28% of scenarios that already contained enough information. When facts were missing, models asked about an average of only 39% of the relevant facts identified by legal experts.

The paper also reports that, in web-enabled trials where models requested every relevant missing fact, 55.6% reached the correct legal conclusion, 32.1% reached an incorrect conclusion and 12.3% gave no conclusion. The authors identify several limits, including limited human validation of the AI helpers, differences in search-tool access across providers, and the possibility that upfront routing altered clarification behavior. They note that not every annotated missing variable is necessary to resolve an instance, so incomplete fact-request coverage does not automatically mean inadequate clarification. The paper's ethics statement says the scores should not be read as evidence that a model is safe for unsupervised legal advice.

The researchers plan to release 50% of the source questions in each category, keeping each underspecified and fully specified pair in the same split, while retaining the rest for private evaluation. Model outputs on the public split and the evaluation pipeline are also planned for release. Scale says it is also exploring further work with IMDA on agentic AI, model evaluation methods and AI safety. The articles do not say when the public subset will be released, how the private portion will be managed over time, or whether the approach will be adopted by other governments.

stories.Headline: Insight Launches Agent Store to Accelerate Enterprise AI Adoption
stories.Summary:
Insight Enterprises announced the global launch of its online Agent Store on November 13, 2026, in Chandler, Arizona. This new catalog provides clients with proven AI solutions and integrated services to deliver measurable business outcomes. The company aims to help organizations move from isolated pilots into production to generate long-term value. These offerings allow companies to achieve business value in as little as days or weeks. Insight deploys these tools independently or as part of broader AI transformation initiatives for its clients.

The store is available across 14 countries, including the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Singapore. European and Middle Eastern locations include Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. Insight added six new offerings to its library, which now contains a total of 15 AI solutions. New tools include Quote Advisor, the NDA Review Agent, and the Parts Order Assist for warehouse staff. Other solutions include TokenScope for cost management and the gamified AI Flight Academy for training and change management.

Jack Azagury, the president and CEO at Insight, stated that the company acted as Client Zero. He noted that Insight drove over 90 percent internal AI adoption to prove its repeatable approach. Azagury believes combining the Agent Store with consulting and managed services empowers clients to move from hype to how. He emphasized that this strategy helps enterprises deploy agentic AI rapidly and responsibly to deliver results. The company used these tools internally in security, finance, and legal departments to improve overall efficiency.

Culligan International became the first external client to implement the AI Flight Academy to build workforce fluency. Global CIO Laura Walsh said that people, rather than technology, are what truly transform a company. She noted that generative AI adoption is far ahead of the learning curve for many teams. Culligan uses Microsoft Copilot, Cowork, Copilot Studio, Azure, and Microsoft Fabric while incorporating governance for cost and responsibility. The company established a functional champions network to make AI adoption an organic and community-led effort.

Insight Enterprises is a global Fortune 500 technology company and a leading Solutions Integrator listed on the NASDAQ. For more than 35 years, the firm has delivered and optimized technology solutions for its various clients. The company maintains a network of over 6,000 partners and experts who provide end-to-end IT capabilities. It is recognized as a Great Place to Work and a Forbes World's Best Employer. The firm is also rated as a Fortune World's Best Workplace for its employees.

The Agent Store is now generally available to help clients solve technology challenges with hardware and software. Insight continues to provide consulting, implementation, and managed services to support these new agentic AI offerings. The articles do not state when additional agents will be added to the current library of 15. They leave open how many more countries will eventually gain access to the online store. stories.Headline: Anthropic Says AI Safety Scores Can Mislead, Urges Overhaul of Model Testing
stories.Summary:
Anthropic published recommendations for building more reliable AI safety evaluations in a research post on Friday, November 13, 2026. The company warned that safety scores can be misleading when tests are easy to game, poorly documented or measure the wrong behavior. Anthropic is a leading developer of large language models. The recommendations cover evaluation design, testing environments, grading and the reporting of results. Anthropic said decisions about whether a system is ready to ship, what guardrails it needs and where future safety work should focus all rest on the quality of the evaluations behind them.

Anthropic said evaluations should assess whether responses raise or lower the likelihood of harm rather than what a model can do. It argued that refusal rates alone are a poor gauge, since declining to engage with a user in crisis is itself a failure. The company called for multidisciplinary evaluation teams, sandboxed testing without internet access, multi-turn conversation tests, human validation of AI graders and published statistical uncertainty. It said it had hardened its own testing environments after incidents, temporarily halted many evaluations that grant models internet access and added real-time monitoring for web-search tests that still need connectivity. Anthropic narrowed its advice to three priorities: define what is being measured before testing begins, validate AI-based grading against human expert judgment, and report statistical uncertainty so readers can tell a real improvement from noise.

Anthropic wrote that when it says a model is safer than its predecessor, it means the model scored better on a set of evals someone built. The company wrote that a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. It wrote that when a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure. Anthropic wrote that in recent months, in response to its own incidents, it had hardened its evaluation environments. It wrote that humans extract harmful information from a model through gradual escalation, so a model that handles the first message well may respond inappropriately by the fifth.

Anthropic said an appropriate response in biology and cybersecurity is rarely a flat refusal, and models should engage with legitimate requests while withholding operational details that could enable misuse. The company said evaluations need to capture both a model's willingness to comply with harmful requests and its tendency to reject harmless ones. It said results can shift on seemingly minor design choices, such as whether a question is multiple-choice or open-ended, or how the answer options are ordered. Anthropic said it runs multi-turn evaluations that grade an entire conversation against rubrics written by domain experts, with a single failure sinking the whole interaction. The recommendations arrive as regulators and enterprise buyers increasingly ask vendors to substantiate safety claims, and as model releases are marketed partly on benchmark performance.

Anthropic distinguished observational designs, suited to understanding how a model behaves, from causal designs, needed to test whether a specific intervention changes outcomes. It called for measurement specialists to decide how responses are sampled and scored, and subject-matter experts to identify realistic risks and define what a sound answer looks like. The company likened the state of the field to psychology a decade ago, when similar problems with measurement were addressed through reforms such as preregistration and better methodology. Anthropic said some evaluations run with standard safeguards switched off so that a model's baseline behavior can be observed, which can let a system reach beyond its intended testing environment. It urged developers to document testing configurations so that independent teams can reproduce results.

Anthropic said that if scores can move with the format of a question, comparisons across models and versions become difficult to defend, weakening the case for evaluation results as a procurement or compliance signal. For AI developers, the practical burden is heavier than running a standard benchmark, since expert-designed rubrics, human validation of automated graders, longer conversational tests and published uncertainty ranges all add cost and time to the release cycle. Anthropic's own account suggests the payoff is a clearer picture of what a model will actually do once deployed, rather than a number that may not mean what it appears to. The articles do not say when Anthropic will publish further recommendations or whether regulators will adopt them. The articles do not say how many incidents prompted Anthropic to harden its testing environments.

stories.Headline: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints | AI (artificial intelligence)
stories.Summary:
A UK housing association complaint investigator has written to The Guardian, in a letter published on 13 November 2026, describing how AI-generated complaints have swamped their work. The writer says the scope of their job changed completely within a few months, after nine years in the role. They respond to an earlier Guardian article from 8 November about UK public bodies facing a flood of chatbot-written grievances. The writer says that hundreds of pages of wordy complaints are hard to sift through, and that the technical language in AI-drafted letters often confuses customers when staff speak with them in person or by phone. They argue that a human-written complaint, even one with spelling mistakes or expletives, comes from the person and gets straight to the heart of the issue.

They also describe regular complainants who send multiple, massive AI-generated complaints each month, which makes staff feel disrespected. The organisation is considering treating this bombardment as a form of harassment. A second letter, from Pete Bibby, takes a different view. Bibby says that using AI as an assistant to seek redress should not be seen as a nuisance, but as a way of extending recourse to people who lack the time or resources to pursue complaints. Bibby argues that public bodies, especially councils, should use AI with a human in the loop to work through likely legitimate complaints, whatever their wording.

Bibby also suggests that the so-called clog may reflect earlier powerlessness among people who could not express grievances before. The letters sit against a backdrop of strain on public services, and the first writer points to the case of Awaab Ishak as an example of why accessible complaints processes matter for tenants. The articles do not say whether the housing association has formally adopted a harassment classification, or what the outcome of the debate will be. The letters themselves are opinion, not reporting on a decision.

stories.Headline: You’re Not Behind on AI Agents Yet. Learn How They Work in 10 Minutes, Before Your Competitors Get Ahead
stories.Summary:
Entrepreneurs are currently building custom AI agents to handle tasks like reporting, video editing, scriptwriting, and marketing. Ben Angel wrote about this trend on November 13, 2026, for the Entrepreneur website. He explains that these tools help business owners focus on running their companies. Some competitors are already using these agents to move faster. This shift allows owners to automate recurring jobs that drain their time.

United Airlines announced a ban on AI agents making customer bookings during the week of November 12, 2026. This policy addresses privacy concerns and the risk of exposing sensitive data to third parties. The airline notes that bots cannot legally acknowledge that travel bags lack explosives. Such actions might violate rules from the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration. These rules ensure that humans verify safety requirements for every single flight.

Ben Angel says that entrepreneurs should identify a worthwhile first job for an agent without automating everything. He warns that moving too quickly can create a new bottleneck instead of removing one. He suggests using his AI Success Kit and his book, The Wolf is at The Door. Angel believes it is not too late for business owners to learn these tools. He emphasizes that the first assignment given to an agent is very important.

United Airlines believes that unintended transactions from bots could bog down the booking process for all users. Uber reported that only 500 of 320 million trips during Halloween week were placed by agents. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said only several hundred orders total were placed by agents since September. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky described agent traffic and bookings as a very non-material number. These companies find that adding agents can be inconvenient for most consumers.

A 2026 G2 survey of 1,019 B2B decision-makers found that 66 percent had agents in production. These agents were running in either limited or scaled production within those specific organizations. DoorDash had previously launched a feature allowing people to text an agent to order food. Many AI makers claimed their agents could handle simple tasks like making various bookings. However, consumers have shown little interest in using these intermediaries for their daily transactions.

Business owners must now decide which specific tasks to hand off to their new AI agents. They need to ensure agents understand their standards and know when to ask for input. United Airlines will continue to block agents to protect sensitive data and follow federal laws. It remains unclear if consumers will ever want agents to handle their personal business transactions. The articles leave open whether AI agents will become material to everyday corporate cash flow.

stories.Headline: Here’s how to teach AI agents to search like human experts
stories.Summary:
Docebo launched Docebo Knowledge and Docebo Agents on November 13, 2026, for customers using its Learn platform. These new tools add a knowledge search layer and AI agents to the company's workforce learning software. The system allows employees to search training materials and connected business systems from one single interface. These tools draw on learning records, skills data, and approved company information held across various systems. The rollout aims to help companies manage skills, knowledge, and workflow context as they increase AI spending.

The tools index content from SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive, Slack, and Docebo's own SCORM and xAPI packages. Four pre-built agents handle course creation, learner support, post-course reinforcement, and content sourcing from third-party providers. A no-code tool allows customers to set an agent's goal, instructions, and permitted actions without writing software code. The Model Context Protocol connects the system to Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude for external access. Users only see information they are authorized to access because the system carries over existing source permissions.

Docebo stated that many businesses are adopting AI faster than they are putting necessary foundations in place. The company cited these findings from its 2027 Skills Intelligence Report to explain the need for these tools. Docebo said that administrators can decide which agents operate and which actions require human sign-off before completion. The company noted that each action is logged and customers can track AI credit usage to monitor costs. These oversight functions were built into the system to ensure proper approval and control over the AI agents.

More than 50 customers in transportation, retail, distribution, and food service sectors took part in the initial pilots. One international electronics distributor reduced manual content curation by about five hours a month for each of its administrators. A global restaurant operator saved store managers about 10 hours a month on training follow-up using the Reinforcement Agent. The Tutor Agent handled 25 percent of frontline training questions without needing an administrator to intervene in the process. A retailer recruiting 2,500 new employees annually expects to save sales managers one to two hours per new hire.

The launch comes as companies increase spending on AI tools while still building systems to manage skills and knowledge. Docebo designed the tools to return answers, procedures, videos, and source links based on approved company material. Users can move from an answer to a related course, certification, practice exercise, or a specific workflow. The agents use information such as a learner's history, identified skills gaps, and organizational taxonomies to act. This effort extends the availability of learning tools outside the primary interface of the Docebo platform.

Employees can now search for content, check progress, and enrol in courses without opening the Docebo platform. Administrators can handle tasks through connected AI assistants and workplace tools to streamline the learning process for staff. The articles do not state the specific costs associated with the AI credit usage for the customers. It remains open how many more pre-built agents Docebo plans to release following this initial launch. The text does not specify the long-term success rates for the custom agents built by the pilot customers.

stories.Headline: Is Mark Zuckerberg's cute new AI assistant a surveillance trap?
stories.Summary:
Meta launched its Muse AI assistant and the Muse Charm keychain companion, and child safety experts are warning about risks to children and teenagers. The rollout began across the US and Canada in September, and Muse has now reached Japan and Singapore, with India soon to follow. Meta has yet to confirm a release date for Europe, but The Times reported on Monday that the UK is first in line. Muse already counts over 1.8 million daily users across the US and Canada. TechRadar published its report on 13 November 2026, quoting experts who spoke to the site.

Muse is an AI agent that can shop online, book vacations, or buy groceries on behalf of its users. Muse Charm is a two-inch wearable with an OLED touchscreen, front and rear cameras, microphones, speakers, 5G connectivity, and USB-C charging. At its visual center sits Jolly, a pink-cheeked, Labubu-style animated avatar that users can personalize by name, appearance, outfits, and voice. Meta officially brands Muse AI as an 18+ productivity assistant, though critics say it looks more like a customizable toy. Meta requires everyone using the Muse app to provide their date of birth, and a spokesperson said age checks will include an element TechRadar's excerpt leaves unstated.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED that "this is a story in search of a story," insisting avatar customization simply brings users joy. Roberts pointed out that the company requires everyone using the Muse app to provide their date of birth. When approached by TechRadar, a Meta spokesperson also explained that age checks will include an element the article does not finish describing. Mark Zuckerberg frames Jolly as a "fun, completely customizable character." Meta has so far rejected claims that Muse is directly targeting children.

AI safety specialist Kavya Pearlman, a former risk advisor during Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal, called the toy-like aesthetic a "deliberate attempt" to attract younger demographics. Pearlman said the company has a lot of information it knows will work towards gaining access to certain age groups. Cuteness researcher Joshua Paul Dale told Fast Company that cute, child-like designs stimulate pleasure centers before users can evaluate risks. Children's digital safety experts at the Canadian group The White Hatter warned that an always-on AI friend could fundamentally alter human attachment to the machine. Critics say Meta is making a product capable of invasive surveillance feel harmless by leveraging nostalgia for Tamagotchis and popular designer toys.

Meta is already at the center of your online social life through Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, and now wants a permanent spot on your desk. Muse Charm brings the AI agent into physical reality, letting users talk to their Muse without opening their smartphone. The cuddly, disarming design, paired with always-on microphones and ambient recording, is raising eyebrows among AI experts and children's digital safety campaigners. Moving beyond screen-based interactions, a wearable charm could tap into innate social emotions, making conversations with ambient software feel as natural as speaking to a person beside you. The White Hatter experts note that such an always-on AI friend could fundamentally alter human attachment to the machine.

As Muse edges closer to a global launch, the articles leave open whether it sets the stage for the next youth privacy disaster and whether we are ready to cope with the aftermath. Meta has yet to confirm a release date for Europe, though reports suggest the company is eyeing the continent with the UK first in line. The TechRadar excerpt cuts off mid-sentence on what Meta's age checks will include, leaving that detail unresolved. The articles do not say what the age checks will involve beyond date of birth, nor how the 18+ branding will be enforced. They also do not say when India or the UK launches will actually happen.

stories.Headline: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global outage, says issue not caused by AI
stories.Summary:
Microsoft apologized on Friday for a global outage that disrupted various public services and businesses around the world. The tech giant reported a broad recovery for Outlook email and other services after the disruption sparked global chaos. This incident began on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and affected several different Microsoft products across many regions. The company ruled out any malicious cyber activity or AI agents as the cause of the service failure. Microsoft stated that the outage was a technical issue and not the result of any external hacking.

The outage disrupted access to Microsoft 365 products for governments, hospitals, schools, and businesses throughout the entire world. It was caused by an underlying infrastructural issue introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a change. Microsoft restored services gradually to validate stability at each stage, which the company admitted took longer than some hoped. The company has now addressed the underlying issue and continues to restore service to remaining customers and regions. This technical failure delayed corporate earnings reports and left schools struggling to communicate with their students and staff.

Microsoft said they are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident caused to their many customers and partners. The corporation stated that they take the responsibility of the trust placed in their services extremely seriously. They reported that they are now seeing broad recovery and stability across their various services after the event. The company clarified that the problem was a technical issue not related to cyber agents or AI. Microsoft promised to provide a full post-incident report once their internal review of the outage is complete.

The outage affected healthcare services and various public sectors, causing significant disruption to essential operations and corporate reporting. Some people speculated that the outage was caused by vibe-coding, given the company's push for company-wide AI adoption. The company's decision to restore services gradually was intended to ensure a stable restoration for all affected users. Many customers and partners experienced chaos as they lost access to critical tools and communication platforms for hours. The scale of demand required a phased approach to bring the systems back online without further stability issues.

Microsoft has laid off roughly 30,000 employees over the last four years as part of a cost-cutting strategy. This includes 10,000 employees laid off in 2023 and 6,000 employees who were let go in May 2025. Another 9,000 employees were laid off in July 2025, followed by 4,800 more a year later in 2026. This later group included 1,600 people at Xbox, with another 1,600 layoffs scheduled to follow those cuts. Last month, the company extended voluntary buyout offers to 60,000 employees to further reduce its total workforce.

The company will release a detailed report after the internal review is finished to explain the technical failure. Microsoft continues to work on restoring full service to all remaining customers and regions affected by the outage. The articles leave open whether the massive layoffs contributed to the company's inability to prevent this technical hiccup. It remains unclear if the company intended to add another word after the term cyber in their official statement. The final report will likely clarify the exact sequence of events that led to the network capacity failure.

stories.Headline: Meta's Muse now calls businesses for you, but many companies might just hang up on the AI
stories.Summary:
Meta launched the Muse AI agent on September 8, which can now place outbound phone calls to businesses. This feature is available to paying subscribers in the United States and was tested in September. The agent handles tedious tasks like calling cable companies, the DMV, and restaurants for its users. Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang stated that the agent now serves more than 10 million users. The tool allows users to book tables, make appointments, and wait on hold without any complaint.

The feature requires a paid subscription, with plans costing 20 dollars or 100 dollars per month. The 20 dollar plan provides 500 million tokens weekly, while the 100 dollar plan offers 3 billion tokens. Muse launched on September 8 and released a Mac app on September 17 for its users. The service is limited to the United States and does not include a free tier for calling. Meta will soon provide the AI agent with its own free email address for these business calls.

Alexandr Wang pitched the tool as a way to handle calls that users do not want to make. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reuters that the company would only roll out features with proper disclosures. A Meta executive later admitted that using human operators without clear disclosure was a mistake for the company. Meta communications reported that human agents could succeed in calls 95 to 98 percent of the time. This human concierge option was tested with half of Meta employees who could choose to opt out.

Many businesses and receptionists hang up the moment they detect an AI agent on the phone line. Users are affected by this, as Muse does not always state outright that it is an AI. The agent tells the recipient it is calling on behalf of someone and is transcribing the conversation. Some staff warned that sensitive details could reach call center contractors without any intention of doing so. This issue echoes Google Duplex, where one in four calls was handled by a human at launch.

Google Gemini, the startup Instinct, and xAI Grok Bot can already place calls, but OpenAI and Anthropic cannot. Meta previously ran a Messenger assistant called M from 2015 to 2018 that used human staff members. That earlier assistant never achieved more than 30 percent automation during its three years of operation. Muse recently reached number two on the US App Store, though its downloads trail behind Threads. The company also launched the Muse Charm keychain gadget and various updates for its smart glasses.

Meta will continue to refine synthetic voices to make AI detection more difficult for businesses to perform. It remains unresolved whether paying customers can currently be routed to a human agent for their calls. The company has not publicly answered what exactly a subscriber gets for the 20 dollar monthly fee. There is no information regarding call limits, per call costs, or geographic limits beyond the United States. It is unclear if the 20 dollar plan alone unlocks calling or if it requires higher tiers.

stories.Headline: FAA Ground Stop and Microsoft Outage: Did AI Play a Role?
stories.Summary:
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, after communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, and technicians were investigating, the agency said in a preliminary statement. Microsoft’s recorded start for incident MO1550821 was November 12 at 18:26 UTC, or 1:26 p.m. EST. AP reported that European departures for the United States were suspended at the FAA’s request from November 13, 22:00 UTC (5:00 p.m. EST), until November 14, 05:00 UTC (midnight EST).

Alaska Airlines’ advisory described the affected U.S. departures as excluding Alaska and Hawaii and offered a flexible change-or-cancel policy. OpenAI moved its Microsoft 365 connector incident to monitoring on November 13 at 16:20 UTC (11:20 a.m. EST), and Anthropic posted at 21:49 UTC (4:49 p.m. EST) that its Microsoft 365 connector incident was resolved. An FAA advisory at 22:46 UTC (5:46 p.m.

EST) said the ground stop remained in effect and allowed coordinated departures as facilities recovered, with another update expected at 04:00 UTC on November 14 (11:00 p.m. EST on November 13). OpenAI marked its Microsoft 365 connector incident resolved on November 14 at 00:18 UTC (7:18 p.m. EST on November 13). Microsoft attributed the disruption to an earlier network upgrade and a subsequent network change, and on November 13 it said, “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.”

Anthropic identified the main impact window for Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector and Claude for Outlook as November 12 at 16:03 UTC (11:03 a.m. EST) through November 13 at 16:40 UTC (11:40 a.m. EST). Microsoft listed Copilot Chat and access to work data among affected functions. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself and said there was no connection between it and Microsoft.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights. Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” that “it appears that this was mechanically driven,” and that officials were “not going to rule that out.” Asked whether officials had seen any evidence of a cyberattack, he said, “We’ve seen zero evidence.” Duffy said the FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began.

Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific, and that aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information. He said the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines,” that “our new IP switches did not go down,” and that “it’s the old hardware that went down.” Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing, and neither official said exactly what that equipment was. The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m.

Pacific, more than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, and medevac, critical cargo and law enforcement flights were allowed to continue. FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon. The FAA unveiled SMART on September 21 and announced expansion on November 10 to the airspace of all 22 centers, and the FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers. According to the FAA’s SMART fact sheet, the cloud-based system analyzes traffic, weather and other operational information to produce planning recommendations, and controllers remain responsible for separating aircraft.

The FAA awarded Air Space Intelligence a contract for the related Flow Management Data and Services, with SMART described as an enhancement, and SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence. Air Space Intelligence denied any connection in a post on X, saying, “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” On October 13, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Democrats asked the Government Accountability Office to review SMART and FMDS, requesting scrutiny of safety work, testing, performance measures, training and deployment. AT&T took over the lead role on replacing the FAA’s legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

In justifying the award, the FAA said its current telecom network “can no longer adequately support” air traffic operations, MeriTalk reported. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency, and the administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported, while Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion. It is the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system. The FAA’s underlying telecommunications failure and Microsoft’s final root-cause analysis remain open questions, and the public material reviewed does not establish a shared cause for the ground stop and the Microsoft 365 outage.

stories.Headline: Uganda: Will Uganda's Youth Power the Ai Economy, or Be Left Behind By It?
stories.Summary:
Uganda faces a choice over whether its young people will benefit from artificial intelligence or be left behind by it, according to a new Commonwealth study unveiled at the leaders' summit in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda, held from November 1 to 4. The inaugural 2026 Commonwealth Youth AI Readiness Index, produced by the Ayre Think Tank, was presented on the sidelines of that gathering. The study found that AI could raise Uganda's GDP by an estimated US$899 million over the next decade, provided the country creates the conditions for young people to benefit. Uganda has one of the most youthful populations in the world and a sizeable entrepreneurial base, but its ability to turn that advantage into productive jobs remains constrained. The article was reported by Ronald Musoke and published on November 13, 2026.

Uganda ranks 23rd among 56 Commonwealth countries, scoring 47.0 out of 100, below the study's readiness benchmark of 53. The country is marginally behind Kenya, which ranks 22nd with 48.7 points, and ahead of Tanzania at 25th with 45.5 and Rwanda at 47th with 38.1. Uganda has 13.4 million people aged 15 to 29, according to the data used in the study. Uganda Bureau of Statistics figures from its 2025 Labour Market Survey put youth unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 at 17.9%, against a national rate of 12.2%. Young women face a 21% unemployment rate compared with 15.2% for young men, and the survey found 89.2% of employment was informal.

The index was produced by the Ayre Think Tank, whose founder, Calvin Ayre, said that AI will change how people work, do business and create wealth. He argued that the race is not one only the biggest or richest countries can win, and that giving young people skills and chances matters most. Ayre said governments now have to decide what they will do about the gaps the index reveals. The study measures the conditions that let young people benefit from the technology rather than directly measuring AI competence or adoption. Uganda's score is based on usable information for 61 of the 102 indicators, and its Data Gap Index is 50.0, which indicates substantial missing evidence.

Young people in Uganda are also affected by the infrastructure gaps the study identifies. Electricity reaches just 55.3% of the population, according to the figures cited, and fewer than half of young people report using the internet. The study found that 41.9% of people aged 18 to 29 were starting or running a new business, while another 20.6% owned an established business. Joshua Pi'Rwot, a consultant at the AVODA Institute of Entrepreneurship in Kampala, said businesses lack a date for when the national AI policy will be completed. The Ministry of ICT is leading the drafting of that policy after a national stakeholders' consultation in May 2026.

Uganda's readiness challenges were identified in a 2025 national AI landscape assessment by the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance, working with the International Telecommunication Union. That assessment highlighted inadequate AI infrastructure, shortages of specialised skills, limited collaboration between academia and technology companies, and the absence of a comprehensive AI policy and regulatory framework. A national task force set up in 2018 developed the Uganda National Fourth Industrial Revolution Strategy, which targets creating 300,000 new earning opportunities by 2040. The strategy also seeks to raise agricultural GDP output by 2% annually.

The Ayre Index places Singapore first with 77.6 points, while Mauritius leads Africa in eighth place with 64.4 points. The articles leave open when Uganda's national AI policy will be finalised and whether the country can close its infrastructure and skills gaps in time. They do not say how the 300,000 earning opportunities target is progressing toward its 2040 deadline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Will NVIDIA’s New CFO Halt AI Financing? The "Jumpy Deer" Who Slashed $250B Data Center Budget by Half & Was Mocked by Jensen Huang as "Just a Finance Person"
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA CEO on December 12, 2026, following an extramarital affair scandal. Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, was named the interim chief executive to fill the vacancy. Huang had previously built a circular financing network worth over 500 billion U.S. dollars for AI. This network used equity investments and credit guarantees to provide capital to the cash burning industry. The founder left in disgrace while the company now faces a major leadership reshuffle.

stories.Headline: Gemini Enhances Personal Finance Insights with Google Wallet Integration
stories.Summary:
Google launched a Gemini app feature connecting to Google Wallet, announced in a blog post, rolling out today for all Gemini users in the U.S. The feature lets users receive personalized financial insights drawn from their spending habits. It is initially rolling out to users in the US on Android, iOS, and the web. Small Business Trends published its report on Nov 13, 2026, by David Wilson. How-To Geek published its report on Nov 13, 2026, at 4:57 PM EST, by Jefferson Mangubat. Users can link Google Wallet via Gemini’s Connected Apps settings and mention @Google Wallet when asking questions about their finances.

Google also allows users to link bank accounts and credit cards to Wallet through Plaid, a financial technology company that helps connect financial institutions to third-party services. The integration is part of Google's Personal Intelligence initiative, which already connects Gemini with Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search. Google is also rolling out an update to its Memory Summary feature that will enable users to review, edit, and delete what Gemini remembers about their preferences and ongoing goals. Google says the integration is read-only, so Gemini can see linked account information but can’t move money, manage accounts, make purchases, or invest for you. Google says connecting Wallet is entirely optional, and users can revoke access at any time.

Google provides several practical suggestions for using the service, such as asking Gemini to look at spending over the last quarter and come up with a plan to save $1,000 over the next three months. Google says the integration is fully opt-in, so privacy-conscious users can keep it switched off. How-To Geek says it still takes a giant leap of faith to give an AI the keys to your transaction history, particularly when chatbots are still prone to the occasional math error and hallucination. Small Business Trends says business owners will need to dedicate time to learn how to fully leverage the capabilities of the Gemini app. Small Business Trends says they must also consider the security implications of linking financial accounts, as this might raise concerns about data privacy and vulnerability.

Small Business Trends says small business owners often face the dual challenge of limited resources and high competition, making financial efficiency crucial. Gemini has evolved from a general-purpose chatbot to a more personal AI assistant by integrating with services like Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search to give it more context about users’ lives. Many small business owners already use a range of Google services, such as Gmail and Google Search. The Gemini app leverages Personal Intelligence to provide tailored responses.

With Google Wallet in Gemini rolling out across both web and mobile platforms, small business owners now have access to a robust suite of tools, backed by the reliability of Google services. Users can ask the app specific questions like, “Can we review my spending from last quarter so I can save $1,000 over the next three months?” With this request, Gemini generates dynamic charts that illustrate cash flow, asset allocation, and budget outlines directly within the chat interface. The question, “What subscriptions am I still paying for, and did any of them go up in price this year?”

can prompt Gemini to search through linked accounts, highlighting recurring charges and alerting users to any price hikes. Users can ask “How much did I spend on gifts and travel last year? stories.Headline: European firms with AI exposure earn higher stock returns, ECB finds
stories.Summary:
European companies with artificial intelligence exposure earned about 1.3 percentage points more in quarterly stock returns than comparable firms without such exposure, research published Thursday by the European Central Bank found. The central bank published “Artificial intelligence and European firms: the cost of market-based financing” on Nov. 12 in its Economic Bulletin. Irene Ferrari, Sofia Gori, Johannes Groß, Fabian Schupp and Sigurd Steffensen prepared the research. The authors examined companies in the STOXX Europe 600 index using quarterly earnings calls from the first quarter of 2017 through the second quarter of 2026. They classified firms as AI-exposed when calls linked the technology to infrastructure, products or improvements in operations and productivity.

The authors also found that AI exposure corresponded to corporate bond spreads about 5 basis points, or 0.05 percentage point, lower in quarterly data covering 2019-26. About 75% of calls mentioning AI discussed product innovation or growth opportunities, while 50% discussed productivity gains, the central bank found. The authors found that technology firms discussed AI product innovation as early as 2017, while other sectors mainly began discussing productivity improvements after ChatGPT launched in late 2022. The stock-return analysis compared AI-exposed companies with firms in the same sector and quarter, accounting for company characteristics, earnings surprises and sector trends. In the bond analysis, the authors accounted for characteristics of individual bonds and issuers.

The authors said the findings depend on investors’ expectations about returns from the technology. Disappointing returns could trigger abrupt changes in stock valuations and bond spreads across businesses beyond those driving AI investment, they said. They called for further analysis to establish the possible scale and effect on euro area financing conditions. The authors said AI could improve expected company earnings and reduce investors’ perceptions of credit risk if they believed businesses were making real progress. But adopting AI could also increase financing costs because it often requires large upfront investments in assets with limited value as collateral, they said.

The advantage extended beyond technology companies supplying AI infrastructure to businesses using the technology in products and operations, the authors said. The authors found that exposed firms also had higher median annual stock returns in most years and tended to command higher prices relative to earnings. They found that AI-exposed companies issued a larger share of bonds maturing in more than 10 years. The authors said longer maturities would typically require higher spreads, making their combination with lower spreads evidence of more favourable financing conditions. Bond spreads measure the extra return investors demand to hold company debt against a benchmark, with lower spreads indicating cheaper financing.

Artificial intelligence has been the dominant theme in global financial markets since late 2022, with equities in the technology sector outperforming substantially. This outperformance has been especially striking in the United States, led by a small group of hyperscalers, and is evident among European firms that occupy upstream positions in the global AI infrastructure buildout. The share of AI-exposed firms has risen markedly since 2022, with AI predominantly mentioned in earnings calls as a source of product innovation and growth. The ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area in June and December 2025 show more innovation-oriented cases of AI use in the IT sector and greater emphasis on cost reduction in manufacturing, construction, trade and other services. AI exposure is measured quarterly from 2017 onwards and treated as time-varying, allowing the analysis to control for firm heterogeneity and sector-specific time variation.

The findings suggest that AI exposure is positively reflected in equity and corporate bond pricing across the wider economy in Europe. AI’s association with lower market-based financing costs is more widely distributed than the concentrated equity rally in the IT sector suggests. However, this relationship rests on expectations about the technology’s returns. Should those expectations disappoint, valuations and spreads could reprice abruptly and broadly, extending well beyond the firms driving the AI investment cycle. Further analysis is warranted to establish the potential scale of this repricing and its effect on aggregate financing conditions in the euro area.

stories.Headline: 🔥 Jensen Huang and the future of the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, after the company's board launched an investigation into his behavior and its possible national security implications. Huang, now 63, had run the company for the 33 years since he co-founded it in 1993. He left after two reported extramarital affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee. The board named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and appointed Harvey Jones as chairman. Nvidia has not replied to repeated requests for comment on the episode.

Kress will serve as interim chief executive until the board finds a permanent replacement, while Jones takes over as chairman of the board. CNBC reported that Huang has agreed to testify before Congress following his resignation. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That figure is up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

Nvidia's board is responsible for choosing a successor, and it must do so without a succession policy, because the company refused to put one in place. Colette Kress and Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees after the announcement, and CNBC published what they said. Huang publicly apologized for being unfaithful to his wife on the Sunday before he resigned, according to the reporting. Nvidia did not respond to the repeated requests for comment that CNBC made. Huang had earlier built the company with no second-in-command, which leaves the board looking for a leader of a firm run by one singular figure.

Kevin Cramer, a Republican senator from North Dakota who sits on the Senate Banking Committee, told CNBC just before the resignation that Huang looked vulnerable to extortion and blackmail. Many US lawmakers demanded investigations, and some demanded Huang's resignation. Former Cisco chief executive John Chambers said that how companies handle a crisis determines their future, and that this will show whether Nvidia is a great leadership team beyond one person. Michael Dell called Huang a visionary of the AI age, and Chris Miglino of the neocloud Axe Compute said the industry would be years behind without him. Tomás Puig of Alembic said Nvidia prepaid two years of invoices after the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, when his firm was down to weeks of cash.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 to make chips for computer graphics, and in the early 2000s he and other executives saw that the chips could serve computationally intense projects. The company became the first to pass a $5 trillion market cap, and in the five years to 2026 it sold nearly 14 million flagship AI chips, which hold 85% of the market. Nvidia has backed the neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius with equity and financial guarantees, and it invested nearly $10 billion across Europe in the last year. In August it said it would provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio. The woman involved was identified by US intelligence as recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, according to The New York Times, and she has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer.

The next test is Nvidia's quarterly report on Tuesday, when analysts expect revenue of $109.2 billion. The board still has to pick a permanent chief executive, and the articles do not say who it will choose or how long that will take. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, but the articles give no date for the hearing or say what he will be asked. It remains open whether the ecosystem of neoclouds and startups that leaned on his sign-off will stay on course, since one source said project finance deals waited on his approval even while he was flying. The articles also leave open what the national security investigation will find, and Azeem Azhar asked whether the dependent ecosystem will stay on the road.

stories.Headline: AI Scams: What families should know this holiday season
stories.Summary:
Veriff, an identity platform company, issued a warning on November 12, 2026, through GlobeNewswire from New York, saying that scams driven by artificial intelligence are set to target holiday shoppers. Its fraud expert Ira Bondar-Mucci shared tips to help shoppers stay ahead of increasingly convincing scams as Black Friday, Cyber Monday and the rest of the holiday sales season approach. The same day, the Alabama station WALA published a segment from Mobile in which gerontologist Rodnée Warr explained what families should watch for this holiday season. The WALA piece said artificial intelligence is making familiar scams more convincing, with deepfake calls, videos and images that can seem to come from loved ones or other trusted people. Both pieces were published on November 12, 2026, and both focus on how AI is changing fraud before the busiest shopping weeks of the year.

The Veriff release lists four habits for safer holiday shopping. The first is to start at the source, entering the retailer's address or opening its app instead of tapping an ad, text or social post, and the second is to treat any celebrity or influencer endorsement as unconfirmed until the same offer appears on the retailer's own website. The third is to keep one-time passcodes private and avoid completing an ID or selfie check through a link someone sent you, on the rule that if you did not start it, you should stop. The fourth is to stay on the platform, pay by credit card for the strongest protection, and treat any request to switch to a bank transfer, gift cards or crypto as a red flag. International Fraud Prevention Week runs from November 15 to 21, and WALA said Warr would explain what to do when something does not seem right.

Bondar-Mucci, who is Fraud Platform Lead at Veriff, said sales events squeeze the time people take to decide, so shoppers click on things they would normally question, and fraudsters build their campaigns around that habit. She said the tricks themselves are familiar, such as fake deals, bogus delivery notices and phony customer support, but AI has made them cheaper to create, more believable and much easier to run at scale. She argued that shoppers should not have to carry this alone and that organizations relying on manual review, or on customers vouching for themselves, are exposed. In her view, retailers, marketplaces and payment providers need checks that do not hinge on what the human eye can see, including confirming a live person is present, making sure the camera feed has not been tampered with, and linking signals across sessions so a reused face or device is noticed. She added that protection should not end at sign-up, because some of the riskiest moments come later, such as a password reset, a new payout account or a large order placed mid-sale, and she said the deepfake arms race is an AI problem that will take AI to solve.

Those most affected include parents, grandparents, neighbors and older loved ones, according to WALA, and the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center 2025 Annual Report found that Americans aged 60 and older reported more than $7.7 billion in fraud losses in 2025, a 59% increase from the previous year. Veriff's Deepfakes Report 2026, produced with Kantar, found that Americans and Britons do only slightly better than chance at telling real visuals from AI-generated ones, and video proved the trickiest format for both groups. Roughly half of Americans, and slightly fewer Britons, said they could reliably spot manipulated media, yet their actual results were close to random guessing, and in the UK more than one in five admit they do not try to verify suspicious content online. About 7% of people fall into an especially high-risk group who struggle to identify fakes, feel sure of themselves anyway, and seldom check a second source. Bondar-Mucci said that is exactly who a well-made deepfake ad is aimed at, because once people feel they cannot be fooled they stop looking for warning signs.

The release explains that scam shops no longer have to rely on a polished website alone, because they can add a video of a familiar-looking face endorsing the offer, a support agent on a live video call, or a cloned voice saying an order is on hold until payment details are confirmed. Generative AI also lets a single fraudster produce hundreds of fake identities, each with a face, a document and a backstory, which are used to set up seller, payment and buy-now-pay-later accounts as well as mule accounts for moving stolen funds. Any one identity may pass inspection, and the giveaway is the pattern, such as the same face, device or network appearing across accounts that supposedly belong to different people. Some scams enlist genuine people instead, approaching targets through a bogus job offer, a prize or refund claim, or a romance or investment chat and asking them to complete an identity check for someone else. The report was an online survey by Kantar of 3,000 adults aged 18 to 64 in the US, the UK and Brazil, and Britons are the most familiar with the term deepfake among the countries surveyed, though that awareness has not sharpened detection.

International Fraud Prevention Week, running from November 15 to 21, falls ahead of the holiday sales season, and Warr's guidance on what to do when something does not seem right was set to be shared with families. Fraudsters often steer victims away from the shopping platform and toward a text thread, messaging app, bank transfer, gift cards or crypto, where buyer protections no longer apply, and the release says genuine retailers do not ask customers to move a conversation or payment off-platform. Neither article says how many shoppers will be targeted this season or how much money these scams may cost them. WALA does not detail the specific steps Warr recommends beyond saying she would explain them. Veriff's release likewise gives no timetable for when retailers, marketplaces and payment providers might adopt the checks Bondar-Mucci calls for.

stories.Headline: Uber Data Breach Exposes Thousands of Drivers Through AI Firm
stories.Summary:
Hackers stole the personal information of thousands of Uber drivers through an AI startup. The ride-hailing company filed security breach notices with several state attorneys general this month. A third-party provider notified Uber of the incident on October 9. Uber determined on October 13 that hackers had accessed its driver data. The breach involved the theft of internal credentials to access the account.

The breach affected 1,873 Rhode Island residents and 3,430 South Carolina residents. TechCrunch reports that 2,567 people in Massachusetts also had their information stolen. The stolen data included driver's license information from the Fireworks AI startup. Notion also lost data, including AI chat transcripts for fewer than 1% of workspaces. Fireworks AI reported that hackers accessed billing information and incomplete AI models.

Fireworks AI said the attack was carried out by a financially motivated cybercriminal group. The company described the practice as LLMJacking, where hackers steal credentials to use or sell AI models. Fireworks AI stated it notified law enforcement and worked with Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. Uber said it immediately cut off all data connections with Fireworks AI. Uber stated it has not identified any misuse of the stolen information.

Affected drivers are encouraged to monitor credit reports and review account statements for suspicious activity. Uber is offering these drivers free fraud assistance and credit monitoring through Cyberscout. Drivers have 90 days from their notification letter date to sign up. Notion customers were affected by the exposure of anonymized chat transcripts. Uber operates a fleet of over 10 million drivers and couriers.

Fireworks AI disclosed that hackers accessed development machines through a separate cloud provider security incident. Uber previously dealt with a security incident in August involving its logistics subsidiary, Uber Freight. A hacking group claimed to have stolen nearly 1 million files from that subsidiary. Uber Freight confirmed unauthorized access to some systems but did not verify the file claims. Uber requires drivers to upload residency, insurance, and bank statements.

Uber will notify all affected workers, though the total nationwide number remains undisclosed. The company recently expanded policies for banning drivers based on public records and background checks. The articles do not state if the cybercriminal group has been identified. It is unclear if any other Fireworks AI clients were compromised. The reports leave the final count of affected drivers open.
