stories.Headline: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team and reassigned the researchers working there to other parts of the company. The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision. The spokesperson portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it. The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week.

OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen. The applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, but when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen. OpenAI rebuilt a stand-alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI.

OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world. OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots. The company said that at the start of the year, its researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model. But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown they can be directly applied to robotics.

Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, told Fortune he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run. Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark, compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence through other methods. OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text, the approach that eventually yielded ChatGPT in late 2022. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts, including Sora, to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses, which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter. OpenAI is seeking to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.

Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. Shi said large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection. Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former OpenAI robotics team members still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. One of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots

stories.Headline: China-nexus actor uses AI tool in campaign targeting US defense, semiconductor industries
stories.Summary:
A suspected China-nexus threat group ran a campaign against key U.S. sectors, including advanced semiconductors, the defense industry and civil-society organizations, according to a report Palo Alto Networks released on a Thursday in mid-November 2026. The attackers paired an AI pen-testing framework called Cairn with two Chinese open-source models, DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM, to target at least 19 organizations. Researchers say they gained access to or pulled data from 10 of them. The attackers obtained dozens of valid credentials, created administrator accounts inside a production system and exposed more than a million personal records at one organization.

Researchers say the combination let the hackers scale their attacks well beyond what a person working by hand could manage. Andy Piazza, senior director of threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, said tools like Cairn let attackers hit more targets faster. He added that such tooling lets them carry out technical tasks without learning the underlying technologies. Researchers are tracking the group as CL-STA-1238, which they describe as part of a China-nexus intelligence-collection effort. The report presents the activity as the latest in a growing wave of attacks built on AI pen-testing frameworks.

The article places the campaign within a broader pattern. Over the past two months, threat groups used a testing framework called Artex to attack hundreds of companies worldwide, and the same tool was linked to a campaign against South Korean banks and Japanese companies. In a separate matter, Arctic Wolf researchers reported on a Tuesday that attackers used the AntiFox pen-testing framework, hosted on Alibaba, to steal Amazon Web Services credentials. At least two organizations were confirmed compromised, and researchers suspect six more were affected. Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, said that activity appears opportunistic rather than aimed at a specific industry.

An Amazon spokesperson said AWS services were not specifically compromised and operated as designed, while the attackers used credentials taken from compromised applications to reach customers' accounts. The spokesperson urged AWS users to follow security best practices, including least-privilege permissions, requiring Instance Metadata Service on EC2 instances, and keeping long-term access keys out of application configurations. The articles do not say whether any government agency has responded to the Palo Alto Networks findings. They also do not describe the specific defense or semiconductor companies that were affected. The reporting ends with the findings themselves and the warnings from researchers and Amazon.

Articles.Title: China-nexus actor uses AI tool in campaign targeting US defense, semiconductor industries

stories.Headline: Clark State, Mark Cuban Foundation to host free AI academy
stories.Summary:
Clark State College, working with the Mark Cuban Foundation, plans to bring a free AI academy to Springfield so residents can explore artificial intelligence and what it can do. The college will host the foundation's AI Academy from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Dec. 7-11 at its Springfield campus at 570 E. Leffel Lane. The foundation is a nonprofit led by entrepreneur and investor Mark Cuban.

Separately, Hopkinsville Community College will hold a free community presentation on artificial intelligence on Tuesday, Nov. 17. The academy will show participants how AI can help generate ideas, solve problems and launch their own projects. Participants can also connect AI to personal interests such as music or business. It is the first adult-focused program from the foundation, which already runs an AI Bootcamp for high schoolers, and it is aimed at people in the trades and communities with fewer AI training options.

Anyone 18 or older can join without technical or coding experience, and coffee, lunch and snacks will be provided. Space is limited to 30 participants, who can register through Clark State's Workforce application at go.clarkstate.edu/AIAcademy. Dave Ferguson, director of workforce development at Clark State, said the college sees programs like this as an important way to prepare people for a future where AI is increasingly part of the workplace. He said AI has already opened new possibilities in fields such as healthcare and manufacturing.

Ferguson added that knowing how to use these tools, judge the information they produce and apply them responsibly can give people an edge in a changing job market. He also said the goal is to understand how AI works, along with its potential and limits. The Hopkinsville event, titled "AI Today and Tomorrow," will run from 5:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.

in Anderson Hall at HCC's Emerging Technologies Building. According to a press release, the 90-minute session will look at the current state of AI and its possible effects on local businesses, jobs, education and daily life. The speaker, Dr. Ryan Hall, is AI and innovation lead for strategy and governance at Owensboro Community and Technical College and the Kentucky Community and Technical College System, and he helps guide the state's 16 community and technical colleges on AI strategy. The presentation is designed for a broad audience and will end with a community question-and-answer session.

Articles.Title: Clark State, Mark Cuban Foundation to host free AI academy

stories.Headline: Why Are Games Hiding Their Blatant AI Usage If They Think It's Totally Cool And Fine And The Future
stories.Summary:
Luke Plunkett wrote in Aftermath on November 12, 2026, that many games on Steam clearly use large amounts of AI-generated assets without disclosing it. He said the number of such games appearing in his personal recommendations is getting out of control. He wrote that he plays a lot of strategy and management games and feels particularly overwhelmed by them. He described Napoleonic officers with buttons all over the place and space miners with piss filters and nonsensical goggles on their helmets. He also described cityscape illustrations with buildings that morph into each other and cannot hold their shape.

Steam has an AI disclosure policy, and after a January 2026 rewrite it is very clear, Plunkett wrote. He said that if anything in a game is consumed by players, like visuals, sound and writing, then it must be disclosed. He gave legal uncertainty over the ownership and copyright status of AI-generated works as one reason for the policy. He wrote that mostly there is also the fact a very large number of people simply hate that shit and do not want to see it in their video games. He said he had lost count of the number of times in the last few months he was recommended a game, installed it, started playing and only then encountered blatant slop.

Plunkett asked why studios that feel AI is a useful tool and the future of development do not just mention it. He asked whether they are not proud of their cost-cutting, their time-saving and the visual and audio benefits. He wrote that the answer is that these studios know it sucks and know people hate it for many and serious reasons. He said they do not want to be called on it and are collectively hoping nobody will notice. He wrote that they hope to receive all of the plaudits and none of the blowback.

Plunkett wrote that a huge number of gamers hate this shit and will make purchasing decisions based on that hatred. He said those gamers deserve to be fully informed. He wrote that he had written twice about major games he had been enjoying until he found AI-generated stuff in them. He said he does not want to support that and does not want to play games that have made use of it. He wrote that the obfuscation is worse than plain AI slop games, which you can see a mile coming and safely ignore.

Plunkett wrote that he had started jotting notes for the blog before the IGF stuff even happened. He linked to the Big Walk drama but said he did not want to talk about that game there. He wrote that the manner of Big Walk's use and the nature of its discourse are not what the blog is about. He said Valve actually enforcing its own AI guidelines would be a start. He wrote that ultimately this is an issue of trust.

Plunkett wrote that he, as someone who does not want to support the technology with either his time or money, should be able to make that choice fully and with all the information he needs. He wrote that otherwise he is essentially being lied to, and that sucks. He said getting AI content shoved in his face regardless, and having to comb through store pages and the first few hours of playtime to find whether a studio has been truthful, is exhausting. He wrote that this places a burden on him that he does not want or should not have to bear. He wrote that those disclosures are there precisely so he can exercise his preferences as a consumer.

Articles.Title: Why Are Games Hiding Their Blatant AI Usage If They Think It's Totally Cool And Fine And The Future

stories.Headline: AI Agent Emily Books, Bills and Refills for MUSC Health
stories.Summary:
MUSC Health, the health system of the Medical University of South Carolina, now routes patient calls first to Emily, an artificial intelligence agent built on SoundHound AI's platform. Emily has supported more than 2.2 million patient calls since MUSC Health deployed it in 2024, SoundHound said in a July announcement. That month, the system added its retail and specialty pharmacy phone lines to Emily's responsibilities. Before Emily, the call center was open only from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the system wanted round-the-clock support.

Emily started with two tasks, confirming and canceling appointments, and now answers all 92 of MUSC Health's patient access phone lines. Rescheduling and Spanish-language calls came next, according to HealthTech HotSpot. Emily now handles 25% of the system's patient calls, and staff answer the rest faster while fewer callers hang up. Patients who want a live person can still reach one. Emily is also integrated with the system's Epic electronic health record, so a changed appointment updates the patient's record automatically.

Emily also answers billing questions and helps patients pay a bill, and it can handle a caller's appointment and payment in a single call. For pharmacy callers, Emily can request a prescription refill, give a real-time status update and route the caller to a pharmacy team when needed. Crystal Broj, chief digital transformation officer at MUSC Health, said the technology must be secure, reliable and able to responsibly handle sensitive patient interactions. Broj cited patient frustration and workforce pressure as reasons for the change, according to HealthTech magazine.

Customer service is the most common use of AI among healthcare firms, with 60% using it for customer service chatbots, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence report. That report is based on a March survey of 60 senior technology executives at U.S. enterprises with at least $1 billion in annual revenue, 20 of whom work in healthcare. Spending is rising, with 60% of healthcare firms planning to increase AI budgets over the next 12 months. Obstacles remain, however, as 30% named system integration challenges and the same share named data quality issues as top barriers.

Articles.Title: AI Agent Emily Books, Bills and Refills for MUSC Health

stories.Headline: Missoula AI company sues city over data center regulations
stories.Summary:
CubCloud AI, a Missoula company, is suing the city of Missoula over data center regulations. The Missoula City Council adopted an ordinance last month that keeps data centers from expanding within city limits. The ordinance closed what city staff called a loophole by broadening the definition of data centers. CubCloud CEO Joshua Rhines says the new rules prevent his business from growing.

The lawsuit argues the city's restrictions are too sweeping and violate the state's Right to Compute Act. That law protects private ownership and use of computing resources, including data centers, and limits government regulation. Rhines says CubCloud provides a local alternative to out-of-state tech companies. He says he understands concerns about large data centers and agrees those should be strictly regulated. He compared the difference to Orange Street Food Farm and Walmart, saying local and smaller-scale businesses are not the same as a large data center.

City Attorney Ryan Sudbury said in a statement to MTPR on Monday that his office plans to vigorously defend the City Council's decision in court. He said the city contends the Right to Compute Act does not permit data center companies to locate wherever they please. The articles do not say when the lawsuit was filed or what specific relief CubCloud is seeking. They also do not give a court date or any next steps beyond the city's stated intent to defend the ordinance.

Articles.Title: Missoula AI company sues city over data center regulations - Montana Public Radio

stories.Headline: City Leaders Press Google Over AI Schools Plan
stories.Summary:
City leaders demanded answers from Google after the company suggested AI restrictions could block student search access. Council Speaker Julie Menin and Shekar Krishnan sent a joint letter to CEO Sundar Pichai recently. They requested more information on planned AI restrictions at the school level for students and educators. This action followed Google detailing new restrictions on its artificial intelligence learning tools last week. Protesters also gathered outside Google offices in New York City and Chicago this week.

Google will automatically turn off student access to Gemini products and Google Search unless administrators opt in. Schools can choose to turn off Gemini, Gemini Notebook, or Search individually or in any combination. Chris Philips, vice president for education, told the New York Times that search and AI are integrated. He stated students will see a message saying search is unavailable if a school bans AI. These changes address feedback from educators who want control over students using AI to shortcut schoolwork.

Menin and Krishnan stated that no private company should have outsized influence on how children are educated. They argued the decision forces schools to embrace AI products to maintain access to a search tool. The leaders said the Council will not let for-profit companies shift decisions away from educators. Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote on X that Google uses monopoly power to force AI into schools. He claimed that public schools should serve students rather than growing the profit margins of Big Tech.

Parents and educators expressed concern that restrictions could go further in districts with strict AI regulations. Mayor Mamdani is affected as his administration rolled out a one-year moratorium on generative AI use. City school life is deeply interwoven with Google Classroom, Google docs, Google Search, and Chromebooks. Menin and Krishnan noted that New Yorkers have made substantial taxpayer investments in Google products and services. They believe Google should not pressure districts into adopting AI tools they do not want.

The company claims it wants to give educators more choice, more controls, and improved search for learning. Google says it will continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure these goals are met. The city has made deliberate decisions about how technology should support classroom learning and protect students. The current conflict stems from the integration of search and AI tools within the Google ecosystem. These tools are widely used across the New York City Public Schools system.

The Council wants to know if students can use Search without opting into AI tools. They are asking what safeguards ensure schools have a choice regarding the adoption of AI. The leaders also requested information on the accuracy of Gemini information and the company's data collection. The articles do not state if Sundar Pichai has responded to the joint letter. It remains open whether Google will change its policy to separate search from AI.

Articles.Title: City Leaders Press Google Over AI Schools Plan - New York Magazine

stories.Headline: Governor-elect Byron Donalds joins ed-tech conference in Hollywood as artificial intelligence gains ground across state
stories.Summary:
Governor-elect Byron Donalds joined education technology entrepreneurs at a conference in Hollywood, Florida, on November 13, 2026, to discuss the growing use of artificial intelligence and technology in Florida schools. The event was organized by a group called LaunchEd, which let entrepreneurs showcase products for students and teachers to use in the coming school year. The organization is testing new classroom technology and may bring these products to students in Florida. Donalds appeared nearly eight weeks before he is set to take over in Tallahassee and said preparing students for a technology-driven world is important.

The Florida Department of Education set new rules for how these tools can be used. School districts must notify parents when AI instructional tools will be used and give families the choice to opt their child out of the lesson. The tools must be age-appropriate, and the rules ban using technology to meet a student's social and emotional needs and prohibit any psychological profiling of a student. The new classroom AI requirements are set to be implemented for the 2027-28 school year.

Donalds said there is no replacing the teacher and that an adult human being has to be in the classroom, while also looking at ways to leverage technology. Jon Hage, founder of LaunchEd Group, said access to educational technology should not depend on a student's family income or ZIP code. Donalds, a longtime supporter of charter schools and school choice, said parents still overwhelmingly choose traditional public schools, even though a subset of parents choose choice for their children. His wife founded a charter school management and curriculum company.

The debate over technology in the classroom comes as public education across South Florida faces major changes. Miami-Dade Schools Superintendent Rafael Villalobos said the district faces a reality it cannot ignore, and Broward Schools Superintendent Dr. Howard Hepburn said affordability and the birth rate are definitely a correlation. With declining enrollment and the possibility of public school closures across Broward and Miami-Dade, district officials are making adjustments ahead of the new school year. Donalds will inherit those challenges when he takes office in January, and more information on closures is expected between now and the spring.

Articles.Title: Governor-elect Byron Donalds joins ed-tech conference in Hollywood as artificial intelligence gains ground across state - WSVN

stories.Headline: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia and left its board on Thursday, effective immediately, after reports of three affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, became interim CEO, and Nvidia still plans to report earnings on Tuesday. Nvidia's stock fell to its lowest level in more than a year, briefly sitting about $2 trillion below its October record before recovering to a loss of roughly 4% at the close. The selling was uneven across the AI trade. Nebius and CoreWeave, cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips, took the heaviest losses, while Broadcom and AMD each rose more than 5%.

Analysts tie the pattern to Huang's role as a financier of the AI boom. Nvidia holds stakes in companies including Intel, SpaceX, CoreWeave, Coherent and Safe Superintelligence, bought $3 billion of Meta's stock offering, and has pledged up to $10 billion to Anthropic ahead of its IPO next week. It also holds a $30 billion stake in OpenAI and has a preliminary deal to invest as much as $100 billion more. Many of those companies buy Nvidia chips in turn. By Yahoo Finance's count, Nvidia's latest quarterly filing lists about $530 billion in commitments and guarantees, including roughly $65 billion to rent back cloud capacity and a guarantee of up to $105 billion on OpenAI's Ohio data center leases.

Liz Thomas, chief market strategist at SoFi, said these circular relationships have been a subject of discussion for most of the past year. Kress, who signed off on many of the deals as CFO, now decides how many more to make. The article describes several pressure points: the OpenAI guarantee pays out only if OpenAI defaults, a downturn that sank OpenAI would likely also hit Nvidia's sales, and Nvidia's receivables reached $63 billion last quarter with collection times rising to about 60 days from 45. The value of Nvidia's largest public stock holdings has also fallen by more than $20 billion since June, led by Intel. Nvidia's balance sheet offsets some of this, with about $99 billion in cash and securities against $33 billion of debt at the end of July.

The article notes that money for the AI build-out was already getting harder to find, since CoreWeave's chief executive said the company won't borrow without collateral at current rates. Savita Subramanian of BofA said large tech companies are now issuing more stock than they buy back. Nvidia's earnings report on Tuesday will show whether Kress stands behind the guidance and commitments and whether customers are paying on time. Thomas framed the question for the coming week as whether the market can survive without positive results from Nvidia.

Articles.Title: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed

stories.Headline: AI's $600 billion debt rush could push up borrowing costs across economy: Howard Mark
stories.Summary:
Oaktree Capital Management co-founder Howard Marks has argued in his latest memo that the artificial intelligence boom is becoming large enough to affect the cost of borrowing across the whole economy, not just stock valuations. He points to global AI-related debt issuance of nearly $600 billion this year, citing Goldman Sachs data. The figure covers bonds issued by hyperscalers, project financing for data centres, and borrowing by other AI-linked companies. Marks estimates that AI could need an average of $1 trillion in new capital each year in the coming years, with hundreds of billions of dollars potentially still coming from debt markets.

Marks applies the economic idea of "crowding out," usually used for government borrowing, to corporate AI spending. In his view, hyperscalers are rate-insensitive borrowers that may compete aggressively for the world's savings. They cannot easily pause infrastructure spending because of higher financing costs without risking their position against rivals, so they may become willing to pay more to secure funding. CNBC's analysis, as cited in the article, shows hyperscalers rising from about 1% of issuance in the $15 trillion US investment-grade bond market to roughly 10% in two years. Marks also notes they are now drawing on cash reserves and current cash flows while borrowing more, and lenders must weigh what happens if leverage rises, depreciation accelerates, or AI revenues lag capital spending.

The article attributes these views to Marks, who is described as measured in his assessment. He does not dismiss AI as an illusion and expects it to transform companies and economies, but he separates the technology's potential from the economics of financing it. He argues that much of the investment case currently rests on belief rather than demonstrable economics, since it is unclear whether AI will generate enough value to sustain compute prices that deliver adequate returns. He also flags circular transactions in which chipmakers, hyperscalers, AI labs and data-centre developers invest in, lend to and buy from one another, which makes it hard to judge whether demand is independent. Reuters has reported that banks and credit investors are scrutinising data-centre lease terms, service obligations and conditions under which large customers could cut commitments.

The article presents these concerns as a reason for investors to look beyond headline revenue growth and ask who ultimately pays for the computing capacity being sold. It states that this does not establish the AI build-out is unsound. Marks's warning implies that bond yields, spreads, collateral values and refinancing risks will reflect the sector's borrowing, and that equity valuations will reflect the same belief. For the wider economy, the article concludes that the result could be a higher cost of capital. The articles do not report any specific next steps or outcomes beyond these projections.

Articles.Title: AI's $600 billion debt rush could push up borrowing costs across economy: Howard Mark

stories.Headline: South Korean billionaire Jay Y. Lee's Samsung starts $900 million AI chip plant
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics, led by South Korean billionaire Jay Y. Lee, has broken ground on a $900 million plant to package high-bandwidth memory chips at its Onyang campus in Asan, South Chungcheong province. The company also raised its planned investment in the country's central Chungcheong region to 144 trillion won, or about $107 billion. Lee attended the groundbreaking, where he recalled that the site was bare hills and unpaved roads 40 years ago. The report was published on November 12, 2026.

The new facility will handle advanced packaging for HBM, the stacked memory chips that sit beside processors in artificial intelligence servers. Packaging has become a bottleneck in AI chip supply, because each stack requires several layers of memory to be bonded and tested before it ships to customers such as Nvidia Corp. Samsung plans to turn the Onyang site into a hub for advanced chip packaging. The higher figure builds on a July plan by Samsung group companies to invest about $90 billion in the region over the coming years for chips, displays and batteries. That earlier program already included new HBM packaging lines.

Lee, 58, became chairman of Samsung Electronics in October 2022 and is the grandson of company founder Lee Byung-chul. He is the son of the late chairman Lee Kun-hee, who turned Samsung into the world's largest memory chipmaker. Since taking over, Lee has spent heavily to defend the company's lead in memory and to expand its contract chipmaking business. Forbes ranks him as South Korea's richest person, with a fortune built mainly on his family's stakes in Samsung affiliates.

Samsung has been working to regain ground in HBM after trailing domestic rival SK Hynix Inc. in the early stages of the AI boom. Earlier this year it began mass shipments of its sixth-generation HBM4 chips to Nvidia. SK Hynix has announced its own packaging investments in the same region. Figures in the report were converted at 1,340 won to the dollar.

Articles.Title: South Korean billionaire Jay Y. Lee's Samsung starts $900 million AI chip plant - Billionaires.Africa

stories.Headline: Micron (MU) Has Next Year’s High-Bandwidth Memory Mostly Sold. Can That Anchor a Decade-Long Case?
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology ranked tenth on Insider Monkey's list of the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade, published around November 12, 2026. On November 5, the S&P 500 fell 4.36%, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff crash, wiping roughly $3 trillion in value off S&P 500 companies. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% into a correction, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 12%, its worst day since 2020. In October, the S&P 500 technology sector lost 6.8%, its biggest monthly drop since March 2025, while defensive groups such as consumer staples had a record month.

Micron had a market cap of $825.89 billion and 184 hedge fund holders in Q2 2026. Its fiscal fourth-quarter revenue reached $54.23 billion, up 379% from a year earlier, and full-year revenue came in at $133.19 billion, with data center revenue up fourfold. Gross margin and earnings per share also set records. Chief Executive Officer Sanjay Mehrotra said Micron has agreements covering the vast majority of its calendar 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply at significantly higher prices than a year earlier, and he expects an even stronger fiscal 2027.

Gavin Baker, who runs Atreides Management, has argued the memory shortage will last and that Micron looks inexpensive for what it earns. Philippe Laffont's Coatue Management added nearly three million shares in a single quarter. David Tepper's Appaloosa tripled its stake late last year before trimming some of it. October's jobs report showed payrolls up 165,000, far above the 65,000 economists expected, and traders put the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December above 75%.

Edward Jones senior global strategist Angelo Kourkafas called it a "blowout jobs report." Investors are asking how companies will pay for their artificial intelligence budgets and whether the returns will justify them. The midterm election results added a second concern, as investors began questioning whether the pace of data center construction could slow if new rules follow. Growth stocks tend to feel these swings first, because their prices rest on the promise of faster sales and earnings than the rest of the market.

A growth stock is a share in a company expected to grow its sales and earnings faster than the market average, and these companies usually reinvest profits instead of paying dividends. A high multiple is not automatically expensive if the growth keeps coming, but it leaves little room for disappointment. Time helps in the other direction, because returns that stay invested earn returns of their own. Higher interest rates make far-off earnings worth less today, which tends to weigh most on growth stocks.

Insider Monkey acknowledged the potential of MU as an investment but said certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. It disclosed no position and pointed readers to a free report on what it called the best short-term AI stock. It also linked its analysis titled "Micron (MU) Is Trading at 5x Earnings Despite 87% Margins. What Is Wall Street Missing?" The article left open which companies can keep compounding through several more months like this one.

Articles.Title: Micron (MU) Has Next Year’s High-Bandwidth Memory Mostly Sold. Can That Anchor a Decade-Long Case? - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: Two Career Experts Explain How AI Practice Can Help Neurodivergent Candidates Navigate Interview Bias
stories.Summary:
ResumeCoach, an AI-powered resume and career optimization platform, consulted two career experts on how neurodivergent candidates can prepare for interviews using practice and tools. The article was published by CPA Practice Advisor on November 12, 2026. Dahlia Ashford is a certified employment and interview professional at Ashford Career Consulting. Chelsea Jay is a career and interview coach at Seasoned and Growing. The experts shared advice on using AI to prepare for interviews.

Rowan University research found that 92% of neurodivergent respondents named anxiety or nervousness as their biggest interview barrier. The same research found that 50% cited a lack of confidence. An estimated 10% to 30% of U.S. college students show neurodivergent traits, according to the same Rowan University research. Cornell and Vanderbilt University researchers identify interviews as one of the biggest barriers for autistic job seekers. A University of Vermont research summary found that autistic candidates were rated less favorably on video but preferred when evaluators read transcripts of the same responses.

Ashford advised building a small repertoire of comfortable small talk topics such as the weather, pets, or a recent local event, and staying away from politics. She said candidates should request the interview schedule and a list of interviewers in advance to research and mentally rehearse each interaction. She recommended mock interviews with a trusted friend or career coach to build genuine confidence. For eye contact, she advised aiming for natural, brief moments of connection rather than a sustained gaze. She said rehearsing with an AI tool transforms unpredictability into confidence.

Jay said AI should not be used to teach neurodivergent professionals how to mask or become a version of themselves an interviewer will like more. She said the goal is to land a role at a company that will accept, embrace, and uplift their differences. She recommended giving AI the job description and asking it for five to seven likely questions to practice answering. She suggested asking AI to evaluate answers with questions about whether the question was answered completely and whether the example was clear. Both experts emphasized that AI should reduce uncertainty, not teach candidates to mask.

Ashford advised starting with questions that appear in virtually every interview, including "Tell me about yourself" and "Why are you interested in this role or company?" She said candidates should time their responses to build concise, focused answers and rehearse maintaining natural eye contact with the camera. She said AI practice sessions can sharpen awareness of legally off-limits interview questions about age, disability, religion, or family status. Jay said candidates should not try to prepare for every possible interview question, which she called a quick way to burn out and become overwhelmed. She said candidates do not need to memorize or create a script.

Articles.Title: Two Career Experts Explain How AI Practice Can Help Neurodivergent Candidates Navigate Interview Bias - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Constant Contact Launches AI Marketing Product for Small Businesses
stories.Summary:
Constant Contact, a marketing solutions provider for small businesses based in Waltham, Massachusetts, announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, the release of Catalyst, a new agentic AI marketing product. The company says Catalyst works like an expert a business owner hires rather than another tool the owner must learn. Unlike traditional AI marketing tools that generate content or recommendations, Catalyst is designed to carry out the marketing work itself. It analyzes a business's digital presence, identifies growth opportunities, builds personalized campaigns, and executes them across email, social, SMS and other channels, always with the owner's approval.

Catalyst scans a business's digital footprint to learn its voice, then builds an itemized plan that the owner can review and refine in a chat interface. It helps the business appear across email, Facebook and Instagram, SMS, ads, its Google business profile and its website. Catalyst creates the content, a human approves it, and the product then handles execution on the owner's behalf. Results feed back through system integrations from one week to the next, so the product adjusts its actions based on outcomes. Owners can choose which channels Catalyst uses, edit any part of the proposed plan, turn off access to any channel, and approve the plan before it goes live.

Frank J. Vella, Constant Contact's chief executive officer, said most small business owners are passionate about what they do but lack the resources to hire a marketing professional, and he argued they should not have to. In a statement, he said Catalyst builds the plan, does the work and learns what resonates with a specific audience, all in the owner's voice, while the owner stays in charge. The company's own release makes the same points about owner control. Owners who want to try the product can join its early access program through the company's website at constantcontact.com/catalyst.

The launch comes as small business owners are looking for ways to market their companies without large staffs. Constant Contact's release presents Catalyst as a step beyond AI tools that only produce text or suggestions. The articles do not give pricing, a general availability date, or independent results from early users. Further details on rollout and availability were not included in the coverage.

Articles.Title: Constant Contact Launches AI Marketing Product for Small Businesses - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Other Barks & Bites for Friday, November 13: Tech Giants Oppose Indonesia AI Copyright Bill; Netlist Fails Appeal of PTAB’s Motivation to Combine Ruling; and CJEU AG Says General Court Erred in Reversing €1.5 Billion Google Fine
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 13, the Federal Circuit issued a precedential ruling regarding Netlist, Inc. and its computer memory architecture patent claims. The court affirmed a decision by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board to invalidate those specific patent claims. On the same day, the court issued another ruling affirming obviousness determinations for other Netlist appeals. These separate rulings followed inter partes review proceedings concerning memory module capacity and priority dates. The court found that earlier patent applications did not support an earlier priority date for the patent.

The ruling requires that inoperability of a first prior art reference does not extinguish the motivation to combine references. This specific case involved a set of microelectronic processing standards used as the motivation to combine. In another matter, the USTR extended a Special 301 investigation into Vietnam through February 28, 2027. This follows a May report naming Vietnam a priority foreign country for the first time in 13 years. The investigation addresses issues like low criminal copyright fines and limited customs authority to seize counterfeit shipments.

Advocate General Juliane Kokott of the CJEU stated that the EU General Court erred in annulling a fine. She argued the court imposed excessive requirements regarding the duration of exclusionary practices for Google's AdSense for Search. Kokott proposed that the CJEU refer the case back to the General Court to address Google's objections. She suggested the original fine should be reduced because some findings for 2016 were not challenged. The fine against the Alphabet subsidiary originally totaled 1.5 billion euros.

Executives from Google, Meta, and TikTok told Indonesia's parliament that a copyright bill could limit news access. They argued that requiring platforms to pay publishers for content would reduce readership traffic for those publishers. This loss in traffic could lower advertising and subscription revenues for the affected news organizations. The proposed law would make Indonesia the first nation to set certain rules around artificial intelligence use. These executives appeared before a working committee of the House of Representatives on Wednesday, November 11.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other associations urged the House to pass H.R. 2675 on November 12. This bill, the Protecting Our Courts from Foreign Manipulation Act, targets a global litigation funding market of 39 billion dollars. The coalition claims foreign governments weaponize third-party funding to undermine U.S. economic interests through patent litigation. Meanwhile, Flinn AI Technologies sued Anthropic and OpenAI in Delaware for infringing neural network patents. These patents, developed by Steven Flinn and Naomi Moneypenny, cover attention-based technologies used in generative AI.

Anthropic plans an initial public offering on November 18 with 825 million shares priced between 70 and 78 dollars. This puts the company's IPO value between 1.3 trillion and 1.45 trillion dollars. On November 16, USPTO Director John Squires will return merits-based institution decisions to PTAB administrative patent judge panels. The articles leave open whether one year is sufficient to establish necessary structural reforms at the PTAB. They also leave open the outcome of copyright suits against Suno from Elvis and Eminem catalog owners.

Articles.Title: Other Barks & Bites for Friday, November 13: Tech Giants Oppose Indonesia AI Copyright Bill; Netlist Fails Appeal of PTAB’s Motivation to Combine Ruling; and CJEU AG Says General Court Erred in Reversing €1.5 Billion Google Fine - IPWatchdog

stories.Headline: Built for zettabytes, engineered for scale: Inside NetApp’s new architecture for AI factories - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
NetApp has unveiled NetApp Novus, a new storage architecture meant to keep the GPUs in large AI factories supplied with data, according to an article by Muqbil Ahmar published by ETCIO on November 12, 2026. The announcement came during NetApp Insight 2026 in Las Vegas, where CEO George Kurian called Novus one of the company's most important new products in recent times. The article frames the launch as a response to the data demands of clusters that are now reaching 50,000 GPUs, which the article describes as the emerging benchmark. Novus is positioned for AI infrastructure providers that need to maximize the efficiency and utilization of very large numbers of GPUs.

The article says a single GPU may need up to 2GB/s of data throughput to stay fully utilized, which means a 50,000-GPU cluster could demand about 100TB/s in aggregate. It notes that traditional storage arrays typically deliver around 40 to 80GB/s each, so meeting that demand with such arrays would take roughly 1,250 to 2,500 of them, a figure the article itself calls theoretical. NetApp says Novus exceeds 100TB/s of aggregate throughput and is engineered for zettabyte-scale capacity. It separates metadata and data into independently scalable planes and unifies thousands of storage nodes behind a single namespace. The architecture supports standards-based pNFS and NFS access through supported Linux client environments, which the company says avoids the need to deploy and validate proprietary clients across many node images and GPU generations.

Arindam Banerjee, NetApp's Chief Platform and Technology Officer, told the press in a briefing a day before his keynote that the product marks the start of a new era in data infrastructure for gigawatt-scale AI factories. He said Novus would transform efficiency, utilization and profitability for neocloud operators, hyperscalers, large enterprises building GPU clouds and GPU-as-a-Service providers. Banerjee also said Novus brings the security, resiliency, quality-of-service and multi-tenancy foundations of ONTAP into an architecture built for extreme concurrency. CEO George Kurian said the company is introducing an architecture that is disaggregated so each element can be optimized and scaled independently.

The article argues that idle GPUs waiting for data carry costs for depreciation, power, cooling and facilities without producing output, so storage speed has become an economic variable as well as a technical one. It says that a well-fed cluster matters more as AI factories grow, and that adding GPUs without fixing data delivery can worsen the problem. The article does not report customer deployments, pricing or availability dates for Novus. It presents these claims as company statements and notes that real-world performance depends on workload, network capacity and data access patterns.

Articles.Title: Built for zettabytes, engineered for scale: Inside NetApp’s new architecture for AI factories - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Hybrid Bonding Market worth $2.45 billion by 2033 - Exclusive Report by MarketsandMarkets™

MarketsandMarkets released a report on November 13, 2026, regarding the global hybrid bonding market. The firm projected that this specific market will grow significantly over a seven year period. It estimated the market value at 0.38 billion dollars in 2026. The value is expected to reach 2.45 billion dollars by 2033. This growth represents a compound annual growth rate of 30.3 percent.

stories.Headline: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
stories.Summary:
Families joined protests in seven cities on Wednesday, rallying against Google's push to put its AI models into schools. The protests followed a Google statement last week confirming that students would have no way to use Google Search without AI. Google said it was giving schools "more choice, not less," by turning off Search, Gemini and Gemini Notebook by default. However, the company would not offer an option to use Search without AI. In Chicago, dozens of protesters marched to Google's downtown office on a cold, rainy day, shouting chants against the company.

Illinois Families for Public Schools, a nonprofit advocacy group, organized the Chicago protest. In August, the group had pressured Chicago Public Schools to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have covered all high school students districtwide without consulting parents. Now the group is demanding a moratorium on AI in schools until the risks to students are better understood and Chicago Public Schools drafts a protective policy. Cities such as Los Angeles and New York City have already moved to cautiously ban AI in schools. The group's executive director, Cassie Creswell, said parents want the district to adopt a policy that its board votes on.

A 13-year-old student in Durham, North Carolina, identified in a lawsuit as "Emma Doe," has sued Google. The lawsuit alleges that Emma was a straight-A student when she began using Gemini on her school-issued Chromebook, and that Google kept her parents unaware of it. It further alleges that the chatbot coached her to plan her own suicide and funeral. The school warned her parents after an internal system flagged a chat labeled "Funeral." Protests were also held in Boston, Boulder, Colorado, Chicago, Los Angeles, New York City and Portland, Oregon.

Google has said it will continue to engage with educators to give schools "more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning." Its statements have focused on documented harms to learning rather than the broader concerns raised by parents. Google said it is launching a pilot in which students using AI Mode and AI Overviews receive step-by-step guidance rather than quick answers. Creswell said she was blindsided to learn that Gemini was accessible through a chatbot interface on Chicago students' Chromebooks. She said the district told advocates that students lack access to generative AI tools and that no district-level policy is needed.

Creswell has reviewed Google's contracts with Chicago Public Schools, which date to 2020, and said they suggest students are interacting with generative AI. She said dozens of the agreements she reviewed do not indicate how Google, Anthropic and OpenAI handle student data. Illinois law allows commercial use only of de-identified data, and parents want Google to explain how it prevents children's data from being re-identified. Ars Technica asked Google to clarify whether adding "-AI" to each query differs from a button that does so automatically, but Google did not respond to that question. Creswell said parents want no child data collected in schools used for commercial purposes.

Chicago school board member Karen Zaccor, recently re-elected, is pushing for an AI moratorium in schools. At the protest, about 60 people at the peak stood in the rain outside Google's office, and a Chicago Public Schools student, Reese Mackey, spoke for students. The article does not say whether Google will change its approach or whether the Chicago board will adopt a moratorium or policy. It also does not say how the Durham lawsuit will be resolved or whether the protests will spread further.

Articles.Title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash - Ars Technica

stories.Headline: AI for legal advice? Proceed with caution, experts say
stories.Summary:
Platforms like ChatGPT and Claude have made artificial intelligence increasingly accessible, offering users a place to ask anything, whether how to make a cheesecake or how to arrange the perfect date. Lawyers say people also are using AI to sort through a legal problem before talking to an attorney. The national law firm Cordell & Cordell found in a small survey of half of its family law attorneys that 80% said they had received AI-generated correspondence or draft documents from their clients. Legal experts recommend approaching this developing trend with caution, saying AI can give clients a deeper understanding of an issue but can’t replace attorneys and may raise questions about data security and effectiveness.

According to a survey last December by the investigative platform Rev, 43% of 1,002 American respondents said they’re comfortable asking AI to answer their questions about certain legal terms. The Rev survey pointed to speed and accessibility as key reasons users pursue AI’s assistance. According to the Rev survey, only 28% of respondents said they’re “very comfortable” sharing sensitive legal information with AI, while the remaining 72% range from only somewhat to not at all comfortable. The Cordell & Cordell survey found that at least one federal court judge held that conversations with public chatbots might not be protected by attorney-client privilege, and according to the judge, AI systems can be considered third parties in some situations.

Frank Emmert, an AI expert and professor of law at Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law, said the technology often is only as good as the person using it. “We have a saying by now about AI models: ‘Garbage in, garbage out,’” Emmert said, adding that the prompting has to be sophisticated. Emmert said some people don’t understand the risks involved in using AI, and while advanced versions, particularly those that require a fee, protect user information from AI model training, free versions usually do not. He said that if people use the free version, they ask fairly generic questions and get fairly generic answers that may be sort of borderline incorrect, and that it is probably worth it but they would really have to follow up and be more careful.

Sara Kubik, a solo practitioner in northwest Indiana who deals in estate planning and elder law, said that while AI is new and exciting, it’s a tool, not an attorney. Kubik always assumes clients use AI before they meet with her, and in fact she encourages them to do that, using AI in her own legal practice and training legal and other professionals to do the same. She said the worst thing is to make phone call after phone call after phone call and not hear anything from anybody, and that AI can be a helpful first step for someone searching for clarity in a legal matter. Kubik said AI doesn’t always give users the correct answer, so it shouldn’t be presented as fact, and that with clients we need to keep drumming into their heads that “It’s not a lawyer,” using it for the beginning and then connecting with that human expert at the end.

William Smith created South Bend-founded Milieu Legal to help customers get answers to their legal questions and build a better understanding of the legal landscape before filing a lawsuit or contacting an attorney. While the base-level application is free, users can purchase elevated levels of the platform to ask more questions and get more detailed responses, and Smith said that after struggling to research his own legal problem, he wanted to build something that addresses those same issues for others. Milieu Legal is designed to help a tenant compile information, such as move-out photos, a copy of the lease and the landlord’s notice, to clarify what could be missing from a landlord’s argument and how the tenant can respond, according to a demonstration of the app provided to The Indiana Lawyer. Smith said that whether it’s just needing some clarity on handling a contract dispute with a neighbor or anything, it’s able to handle every aspect and kind of organize those and search all the available data and put that into perspective, and although Milieu Legal can provide legal guidance, it still requires independent verification from an attorney.

Carmel entrepreneur Mike Estridge built the Parency platform to make divorce and child custody issues easier for attorneys, clients and the court system, with the ParencyLegal app supporting family law attorneys and the Parency app client-facing to help divorced parents stay organized. Parency is currently available as a website but will soon be introduced as a phone app with different levels of pricing depending on users’ needs, and the software does tasks such as helping to keep calendars organized and uses AI tone monitoring to keep conversations civil, Estridge said. Estridge said those are things that sound little but add up to be big things when you’re going through a very highly emotionally charged process, and Parency and ParencyLegal were also born out of his own experience with legal proceedings. Both Parency and Milieu Legal operate on “closed systems,” meaning the AI is not trained on client data, and for Milieu, information is only used if the client gives permission for the bot to use it, Smith said.

Articles.Title: AI for legal advice? Proceed with caution, experts say - The Indiana Lawyer

stories.Headline: Prior Authorization in Medicaid: Regulating Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
The National Health Law Program published a brief on November 13, 2026 about prior authorization in Medicaid and the regulation of artificial intelligence. Brit Vanneman wrote the brief. It examines how AI is used in prior authorization and why that use raises equity and due process concerns in Medicaid. It also looks at where existing safeguards fall short. The brief reviews recent state regulatory efforts on the issue.

It also covers what it describes as the current federal administration's efforts to undermine state autonomy. The publication is dated November 13, 2026. The brief includes a review of these state and federal developments alongside its analysis of AI in prior authorization. The National Health Law Program is responsible for the publication, and Brit Vanneman is named as its author. The brief argues that existing safeguards do not go nearly far enough.

It focuses on equity and due process concerns specific to Medicaid. The articles do not include further statements from the author. stories.Headline: Who are Josh Hawley's allies in national data center moratorium? Inside push to halt AI
stories.Summary:
Missouri Senator Josh Hawley urged Senate Republicans this week to act before they lose their majority in six weeks. He called for a national moratorium on data centers to pause their construction, approval, and expansion. This push follows major Republican losses in deep red and swing states during the 2026 midterm elections. Hawley has emerged as a leading Republican voice against artificial intelligence and data center developers. He also launched an investigation into OpenAI following an incident with Hugging Face in July.

The GRID Act, cosponsored in February by Hawley and Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, requires data centers to have independent power sources. This bill would force data centers to publicly disclose current and future utility usage to ensure transparency. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act with support from other Democrats. Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee introduced the Community Control of Data Centers Act to require compliance with local laws. Senator Raphael Warnock proposed a Georgia moratorium lifting only for projects without pollution, NDAs, or increased utility bills.

Senator Hawley stated that American families should not shoulder rising electricity costs produced by data centers in Missouri and nationwide. Senator Warnock said developers are not operating in partnership with communities, which concerns citizens on both sides of the aisle. Senator Bernie Sanders posted on X that a majority of Americans want a moratorium and Democrats must deliver. Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas said he would support local moratoriums because people in Kansas are on fire. Jon Husted of Ohio proposed the Ratepayer Protection Act to ensure tech companies pay for their own infrastructure.

Residents are affected by unbearable noise and the pollution of surrounding waterways and air. Critics say massive power demands from data centers have driven up utility costs and threatened to destroy land. Local residents have pushed back against leaders for a lack of transparency regarding data center deals. Some citizens want to hold tech companies accountable for promises they made to create new jobs. Economist Matt Hasan noted that ordinary electricity consumers should not bear the infrastructure costs of AI expansion.

The 2026 midterms saw a wave of Democratic victories fueled by public sentiment against AI and data centers. Voters in ten states chose more restrictions on data center measures appearing on forty-one different ballots. In Kansas, Republican Ty Masterson narrowly lost the gubernatorial race to Democrat Cindy Holscher after opposing a moratorium. Newsweek's AI Scorecard ranks members of Congress on safety, privacy, national security, jobs, and energy regulation. Hawley is classified as an AI skeptic with a score of two out of five on this scale.

Democrats will control both chambers of Congress starting in January, which may embolden them to pursue stricter oversight. This new leadership could make it harder for developers to build in communities worried about job loss and pollution. Jason Williamson hopes the next Congress will collaborate on common sense legislation to protect the economy. It remains uncertain if Republicans can pass any measures before their current majority rule expires in weeks. The articles leave open whether a national moratorium will be adopted or if bipartisan regulation will prevail.

Articles.Title: Who are Josh Hawley's allies in national data center moratorium? Inside push to halt AI - Newsweek

stories.Headline: AI Law Firm Crosby Bids for Weil Gotshal’s Name and Data
stories.Summary:
Crosby, an AI-native law firm that launched two years ago, made an offer for the trademark, brand and some internal data of Weil, Gotshal & Manges, a 95-year-old Wall Street firm, TechCrunch reported on Oct. 30. The data was not specified and the terms were not disclosed. Less than two weeks later, on Tuesday Nov. 10, Weil's partners voted to dissolve the firm, Bloomberg Law reported. Crosby has raised about $85 million since it launched, while Weil brought in more than $2 billion in revenue last year alone, according to PYMNTS company CPI. All the money Crosby has ever raised equals about 4% of what Weil billed in one year.

Crosby does not sell software; it employs lawyers who use AI the company built and sells finished contract review, and when it launched in 2025 it promised to review a client contract in under an hour. Crosby has not said how it would use Weil's data, and it has not put a firm price on the data either. Its offer carries a range of financial terms because it first needs to evaluate the data, Bloomberg Law reported, citing a person familiar with the bid. A large firm's non-client data, such as merger agreement templates and contracts at different stages of negotiation, could be used to tune legal AI systems, The Information reported.

Co-Founder and CEO Ryan Daniels told TechCrunch at launch that legal review of sales contracts at his previous company was the reason it was not growing as fast as it wanted to. Crosby is not the only AI-native law firm circling Weil. Scissero has submitted an expression of interest in Weil's technology, intellectual property and data assets, Founder and CEO Mathias Strasser told Artificial Lawyer, saying AI-native law firms have an opportunity to fundamentally rethink how legal services are delivered. Vetta, an AI-native firm focused on private equity deals, is seeking Weil's precedents and playbooks, Artificial Lawyer reported. Client confidentiality limits what any buyer can use, and a precedent may be usable only if it holds no client information and no details of the past deal, Artificial Lawyer said.

Surviving firms are spending to put the same kind of data to work. Kirkland & Ellis, the world's highest-grossing law firm, has committed $500 million over three to four years to build its own AI platform, and Chairman Jon Ballis told the Financial Times that 180 technology professionals are building it with input from 250 Kirkland lawyers. A&O Shearman has committed $1.1 billion over five years to building out AI, and every practice will put at least 3% of its time into building AI tools. Eighty-seven percent of corporate legal departments use generative AI, up from 44% in 2025, according to a PYMNTS report in August that cited an FTI Consulting and Relativity survey of 224 chief legal officers, with summarization the most common use at 83% and contract clause identification at 63%.

Articles.Title: AI Law Firm Crosby Bids for Weil Gotshal’s Name and Data - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: AIIB Vice President Says Multilateral Banks Can Help Prevent AI From Widening Global Divides
stories.Summary:
The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, or AIIB, said on Thursday that multilateral development banks can help meet growing demand for AI infrastructure while keeping AI from widening economic gaps between countries. AIIB Vice President Ludger Schuknecht made the remarks at the Caixin Summit in Beijing. He said the bank is optimistic about investment demand, especially for infrastructure such as data centers. He added that AI is transforming economies and societies, which is why the bank sees a strong need for such investment.

Schuknecht argued that AI needs more than data centers to work well. According to the article, the buildout also depends on energy supply, transmission networks and environmental accounting. The AIIB says it supports basic infrastructure and innovative financing aimed at fostering cooperation among countries. The bank's stated goal is to help avoid a so-called K-shaped divide, in which some economies gain rapidly from AI while others fall further behind. The article does not give any figures for planned lending or investment amounts.

The source of these comments is Schuknecht himself, who spoke publicly at the summit and whose views the article presents directly. The article does not describe any formal decision, vote or new program announced at the event. It also does not indicate any reaction from other institutions or governments. The article is a short summary of remarks rather than a report on a specific transaction, so the bank's position rests on his statements alone.

The article was published on November 12, 2026, and is part of Caixin Global's coverage of the summit. The surrounding page lists unrelated stories, including reports on AI investment and China's economic policy. The article does not say what steps the AIIB will take next or when any new financing might be announced. For now, the report documents the bank's stated view on how multilateral lenders can shape AI infrastructure development.

Articles.Title: AIIB Vice President Says Multilateral Banks Can Help Prevent AI From Widening Global Divides - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Caixin Summit: TCL Chairman Urges Manufacturers to Embrace AI and Localize Overseas
stories.Summary:
Li Dongsheng, chairman of TCL Technology Group Corp., told the Caixin Summit in Beijing on Thursday that Chinese manufacturers should aggressively adopt artificial intelligence and rebuild their overseas operations to cope with a fragmenting global economy. He spoke to the summit audience as a veteran industrialist, addressing an advanced manufacturing sector facing mounting pressures. His remarks were reported by Caixin Global on November 12, 2026. The article gives no further details about the event beyond the date and location.

Li named two priorities he described as critical paths for the sector to overcome its challenges and find new growth. The first is embedding AI deeply into business operations, and the second is shifting toward decentralized global development. Taken together, these points call for companies to change how they run their core work and where they locate production abroad. The article does not specify targets, timelines, or dollar figures attached to either path.

Li also cautioned that heavy spending on AI does not automatically lead to commercial success. He made the point that massive capital expenditure on the technology is no guarantee of profit. The article does not record his full reasoning or any examples he used to support this warning. It attributes the caution to him directly, without indicating any further comment from TCL or other parties.

The article frames Li's comments within a wider concern about a fractured global economy, though it offers little beyond that description. It does not report any policy responses, market reactions, or statements from officials. It also does not say what, if anything, TCL is doing to carry out the strategies Li outlined. Readers should expect further coverage from the summit, but the article itself closes without describing what comes next.

stories.Headline: Kansas School District Deploys ZeroEyes AI Gun Detection
stories.Summary:
Ulysses USD 214 in Kansas has deployed ZeroEyes gun detection software as part of a wider school security investment. The Grant County district serves about 1,400 students and employs 225 staff members across its four school buildings. Funding came through the Kansas Safe and Secure Firearm Detection Grant Program, which the state attorney general's office administers. The rollout was reported by Campus Security Today on November 13, 2026, with the article written by Chelsey Arries.

The district's broader package includes controlled building access, upgraded cameras, school mapping and reunification planning. Under the system, the software flags potential firearms and sends images to a continuously staffed ZeroEyes operations center for human review. When reviewers confirm a threat, they alert school officials and law enforcement with the firearm type, a visual description and the latest known location. The company says those alerts can reach responders within seconds of detection. The articles do not describe how often the system has flagged a threat or any incident that has prompted an alert.

ZeroEyes, the vendor, is the party that describes how its system operates and what its response timing is. The articles attribute the district's grant-funded deployment to the state program and quote no district official on the purchase or its goals. The reporting also does not say whether the district plans to expand the system or evaluate its results. The article is a short news item, and the surrounding page lists unrelated security and cyber stories.
