stories.Headline: Fake content, false impression: Pennsylvania’s AI ad disclosure law takes effect December 21
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed SB 806 on October 22, 2026, creating the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, also known as Act 99 of 2026. The law takes effect December 21, 2026, making Pennsylvania the third state after New York and California to require disclosures for certain AI-generated advertising. Unlike those states, Pennsylvania's law does not focus on synthetic performers. It applies only when AI content creates a false consumer perception. The article's author, a Reed Smith counsel, argues that advertisers should already avoid such ads because misleading advertising is illegal everywhere.

The statute requires that an advertiser not create or disseminate an ad using synthetic content in a way that misleads consumers about the nature, origin, or authenticity of what is being sold, unless a clear and conspicuous disclosure is included. Synthetic content means an image, video, audio clip, or text that has been significantly modified or generated by AI, though text-only content is excluded. The law does not define false consumer perception, so the author expects Pennsylvania to borrow the FTC framework on whether a message is likely to mislead a reasonable consumer and whether it is material. A required disclosure must state that the ad contains AI-modified or AI-generated content, appear the first time the content is shown, and appear in the same medium. The law also sets penalties of up to $3,000 per violation, plus attorney fees and costs, enforced by the Attorney General or district attorneys.

The author notes that the statute has no knowledge requirement, since the final bill removed "knowingly, recklessly or willfully," so advertisers may be liable for the messages they release. The author argues the disclosure cannot cure an ad that is misleading at its core and that adding one could be read as an admission of deception. The author's view is that the law's practical use will be as an added tool for prosecutors against deceptive AI ads already vulnerable under other laws, and that "violation" is undefined, so exposure could grow quickly across high-volume campaigns. The article compares the three state laws, noting that New York's law has a knowledge requirement and California's and Pennsylvania's do not, and that Pennsylvania has the broadest coverage. It recommends eliminating deception rather than designing a disclosure, reviewing routine AI uses, and tightening oversight of agencies and vendors.

Articles.Title: Fake content, false impression: Pennsylvania’s AI ad disclosure law takes effect December 21 - Reed Smith LLP

stories.Headline: AI needs the kind of federal regulation that has made air travel safe [letter]
stories.Summary:
The Wright brothers made their first powered airplane flight on Dec. 17, 1903, near Kill Devil Hills and Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Orville Wright piloted the flight, which covered 120 feet over the ground and lasted 12 seconds. Federal regulation of flight later led to the 1958 creation of what is now the Federal Aviation Administration. That agency manages more than 5.3 million square miles of U.S. airspace through a layered system of control.

The system has three main tiers that work together. Airport traffic control towers handle ground movement on runways and taxiways along with takeoffs and landings near the airport. Terminal radar approach control systems guide aircraft during arrival and departure, up to roughly 10,000 to 17,000 feet, and often serve several regional airports at once. Air route traffic control centers oversee planes as they cross states and time zones. FAA rules and regulations, published in hundreds of pages and documents, direct how these systems are built and run.

In a letter to the editor published Nov. 13, 2026, Dennis Dezort of Marietta argues that artificial intelligence should be governed by a similar framework. He writes that AI today is at roughly the same stage the Wright brothers' airplane was in 1903. He says that systems and rules should be designed now to govern the technology. The letter appeared in LancasterOnline's opinion section and does not describe any proposed legislation or agency action.

Articles.Title: AI needs the kind of federal regulation that has made air travel safe [letter] - LancasterOnline

stories.Headline: Slow and steady characterizes nation’s rational AI buildout
stories.Summary:
The recent swings in US chip stocks, driven by midterm-election worries over data-center regulation, were highlighted in a China Daily commentary published on November 10, 2026. The piece argues that such volatility shows how dependent the American AI buildout has become on a policy and regulatory landscape that could shift quickly. It contrasts this with China's approach, which it describes as demand-driven, self-reliant and coordinated with the power grid. The commentary presents this as a structural difference rather than a boast of superiority.

The piece points to several figures to support its case. Wang Weiming, chief engineer of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, said that in the first three quarters of 2026, computing power driven by domestic AI chips and large language models grew more compatible, with more than 1,000 application scenarios taking shape across 20 industries, including steel, automobiles and pharmaceuticals. Xie Cun, an MIIT spokesman, said China's intelligent computing capacity reached 2,592 EFLOPS by the end of September, up 146 percent year on year. Jiang Yi, a spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, said estimates put new direct investment in computing network construction during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30) at 4 trillion yuan, or about $599.59 billion, with enterprises as the main investors.

The commentary credits several policies for this approach. It describes the "East Data, West Computing" initiative, which links computing demand in eastern China with resources in the western regions. It also cites the separation of industrial and residential electricity pricing, which it says keeps the cost of the buildout from falling on ordinary households. By contrast, the piece describes US data centers competing with homeowners for water in drought-stricken states, pushing up household power bills, and facing projects halted by litigation and protests.

The commentary is not uncritical of China's own path. It warns that rapid growth in computing capacity can invite overheating, and it urges building what is needed, where it is needed, with chips, power and users in place. It frames China's patient, long-term planning as a strategic advantage that must be protected from the temptation to overreach. The article carries no reported reaction from US officials or industry groups, and it does not describe any specific next steps beyond calling for steady and deliberate growth.

Articles.Title: Slow and steady characterizes nation’s rational AI buildout - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: 1 UCL Claim Could Freeze Frontier AI: Lawsuit [2026]
stories.Summary:
Four nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco on November 12, 2026, asking a judge to stop the five biggest frontier AI developers from building anything more capable than what they have today. The plaintiffs named in reporting are Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and The Alliance for Secure AI. The defendants listed by exchange4media are OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and SpaceX. The complaint names ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude among the products at issue. No judge has ruled and nothing is frozen.

The legal basis is California law against unfair business practices, including the state's Unfair Competition Law. The plaintiffs ask for an order stopping the defendants from developing or deploying more advanced AI models until the systems can be shown to be under adequate human control. Reuters carried the story on its wire on November 12, and one smaller outlet dated the complaint a day later. Coverage names three consumer products and two chief executives, Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Elon Musk of SpaceX. It does not confirm which specific model versions the complaint targets, and no case number, exact filing time, damages amount or ruling has been reported.

Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of Alliance for Secure AI, said in a statement carried by CBS News that for years the executives building these systems have warned that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks. He said they keep racing to develop and market increasingly powerful AI that they admit they cannot reliably control, and are now handing over AI research and development to AI itself. A spokesperson for the plaintiff coalition, whose name the release does not give, said they must freeze frontier AI development until the technology is under control and the American people have a say and a stake in its future. Machine.net's coverage cites Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei saying that we do not understand how our own AI creations work. The defendants have not been quoted in the sources reviewed with a substantive reply.

Reporting says the complaint claims AI systems have bypassed safeguards and accessed computer systems without authorization. The allegations center on risks to public health, safety and property, and the plaintiffs lean on the defendants' own words, wanting executives' warnings read as admissions. AF.net's account frames the case as a shift from voluntary corporate commitments toward state-level enforcement and says the plaintiffs rely on the labs' own research and promotional claims as evidence. That account also describes the requested relief in broader terms than other outlets, including oversight proposals, which other reports do not repeat. Private plaintiffs under the statute generally have to show they personally lost money or property because of the conduct they challenge.

In March 2023, a widely circulated open letter called for a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than the leading model of that moment, and labs did not pause. Since then, the policy path split in two, with one track producing rules on transparency and incident reporting and the other producing litigation, first over copyright and privacy, and more recently over patents and product harms. The new filing is the first one seen to ask for a development freeze under a consumer-protection law. Most AI cases ask for money, as copyright plaintiffs want licensing fees and patent holders want royalties. The Flinn patent suits against Anthropic and OpenAI target five patents per defendant and fit that familiar pattern.

No hearing date is set and the defendants have not answered the substance publicly. Reporting says no emergency relief motion has surfaced yet, and the plaintiffs may eventually seek one. A court would need an expert-written definition of "more advanced," and each side would hire experts to bend it. Enforcement would depend on the labs' own disclosures, since outsiders cannot audit training runs from the sidewalk, and a judge would likely appoint a special master or demand sworn certifications.

Articles.Title: 1 UCL Claim Could Freeze Frontier AI: Lawsuit [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: What this S’pore bank weighs in tailoring its AI tools across Asean
stories.Summary:
UOB, Singapore's third-largest lender, is shaping how it rolls out artificial intelligence across Asean, where a tool that suits a customer in Singapore may not suit one in Indonesia. The bank says differing regulations, customer needs and levels of digital maturity shape how its AI solutions are designed, deployed and governed in each market. Lawrence Goh, head of Group Technology and Operations at UOB, said that Indonesia requires customer-facing AI applications that handle personal data to be hosted onshore. The bank runs a standardised central platform and adapts deployment to local rules.

Markets with rich financial data, such as Singapore, can support AI-powered credit assessments. The bank's example is B-Score 2.0, an AI-enabled tool for its Commercial Banking Portfolio launched in August 2025, which draws on more than 3,000 data points to flag early signs of borrower distress among business accounts in Singapore. A regional rollout of the tool is in progress. UOB aims to become the "No. 1 trade bank in Asean" and help businesses trade across borders. Operating income from the Asean-4 markets of Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam grew 5 per cent year on year in the financial year ended December 31, 2025, and those markets contributed 28.5 per cent of operating income, second only to Singapore's more than half share.

Goh said the bank is building its technology on trust, control and reliability, so it can use regional scale where suitable, localise where needed and scale AI responsibly. Any technology it deploys must answer questions about whether the data is trustworthy, whether the party interacting with the bank is authentic, what it is authorised to do, and whether it can operate securely and consistently at scale. These questions matter more as UOB expands its use of agentic AI, in which AI agents act on behalf of people. Goh expects organisations to move from experimentation to enterprise-scale deployment of agentic AI over the next two to five years.

Trust is a concern for customers as well. UOB's Asean Consumer Sentiment Study 2026, which surveyed 5,000 consumers in Singapore and the Asean-4 markets in June 2026, found that 62 per cent trust AI-powered tools to act in their best interest on financial decisions, 14 percentage points below the 76 per cent who trust their primary bank to do so. Goh said AI may change how banking is delivered but not what customers value most, namely confidence that their money is safe, that their interests are protected and that someone remains accountable. He argued that the institutions that succeed will be those that use AI to strengthen that confidence. The article was produced in partnership with the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Global Finance & Technology Network.

Articles.Title: What this S’pore bank weighs in tailoring its AI tools across Asean - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Nscale Has a $100 Billion AI Dream and a Very Expensive Funding Problem
stories.Summary:
Nscale said in an amended IPO filing that preliminary revenue reached $307.5 million in the nine months through September, up 1,344% from $21.3 million a year earlier. Its expected net loss widened to roughly $1.7 billion from $433 million. The London-based company builds AI computing infrastructure, including data centers packed with Nvidia GPUs. It has marketed more than $100 billion of contracted revenue to major AI customers, with the largest prize a deal with Anthropic that could generate as much as $44.6 billion.

Nscale plans to deploy Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin systems at its Monarch Compute Campus in West Virginia, but its filing says it has not yet secured binding commitments for the financing required to fund that project. Nscale says it has raised more than $13.4 billion through equity, project financing and credit facilities. It nevertheless warned that bigger 2027 commitments mean more financing will be needed, reversing the message in its September filing that existing resources were sufficient for at least 12 months. Nscale has considered delaying the listing until next year and has been targeting a valuation around $30 billion to $35 billion, while Bloomberg reported that some investors think something closer to $16 billion to $19 billion would be easier to sell.

Nscale itself warns that there is no guarantee the required financing will be available on acceptable terms. That risk matters because the company expects about $5.5 billion of debt while its current revenue base is still relatively small. It has also suffered customer changes, including Microsoft declining to expand one Texas arrangement and a separate London project being delayed by grid constraints. The filing says management believes it can lock down financing for the Anthropic buildout, but binding commitments are not yet in place.

Investors will watch whether the IPO proceeds this year and where the valuation lands. A successful listing near $30 billion to $35 billion would show public markets are still willing to finance aggressive AI infrastructure expansion despite huge losses. A delay or sharply lower valuation would send the opposite message. Nscale has no shortage of customers wanting compute, and its challenge is proving that demand can be turned into profitable capacity before the bill for building it arrives.

Articles.Title: Nscale Has a $100 Billion AI Dream and a Very Expensive Funding Problem - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: T-Robotics, KAIST Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute Sign MOU to Strengthen Commercialization Cooperation
stories.Summary:
T-Robotics, a robot manufacturer, announced on November 13 that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST). The agreement is meant to advance the development and commercialization of the physical artificial intelligence industry. Both sides plan to build a framework for cooperation on standardization in the sector. They also intend to pursue commercialization and expansion into global markets based on technology demonstrations.

The partners aim to bring physical AI technologies into use at industrial sites and to revitalize the domestic ecosystem for related industries. T-Robotics had already taken part in the KAIROS project, a physical AI manufacturing demonstration platform led by KAIST. The company is now testing whether its own humanoid robot, TR-WORKS, and its autonomous mobile robots can be applied on site for manufacturing and logistics automation. The articles do not say what milestones or timelines the new agreement sets.

T-Robotics has built its business on vacuum robots used in display manufacturing and is now expanding into autonomous mobile robots and smart factory systems. It is also developing next-generation robots, including humanoids, along with technologies for robot mobility, task execution, and manufacturing process automation. The company says it wants to meet automation demand across a range of industrial sites. A company official said the agreement will widen existing cooperation with KAIST and help define concrete chances to demonstrate and commercialize physical AI. The official added that combining robot manufacturing with physical AI should improve the technology's fit at industrial sites and strengthen the company's competitiveness abroad.

stories.Headline: Howard Marks' Latest Memo: Who Can Actually Profit From AI Investments?
stories.Summary:
Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital, released an investment memo titled "A Layman Thinks About AI" on November 11, 2026. The memo followed "Is It a Bubble?", which Marks had updated in December 2025, and it again took up AI investing. This time he focused on the sales volume and price of computing power. He asked whether the value AI creates for users could support trillions of dollars in infrastructure investment. He also asked which companies would be able to make profits from it.

In December 2025, Marks used railways and the internet to show that speculation can build infrastructure early and speed up the spread of technology. He warned that the first investors who put in capital may lose money even when the data centers prove useful. In February 2026, in "AI Hurtles Ahead," he argued that the technical potential of AI is more likely to be underestimated. He kept his earlier advice to participate moderately, select targets carefully and invest prudently. In his latest memo, Marks split the bubble question into three judgments about the technology.

Those three judgments concern what the technology itself can achieve, whether enterprise capital spending will earn sufficient returns, and whether the prices investors pay for stocks and bonds are reasonable. Marks still believes AI will transform enterprises, the economy and daily life. He argues that no judgment on capital spending or security prices can be made until investors understand AI's use cases, profit attribution and infrastructure returns. If several models perform similarly on the same task, suppliers may be forced to cut prices, leaving more of the efficiency gains with users. Marks also pointed to debt across the whole market, not just individual deals.

In December he questioned whether the narrow spread on 30-year bonds issued by cloud vendors could compensate for long-term technical uncertainty. In November he cited Goldman Sachs data showing that global AI-related debt issuance in 2026 had approached $600 billion by the memo's release. About $400 billion of that had entered the US investment-grade bond market, more than one-fifth of the market's new supply for the year. Marks questioned whether cloud vendors could keep their credit ratings as they keep borrowing. He also asked whether the AI industry's financing needs would raise capital costs for other borrowers.

The memo also changed how he views investment portfolios. An equity stake in a frontier model company and a data center loan backed by a long-term lease, he noted, call for different judgments. The equity depends on technology, competition, pricing and valuation, while the loan depends on tenant credit, contract terms, power supply and residual asset value. Yet a tech stock, a data center loan and an investment-grade corporate bond may all depend on growth in computing power demand. In that case, holding different assets could mean taking on the same type of risk.

At the end of the memo, Marks poses questions for investors to answer themselves. He asks how many assumptions must hold at once for a return to be reasonable, and what the maximum loss would be if the core assumption is wrong. He also asks how much optimism the current price already reflects, and whether the investment will diversify the portfolio or amplify existing risk. Marks writes that the goal is to pose the right questions rather than give direct answers, and he has long stressed knowing what one does not know.

The articles do not report whether any of these questions has been answered. The articles leave open whether AI will create enough value to justify trillions of dollars in investment, and which companies will earn returns on it. They also do not say whether cloud vendors' debt will affect their credit ratings or raise borrowing costs for others. Marks' memo ends with questions rather than conclusions, so the articles offer no forecast of the outcome.

Articles.Title: Howard Marks' Latest Memo: Who Can Actually Profit From AI Investments? - 36Kr

stories.Headline: The AI Productivity Revolution: Why a "New Factory Building" Is Essential for Modern Business Growth
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a discussion at the 2026 Baidu World Conference, where Li Yanhong was asked in a digital human interview video whether a digital human could be a CEO and answered no. The question arose against a backdrop of AI being integrated into code development, copywriting and customer service. Li Yanhong framed the broader issue as why enterprises' operational efficiency and profits do not always rise alongside employees' AI capabilities. The conference is where he put forward the metaphor that AI is the new electric motor and the intelligent organization is the new factory building. Ten years earlier, he had compared AI to new electric energy.

Li Yanhong's thinking on AI productivity has moved through several stages across recent conferences. The 2025 Baidu World Conference emphasized internalizing AI as a native enterprise capability. The 2026 Create Conference proposed mixed teams of humans and agents to drive organizational self-evolution. This year's conference focused on intelligent organizations. The articles say his argument is that a new motor installed in an old factory will not fully unleash productivity, so organizations must be redesigned.

They also say AI tasks still require human decisions and professional judgment in complex businesses. The articles say Li Yanhong's proposition is a judgment about where productivity bottlenecks now sit, and the responsibility for redesign falls on enterprises. He argues that technology is no longer the only constraint, so companies must reexamine their own organizational methods. The articles attribute to him the view that the question has shifted from what AI can do to how organizations are structured around it. They present this as a continuation of his earlier statements, not a new departure.

The articles report his position in paraphrase rather than as a set of formal commitments by Baidu. Analysts and surveys cited in the articles point to a gap between individual and organizational gains. A McKinsey global AI survey released in August 2026 found that 80 percent of respondents said AI had improved individual productivity, while only 37 percent said it had a positive impact on EBIT. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index calls this the enterprise AI transformation paradox, in which employees use AI but processes and evaluation remain unchanged.

Microsoft found that only 19 percent of respondents had both high personal AI capability and strong organizational support. The articles say employees and enterprises alike are affected, since individual gains may not translate into company results. The articles give background on how enterprises have organized work. Since the industrial era, companies have relied on specialized roles and departmental handoffs, a system suited to human-dominated labor.

The articles cite the example of China Southern Power Grid, which worked with Baidu Dazi to convert power fault analysis, previously dependent on senior experts, into a capability that draws on historical fault data, line information and expert experience. They also describe a common enterprise problem in which valuable knowledge sits with a few senior employees and leaves when they do. The articles note that BCG advises companies to be redesigned for AI rather than making AI adapt to existing structures. The articles leave open how far the redesign will go and how quickly enterprises will adopt it.

They describe three areas of change: role boundaries giving way to task-based organization, knowledge shifting into reusable organizational assets, and growth moving from periodic reform to continuous evolution through measurable, looping processes. They do not say how these will be implemented across industries or what outcomes they will produce. They also do not specify how responsibility will be allocated when agents perform cross-role tasks. The full text of the article is cut off before its discussion of Li Yanhong's three principles of organizational evolution, so their content is unknown.

Articles.Title: The AI Productivity Revolution: Why a "New Factory Building" Is Essential for Modern Business Growth - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Character.AI Faces Imminent Bankruptcy: How the AI Companionship Industry Is Quietly Raking in Massive Profits
stories.Summary:
Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code on October 12, planning to sell the company's assets under court supervision, according to a report published on November 12, 2026. The company was once the most promising AI companion unicorn, with more than 20 million monthly active users who spent an average of two hours on it every day. In 2023, less than two years after its establishment, Character.AI secured $150 million in financing led by a16z, reaching a valuation of $1 billion. If no suitable buyer is found in the end, this once globally popular AI application may even face shutdown. The report said Character.AI is on the verge of bankruptcy, yet the AI companionship industry has quietly started raking in massive profits.

According to bankruptcy filings, as of August 2026, the monthly revenue of Character.AI only reached about 5.3 million U.S. dollars, including 2.8 million U.S. dollars in subscription revenue and 2.5 million U.S. dollars in advertising revenue. In August 2026, the company's monthly operating expenses were about 13.3 million U.S. dollars, and the monthly loss still reached 8 million to 9 million U.S. dollars. Among the expenses, the computing power expenditure alone reached 5.61 million U.S. dollars, accounting for about 45% of operating expenses. In the early stage, Character.AI mainly monetized through a $9.99 monthly membership subscription, and a large number of free users could chat unlimitedly. According to data from Sensor Tower, in August 2024, the global monthly active users of Character.AI hit a record high of 22 million, ranking first in the AI companion track.

Noam Shazeer, founder of Character.AI, once put forward a view that the global entertainment industry is as large as 2 trillion U.S. dollars every year, and one core essence of entertainment consumption is that humans build emotional connections with fictional characters. He and his team believed that the interaction process itself can also become a kind of experience with commercial value. They said virtual characters powered by large language models can not only have free conversations with users, but also continuously adjust their interaction methods based on users' preferences and experiences. According to the report, this means that entertainment content that users could only passively watch in the past has begun to turn into two-way interaction that users can continuously participate in. The report said Character.AI never managed to answer a more important question: how on earth can this time be converted into revenue.

According to data from Sensor Tower, the mobile revenue of the AI companion track surged from 316 million yuan in the single month of January 2026 to 656 million yuan in August 2026, doubling in total. According to statistics from Appfigures, in the first half of 2026, 214 global romance and adult-oriented AI companion applications generated a total of 162.8 million U.S. dollars in mobile user consumption. Among them, South Korea's Zeta ranks first with 33 million U.S. dollars, Tipsy Chat follows closely with 15.2 million U.S. dollars, and Crushie AI also reached 8.8 million U.S. dollars. Scatter Lab, the South Korean company behind Zeta, recorded 70.9 billion won in revenue in the first half of this year, 2.7 times the 26.7 billion won revenue for the whole of last year, and posted an operating profit of 5.2 billion won at the same time.

Another AI social application named CHAI disclosed in October this year that its annualized revenue run rate has reached 120 million U.S. dollars, with a team of only a dozen to 20 people. In March 2023, Character.AI secured $150 million in financing led by top Silicon Valley venture capital firm a16z, reaching a valuation of $1 billion and becoming one of the earliest AI application companies to enter the unicorn club. Less than a week after the launch of Character.AI's mobile application, its downloads exceeded 1.7 million times. In September of the same year, according to data from Similarweb, Character.AI reached 4.2 million monthly active users on U.S. mobile devices, close to the roughly 6 million MAUs of ChatGPT's mobile version in the same period.

According to statistics from Sensor Tower, active users of Character.AI spend more than 90 minutes on the platform on average every day, initiating about 25 conversations on average. At that time, even TikTok, which is famous for its high user stickiness, only had an average daily usage time of a little more than 70 minutes. In March this year, Zeta adjusted the content unit on the platform from "character" to "plot", further emphasizing the importance of the story itself. To further lower the threshold for users to participate in the plot, Zeta launched the AI plot option feature in April this year.

According to the official explanation, the content on the platform now is no longer limited to a certain virtual character, but has gradually evolved into a story that includes protagonists, supporting roles, character relationships and a complete worldview. Tipsy puts more emphasis on interactive plots, and users can directly choose their favorite characters, enter a virtual world with pre-set character relationships and story backgrounds, and push the plot forward in the process of interacting with AI. The platform can also generate images and videos based on the plot, so that users no longer have to rely solely on text to imagine characters and scenes. More to follow.

stories.Headline: From software-defined to AI-native: Automotive’s next operating model
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA published an article on November 12, 2026, written by Ralf Malter, Managing Director for Global Automotive, Business Consulting and AI at NTT DATA DACH, titled around the shift from software-defined vehicles to an AI-native operating model. The piece draws on the company's 2026 Global AI Report, which argues that most automakers and suppliers have moved past pilot projects and proofs of concept. It says the real question now is whether leaders are using AI in ways that change how the business actually runs. The article describes AI as becoming the operating model itself rather than a complement to it.

The report's data shows a widening gap between leaders and laggards. Of leaders, 38.6 percent are already rebuilding applications with embedded AI, compared with 12 percent of laggards. Leaders focus on redesigning high-value workflows end to end, including engineering, change management, quality escalation, warranty triage and procurement exceptions. The article contends that the main constraint is no longer model quality but workflow design. It also says 93.2 percent of leaders apply AI in core operational workflows, against 68.8 percent of laggards.

The author argues that the rise of software-defined vehicles points to a broader change, since AI in engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and in-vehicle experiences makes the whole value chain driven by data-based decisions. He describes agentic AI as able to carry out and adjust workflows as conditions change, with examples such as coordinating over-the-air updates, simulating test conditions and adapting in-vehicle experiences to usage. The article notes that many organizations still treat AI mainly as a tool for efficiency, which it attributes to viewing AI as "better automation." Governance is presented as essential in a sector where safety and compliance are non-negotiable, and 67.6 percent of leaders have adopted centralized AI governance compared with 38.4 percent of laggards.

The article is promotional in nature and is written by an NTT DATA executive, so its figures come from the company's own research and have not been independently verified. It describes the report as offering a playbook for automotive AI leaders and invites readers to download it. The piece does not describe any regulatory action or external deadlines. It concludes that competitive advantage will come from how well organizations align their operating models with AI, and it frames the future of automotive as both software-defined and AI-native.

Articles.Title: From software-defined to AI-native: Automotive’s next operating model - NTT Data

stories.Headline: Jones County Industrial Forum explores AI in manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Industry leaders gathered at an AI manufacturing forum at Jones College in Jones County, Mississippi, on November 13, 2026, WJTV reported. The forum explored how artificial intelligence is changing the way businesses operate and how Mississippi manufacturers can use the technology. Dr. Kollin Napier, with the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Network, and Thomas Cagle, IT director from Taylor Group of Companies, spoke at the event. Organizers said the goal is to help Mississippi move beyond discussing the possibilities of AI and start putting the technology into practice. The forum was covered by WHLT and posted by Danielle Willis on November 13, 2026.

Leaders said AI can help employees work more efficiently by using technology to build on their existing knowledge and skills. Napier said AI is already used for cameras, quality control and inspection on the production line, and there is absolutely a usage for worker safety. Napier said companies that have not embraced the technology can ask questions to get no-cost resources and understand the power and benefit of AI. Cagle said employees will need to keep learning and adapting as AI becomes more common in the workplace.

Organizers said preparing Mississippi's workforce to adapt and take advantage of the technology will be key to the state's future. Napier said manufacturing can be seen as an investment in not only the production line, but the people and then the consumer in that process. He said AI is able to achieve things at a greater scale, with more efficiency, more productivity and more accuracy if something is being produced. Napier said that is just going to lead to better benefits across the board.

Cagle said AI is an efficiency multiplier, so knowledge workers can take what they do and use AI tools to make themselves more efficient. Cagle said he does not think AI will replace a human in our departments and in what we do, but eventually somebody using AI will probably be in your position. Napier said AI is not a perfect system, just like there is no perfect human, and AI is not a perfect solution, but it is absolutely a competitive advantage now and going forward. Cagle said if you are not on board with AI now, he feels there is going to be a point where you will have to make a decision.

The forum was held as AI becomes more common in the workplace and Mississippi manufacturers look at how the technology can improve production. Industry leaders gathered to discuss how the technology could benefit businesses across the state. The event was held at Jones College on November 13, 2026. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Jones County Industrial Forum explores AI in manufacturing

stories.Headline: ‘Fight AI with AI’: Singapore banks warn against third-party AI agents as observers flag liability risk
stories.Summary:
Singapore's three major banks, DBS, OCBC and UOB, are warning customers against using artificial intelligence agents to access their accounts. The warning comes as financial institutions around the world grapple with security risks and with the question of who should bear responsibility when autonomous bots carry out unauthorised transactions. The report was published on November 12, 2026, and the account is dated November 13, 2026. Although the local lenders have not yet seen customers use such agents, market observers say their adoption is inevitable. DBS chief executive Tan Su Shan said at the bank's third-quarter results briefing that every bank now has to review its terms and conditions.

The review would decide whether a third-party AI agent used by a first-party client should be treated as a first party or a third party. That classification matters because it determines who answers for a transaction an agent carries out. The articles do not give figures or deadlines for any change to the terms. Tan's remarks put the responsibility question at the centre of the debate.

Her position, as reported, is that the banks have to settle the classification in their own contracts before agents become common. The articles do not record any statement from OCBC or UOB on the same point, and they do not say whether the banks have set a timetable for revising their terms. The piece sits within a wider global debate about AI agents operating accounts on a customer's behalf. The articles do not say what action regulators or the banks will take next, so the outcome of the review remains unknown.

Articles.Title: ‘Fight AI with AI’: Singapore banks warn against third-party AI agents as observers flag liability risk - The Business Times

stories.Headline: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, Hugging Face published a blog post by Suvaditya Mukherjee, merve and Pedro Cuenca titled "The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models." The post provides fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model, on 3D assets. The scripts can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. Users can run the scripts with few arguments, assuming they updated their dataset to Hugging Face Hub, or tinker with them using the linked repository. The post also goes through how the script works.

The experiment uses a subset of GSO with 188 footwear objects, out of the 1,030 objects in GSO. The configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. Rank 8 adapters are used in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT, and rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The sparse-structure flow DiT makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8, and a VAE decoder changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Another VAE decoder changes the shape latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512, and the pipeline exports the result as a GLB file.

The authors say choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. They add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT, because these DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. They freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities, because their dataset has diffuse color maps but lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. They say training the texture flow DiT on these maps can teach it to show lighting as a surface property and can cause catastrophic forgetting. They say LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning for a dataset this small, because full fine-tuning costs much more and can overwrite the model's learned priors.

The post says the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect, and the test checks whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. It says a general-purpose model such as TRELLIS.2 can make errors in details important for a specific application, for example accurate geometry for furniture models. It says 3D generation has uses in robotics, simulation, media and entertainment, where it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. It lists file formats such as GLB and PLY and representations such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS), each with different advantages and disadvantages. It says the pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry and materials, so only the components important for the task are fine-tuned.

The post says TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation called a unified latent representation, whose decoders convert it into 3D models in the required output format, so different models are not needed for each representation format. It says the same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure, but neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. It says TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. It says BiRefNet removes the background, DINOv3-L encodes the image into feature tokens, and the sparse-structure flow DiT, a dense transformer, predicts the coarse shape. It says the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers that use structured sparse latents from TRELLIS, and the model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid.

The post says the preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object, run without a display through the xvfb-run utility, and for the 188 objects the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. It says the hardware used is a100-large (80 GB), and users can see all options by running hf jobs hardware. It says the token from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login is sent to the job as an encrypted environment variable and is not written into the image. It says preprocessing skips finished objects and training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to, and that the training container records metrics with Trackio. It says the 'ss' mode fine-tunes only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT and the 'shape' mode fine-tunes the Shape Flow DiT, referencing different config.json files for each stage.

Articles.Title: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy Advances AI Data Center Power With New Testbed
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy announced on November 10, 2026 that it has joined StabilityMax, a three-year research project led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory. The company said it will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut as part of the work. The project will develop and validate integrated power system architectures designed to support the rapidly evolving energy requirements of artificial intelligence data centers. FuelCell Energy is a U.S. clean energy technology company based in Danbury, Connecticut, and its shares trade on NASDAQ under the symbol FCEL. The announcement was issued as a press release from Danbury, Connecticut, on November 10, 2026.

StabilityMax will develop and validate a testing and modeling framework to evaluate how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics can work together to deliver reliable, responsive power for AI data centers. The project duration is three years. FuelCell Energy will fund and build its share of the test facility in Connecticut, creating a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions for AI data centers. NLR will develop data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power demands of modern computing infrastructure. Argonne National Laboratory will complement this work with techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to help identify commercially appealing, cost effective deployment strategies.

Shankar Achanta, Chief Product and Technology Officer of FuelCell Energy, said AI infrastructure is creating unprecedented demand for reliable, flexible and resilient power. He said StabilityMax brings together the company's operating experience and fuel cell technology with the expertise of leading national laboratories to better understand how integrated power systems can support the evolving needs of AI data centers. He said the insights gained will help optimize system designs, validate performance under real-world conditions and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions for digital infrastructure. Zhiwen Ma, Principal Investigator at NLR, said fuel cells collocated with data centers provide unique solutions to meet the power demands of AI infrastructure. He said NLR will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can rapidly respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers.

Eric Strayer, FuelCell Energy's Head of Global Sales, said the company is actively working with customers and partners deploying power solutions for digital infrastructure, and the project will provide valuable data and operating experience that can inform future deployments. He said demand for AI infrastructure continues to accelerate and load profiles evolve with each new generation of chips, and the insights gained will help refine system designs and deployment strategies for integrating fuel cells, energy storage and power electronics in data center environments. The release announces no contract, order or revenue, and the project's results are still to come. The company will fund and build its share of the test facility, adding to its spending before any commercial return is shown. FuelCell Energy's fuel cell systems generate electricity on-site at the point of use, providing reliable power for data centers, industrial facilities, utilities and distributed-generation customers.

The project builds on FuelCell Energy's ongoing development of integrated power solutions for digital infrastructure. Earlier this year, the company announced a collaboration with Siemens to advance a layered architecture approach that combines multiple technologies operating across different timescales to support the evolving power requirements of AI data centers. Insights generated through StabilityMax are expected to further inform system design and deployment strategies for future digital infrastructure applications. StabilityMax is part of a broader initiative by NLR to support the growing energy needs of AI-enabled digital infrastructure, through new modeling tools, planning platforms and test environments. FuelCell Energy provides proven utility-scale solutions for cleaner, more resilient local energy and has global deployments approaching one gigawatt.

FuelCell Energy currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Woodside Energy Group's 2026 earnings indicates 23.9% year-over-year growth, for XPLR Infrastructure 393.3% growth and for Bloom Energy 338.2% growth. Woodside and XPLR each sport a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) at present, while Bloom Energy carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). FuelCell Energy's systems are compact and modular by design and deliver quiet, low-emission power while minimizing impacts on surrounding communities. The articles leave open what the testbed's results will show and when any commercial deployment may follow.

stories.Headline: China's trade surplus soars past $1 trillion as AI boom powers exports
stories.Summary:
China's customs data released on Tuesday, Nov 10, showed that the country's trade surplus surged past US$1 trillion in the first 10 months of the year. A global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand in the world's second-largest economy. Exports rose 35.2 per cent in October from the same month a year earlier, measured in US dollar terms. That was only a touch slower than the 36.3 per cent surge recorded in September, but ahead of economists' forecast for a 33.5 per cent increase. The reporting on the data comes from Reuters, with the Channel NewsAsia and Jakarta Post versions carrying the same account.

The surplus reached US$1.04 trillion across the first 10 months, topping US$1 trillion for a second consecutive year. It reached that milestone a month earlier than it did in 2025. Imports grew 41.6 per cent in October, beating the median forecast of a 32 per cent increase in the Reuters poll. That marked an acceleration from the 31 per cent growth in imports recorded in September. China on Monday officially announced a two-month extension of its trade truce with Washington, which had been due to expire on Nov 10.

On the trade truce, China said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of the agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement. The articles attribute the figures to customs data released by Beijing, while the reporting itself comes from Reuters journalists Yukun Zhang and Ryan Woo. Beijing is described as relying increasingly on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump. Car exports from China maintained a solid pace of growth in October, according to separate data from an industry association. That same association data showed domestic vehicle sales recorded a 12th straight month of declines.

Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China, said the risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027. He linked that risk to Chinese manufacturers continuing to expand their presence in overseas markets. Macquarie analysts wrote that the outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last. They expect China's exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter, before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027. In the European Union, leaders have called for more trade curbs with China, even after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit exports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to the bloc.

Consumers in China remain reluctant to spend, constrained by a property market downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook. Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. The articles say the swelling surplus could fuel further tensions with the European Union and with other major trading partners. Greater reliance on exports leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand. Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by the global push to expand AI infrastructure.

China's trade surplus hit a record US$1.2 trillion last year, according to a video report from Channel NewsAsia at China's flagship import expo in Shanghai. That report said China wants the world to keep buying its goods, while also wanting to show that it is buying more from the world. The balance is described as becoming harder to sell after last year's record surplus. The articles describe the global AI investment boom as expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027. They add that the same boom risks deepening domestic imbalances and fuelling trade frictions with partners including the European Union.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit will take place next week in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese tech and innovation hub. Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet there for the third time so far this year. The EU measures limiting Chinese hybrid vehicle exports have yet to take effect, so factories are expected to bring forward shipments. That front-loading is expected to bolster exports in the near term. The articles leave open how long the AI boom will last and whether the tariff-reduction arrangement with Washington will be implemented, and they give no figure for the extent of the EU's planned limits.

stories.Headline: Kazakhstan-linked hackers used AI to steal Tajik government documents, researchers say
stories.Summary:
A hacking group linked to Kazakhstan used an artificial intelligence agent to steal more than 2,000 national security-related documents from Tajikistan, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Singapore-based cybersecurity company CloudSEK. The firm said it found the operation after the attackers accidentally left a server exposed to the internet. The group, which researchers call Silent Lynx, relied on Hermes, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents, and the data CloudSEK recovered shows the hackers began reconnaissance around mid-August before breaking into Tajikistan's electronic document system a couple of weeks later. The server also held more than a dozen gigabytes of material, including stolen government files, hacking tools and records of how the agent was used.

According to CloudSEK, the hackers configured the agent to act as an offensive security expert, and it handled reconnaissance, data collection and the erasing of traces from compromised systems. The agent was also set up to run certain potentially destructive commands without additional approval, and the operator issued instructions in Russian through a Telegram bot, which let them direct it from a phone. The AI models behind the system were mainly developed by the Chinese company DeepSeek. Once inside Tajikistan's systems, the group used the credentials of a single railway employee to log into the national platform that ministries use to exchange official correspondence, then built tools to download large volumes of files, including thousands sent to or processed by the Defense Ministry in 2026. The stolen material also reportedly touched the National Guard, the State Committee for National Security and the State Investment Committee, and information about more than 100 government organizations.

CloudSEK said it assessed with medium confidence that Silent Lynx has ties to Kazakhstan, pointing to Russian-language communications and test connections from a residential internet provider in the country. The company's findings align with earlier assessments that the group is probably based there, though they do not establish any link to the Kazakh government, and Kazakh and Tajik officials did not respond to requests for comment. The researchers also found evidence of a compromised server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative and malicious files posing as official Turkmenistan documents that were created in October, which suggests another phishing campaign was being prepared. Silent Lynx, also known as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper, has been active since at least 2022 and has previously targeted government and diplomatic bodies across Central Asia, Russia and Europe. Efforts to reach the group were unsuccessful, and the researchers did not determine whether the Turkmenistan attacks succeeded.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud introduces Professional Agentic Architect certification
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud has announced a new Professional Agentic Architect certification, a credential meant to show that a person can deploy secure, enterprise-grade agents that automate workflows spanning several steps and applications. The certification was introduced on November 11, 2026, according to Google Cloud's blog, and TechGig reported the launch on November 13, 2026. It is positioned as the latest milestone in the company's Gemini Agent Ready initiative, which the blog says nearly one million developers are using to learn about agents. Google Cloud first used the curriculum internally, training thousands of its forward deployed engineers and strategic partners over the past four months before opening it to outside developers.

The certification uses a hybrid format rather than a traditional exam. Part one is a proctored multiple-choice test covering system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance. Part two is a set of hands-on labs on Google Skills, where candidates build, test, and debug live agentic workflows in an active cloud environment. Candidates who pass both parts can claim a digital badge. The curriculum covers building agents with low-code tools, using coding agents for development, developing custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks, evaluating and deploying agentic workflows, and securing and governing them.

Google Cloud is the body setting these requirements, and its managing directors for forward deployed engineering and learning framed the program as a way to standardize skills across customers, partners, and Google's own staff. The company says the certification is intended for developers, cloud architects, and engineers who build and deploy agents on Google Cloud. Google says it commissioned research with Ipsos, and TechGig cites that research to report that over 80 per cent of certified individuals said the credential opened new career opportunities and helped with promotion. The same figures indicate that 82 per cent of respondents said certifications help them earn higher salaries.

The announcement comes as enterprise demand for agentic workloads grows and customers move beyond simple AI prompting to run business-critical work on Google Cloud. Google says it has used the program to prepare engineers who are embedded with customers worldwide, and it has made the training available at no cost to some participants. Customers can join a cohort-based, guided certification journey through Get Certified, while partners can register for Partner Certification Kickstart. Candidates are directed to review the exam guide, learning path, and sample questions, and to use hands-on labs before sitting for the exam.

stories.Headline: NTT partners Sompo Holdings to develop physical AI for care sector
stories.Summary:
NTT, the Japanese telecommunications company, has signed a partnership agreement with Sompo Holdings, the insurance and financial group, to explore how physical AI can be used in the care sector. The aim is to address labour shortages and operational pressures in Japan's ageing society. The agreement covers identifying where physical AI can be applied in care work. It also covers developing ways to fit the technology into day-to-day care operations, moving from research and trials through to deployment and commercialisation.

Separately, Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri has announced a strategic partnership with Poste Italiane and the telecoms company TIM to build what it describes as Italy's first integrated national physical AI ecosystem for shipbuilding. The initiative, called Fincantieri Ontology, forms a central part of the company's 2026 to 2030 industrial plan, known as F4, which prioritises digitalisation, automation and protecting industrial knowledge. The three companies plan to create a secure digital infrastructure that brings AI into ship design, construction and vessel management. A parallel effort, Navis Sapiens, is aimed at digitalising the ships themselves to support increasingly autonomous vessel operations.

Fincantieri's plans involve creating digital representations of industrial processes, capturing technical expertise and using AI models to optimise manufacturing. The companies intend to build four-dimensional design and construction models so that shipyard workers and robotic systems can receive AI-optimised work packages and daily production instructions. The work supports an industrial workload valued at about $81 billion (€70 billion) extending through 2036. Its supply chain includes 7,000 small and medium-sized enterprises across 18 shipyards worldwide, and roughly 100,000 people access its facilities each day. Fincantieri says the partnership will also run a protected computing environment that combines local AI processing with secure cloud infrastructure to safeguard sensitive data.

Fincantieri's chief executive and general manager, Pierroberto Folgiero, said that data and artificial intelligence are the driving forces behind the 2026 to 2030 industrial plan. He argued that the partnership goes beyond digitalising a process, describing it instead as documenting and protecting the company's technical culture. The articles do not give comparable statements from NTT or Sompo Holdings about their agreement. Both initiatives reflect a wider push by industrial and service companies to bring physical AI and robotics into operations facing workforce pressures. The articles do not say what results the NTT and Sompo trials will produce or when any care-sector deployment will begin, and they give no timetable for the Fincantieri initiative beyond the 2026 to 2030 plan period.

stories.Headline: 7th World Media Summit opens in Beijing, highlighting media transformation in AI age
stories.Summary:
The 7th World Media Summit opened in Beijing on Saturday, November 7, 2026, under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action." Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government jointly organized the summit, which runs from Thursday to Monday. It drew nearly 500 representatives from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks and government bodies across 112 countries and regions, along with the United Nations and other international organizations. The gathering highlights how media is changing as artificial intelligence spreads through the industry.

Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and head of its Publicity Department, delivered a keynote speech at the opening ceremony. Yin Li, also a Political Bureau member and secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, addressed the ceremony as well. Delegates discussed the role of media in the age of artificial intelligence and how the industry should respond to the challenges it poses. They called for closer cooperation to broaden access to advanced technologies and help media organizations worldwide develop together. Speakers also urged concrete steps to uphold journalistic ethics and protect the authenticity of news content as AI use expands.

The summit's organizers and speakers framed the discussions around shared goals, with a focus on moving from agreement to practical measures. Their remarks stressed cooperation between outlets in different countries and the need to keep news reliable while new tools reshape how stories are produced and shared. The articles present these views as the positions voiced at the event rather than as independent assessments. A separate report published on November 9, 2026, described a preview video released for the summit titled "AI-Powered, Toward a Shared New Future," though that report was brief and gave few further details. The articles do not say what specific commitments, if any, the delegates reached by the close of the summit.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) Blowout Quarter Signals Robust AI Infrastructure Demand, Lifting Nasdaq 1.6%
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, listed on the Nasdaq as CRWV, reported record quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion on Wednesday, November 11, and the results lifted the broader market. The company also raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook, which eased worries that corporate demand for computing capacity might not justify the heavy spending required to build it. Its shares jumped 24.71% during the session, and the stock has risen 52% since it went public in 2025. The results gave a lift to technology stocks as well, with the Nasdaq Composite climbing 1.60% to close at 25,466 after declines caused by Tuesday's inflation concerns. The S&P 500 gained 1.29% to finish at 7,618.

The rally was concentrated in technology and semiconductor names rather than spread evenly across sectors. Micron Technology rose 11.89% as chipmakers recovered from losses earlier in the week. Nebius Group closed 15.44% higher and Applied Digital finished up 7.37%, as investors reassessed the near-term earnings potential of companies tied to AI infrastructure. The article describes CoreWeave's report as a confidence reset for a part of the market that had been pressured by valuation worries and doubts about how long AI-related capital spending could last.

The story frames the gains as a reaction to that single catalyst. Several risks remained after the rally, according to the article. The 10-year Treasury yield kept moving toward the 5% level, which the piece notes has historically created headwinds for growth stocks. Higher yields raise the discount rate applied to future earnings, which can leave richly valued technology shares more exposed if the upward drift continues.

The article also questions whether the gains reflect broad market strength, since they were confined to a narrow group of AI and semiconductor companies. The article's author, David Prior, a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, presents CoreWeave's results as having restored credibility to the AI trade for now. He says investors will be watching whether that momentum holds as macroeconomic pressures build. The piece does not specify any further scheduled events or outcomes beyond that.

stories.Headline: See what AI looks like in production at Microsoft Ignite
stories.Summary:
Armanino built an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry and cut production time for new AI applications by 89%, Microsoft reported on 11/11/2026. The accounting, consulting, and technology firm is headquartered in San Ramon, California, and aimed to grow its business by meeting rising customer demand for AI solutions. Armanino used Microsoft Foundry and GitHub Copilot to establish the AI App Factory, which standardizes and accelerates application delivery. The firm needed to scale innovation faster without proportionally increasing resources, then deliver enterprise-grade AI capabilities to mid-market customers. The AI App Factory gives teams a highly secure, reusable foundation to build and deploy AI solutions faster.

Armanino cut production time for new AI applications by 89%, and its consultants now turn a two-hour client session into finished requirements in 30 minutes. The firm reports 89% less production time per new application and 90% fewer version revision cycles. Armanino now builds solutions it once found too costly to attempt. Creating a convincing prototype takes days, and turning it into a governed, audited, supportable application that a regulated client will run on can take months. That lag is a common reason AI programs fail to move from pilot to production.

Carmel Wynkoop, Partner, Artificial Intelligence Solutions at Armanino, said the firm recognized early that meeting the opportunity ahead meant more than adopting AI tools. Wynkoop said it meant deeply reengineering delivery workflows to be AI-native. Drew Armanino, Lead, Artificial Intelligence Solutions at Armanino, said the core developer team is small and the business is large. Drew Armanino said the ambition was to reengineer workflows across the entire firm, which meant a small team had to produce incredible output. Drew Armanino said that constraint became the catalyst.

Mid-market companies are asking their service providers for AI that is capable of reaching production, rather than another pilot. In professional services, proving that an AI model can do the work is not the hard part, and shipping a scalable solution is. Two technical challenges stood between the ambition and delivery, and the first was extensibility. A talent acquisition tool, a technical accounting memo drafter, and a client intelligence engine each have very different user workflows and domain logic. They rest on the same underlying infrastructure, though, and each new build must fit it.

Armanino set out to engineer that lag out of its own business. The firm's constraint was arithmetic, according to Drew Armanino. Armanino's core developer team is small and its business is large. The ambition was to reengineer workflows across the entire firm. The AI App Factory standardizes and accelerates application delivery for Armanino's teams.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond Armanino's current use of the AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry. The articles leave open the second technical challenge that stood between the ambition and delivery, which the Microsoft story names but does not describe. The articles do not give the date the AI App Factory was established or the number of applications it has produced. The articles do not say how many consultants work in the AI App Factory or which clients use the resulting applications. The articles do not give the size of Armanino's core developer team or the cost of the solutions it once found too costly to attempt.

stories.Headline: With less than a week left, AI assistants, multilingual translation terminals and driverless shuttles appear in Shenzhen to greet visitors
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen is preparing for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting which will be held on November 18 and 19 in Guangdong Province. The city has entered a period called APEC time to welcome international visitors with various new technological innovations and smart services. AI assistants, multilingual translation terminals, and driverless shuttles have appeared across the city to greet the arriving delegates and other guests. These advanced tools aim to showcase how technological innovation is reshaping urban life and facilitating international exchanges for the global event. Preparations are currently in full swing to ensure the city is ready for the high profile meeting starting in less than a week.

Bao'an International Airport has launched an AI travel assistant and translation terminals supporting 38 languages at the service center and transportation desk. A facial recognition boarding system allows passengers to submit entry information via QR codes, completing immigration clearance in as little as one minute. Level 4 autonomous minibuses with over 20 sensors, including LiDAR and cameras, operate on a downtown route near the Luohu Port. These vehicles feature central control screens, voice commands for music and temperature, and the ability to navigate complex intersections and traffic lights. Ultra-high-bandwidth networking provides peak downlink speeds of 1.5 gigabits per second and stable speeds of 10 megabits per second during peak periods.

The Shenzhen municipal statistics bureau released data on October 23 regarding the growth of the city's high tech and advanced manufacturing sectors. Officials state that the city will showcase its industrial ecosystem in robotics, new vehicles, and the digital economy to connect Asia-Pacific markets. They report that high tech manufacturing value-added output rose 11.6 percent, while advanced manufacturing increased by 11.9 percent in the first three quarters. Production of industrial robots grew by 44.1 percent, lithium-ion batteries by 38.5 percent, and 3D printing equipment by 77.8 percent this year. These figures highlight the city's reputation as China's Silicon Valley and a global hub for embodied intelligence and artificial intelligence.

Modern Diplomacy noted that Shenzhen was chosen for the APEC meeting because of its status as a global hub for AI technology. International delegates and visitors are the primary people affected by the new smart services and the upgraded communications infrastructure at border checkpoints. In a separate development, Johannes Wigand, founder of LiveVoice, said AI translation allows congregations to welcome visitors in their own languages. Simon Egli from ICF Church stated that the LiveVoice platform is simple to use for both the interpreters and the listeners. Jan Hendrik of Willow Creek noted that the tool accommodates the needs of both their on-site and their online audiences.

LiveVoice is an Austria-based platform in Salzburg that has now surpassed 150,000 multilingual church services using AI translation in over 70 languages. The system allows worshippers to hear sermons on their own phones via QR codes, replacing expensive rented receivers and interpreter booths. This cloud-based technology has seen over 850,000 app downloads and 50,000 admin users across more than 100 different countries and various venues. It is used by ministries like Hillsong, Alpha, OM, and ICF, as well as sports events like the Biathlon World Cup. The platform can lower costs for smaller congregations by 80 percent while avoiding hygiene concerns associated with using shared headsets.

The APEC meeting will soon demonstrate Shenzhen's advanced robotics and digital economy to leaders from across the Asia-Pacific region during the summit. LiveVoice continues to expand its reach by offering participant-based pricing and pay-as-you-go AI translation for churches and other large scale events. The articles leave open how the APEC delegates will react to the Level 4 autonomous driving and the AI airport assistants. It remains unclear if other cities will adopt the specific ultra-high-bandwidth networking technology used at the Shenzhen transportation hubs and checkpoints. The future growth rates for Shenzhen's high tech manufacturing products beyond the third quarter of the year are not provided.
