stories.Headline: AI Spending Lifts Global Trade to 30-Year High, Raising Bust Risk
stories.Summary:
AI spending by U.S. Big Tech is driving global trade to its strongest growth since the early 1990s, excluding rebounds after the pandemic and the global financial crisis, according to the articles. Up to 80% of the recent rise in global exports is concentrated in AI-related goods, and analysts warn that Asian exporters including South Korea, Taiwan and China would take an immediate hit if U.S. investment cools. The Wall Street Journal reported on the 11th, citing analysis by Capital Economics, that a cooling of the AI investment boom could tip the world economy into recession. In October, South Korea's total exports rose 93.7% from a year earlier and semiconductor exports soared 259.4%, while Chinese exports rose 35%. Moody's Analytics head of international economics Gaurav Ganguly said a sharp drop in AI-related stocks combined with other shocks could lead to a global recession.

The U.S. government is finishing a plan to extend export restrictions to Southeast Asia, which has been identified as a detour route for AI chips bound for China. The Bureau of Industry and Security at the U.S. Commerce Department is pushing to add Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, Norway and South Africa to its semiconductor export control list, The Information reported on the 11th. Under the proposed rules, imports of Blackwell-class or more advanced chips would require U.S. government approval, with end users and intended uses also subject to disclosure. Singapore accounted for 18% of Nvidia's total revenue in fiscal 2025 on a billing basis, but chips actually shipped into Singapore generated only 2% of revenue. Congress is seeking to attach the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act to the National Defense Authorization Act.

Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang's future is uncertain, and Wall Street has cut ratings and price targets on the company as a result of the possibility that he steps down. Baird on the 11th lowered its rating to neutral from outperform and cut its price target 60% to $200 from $500, while Bernstein halved its target to $200 from $400. Nvidia shares fell 9.51% over two days after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on the 8th. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning pushed back, saying the United States should stop fabricating spy narratives. Nvidia has provided a combined $300 billion in financial support to customers over the past three years, according to Bloomberg, and in August it unveiled a $500 billion AI infrastructure investment vehicle with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and others.

South Korea has announced at least $510 billion, about 680 trillion won, in joint projects with Nvidia over the past year, and SK Group signed a letter of intent worth more than $500 billion in July. NAVER received $1 billion from Nvidia in exchange for a 4.13% stake. According to the Korea Securities Depository, domestic investors held $13.64744 billion worth of Nvidia shares as of the 10th, or about 18 trillion won, the second most held foreign stock after Tesla. Advantest, the Japanese chip test equipment maker, reported second-quarter revenue up 81.7% from a year earlier to 477.7 billion yen. Its gross margin reached a record 71.1%, and it raised full-year revenue guidance to 1.863 trillion yen.

Huang's exit and the U.S. chip curbs are the two risks that the articles frame as threatening Nvidia and the broader AI supply chain. The Fair Trade Commission imposed a record 1.6 trillion won in fines on 15 banks and securities firms for colluding in government bond auctions from January 2020 to June 2023. A 2.2 trillion won auction of 10-year treasury bonds scheduled for the 16th is expected to be the first test of how the market has changed since those sanctions. The articles do not say whether Congress will pass the bills, whether the Southeast Asia restrictions will be finalized, or whether Huang will step down. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Democrats encouraged to scrutinize Trump and AI
stories.Summary:
Democrats face pressure from AI safety groups to scrutinize the Trump administration's AI policy when they take power next year, according to two letters shared first with Semafor. The AI safety group Guardrails Action and nine other groups wrote to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, arguing that voters made clear in the midterms that they want accountability. The groups pointed to the recent Nvidia controversy and demanded hearings with now-former CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Department officials. A second letter, from the Alliance for Secure AI and the Tech Oversight Project, addressed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directly and demanded that he support strengthened export controls. Both letters frame the concentration of power and wealth from AI as a serious danger that Democrats should challenge.

Silicon Valley's close alignment with Donald Trump, which followed his reelection in 2024, has produced results that the tech leaders did not anticipate. The Atlantic argues that the pivot failed on its own stated goals. Over the past 18 months, China has been closing the gap with the United States on model performance and chip development. American public attitudes toward AI have also grown more negative than they were under President Biden, and worse than in almost any other country. Meanwhile, anti-Big Tech sentiment has risen in many parts of the world, with economies such as Canada's, India's, Germany's, and Brazil's seeking less of what Silicon Valley produces.

The article describes this as a scorecard in which China is strengthened, domestic support weakened, and global markets angered. The author, Nick Clegg, a former Meta executive who announced his departure a few days before Trump's 2025 inauguration, places the fault on a herd mentality rather than on individual leaders. He says some tech figures were more restrained than others. Clegg suggests that fear of missing out drove the rush after Elon Musk spent Election Night 2024 at Mar-a-Lago. He also cites a desire for payback against traditional media, academia, and the Biden administration, along with a tendency among wealthy people to overestimate their grasp of politics.

Clegg adds that tech hype cycles led executives to read Trump's narrow popular-vote win as a mandate, and that venture capitalists such as Marc Andreessen and David Sacks overreached after success on crypto regulation. Voters across the political spectrum are affected by these choices, according to the article, because many Americans dislike the cozy relationship between the government and the Valley. Clegg notes that many voters abhor what he calls the self-serving cliquishness and extremism of the second Trump administration, and its apparent indifference to their economic plight. He compares the situation to Brexit, after which a significant majority of Britons came to think the referendum was a huge mistake. The article also notes that many tech chief executives assumed Trump's victory marked a permanent political shift, so they doubled down rather than hedge.

The articles leave the next steps uncertain. The safety groups' letters ask Democrats to act once they take power next year, but neither article says whether Democrats will schedule the requested hearings or pursue export-control measures. The White House and Department of Transportation have separately urged Congress to approve a further $30.1 billion for aviation reform, and a Politico report describes climate funders' data center forum as having triggered a reckoning. Clegg's analysis ends without predicting whether the tech sector will recalibrate its political strategy, or how the relationship between Silicon Valley and the administration will develop.

stories.Headline: Foundation Models framework
stories.Summary:
Apple has released an updated Foundation Models framework, a native Swift API for integrating large language models into apps, according to its developer site dated 12 November 2026. It gives direct access to the Apple Foundation Models both on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Guided generation, tool calling, image understanding and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so developers do not need to add them separately. Separately, Microsoft has begun rolling out its own foundation models under its Microsoft AI program, known as MAI, according to InfoWorld. Microsoft's models are offered mainly through its Foundry platform, which the article says gives access to more than 11,000 different models.

Apple's framework now accepts multimodal prompts, so an app can pass images alongside text and reason about visual content. The Vision framework is integrated, giving the model tools such as OCR for text extraction and barcode readers, all on-device. The framework also extends to server models, including Claude and Gemini, through the same Swift API, with support for tool calling and guided generation. Developers in the App Store Small Business Program with fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can use the Apple models on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost. A new fm command line tool arrives in macOS 27, and an Evaluations framework lets developers test prompts and validate features.

Apple says any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol, which lets developers choose the right model for their app. It describes Dynamic Profiles as declarative APIs for updating a session's model, tools and instructions on the fly. Each profile carries its own model, temperature, reasoning level and toolset, and the session transcript is shared across every profile switch. Apple says the Evaluations framework is meant to give developers confidence that their app's behavior holds up before shipping. It also says the Private Cloud Compute option ensures user data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else.

InfoWorld's Simon Bisson reports that Microsoft's MAI models focus on offering a lower token cost than competitors, which he says fills a gap in the market. He writes that the era of free and low-cost tokens is over, as hyperscale vendors try to recoup their multi-billion-dollar data center investments. MAI describes its approach as humanist, with a focus on safety and environmental impact. The affected users include developers who can call MAI models through existing Foundry Azure OpenAI APIs, and who can set limits on tokens used per request. Microsoft also offers a tuning service that lets customers build custom versions of the models using their own data.

Apple's framework also offers open source pieces, including a utilities package with custom skills, context management helpers and a Chat Completions client for a hosted model of your choice. A Foundation Models SDK for Python extends the framework into the Python ecosystem. Apple publishes Acceptable Use Requirements that prohibit certain uses of its models, and cites Article 53(1)(b) of the AI Act in making documentation available for AFM 3 Cloud. On the Microsoft side, Foundry started from a partnership in which OpenAI trained models on Azure infrastructure and Microsoft became the first commercial partner to use them. Its stable later grew to include Anthropic, Hugging Face, Meta, Mistral and DeepSeek models, alongside its Phi series and Cognitive Services models, and Microsoft Research has long topped benchmark tables with focused models.

Among the MAI models, MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is used in the GitHub Copilot service and MAI-Cyber-1.1-Flash in Microsoft's MDASH security system, while MAI-Thinking-1 handles the most complex applications. MAI-Code-1.1-Flash needs more than 120GB of RAM, so it is not yet small enough for Copilot+ PCs, while a Surface Ultra with an NVIDIA RTX Spark and at least 128GB of RAM should be capable. MAI-Cyber-1.1-Flash handles 90% of tasks once done by larger models and is 18% cheaper to run than version 1.0. The Maia 300 accelerator raises compute by 36%, improves high bandwidth memory performance 2.5 times, and gives roughly a 2x gain per watt, with 96 accelerators per rack. The articles leave open how much local operation would save over cloud servers, and they give no release date for the new Apple tools beyond macOS 27.

stories.Headline: AI SRE agents: data flow, security questions for engineering teams
stories.Summary:
AI SRE agents aim to reduce the time engineers spend investigating production incidents, retrieving logs, traces, metrics, and deployment history to suggest root causes, TechGig reported on Nov 13, 2026. Production telemetry can contain sensitive information, including customer identifiers, internal service details, API paths, and error payloads, which may not be intended for external systems. Effective investigation requires the agent to access context such as application events, exceptions, stack traces, CPU, memory, latency metrics, distributed traces, error data, session context, and Git/deployment metadata. A typical AI investigation involves several stages, each raising different data-handling questions, including data collection from applications and infrastructure, context retrieval from relevant data sources, AI inference where models reason over evidence, and results/remediation with root-cause hypotheses or suggested fixes. Questions arise about telemetry storage, context assembly, model processing, and prompt/response retention, which are not fully answered by the observability database location alone.

Three main deployment models for AI SRE agents exist: Vendor-hosted SaaS, Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC), and Bring Your Own Key (BYOK). In Vendor-hosted SaaS, telemetry is sent to vendor-operated infrastructure, and some context may be processed by an AI model provider. BYOC runs the platform inside customer-controlled infrastructure, retaining control over the cloud account and environment where telemetry is stored and processed. BYOK allows customers to connect their own AI model API key or deployment, such as Azure OpenAI or Amazon Bedrock, for inference. BYOC controls where the platform runs, while BYOK controls model credentials and inference deployment, and both address distinct parts of the data architecture.

Before connecting an agent to production, engineering and security teams should ask vendors specific questions, including where telemetry is stored, whether raw application data leaves the cloud environment, which AI model receives investigation context, and if prompts/responses are retained by the model provider. Other critical questions involve whether customer data is used for model training, if customers can use their own model key, and the permissions the agent requires. Teams should also inquire about auditing data retrieval and actions, initial read-only access, and architectural verification through cloud and network logs. An agent that can only read telemetry and suggest fixes has a very different permission model from one that can modify infrastructure, execute commands, or deploy changes. A phased adoption approach is recommended, starting with read-only investigation and gradually introducing approval-based remediation, and an agent could generate a pull request for a code fix, which an engineer would then review and merge, maintaining engineering control.

As AI agents move into production on Kubernetes, cloud engineering teams at financial companies face a security problem that encryption alone can't solve, SiliconANGLE reported on Nov 11, 2026. Container orchestration has become the default foundation for AI workloads, and the data those agents use is now the main target. Payment networks feel that pressure more than most because every transaction carries customer data and regulatory exposure, and protecting data while it is being processed, and not just while it is stored or moving, has become central to running agents at scale, according to Krishna Mayuram, senior principal engineer and vice president of cloud engineering at Mastercard Inc. Mayuram spoke with theCUBE Research's John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. Mastercard runs its platforms on Red Hat Inc.'s OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform that Red Hat is extending to support AI agents, and Red Hat has also brought confidential containers to OpenShift on bare metal.

Mayuram said confidential computing is when you are launching these applications in highly secure, virtualized secure environments or confidential environments or confidential containers, and you are able to protect the data in use. He said we have protected data at rest, data in motion, and now the question is what is happening to the data in use. Agents act much like microservices and need the same elastic infrastructure, Mayuram explained, and he said we need to scale the platform, that's Kubernetes which gives horizontal scaling, vertical scaling, if you will, and also the agents, just like applications, require all the elastic capabilities of Kubernetes. Scale increases the risk, especially for a company that operates under many countries' laws, and Mastercard recently added trust services for agentic commerce. Internally, the same idea applies, with guardrails at every step from development to deployment, according to Mayuram, who said the business is distributed, the industry is very distributed, and we have different laws of the land, so all these things need to be encompassed with guardrails.

Mayuram said whether agents or regular, the guardrails remain the same, and the enterprise security remains same. TheCUBE is a paid media partner for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, and sponsors of theCUBE's event coverage do not have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE. The goal is to reduce investigation effort without removing human oversight, according to TechGig. stories.Headline: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
stories.Summary:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, and the findings were published in November 2026. Structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption. Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotstar, led the comparison of filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. The team tested these approaches on subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, plus a custom question-answering harness built for JioHotstar's codebase.

The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability. The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked-out repositories and standard search, stayed competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which offers indexed text search and symbol definitions, beat the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results. CodeScaleBench showed that semantic retrieval helped most when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions.

Bansal's team at JioHotstar conducted the study and published its results. The report stressed that tool design matters, since agents often preferred familiar operations such as text search and file reading over higher-level abstractions. Siddharth Vaithinathan separately raised a broader question in a LinkedIn post about whether coding agents should understand the company behind the code, not just the code itself. He suggested extending agent knowledge to architecture, constraints, decisions, and incidents, so agents could assess existing design choices before proposing changes.

The results matter most to engineering teams building or using AI coding agents on large codebases, and to the developers whose work those agents assist. JioHotstar recommends keeping filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems, and using semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. The team also advises measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to see whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. Tarun Bhargava raised a point about interpreting benchmark results, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.

The study's background includes the use of SWE-bench, CodeScaleBench, and the Model Context Protocol and retrieval-augmented generation approaches that form the context for these comparisons. The articles describe the evaluation as a comparison of retrieval layers for coding agents, with JioHotstar presenting the work through its blog and both TechGig and InfoQ reporting on it. The articles do not say whether JioHotstar plans to adopt any particular tool across its engineering teams. They also do not report how many runs were performed per setup, which Bhargava flagged as a question for interpreting the numbers.

stories.Headline: Indian startups target AI inference to scale models
stories.Summary:
Indian startups are building AI inference platforms to run AI models faster, cheaper and more reliably at scale. The coverage, published on November 13, 2026 by TechGig and on November 11, 2026 by Inc42, describes this as a shift from building larger models toward running them efficiently. Inference is the stage at which a trained model uses what it has learned to answer new inputs. The articles say that as AI moves into everyday products, companies find it hard to run models at scale without rising costs. Platforms that deploy, manage and optimise models are emerging to fill that gap for businesses.

Simplismart, an Indian inference startup, claims it reduced inference costs by 53 per cent for voice AI platform Sanas while keeping 99.99 per cent accuracy through model quantisation. For customer support platform Exotel, Simplismart says it cut costs to ₹0.90 to ₹1.30 per minute from ₹2.10 for a closed-model API. The same work lowered latency from 1.1 seconds to under 300 milliseconds. Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding in October, with NVIDIA among the participants. Vishnu Subramanian of JarvisLabs, which E2E Networks acquired, identified four ways businesses consume inference.

Subramanian described inference platform as too generic a term, and he listed shared model APIs, managed inference, self-managed inference and dedicated infrastructure as the four consumption methods. Shared APIs give access to ready-to-use models, with the provider managing the infrastructure. JarvisLabs' Token Factory offers hosted open models through an API, with the platform managing GPU capacity. Managed inference provides dedicated deployments that the provider largely sets up. Self-managed inference lets businesses deploy and scale their own models, while dedicated infrastructure reserves capacity for predictable performance.

Apna, a jobs and networking platform, uses AI for tasks such as improving candidate profiles and onboarding employers. Its CTO, Abhishek Ranjan, aims to make the company's AI faster, more efficient and economically viable. Apna uses external inference platforms for flexibility across models without managing serving infrastructure. Its subsidiary Blue Machines AI, where Ranjan is also CTO, built its own platform for conversational AI, which needs faster responses and must serve many users at once. Pipeshift, E2E Networks and other Indian startups also operate in the space, and Pipeshift has partnered with Neysa.

The articles describe the inference sector as fragmented, with startups building different layers of the stack. Pipeshift focuses on production inference for open-source models where latency matters, and it has partnered with Neysa to combine its managed serving layer with Neysa's sovereign AI cloud. The collaboration targets voice agents, coding agents and enterprise copilots for Indian businesses. Globally, startups such as Hopper and RouterPlus address specific inference problems, with Hopper focused on real-time voice agents. The articles say the opportunity is unlikely to settle into a single category.

The articles name Simplismart, Pipeshift, E2E Networks, JarvisLabs, Apna and Blue Machines AI as participants, and they say businesses across sectors must decide how much control they need over models and infrastructure. Customers such as Sanas and Exotel are described as beneficiaries of lower costs and faster responses. Subramanian says startups experimenting with open models may favour shared APIs, while high-volume voice applications may need dedicated capacity. Regulated enterprises may want more control over their models, data and deployment environment. The articles do not quantify how widely these platforms are adopted.

Inc42 notes that global cloud giants and AI providers are competing for a share of the growing inference market. The articles say Sarvam AI launched Prism, an open-weight decision model for structured decisions in enterprise workflows. They also note that E2E Networks offers managed and self-managed inference. The articles frame the sector as one where the Indian startups must build sustainable businesses. They do not say how that competition will resolve.

The articles leave open whether Indian startups can win against global cloud giants and AI providers. They do not say whether Simplismart's reported savings will hold across other customers, or how Pipeshift and Neysa's partnership will perform. The coverage does not give adoption figures for these platforms or their revenue. It also does not settle which of the four consumption methods will dominate. The next steps for the sector are not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: South Korea's AI Strategy Committee Launches Cyber Resilience Task Force
stories.Summary:
South Korea's National AI Strategy Committee launched a National Cyber Resilience Task Force on November 12. This new initiative aims to supplement security policies that focus on defense. The committee created this group because cyberattacks are becoming more sophisticated. These attacks are growing more complex due to advances in artificial intelligence. The task force will now address these evolving threats to national security.

The committee will establish a national cyber resilience strategy by the first quarter of 2027. An implementation roadmap will cover the years 2027 and 2028. The strategy includes at least 10 key action items and more than 20 assessment criteria. It will develop three scenarios for recovery at AI data centers and other essential facilities. Two pilot project proposals will also be included in the final plan.

Lee Won-tae, a Kookmin University professor, leads the task force as chairman of the Special Committee on Security. Lee stated that the ability to maintain daily life during cyberattacks is what matters most now. He said the group will develop measures to enable rapid recovery after a security breach. Vice chairman Ha Jung-woo said he will personally oversee the efforts of government and private sectors. Ha wants to ensure the task force delivers results by identifying and implementing key initiatives.

The task force includes 11 private sector members from security, regional, defense, and global cooperation divisions. Government agencies like the National Intelligence Service and Ministry of Science and ICT will also participate. The Ministry of the Interior and Safety and Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment are involved. Small and medium enterprises and local community facilities with limited cybersecurity capabilities are affected. These entities will receive guidance on improvements, recovery measures, and simulation exercises.

AI allows attackers to automate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement more quickly. Enterprises are embedding AI into workflows, which creates new dependencies on autonomous systems and data. This complexity means disruptions can have wider and faster consequences for business operations. Recovery is now about bringing back clean data to a safe space after a compromise. Traditional IT governance and controls around identities and access still remain essential requirements.

The task force will analyze emerging cyber threats and policy gaps in existing response systems. It will identify measures to ensure the continuity of essential services and critical national functions. Members will assess vulnerabilities at individual companies and institutions to provide specific recovery guidance. The articles do not state the specific names of the 11 private sector members. They also leave open the exact details of the two planned pilot project proposals.

stories.Headline: How Nvidia became the backbone of the global artificial intelligence industry
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the global AI industry, has come under scrutiny after allegations linked to its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and a suspected Chinese intelligence operative accused of facilitating access to restricted computing chips. Huang has resigned as chief executive, and Nvidia has appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim chief executive while it searches for a successor. The allegations, which China has dismissed, emerged as governments restrict advanced semiconductor exports and major technology companies try to reduce their reliance on Nvidia. A separate report, published on the moneycontrol.com site on November 13, 2026, described a researcher's finding of numerical patterns matching Nvidia Blackwell hardware in AI models from six Chinese developers. The company's dominance rests on hardware and on the CUDA software platform that Nvidia introduced in 2007.

Nvidia was originally known mainly as a maker of graphics processing units for computer games, and Huang co-founded the company in 1993. Huang insisted that CUDA be included in every GPU Nvidia sold, adding to production costs even though most purchasers never used it. The strategy gained importance in 2012, when researchers increasingly used CUDA for artificial intelligence, and AlexNet demonstrated better image recognition than existing techniques. In 2016, Nvidia introduced the DGX-1, a system containing eight GPUs, and Huang personally delivered the first unit to OpenAI. That year Google's DeepMind used 176 GPUs in January against Fan Hui, then 48 tensor processing units by March when AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol.

The United States introduced restrictions in 2022 on exports of advanced computing chips to China, covering many of Nvidia's highest-performance products. The measures are intended to limit China's progress in artificial intelligence and prevent military use of the technology. The allegations concern Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, a claim China rejects. According to the Financial Times, she told Chinese investors she could secure access to Nvidia GPUs. The Information reported she was involved in a proposed deal to purchase 240,000 restricted GPUs.

The Financial Times and The Information are cited as the sources for these claims, and Alice Huang has not publicly responded to them. The New York Times reported allegations of a second affair involving Jensen Huang and an Nvidia executive, which he has not confirmed. Nvidia's valuation had reached $4.5 trillion before the controversy, making it the world's most valuable company. News of the initial allegations wiped almost $500 billion from its market value, and further share-price declines followed the announcement of Huang's departure. Investors and businesses whose AI operations depend on Nvidia hardware and software are affected by the leadership change.

The company has operated as a central supplier to the AI industry since its transformation from a gaming hardware maker, and competitors including Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are developing alternative chips. Google continues to use its TPUs, while Nvidia retains dominance supported by software built around CUDA over decades. Researchers and companies that have invested in this ecosystem face substantial difficulties in moving to competing platforms. Nvidia must now identify a new chief executive while Colette Kress serves as interim leader. The articles do not say who will succeed Huang, what the outcome of the intelligence allegations will be, or whether the Chinese AI model findings constitute export violations.

stories.Headline: 'Artificial Intelligence enhances private sector competitiveness'
stories.Summary:
Qatar Chamber Chairman Sheikh Khalifa bin Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani told the opening session of the 13th Gulf Quality Conference in Doha that quality is now an integrated corporate culture. He said artificial intelligence is a key driver of institutional performance, improving service quality, data analysis and operational efficiency. The remarks were made on 12 November 2026 at Sharq Village & Spa in Doha, under the theme "AI and Customer Service Quality." The session was attended by Minister of State and President of Qatar National Library Dr. Hamad bin Abdulaziz Al Kuwari, along with officials, experts and representatives of public and private institutions. The event was organised by the Gulf Quality Centre for Consultancy and Training as a platform for sharing AI applications that enhance customer services across Gulf institutions.

Sheikh Khalifa said adopting international quality standards and AI applications would help private sector companies, particularly SMEs, raise productivity and competitiveness. He reaffirmed the Qatar Chamber's commitment to supporting technological advancement and best institutional practices. He expressed hope that the conference would end with practical recommendations to promote innovation across the GCC. He also commended the Gulf Quality Centre for organising the event. Mohammed Al Hamad, Director of Communications at the Gulf Standardization Organization, highlighted how digital transformation and AI improve services, communication and data-driven decisions.

Mohammed Al Hamad also described the GSO's work with national standardisation committees to develop standards and technical regulations across the GCC. Mohammed Saleh Al Kuwari, Chairman of the Gulf Quality Centre and President of the conference, said the theme reflects the growing importance of modern technologies. He pointed to ISO 10004:2018, which covers monitoring and measuring customer satisfaction. He hoped the discussions would encourage companies to strengthen their commitment to international quality standards. Al Kuwari announced three new services by the Centre, coinciding with World Quality Day.

Those services are the "Mi'yar" platform, which uses generative AI to analyse customer feedback, the "Ma Qalla Wa Dalla" series of short AI-produced training films, and the "Creative Ideas Bank," managed by an AI agent. The conference's focus on customer service quality concerns institutions across the Gulf and the private sector companies that the chairman singled out. The articles identify SMEs as a group that would benefit from adopting these standards and applications. Speakers presented these tools as ways to improve services for customers in the region.

Separately, on 12 November 2026, Navatar, a Salesforce-based CRM for private equity and M&A firms, announced enhanced Salesforce Model Context Protocol capabilities in New York and London. The capabilities bring information from documents into Claude-assisted work, even when users do not know which document holds it. The supported sources are documents in Navatar CRM, SharePoint, other connected document management systems and shared drives. Professionals can verify findings, select relevant information and add it to the right CRM fields, and firms need not move documents into a single repository.

Navatar's announcement says that important deal information often sits outside structured CRM fields, such as in management presentations, meeting notes or diligence files. Without document access, a professional asking Claude about a deal may miss a relevant detail. The company says the enhanced connection lets Claude use that document information alongside CRM data, with results returned to Navatar. Navatar's Claude-native deal engine is now available for private markets firms. The company describes itself as powering private markets and investment banking firms worldwide, including private equity, venture capital and private credit firms.

The Peninsula article gives no figures on the conference's outcome, attendance, or the adoption of the AI tools by companies. The Navatar release does not say how many firms use the service or the pricing terms. Neither article reports whether the GCC recommendations will be issued or how the Mi'yar platform and other Centre services will perform. The articles also do not state whether companies in Qatar will adopt the Navatar tools. Both sources leave open how widely these AI services will be taken up in their respective markets.

stories.Headline: New private school in downtown Chicago using artificial intelligence to teach students
stories.Summary:
Alpha Chicago opened a new private school in downtown Chicago during its first year of operation in 2026. This institution uses AI-powered software to teach students core subjects like reading, science, and math. Students spend two hours every morning learning these specific core subjects on a computer. The rest of the school day focuses on developing real-world skills like cooking and sewing. Students also learn how to navigate public transportation and practice leadership and teamwork.

The school is located in the Lakeshore East neighborhood and currently has around 50 enrolled students. The facility can hold up to 500 students, while Alpha Schools has 1,500 students across 50 campuses. Tuition for one student costs nearly 55,000 dollars, and the school uses a program called 2 Hour Learning. The school employs guides instead of traditional teachers, and only one-third have education degrees per a February analysis. This analysis was conducted by the University of Colorado's National Education Policy Center, which is a nonpartisan think tank.

Lead guide Carrington Haas stated that AI is a component, but the magic is teaching life skills. These skills include financial literacy and public speaking, which Haas believes are the most impressive parts of Alpha. Dean of parents Dr. Brian Howell, a former anthropology professor, said people often have misunderstandings about this education. Howell noted that most families are from the Chicago area, though one family moved states to attend. He expressed a desire to expand the model so it is not just an exclusive education.

Student Owen enjoys the platform but says the software sounds like a robot rather than a human. Associate professor Charles Tocci of Loyola University Chicago questioned if the AI component is truly an innovation. Tocci suggested the goal might be scaling the software platform to serve a billion students within 20 years. He also noted that some of the school's approach is similar to the existing Montessori education model. Other parents and teachers in Chicago are protesting Google's AI policies at an office on North Morgan Street.

Google announced that K-12 schools will lose search engine access if they switch off all company AI tools. This includes AI Overview and AI Mode, which executives say are too deeply integrated to shut off. Chicago Public Schools has blocked AI chatbots like Claude, ChatGPT, and the Gemini App on student devices. Twelve elected board members, including president-elect Jessica Biggs, signed a pledge for a three-year generative AI moratorium. This pledge also called for the appointment of a chief privacy officer and limits on classroom screen-time.

Alpha Chicago has applied for a zoning permit to renovate an old school in Evanston to expand. This request is currently going through the city approval process to determine if the renovation can proceed. Chicago Public Schools is exploring options to independently suppress AI Mode and AI Overview in the Google Search engine. If these efforts fail, the district spokesperson said officials may consider using an alternative search engine for students. The articles leave open whether Alpha will reach its goal of serving a billion students in 20 years.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as spy scandal stirs fear of US curbs
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres outside China, according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to Reuters. They worry a scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang could push Washington to tighten limits on their remote use of advanced processors. A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some firms have contacted data centre operators about reserving it. Smaller AI labs are considering similar steps, including approaching major providers of rented computing power in South-east Asia, two of the sources said. Huang said on Sunday, Nov 8, that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and the story was published on Nov 12, 2026.

The companies fear the controversy could add political momentum to the Remote Access Security Act, known as Rasa, a US bill giving the Commerce Department authority over remote, cloud-based access to restricted technology. The House of Representatives passed the bill in January by a vote of 369 to 22, and it now awaits action in the Senate. Washington already restricts exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips, yet Chinese firms can reach such processors by renting computing power at overseas data centres. Restricting overseas cloud access would make it harder for Chinese developers to obtain high-end computing power without importing the chips directly. The prospect of tougher enforcement has also fuelled demand in China's grey market, where traders and intermediaries have begun stockpiling restricted Nvidia AI chips, two of the sources said.

The people who described these moves declined to be identified, and would not name the cloud provider, because of the sensitivity of the matter. Nvidia, Megaspeed and the US Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tencent and Alibaba also did not immediately respond, and Reuters said it could not independently verify the allegation that the woman involved was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied that allegation, and Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting chips to China. Seoul Economic Daily, citing Reuters, The Information and other foreign media, reported that Alice Hwang, whom it describes as an alleged Chinese agent, built a multilayered business structure linking China, Singapore and Malaysia.

The New York Times reported that the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed, and that US authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Alice Huang had business dealings and investment ties with several leading Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba, according to two people familiar with the matter. Singapore business filings show that Alibaba subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions provided financing to Speedmatrix, a Malaysian company linked to Megaspeed, according to records Reuters reviewed. Singapore authorities summoned her over suspicions of false import declarations but closed the investigation for lack of evidence. Taiwanese authorities also monitored her visits at Washington's request, and she later left for Shanghai, although Megaspeed's business continues.

Washington has struggled to stop Chinese access to advanced chips, and the articles point to several earlier cases. A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips in October despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show. US prosecutors in March charged Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips to China through a South-east Asia-based company. Prosecutors said that company bought about US$2.5 billion of servers from Super Micro between 2024 and 2025, and that a substantial portion went to China, while the defendants have not been convicted. Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese customers gain access to restricted chips, and Seoul Economic Daily reported that its Malaysian arm Speedmatrix pledged servers and intellectual property to Alibaba affiliate Apex as collateral.

Seoul Economic Daily reported that Alice Hwang's chip dealings were estimated at about 240,000 units, including H100, H200 and A100 processors, either smuggled into China or supplied as leased data centre capacity. The paper said the Malaysian figures linked to her have reportedly pressed ahead with data centre construction in Malaysia. The articles do not say when the Senate will act on Rasa, or whether the Commerce Department will take any step against remote access. They also leave open whether Chinese firms will succeed in securing overseas capacity, and whether a wider US crackdown on smuggling of chips and AI servers will follow. Headlines linked to the story say Nvidia is preparing to oust Huang, though the articles give no detail on that.

stories.Headline: AI-era trade challenges demand cooperation
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, China's General Administration of Customs reported that foreign trade in goods kept growing strongly in the first 10 months of the year. Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year to 44.81 trillion yuan, about 6.67 trillion U.S. dollars, accelerating from 18.8 percent over the first nine months. Imports surged 23.6 percent, while exports rose 17.6 percent during the January to October period. Booming artificial intelligence demand lifted exports of electronic components, and imports posted especially robust gains. Both imports and exports have now recorded double-digit growth for six consecutive months through October.

Goods trade in October alone expanded 31.2 percent. Mechanical and electrical products rose 25.2 percent over the period and accounted for 64.7 percent of total exports, up 3.9 percentage points from a year earlier. Exports of integrated circuits and memory components surged 101.9 percent and 132.5 percent, while 3D printers, digital cameras and industrial robots rose 104.8 percent, 41.4 percent and 17.8 percent. Exports of the so-called new three, electric vehicles, photovoltaic products and lithium batteries, grew 46.5 percent, electric motorcycles and bicycles rose 33.3 percent, and wind turbines and their components gained 19.7 percent. By trading partner, trade with ASEAN grew 24.2 percent, trade with the European Union rose 8.5 percent, and trade with the United States expanded 6.3 percent, while trade with Belt and Road participating countries grew 18.5 percent.

Lyu Daliang, director of the customs administration's Department of Statistics and Analysis, said China's foreign trade has kept up its momentum this year, showing greater resilience and vitality. He said imports from more than 150 countries and regions recorded growth in the first 10 months. Imports from ASEAN, Latin America and Africa all reached record highs for the same period. In his words, China's vast market continued to offer opportunities to the world. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said several factors kept export growth elevated in October.

She noted that the global AI investment boom continued to push up prices of chips, other electronic components and computer parts, which drove strong growth in export value. She added that domestic manufacturing upgrades in recent years have also strengthened the competitiveness of new energy vehicles and high-tech products. Separately, Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio told a high-level virtual meeting convened by French President Emmanuel Macron that African and other developing nations must have a meaningful voice in shaping global standards for frontier AI. He said no country can adequately address these challenges alone and that sovereignty means choosing the terms on which countries work together. The Sierra Leone presidency said the meeting, held on Monday, November 9, focused on strengthening international cooperation on frontier model security.

Attendees included the prime ministers of the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Norway and the Netherlands, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Bahrain's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa also took part, along with technology leaders Brad Smith of Microsoft, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Arthur Mensch of Mistral AI. Bio recalled that Sierra Leone endorsed the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models at the AI Middle Powers Roundtable at the United Nations General Assembly in September, co-hosted by Kenya and Finland. He said the country has completed its National AI Readiness Assessment, which will inform its first National AI Strategy, and that it is exploring AI in agriculture, healthcare, education and public service delivery.

He also cited the proposed Regional Data Embassy Framework under ECOWAS, which aims to expand shared infrastructure while safeguarding national control over data. A commentary carried by China Daily Global Edition, drawing on interviews with Zhang Monan of the China Center for International Economic Exchanges and Wang Zhimin of the University of International Business and Economics, examined how AI demand moves along global supply chains. It said AI is spreading into manufacturing, automobiles, robotics and smart devices, and that it helps firms overcome language and information barriers in cross-border trade and improves logistics. It warned that AI could widen the digital divide because of gaps in technology, infrastructure and talent, and said China has worked with various countries on digital infrastructure and smart cities through the Digital Silk Road.

It also said data, algorithms and intelligent services are raising questions about market access, cross-border data flows, privacy, intellectual property and security certification. Bio told the meeting that common standards for evaluating advanced models, clear accountability for developers and deployers, and mechanisms for reporting serious incidents are essential, and that countries should not simply adopt standards set elsewhere. Experts quoted by Xinhua expect strong exports to continue through the end of the year. Zhang Di, a macro analyst at China Galaxy Securities, said that as the AI cycle remains in an upswing, China will keep benefiting as a global hub of electronics supply chains.

She added that the global green and low-carbon transition, combined with China's rising competitiveness in mechanical equipment, will sustain strong growth in new energy vehicles, ships and other transport machinery. Bio welcomed the proposed Paris Declaration and called for its commitments on common evaluation standards, accountability and incident reporting to become practical measures. He said Sierra Leone is ready to work with international partners and wants greater investment in scientific expertise, institutional capacity and evaluation tools for developing countries. The articles do not say when the Paris Declaration will be finalized, and the China Daily commentary does not name specific rules or agreements that would follow its call for cooperation.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Claude down: Why it said it was unable to authenticate code
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Claude AI assistant went down on the morning of November 13, 2026, with users unable to authenticate to Claude.ai and Claude Code, according to the company's status page. The disruption came as a massive outage affecting multiple Microsoft services was still unresolved that day. Anthropic wrote on its Claude Status page that it was investigating an issue with user authentication and would provide an update as soon as possible. Mashable's own staff could log into Claude without trouble, though some users reported on X that they could not. It was unclear whether Anthropic's problems were connected to the Microsoft troubles.

Separately, Anthropic announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, a set of new workplace tools led by Claude Meetings, which lets the chatbot join Google Meet calls as a participant. During meetings Claude can answer questions in the meeting chat, pull information from connected work apps, and create plans and timelines as participants discuss them. Notes, action items and other work products remain available afterward inside Claude. Claude Meetings launches in beta for Team and Enterprise customers. Two further tools, Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets, let teams brainstorm on a shared whiteboard or create and edit spreadsheets with AI help, and both launch in beta for paid subscribers.

Anthropic is the company responsible for Claude, and its status page carried the statement about the authentication problem. The company described the workplace tools as a move to make Claude as indispensable to knowledge workers as it has become for many coders, according to the article's framing of the announcement. Anthropic's own statements, as quoted in the coverage, were limited to acknowledging the authentication investigation and promising a further update. The workplace announcement was attributed to the company's launch of its new tools.

The authentication failure affected users of Claude.ai and Claude Code, while the Microsoft outage affected multiple Microsoft services. Mashable reported that the Microsoft outage had brought many people's workdays to a halt, and that Microsoft 365 services were beginning to come back online. Users who relied on Claude for coding or work tasks were left unable to log in during the disruption. Knowledge workers were the audience targeted by the new Claude Meetings, Whiteboards and Sheets tools announced days earlier.

Mashable's coverage of the Microsoft outage noted that Microsoft said failed server checks may have played a role in its November 12 outage. Earlier in the same period, Anthropic had also updated its Usage Policy and launched Claude Opus 5.5, which it said rivals Fable 5.1 on most tasks at 40 percent lower cost than Opus 5. Anthropic had also made Claude able to send Gmail emails without first asking for approval. These were separate product and policy moves reported in the same coverage stream as the outage.

The articles leave open the cause of the Claude authentication failure and whether it was related to the Microsoft outage. They do not say when service was restored or when Anthropic's promised update would arrive. The Microsoft Outlook outage fix timing was also still unresolved when the coverage ended. The Claude Meetings beta's broader availability and the final shape of the Whiteboards, Sheets and Data tools were not stated in the articles. Mashable said it would update its story when more was known.

stories.Headline: Google's Gemini Glasses Start at $395, With Preorders Open Ahead of December Launch
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 12, 2026, that its Gemini glasses had moved from preview to preorder, according to AndroidGuys. Google confirmed Warby Parker frames starting at $395 and Gentle Monster models from $449. Retail availability is set for December 10, 2026. The Samsung-engineered glasses combine hands-free Gemini assistance, navigation, translation, audio, and a 12-megapixel camera. Google rates battery life at up to nine hours, depending on use.

Support covers Pixel 7 and newer with the Android 17 September 2026 update or later, specified Galaxy models on One UI 9.0 or later, and iPhone 13 Pro and newer. Setup requires a compatible Google Account for an adult in the U.S. or South Korea. Guided Vision's spoken visual descriptions and Aira's human interpreter service require a compatible Android phone at launch and may require a subscription or membership. Guided Vision is not a mobility aid or a replacement for a white cane, and Audible is also Android-only at launch. Google's privacy breakdown says visuals used for Gemini assistance aren't saved in Gemini History or used for AI training or ad targeting.

Google says photos and videos you deliberately capture still go to your gallery. The glasses are designed to redact bystanders' faces before Gemini processing and block photo or video capture if the recording indicator is covered. Private AI Compute is planned for later, and Google hasn't provided a date. Preorders are available through Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, with demos at selected retail locations. Google's privacy breakdown addresses what happens to the camera data.

MarkTechPost reports that Google launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 (gemini-decision-1). The API does not generate text, and it scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. Google prices it at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with zero output tokens billed. Context is 262,144 tokens (256K) across shared input and all questions, and it runs on the Google-hosted API only (Gemini Developer API, v1beta), with no open weights or self-hosting.

Google reports that Gemini Decision 1 leads 7 of 9 accuracy benchmarks in its table, with the lowest calibration error. Its worst result is 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, its lowest score, and it trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%). Google calls it best for multimodal, calibrated decisions in 150-250 ms, but not the cheapest, since Jev 1.14 costs $0.68 vs $0.88 on the shared suite. Gemini Decision 1 is a specialized multimodal model from Google built for closed-set decisions, reading text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one prefill pass.

Output token usage is always 0, and your code branches directly on the returned numbers. Each request has 3 parts: a model ID, a shared input, and a map of questions, and the docs define 3 question types. The noul (yes/no) type returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99, while choice picks 1 of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for every option. The score type rates input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score, and every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1.

Google suggests routing low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer, and questions are scored in parallel and cannot see each other. Standard models decode an answer token by token, then your code parses it, but Gemini Decision 1 instead scores your candidate options in one forward pass. Google reports median model compute of 50-100 ms and 150-250 ms end to end, which holds for inputs up to 16K tokens and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. The shared input is billed once per request, however many questions you ask, and each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens. There are no thinking-token, transcription or OCR charges.

Google tested Gemini Decision 1 against 3 rivals: TypeSafe Jev 1.14, GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI Decisions and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, and all figures are self-reported by Google. Refusals and safety blocks count as incorrect. On JevBench (public split) Gemini Decision 1 scored 92.2%, TypeSafe Jev 1.14 90.0%, GPT-6 Luna 90.9% and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 86.6%. On Amazon ESCI (Macro-F1) the scores were 58.7%, 56.7%, 54.7% and 47.2%, and on New Yorker Caption (text-only) they were 79.7%, 72.0%, 68.4% and 73.7%.

On Mind2Web Multimodal the scores were 86.2%, 86.8%, 81.8% and 78.0%, and on PubMedQA they were 79.8%, 78.2%, 74.4% and 77.6%. On Global-MMLU-Lite (non-English) the scores were 86.0%, 85.0%, 79.6% and 78.8%, and on When2Call they were 79.9%, 82.0%, 70.4% and 60.9%. On MMAU (audio) Gemini Decision 1 scored 71.8% and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 67.7%, with the other two not reported. On Video-MME (no subtitles) Gemini Decision 1 scored 69.1% and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 63.3%, with the other two not reported, and Top-1 ECE (lower is better) was 0.02.

stories.Headline: OpenAI faces civil racketeering charges over $30bn data center planned in Effingham County, Georgia
stories.Summary:
The civil racketeering lawsuit over OpenAI's planned Project Camellia data center in Effingham County, Georgia was filed by residents against the company, two of its affiliates and several county officials. The complaint alleges that the defendants kept residents in the dark about the project. It is the third lawsuit related to Project Camellia filed since the 3.2 GW campus was announced in July. Among the allegations are civil conspiracy, improper zoning procedures, and civil racketeering involving false statements, perjury, and forgery. The complaint does not detail specific statements that might constitute racketeering.

The project is a $30 billion data center campus planned on a 1,440-acre parcel at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon. It would have four data center buildings with a total footprint of 4.4 million square feet, or 408,775 square meters. Construction could start in 2028 if final permission is granted. A Supervisors' board decision that had been due on November 4 has been shifted to November 19. Tom's Hardware reports the site is expected to cost between $20 billion and $30 billion, built across five phases.

The lawsuit was filed by the law firm Savage Turner Pinkney Savage Sprouse & Gilluly on behalf of three Effingham County residents, identified as Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver. The named defendants include county commissioners Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly and Phil Kieffer, County Manager Tim Callanan, and Industrial Development Authority CEO Brandt Herndon. Also named are the Industrial Development Authority, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, which operates the data center for OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC. OpenAI was contacted for comment, and the articles do not report a response.

The plaintiffs say offers to buy nearby properties have been reduced or withdrawn, and that the project has affected their property values, so they seek civil damages. The complaint alleges the defendants used non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements to keep residents unaware of the project's nature for as long as possible. Residents say the county tried to secure land, tax incentives and zoning approvals without informing them until key decisions were final and contracts signed. The plaintiffs describe the actions as affecting residents of Effingham County, whose property values they say have declined.

OpenAI has promised that the project will not raise the community's utility costs, since it will pay for all required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will use minimal water through a closed-loop system. The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act was originally conceived to counter organized crime, but Georgia's version is less stringent than the federal one. Georgia's RICO statute was used in the 2023 election case against Donald Trump and 18 others over the 2020 presidential election results in the state, and in Young Thug's trial. Georgia State University professor Volkan Topalli, quoted in Atlanta Magazine, said critics consider the state version too encompassing. Developers say they use NDAs to avoid running afoul of insider trading rules, though West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana closed a data center deal without one.

Two other lawsuits related to the project were filed earlier this year, one over zoning and another over the Effingham County Industrial Development Authority's role in advancing the development. None of the three cases has yet reached court. The articles do not say whether the November 19 board decision will proceed as scheduled or how the courts will rule on the claims. They also do not report whether OpenAI or the county has responded to the allegations in court.

stories.Headline: Elevated errors on claude.ai, Claude Code, and platform.claude.com
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, an issue affected users authenticating to Claude.ai and Claude Code, according to a status page incident report. The incident affected claude.ai, Claude Console at platform.claude.com, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. The investigating update was posted on November 13, 2026, at 09:58 UTC. A fix was deployed for the issue affecting Claude services, and the team monitored for recovery at 11:05 UTC. The incident was resolved, and the issue affecting claude.ai and Claude Cowork was resolved at 11:58 UTC.

The incident affected claude.ai, Claude Console at platform.claude.com, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. The status page offered email and text message subscriptions for updates on the incident. Subscribers would receive email notifications when incidents were updated and text message notifications when Claude created or resolved an incident. The page listed country calling codes from Afghanistan at +93 to Zimbabwe at +263 for SMS signup. The page stated that message and data rates may apply and that subscribers agree to the Privacy Policy, the Atlassian Terms of Service, and the Atlassian Privacy Policy.

The status page said the team was investigating an issue with users authenticating to Claude.ai and Claude Code and would provide an update as soon as possible. It said a fix had been deployed for the issue affecting Claude services and that the team was monitoring for recovery. It said the issue affecting claude.ai and Claude Cowork had been resolved. The page was powered by Atlassian Statuspage. The page stated that the site was protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service.

ZDNET's David Gewirtz, a senior contributing editor, wrote that he used Claude Code to set up and manage his local OpenClaw server. He wrote that two Macs and separate accounts kept it isolated from the real world. He wrote that Claude checks OpenClaw on demand for problems, breaches, or trouble. He cited ZDNET's Charlie Osborne saying OpenClaw is also a security nightmare. He wrote that OpenClaw and its local agentic buddies like Hermes and NemoClaw are self-contained local agentic AI that can run commands, send messages, and perform operations 24/7.

Gewirtz wrote that he installed OpenClaw on a dedicated Mac Studio with internet access but no access to home servers or personal accounts. He wrote that he ran Claude Code on his personal Mac to configure, lock down, and help manage it daily. He wrote that he pulled a 2020 64GB M1 Mac Studio out of storage for OpenClaw. He wrote that the OpenClaw instance is named Colossus, after the AI in the 1970 film Colossus: The Forbin Project. He wrote that Colossus has its own account called Forbin, with no access to personal accounts on the network or in the cloud.

Gewirtz wrote that Claude runs on his personal work machine, a 2025 M4 Mac Studio, and uses an encrypted SSH tunnel to connect to Colossus. He wrote that Claude acts as the warden with full access to Colossus' administrative functions but only runs when he actively controls it. He wrote that he set up a flat-rate $20-per-month Ollama Cloud subscription and ran GLM-5.2, made by Z.ai, formerly Zhipu AI, a Tsinghua University spinoff and the first publicly traded foundation model company in China. He wrote that Colossus tried to break out 11 different ways and every one failed. He wrote that after the test he shut down Colossus and had Claude remove every memory of the test and every element about an admin side or a warden.

stories.Headline: SE3 Raises $30 Million Series A Led by Accel for Spatial AI for Drones and Autonomous Systems
stories.Summary:
Munich-based SE3, which builds spatial AI for drones, raised $30m in Series A funding led by Accel on 12 November 2026, with Keen Venture Partners, Seedcamp and Lakestar participating. The defense tech company closed the round at $30 million, around €27 million, as reported by trendingtopics.eu on the same date. SE3 emerged from stealth only in June with €5.5 million in seed funding led by Lakestar, so the new round is roughly five times as large. The startup launched roughly two years ago and says it is working on contracts with Germany and Ukraine. Accel partner Matt Robinson pointed to the team from one of Europe's leading research departments.

SE3 is a spin-off from the chair of computer vision and A.I. at the Technical University of Munich, where CEO Lukas Köstler and CTO Simon Klenk did their PhDs in computer vision and robotics. Chair holder Daniel Cremers is a co-founder and a recipient of the Leibniz Prize, Germany's most prestigious research award. The software fuses sensor data from drones and ground vehicles made by different companies into a shared 3D picture of the terrain and uses it to direct an entire swarm. Operators control it by voice, and the software runs entirely on the devices themselves, designed to keep working when satellite navigation is disrupted. SE3 supplies the software that lets drones understand their surroundings, while the aircraft themselves come from other manufacturers.

CEO Köstler said working in defence means the company's technology has to deliver under pressure in the field. Auterion CEO Lorenz Meier said autonomy only counts if it holds up when satellite navigation is jammed and one operator is responsible for many vehicles. Robinson pointed to the team from one of Europe's leading research departments, which is building spatial A.I. for autonomous systems, something defence primes have found so difficult to do. According to SE3, the company has shipped thousands of systems over the past two years and is working on several contracts with Ukraine and Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr. SE3 works as an A.I. partner to defense contractor Hensoldt and to scale-ups such as Auterion and ERC System.

SE3's software runs, for example, on Skynode, Auterion's onboard computer. In Ukraine, where SE3 says it is already deployed, electronic warfare jams GPS signals on a massive scale, and large drone fleets overwhelm the people tasked with supervising them. How risky dependence on outside infrastructure can be became clear recently when SpaceX throttled Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian drones. SE3 deliberately positions itself as manufacturer-neutral, and procurement programs such as the Modular Open Systems Approach in the United States and MOSABw in Germany are designed to make it easier for armed forces to combine systems from different suppliers. That benefits software that works across many platforms without selling vehicles of its own.

The big fundraise comes as European defence rollups are becoming a bigger trend, and some VCs are sceptical of the strategy, which is commonly used in private equity to acquire smaller companies and make them more efficient. Munich's front-runner Helsing recently raised $1.8 billion and develops its own A.I. for drones and targeting, while in the United States, Anduril with Lattice and Shield AI with Hivemind offer software for autonomous swarms. Partners such as Auterion are also working on autonomy features of their own. The recent Dual-Use Founders Handbook shows that Europe's defense start-ups lack government customers more than investors, and procurement remains slow. SE3 does not disclose revenue or order volume, and the figures on shipped systems come from the company itself.

SE3 plans to use the funding to expand its engineering, commercial and operations teams so it can fulfill further contracts. Alongside Germany and Ukraine, the company is opening an office in the U.K. and plans to expand to other European countries. From 2027, it also wants to add civilian applications, for example in robotics and emergency response. The EU aims to mobilize up to €800 billion for defense by 2030 and is planning a drone wall on its eastern flank. The articles leave open SE3's revenue and order volume, which the company does not disclose.

stories.Headline: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
stories.Summary:
Perplexity released the open-weight decision models pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 on November 13, 2026. These models return probabilities for answers instead of generating text for the user. They can answer multiple-choice, score, and yes or no questions about images or text. The latest version introduces Locate to extract exact text spans based on instructions. These models succeed the previous v1.2 and Flash v1.2 versions.

The v1.3 model uses Qwen3.8-27B with 27B parameters, while Flash uses Qwen3.5-4B with 4B parameters. Hugging Face lists them as 26B and 5B parameters, shipping under Apache 2.0. Local defaults are 32,768 tokens, but the API supports under 256K tokens. v1.3 requires a CUDA GPU with 49 GiB of BF16 weights, while Flash needs 8.5 GiB. Both models are available on OpenRouter and the Perplexity Decisions API.

Perplexity stated that the models adapt a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. They used a linear decision head and bidirectional full-attention layers to improve performance. The company explained that Flash v1.3 was distilled from the larger model using KL divergence. They noted that the new attention system prevents answers from shifting between different questions. Perplexity also added a LoRA adapter and a span head for the Locate feature.

The models are inspired by Jev from TypeSafe, which was described as a System One model. These decision models affect tasks like PII detection, NER, and extractive QA. They outperform Jev 1.14 on most self-reported evaluations, including a 91.6 percent mean accuracy. They also beat Qwen3-Reranker-8B on retrieval tasks with an 83.99 mean nDCG@10. The models show a low answer-flip rate of 0.27 percent on real-world requests.

Decision models differ from traditional classifiers because their output classes are not baked into the head. They avoid the computational overhead and schema errors common when LLMs generate JSON objects. Traditional classifiers require retraining to add new labels, but decision models evaluate predefined primitives. Zero-shot classification allows candidate labels to change from one request to another at inference. This approach replaces autoregressive decoding when an application only needs to choose between options.

The models will be used for domain classification, where v1.3 leads Jev 1.14 in seven domains. They will also handle multilingual tasks across eight languages with 88.16 percent accuracy for v1.3. Production requests cost 26.47 dollars per 1M requests according to the company. The articles leave open whether these self-reported figures are accurate since no external audits are mentioned. It remains unclear how the models perform on tasks outside the provided benchmarks.

stories.Headline: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
stories.Summary:
AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local tool that simulates more than 200 of its cloud services on a developer's own machine. The emulator works with the AWS CLI and SDKs, so no AWS account or service fee is needed to run it. The release, announced in November 2026, stands out because autonomous AI agents wrote all of its code, and AWS says its team has not written or reviewed any of it. Developers and coding agents can use the tool to run quick, low-cost tests against AWS-style APIs. The emulator is built from 438 AWS API models and ships as one Rust crate per service.

It runs on Linux through RPM or Debian packages, or in Docker on macOS and Windows with a 2 GiB memory limit. Building it from source requires 100 GB of free disk space. In release v1.0.322, it passed 24,243 of 42,857 scored fidelity tests, or 56.6 percent. Its strongest result was AWS KMS at 93.9 percent, while AWS CloudFormation was the weakest at 15.8 percent. Resources live in memory and disappear when the program stops.

AWS attributes the work to a coordinated group of AI agents. The project began with a prompt to Kiro, which produced a basic Amazon SQS emulator in about 15 minutes, and the work was then split among three agent teams that wrote test scenarios, found failures and submitted fixes. Every change must pass a merge gate covering build, code review, security and fidelity checks, and several security agents run adversarial reviews. Matthew Goldberg is cited as reporting that hundreds of agents work at once on thousands of issues each day. The articles say the release pipeline runs on AWS Developer Tools, with CodeCommit as the agents' repository and GitHub receiving the code last.

The articles place the emulator among competing tools such as LocalStack, Moto and Floci, which differ in licensing, pricing and service coverage. AWS publishes a scores file with each release, so outside observers can review the test results. Its published fidelity figures show that control-plane operations match AWS most closely, while support for data-plane services, CloudFormation, Terraform and CDK varies widely. Operations not yet implemented return an HTTP 501 response, and the failing tests remain public in the evaluation suite.
