stories.Headline: Guide to Expanding AI Within the Company and Across Portfolio Companies for Investment Funds: November 2026 Edition
stories.Summary:
AIworker, a company based in Minato, Tokyo and led by representative director Takao Sugimoto, released a free report on November 13, 2026, about how investment funds can spread AI use inside their own operations and across the companies they invest in. The report is the November 2026 edition of a guide aimed at fund partners, value-up staff, and middle and back office managers. It draws on the company's work helping funds set rules for AI use and put it into practice. The report also includes results from actually running AI on sample monthly reports.

The report says M&A deals involving Japanese companies rose to 5,115 in 2025 from 4,700 in 2024, citing the 2026 Small and Medium Enterprise White Paper. It notes that fund internal work grows heavier as portfolio companies increase, because monthly reports differ in format and account names, so manual middle and back office work keeps rising. It also says much portfolio information must not leave the fund, so rules need to be set before AI use begins. The report covers use rules, real internal use cases by job type, and a method for building AI into a post-acquisition 100-day plan. It also includes a way to measure and estimate value-up effects and answers to likely questions from partners and portfolio company presidents.

In a test using fictional monthly reports from six portfolio companies, four in Excel and two in Word, AI built a summary list converted to millions of yen in 69 seconds. Asked to compare it with the previous month's list, it took 92 seconds to rank eight check points by importance and attach question text that could be sent to the companies. The AI caught unit errors in tables, mismatches between text and tables, corrections to figures received the previous month, and net assets close to a level promised to a bank. At a fund AIworker supported, the user base grew to 25 people in about two weeks, and in a follow-up survey of five respondents, four used it almost daily and usefulness averaged 4.6 out of 5.

The report cites statistics from the 2026 Small and Medium Enterprise White Paper and IPA's DX Trends 2025. Company names in the cases are withheld, and the monthly reports processed by AI were made up, with all company names, personal names, and numbers fictional. AIworker was established in July 2024 and works on AI agents, business AI development, FDE support, corporate generative AI training, and hands-on AI support. The report is available free through the company's website.

Articles.Title: Guide to Expanding AI Within the Company and Across Portfolio Companies for Investment Funds: November 2026 Edition

stories.Headline: TSMC signs seven-year deal with Xintec to expand CoWoS packaging
stories.Summary:
TSMC signed a seven-year agreement with Xintec Inc. to expand its advanced packaging capabilities. The deal was approved by the Xintec board on November 13, 2026. This partnership focuses on building and operating a production line in Taiwan. The contract is scheduled to last until December 31, 2033.

The project requires Xintec to build a line for the on-substrate portion of CoWoS technology. This facility will be located within a TSMC site in the Central Taiwan Science Park. Xintec will provide the staff and equipment, while TSMC provides the building. To fund the equipment, Xintec plans to raise NT$15 billion through convertible bonds. Mass production for this specific line is expected to begin in 2029.

TSMC is responsible for the overall strategy to increase capacity for AI and high-performance computing chips. The company is outsourcing part of its workload because demand from AI customers continues to exceed supply. TSMC owns about 41% of Xintec, and the affiliate already gets over 70% of its revenue from TSMC. This arrangement allows TSMC to widen its production pipeline through a trusted partner.

This deal is part of a larger push that includes a $2 billion agreement with GlobalFoundries for US production by 2028. TSMC also bought plants from AUO to gain more cleanroom space. While supply constraints should ease by 2028, the 2029 Xintec target shows that long-term demand remains high. Future milestones include the bond raising and construction updates in Taiwan.

Articles.Title: TSMC signs seven-year deal with Xintec to expand CoWoS packaging - Crypto Briefing

stories.Headline: Trustpoint Xposure Launches Program to Help Startup Founders Check How AI Search Platforms Describe Their Companies
stories.Summary:
Trustpoint Xposure, a public relations agency based in New York, launched its Startup Visibility Program on November 13, 2026. The program helps startup founders review and improve how AI search platforms such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews describe their companies. It uses methods the agency calls Answer Engine Optimization. The announcement was distributed as a press release through Newswire.com.

The program begins with an AI visibility audit that records how those platforms describe the company and its founders. Based on the audit, the work can include aligning company and founder details across online profiles, adding structured schema markup to the company's website, and identifying credible third-party sources that confirm company facts. The audit is then repeated to document what has changed. Founders can request a complimentary AI and Media Visibility Audit to see the current picture before deciding whether to proceed. The release presents accurate, consistent information as the basis for making a company easier to identify and describe correctly.

Trustpoint Xposure says that it does not guarantee that any AI platform will mention or recommend a company. It also says it does not guarantee search rankings, website traffic, investor interest, or funding, since those depend on factors outside any agency's control. The release notes that the agency's AEO Certification Framework is its own proprietary standard and is not an independent third-party certification. Jack Smith, the agency's media director, is listed as the media contact. The release also says that no AI platform publishes its exact rules for selecting sources.

The release places the program within a broader shift in how buyers, investors, and job candidates research companies. Founders increasingly find that people check outside sources before trusting a company's own claims, and those sources now include AI platforms that can draw on public information. The agency has also launched other AEO programs in recent weeks, including one for real estate professionals and another for published authors. The articles do not describe any further timeline or next steps for the Startup Visibility Program.

Articles.Title: Trustpoint Xposure Launches Program to Help Startup Founders Check How AI Search Platforms Describe Their Companies

stories.Headline: LEOTEK Highlights AI-Enabled Transportation and Energy Management for Resilient Cities at COP31
stories.Summary:
LEOTEK, a smart transportation and energy management company, used the COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye, to highlight its AI-enabled systems for traffic and energy management, according to a press release dated November 13, 2026. The company presented its work as a way to help cities manage traffic in real time, improve roadway safety and respond to changing energy needs. The release points to U.S. policy context, noting that the Department of Transportation's SMART program funds public-sector demonstrations of smart traffic signals, sensors and connected vehicles, and that the Department of Energy sees energy storage as a tool for balancing electricity supply and demand. COP31, the release says, is focusing on energy and transport, resilient cities and technology innovation, including electrification, smart mobility and artificial intelligence.

LEOTEK's Interlux AI Traffic Signal System combines camera and radar sensing, edge AI computing and digital twin technology to monitor traffic and pedestrians and to model traffic scenarios before field changes are made. The system supports adaptive signal control and priority passage for emergency vehicles. The company says Interlux is being evaluated at Curiosity Lab in Peachtree Corners, Georgia, and that it was deployed at intersections near a medical center in eastern Taiwan as part of an ambulance-priority signal trial. A companion product, LEOLink, connects roadway lighting, traffic signals and other municipal assets through IoT connectivity and cloud management, and the company reports 49 new and pilot deployments across 19 U.S. states, along with experience in more than eight countries and regions.

The company's cloud platform, RenAI, brings asset status, energy consumption, fault detection and maintenance data into one environment, and LEOTEK says its analytics and predictive maintenance can help operators reduce costs and improve reliability. An AI assistant within RenAI, called LiSA, lets operators ask natural-language questions about their equipment and receive recommendations. LEOTEK is also extending RenAI to electric vehicle charging infrastructure and battery energy storage systems so that charging demand, equipment performance and storage availability can be managed together. Bob Flaherty, Vice President of IoT at LEOTEK, described the platform as simplifying operations for users regardless of technical expertise, and Torrent Chin, President and Chief Sustainability Officer, said cities need infrastructure that can sense conditions and respond.

Articles.Title: LEOTEK Highlights AI-Enabled Transportation and Energy Management for Resilient Cities at COP31 - PR Newswire

stories.Headline: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions
stories.Summary:
A team of physicists and computer scientists led by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's Brookhaven National Laboratory developed a new artificial intelligence approach that learns on its own to separate high-energy particle jet signals from background in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The work was published in Scientific Reports in a paper by Yeonju Go and colleagues, including researchers from Columbia University and the University of Colorado Boulder. The team tested the model on simulated data captured by calorimeters at sPHENIX, a detector that operated during RHIC's final three runs. RHIC, a DOE Office of Science user facility for nuclear physics research, completed operations in early 2026. The article was published on November 13, 2026, and was edited by Lisa Lock and reviewed by Robert Egan.

The method is a generative AI approach that separates jet signals from collision background without requiring paired signal-and-background examples for training. It is described as the first use of an "unpaired, unsupervised" model that learned directly from simulated physics collision data rather than from labels fed by scientists. Researchers provided the model with simulated detector data that included collision background, along with separate simulated jet images without background. In simulated sPHENIX data, the model more accurately reconstructed jets' positions, energies and internal structure than conventional background-subtraction methods, particularly for larger jets where background fluctuations are strongest. sPHENIX collected nearly 300 petabytes of data during its runs, a cache equivalent to tens of billions of smartphone photos.

Yeonju Go, a Brookhaven Lab physicist and Stony Brook University assistant professor working on RHIC data analysis, said improving background subtraction can enable more precise measurements of how quarks and gluons interact under extreme conditions. Go said the detector sees a crowded "image" in which the signal is buried inside a dense spray of other particles, and the AI method learns to split that image into the jet signal and the background without one-to-one "answer key" examples. Dmitrii Torbunov, a Brookhaven Lab computer scientist, said the problem with the traditional approach is that it requires a lot of human work to annotate all the data. Torbunov said the newer generation of machine learning algorithms focuses on the so-called unsupervised learning paradigm. Torbunov said the new framework does not need to be told what corresponds to a cat or a dog, and unsupervised methods can learn useful concepts and patterns directly from the data.

Torbunov said the algorithm looks at a collection of pure background data produced by the QGP and at ideal jet simulations, then automatically figures out how to extract the underlying jet signal while removing the background. He said this paradigm is useful for science because scientific data can contain very large backgrounds, and it may be difficult or even impossible to manually determine how much of each data point comes from background and how much from jet signal. Go said the physicists of sPHENIX are privileged and lucky to work with computer scientists at Brookhaven Lab, whose contributions on the model were big. Go said they have been working on multiple projects together and this is not a one-time project. The advance could help scientists make more precise measurements of the quark-gluon plasma, a hot, dense state of matter that existed a microsecond after the Big Bang.

At Brookhaven Lab, physicists recreated early-universe conditions that produce the QGP, a "soup" of free quarks and gluons, in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC. Physicists use jets, collimated sprays of high-energy particles produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, as one of the best probes of the QGP. As jets stream through the QGP, the many particles within them lose energy and experience changes to their internal structure. Separating jet signals from the enormous background produced in heavy-ion collisions has long limited the precision of jet measurements. The new machine learning approach comes amid a growing focus across DOE national laboratories and other research institutions on harnessing AI to accelerate scientific discovery.

Looking ahead, researchers aim to apply the model to the wealth of physics data collected by sPHENIX and possibly apply it to future experiments at the Electron-Ion Collider. Go said they definitely want to use the model on their experimental data, especially as sPHENIX has a very large data set, and that extracting the physics results is the next step. Go said this would be the first use of this kind of model in the nuclear and particle physics community, not just RHIC, and they expect it to be applicable to calorimeter-based measurements at the EIC or the Large Hadron Collider in Europe. Because the framework works directly with image-like detector data, researchers say its potential extends beyond high-energy particle jet studies to other experiments that must disentangle overlapping signals. The article's summary states that validation on experimental data remains pending.

Articles.Title: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions - Phys.org

stories.Headline: SC26 Preview: AI-HPC Convergence Takes Center Stage in Chicago
stories.Summary:
Ahead of the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, Data Center Frontier aired a preview episode of its podcast hosted by contributing editor Doug Black. The conversation brought together Lois Curfman McInnes of Argonne National Laboratory, Addison Snell of Intersect 360 Research, and Earl Joseph of Hyperion Research. The episode also launched the outlet's new Frontier Computing channel. The conference runs November 15 to 20, and the article was published on November 13, 2026. The panel's central theme was that artificial intelligence is changing how scientific computing itself is carried out, rather than serving only as an add-on to traditional supercomputing.

McInnes said the field is moving beyond simply building bigger and faster machines toward integrating AI into software development, simulations, and research workflows. Joseph cited new Hyperion research finding that 70 percent of respondents already use AI for code generation. The panel also discussed the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, an effort to link supercomputers, large-scale AI infrastructure, and cloud resources for scientific discovery. The speakers raised concerns about the economics and sustainability of the AI buildout. Snell said the industry's focus on rapid construction has outpaced serious discussion of infrastructure lifecycles and upgrades.

Joseph said it is increasingly hard to finance supercomputers costing $100 million or more when new GPU generations arrive roughly every 12 months. He also argued that the industry has not done enough to explain the societal value of its infrastructure investments amid growing public opposition to data center development. The discussion also looked ahead to the SC26 exhibition floor, touching on quantum computing's longer-term prospects, photonics, advanced cooling, processor sovereignty, and whether traditional high-performance computing capabilities can be preserved as hardware becomes more optimized for AI. The article presents these topics as a preview of a conference defined as much by the trade-offs of building next-generation AI and scientific infrastructure as by raw computing performance. Listeners were directed to the full podcast episode for the complete conversation.

Articles.Title: SC26 Preview: AI-HPC Convergence Takes Center Stage in Chicago - Data Center Frontier

stories.Headline: How crypto and AI lost the midterms, and why they say they didn’t
stories.Summary:
Crypto and AI super PACs spent $250 million trying to hand-pick the next Congress in the 2026 midterms, and most of that money backed candidates who lost in the races where it could make a difference. The most expensive loss came in the Ohio Senate special election to fill the seat vacated by JD Vance, where the industry spent $64 million to keep Sherrod Brown from returning and Brown won anyway. In 2024, when Brown lost his Senate seat, the crypto industry's flagship Fairshake super PAC took credit almost immediately, saying "thanks to our efforts, he will be leaving the Senate." This year Fairshake has had much less to say after that $64 million Ohio loss. A Fairshake spokesman handed one industry newsletter a statistic that the network backed winners in 86 of the 93 races it spent in, a roughly 92% success rate.

Fairshake went 74 for 74 in races where its candidate was a clear or likely favorite, but just 10 for 18 in races that were actually competitive. About half of the $154.5 million it spent had backed candidates who lost. Industry super PACs spent $48.5 million in competitive primaries and runoffs, and $30.8 million of it backed winners including Republicans Barry Moore of Alabama and Andy Barr of Kentucky and Democrats Christian Menefee of Texas, Adrian Boafo of Maryland, and Jasmine Clark of Georgia. The PACs spent $10.3 million in a failed attempt to defeat Democrat Juliana Stratton in the Illinois Senate race, $2.5 million against Democrat La Shawn Ford in Illinois' 7th District, and $2.1 million against Democrat Oliver Gilbert in Florida's 24th District, and all three won in November. In the competitive general election races, Fairshake lost three of the four, and those three losses, Republicans Jon Husted in the Ohio Senate race, Bill Huizenga in Michigan's District 4, and Bryan Steil in Wisconsin's District 1, accounted for $58.6 million of crypto's $170 million in midterm spending.

Fairshake's one competitive win was in the Nebraska Senate race, where it spent almost $13.5 million to oppose independent Dan Osborn in his race against incumbent Pete Ricketts, whose seat on the Senate Banking Committee drew crypto's support. Brown chaired the Senate Banking Committee until his 2024 defeat, and Tyler Winklevoss, co-founder of the crypto exchange Gemini, celebrated the ouster of a "crypto public enemy" and "Elizabeth Warren co-conspirator." Brown is not expected to retake his Senate Banking chairmanship, but Warren looks likely to take the spot, and Brown may well end up heading the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the CFTC. Huizenga, the vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, lost to Democrat Sean McCann, and Steil, who chairs the committee's digital assets subcommittee, lost to Democrat Mitchell Berman. Next year, House Financial Services will likely be run by Maxine Waters, who is reportedly already working to expand her "Crypto Investor and Consumer Bill of Rights," originally proposed as an amendment to the Clarity Act, into a full market structure bill of her own.

The Winklevoss-funded, explicitly pro-MAGA Digital Freedom Fund spent all of its $9 million across three Senate races and lost all three, most of it going to Ohio, where it added $7.5 million to oppose Brown and support Husted. It also spent about $870,000 trying to stop James Talarico and boost Ken Paxton in Texas, and about $700,000 against Josh Turek and for Ashley Hinson in Iowa. First Principles Digital, a crypto PAC linked to Senator Cynthia Lummis, went 0 for 2, spending $810,000 backing Mike Rogers against Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and $200,000 trying to unseat Democratic Representative Shomari Figures in Alabama's 2nd District, a crypto ally the industry had helped elect in 2024. Across all crypto super PACs, they went one for six in competitive general election races, and of the $82.2 million spent on these races, 84% was spent on the losing side, while in races rated safe or likely they spent $9.1 million and went 29 for 29. In 2024, Fairshake spent heavily on Democrats, including more than $10 million each to help elect Elissa Slotkin in Michigan and Ruben Gallego in Arizona, but this cycle, outside of primaries, crypto super PACs did almost no significant spending to help Democrats.

The AI industry's super PACs, which spent about $80 million this cycle, had problems too, and the Leading the Future network, funded by Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI's Greg Brockman, followed the same back-the-winners strategy as Fairshake. In the primaries, where it spent $27.8 million, only seven of 37 races were competitive, but its big win in New York's District 12 was a costly one, spending $8.2 million opposing Democrat Alex Bores, who ran on a platform of "AI safety," only for Bores to lose to Micah Lasher, who campaigned on the same. Greg Brockman reportedly canceled a planned second $25 million donation amid pushback from OpenAI employees, and venture capitalist Ron Conway, the network's only publicly known Democratic funder, said he wouldn't contribute again. Despite announced plans to dump $125 million into the midterms, the network ultimately spent less than a third of that, and in the general election it spent just under $10 million to back 21 sure winners.

It supported only a single candidate in a competitive race, Darline Graham, who lost her South Carolina Senate race despite $4.8 million in support from the network, its largest general election expenditure and second largest overall. The conservative, pro-AI Alliance for a Better Future, whose advisory council lists members from groups including the Heritage Foundation, the NCOSE anti-pornography organization, and the effective altruist-aligned Future of Life Institute, spent $2.1 million on four Republican Senate candidates, all of whom lost: Mike Rogers in Michigan, Susan Collins in Maine, Ashley Hinson in Iowa, and Roger Marshall in Kansas. The Public First network, funded mostly by a dark money group backed by Anthropic, spent $13.2 million of its $24.2 million in primary spending to back Alex Bores, who lost, and like Leading the Future it largely stayed out of the general election, spending just $5 million across four races. Its clearest win came in California's District 11, where it spent $4.7 million to back Democrat Scott Wiener and oppose his Democratic opponents, Connie Chan and, in the primary, Saikat Chakrabarti.

Wiener earned their support through his AI regulation credentials in the state senate, where he authored SB 1047, a frontier AI regulation bill vetoed in 2024, and its narrower successor SB 53, which became law. Public First co-founder Brad Carson boasted of the network's "crushing blow to the AI industry's anti-regulatory efforts," and the group claimed that 10 of the 17 congressional candidates it backed won their races. Following its spending through the whole cycle, only about $10.9 million of its $29.2 million helped winning candidates, and about $5 million went to candidates who won their primaries only to lose in November, like Republican Rhett Marques in Alabama's 2nd District, whom the network spent $960,000 boosting in his primary. More to follow.

Articles.Title: How crypto and AI lost the midterms, and why they say they didn’t - Citation Needed by Molly White

stories.Headline: Huang's exit could give Korean HBM makers more leverage, raise doubts over Nvidia's AI ventures
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 13, 2026. He co-founded the company in 1993 but left following reports of extramarital affairs. One of these relationships involved a woman suspected by US officials of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia has appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim CEO.

The company intends to keep its product plans and customer commitments. However, market shares may shift, with Nvidia's HBM demand expected to drop from 66 percent in 2025 to 57 percent in 2026. Morgan Stanley predicts its share will fall further to 37.3 percent in 2027, while Google reaches 36 percent. SemiAnalysis suggests SK hynix could charge Nvidia $3 to $3.30 per gigabit for HBM4 in 2027. Other customers like Amazon and Broadcom may pay $3.70 to $4.10.

Ahn Ki-hyun of the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association believes this change could benefit Korean makers. He stated that Nvidia still needs high-bandwidth memory regardless of who leads. Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis noted that Huang's personal influence secured capacity in Taiwan and South Korea. Patel believes the preferential treatment Nvidia received may now weaken. This shift could allow suppliers to spread their products across more customers.

There are now concerns regarding AI factories, robotics, and physical AI projects that Huang personally led. An anonymous official worried that these ventures might not move as quickly under new leadership. Analyst Hwang Soo-wook warned that more conservative financial support could slow neocloud expansion. Existing contracts are expected to remain, but long-term investments face uncertainty. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have declined to comment on the situation.

Articles.Title: Huang's exit could give Korean HBM makers more leverage, raise doubts over Nvidia's AI ventures - The Korea Herald

stories.Headline: Texas Has A Power Grid Unlike Any Other State, And AI Is Exposing Its Biggest Weakness
stories.Summary:
Texas is facing a growing strain on its electricity grid as demand from AI data centers surges. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has received interconnection requests from data center developers that the grid cannot supply. The state's grid reached an all-time high demand of about 91.1 gigawatts on July 22, 2026, while current project proposals, about 90% of which are for data centers, total more than five times that July peak. Texas grid operators are largely isolated from other states, and much of its generation comes from renewable sources such as wind, which the article notes is the largest number of turbines in the country.

Senate Bill 6, which Gov. Greg Abbott signed into law on June 20, 2025, requires AI data center developers to share the cost of infrastructure upgrades needed to deliver power to their facilities, costs that had previously fallen on ratepayers through their power bills. The law also sets guidelines that could mandate shutting down data centers during emergencies like Winter Storm Uri in 2021, which caused the largest controlled outage in U.S. history. After the law took effect, Abbott ordered a comprehensive audit of ERCOT's interconnection requests. As a result, ERCOT delayed its Batch Zero screening process, and new approvals for large data centers are on hold until the audit is finished.

The article credits Texas lawmakers and Abbott with these actions, and it describes the state's response as an effort to bring interconnection requests in line with what the grid can support. It also notes that many proposed data centers are not viable because they lack funding and support. According to the article, the audit will significantly affect the timelines and feasibility of some affected developments, but it is expected to help Texas maintain a stable electricity supply. The article does not give a completion date for the audit or say when approvals might resume.

Articles.Title: Texas Has A Power Grid Unlike Any Other State, And AI Is Exposing Its Biggest Weakness - BGR

stories.Headline: Independent AI auditors have a recruitment problem - Transformer | Substack
stories.Summary:
Independent AI auditors have been drawing attention because there are not enough qualified people to staff the oversight bodies that policymakers want. The article describes a growing consensus among safety-minded lawmakers and policy researchers that frontier AI companies will need ongoing monitoring by third-party organizations not tied to industry or government. These bodies are called independent verification organizations, or IVOs. Researchers and advocates are now sounding the alarm that the talent pool is too small for the demands of strong proposals. The strongest proposal discussed is in Massachusetts, where an IVO regime would give auditors advance access to models and the power to question AI firms and make recommendations.

Under that bill, which is part of the Mass Wins Act and currently in conference in the state legislature, auditors would conduct annual compliance audits and independent catastrophic risk evaluations of models roughly every four months. Illinois passed an auditing regime in July that measures companies against their own promises, a lighter requirement than Massachusetts. The federal FRONTIER Act, introduced by House Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, would require independent third-party audits of the largest AI companies' risk monitoring and mitigation practices. Reps.

Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer told Transformer they are working on IVO legislation that would include a protocol for ramping up capacity. Kevin T. Frazier, a professor at the University of Texas School of Law, says the AI field is very small and few people can answer the technical and governance questions involved. Nat Purser, director of US policy at the AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute, calls ongoing auditing a really intensive ask that will not be insurmountable but needs a concerted effort. OpenAI spokesperson Shana Mansbach said the company is concerned about capacity regarding the Massachusetts bill. Ben Snyder, Encode's director of state policy, said the Massachusetts bill is stronger than any AI safety regulation on the books today.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a third-party auditing regime in September. Existing evaluators include METR, Redwood Research, FAR.AI, RAND and SecureBio, and in October Anthropic gave six METR staff employee-like access to assess its models. METR's president, Chris Painter, has said that staff capacity constrains the organization's work. Ajeya Cotra, a METR researcher, drew criticism because she is married to Paul Christiano, who recently joined the OpenAI Foundation board. METR says it does not receive payment for frontier company assessments and points to its disclosure policies.

Patricia Paskov, director of standards at AVERI, says three categories of workers are needed: model and system evaluators, hardware evaluators, and governance analysts. Anka Reuel says technical evaluators need both frontier model knowledge and evaluation domain knowledge, and most such people join well-paying frontier firms. Frazier says adequate training for model-level evaluation does not currently exist. Several fellowships and bootcamps, including MATS and GovAI, train people to move into AI safety.

Paskov has discussed a certificate program with the University of Wisconsin, Madison, and the AI Evaluator Forum has a stated goal of building a pipeline of qualified candidates, though Paskov says it is still working out what that will look like. Patricia Paskov argues that talent from cybersecurity, IT, policy, accounting and business can be drawn into the field. Most training programs for senior-level model evaluation are still in development. The articles leave open how quickly these programs can produce enough qualified auditors, whether the Massachusetts and federal bills will pass, and how the ramp-up protocol described by Jacobs will work.

Articles.Title: Independent AI auditors have a recruitment problem - Transformer | Substack

stories.Headline: China’s great AI chip loophole: How American espionage stopped China — this time
stories.Summary:
The articles report that a suspected Chinese intelligence operation sought to obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips through companies in Singapore and Malaysia, and that American intelligence uncovered it, as reported on November 13, 2026. The New York Times reported that American intelligence concluded Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed International, had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed acquired Nvidia processors for cloud-computing operations, and American intelligence officers reportedly identified concerns about Huang's activities and her relationship with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. The articles state that approximately 50,000 Nvidia processors could not be reconciled with the company's reported inventory records. Nvidia later said it located hardware in additional warehouses, but full public reconciliation and independent verification of final locations remained unknown.

The articles state that Nvidia's H100, H200 and newer Blackwell-family processors are among the most strategically important technologies underlying modern artificial intelligence. President Trump has spent years restricting Chinese access to the most advanced versions of these technologies. A November 11 letter from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Christopher Coons stated that Megaspeed had purchased more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024. Reuters reported on November 12 that Chinese AI companies were seeking additional overseas Nvidia computing capacity amid fears that Washington might close this regulatory gap. Bloomberg reported a discrepancy of roughly 50,000 processors between Nvidia's initial government tally and shipments made through hardware partners.

The articles state that the individuals who uncovered the suspected operation have not been publicly identified. The articles state that the public record does not yet establish whether Alice Huang actually transferred Nvidia secrets to Chinese intelligence, whether Jensen Huang knowingly assisted any intelligence activity, or whether their romantic relationship directly influenced illegal chip shipments to China. The articles state that Congress and the CIA will have to establish how much China got away with and who helped them defeat America. The articles state that the question Congress must resolve is whether the processors can be physically identified, their serial numbers verified, and their locations traced. The articles state that Bloomberg and The New York Times reported that Nvidia representatives communicated with senior Commerce Department officials while investigators examined the matter.

The articles state that China's intelligence services and commercial intermediaries may have identified weaknesses in precisely the system designed to keep them out. The articles state that the MSS has a long history of seeking valuable foreign technology, political intelligence, and relationships with influential individuals. The articles state that Singapore and Malaysia have developed substantial cloud-computing industries, and that companies in these countries can legitimately purchase American technology, install processors in data centers, and rent computing capacity to customers worldwide. The articles state that processors ostensibly destined for facilities outside China might subsequently be physically diverted to Chinese customers, and that such unauthorized reexports could violate American export restrictions. The articles state that Chinese companies might obtain access to advanced American processors without importing the physical chips at all by renting computing capacity in overseas data centers.

The articles state that China may have discovered a remarkably effective way around America's restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips by obtaining processors through ostensibly legitimate companies in Singapore and Malaysia, exploiting weaknesses in American export enforcement, and using personal relationships to influence the leadership of the world's most important AI chipmaker. The articles state that the unfolding Nvidia scandal raises the possibility that an elaborate Chinese intelligence operation came dangerously close to succeeding, and that some of the technology may already have reached Chinese customers. The articles state that the apparent weakness involved the distinction between selling advanced processors directly to China and selling them to companies operating data centers elsewhere in Asia. The articles state that the second method is not necessarily illegal under existing regulations and exposes a distinction between controlling the shipment of advanced processors and controlling who ultimately benefits from their computing power. The articles state that the discovery illustrates the importance of counterintelligence in detecting foreign activities that may be deliberately concealed behind ordinary commercial relationships.

The articles state that Nvidia has not publicly disclosed exact counts, leaving open whether every processor can be accounted for and verified against unauthorized diversion to China. The articles state that it remains unknown whether every processor can be accounted for and verified. The articles state that the full public reconciliation and independent verification of final locations remained unknown. The articles state that Congress and the CIA will have to establish how much China got away with and who helped them defeat America. The articles state that the question Congress must resolve is whether the processors can be physically identified, their serial numbers verified, and their locations traced.

stories.Headline: After $604M verdict, fleets face AI camera blind spots
stories.Summary:
A Dallas County judge upheld a $604 million jury verdict against C.H. Robinson days before a panel at the American Trucking Associations’ Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina. The case stems from a 2021 crash in Jackson, Mississippi, that killed three people and the truck’s driver. Defense attorney Doug Marcello, a shareholder at Saxton & Stump, spoke on the panel with Sean Ritchie, a vice president at Solera Fleet Solutions. Marcello said nuclear verdicts against trucking companies rarely grow out of the facts of the crash itself. He said plaintiff attorneys look for evidence of systemic failure, and AI-only dash cams give them a new place to find it.

Marcello said fleets should treat any footage they hold as discoverable. He said the defense of saying AI did not pick it up is not going to be an excuse. Ritchie said early video-based safety systems recorded an event when an accelerometer sensed G-forces past a set threshold. He said that as recently as five or six years ago almost every video passed through a human layer before it reached the fleet. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s windshield rule allows safety technology mounted no more than 8.5 inches below the top of the area swept by the wipers.

Marcello received the Trucking Associations Executive Council’s J.R. “Bob” Halladay Award in July. He said juries will set a standard for AI review because there is no government standard. He said it will be an economic governance by what you do or fail to do with that AI. Ritchie asked who in the room used dash cams, and every hand went up. He asked who knew their false-negative rate, and every hand went down.

Ritchie said Solera analyzed AI-triggered videos and found up to 30% held other risk the AI did not flag. He said the company has not published the sample size or method behind the figure, a version of which it has cited since at least August 2025. He said rates vary by vendor and by type of risk, and drowsy driving was the most common miss. He tied the misses to vendors’ efforts to cut down on false alerts. He said dialing down sensitivity creates more opportunity for something risky to go unlabeled.

Marcello ran a mock trial with a Philadelphia focus group about a 35-truck carrier whose driver came over a hill, hit a line of traffic and killed two people. He said the driver had several overspeeds and hard brakes the week before, and the company’s lone safety director had not caught up on them. He said the mock jury was totally unsympathetic. He said the jury in the C.H. Robinson case assigned 23% of fault to the broker and 45% to the driver, Gorgonio Gonzalez. He said the jury found Gonzalez was subject to control by C.H. Robinson as to the details of the mission.

Marcello said he pulled the filings from the docket and that plaintiffs argue the finding makes Gonzalez a borrowed employee of the broker. He said that would combine the two shares above 50% and leave C.H. Robinson owing the full verdict. He described the reptile theory as primarily a strategy for maximizing verdicts based upon engendering fear in the jury. Ritchie said most people are wearing multiple hats and these are very lean organizations that are getting leaner by the day. He said providers typically hold video with no identified risk for 30 days at most and video with any flagged risk for six months or longer.

Ritchie split vendors into three groups: some send video straight into the fleet’s workflow, some use human reviewers only to remove false positives, and others review for both false positives and false negatives. He said dropping the AI would not help and that human review alone is no better, just as the AI alone is not better. He said he sells AI cameras and feels compelled to have this conversation because he has not heard anybody talk about a false negative. Motor carriers ranked lawsuit abuse reform as their top concern in the American Transportation Research Institute’s 2026 Top Industry Issues report, released Oct. 18 at the conference. Lawsuit abuse reform also ranked second overall.

Articles.Title: After $604M verdict, fleets face AI camera blind spots - FreightWaves

stories.Headline: Executive Perspectives: Iowa leaders share their AI outlooks
stories.Summary:
The Business Record published on Nov. 13, 2026, at 6:00 am an Executive Perspectives feature in which Iowa leaders shared their outlooks on artificial intelligence in business. The piece ran 2,708 words with an 11 min read time and appeared under All Latest News, Innovation and Entrepreneurship and Premium. It followed the Business Record’s final Power Breakfast of 2026, which featured speaker Mike Stitt. The Business Record newsroom reached out to several more leaders to add their thoughts after local executives shared perspectives at the event. The perspectives covered business decisions and outcomes, present and future, and leading strategy and the division of work between humans and AI.

Joel Veenstra, president of Baker Group, said the biggest shift has been in the office, not on the jobsite. Baker Group is embracing AI for internal processes including contract review, proposal generation, takeoffs, estimating, submittals, RFIs, document review and coordination. Veenstra said the firm is investing in four areas: data, governance, people and flexibility. Baker Group formed a cross-functional steering group and is building policies for data handling and acceptable use. Veenstra said AI does not take away human accountability and the firm is building AI literacy across the company.

Mike Harryman, general manager of McGough Construction, said AI has the highest potential to improve efficiency by reducing the time required to process information and identify risk. He said AI can accelerate quantity analysis, document review, scope comparison, scheduling and cost forecasting. Harryman said the Iowa office is focusing on the quality, consistency and accessibility of project data and on early VDC planning, model-based coordination, disciplined estimating and scheduling practices. He said the team will use AI as an extension of their expertise, not a replacement for field knowledge, judgment or relationships. He said he is certain he will be amazed at where AI will be in three to five years.

Ryan Wiederstein, broker-owner of WB Realty Co., said AI creates an opportunity to reduce operating costs while improving service to tenants for owners and operators of commercial real estate. He said it allows smaller, more nimble companies to compete with larger organizations because they can accomplish more without adding significant overhead. Wiederstein said he believes there will be greater demand for highly amenitized projects that offer experiences and opportunities for collaboration difficult to replicate remotely. He said well-located, well-managed buildings that give people a compelling reason to come to the office will become even more important if overall office demand decreases.

He said the approach is to stay nimble and be prepared to pivot quickly as the technology evolves. Neil Schroeder, chief information officer of Des Moines Public Schools, said the biggest near-term gains are behind the scenes. He said finance, payroll, human resources, enrollment and technology support all run on repetitive processes that AI can draft and check. Schroeder said AI can help teachers tailor lessons to each student at a scale that isn’t possible without it.

He said he expects families, students and employees to have personal AI assistants working for them within five years. He said traditional IT practices such as privacy, data security and appropriate permissions will be more important than ever. Brianne Schulte, vice president of strategy, risk, information technology and financial planning at Vermeer Corp., said AI can materially change the industry in the speed to solve problems and build solutions to derive insights. She said this shortens development times in delivering value internally for teams as well as value to distribution and customers.

Schulte said the company is driving the organization to set up strong data systems and integrations versus being dependent on individual software ecosystems. Joe Murphy, president of the Iowa Business Council, said the AI tool has the potential to have an impact on virtually everything. Murphy said the question becomes how to utilize the tool to put the company and its products at a competitive advantage in the marketplace. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Executive Perspectives: Iowa leaders share their AI outlooks - Business Record

stories.Headline: The Five Nine: Can Voice AI give telecom a new voice?
stories.Summary:
Voice AI, the use of artificial intelligence within live phone calls, is being pitched by vendors as a way to revive voice services that many in telecom consider stale. Fierce Network's Diana Goovaerts hosted an episode of The Five Nine on the subject, published on November 13, 2026. Guests Brandon Larson of Mavenir, Dag Peak of Alianza and Kris Efland of Deepgram appeared in the episode. The episode examines whether AI can give the oldest service in the network a second life, and it covers both the promise and the difficult parts. Those difficult parts include latency, consent, data privacy, where the AI should run and how to price it.

Voice AI is a broad label that can describe several different things. Peak and Larson divide it into three categories: AI-handled calls, applications that engage in live conversations, and post-call intelligence. Larson offered examples such as real-time translation between two people speaking different languages, an AI receptionist for small businesses, and AI that detects deepfake voices, non-human voices or social engineering. Peak argued that human conversation is the richest form of communication and that bringing calls into the application and AI space opens many possibilities. Larson said operators' product teams see an opportunity to create value that does not depend entirely on handset makers such as Apple and Samsung.

Larson said operators could use these services to raise revenue through uplifts, step-up plans and add-on plans. Peak said operators are losing subscribers, lines and SIP trunks to vendors such as Twilio that bring intelligence to voice or messaging. He described bringing AI-powered services into operator networks as a defensive move that could help them keep customers, as well as an offensive move that could generate revenue. Larson advised operators to begin with a customer problem, estimate how many people have it, determine what they would pay to solve it, and then work backward to the technology. Efland said successful voice AI depends on low latency, accurate speech recognition and reliable turn-taking, and he noted that accuracy matters more in specialized fields such as healthcare, where recognizing drug names is important.

Efland said the highest value for enterprises comes from integrating AI with their data and systems, and he said Deepgram deploys wherever customers operate, including air-gapped devices, their own infrastructure, virtual private clouds and data centers. He added that Deepgram spends considerable time understanding customers' use cases and outcomes before working back from those outcomes. Efland used a drive-through example, describing a parent ordering while children shout, to illustrate the unpredictable conditions these systems must handle. Larson said context engineering, including knowing a subscriber's preferences and history, can matter more than choosing a more powerful model. Peak said the major problems have been identified and that the pieces are coming together.

The three guests disagreed about how much of the work remains unfinished. Larson described a design in which the other caller hears an announcement and actively accepts before the AI begins, while Peak said Alianza's trust framework covers consent, announcements and data collection along with vetting the experiences attached to calls. Peak and Larson described these as their own companies' approaches rather than a universal legal rule for every service or location. Peak said trust, privacy and consent remain central to getting people comfortable with such services. Efland said users need to understand when AI is involved in a conversation.

The guests all said the test is whether the whole system works for the person using it. The episode was written and hosted by Diana Goovaerts and edited by Goovaerts, Matt Rickman and Nikki Grcic, with Liz Coyne as executive producer. The articles do not say how the services discussed will be regulated, priced in the market or adopted by operators. They also do not say how far the consent designs described by the guests will be used across the industry. Whether operators will turn these pitches into revenue remains an open question in the coverage.

Articles.Title: The Five Nine: Can Voice AI give telecom a new voice?

stories.Headline: Nvidia Interim CEO Vows Central AI Role as Permanent Successor Race Opens
stories.Summary:
Nvidia abruptly dismissed its chief executive Jensen Huang after he led the company for 33 years. The company named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive to stabilize the organization. This leadership change occurred around November 12, 2026, according to the provided reports. Kress now faces the task of managing the firm during an extremely difficult time. She aims to return the organization to normal operations following this sudden transition.

The company plans a quarterly earnings release on November 17 and a company-wide meeting on November 18. Kress previously worked at Microsoft and Cisco before joining Nvidia as the CFO in 2013. She reduced a $250 billion financial guarantee for an OpenAI Ohio data center project by half. Nvidia is pursuing a $500 billion AI chip financing program with Wall Street partners. These partners now demand that the guarantee ratio be raised from 25 percent.

Interim CEO Colette Kress told staff that the company plays a pivotal role in the AI revolution. She wrote an email on the 12th thanking employees for their professionalism and unwavering dedication. Kress believes that important challenges lie ahead for the organization as it moves forward. She is expected to shift management toward a more cautious investment strategy than her predecessor. This shift follows her previous concerns regarding the circular financing used under Jensen Huang.

Some observers say Kress lacks the engineering background needed to lead the world's largest AI chipmaker. Vice President Ian Buck is a rival candidate who developed the CUDA software for graphics processing units. Other potential successors include Arm CEO Rene Haas and Nvidia co-founder and adviser Chris Malachowsky. Reuters reported that Kress had previously clashed with Huang over investments in AI infrastructure. These internal tensions highlight the competition for the permanent role of chief executive.

The articles mention that three semiconductor bills may clear the U.S. Congress this year. These include the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, and the MATCH Act. House Speaker Mike Johnson said on the 12th that the current episode could change thinking. Chairman Brian Mast said these bills likely fit into the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. This legislation must pass this year to implement the proposed security and oversight measures.

Nvidia will hold its employee meeting on the 18th to discuss the response to the dismissal. The company must decide if it will complete the $500 billion AI chip financing program. It remains open whether Kress or a rival like Ian Buck will become permanent CEO. The articles do not state if the U.S. Congress will officially pass the three bills. They leave the final outcome of the successor race and the legislative process undecided.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Interim CEO Vows Central AI Role as Permanent Successor Race Opens - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Shifting HBM4 Controller Functions Closer To Memory (UC Riverside) - Semiconductor Engineering
stories.Summary:
Tharunya Yogananda and Wantong Li published a technical paper on November 13, 2026. These researchers are from the University of California, Riverside. Their work focuses on shifting controller functions closer to memory. The paper is titled Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies. It was released on the arXiv server as 2611.10930.

The study examines high bandwidth memory, specifically the HBM4 generation. It requires using a logic process for the base die of the memory stack. This process allows complex controller functions to exist next to the DRAM. The researchers used a silicon interposer for their quantitative study. They evaluated four placements for the controller functions.

Yogananda and Li are responsible for this systematic quantitative study. They divided the memory controller into its main functions. The authors evaluated moving maintenance or scheduling to the base die. They compared a complete host controller against a complete base die controller. They also tested intermediate placements for these specific functions.

The paper explores how partitioning affects the host and the HBM4 base die. It targets the interface between the host and the memory. The study focuses on the die to die interface. It addresses the placement of functions on a silicon interposer. This research affects the design of high bandwidth memory systems.

The background involves the evolution of high bandwidth memory generations. Recent HBM4 designs allow the base die to use logic processes. This is a change from previous generations of memory stacks. The research utilizes 2.5D integration and advanced packaging techniques. It focuses on the relationship between the host and DRAM.

The authors provide a quantitative analysis of function level controller placement. They determine the best location for maintenance and scheduling tasks. The articles do not state which of the four placements is best. They do not list the specific performance results of the study. The future impact on commercial HBM4 production remains open.

Articles.Title: Shifting HBM4 Controller Functions Closer To Memory (UC Riverside) - Semiconductor Engineering

stories.Headline: Kudu has given Leidos a cyber boost and an AI surprise
stories.Summary:
Leidos, the defense contractor, has been reporting gains from its 2025 purchase of Kudu Dynamics, a cyber company it bought for $300 million. In October, Leidos won two contracts from U.S. Cyber Command: a $160 million operations support contract and a $99 million other transaction authority contract to keep developing a cyber mission planning platform that Kudu brought over from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. Together these amount to nearly $260 million in new business over the next several years. Leidos Intelligence president Jason O'Connor said the customers are ones the company had not really worked with before.

The acquisition was announced in May 2025, when CEO Tom Bell said it moved Leidos into offensive cyber by 18 months compared with building those capabilities internally. Kudu brought roughly 170 employees, and much of its earlier work was in research. O'Connor said the company's artificial intelligence work has also benefited, pointing to Parcata, an AI-driven tool that finds and ranks software vulnerabilities so teams can fix the most serious ones first. Leidos introduced Parcata in August, and it grew out of Kudu's work on DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge. O'Connor said Leidos is testing it on its own software before a commercial release, and Bell discussed it on a November 5 earnings call as part of a cyber product business the company hopes to launch later this year.

O'Connor credited Kudu with a broader effect he called a "halo," in which its offensive background lets Leidos view the systems it builds the way an attacker would, which he said has improved the company's chances on engineering, software development and analytics bids as well. He said Leidos has worked to protect Kudu's culture, which had a 47,000-employee parent to worry about, and that Kudu engineers are now being placed on traditional Leidos contracts to coach and mentor staff. O'Connor linked the shift to fixed-price, outcome-based contracts and to rapidly changing technology, saying customers now expect solutions that are ready to go. He described the Leidos Intelligence cyber business, which sits in one of five sectors the company formed on January 1, and said the company is "just getting started," with possible wins in weapon system and communications cyber.

Articles.Title: Kudu has given Leidos a cyber boost and an AI surprise

stories.Headline: Hacking of AI Vendor Exposes Data of 818 Startup Program Participants
stories.Summary:
An external hacking attack exposed the personal data of 818 participants in a government project. The breach occurred at Amicus Lex, a private AI vendor, on November 11, 2026. This company provides a legal document drafting tool called LawForm. The attack targeted the vendor rather than the systems of the Ministry of SMEs and Startups.

The breach affected 20,028 people in total, including the 818 participants of the second Startup for All project. Leaked information consisted of names, email addresses, and phone numbers. Amicus Lex responded by blocking overseas IP access immediately after the event. The company then notified the affected users on November 13, 2026.

The Ministry of SMEs and Startups and the Korea Institute of Startup and Entrepreneurship Development are managing the response. They informed the victims about the leak and gave advice to prevent smishing. A ministry official stated that they will work to stop further damage. They also asked the other 49 AI providers in the project to inspect their own security.

The government will now monitor how all project vendors handle data protection. This includes checking access rights to personal information. They will also verify if data is deleted after the retention period ends. These steps aim to ensure better management of personal data across the program.

Articles.Title: Hacking of AI Vendor Exposes Data of 818 Startup Program Participants - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
stories.Summary:
The American Medical Association, the nation's largest physicians group, has called for federal and state legislation that would shield doctors from liability when AI products injure patients, even when physicians use those tools as intended. The announcement came this week, according to Axios, which reported it on November 13, 2026. The push reflects growing concern that AI systems are taking on more consequential medical tasks, such as deciding whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug, with less direct oversight. The question of who is responsible when something goes wrong has become more pressing as a result.

The AMA policy also asks lawmakers to require AI companies to carry adequate liability insurance and to disclose product limitations and performance data. It states that hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should bear responsibility if the required use of a specific AI product leads to harmful errors. The group points to particular risks, including triage errors in which an AI system misjudges how severe a case is without the attending doctor knowing. It also warns that a physician may be unable to verify inputs such as incomplete laboratory results or outdated diagnoses. In such cases, the AMA argues, liability should fall on manufacturers and vendors, and possibly on health systems that require the tools, rather than on physicians through malpractice claims.

The AMA's position is shaped by earlier lawsuits over algorithm-driven medical decisions. Axios cited a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities, where the software developer was not held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors. Martin Hilbert, a professor at the University of California, Davis who studies digital information and algorithms, told Axios that courts around the country are concluding that companies designing, training and deploying AI systems bear responsibility for what those systems do. He said different parties are responsible for different cases and that the end user cannot simply be held responsible for everything. Hospitals have generally supported placing monitoring duties on developers and vendors, citing the "black box" nature of many systems.

The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices, though its authority covers only software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all AI used in health care. AdvaMed, the trade group for device makers, has urged the FDA to keep its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled devices and to avoid post-market monitoring burdens unrelated to a product's actual risk. Axios reported that the AMA's proposals are aimed at situations where use of an AI system is mandatory. The article did not report whether any legislation has been introduced or what action lawmakers have taken so far.

Articles.Title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes

stories.Headline: Is AI contributing to CPA burnout or making us more productive?
stories.Summary:
A recent Wall Street Journal report concluded that artificial intelligence boosts individual productivity and significantly cuts down on repetitive tasks, according to an article by Randy Crabtree published November 13, 2026, in Accounting Today. The same report said AI also increases work intensity, pace and cognitive pressure for most employees. The annual CPA Career Satisfaction survey that Crabtree co-authors echoed the Journal's sentiment. Nine in 10 accountants, or 92%, told the survey they expected AI to benefit their firms long-term. Over the near term, most respondents felt AI would contribute to personal stress and burnout risk.

Only one in five, or 20%, feared losing their job or being demoted, while nearly three in five, or 56%, said they were very concerned about the endless learning curve needed to keep up with AI developments and options. One in three, or 31%, felt the scope of what counted as their job had expanded exponentially, and another third, or 30%, were frustrated by the lack of reliable training and resources for using AI better. At least one in five respondents felt their workday never ended. A recent University of California, Berkeley study identified three main forms of work intensification driven by AI: job scope expanded, less downtime and multitasking.

Crabtree wrote that he is also concerned about AI creating downward pressure on pricing for accounting firms. He said that if clients sense routine work is taking CPAs less time, they will expect lower bills. He warned that if firms keep working the same hours, reduce fees for tax returns and replace those hours with lower-value work, they will only add to worker stress. He said AI offers real benefits when used correctly, with vendors automating upfront tax preparation work such as streamlining data collection, populating tax returns and encouraging more clients to upload documents through firm portals. He said AI is moving into the general ledger itself, with tools to automate transaction categorization, account reconciliation and much of the monthly close.

One respondent said their firm is still in the Wild West and that they keep imploring for AI policies to be communicated and are told "we are working on it." Another respondent said audit clients are using AI to develop procedures or policies that they don't read or understand. The Cal Berkeley study noted that expectations of productivity gradually reset thanks to AI, and that what was once considered extra effort becomes standard performance. Researchers said constant switching and reduced recovery over time can impair judgment and increase errors. One respondent observed that clients are running their issues through with poor prompts and getting erroneous answers, and that accountants need to convince them they are wrong.

Another respondent resented the time spent double checking the AI to find that AI was wrong and having to do the research themselves. Crabtree wrote that prompting skills will become increasingly important and that accountants will be responsible for training their AI agents to understand what they are really looking for. He said critical thinking is equally important and that accountants cannot blindly trust AI output. He said technical skills will always matter but that accountants must get better at nontechnical skills machines lack, particularly communication. He said the decision tree for AI tools has gotten very large, with options ranging from ChatGPT and Claude to industry-specific tax AI.

Crabtree wrote that accountants are generally not permitted to input confidential client data into most general AI platforms, which limits useful experimentation. He recommended building intentional pauses into the workday, batching non-urgent updates, protecting focus windows and protecting time for check-ins, shared reflection and dialogue. He said accountants should not be afraid to ask for help and that managers should make sure their team feels safe doing the same. He said the survey shows accountants at firms that make mental health resources readily available without stigma are significantly more likely to find their careers rewarding and less likely to leave the profession. He concluded that AI holds real promise for accounting professionals but only if adopted thoughtfully, and that productivity gains mean nothing if they come at the cost of wellbeing.

Articles.Title: Is AI contributing to CPA burnout or making us more productive? - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: Nvidia's Huang Forced Out, Shaking AI Circular-Deal Ecosystem
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang would immediately resign as president, CEO, and board member. Major financial outlets reported that Huang was effectively ousted from the company over workplace affairs. He faced three infidelity allegations, including a relationship with a woman suspected of Chinese espionage. Huang apologized on November 8, stating his actions hurt his wife and children. The company began the process of selecting a permanent CEO following his departure.

Colette Kress, the CFO since September 2013, became interim CEO while keeping her existing roles. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO, was appointed as the first board chairman. Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore based Megaspeed. He also dated Kimberly Powell, a vice president who joined Nvidia in 2008. Reuters reported a third affair with an unidentified female employee on November 12.

Interim CEO Colette Kress told employees in an email that this was an extraordinarily difficult time. She announced a company wide meeting for November 18, following the November 17 earnings release. Jensen Huang apologized for his actions but did not name the women involved in the affairs. Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Tim Cook should replace the departing legend. Mandeep Singh said Nvidia's aggressiveness in beating targets will now be gone.

Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons expressed grave concerns about national security and technology controls. They requested that officials preserve all documents regarding Chinese intelligence and communications between Trump and Huang. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast summoned Huang to testify before congressional committees next week. Chinese spokeswoman Mao Ning said the United States should stop fabricating espionage narratives for blockades. Shareholders and memory chip suppliers like SK hynix and Micron saw their values fall.

Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, co-founded Shanghai Hexi, which held stakes in Huawei linked data centers. Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore revenue in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, after earning $10.2 billion. The U.S. Commerce Department may block AI companies from accessing chips in seven additional countries. Huang previously funded AI developers like OpenAI and Anthropic to create a circular trading ecosystem. This system allowed recipients to use investments to buy more Nvidia chips.

Nvidia shares fell 13.08 percent at the open before closing down 4.34 percent on November 12. Citigroup and Bernstein lowered their price targets for the company to $225 and $200 respectively. Rivals including AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet, and Samsung Electronics may benefit from a diversified supply chain. Huang has tentatively agreed to testify behind closed doors, though Brian Mast may issue subpoenas. The articles leave open how the AI ecosystem will reshape without Huang's central link.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's Huang Forced Out, Shaking AI Circular-Deal Ecosystem - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
stories.Summary:
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel published his two incompleteness theorems in 1931, transforming mathematics and paving the way for the digital age. Since 2017 the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand 16 notebooks Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. In September von Plato enlisted the AI model Claude, which within a couple of days provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material. Claude revealed that Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about. The most famous logician of modern times had discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

The material, called the workbooks, is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic, much of it in the German shorthand Gabelsberger. Von Plato received a €2.5m grant from the European Research Council and taught himself the shorthand, saying he is one of only six people in the world who can read it. Claude produced a 650-page explanation of the workbooks, which had to be controlled page for page. Claude found 663 theorems for which Gödel had a proof, a sketched proof or an idea for a proof. When these were put into the proof assistant Coq, about 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired and about 50 were false.

Von Plato said he was flabbergasted, that the workbooks contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, and that they contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. He said Gödel was far ahead of his time, and that humans read one page at a time and take a year to read about 50 pages. He said the AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages and see all of Gödel's writings as one piece. He said the first task he set Claude was to discover if the workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice. The answer came back yes, almost, and von Plato said Gödel was just one step away, with one definition wrong but the right definition two years earlier.

Von Plato ran Claude's reconstructed proof through Coq and it passed, and he believes Gödel would have won the 1940 Fields medal had he published his work on the axiom of choice. Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude's reconstruction but said that if it stood up it is remarkable and historically interesting, though how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians. Hamkins said the fact that there are things in there that resemble Cohen's proof does not mean Gödel had it, and that you don't get credit for work you don't tell anyone about. He said Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising his notebooks are full of exciting things. Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis in 1940 and settled in Princeton, New Jersey, where he became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow, about a page a week, until September. In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested he co-opt Claude, and on his return to Helsinki he showed Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks and six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature. Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved nor disproved, and his work inspired Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation. In 1966 the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal for showing the independence of the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice, and Gödel reacted by saying he had already proved the result in the 1940s but was unable to reconstruct a proof when pushed by his peers. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, Gödel refused to eat food not cooked by his wife and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he is sure continued study of Gödel's manuscripts will reveal further treasures, and that Claude says the workbooks contain more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics not found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. He said Gödel's physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory he plans to start exploring once he is finished with his present logic projects. Von Plato started the project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. The articles do not say what became of the 14 unpursued themes or the more than a dozen further themes beyond von Plato's stated intention to explore them. The articles also do not say whether the reconstructed proof will be published or how historians will separate Claude's contribution from Gödel's.

Articles.Title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

stories.Headline: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters.
stories.Summary:
A study of native ads on news sites found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising, and in a Contently survey two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived when they realized an article or video was sponsored by a brand. According to an impact.com survey, 47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI, and Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse. OpenAI’s answer to the disclosure question so far is the citation link, since launching ChatGPT search it has included links to sources in answers so users can check them for themselves. One study found that about a quarter of the pages cited by ChatGPT, Google’s AI Overviews and Perplexity carried a commercial disclosure, and 86% of answers cited at least one such page.

In the impact.com survey, 24% of shoppers said they use AI to avoid sponsored results and ads, and Pew found people clicked a link inside an AI summary on just 1% of visits. According to impact.com’s survey, Gen Z is split between those who never click through at 11% and those who always do at 21%. In a University of Michigan study, people rarely noticed when a chatbot wove ads into its responses, many preferred those answers, and even when the ads were labeled about half the participants did not spot them. Early research from the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management found shoppers who clicked ChatGPT ads bought at a rate of 0.37%, versus 2.21% for those who arrived through ChatGPT’s regular answers.

OpenAI’s ad principles promise that “ads do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives you,” and ads only appear in ChatGPT’s free and Go tiers, always separate from the answer itself. Perplexity made similar promises when advertising was part of its business model, though it walked away from ads earlier this year, with one executive saying “A user needs to believe this is the best possible answer.” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on Meta’s October earnings call that the company will “build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate.” In the writer’s tests with Meta’s Muse, when asked which robot vacuum was best, it recommended a model that could be checked out right there but was not the top model on the review it cited.
