stories.Headline: ChatGPT agents could reshape internet browsing, brand discovery
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has introduced a way for businesses to set up a presence inside ChatGPT, adding two features called Business Hub and Business Agents. TechGig reported the rollout on Nov. 11, 2026, noting that it begins as a beta limited to eligible e-commerce and online service businesses in the United States. Business Agents are verified, brand-specific AI representatives that users can talk to for tasks such as comparison shopping. A follow-up TechGig piece on Nov. 13 examined what the launch could mean for how people browse the internet and find brands.

Under the new setup, a company can use the Business Hub to claim its organisation, go through verification, update key information and share product feeds for ChatGPT queries. Businesses can also build a Business Agent, configuring it with specific instructions and context that guide its answers about products and services. OpenAI says conversations with these agents will be clearly marked and kept separate from regular ChatGPT interactions. The Hub also gives companies insights, including how often they are mentioned in ChatGPT responses and the top "discovery topics" in which they appear. In addition, OpenAI's sponsored Business Agents act as destinations for ChatGPT Ads, which the report describes as an early sign of new commercial opportunities.

OpenAI is the company behind the changes, and it describes the launch as an initial step toward bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT, with the aim of improving how users make decisions and opening new ways for businesses to take part. The company also states that its recommendations remain independent of whether a business has claimed a profile or created an agent. TechGig's analysis, rather than anything OpenAI said, supplies the broader reading of the move. It argues that if consumers discover products, compare options and look up information through AI agents, they may no longer need to visit individual websites, which challenges the premise on which conventional browsing was built.

That shift could affect website traffic, search engine optimisation and digital advertising, since brands have long relied on websites, search engines and ads to attract attention. TechGig says brands may need to reconsider their investments in digital visibility, because discovery will increasingly depend on AI systems being able to access and understand their information. Websites are expected to remain as original sources, but they would need accurate, updated and structured data, with product descriptions, prices, availability and return policies becoming key inputs. In that scenario, the report suggests, websites could move from being discovery destinations to information warehouses supporting AI platforms. The articles do not say when the beta might expand beyond the United States or beyond its current business categories.

stories.Headline: Vietnam pilots $120K AI grant program for SMEs
stories.Summary:
Vietnam's Ministry of Science and Technology has launched a pilot program offering small and medium-sized enterprises grants of up to 3 billion VND, or about $120,000, for adopting artificial intelligence. The program was announced by Minister Vu Hai Quan during a question-and-answer session of the 16th National Assembly on November 12, 2026. It is modeled on a Singapore framework and is meant to place scientific experts directly inside participating firms. The aim is to tackle innovation bottlenecks in the private sector, where, according to VCCI data cited in the report, only 8.8 per cent of domestic firms engage in product innovation.

The same data show that just 3.9 per cent of domestic firms partner with others on scientific research, which the program is designed to change. Under the scheme, the ministry will connect SMEs with research institutes and universities. Each grant supports a single project, and the stated goal is to speed practical AI use across commerce and manufacturing. The ministry is responsible for the program and its minister presented it to lawmakers. Vietnam's approach is set against a wider push for technology partnerships.

Separately, the Vietnam-Korea AI and Semiconductor High-Level Summit 2026, held in Hanoi under the ministry's auspices, marked a shift in bilateral cooperation from traditional manufacturing toward joint research. Partnership areas include AI semiconductor architecture design, shared sovereign computing infrastructure and deep tech talent exchanges. Tran Dang Hoa, chairman of FPT IS and FPT Semiconductor, outlined a roadmap that puts specialized talent first, ahead of Vietnam's first commercial outsourced semiconductor assembly and test plant, and expands AI Factory infrastructure in Vietnam and Japan with Naver Cloud. The article places these moves within a broader national semiconductor strategy.

Global developments are also part of the context. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid personal conduct scrutiny and US export compliance investigations, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. Chinese AI labs are reportedly securing overseas Nvidia GPU instances in anticipation of tighter compute export sanctions. The article says these shifts reinforce Vietnam's push toward multi-vendor compute architectures and sovereign fabless chip capabilities. stories.Headline: AI-generated lesson plans save teachers time. Just don’t let the kids know.
stories.Summary:
The AI Hub for Education, part of Stanford University’s SCALE Initiative, released a review of 52 studies on artificial intelligence in educational settings on Tuesday, November 13, 2026, Chalkbeat reported. The review found that most AI tools do not help students learn and that education-specific AI tools are not necessarily better than general purpose chatbots. It also found that even tools that help teachers save time can have unintended consequences for students. The report’s authors said they are not throwing in the towel on AI in education. The review is the AI Hub’s second AI research review and incorporates 32 new studies.

The included studies were selected from hundreds in the field and are either randomized controlled trials or have a quasi-experimental design providing strong causal evidence. The goal is eventually to have a robust research repository that teachers and districts can use to inform decisions about whether and how to use AI. The review is a synthesis of findings from high-quality studies, not a meta-analysis. AI in education is not just one thing, with too many different tools used in too many different ways to pile studies together and reach strong conclusions. Many of the studies come from other countries or involve college students, and there is still very little research on AI in K-12 settings in the United States.

Susanna Loeb, faculty director at the SCALE Initiative and an author of the report, said AI tools can be quite powerful to differentiate lessons for students at different levels or support students learning a new language. She said you just have to use them thoughtfully and track how they are doing and whether they are really benefiting students. Loeb said that if a district does not want to think about it and does not want to design its classwork, homework and school day to leverage these tools well, she would not use them. She said that on their own without thought, the tools have some negative effects on learning. She said teachers and district leaders need to proceed thoughtfully and that if they do not have the capacity to do so, it is better not to use AI at all.

Collectively, the studies suggest students do not learn much when they use AI to produce essays or solve problems, and when those students later do work without AI, they do worse than other students. AI shows more promise when students use it to explain concepts and help them practice, but even then the results are mixed or do not show much benefit over traditional study methods. AI tools that provide interactive formats and adaptive practice questions may improve student learning more than static digital textbooks, and students sometimes experience AI-generated feedback as clearer and more motivating than feedback from teachers, but even where students reported positive experiences the evidence of learning gains was mixed. Teachers who used an AI tool to do the first pass on grading assignments provided more and more detailed feedback in one study, and teachers who used AI progress-tracking tools saw students complete more assignments, though students’ grades on those assignments were not necessarily better.

Studies found teachers could save time using AI to generate lesson plans without reducing the quality of those lessons, but students who believed a lesson was AI-generated reported being less motivated, and in one study from Turkey students did worse when teachers who already were lower-performing used AI to generate lesson plans. The review comes as school districts are navigating competing pressures to adopt AI rapidly and to limit technology in the classroom. Google caused an uproar this month when it said that school districts that ban AI will not be able to use Google Search. The American Federation of Teachers has embraced training teachers to use AI while pressing major tech companies to agree to guardrails.

A forensic audit found serious flaws in a number of previous meta-analyses that found positive outcomes for AI in education, such as hallucinated references and statistics that did not make sense, according to The Hechinger Report. Another challenge with studying AI in education, particularly with younger students, is that they often do not want to use the tools. The report’s authors said the technology has potential to provide personalized assistance for students and remove some of the tedium from teachers’ jobs, and Loeb said that potential is worth developing. The articles do not say what specific steps districts or the AI Hub will take next.

The articles do not say how the 52 studies break down by country or age group. The articles do not name the other authors of the report. The articles do not say when the AI Hub’s research repository will be complete. The articles do not say how Google’s statement will affect districts that ban AI.

stories.Headline: Island launches enterprise browser to control AI agents
stories.Summary:
Island launched an Enterprise Browser for Agents on 13 November 2026, according to IT Brief Australia. The software lets AI agents use software-as-a-service tools, internal applications and public websites while working under enterprise policies. Island says the product extends the browser controls already used for human employees to software agents that browse, read and act across systems. Businesses are starting to use agents for routine work such as updating customer records, onboarding staff and processing invoices.

The controls apply at the browser activity level rather than to the agents themselves, and Island says end users and agents cannot disable or bypass them. Policy can set permissions by agent and by application, define which document object model operations are allowed, and decide whether an agent can write or only read. Agents inherit the user's identity and permissions, and policy can apply to the user alone, to the user and agent together, or to the agent separately. Logs record whether a human or an agent took an action, and sessions can be recorded for visual playback of pages, clicks and form submissions.

A read-only mode lets agents extract information from systems such as enterprise resource planning platforms without changing, submitting or deleting data. Dan Amiga, Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder at Island, said the company already had what agents need, including identity federation, data boundaries, credential isolation and full attribution, all proven in production. He said agents inherit Island's security model from day one, with policies built specifically for them. He also said that within a few years most enterprises' browser activity will come from agents rather than people, and that organisations treating agent browsing as a separate problem end up running a second workforce nobody can see.

The launch comes as technology suppliers race to define how AI agents should operate inside corporate systems. Island argues that many organisations have relied on patchwork arrangements built on consumer browser infrastructure, which it says can create risks around credentials, data handling and changes to records. The browser can be deployed on devices and in the cloud, covering local and remote agents without a cloud-hosted browser running outside the customer's environment. Island says it helped define the enterprise browser category and has applied the same policy framework used for human workers to this new product.

stories.Headline: InMobi founder: AI's future business is advertising

InMobi founder and CEO Naveen Tewari has said that advertising will become the main way artificial intelligence reaches consumers at scale, much as it paid for free access to search engines and apps. Tewari expects advertising budgets to move from traditional search toward AI-powered answer engines. He said the same economics should extend to conversational AI, with platforms such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini adopting similar ad models.

Glance, InMobi's consumer technology platform, is building an AI-powered personal shopping agent. Tewari predicted that half the global population could use such an agent to shop within the next two years, which he said could improve purchasing decisions and reduce unnecessary buying. He also argued that India has the opportunity to build global technology companies, saying that competing in international markets pushes companies toward higher quality and innovation. Tewari said AI has lowered the barriers to creating products, so distribution and speed have become the decisive competitive advantages. He advised founders to move fast and accept failure, noting that technology cycles have shortened to two or three years. He stressed that companies must earn consumer trust, particularly because platforms like Glance collect personal information to run AI services. He also said he uses AI agents, each trained on an individual business unit, to help manage InMobi, which frees his team to focus on analysis and problem-solving rather than routine information gathering.

stories.Headline: Chariot launches multilingual TTS model supporting 11 Indian languages
stories.Summary:
Chariot, an Indian AI research lab, has launched Chariot-1-TTS-Multilingual, a text-to-speech model that supports 11 Indian languages and English. The model offers more than 50 voices, allows code-mixing between any two supported languages within a sentence, and can clone a voice from a few seconds of reference audio. It can generate speech from up to 1,000 characters in a single request. Developers can access the voice catalogue or create custom voices using reference recordings.

Unlike conventional systems, the model applies contextual reasoning to pronunciation, which lets it tell apart homographs such as "B+" as a blood group or as a grade. It also handles currency amounts, dates, abbreviations and technical expressions according to context. Chariot says the model ranks first on several measures against selected offerings from ElevenLabs, Cartesia, Microsoft, OpenAI, AWS and Sarvam. The company reported a character error rate of 7.60 per cent for Hindi and 6.47 per cent across nine other Indic languages. It also reported 93.78 per cent accuracy on an English verbalisation benchmark covering more than 1,000 sentences.

Chariot, previously known as Gan.ai, is a Delhi-headquartered frontier AI research lab founded by Parth Sarthi and Suvrat Bhooshan, who were formerly researchers at Google DeepMind and Meta's Fundamental AI Research lab. The company says the model will be deployed in voice agents, customer service, educational platforms and multilingual public helplines. The company is backed by the IndiaAI Mission, which was launched in March 2024 with an allocation of ₹10,372 crore to support indigenous AI development. Chariot is one of 12 organisations selected under the Mission's Foundation Models pillar.

stories.Headline: Why Silicon Valley’s Knives Came Out for Anthropic
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley executives have turned against Anthropic and its chief executive, Dario Amodei, according to a New York Times report published on November 13, 2026. The article, written by Kalley Huang, Mike Isaac and Cecilia Kang, says the company has grown into a rival that peers increasingly view as a nuisance. Anthropic and OpenAI had been lobbying the White House to keep some advanced A.I. models from being developed and widely shared, arguing they were too dangerous. Companies such as Nvidia and Microsoft, however, saw those models as a major business opportunity.

At the end of July, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Jensen Huang, then the chief executive of Nvidia, moved against that effort. According to four people familiar with the discussions, they exchanged drafts of a letter calling for those models to stay open. Two dozen companies agreed to sign before the letter became public, and over the following week about 200 more joined, including OpenAI. The article also says Amodei has spent years frustrating rivals with warnings about extreme A.I. risks, even as his company builds some of the most powerful systems available. Frustration grew as Anthropic moved into the lead in A.I. development and reported rapid revenue growth.

The article describes Anthropic as a company that has cultivated an image of doing the right thing while also gaining a reputation for playing hardball. It reports that Anthropic has cut some customers off from its service and lobbied against free alternatives offered by other companies. More than 20 people in the technology industry told the newspaper that competitors and investors have organized to push back over the past year. Many of those sources spoke on condition of anonymity to protect their relationships with Anthropic. The report notes that the company is moving toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever, expected later in the month.

Articles.Title: Why Silicon Valley’s Knives Came Out for Anthropic

stories.Headline: Developer builds open-source AI creative suite Enigma Ray

The application combines image, video, audio, lip sync, and visual workflow generation into a single tool. Aziz developed the project in Pakistan, and the code is publicly available on GitHub along with a live online demo. The suite is presented as a free resource that developers can examine, run, and build upon.

The platform is organized around 17 specialized studios, each handling a different creative task. It supports a broad catalog of AI models for different generation workflows, rather than relying on a single model. The application uses a modular monorepo architecture built with Next.js 15, React, Node.js, and Electron, with JavaScript, npm Workspaces, and C++ inference integrations. Its design includes both a desktop application workflow and a web application, so the same project can be used in either form. Together, these choices let the software be extended and maintained as separate components.

Aziz is working on local inference integrations using stable-diffusion.cpp and Wan2GP, which would allow users to run supported models on their own hardware. The article notes that this would reduce dependence on cloud services for generation tasks. Aziz has asked other developers for feedback on possible additions, improvements, or alternative approaches to the project. stories.Headline: Technical debt is social, not just poor engineering, says Xin Yao
stories.Summary:
Technical debt is not always a sign of poor engineering, according to Xin Yao, who made the point at the GOTO Copenhagen conference, as reported by TechGig on November 13, 2026. Yao argued that debt can be the cost of learning from software while it is in use, and that releasing imperfect code lets businesses and users give feedback. On this view, debt can be a deliberate business strategy rather than an accident of careless work. The article's highlights add that the strategy depends on balancing feature delivery against keeping future architectural options open.

Yao described debt as arising when software is designed with incomplete knowledge. Every feature added brings complexity and closes off some future options, and the article ties this to Kent Beck's book "Earn and Learn." Yao warned that producing too many features, possibly with large language models, can eventually leave a team's capacity entirely consumed by fixing existing code, leaving no room for new releases. She also suggested that technical debt can serve as an economic argument that management can use to justify postponing architectural improvements. The central question, in her framing, is whether the learning gained from the debt justifies its cost and whether the debt is eventually repaid.

Yao linked the problem to AI, which she said is changing the picture because software is now produced faster than people share an understanding of how it behaves and why its design decisions were made. Agentic coding, the article reports, makes repayment harder because teams must close the gap between what software does and what people can comprehend. The challenge goes beyond cleaning up badly written AI-generated code and includes making sure the code evolves in line with the domain and the architecture. Yao concluded that paying off this debt is a sociotechnical task, one that requires people and their shared understanding as well as technical work. The article does not report any further steps or next events.

Articles.Title: Technical debt is social, not just poor engineering, says Xin Yao

stories.Headline: CERT-In warns Google Chrome users of critical vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In, has issued a critical warning to Google Chrome users, urging them to update their browsers immediately. The agency's notice, reported by TechGig on November 13, 2026, covers multiple vulnerabilities in Chrome versions earlier than 157.0.8103.50 and Extended Stable versions earlier than 156.0.8078.96. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is already being exploited in the wild. The warning describes the risk as high, since attackers could use these weaknesses to run harmful code or bypass security controls.

The flaws span several parts of the browser. The agency listed use after free in XML, type confusion in V8, an out-of-bounds write in the GPU component, incorrect authorization in FileSystem, a buffer overflow in Compositing, and uninitialized resource bugs in WebGL and the GPU. Google has released stable channel fixes, with version 157.0.8103.50 or 157.0.8103.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Users who have not installed these builds remain exposed to the listed weaknesses. Those running the affected versions should move to the fixed release as soon as possible.

CERT-In is the government body that issued the advisory, and it stated that remote attackers could exploit these flaws against targeted systems. Google, the maker of Chrome, has confirmed that it is aware of an exploit for CVE-2026-125350. The company said its updates would roll out over the coming days and weeks, which means some users may not receive the fix immediately. The reports do not say how many systems have been compromised or who is behind the exploitation. More to follow.

Articles.Title: CERT-In warns Google Chrome users of critical vulnerabilities

stories.Headline: If an AI Bubble Triggers a Bear Market, History Says This Is the Best Move Investors Can Make
stories.Summary:
Several major AI stocks have entered correction territory, with Nvidia shares down more than 25% over the past month and shedding more than $1 trillion in market value, Ryan Vanzo wrote for The Motley Fool on November 12, 2026. A bear market has hardly arrived, as many AI stocks including BigBear.ai, Amazon and C3.ai have continued to gain value during the rout. The article asks how investors should respond to the popping of an AI bubble and says the history of the dot-com crash offers clear advice. It says the potential impact of a bear market in the AI sector is difficult to ignore because overly optimistic valuations may shrink even as demand remains strong. It says it won't be difficult for a downturn in AI stocks to impact the rest of the market.

The article says nearly half of the S&P 500's value is now tied to AI companies, whether AI developers themselves or suppliers to the industry. It says the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 80% over a 31-month bear market during the dot-com bubble. According to data from the U.S. Federal Reserve, 36% of Americans were active internet users in 1999, 43% in 2000, 49% by 2001 and nearly 60% by 2002. The article says there has never been a bad time to buy an index fund tracking the S&P 500, and a portfolio bought at the height of the dot-com bubble and doubled down just before the financial crisis would still be in the black with a long enough time horizon. It says nearly half of the components in many popular indexes are businesses tied to the AI economy, and it may be wise to look at small-cap or international index funds, which are far less dominated by U.S. mega-cap AI companies and often trade at lower valuations.

New research from Barclays stresses that AI demand remains strong and that what the market is questioning is funding, as hyperscalers keep lifting capex while free cash flow evaporates. Barclays' research affirms that AI fundamentals remain very strong in absolute terms. The article says the issue is a matter of logistics and timing, not a matter of demand prospects. It says it is still far too early to know who the ultimate winners will be, whether GPU producers selling to AI software developers or the end users of that software development. It says predicting the future of a game-changing technology is more difficult than many suppose, as the dot-com bubble proved.

The article says investors should accept that AI adoption growth isn't going anywhere, and that while market valuations plummeted during the dot-com crash, the internet continued to experience sustained success. It says nearly every business on Earth, not just technology companies, ultimately benefited from the internet's rise, so betting on the internet did not require buying only dot-com companies. It says the wisest long-term decision may have been the simplest, maintaining exposure to broad market indexes so a portfolio benefits no matter how the internet's success is distributed. It says the same should prove true for the current AI craze, with AI companies soaring in valuation and accounting for massive chunks of broader market indexes. It says if the AI segment of the market struggles, it could disproportionately impact an entire portfolio.

The article says the Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team identified 10 best stocks for investors to buy now, and the Nasdaq Composite Index was not one of them. It says Netflix made the list on December 17, 2004, and $1,000 invested at the time of the recommendation would be worth $348,060. It says Nvidia made the list on April 15, 2005, and $1,000 invested at the time of the recommendation would be worth $1,067,492. It says Stock Advisor's total average return is 849%, compared with 210% for the S&P 500, with returns as of November 12, 2026. It says Ryan Vanzo has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, and the Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon and Nvidia and recommends C3.ai.

The article says the first takeaway is not to overthink the current environment, and the second is to understand how exposed you are to an AI bear market. It says if you're concerned about AI valuations, you don't necessarily have to sell your existing positions for something else. It says the article was originally published by The Motley Fool. It says the Motley Fool has a disclosure policy. It says the above button links to Coinbase, Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading, and Coinbase pays Yahoo for certain activity generated through the link.

Articles.Title: If an AI Bubble Triggers a Bear Market, History Says This Is the Best Move Investors Can Make

stories.Headline: Saying no to AI spend is how we protect AI value
stories.Summary:
On the 17th of July, an engineer at Paessler asked for more credits for Claude after already spending $4,000, and soon after alerts went out that the company had reached 75% of its allocated monthly spend limit. Jay Miller, CISO at Paessler, and Ashley Rice, VP of strategic delivery and operational excellence, wrote the account, published on Nov 13, 2026. Earlier this year, Paessler held its first AI-focused dev day and offered a $5,000 prize for the best feature built into its network monitoring platform. The team produced a record 29 submissions, with some deliberately choosing more expensive approaches to build things that would otherwise have been impossible. The applications ranged from context-aware assistants to root cause analysis helpers, and Paessler gave a very long leash on cost because it had never done this before.

Paessler's answer is hard-and-fast rules such as group limits, set at rollout, with token limits aligned to spending limits. The company suggests working backward from how much you are comfortable spending per person or team, and treating AI like any other resource by setting a maximum spend limit and raising it when value shows up. Paessler unites around an AI Center of Excellence, a cross-functional group of decision makers from IT, information security, human resources, finance, legal and operational excellence who meet weekly. Before approving a new tool, the group asks whether something already paid for can do the job through an integration, and a pen tester tries to break new AI apps by accessing data he should not see. Claude lets users select the amount of effort needed to answer a question or perform a task, and more thorough responses require higher token usage and therefore higher cost.

Miller and Rice said employees are not doing anything wrong and are understandably excited and legitimately experimenting, usually with positive results, but too much of a good thing can hit the bottom line. They said the right culture is just as important as spend controls, and if employees know to be cost-aware they will be cost-aware. They said caps do not get in the way of innovation but act as a sense check between employee and employer, surfacing genuine use cases and ensuring alignment between spend and outcome. They said an executive who hits a monthly cap during heavy analysis before a board meeting should not be impeded, so a warning can evolve into a quick check and an increase, while a manager may pause spending on experiments not yet tied to a critical business need. They said "no" should be the most valuable word in your AI vocabulary in the year ahead, not because AI is not valuable but because maximizing its value comes through meaningful constraint.

McKinsey reports that more than 9 out of 10 companies, or 93%, are exceeding their AI budgets, and a CIO in Paessler's network shared that their annual AI budget evaporated within two months. Gartner predicts that by 2028 AI coding costs will overtake the average developer's salary, meaning the tools could cost more than the developer using them. Two-thirds of office professionals at large companies say they have used AI tools at work they believed were not permitted, which wastes resources and creates an attack surface. Paessler consolidated one app that jumped in costs unexpectedly once it realized its main AI platform could handle the job anyway. Paessler's PRTG network monitoring platform is used by more than 500,000 users worldwide to oversee their IT, OT and IoT infrastructure.

Miller spent more than 20 years building cybersecurity solutions in both the public and private sectors and continues to bridge the gap between technical teams and executive leadership across a global monitoring company. Rice, chief of staff to the CEO, chairs the AI Center of Excellence and brings almost two decades of leadership and hands-on expertise in public and private technology-driven companies. Paessler, like many companies, is building the AI boat as it sails it, and spend leaks are common in the wild waters of automation. The authors said value-vs-spend checks serve as a necessary compass and a cross-functional AI team keeps the ship structurally sound, preventing things like shadow AI or unchecked agents from sinking the budget. They said they learned the hard way that protecting AI value means being willing to sometimes say no, putting the processes and the people in place to make that call before the bill arrives.

The CoE is now Paessler's single voice on publishing guidance, approved use cases, education and training, so employees know where the company is heading and where to bring their questions. An AI tool repository backed by one set of usage standards means Paessler always knows what is running and why, which also matters for compliance. The process is ongoing: evaluating performance, aligning spend with business goals and, when needed, declining a tool. The authors said many have gotten swept up in the hype and forgotten that AI is a tool that requires a business case, and that this is not about shutting down new ways of doing things but giving visibility into where efforts are going. The articles do not say what Paessler's total AI budget is, how many employees use AI tools, or which specific tools the CoE has declined.

Articles.Title: Saying no to AI spend is how we protect AI value

stories.Headline: Leading AI safety advocate likely to run for president
stories.Summary:
Brad Carson, a former Oklahoma congressman and a leading AI safety advocate, is likely to run for president, according to two people directly familiar with his plans, as reported by Politico on November 13, 2026. The Democrat, who served as a "blue dog" lawmaker, is reportedly considering the bid. Those close to him say a push from like-minded donor groups has also encouraged the idea. The report describes Carson as someone who helped build the political infrastructure of the AI safety movement.

The timing is tied to the midterm elections, in which many Democrats won while campaigning on backlash against data centers and skepticism toward big tech. The article says this has left AI safety advocates feeling emboldened. Carson has become a central voice in the debate over how far the companies developing AI should be restrained. The report presents his interest as part of a broader political shift rather than a formal policy change.

The article also makes clear the run would be a major long shot. Carson has a military background as an Iraq War veteran and once served as undersecretary of the Army, which the report says could sound presidential. However, he has not served in Congress since 2005 or in government since 2016. One person familiar with his plans called it a "keyhole shot," while stressing that no final decision has been made.

Politico's Decoded newsletter carried the report, which is based on people with direct knowledge of Carson's thinking. The article does not describe any formal announcement or filing. It offers no timeline for a decision. Readers should expect further reporting on whether Carson moves forward with a campaign.

Articles.Title: Leading AI safety advocate likely to run for president

stories.Headline: How Northstar landed in AI boom
stories.Summary:
Northstar Technologies, a Bonita Springs-based manufacturer of modular data centers, has seen explosive growth in the artificial intelligence infrastructure market, according to a Naples Press article published on November 13, 2026. The company, an offshoot of a 26-year-old construction company, originated in Naples in 2020 during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. It had makeshift offices at Naples Smoke Shop in Neapolitan Way Shopping Center, then in the hallways of Naples Bay Resort and later on a yacht anchored there. CEO Paul Inglese said Northstar is on track for its annual revenue to grow more than 100 times over three years. The company started at $4.3 million in 2024, grew to $11.5 million in 2025 and leaped to a projected $450 million this year, with about $1.3 billion in committed sales this year.

Most of Northstar's modular buildings measure about 12 feet wide, 12 feet tall and 60 feet long, about 720 square feet, roughly the size of two steel shipping containers. They are being built inside a 153,000-square-foot warehouse off Oriole Road, near where Alico Road and Interstate 75 intersect in Lee County. The assembly line process takes about two days to build one, and the factory uses a combination of humans and machines, such as a saw, during the milling process. Instead of using concrete and steel, Northstar assembles the buildings out of fiber-reinforced polymer, made out of high-strength fibers such as glass, set in a polymer resin matrix. The modular data centers have passed tests, certified as Category 5 hurricane- and EF5 tornado-resistant, Inglese said.

Inglese said the composite material is similar in insulation capability to a Yeti cooler, which is made from polyethylene with polyurethane foam insulation. He said the claim is ice lasts for three days or more in a Yeti cooler, and the same concept goes for the data center, which is not taking on heat from the outside. Inglese said Northstar is 80% lighter than steel but stronger than steel on a weight-to-strength ratio, which makes a 60-foot module more transportable across the country or globally. He said that aspect has led to clients such as the U.S. government, including the Department of Defense. Inglese said the government contracts, exponential growth and the billion-plus dollars in sales would not have been set in motion had he not witnessed the days after Aug. 13, 2004, when Hurricane Charley devastated Charlotte County.

Jason Hick, director of modular data centers at Alliance Technology Group, said Alliance surveyed 25 modular data center builders and Northstar rose to the top. Alliance is one of Northstar's biggest clients, and Alliance has projected its own modular data center revenue this year at about $100 million, Hick said. Hick said hyperscale data centers are a very dirty environment with tools flying everywhere, not an environment for a computer, which needs filtered air and liquid cooling and a lot of power. He said Alliance's clients are trying to monetize their buildings before they get completed, which isn't easily feasible in a cavernous building. Multiply one Northstar modular data center by about 700, and you get a hyperscale data center, a massive building eclipsing half a million square feet, which have been facing opposition from communities, voters and elected officials.

Inglese said that when Hurricane Charley and Wilma hit, the company was doing just small residential buildings, conventional block and such, up in Port Charlotte and Punta Gorda. He said a concrete block panel had blown through the side of a garage, through the car inside and onto the car seat, and he thought there had to be a better way. Inglese spent almost the next 20 years in construction while doing research and development and trial and error, leading him to building a three-story, 3,100-square-foot, $1.7 million luxury home in Naples Park on 111th Avenue North. It is Collier County's first home made out of fiber-reinforced polymer, nicknamed the "Lotus home," and its then-windowless shell was completed in time to endure Hurricane Ian's devastating winds in 2022. Northstar posted about the home's resiliency on LinkedIn, which was when Dan Smith, executive vice president and chief growth officer of Toledo, Ohio-based Owens Corning, saw it and said, "If you have what I think you have, we've got to talk.

We're flying down." Owens Corning dispatched about 10 employees to Naples to meet with Inglese and look at the Lotus home, and one of them said he had been in composites all his life and didn't think he would live long enough to see a 100% composite-built home. Inglese said the engineering department ran the calculations and found 87,000 pounds of glass just in the structure of that home. A few weeks after the Naples visit, Owens Corning invested about $5 million into Northstar, Inglese said.

Inglese said the deal gave Northstar access to Owens Corning's science and technology lab, where the company developed Northstar materials at the material science level and developed the glass mats it uses. The first product the company began selling was a storage compartment for EV batteries, and Porsche North America began ordering and deploying them to dealerships across the country. Inglese said the EV battery in a Porsche is the whole length of the car, about $80,000 and about 1,400 pounds, and when these batteries are damaged, fire code does not allow them to store the batteries in the service bays. Northstar developed an EV battery enclosed building, which Inglese called the company's first modular build, moving from residential, which it called panelized and erected like tilt-wall.

Canadian-backed owners bought Dallas-based Compass Datacenters in late 2023, and it was building modular data centers for the U.S. military. Some of Northstar's modular buildings end up in large, hyperscale data centers, Inglese said, but others are deployed as standalone buildings, allowing them to face less scrutiny from neighboring property owners. By building a data center miniature in scale, Northstar has positioned itself to pioneer a nascent industry, Hick said. More to follow.

Articles.Title: How Northstar landed in AI boom

stories.Headline: Fall event highlight - Boomi's Michael Bachman shakes up the enterprise AI conversation at CCE 2026
stories.Summary:
Michael Bachman, Boomi's Head of AI Research and Emerging Technology Strategy, spoke with diginomica at Constellation Connected Enterprise in a fall event season where AI vendors got some things right but also fell short. The conversation took place at the end of that season and covered agentic truth and the data architecture needed to reach it. Bachman was also up for a spirited review of two controversial AI buzzwords, reasoning and grounding. The interviewer called him the sharpest enterprise AI thinker sat down with in quite a while. Bachman did not know ahead of time that he would be the foil for the interviewer's grouchiest enterprise AI questions.

The interviewer asked why machine reasoning is conflated with human reasoning and why vendors use the term grounding, which sounds sexy but is technically inaccurate for current architectures. The interviewer said quality data does not mean an agent will do the right thing at inference time. The space seen for Boomi to take up lies between that lazy understanding of data quality and getting exactly what the agent needs at that moment. Bachman began with the blurring of lines between analytical and operational data. He said you need a data lake for data models, hygiene and analytics, but operational and analytical data are coming together at rapid speed.

Bachman said an inference time engine must be concerned with the intersection of those two domains, and that is what Boomi does. He said Boomi needs layered data quality, with data quality in the data lake, change data capture and ELT. He said a lightweight data hub is also needed to provide an intermediate layer of cleaning. He said lineage information and ontologies are needed to look things up faster, with a good semantic layer in between. He said metadata created actively by something autonomous in the background gives better pictures of context so we know where to get data at runtime.

The interviewer said he would not turn an LLM reasoning engine loose onto a massive context layer and wants a concise list of the best sources for the query. Bachman said putting a massive LLM against your data structure is one way but not necessarily the recommended way, which is why Boomi made a pickup of a company called Lunar. He said the idea is to channel the right logical system for the call being made and to know who is making the call. He asked whether an agent is an extension of Jon, Kristen or Bachman, and what entitlements each has back in the system. He said access to the same systems can mean different objects within that system.

Bachman said pulling the right object and integrating it with other objects at runtime is tricky business, which is where Boomi's distributed architecture comes in handy. He said distributed runtimes can be located publicly, privately or hybrid, and that architecture makes the decision process easier. He said it supports the human and the human extension at the right place, time and cost, whether monetary or the cost of getting information as grounded as possible in that moment. He said a well-defined semantic layer is essential but it is more essential for that layer to adjust toward change and variation. He said he has written patents on mapping using a different set of semantic systems and the semantic layer.

Bachman said those patents are meant for mapping source and target endpoints but can also incorporate how semantics change relative to different types of systems of truth. He said one of the most important things is capturing nuanced metadata dynamically so semantics knows and has the right pointers to where data is located. He said it is not about giving MCP carte blanche to the systems but using MCP effectively with APIs, which he thinks Boomi can figure out well. The interviewer said grounding drives him particularly bonkers because it implies a base foundation and an innate structure, as when humans are grounded in the physics of the world. He said agentic context is fragile and not innate, and an agent has to be re-grounded at every different point of inference.

Articles.Title: Fall event highlight - Boomi's Michael Bachman shakes up the enterprise AI conversation at CCE 2026

stories.Headline: AI helps conservators uncover lost details in William Merritt Chase painting
stories.Summary:
AI has helped conservators reveal how a William Merritt Chase painting changed over the years. The work, A Comfortable Corner (around 1888), was studied by a team from Modern Art Conservation working with the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, and the story was published on 13 November 2026 by The Art Newspaper. The painting had been altered by at least two earlier restorations, including a significant effort in the 1960s. Those interventions had added a heavy lining, retouching, inpainting and uneven varnishes, some of which discoloured or changed the surface texture.

The key evidence was an early black-and-white photograph, believed to predate the 1960s restoration, which showed that more of the composition had once been visible. The painting appears to have been reduced in size during that restoration, perhaps to fit a new stretcher or because damaged edges were folded over and removed. The photograph also showed missing details, such as a curl of hair beneath the sitter's ear and faded parts of a decorative screen. Using AI, the team combined the historical photograph with a colour image of the painting to create a composite showing where the two differed. The software proved faster than manual comparison, and the work was supported by a Bank of America grant.

Conservator Suzanne Siano, who leads the studio's work on the project, said it was difficult to establish whether all the changes resulted from earlier conservation. She suggested that some earlier cleaning may have removed marks or additions made by Chase himself, which would make them pentimenti. The team did not simply restore every difference the software flagged, since the photograph was not high resolution and was not necessarily a record of the painting's earliest state. Instead, its findings were checked against magnified examination, ultraviolet imaging, knowledge of Chase's materials and comparison with his other works. One notable finding was that Chase's signature had become very faint, and Siano believes it may have been mistaken for part of the carpet pattern during an earlier restoration.

The restored painting will be shown in the exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End, which runs from 14 November 2026 to 21 March 2027 at the Parrish. Kaitlin Halloran, the museum's associate curator, described the work as important within Chase's output because it reflects 19th-century art and the influence of Japanese art and design on him. Siano said this was the first time her studio had used AI as an aid in a painting's conservation, and she expects its use to remain specific to each case. She added that AI may prove more valuable as a research tool, for example in locating historical images, but that the nuanced judgments conservators make are unlikely to be replicated by a machine.

Articles.Title: AI helps conservators uncover lost details in William Merritt Chase painting

stories.Headline: Taiwan Wants an AI Model That Understands It
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's government is seeking what it calls "sovereign AI," meaning AI models that reflect Taiwanese language, culture and values rather than relying mainly on Chinese-language data or on models built by U.S. companies such as Google and OpenAI. The push was described in a Domino Theory report published on November 13, 2026. Ling-Jyh Chen, chief executive of Taiwan AI Academy, said that earlier ChatGPT versions could not answer a basic question about Taiwanese cuisine, noting that beef soup noodles do not contain chunks of meat. He said earlier models were trained on 190 million Chinese words, mostly in simplified Chinese originating from China, and that Chinese-language skill does not equal awareness of local context.

The effort rests on a ranking system run by the AI Evaluation Center, which operates under the Ministry of Digital Affairs and began scoring models in September. Models are scored on language proficiency, understanding of Taiwanese society and culture, and understanding of Taiwanese values. The first two measures rely on questions from Taiwan's university entrance exam, the GSAT, which Chen considers too easy to game because the questions are public. Taiwanese startup APMIC rose from 15th to 1st place between September and October after its GSAT score improved by nearly 17 percentage points, which the report attributes to fine-tuning on data the Taiwanese government made public. The report also notes that Taiwanese models generally outrank major U.S. models only on the values measure, and fall sharply when that measure is removed.

The Ministry of Digital Affairs has said in a blog post that authoritarian regimes use AI to rewrite the past and shape the future, and that Taiwan must control its own data, language and perspectives. The AI Evaluation Center told Domino Theory that it measures understanding of Taiwan's historical experience and democratic institutions, and that it does not aim to make models agree with Taiwan's positions. Alice Yang of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research questioned whether a specifically Taiwanese value can be defined objectively, and suggested the government mainly wants to limit Chinese influence on younger people's thinking. Audrey Tang, a former minister of digital affairs, argued that Taiwan has 20 national languages, 16 recognized Indigenous peoples and 42 language variations, so no single voice can represent it. She said sovereign AI should be governed at the local level and that a state-built national model based on everyone's data would be misguided.

Articles.Title: Taiwan Wants an AI Model That Understands It

stories.Headline: Cisco’s 4 pillars for achieving agentic AI transformation
stories.Summary:
Cisco Systems is using agentic AI, traditional AI and automation to transform its business, the company said in an article published by CIO.com on November 13, 2026. Liz Centoni, executive vice president and chief customer experience officer, leads the effort at the networking, cybersecurity and AI company. She runs Cisco's $15 billion services business, an organization of 20,000 employees. That business covers professional services, customer success, technical support and the renewals engine for software and services. In 2024 she led Cisco's $28 billion acquisition of Splunk, and she is a 26-year Cisco veteran.

Centoni said Cisco did not simply start bolting on AI and instead looked at underlying workflows to understand how work could be redone. When she took her current position two years ago, she reviewed customer feedback and found frustration with the path to the right expert, which often required handoffs between engineers. The team first built an agent to speed up finding the right engineer, which Centoni called a misstep. She said the agent upset customers more because it showed five handoffs behind the scenes and surfaced them faster. She said the team should have asked why handoffs existed before creating an agent.

Centoni said users are an essential part of the technology stack and that subject matter experts and users must outline the workflow. She said leaders must get close to the work and that if they cannot, they have no right designing. She said Cisco treated every customer like a bespoke model when she came into the business, but over 40-plus years it has solved these problems tens of thousands of times. She said the company built a knowledge base and playbooks from 40 years of engagements for AI agents and human experts. She said an expert agent brings in all the prior experts and democratizes the knowledge base, giving customers consistency, security and better time to project completion.

Centoni said human experts are always in the loop and the team would have more bandwidth for customer conversations. She said Cisco's focus has been on how fast it can reach root cause analysis, asking whether three hours could become 30 minutes. She said Cisco now uses AI to stop issues before they hit a customer by monitoring environments and recommending next best steps. She said that in 12 months she would like to tell a customer they would have had 10 outages last year and Cisco prevented eight. She said Cisco asks whether automation can do a task before going down the AI path, using automation for rules-based work and AI when multiple signals drive a prediction.

Centoni said Cisco's AI assistant for renewals combines a renewals agent, a sentiment agent, a risk agent and an install base agent and is based on Mistral because it was one of the few on-prem models with full capabilities. She said Cisco customized that model using a private instance and uses automation along with it. She said measuring adoption leads users to check the box and then use old processes, which she calls compliance theater. She said she instead checks whether workflows have changed and whether the renewals team showed greater capacity. She said an agent is about 60% of the way there in its first iteration in terms of usability, with the user part of the tech stack giving feedback.

Centoni said Cisco's internal support agent runs in the support workflow and pulls in a customer's relevant history and context as soon as a case opens. She said that saves the first 30 minutes a support worker would spend asking what went wrong and provides the next best action. She said the quality Cisco has today is the floor, not the ceiling, and that AI capabilities evolve rapidly. She said leadership, not technology, is the limiting factor and leaders need to find and support leaders underneath them. She said the status quo is not an option because customer expectations will grow and revenue growth and good margins are no reason to rest.

The article was written by Thor Olavsrud, a senior writer for CIO.com with more than 20 years of experience covering IT and the tech industry. It appeared alongside CIO.com news items on Northern Trust, Microsoft, Salesforce, Nvidia, Anthropic and Tableau. The article did not say when Cisco began the transformation or how many agents it has deployed. It did not give the cost of the AI effort or a date for the 12-month goal beyond Centoni's remark. It did not name the customers involved or say whether the renewals assistant is sold externally.

Articles.Title: Cisco’s 4 pillars for achieving agentic AI transformation

stories.Headline: The AI at the source of water management reform
stories.Summary:
Korea Water Resources Corporation, known as K-water, manages water in dams, treats it at purification plants, and supplies it to local municipalities. The company is now using AI to connect the flow of water from one end of that process to the other. K-water has a long history of using technology to operate dams, but it once relied mainly on historical climate patterns and years of operating experience. As climate change brings more frequent and unexpected extremes of rainfall and drought, those methods have become harder to rely on, so K-water needed new analysis and forecasting tools.

Flood damage downstream of dams in 2020 prompted K-water to adopt AI and digital twin technology in earnest. In late 2025 it established the AI Division, which brings together internal specialists from IT, administration, civil, mechanical, electrical, environmental engineering and telecommunications. The division's task is to merge technologies developed separately, including digital twins for water management, AI-powered treatment plants and smart distribution network management, into one framework. That framework covers the whole process of managing dam water, treating it and delivering it to users. K-water also plans an AI data center in Sejong, which it aims to build by 2030.

Ha-Dong Jung, the division's VP, joined K-water in 1997 and became its first head. He describes the division's creation as a natural progression of the company's consistent use of technology to drive internal innovation. Jung says the purpose of earlier data work was to collect, store and display information for people to read at a glance. Today, he says, that accumulated data is just a collection of numbers that must be defined and related to each other before AI can use it. K-water is investing in an ontology that defines data concepts and relationships, combined with RAG.

Jung also described practical obstacles, including extraction of large data volumes sometimes stopping existing equipment, which K-water had to address by adding multiple routes for data acquisition. He said the equipment was designed for its original tasks, not for the data extraction AI projects require. K-water has also changed the AI tools available to employees, first building K-water GPT on Meta's Llama models before introducing external services. Jung said employees compare internal tools with ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, and that external services let them choose among major models in a more secure environment.

Jung said an IT project typically takes six months to a year to prepare, about a year to implement and roughly six months more to close out, while AI models keep changing throughout. He said the company may eventually need an environment where its own employees respond directly rather than relying entirely on outside contractors. The article notes that public enterprises are often seen as slow to change, yet K-water is regarded as one of South Korea's leading public enterprises in AI. OpenAI has highlighted K-water as a prime example of AI use in disaster response, drawing attention to its water management capabilities.

K-water's AI division aims to make the company a global water company leading the response to climate change. Jung said his role is to help employees keep taking on challenges and to remove obstacles he can resolve as a leader. The article says the progress so far is only the beginning, with the company's AI use still in early stages. It gives no timeline for when employees might respond directly to AI work, and no detail on how the Sejong data center will be funded or staffed beyond the 2030 target.

Articles.Title: The AI at the source of water management reform

stories.Headline: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on a Thursday, following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. The resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, and rival chipmakers appear eager to take advantage of the uncertainty. Shares of Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices rose that day as investors predicted that Nvidia's customers would look to diversify their suppliers. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, has become interim chief executive.

Huang was the public face of a company that dominates the market for the computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, he had predicted that Nvidia would face a backlog of $1 trillion in chip orders by the end of the year, double his estimate from a year earlier. Nvidia trades with Apple as Wall Street's most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Analysts say the shake-up could turn a near monopoly into a more competitive market, though one expert noted that Nvidia's losses would outweigh its rivals' gains.

Analysts said Nvidia built its early lead by adapting graphics processing units, first used for video games, to train AI systems. Competitors named in its filings include AMD, Intel, Broadcom, and the cloud companies Google, Amazon and Microsoft. Huang, a celebrity figure in the industry, had close ties with President Donald Trump and pushed for light regulation of AI. Analysts say his departure creates uncertainty well beyond the company, given how heavily the AI industry relies on Nvidia's chips. One analyst also warned that the scandal could spur tighter export controls, which might benefit the Chinese chipmaker Huawei.

Nvidia's ties to its customers are also drawing scrutiny. The company has many partnerships and investments in firms that buy its chips, including CoreWeave, in which it holds a stake of nearly 13 percent. CoreWeave's shares fell almost 7 percent on Thursday. Experts will be watching how the fallout affects the planned public listing of Anthropic, which is valued at $1.3 trillion, as well as a political climate shaped by midterm elections and growing hostility toward data centers. The coming weeks are expected to reveal how these pressures play out across the sector.

Articles.Title: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom

stories.Headline: From potato farm to data farm: Inside the Chinese city powering the country’s AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
In the vast grasslands of northern China, in the city of Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, massive data centers are being built at breakneck speed. NBC News reporters Janis Mackey Frayer, Dawn Liu, Erin Tan and Mithil Aggarwal describe how the landscape is being transformed as the country races to build the computing power it needs for artificial intelligence. The reporting, published on November 13, 2026, presents the buildout as part of a broader effort to compete with the United States for global AI leadership. The city's shift from farmland to a hub for computing is the central subject of the piece.

The articles provided are only partial, consisting mostly of the headline, the opening of the story and a long list of unrelated headlines from the NBC News site, so they do not give the specific figures, dates, project sizes or investment amounts that a fuller account would contain. They also do not spell out what regulations or policy changes, if any, accompany the expansion. What they do establish is the scale and speed of the construction and the strategic goal behind it. Without more detail, the requirements and changes flowing from the buildout cannot be described from these sources.

The reporters' framing ties the data center boom directly to China's ambition to challenge the United States in AI. The articles do not include direct statements from named officials or companies, so no specific responsibility or testimony can be attributed beyond the reporters' own account. The surrounding headlines on the page touch on other AI and chip matters, but they are not connected in the excerpt to this project. The provided material does not say what comes next for the Ulanqab facilities or how the expansion is expected to develop.

Articles.Title: From potato farm to data farm: Inside the Chinese city powering the country’s AI ambitions

stories.Headline: AI data centres and renewables to generate $202 bn in insurance premiums
stories.Summary:
Swiss Re Institute forecasts that investment in AI data centres and renewable energy projects could generate $202 bn in cumulative commercial insurance premiums between 2026 and 2030. Of that total, AI data centre construction and operations are expected to account for $91 bn, while renewable energy projects could contribute $111 bn. The combined figure is equivalent to roughly 12% of projected global commercial property insurance premiums over the same five-year period. The articles present these numbers as a forecast rather than a settled outcome.

Construction activity will drive demand for engineering, surety and liability cover, since these projects involve works under construction, equipment and materials supply chains, financing-related risks and obligations that arise during development. Large and technically complex projects with high insured values will require substantial underwriting capacity, often drawing on both commercial insurers and reinsurers. As facilities move through commissioning, their needs shift toward operational property and liability policies. Those policies replace much of the construction-specific protection and create recurring premium streams over the assets' working lives.

The articles also highlight exposures that reach beyond individual facilities. Electricity grids, water systems and transport networks connect many businesses, so damage to one component can interrupt operations elsewhere even without direct physical loss. A single infrastructure failure could therefore generate business interruption claims across multiple insureds at once. Common suppliers and shared providers can create concentrations of exposure, meaning one event may trigger simultaneous losses under several policies. Insurers must account for this possibility when pricing and managing their portfolios.

The source attributes the forecast to the Swiss Re Institute, which is the research arm of the reinsurer Swiss Re. The articles say the ability to turn this investment into premium income will depend on the availability of insurance capacity, though the excerpt ends before fully explaining that point. The articles do not describe any specific policy changes, regulatory responses or timelines beyond the 2026 to 2030 forecast window. Whether the projected premiums materialise will therefore depend on how quickly projects proceed and how insurers respond to the risks described.

Articles.Title: AI data centres and renewables to generate $202 bn in insurance premiums

stories.Headline: Huang Exit Puts $3.2B of China AI Projects at Risk [2026]
stories.Summary:
Reuters reviewed more than 150 Chinese documents, including procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, and found computing projects worth over 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion) built around Nvidia processors the company says it can no longer sell into China. The findings were published on November 13, 2026, one day after Reuters reported that Jensen Huang had resigned as Nvidia chief executive. The projects are tied to H100 and H200 chips that Nvidia has said U.S. export controls effectively bar it from selling in China. Chinese AI builders now face the awkward position of having planned around those chips at the same time U.S. scrutiny, board investigations and political pressure are intensifying in Washington. The reporting frames the risk as exposure, since the sources do not confirm that any specific project has been cancelled, frozen or blocked.

The largest named project is a proposed AI computing center in Xianyou county, Fujian province, carrying a 6.2 billion yuan price tag, about $873 million, and specifying Nvidia H100 chips. In Shaanxi province, a 3 billion yuan computing center has documents specifying both H100 and H200 processors, and the state-owned engineering group Sinomach said a subsidiary won a related contract. A government prospectus issued in April describes a 2.26 billion yuan project in Jilin province that combines Nvidia H100 processors with Chinese-developed chips. The three named projects total roughly 11.5 billion yuan, about half the headline figure, though Reuters did not say whether all three sit inside that total. Reuters noted that the Xianyou project is still seeking commercial partners and that the Jilin developer is expected to fund about 80% of its investment with bank loans, according to a single reported source.

Reuters' review is limited to public paperwork, so it captures only plans that were published and does not show how many restricted chips are physically installed in China. A procurement notice or prospectus describes what a developer wants to buy and does not prove delivery. Nvidia has said U.S. export controls shut it out of China's AI data-center market, and in comments cited by CNBC, Huang said in October 2025, "We are 100% out of China." Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation after recent reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and the board's statement does not announce any finding about his conduct. Reuters reported that Huang resigned on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim chief executive while the company searches for a permanent successor.

Huang was Nvidia's most visible advocate for access to the Chinese market, and Reuters presented the loss of that advocacy as a potential shift in how Washington weighs the industry's case. The planning risks described in the documents were visible before Huang's resignation, as shown by the hybrid design in Jilin, which appeared in an April prospectus. Projects financed mostly by bank debt that depend on a restricted part also carry exposure for lenders, since their economics rest on chips that may not arrive. Mixed clusters of Nvidia and domestic chips require engineering work because training frameworks tuned for CUDA do not move easily to other accelerators, which can slow onboarding and create uneven performance for model developers who rent capacity. The reporting also notes that Chinese AI firms are seeking Nvidia capacity outside China, which the articles present as part of the same pressure.

Reuters reported that the Chinese projects remain under reported risk and heightened scrutiny, but the sources do not show that any contract has been cancelled, frozen or blocked. Chinese shares fell on Friday, November 13, 2026, according to the market reporting in the articles. The articles leave open whether Xianyou and the other projects will shift to domestic accelerators or hybrid designs, and whether partner announcements will continue to name H100 chips. They also leave open how many of the specified chips will ever be delivered, through which channels, and at what price. The independent investigation at Nvidia has no announced conclusion, and the articles do not say when Nvidia will name a permanent chief executive.

Articles.Title: Huang Exit Puts $3.2B of China AI Projects at Risk [2026]

stories.Headline: How Cisco Is Rewiring Its Corporate Structure for the AI Era
stories.Summary:
Cisco Systems President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel spoke with Steve about rewiring the corporation for AI in an interview recorded on October 28, 2026. The interview was published by the Wall Street Journal on Friday, November 13, 2026 at 4:00 AM CST. Patel said Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins made the first big change by putting the entire product organization under one umbrella. Patel said Cisco had made 250 acquisitions, and each acquisition had a general manager who wanted to build his own fiefdom. Patel said Cisco blew that up and moved to a functional organization at its size and scale.

Patel said Cisco's revenue this year will be like $70 billion plus. He said Cisco built a vertically integrated platform that is a co-design full stack, building its own silicon, photonics, hardware systems and software. He said Cisco has its own platforms for security, observability and data, and its own models, applications and agents. He said Cisco is the largest networking company in the world and also one of the largest security companies in the world. He said Cisco's security friends don't have networking and its networking friends don't have a security platform.

Patel said the hardest thing is the cultural shift and getting people to not be afraid of AI. He said Cisco told engineers that if they don't use AI they will lose their job. He said every major step function of AI improvement has created a human bottleneck someplace else. He asserted that Cisco will have more engineers in the future rather than less, and none of them will be syntactically writing code. He said those engineers will focus on technologies that get diffused to 8 billion people on the planet more easily than ever before.

Patel said a CIO has to be concerned because the risks exposed by trust and safety and security are material risks that must be mitigated. He said that when all you have is a collection of products that don't talk to each other, you don't get any advantage. He said Cisco wanted a compounding effect where the marginal cost of ingestion of every new technology customers buy goes down precipitously. He said Cisco tightly integrated the technologies but loosely coupled them to keep an open ecosystem. He said Cisco is in the quiet period right now so he won't comment about this quarter, but every other for the past couple years has seen positive effects.

Patel said the name of the game is to prevent lateral movement if you assume an attacker has already infiltrated your environment. He said lateral movement happens on the network and Cisco has the most amount of telemetry on the network. He said fusing security into the fabric of the network changes the entire equation of how security can be enforced within the fabric. He said that would be very hard to get done while operating like a holding company. He said the second change was the composition of the workforce, applying a rule of thirds.

Patel said a third of the people within his leadership team should be at-scale operators who know how to maneuver within the machinery of Cisco. He said the second third are people hired from the outside who are also at-scale operators but come with a market perspective and are systems thinkers. He said the last third is the one that's the most unique, and the transcript ends there. The articles give no further details on the last third, on what happens next, or on any response from employees or customers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: How Cisco Is Rewiring Its Corporate Structure for the AI Era

stories.Headline: The AI Trade Just Cracked. Here’s the Price at Which I’d Start Buying Nvidia.
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's stock fell sharply on November 12, 2026, after CEO Jensen Huang resigned from his posts as chief executive and board member. The Motley Fool reported that the sell-off came after reports that Huang had extramarital affairs with two Nvidia employees and a business executive suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. The article's author, Adam Spatacco, reported the news on November 13, 2026. Nvidia's stock briefly fell below $150 that day, down from a record high of roughly $243 per share in October. Investors also sold related names in the artificial intelligence landscape as the shares declined.

Nvidia announced that CFO Colette Kress would take on the chief executive role on an interim basis. The article says the change introduces uncertainty about the company's strategy, customer relationships, and future execution. The article also notes that the company's shares traded in a day's range of $148.80 to $167.14 on the most recent session, with a 52-week range of $148.80 to $243.37. Its market capitalization was listed at $4.01 trillion, and its gross margin at 74.67 percent. The article also gives the stock's dividend yield as 0.31 percent.

Huang resigned as CEO after reports of the affairs, and the company's board of directors accepted his departure. The article attributes the decision to the company's announcement on November 12 that Huang had stepped down. Spatacco writes that Nvidia was already under pressure before the resignation. He points to investor doubts about whether hyperscalers can earn adequate returns on their AI infrastructure spending. The article ties Nvidia's pressure to the broader market, where the Magnificent Seven account for nearly one-third of the S&P 500's total market capitalization.

The article says Nvidia's problems could spread to the wider technology sector and to the index itself. Spatacco writes that if investors reassess AI-related growth assumptions across big tech, selling pressure could drag major indexes lower. He notes that Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices also attracted investors seeking AI semiconductor exposure. The article also says utilities, energy producers, and electrical equipment makers attract attention because data centers require large amounts of power. Hyperscalers named in the article include Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Oracle.

Nvidia's rise began after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022. The article reports that between late 2022 and year-end 2025, Nvidia's stock price rose roughly tenfold. The company's graphics processing units became critical infrastructure for training and deploying generative AI models. Nvidia introduced successive architectures, including Hopper, Blackwell, and Vera Rubin, and its CUDA software platform helped keep developers within its ecosystem. The article describes the company's evolution from a gaming GPU maker into an AI infrastructure leader.

The article states that Nvidia's forward price-to-earnings ratio was around 11 as of November 12, a steep discount to its historical valuation. Spatacco writes that he would become interested in buying the stock between $155 and $160 per share. At that range, based on Wall Street's fiscal 2028 earnings per share estimate of $15.91, the stock would trade at 9.7 to 10.1 times earnings. The article notes that the midterm elections introduced uncertainty over potential regulation of data center construction and electricity costs. It does not say whether the board has named a permanent successor, and it leaves open how far the scandals will affect the wider AI trade.

Articles.Title: The AI Trade Just Cracked. Here’s the Price at Which I’d Start Buying Nvidia.
