He described how arbitrators can receive several differing document bundles from the institution, the parties and the electronic presentation of evidence provider, and suggested a single secure repository would keep annotations confidential. He also said DIAC could cover 16 languages, and that AI could support translation, real-time transcription and natural language search of its website. Ms. Hussein said CRCICA is close to completing case automation, expected to be implemented by the beginning of 2027, and uses AI internally for research, reporting and case statistics.

Mr. Stephen warned that AI raises serious concerns about sensitive information, data breaches and unauthorised access, and said institutions must ensure providers keep infrastructure secure. He cited DIAC's ability to move data to Europe because of recent regional conflicts. Ms. Hussein said CRCICA is still training staff and assessing appropriate use before applying AI to arbitrator appointments, conflict checks and award scrutiny. The panel's discussion is aimed at arbitration users and institutions in the region and beyond, as they face the same questions about confidentiality, reliability and fairness. Dr. Arab noted that the use of AI would continue to generate disputes and legal questions.

Dr. Arab referred to a construction award issued through an AI arbitrator by the American Arbitration Association (AAA), reported by the Global Arbitration Review, and raised doubts about whether such an award would be correct and satisfy the parties. Vagenheim said the AAA has expanded its AI Arbitrator initiative beyond construction to other industry cases involving documentary records. Dr. Arab also cited concerns over undisclosed AI use before the Qatar Financial Centre Court and the Abu Dhabi Global Market. He further mentioned a Dubai Court of Cassation decision upholding a university's rejection of a student's thesis after it was found to contain AI-generated material and fake sources.

The panel's discussion continues through the rest of the week, which ends on 13 November 2026. The articles do not report what conclusions the panel reached on common guidelines or institutional standards. Whether CRCICA's appointment and award-scrutiny applications will proceed, and when, remains open. The articles also do not say whether the AAA's AI Arbitrator initiative will expand beyond its announced scope.

Articles.Title: AI in Arbitration: Institutional leaders at Dubai Arbitration Week 2026 discuss how arbitral - SCC Online

stories.Headline: What the OpenAI Incident Reveals About the U.S. 'Frontier' Model and China’s Open-Weight Alternative - Monthly Review
stories.Summary:
On October 6, 2026, Sifted reported that the United Kingdom was examining whether training frontier artificial intelligence models could be illegal under existing laws. The article said the question arose because frontier AI development may involve risks that current UK rules do not clearly address. It explained that the legal uncertainty could affect companies working on the most advanced systems. The report did not name a specific incident but framed the issue as a general regulatory problem. It suggested that developers might face legal exposure without clearer guidance.

The October 15, 2026 press release from Alice said that Alice, Inflection AI, and AI21 had collaborated to show that NVIDIA Nemotron open models could be trained for frontier safety. The work used Alice’s safety data to post-train the models for company-specific safety and security policies. The release said the collaborations demonstrated that powerful open models could be aligned to safety requirements without losing capability. It named NVIDIA Nemotron as the model family involved and Alice as the provider of the safety data. The announcement was made from New York and dated October 15, 2026.

Alice said the results showed a path to responsibly deploying customizable AI. Inflection AI and AI21 were described as the partners that post-trained the NVIDIA Nemotron open models. The release stated that the collaborations focused on aligning the models to company-specific safety and security policies. Alice presented the work as evidence that open models can meet frontier safety challenges. No direct quotes from individual executives were included in the press release.

The Sifted article indicated that the UK legal question could lead to new regulatory clarity or enforcement action in the future. The Alice release did not describe any next steps beyond the demonstrated collaborations. Together, the articles suggest that open-weight models are being positioned as an alternative to closed frontier systems. The press release framed the Alice work as a practical demonstration rather than a regulatory response. Neither article stated what specific legal or policy changes would follow.

Articles.Title: What the OpenAI Incident Reveals About the U.S. 'Frontier' Model and China’s Open-Weight Alternative - Monthly Review

stories.Headline: How AI tools are quietly reshaping working conditions in hospitals - Association of Health Care Journalists
stories.Summary:
Health care organizations are deploying artificial intelligence tools in a largely unregulated environment, and panelists at the Association of Health Care Journalists' 2026 Fall Summit in Los Angeles warned that the tools could harm clinicians and other workers. The discussion, reported by Farah Yousry and published on November 12, 2026, featured Sukhbir Singh, D.O., a hospitalist and board member of the Union of American Physicians and Dentists, and Mishal Khan, Ph.D., a senior researcher with the Technology and Work Program at the UC Berkeley Labor Center, with Barbara Feder Ostrov, editorial director of Medscape, moderating. Tech companies and health system executives have promised that generative AI, which summarizes clinic visits and writes chart notes, will ease burnout and administrative load. Singh said that promise has not matched daily reality for physicians.

Singh said clinicians must review, correct and sign AI-generated chart notes, which keeps full legal liability with the physician and adds a layer of mental work. He said administrators treat the resulting time savings as efficiency gains, using them to assign larger patient panels and reduce support staff. He also described how electronic medical records track metrics such as patient length of stay, discharge times and physician chart usage, which he called a "productivity ratchet" that keeps raising the bar for doctors. Khan said nurses and other staff face risks from AI tools and algorithms that are often untested and unregulated, and that employers increasingly use data-driven systems that affect wages, working conditions, gender equity and collective bargaining. She cited digital staffing platforms that have nurses bidding for shifts through algorithms that adjust pay based on worker data, and she said some automated sepsis systems can strip nurses of decision-making authority, leading to de-skilling and alert fatigue.

The panelists also described a gap in federal oversight that has prompted action at other levels. Some nursing groups are drafting their own workplace AI "bill of rights," and California has passed a law barring employers from making employment decisions without human oversight, with a forthcoming ban on workplace monitoring in restrooms and on neural data collection. Pending Illinois nursing legislation would bar AI from automating core clinical duties such as triage, care planning and discharge, and other states are moving to make it illegal to advertise AI chatbots as licensed health care professionals. Khan argued that "human in the loop" requirements are insufficient, since clinicians under pressure can turn them into corporate rubber stamps, and she called for new labor standards for the 21st century. The article also lists reading for reporters, including research from MIT Sloan, JAMA Network Open, Annals of Emergency Medicine, the AMA and the OECD, and notes that the full panel recordings are available on the AHCJ website.

Articles.Title: How AI tools are quietly reshaping working conditions in hospitals - Association of Health Care Journalists

stories.Headline: Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures
stories.Summary:
Google has open-sourced AQuA, the Ambient Quality Agent, a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns, and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging, or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters, and tracking issues. Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics, and AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment, or on demand.

For root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment. Its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges, and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs, or retrieved data, but it does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically. AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING, or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed. Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints.

Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters. The verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation. After developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero, and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13, though these results came from controlled replay, not production traffic. The Google blog post states that an insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score, and that findings link to supporting traces.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn, Dmytro Aprelenko, engineering manager at Redcore, wrote that agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code. Its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows.

Articles.Title: Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures - infoq.com

stories.Headline: MIT Researchers Create Roadmap to Help Organizations Mitigate AI Risks
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MIT created a roadmap to help organizations mitigate risks from artificial intelligence. This project was announced on November 13, 2026, in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The team developed a free public database called the AI Risk Mitigation Repository. It catalogs 2,206 proposed safeguards drawn from 47 existing governance and risk-management frameworks. This resource helps organizations identify practical ways to manage risks and find important gaps.

The repository organizes each safeguard by the risk it addresses and the responsible actor. It also tracks when action should occur during the AI lifecycle and how it reduces risk. The project involved MIT FutureTech, the MIT Sloan School of Management, and the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Collaborators included the University of Queensland, IBM Research, Stanford University, the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, and the United Nations University. The team also created a reporting framework called PRIMER for consistent and transparent descriptions.

Neil Thompson is the director of MIT FutureTech and a principal research scientist. He stated that organizations recognize the need to address AI risks but lack practical action steps. He noted that a common way to organize safeguards is necessary to coordinate efforts and evaluate options. Peter Slattery is a research scientist at MIT FutureTech and a contributor to the study. He said the resource helps decision-makers understand existing options and where critical gaps remain.

The study found that 55 percent of mitigations focus on AI systems, while others target organizational processes. Developers are responsible for 41 percent of safeguards, and deploying organizations account for 33 percent. Governance actors, including regulators and policymakers, are responsible for another significant share of the proposed interventions. Companies can use the repository to support internal risk-management efforts for their specific AI systems. Policymakers can explore different regulatory approaches, and researchers can investigate which safeguards are actually effective.

The AI Risk Mitigation Repository is part of the MIT AI Risk Initiative led through MIT FutureTech. This initiative previously launched the AI Risk Repository, which focused on cataloging potential AI risks. The current project shifts the focus toward identifying and organizing solutions to those risks. The repository covers technical improvements, organizational policies, industry standards, audits, transparency measures, public oversight, and international coordination. It includes an interactive explorer to search safeguards by category and relate them to different risks.

The researchers found that organizational accountability and responsibility was the largest category at 13.4 percent. However, human oversight of autonomous agents and society's resilience from disruptions each accounted for less than 2 percent. Stewardship of computing resources for advanced AI systems also represented less than 2 percent of documented mitigations. These underrepresented areas are identified as important opportunities for future work as AI systems become more capable. The articles leave open which specific mitigations will prove most effective in practice over time.

Articles.Title: MIT Researchers Create Roadmap to Help Organizations Mitigate AI Risks

stories.Headline: NBIS Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on AI Cloud Growth, Asset-Light Gains
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. reported third-quarter 2026 results on November 13, 2026, with adjusted earnings of 30 cents per share against an adjusted loss of about 42 cents a year earlier, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of a 61-cent loss. Revenue rose 571% year over year to $980.8 million, above the $917 million consensus. AI Cloud revenue was $973.8 million, up 643% and about 99% of consolidated revenue, and annualized run-rate revenue reached $6.4 billion, up 1,062%. The quarter included roughly $325 million in nonrecurring revenue from the first phase of an asset-light model in which partners fund computing capacity while Nebius provides its architecture and cloud platform.

Remaining performance obligations were $38.7 billion at the end of September, up 3% sequentially, and customers committed more than $12 billion in total contract value since the start of the third quarter. Annual contract value per megawatt exceeded $25 million, compared with $20 million to $25 million in the prior quarter, and average GPU-hour pricing rose more than 20% sequentially. More than 90% of contract value signed in the quarter included customer prepayments, which covered more than 100% of associated capital expenditures, compared with 50% to 60% in the second quarter, and the average payback period shortened to one year and seven months from one year and 10 months. Nebius also signed multiyear agreements with Databricks, Datadog and Snowflake, and its Token Factory platform neared a multi-hundred-million-dollar annual revenue run rate, with contract value up 17 times sequentially.

Adjusted EBITDA was $465.8 million against a loss of $5.2 million a year earlier, and the margin improved to 47.5% from 40.6% in the second quarter, with the AI Cloud business at 53.2%. Total operating costs and expenses rose 237% to $930.4 million, and capital expenditures were about $7.3 billion. Nebius ended September with $7.43 billion in cash and equivalents, a net loss from continuing operations of $37.5 million, and net cash used in operating activities of $273 million. During the quarter it completed a $5.75 billion convertible senior notes offering, secured a $775 million asset-backed financing facility and raised about $1 billion in net proceeds through an at-the-market equity offering.

Nebius now expects 2026 revenue of $3 billion to $3.2 billion, down from $3 billion to $3.4 billion, citing delays in bringing third-party data center capacity online, particularly in New Jersey. It kept its full-year adjusted EBITDA margin expectation at about 40% but raised projected capital expenditures to around $27 billion from $20 billion to $25 billion. For 2027, management expects revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, capital expenditures of $40 billion to $45 billion with 75% to 85% financed through customer prepayments and asset-backed financing, customer prepayments of $17 billion to $20 billion, and pretax breakeven in the fourth quarter of 2027. NBIS carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

Articles.Title: NBIS Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on AI Cloud Growth, Asset-Light Gains - TradingView

stories.Headline: 'Big Short' investor Michael Burry is vindicated as AI stocks like Nebius tumble — and he's warning of a coming chip glut
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry bet against the artificial intelligence boom during a volatile market week. His short positions paid off as AI stocks tumbled on November 13, 2026. Nebius shares dropped significantly on the Nasdaq on Thursday. Nvidia also lost about a third of its value since early October. CEO Jensen Huang faced allegations of extramarital affairs and spying for China.

Nebius shares fell 17.5 percent to under 128 dollars from Wednesday's 155 dollar close. The stock peaked at nearly 287 dollars in June. Revenue for the year will hit the low end of 3 billion to 3.4 billion dollars. Computing capacity expected this year is now scheduled for the first half of 2027. Prepayments and financing will cover 75 to 85 percent of next year's capital expenditures.

Michael Burry said the Nasdaq was historically overvalued and top heavy in September. He wrote in August that Nebius represented what the top of a boom looks like. Burry believes the semiconductor industry will return to its traditional boom to bust cyclicality. He predicts a chip glut will occur over the next two years. He claims memory will have a down cycle as production catches up.

Jeremy Grantham called current AI valuations an obvious bubble that will eventually burst. Jeffrey Gundlach warned of fallout and losers leading to a significant drawdown in risk assets. Sujai Shivakumar said Chinese overcapacity in the chip sector is a major risk for Micron. Alphabet suffered a disastrous quarter, and the Nasdaq plunged 5.5 percent in early November. Micron Technology and AMD both suffered double digit routs.

Burry cited Acer CEO Jason Chen, who said there is absolutely no memory shortage. Chen noted that production capacity in China has been consistently increasing. Nebius reported quarterly revenue of 980.8 million dollars, which beat expectations. The company reported losses of 0.13 dollars per share. Burry previously disclosed short positions at the 212 and 247 dollar levels.

Gundlach recommends high quality bonds, gold, emerging market debt, and a commercial real estate ETF. He also suggests an equal weighted ETF tracking Fortune 500 companies to avoid AI overconcentration. Shivakumar warns that Chinese production may lead to future surplus, dumping, and trade friction. The articles do not state when the next significant drawdown will occur. They leave open whether the AI bubble has fully burst.

Articles.Title: 'Big Short' investor Michael Burry is vindicated as AI stocks like Nebius tumble — and he's warning of a coming chip glut - MoneyWise.com

stories.Headline: The great Generative AI unraveling
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the US stock market fell sharply, with about $1 trillion wiped out in 40 minutes, according to a post by The Macro Paper cited by Gary Marcus. Marcus wrote that Nvidia was down 29% over six months, Oracle 35%, CoreWeave 54%, and Anthropic's perceived valuation 25% in weeks. He said Anthropic had hoped for a $2 trillion valuation at IPO and would now count itself lucky to get $1.5 trillion. He also said a neocloud company called N-Scale was in serious trouble after overcommitting, and that the news broke during his appearance on CNBC's Fast Money with host Melissa Lee.

Marcus said generative AI companies followed the same path with similar techniques and datasets, so OpenAI could not keep its lead, nobody had much of a technical moat, and price wars would make profits hard. He said training is very expensive and getting more so, citing a reported $10 billion cost to develop the Claude 5.5 model family, and that inference is expensive too. He said studies show a lack of return on investment and that the systems remain poor at following instructions. He also pointed to the Klarna effect, in which companies rehire humans after making extravagant claims about AI.

Marcus said Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, may be less inclined than Jensen to make big bets, and might refuse to prop up Nscale. He said that if Nvidia stops acting like everybody's banker, a bunch of neocloud companies are in trouble and Anthropic's IPO could be jeopardized. He cited a Bloomberg post by Jesse Felder saying banks are dumping AI loans, tech bond buyers are saying no more, and hedge funds are selling. Marcus said OpenAI, Anthropic, Nscale and CoreWeave have never been demonstrably profitable, apart from one quarter when Anthropic received heavy subsidies from Musk, and that they may now have to stand on their own.

Marcus said he had warned since August 2023 that generative AI might be a financial dud, and that hypey valuations lasted longer than he expected. He said the change in regime at Nvidia may have massive repercussions because so much rested on Jensen making big bets on companies Nvidia was effectively subsidizing. He said his sense, which could be wrong, is that the market has finally picked up on the irrationality of generative AI's economics. He said we may soon see a lot more moments like the N-Scale one.

Articles.Title: The great Generative AI unraveling

stories.Headline: IRS eyes agentic AI tool to help staffers process potential fraud cases
stories.Summary:
The IRS is piloting an agentic AI tool to help staff process potential fraud cases, as announced on Friday, November 13, 2026. Jim Clifford, the director of return integrity and compliance services in the Taxpayer Service Division, shared these plans during a panel at the ACT-IAC Service Delivery and Experience Summit. The agency already uses machine-learning models to flag anomalies in tax returns. This new tool will focus on the back end of the process to make employees more efficient.

The technology will handle clerical and rote tasks, such as organizing taxpayer correspondence and reading submitted documents. Specifically, the AI will review responses, summarize information, and build a case before handing it to a human. This change aims to reduce the constraints on how fast workers can operate, though humans will still make all final judgments. While there is no official deployment timeline, the pilot will eventually scale to other IRS areas if it is successful.

Jim Clifford stated that the agency is already very accurate at stopping identity theft refund fraud, but the overall cost of fraud remains too high. He noted that fraudsters make about 1 billion attempts every month to steal taxpayer information. According to the Government Accountability Office, the federal government loses between $116 billion and $304 billion annually to tax fraud. Clifford believes the agency is generally good at protecting data, despite a few instances of inappropriate releases.

The IRS is also looking for more interoperability and data-sharing with state, local, and other federal governments. Clifford mentioned that current legislative and regulatory constraints limit this sharing, but APIs and AI could allow for safe information exchange. He believes these breakthroughs would better protect and serve American taxpayers. The agency will continue testing the agentic AI tool as part of a separate workstream.

Articles.Title: IRS eyes agentic AI tool to help staffers process potential fraud cases

stories.Headline: Luxembourg and NTT explore photonic networks, sovereign AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Luxembourg and NTT are exploring cooperation on photonic networks, AI and quantum technologies, according to Telecompaper. The talks include a proposed project to connect two data centres in Luxembourg using optical networking technology. The NanoAI initiative, led by NTT Data Luxembourg, would link the two facilities over a connection of roughly 70 kilometres. It would use the All-Photonics Network technology of the Innovative Optical and Wireless Network Global Forum, known as IOWN.

The project aims to investigate whether computing resources in geographically separate locations can work together as one system. The report was published on 13 November 2026. The article does not give the names of the two data centres or a start date for the project. It also does not say how much the work would cost or how long it would run.

Responsibility for the initiative sits with NTT Data Luxembourg, which is leading NanoAI. The articles do not include direct statements from Luxembourg officials or from NTT about the plan. No named person is quoted on the record in the text provided. The cooperation is described as being explored, not agreed.

The context is a wider interest in sovereign AI infrastructure and in optical networking as a way to share computing power. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the exploration of cooperation. No timeline is given for a decision on the proposed project. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Luxembourg and NTT explore photonic networks, sovereign AI infrastructure - Telecompaper

stories.Headline: NiCE's next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them
stories.Summary:
NiCE Ltd. launched the next generation of NiCE Cognigy this week, SiliconANGLE reported on November 13, 2026. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio and an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents. It adds reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support. Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price. Premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic are available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, opened an analyst briefing with a chart showing AI worked on its own for seconds in 2020, minutes in 2024 and roughly 16 hours this year. The footnote calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. Clement Boutier, director of product management, said the large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down. The new studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while full access to the agent’s system prompt sits in advanced sections. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies.

Ho said capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing, and that is exactly where the platform matters. Boutier said hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” while fully agentic deployments are at the beginning of the adoption curve. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged. Boutier said you can have the best builder experience, but without a feedback loop on what you are building you will never build a great agent. Boutier said responsibility is shared: “We offer the tools and the platform, but we cannot 100% control what they put in it.”

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. Boutier noted buyers are open to a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” Cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet.

Cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. NiCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Boutier said each guardrail adds tokens and latency, and “the more you add, the more bloated your agent becomes.” Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting, and wrote the article for SiliconANGLE.

The challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. Regional rules on AI disclosure and human escalation must be built in by the customer. Companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents. The article leaves open which personal agents enterprises will accept and what they can do.

Articles.Title: NiCE's next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

stories.Headline: NTT develops AI credit assessment tech to improve default risk prediction
stories.Summary:
NTT and NTT TC Leasing have developed an AI credit assessment technology, Telecompaper reported on 13 November 2026. The companies say it improves the accuracy of loan default predictions by up to 30 percent compared with existing AI models. The technology was built to address challenges in financial data, including variations in numerical distributions and outliers. It also handles differences in contractual conditions such as repayment terms and loan durations.

The reported gain is a rise of up to 30 percent in the accuracy of default predictions over existing AI models. The article gives no other figures, dates or names beyond NTT, NTT TC Leasing and the 13 November 2026 report date. The technology targets financial data problems, namely variations in numerical distributions, outliers and differing contractual conditions. Those conditions include repayment terms and loan durations.

NTT and NTT TC Leasing are named as the developers of the technology. The article does not say who at either company led the work or who will use the system. It also carries no direct statements from the companies about the project. The only claim attributed to them is the improvement in default prediction accuracy.

The article does not describe the context behind the development or any plans for deployment. It does not say when the technology might be used or by which lenders. No next steps, trials or timelines are given. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NTT develops AI credit assessment tech to improve default risk prediction - Telecompaper

stories.Headline: EU plan for cloud and AI falls short on digital autonomy
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Institute for Information Law at the University of Amsterdam say the EU's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act falls short of its goal of strengthening Europe's cloud and AI sectors. The proposal is intended to reduce Europe's dependence on providers from outside Europe. The European Commission proposed the act, known as CADA. The researchers also are concerned about the rapid expansion of data centers and the limited attention paid to sustainability and social impact. The analysis was published on November 13, 2026.

The European cloud market is highly dependent on three U.S. tech giants, which together control more than 70% of the market. The EU spends €264 billion a year on predominantly U.S. IT products and services. The proposal aims to make investment in large-scale data center expansion more attractive, including by reducing administrative red tape and simplifying permit requirements. It also introduces rules for public-sector procurement of cloud services. The proposal introduces four Union assurance levels, with increasingly strict requirements for cloud services.

Kristina Irion, one of the researchers, says the proposal could undermine Dutch ambitions to achieve greater digital sovereignty and reduce dependence on Big Tech, at a time when the Netherlands is taking steps in that direction. The researchers argue that the proposal would limit public authorities' ability to set additional requirements for many services and thereby reduce their dependence on a handful of third-country providers. Irion says that as currently drafted, the EU proposal could even prevent public-sector organizations from consciously choosing a European alternative. Co-author Plixavra Vogiatzoglou says that under the proposal, providers and developers from outside the EU would retain a strong foothold. Irion says greater digital autonomy also requires clear sustainability rules, democratic participation, stronger public procurement requirements and more support for European and open alternatives.

The researchers assessed the proposal across five areas: cloud and AI leadership, expanding data center capacity, digital sovereignty and public procurement, Union assurance levels, and open source and cloud federations. They say the proposal focuses too heavily on growth and AI's potential benefits, and that the effects on fundamental rights, employment, local communities and the environment receive too little attention. They also call for stronger safeguards for transparency, participation and local involvement. The researchers say sustainability and social impacts are not adequately safeguarded, and they question whether the proposal explains convincingly why data centers should take priority over other demands for energy, water, land and electricity grid capacity. Many public services would be assigned the lowest Union assurance level, which the researchers say limits public authorities' ability to set additional procurement requirements for many services.

The researchers say the criteria do not automatically exclude large U.S. providers, which may be able to meet many of the requirements at the two lower levels. The European Commission estimates that only 10% of use cases would require the highest levels, from which third-country providers are excluded. The researchers say that support for open source is limited and largely optional. They also question how organizations can share cloud services when they rent the infrastructure from a provider rather than owning it themselves. The proposal aims to speed up data center construction, including by creating special zones where permits can be issued more quickly.

Articles.Title: EU plan for cloud and AI falls short on digital autonomy

stories.Headline: 25 November: Your Chance to Understand the Biggest Question in AI – Who Is Accountable?
stories.Summary:
ET TechGig is hosting a free live online masterclass on 25 November 2026 that asks who is accountable when an AI system makes a wrong decision. The session, titled "Who Is Accountable When AI Makes the Decision?", runs for 60 minutes, from 11:30 AM to 12:30 PM. The announcement was published on 12 November 2026. It frames the question as one of the biggest challenges facing the technology industry as AI takes on more autonomous roles.

The article describes AI as increasingly influencing decisions in recruitment, healthcare, finance, business operations and technology. It gives the example of an AI recruitment system rejecting a qualified candidate because of biased training data. The piece says organisations need clear accountability structures, ways to review automated decisions and processes that let people challenge outcomes. Participants will be shown a practical five-question Accountability Test that examines a hypothetical AI-assisted hiring decision. The session is free and offers a Certificate of Participation, and no specialised technical or legal background is required.

The masterclass will be led by Dr. Smrite Goudhaman, who is named as Pre-Sales Solutions leader at Datamatics and Global Professor of Practice at Golden Gate University. The article says the session will examine who is responsible among developers, deployers, managers and affected communities, and whether accountability should rest with individuals or with the institutions that deploy AI. It lists global frameworks the session will cover, including UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, the OECD AI Principles, the European Union's AI Act and India's IndiaAI initiatives. The article is aimed at AI developers, engineering managers, product leaders, data professionals, governance specialists, HR leaders and CXOs. Registration is available through a link on the TechGig website.

Articles.Title: 25 November: Your Chance to Understand the Biggest Question in AI – Who Is Accountable?

stories.Headline: Gondola doubles revenue as its team builds more with Codex
stories.Summary:
Gondola, a startup founded by Jared Kleinstein, has more than doubled its revenue year over year, according to an OpenAI customer story published November 12, 2026. The company's small team uses Codex to build more software and ChatGPT to simplify daily operations. Gondola's monthly engineering output is up 25% across the team and up 50% for its lead engineer. The company is a North American media, entertainment and sports startup with an SMB-sized team. Kleinstein said that using OpenAI has increased the ambition of what a company of Gondola's size can build.

Business teams now prototype features with Codex Cloud before engineers step in, rather than writing requirements and waiting for engineering capacity. Jared Kleinstein and Creator and Client Partnerships Manager Jojo Hesketh have each merged their first code contributions into the main codebase. Gondola built Programs, a tool that helps companies find creatives, review applicants, manage projects and track budgets, with plans to coordinate contracts and payments. The team started Programs with GPT-5.4, did most of the work with GPT-5.5, and used GPT-6.1 for later features, optimizations and bug fixes. Engineers use Codex through the command-line interface, editor tools and GitHub pull request reviews, while remaining responsible for architecture, security, data handling and production readiness.

Kleinstein says Codex saved days, if not weeks, of development time on Programs and helped the team launch it with fewer bugs. Gondola used Codex this summer to build and test a World Cup Creator Map that let brands, teams and agencies find photographers and videographers in World Cup host cities. Hesketh sponsored the Creator Map and built a working prototype with Codex, and engineers polished it for launch shortly afterward. Kleinstein described the build as incredibly quick because of its small, self-contained scope and hard deadline, and he believes both projects launched with fewer bugs and more polish. The article does not name any party other than Gondola and its staff as responsible for these results.

Gondola also uses ChatGPT to prepare proposals, manage schedules, find information across company systems and automate tasks. The company built a daily report template that employees use each morning, integrating Google Workspace, Asana, Slack, QuickBooks and weather information. Kleinstein said preparing such a report manually would take hours and hours of work. A person still reviews consequential work before it is sent externally or used for a business decision. Since adopting Codex in early 2026, the lead engineer's merged changes per month have risen about 50%, while team-wide output rose about 25% without any change in engineering headcount.

The company also reports that brands hired 2.5 times as many creators year over year. Kleinstein has said Gondola was built to help creatives show what they made, prove its impact and turn their work into their next opportunity. He said that OpenAI gives product people more ability to build, engineers more time for difficult engineering, and the business team more time with customers, partners and creatives. The article notes that Kleinstein founded Gondola after running his creative production agency, Fresh Tape Media, and noticing that social media creative work went uncredited. Gondola reports no added payroll costs or significant overhead alongside its revenue growth.

The company is also shipping larger changes while pull request review time has held steady. Looking ahead, Gondola wants AI to complete more of the work connecting companies and creatives, including reducing coordination in finding talent, managing budgets and approvals, handling contracts and getting people paid. The company aims to keep expanding what its small team can deliver. The article does not say when the contract and payment features will launch or how much additional capacity they will add. It also does not report Gondola's actual revenue figures or the size of its team beyond describing it as small.

Articles.Title: Gondola doubles revenue as its team builds more with Codex

stories.Headline: Holiday Extras is rethinking what it can build with Codex
stories.Summary:
Holiday Extras, a travel company that helps customers search, book and manage trips, has been rethinking how it builds software with OpenAI's Codex. The company, which is mid-market and based in Europe and the UK, reported the results in an OpenAI customer story published on 12 November 2026. Working with Codex, the team rebuilt its main mobile app in two weeks, a job that would previously have taken more than six months. The article credits the change to a company-wide rollout that began with ChatGPT Enterprise and extended to Codex for building software.

The reported results are a 32.5% increase in open-to-book conversion on the rebuilt app and a fall in its error rate from 19% to 9%. The main app also moved from an annual major release to weekly releases in the first month after the rebuild, with each release containing multiple new features. The article says the rebuilt app offers a more personal experience based on customers' bookings, trips and history, and that iOS and Android features can now be developed together. Small, documented packages were used to create reusable foundations, while engineers focused on architecture, security and development workflows. Operations have changed too, with an automated system turning airport-transfer customer chats into tickets the team can act on.

CEO Matthew Pack said the shift is about giving people who understand customers and operations the ability to improve them directly, and he said that goes beyond a single team. Liam Thompson, VP of AI Innovation and formerly Head of Design, worked with engineers to turn his knowledge of customers into software, and he said the question is now how he would build something rather than whether he can. David Lee, Director of Innovation and Growth, described an experienced accountant who rebuilt finance systems around his knowledge of the business. Pack said the company wants more of its systems administered through AI, with employees directing the work, and he asked leaders to reconsider the scale of their ambitions.

Articles.Title: Holiday Extras is rethinking what it can build with Codex

stories.Headline: Supporting research on AI and children’s safety
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, OpenAI announced that it had signed the Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children at the Paris Peace Forum earlier that week. The company also committed $2 million to support a scientific research network under the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI. The announcement said the contribution would fund shared measurement work, meaning tools that researchers can use to better understand and measure AI's risks and opportunities for children. OpenAI framed the move as a follow-on to its earlier call for global standards on youth AI safety.

The charter sets out shared principles for safe, age-appropriate AI, along with a research programme and safeguards for its independence. Research teams keep control over their own conclusions, and findings will be published, including negative or inconclusive results. OpenAI said the work is meant to build the evidence needed to support the benefits of AI for young people while addressing risks to their safety and development. The company also reiterated its support for comprehensive youth AI safety legislation that keeps access to tools for learning, creativity and opportunity. It listed age-appropriate safeguards by default, tools for parents, regular risk assessments and mitigation, and meaningful accountability as elements such legislation should include.

The announcement came from OpenAI, which described the research funding and its policy positions in its own words. The company said it looks forward to engaging with European policymakers as the EU Kids Act develops, and with partners around the world to advance stronger protections for young people. The articles provide no independent response from the coalition, researchers, regulators or other signatories. They also do not say when the research network's first findings are expected or how the $2 million will be divided among teams.

Articles.Title: Supporting research on AI and children’s safety

stories.Headline: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
stories.Summary:
LLMON, an LLM-native markup language, was announced on November 12, 2026, by IBM Granite researchers, including Abraham Daniels, Basel Shbita, Chad DeLuca, Dan Gutfreund, Michael Hind and Shub A, on Hugging Face. The team released two experimental preview models derived from Granite 4.1 base models, named granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. They also released a GitHub repository containing a toolkit, examples of workflows and templates for working with LLMON. The announcement describes the models as trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text. The article was published at 06:00 UTC that day on huggingface.co.

LLMON uses reserved special-token delimiters to wrap semantically coherent components, each marked with a meaningful tag. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a form the authors say a causal LLM can read unambiguously. Unique IDs let each instruction point to specific data, wherever that data sits in the context. Existing JSON can be converted to LLMON and back without loss using the released converters. Users can also define their own tags and tune a LoRA adapter on top of the LLMON models to understand them.

The preview models ship with their own chat template, so messages are passed through apply_chat_template as usual. The authors state that they built LLMON because LLMs, especially smaller ones, are brittle, and that unstructured context can be exploited through prompt injections. They say JSON was designed for parsers rather than causal language models, since the same tokens can mark both structure and ordinary text. LLMON is described as an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are single reserved tokens, separate from content. The authors say LLMON enriches existing chat templates rather than replacing them, telling the model what each component means as well as its role.

The models were trained from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints, with decoy blocks added during training and reinforcement learning stages followed by a final DPO stage. On the OPI benchmark, the authors report that LLMON reduces attack success, with robustness defined as one minus attack success rate. They say LLMON avoids 47% more attacks than the best frontier model tested and 95% more than the best open-source model tested. The article reports similar trends on the ASB and StruQ benchmarks, which test static indirect prompt injections. The authors state that LLMON performs on par with Granite 4.1 Instruct models across standard benchmark categories.

They describe the security gains as coming from explicit separation of instructions from data, and say the instruction-following behavior is learned rather than guaranteed. The authors describe the approach as a way for developers to stop forcing LLMs to observe JSON structure and to reduce the effect of hidden instructions in retrieved documents, tool outputs and user data. Mellea, a framework that automatically converts its LLM calls to LLMON, is named as a place to try it. The authors also describe a ScienceWorld experiment, where a custom vocabulary of tags was used to structure planning trajectories for an agent completing elementary science tasks. The article points readers to an LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces to examine attention patterns in LLMON models.

The authors say they are actively working on improving robustness to adaptive attacks that unfold over many chat turns, which the current benchmarks do not test. The article describes the models as experimental previews and does not give a release date for a non-preview version. It does not report results for ScienceWorld beyond describing the setup, and it does not specify how the LLMON models perform on tasks beyond the benchmarks named. It also leaves open how the approach holds up against attacks outside the static prompt injection benchmarks cited.

Articles.Title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

stories.Headline: AI Training Data Firm Mercor's Valuation Doubles to ¥3.2 Trillion; Nvidia Also Invests
stories.Summary:
Mercor, a company that supplies human-generated data for training and evaluating AI models, has raised $750 million in a Series D round, according to its announcement on November 12, 2026. The round valued the company at $20 billion, roughly ¥3.2 trillion, about double the $10 billion valuation it received at its Series C round in October 2025. The round also included a tender offer that let employees sell some of their shares. Investors named in the article include Benchmark, Felicis, General Catalyst, Nvidia, Salesforce, Zoom, a fund affiliated with Apollo, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group and XTX Ventures.

Mercor's business connects professionals such as doctors, lawyers and programmers with AI developers, who pay them to evaluate AI responses and design training tasks. The company says its network includes more than 5 million registered experts across more than 800 occupations in the United States alone. Its revenue has so far come mainly from frontier labs building advanced models, but it is now shifting toward mainstream enterprises. For those customers it designs evaluation metrics tailored to their workflows, measuring how well AI agents handle internal systems, policies and quality standards. It also acquired Deeptune this year, a firm that builds environments in which AI agents can practice work tasks.

Co-founder and CEO Brendan Foody said in an official blog post that companies starting from capable open models can carry out post-training with a small fraction of the resources needed for cutting-edge development. He argued that model developers and compute providers build the foundation, while Mercor supplies companies with the data and evaluations needed to tailor those models. The article also quotes him expressing the view that the usefulness of AI depends on the human expertise behind it. The company has opened offices in New York and London in addition to San Francisco. The proceeds will fund infrastructure and research for evaluation and post-training, along with expanded environments for agents to learn complex work tasks.

The article frames the funding as a sign that the generative AI race is moving from building models to adapting them to a company's own operations. It notes that evaluation data and business-specific additional training often become barriers when companies try to move AI agents into real use. It also points out that Nvidia and Salesforce, both positioned to benefit from wider AI adoption, are among the investors, suggesting compute and business-software providers are now putting money into data infrastructure. The article cautions, however, that Mercor has not disclosed customer names, revenue, or how much of the $750 million came from new capital versus the tender offer. It adds that private valuations reflect fundraising conditions and that views on the company's actual earnings are likely to remain divided, with its enterprise growth the key thing to watch.

Articles.Title: AI Training Data Firm Mercor's Valuation Doubles to ¥3.2 Trillion; Nvidia Also Invests - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Don't like AI in games? Crimson Desert studio Pearl Abyss ain't care: it's expanding AI use 'throughout our entire development pipeline'
stories.Summary:
Pearl Abyss said in its Q3 2026 earnings letter that it will expand its use of AI throughout its entire development pipeline, PC Gamer reported on 13 November 2026. The Crimson Desert studio made the statement midway through the letter, which Eurogamer covered. The studio had apologized earlier this year for the presence of AI-generated art in Crimson Desert. It apologized not because it had used generative AI, but because players saw it. The letter said the studio now uses AI to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation.

The letter said Pearl Abyss previously validated game systems only after implementing them manually. It said the new approach enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed. The studio said AI is being utilized across various stages of development, including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization. It said it is expanding AI implementation throughout its entire development pipeline. The studio said it views AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality.

Pearl Abyss said AI serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity. It said gameplay and content development remain fully driven by its development team. The studio said it is integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality. It said it will continue to expand its application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously. In February, the studio acknowledged that some 2D visual props had been created by AI during the early stages of development.

The studio said those props were supposed to be replaced following final work and review by its art and development teams, with work that aligned with its quality standards and creative direction. It also admitted that it had not clearly disclosed its use of AI in the development process. The studio promised to be more transparent about it in the future. PC Gamer said the letter could be seen as a step in that direction. The article did not name any other parties affected by the change.

The February statement followed players discovering the presence of generative AI art in Crimson Desert. The studio said the AI-made 2D visual props dated to the early stages of development. It said the props were meant to be replaced after review by its art and development teams. The studio said the replacements would align with its quality standards and creative direction. It also said it had not clearly disclosed its use of AI during development.

Pearl Abyss said it will continue to expand its application of AI. The letter did not give a date for the expanded pipeline use or name specific tools. The articles did not say how players responded to the Q3 2026 letter. The articles did not give sales figures or a release date for Crimson Desert. The articles did not say whether the studio set any limits on which tasks AI may handle.

Articles.Title: Don't like AI in games? Crimson Desert studio Pearl Abyss ain't care: it's expanding AI use 'throughout our entire development pipeline'

stories.Headline: UNESCO joins EU-funded CULTURAI project to advance responsible AI in the cultural and creative sectors
stories.Summary:
UNESCO has joined CULTURAI, a new four-year international research and innovation project that the European Union's Horizon Europe programme has funded with nearly €5 million for a consortium of eleven partners. The project explores how artificial intelligence can be used responsibly in the audiovisual sector and public cultural institutions while protecting human creativity, cultural diversity and artistic freedom. Its central question is how cultural diversity and creative autonomy can be protected in the age of generative AI. The work gives particular attention to ethics, governance, labour market impact, inclusivity and AI literacy, addressing four gaps that limit the cultural sector's ability to benefit from AI.

UNESCO's role centres on closing the lack of value-driven governance frameworks that protect diversity, pluralism and freedom of expression. As a consortium partner, it leads a comparative review of AI governance frameworks specific to the cultural sector in seven jurisdictions: the European Union, Australia, Brazil, the Republic of Korea, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States. UNESCO will also design a survey of some 800 audiovisual professionals working in film, television, radio, video and on-demand services to examine how AI affects their creative autonomy and working conditions. The survey results will feed into policy recommendations on AI for the European cultural and creative industries. UNESCO says its work builds on its existing standards, including its 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and its 2005 Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions.

Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO's Assistant Director-General for Culture, said that responsible AI governance depends on moving from principles to practical implementation, and that culture is no exception. He said UNESCO would help build the knowledge, tools and partnerships needed to turn ethical AI commitments into action for the cultural sector. The project is coordinated by KB National Library and includes universities, research institutes and cultural organisations from Belgium, Croatia, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, South Africa and the United Kingdom. Within the consortium, UNESCO connects the project's findings to intergovernmental policy processes on AI and culture. The article notes that the views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or its executive agency.

Articles.Title: UNESCO joins EU-funded CULTURAI project to advance responsible AI in the cultural and creative sectors - UNESCO

stories.Headline: UNESCO, Bayelsa govt begin digital education, AI training for teachers
stories.Summary:
UNESCO, in partnership with the Bayelsa State Ministry of Education, has begun a three-day master trainers programme on digital pedagogy and artificial intelligence for ICT lecturers in the state. The training, reported on November 10 and 12, 2026, was opened in Yenagoa and is part of the Expand, Integrate and Strengthen Systems project. The project is funded by the European Union and implemented by UNESCO, with technical support from the Federal Ministry of Education and the Universal Basic Education Commission. The training targets 40 master trainers who will prepare 1,445 teachers to use digital technologies and AI-supported approaches in classrooms. Esther Ikenye, UNESCO Programme Assistant, spoke at the event in Yenagoa on Tuesday.

From November 16 to 21, the 40 master trainers are to train the 1,445 nominated teachers at centres in Yenagoa, Kolokuma/Opokuma and Sagbama Local Government Areas. The teachers will then continue learning through self-paced online modules after the physical sessions. The programme will equip them to use digital tools and AI in lesson planning, learner engagement, assessment and classroom management. Trainees who finish the programme can register on the online learning portal, access free modules and obtain certificates. By the end of the three days, the master trainers are expected to navigate the platform, complete quick checks and earn a certificate.

Ikenye said the project works on three fronts, supporting policies on teacher shortages and working conditions, strengthening skills of in-service and pre-service teachers, and building connections between teachers, colleagues and learners. She described Bayelsa as one of six project focal states and said the training is a clear example of the second front in action. Commissioner for Education Gentle Emelah, represented by Monday Ake, said the training aims to improve teachers' knowledge and capacity in AI and digital teaching methods. Adam Sadiq of the UBEC Innovation and Instructional Technology Department in Abuja said many children are digital natives, so teachers need these competencies.

The EISS project is designed to strengthen Nigeria's education system through better governance, teaching and learning, and it rests on the principle that teachers are the most important in-school factor in learning. Ikenye said digital tools and artificial intelligence are already part of contemporary teaching and that the project intends to support their use for the overall benefit of society. Representatives of the European Union, the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria, the Nigeria Union of Teachers and the SUBEB Teachers' Professional Development Directorate attended the opening. Ikenye told the 40 master trainers that the programme's success in Bayelsa State depends on them.

Before the training, the programme's theme was given as "Education and Youth Empowerment in Nigeria: Expand, Integrate and Strengthen Systems to Build Teachers' Capacity and Resilience." Ikenye said the programme was designed to strengthen teachers' professional competence and promote inclusive, technology-driven education. The master trainers will also support teachers through a 26-question final assessment with a 70 per cent pass mark and module ratings required for certification. They are also expected to produce a state cascade plan with targets, timelines and support arrangements. The articles do not say how many teachers will complete certification or what the cascade plan will contain.

Articles.Title: UNESCO, Bayelsa govt begin digital education, AI training for teachers - The Sun Nigeria

stories.Headline: Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec, a streaming speech codec with about 74 million parameters, which it built to power its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. The codec turns speech into tokens that a language model can predict, then converts those tokens back into audio. According to the company, it had two goals: tokens that are easy to predict, and fast conversion back to speech. The model card lists 73.6 million parameters, 24 kHz audio, 12.5 Hz frames and 12 codebooks, and the weights are available on Hugging Face. LiquidCodec replaces Mimi, a codec from Kyutai with 96.2 million parameters that Liquid AI used in its earlier LFM2-Audio-1.5B model.

The codec runs on a single CPU thread, and Liquid AI tested it on an Apple M4 Max laptop in FP32 precision. It also works on CUDA GPUs through Transformers and comes in Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. The system uses an encoder, a quantizer and a decoder, with blocks from Liquid AI's LFM3 architecture in both halves. Instead of residual vector quantization, it uses grouped finite scalar quantization, so all 12 codebooks can be predicted in parallel. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly, which avoids a common cost in waveform decoders.

Liquid AI trained the codec in two stages, first on 264,000 hours of speech across 107 languages and then on 55,000 hours of full-band speech with adversarial critics to remove metallic artifacts. A final quantization-aware training step targets edge inference. On self-reported figures, LiquidCodec encodes about 361 times faster than real time on one CPU thread, with an encode real-time factor of 0.0028 against 0.0361 for Mimi. The company tested eight sets against X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi, and reported the best ViSQOL and lowest mel distance on all eight. On LibriSpeech, its ViSQOL score was 4.319, compared with 4.031 for Mimi.

Liquid AI also trained identical text-to-speech models on each codec's tokens and reported that LiquidCodec scored highest on UTMOSv2 across all eight sets and had the best word or character error rates on four of them. Its LibriSpeech word error rate was 3.15 percent, against 6.27 percent for Mimi. The results were said to hold with a Qwen3-1.7B backbone as well. The company's own comparison also shows weak points, since NanoCodec scored higher on PESQ (WB) in seven of eight sets and led on LibriSpeech speaker similarity. Liquid AI's benchmark figures are self-reported, and the articles give no independent verification of them.

Articles.Title: Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec

stories.Headline: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance
stories.Summary:
CopilotKit released OpenBot 1.0 on November 9, 2026, an agent workspace published under the MIT license that can be self-hosted. The company positions it as an alternative to vendor-locked AI coworker products, letting customers choose their own models, agents and infrastructure. Every action a Bot takes is checked against a policy before it runs. The release was reported by MarkTechPost on November 12, 2026.

Each Bot runs inside its own container with a dedicated Chromium browser, its own logins and files, and access only to the tools a user has granted. Every browser click, file write, tool call and component passes through a single gateway that evaluates a CEL policy and writes an audit record before acting. Deny rules take precedence over allow rules, and a malformed rule causes the action to be refused rather than permitted. The workspace supports single sign-on through Google, Microsoft Entra and Okta, along with SAML and OIDC, plus SCIM sync for users and groups. Administrators can set per-Bot tool grants, approval routing for sensitive work, spend limits, and a full audit trail with SIEM export.

CopilotKit, the team behind the AG-UI protocol, is the party responsible for the release. The article says the company designed the product so organizations keep control of their data and rules instead of ceding them to a vendor. The article also states that the platform supports eight agent frameworks listed on the company's site, including Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK and LangChain, and several more in the repository. For models, teams can use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or Grok through existing subscriptions or API keys, as well as open models such as Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen, Nemotron and Mistral.

For companies, the platform deploys through a single Helm chart onto AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google Cloud GKE or any Kubernetes cluster. Personal use is free and runs locally. The business tier, OpenBot for Business, costs up to $29 per active user per month, with a 5% charge applying only to model spend above $5,000 per month. An Annual plan adds air-gapped deployment and 24/7 support, and forward-deployed engineers help teams roll it out. Early access is listed for iOS, Android, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and the article gives examples such as support ticket triage, expense review and operations workflows.

Articles.Title: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance

stories.Headline: Unstructured Data Governance: A missing foundation for agentic AI at scale
stories.Summary:
Gustavo Espinosa, Head of Data & AI at NTT DATA International Clients USA, NTT DATA, Inc., published an article on November 10, 2026, on nttdata.com titled “Unstructured Data Governance: A missing foundation for agentic AI at scale.” The article says enterprise data governance has for years focused primarily on structured data such as tables, fields, models, lineage, quality rules, access controls and ownership. It says generative AI and now agentic AI are pushing organizations beyond databases and analytical datasets into the much larger universe of unstructured enterprise data and content. That content includes documents, presentations, emails, contracts, policies, conversations, images, audio and video, where much of the knowledge and context of the enterprise lives. The article says most of that content was never created or managed with AI consumption in mind.

The article says the principles of data governance remain but the capabilities must evolve, because organizations still need ownership, metadata, quality, lineage, security, retention and accountability. It says a customer table has fields, while a contract has clauses, dates, entities and obligations that first need to be extracted and understood. It says an AI pipeline may convert a document into text, divide it into chunks, create embeddings and place those representations into a retrieval index, requiring controls to propagate across every derived representation. It says an audio recording may need transcription and speaker identification before its meaning becomes machine-usable. The article lists expansions: cataloging evolves into repository discovery and content inventory, profiling expands into OCR, transcription, parsing and multimodal inspection, classification expands into topic, entity and sensitivity detection, lineage extends into documents, chunks, embeddings and AI responses, and quality expands into readability, structural integrity, semantic consistency, extraction accuracy and relevance.

Espinosa writes that the goal is not simply to control files but to transform fragmented enterprise content into information assets that are discoverable, understandable, trusted, protected and reusable. He says governance must balance risk reduction with value creation and efficiency, and that accessibility alone is not enough in the AI era. He notes a document may be accessible and still be outdated, correctly classified and still duplicated, searchable and still lacking business context, or technically available to an AI system but unsuitable for the use case. He says governance must therefore answer not only whether information can be accessed but whether it should be used, for what purpose, by whom or by what agent, and under what conditions. He describes a continuous operating model of visibility, understanding, control and qualification, and activation, with policies executable and continuously enforced rather than documented separately and applied manually after the fact.

The article says enterprises moving toward AI agents need more than isolated knowledge bases, and describes a persistent enterprise context layer called the Company Brain. It says the Company Brain is not simply an enterprise search engine or a collection of documents connected to an LLM, but a living representation of what the organization knows, what that knowledge means, where it came from, who owns it and under what conditions it can be used. It warns that outdated documents lead agents to reason over outdated context, conflicting versions without clear authority may lead agents to select the wrong source, and permissions not carried into AI retrieval may let an agent expose information a user could never access directly. It adds that missing semantics may cause an agent to retrieve the right words while misunderstanding their meaning, and absent provenance leaves organizations unable to explain which information influenced a response or action. It says unstructured data governance is one component of a broader enterprise context governance discipline ensuring knowledge made available to people and agents is current, understandable, traceable, protected and accountable.

The article says generative AI already made unstructured information important, and agentic AI makes its governance critical, because a chatbot retrieving an incorrect policy may produce an incorrect answer while an agent may use that same policy to initiate a workflow, modify a system or recommend an action. It says the consequence of poor context can become poor execution, and that it is not sufficient to protect the original document if an AI pipeline divides it into chunks, generates embeddings and places those representations into a retrieval index without preserving the original permissions. It says governance needs to travel with the information, and that lineage must extend from source content to extracted text, chunks, embeddings, retrieval and ultimately the AI interaction itself. It says a governed document is not necessarily a good AI input, since it may satisfy security and retention policies while being unreadable, obsolete, internally inconsistent or poorly extracted. It says NTT DATA has been working with assets and accelerators that evaluate unstructured content across semantic quality, visual and structural quality, and compliance and risk, producing a quantitative assessment and a disposition that acts as an AI-readiness gate.

The article says the scale of enterprise content means governance cannot rely primarily on manual controls, and describes a chain from policy to standard to control to evidence: a policy may say sensitive customer information must be protected, a standard defines that content as restricted, a machine-readable rule applies that classification when sensitive information is detected, a control masks the content and prevents unauthorized retrieval, and evidence records what was detected and enforced. It says the rise of agentic AI requires organizations to extend what they have learned about data governance, as enterprise knowledge increasingly spans structured data, unstructured content, semantic models and broader business and institutional context. It says the objective is no longer simply to govern datasets but the broader body of enterprise information that becomes the context machines use to understand the organization and act within it. It says organizations that succeed with agentic AI will not necessarily be those that connect the largest number of documents to an LLM, but those that can turn enterprise information into trusted, governed and machine-usable context. It says that makes unstructured data governance one of the core foundations for enabling agentic AI at scale, and it directs readers to read more about NTT DATA’s AI services to learn how to operationalize AI throughout an organization.

Articles.Title: Unstructured Data Governance: A missing foundation for agentic AI at scale - NTT Data
