stories.Headline: As Test Takers Turn to AI for Answers, Exam Security Must Catch Up
stories.Summary:
Test takers are turning to artificial intelligence to answer questions on IT certification exams, Dark Reading reported on November 11, 2026. Marielle Carlos, a data forensics scientist at Caveon, said AI has significantly changed the testing game for IT certification. Caveon added a new category to its testing security threats taxonomy called unknown. Casey Marks, chief operating officer at ISC2, said widespread irregular exam results and verified cheating attempts were found during the nonprofit's online proctoring pilots. ISC2 then required in-person testing for its exams.

ISC2 implemented what Marks called the most stringent security protocols available to analyze each result and detect irregularities, including biometric and identity verification. ISC2 is exclusively test-center based for all exams, which Marks said ensures no access to outside resources or technology during exam administration. The testing environment mirrors the most stringent conditions used by licensed professions such as doctors. Certifications range from entry-level cloud and cybersecurity knowledge and cover Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services updates. In industries like government, banking, and financial services, certified IT departments are required to stay current on compliance regulations.

Carlos said it is hard to know if an exam is measuring actual competence or someone's ability to use AI to answer the question. She said this challenges the usefulness of that exam. Marks said the candidate, the employer, and every other professional holding that credential depend on the credibility of the process. Carlos urged programs to have conversations around protecting score validity across the entire process, including secure exam design, control during administration, analysis of results, and a clear process for responding to security concerns. She said a layered approach is crucial because tools can indicate possible AI use but it is hard to pinpoint exactly.

Carlos pointed to research by Sarah Toton, director of data forensics at Caveon, who conducted an experiment comparing AI and human test taking based on test results and response patterns. Carlos said Toton has seen distinct differences in response timing, with someone using AI often six to 48 times faster compared to an individual test taker. Carlos said AI can get some things wrong, particularly questions that involve some realm of human judgment. Marks said certifications remain one of the most universal ways for employers to validate a candidate's necessary knowledge and skills when making hiring or promotion decisions. Carlos noted a huge boom of people testing fast and receiving high scores, though no concrete data exists that says it is all due to AI.

Carlos said traditional threats like harvesting pre-knowledge, plagiarism, or collusion proxy testing have evolved as people use AI as an unauthorized aid. She said the problem is still in its infancy stage. Exam administrators face a growing list of risks to monitor, from Meta Glasses to AI browsers and deepfakes. The industry is shifting toward more in-person testing and stricter fraud-detection protocols to keep certifications credible. Carlos said she and her team will look more at the trend of fast testing and high scores because of organizational interest and concern over its growth.

Marks said many certifications, like ISC2's Certified Information Systems Security Professional, have and continue to evolve to address how AI is impacting security best practices. He said new AI-specific security certifications are also entering the market. The Computing Technology Industry Association launched SecAI+ to help organizations secure, govern, and responsibly integrate AI into their cybersecurity operations. Marks said that as certifications evolve, especially with AI playing a key role in so many facets of work, the value of certifications for employers is increasing. Carlos said cheating is a risk that has existed for as long as testing has.

Articles.Title: As Test Takers Turn to AI for Answers, Exam Security Must Catch Up - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Does state-and-local AI need a rebrand?
stories.Summary:
In September, President Donald Trump signed an executive order mandating that artificial intelligence be known as “super intelligence,” arguing that AI makes the technology sound fake. The order applies only to federal agencies and departments, and some have already adopted the term. The effort has some state and local leaders wondering if they should follow the federal government’s lead. Speakers at the Public Technology Institute’s GOVIT Leadership Summit and Symposium in Minneapolis this week said deemphasizing AI as a term might be an interesting path forward. They also said government leaders should spend more time selling the technology and its benefits to the public, regardless of what it is called.

John Matelski, chief information officer at the National Association of Counties, said during a panel discussion that AI was here 50 years ago and was just called machine learning or something else. He said he has looked at it not as artificial intelligence but more as augmented intelligence. He said he has never liked the term “artificial intelligence.” PTI Senior Fellow Alan Shark suggested on stage that leaders instead be “talking about office automation” and talk about solutions while leaving out the word “AI.” Shark said the external universe sees AI as a negative term and that people have a right to be fearful.

Williamsburg, Virginia CIO Mark Barham said the government there has taken to calling data centers “co-location facilities.” He said he knows that if leaders disclose they are meeting with data center vendors, “alarm bells go off” in the community. Amy Cheney, Bloomington, Minnesota’s CIO, said her city has seen a dramatic uptick in people using AI to submit requests under the Freedom of Information Act. Cheney said requesters are using AI to create really complicated requests that staff cannot keep up with, and the city is looking at how to automate that process. Ben Bowen, vice president of U.S. sales at software company Claro Enterprise Solutions, said you can call it AI, super intelligence or whatever you like, but it is efficiency that it is going to help create.

Last week voters in numerous localities rejected ballot initiatives related to data centers, which provide the infrastructure AI operates on but have been blamed for rising energy costs and other impacts. Government leaders at the state and local level have for some time argued that messaging around AI should focus on how it helps make employees’ work easier and more efficient. Those who work for small and rural governments have said previously that the technology has given them “breathing room.” More to follow.

Articles.Title: Does state-and-local AI need a rebrand? - Route Fifty

stories.Headline: Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong quarterly results
stories.Summary:
Shares of Nebius Holdings NV, an artificial intelligence cloud operator, fell 17% on November 12, 2026, after the company released its third-quarter financial results. The results themselves beat expectations, with adjusted profit and revenue both coming in above forecasts. The drop was attributed in part to a full-year forecast that came in below the consensus estimate. Some reporting also suggested the sudden departure of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang may have contributed, since Nvidia is an investor in Nebius.

Nebius raised its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion, which CNBC reported is $4.15 billion above what Wall Street had expected. Its plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year also exceeded the consensus estimate by a wider margin. The spending is linked to a shift away from colocation facilities, since about 90% of the company's infrastructure is currently in rented data centers. The next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity will be mostly powered by data centers the company operates itself. Nebius also expects full-year revenue at the low end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range, below the $3.37 billion analysts expected.

Founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh said the company remains focused on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term. He said Nebius will keep investing in capacity and infrastructure, in its platform and products, and in its team. The company swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year earlier to a $90.9 million adjusted profit, or 31 cents per share, against analysts' expected loss of 69 cents per share. Revenue rose 517% year over year to $980.8 million, well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus.

Growth was driven partly by Token Factory, a service for running open-source AI models that launched a year ago and is nearing a "multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate." Nebius signed $12 billion in contracts in the three months ended September 30, including multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. The company uses customer prepayments to finance data center projects, and says prepayments received in the quarter exceeded capital expenditures. That ratio is expected to decline as data center spending ramps up. For 2027, Nebius forecasts revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion.

Articles.Title: Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong quarterly results - SiliconANGLE

stories.Headline: Nebius Bets $40B on Customer-Funded AI Cloud Expansion
stories.Summary:
Nebius, the former Yandex cloud unit, is pushing ahead with a $40 billion AI infrastructure expansion that relies on customer prepayments and loans instead of traditional equity or bond sales. The plan was reported in an article published by The Tech Buzz on November 12, 2026. Delays at a Microsoft data center project that Nebius is involved with have already raised questions about the approach. Shares of the company tumbled 10% just days before the report after it delivered disappointing 2026 guidance. The company is betting that the capital crunch hurting its competitors can be avoided.

The neocloud model asks GPU clients to pay months or years in advance for capacity that does not yet exist. Nebius takes that cash, secures additional loans against the guaranteed revenue stream, and then orders Nvidia H100 chips and builds facilities. The articles say Nebius has not disclosed which customers are providing prepayments or how much of the $40 billion will come from loans versus advance payments. The company also announced news of a massive capital expenditure surge alongside its weak guidance. The expansion would be roughly ten times larger than anything the company has attempted before.

Nebius is the company responsible for the expansion, and the articles report that it is pursuing this financing strategy. The company's pitch to investors is that customer prepayments are a more sustainable funding source than debt markets, which can freeze during downturns. The articles report that the company's logic is that it does not depend on bond buyers or venture capitalists if it already holds the customer's money. Nebius has not publicly addressed the Microsoft data center delays in the articles. The articles present its strategy as a bet that critics are wrong or premature.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk warned of "guppy-level death" for hundreds of GPU providers, which the articles say triggered a selloff across neocloud stocks. Musk argued that most of these companies are too small, too leveraged, and too dependent on a single customer or use case to survive consolidation. CoreWeave, a GPU cloud provider that has used debt-fueled buildouts, has delivered impressive revenue growth but raised concerns about leverage. S&P Global Ratings revised Meta's outlook to negative over worries that AI infrastructure spending is outpacing free cash flow. Customers that pay upfront and any investors holding Nebius shares face the consequences if capacity is delivered late.

The articles say Nebius is a startup that spun out of Yandex less than two years ago. Meta recently announced a $25 billion bond sale to fund its AI infrastructure, and SoftBank is reportedly considering a $50 billion investment in Malaysia for AI and data centers. Hyperscalers have long used capacity reservation agreements to lock in revenue, but Nebius is extending that practice further. CoreWeave has tested a similar model, and Dropbox spent $350 million acquiring Tigris Data to power its AI developer tools. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon has said investor appetite for AI infrastructure remains strong despite market volatility.

The articles say the outcome will show whether customer-funded AI infrastructure is viable. If Nebius delivers capacity on schedule and keeps prepayment customers satisfied, the model could become a playbook for neoclouds without cheap debt. If delays continue and customers demand refunds, the sector could face a reckoning over growth strategies. The articles do not say which customers are paying in advance, how much of the $40 billion is covered by loans, or how the Microsoft data center delays will be resolved. They also do not say whether Musk's prediction will come true for companies like Nebius.

Articles.Title: Nebius Bets $40B on Customer-Funded AI Cloud Expansion - The Tech Buzz

stories.Headline: Nebius Deal Prepayments Exceed Capex as Colocation Delays Shift Revenue
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $980.8 million on November 12, 2026, up 571% from a year earlier. Customers had committed more than $12 billion in contract value since the start of the quarter. Delays at third-party data centers also pushed some expected revenue into 2027. The company's shareholder letter said prepayments on Q3 agreements covered more than 100% of their associated capital spending, up from 50% to 60% in the second quarter. Expected payback on comparable one-to-three-year contracts improved to one year and seven months from one year and ten months.

The core Nebius AI Cloud business made up about 99% of group revenue. Roughly $325 million of the quarterly total was non-recurring revenue from the first phase of an asset-light rollout, in which partners fund capacity using Nebius's architecture and platform. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, was $465.8 million, while the GAAP net loss from continuing operations narrowed to $37.5 million. Purchases of property, equipment and intangible assets totaled about $7.3 billion, mainly for GPUs, hardware and data center expansion. Because that spending is so large, the improved prepayment terms are central to how the build-out gets financed.

Delivery dates at several third-party colocation sites moved into the first half of 2027, including the remaining New Jersey tranches. Nebius expects to have delivered more than half of the New Jersey capacity contracted with Microsoft by the end of 2026, with the rest due in the second quarter of 2027. The company said the contracts remain in place and affected customers have been informed. Following the delays at DataOne, Nebius is scaling Bloom Energy fuel cells to serve as the site's main power source, and it said its owned sites were on time or ahead of schedule.

As a result, Nebius now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3.0 to $3.4 billion range. Its 2026 capital expenditure forecast rose to about $27 billion from $20 to $25 billion. The initial 2027 outlook calls for pre-tax breakeven in the fourth quarter and $40 to $45 billion of capital spending for more than one gigawatt of new capacity. Management expects customer prepayments and investment-grade asset-backed financing to cover 75% to 85% of that spending. Nebius's 2027 breakeven target therefore depends on turning these commitments into operating capacity on the revised schedules while arranging the remaining financing.

Articles.Title: Nebius Deal Prepayments Exceed Capex as Colocation Delays Shift Revenue - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Caixin Summit: China’s AI Push Needs More Than Better Model Rankings
stories.Summary:
Tony Chan spoke via video on November 13 during the 17th Caixin Summit. He is a former president of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and a member of the U.S. National Academy of Engineering. Chan addressed the current state of the artificial intelligence industry in China. He urged the nation to prioritize genuine innovation over simple model rankings.

The speaker suggested that China should leverage its supply chains, traditional industries, and culture. He argued against merely increasing parameter counts for large models or trying to avoid export sanctions. Chan noted that Chinese models reach 90 to 95 percent of benchmark performance compared to U.S. versions. He estimated that the gap between the two countries is less than six months.

Chan stated that China currently leads in AI applications, mature-process chips, and renewable energy. However, he acknowledged that the U.S. maintains an advantage in capital markets, advanced chips, and top scholars. He expressed doubt that increasing computing power alone would lead to artificial general intelligence. He believes the industry must earn respect through original approaches.

The context of these remarks involves a competitive landscape where open-source models and lower costs pressure U.S. firms. Chan believes that focusing on these strengths will better position China in the global market. He emphasized that the goal should be creating value rather than chasing rankings. The summit provided a platform to discuss these strategic shifts for the future.

Articles.Title: Caixin Summit: China’s AI Push Needs More Than Better Model Rankings - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Nebius says customer prepayments now cover its AI build-out costs
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group, the Amsterdam-based AI cloud infrastructure provider listed on NASDAQ as NBIS, said in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, released November 12, 2026, that customer prepayments on contracts signed during the quarter now exceed 100% of the related capital expenditures. That is a sharp change from the prior quarter, when prepayments covered roughly 50% to 60% of associated capex. The company credited better customer terms, including longer commitment periods, larger upfront payments, and higher pricing that tops $25 million per megawatt annually. Nebius also said the payback period on its investments shortened to about 1 year and 7 months, down from 1 year and 10 months in Q2.

The company is spending more, not less. It raised its 2026 capex guidance to about $27 billion and expects $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027, aimed at adding more than 1 GW of new capacity. Most of that future spending is expected to come from customer prepayments and asset-backed financing tied to investment-grade contracts. Q3 revenue reached $980.8 million, up 571% year over year and ahead of analyst expectations, but Nebius now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion range, which it attributed mainly to delays in third-party capacity. It projects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, and it has a contracted backlog above $40 billion, including a Microsoft deal valued between $17.4 billion and $19.4 billion.

According to the article, Nebius framed the prepayment shift as a route to relying less on expensive debt and said it targets pre-tax profitability by late 2027. Shares nonetheless fell between 16% and 23% after the report, amid broader sector volatility. The article's analysis notes that the stock reaction reflects the sharp rise in capex guidance alongside the lower end of the 2026 revenue range, and it points to concentration risk given the size of the Microsoft contract within the backlog. Going forward, the article says investors should watch whether prepayment coverage stays above 100% on new contracts, whether third-party capacity delays clear before the 2027 revenue target, and whether the payback period holds, with the late-2027 profitability goal sitting behind all three.

Articles.Title: Nebius says customer prepayments now cover its AI build-out costs - Crypto Briefing

stories.Headline: Does the Trump Administration’s Campaign to Rebrand AI as ‘Super Intelligence’ Matter?
stories.Summary:
Secretary Markwayne Mullin promoted the term Super Intelligence during a press briefing on Friday, November 13, 2026. This occurred while a nationwide ground stop for all flights was in effect across the United States. Mullin corrected a reporter who used the term artificial intelligence when asking about a telecommunications failure. The Homeland Security secretary indicated that the cause of the coast to coast travel disruption was not yet ascertained. He used the moment to push President Donald Trump's campaign to rename the technology as SI.

The change requires the federal government to use Super Intelligence and not acknowledge artificial intelligence in official contexts. This policy was established by an executive order signed on September 29 titled Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence. Trump first expressed dislike for the word artificial in July 2025 during his AI Action Plan launch. He later floated supreme intelligence in December and polled options on Truth Social on September 19. He officially chose Super Intelligence during a United Nations General Assembly speech on September 22.

President Trump stated that the term artificial implies a defect and that the technology is actually pure genius. He believes the new name is more accurate and reflects the transformative capabilities and limitless opportunities of the technology. Trump said that whoever wins Super Intelligence wins, and he wants to maintain global technological dominance over China. A State Department official instructed diplomats to change all references in documents, positions, and press elements. Michael Kratsios of the OSTP adopted the term in his remarks at the UN the next day.

Social media users and technology writer Charlie Warzel called the focus on branding during an aviation crisis absurd. Harvard political scientist Ryan Enos noted that prioritizing regime approved rhetoric during an emergency is a sign of authoritarianism. Emily Tucker of Georgetown Law suggested the renaming might preempt arguments or make it harder to resist power abuses. Dave Karpf of George Washington University said the insistence on the term shows Trump is out of his depth. Jenna Ruddock of Free Press said industry leaders play along for lucrative contracts and regulatory fast tracks.

Trump has a history of renaming things, including the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on day one. In September 2025, he ordered the Department of Defense to be called the Department of War. He also renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America and suggested calling the Strait of Hormuz the Trump Strait. Industry leaders like Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang have adopted the SI branding in their companies. Musk planned to rename the SpaceXAI unit to SpaceXSI, and Zuckerberg used the term in earnings calls.

The federal government will continue to use the term Super Intelligence to the maximum extent permitted by law. The administration aims to achieve and maintain unquestioned and unchallenged global technological dominance through this technology. Trump mentioned America.gov as a new website used to query government information. The articles leave open whether the telecommunications failure that stopped all flights was actually related to SI. The cause of the Friday air travel crisis remains unclear as of the time of publication.

Articles.Title: Does the Trump Administration’s Campaign to Rebrand AI as ‘Super Intelligence’ Matter? - Tech Policy Press

stories.Headline: Fermi gets $200 million hyperscaler prepayment for 600 MW and ends TensorWave lease
stories.Summary:
Fermi said on Thursday that an undisclosed investment-grade hyperscaler committed about $200 million up front to advance an initial 600 megawatts at Project Matador, its private-grid data center campus in the Texas Panhandle, beginning in 2027. The customer signed a $200 million prepayment agreement and a $15 million early construction and site development agreement. Fermi and TensorWave terminated the Data Center Lease and Services Agreement they signed in August 2026, and the AMD credit support agreement tied to it is also terminated. The release gives no reason for the termination. Fermi scheduled a call for 9 a.m.

ET on Thursday. The deal is not a lease, and the parties continue to work toward a definitive long-term lease and a $90 million structural steel and building materials purchase agreement. The steel agreement, still being finalized, would let the customer use long-lead materials Fermi already secured to speed construction of multiple data center buildings on the site. The prepayment provides upfront customer funding for the proposed 600 MW development, and the $15 million agreement sets a framework for site preparation and construction to start as soon as possible. The customer's identity remains confidential.

The investor presentation shows the 600 MW as reserved for 2027 by a "major hyperscaler." Chief executive Lee McIntire said Fermi's headstart in speed to power is a key reason an investment-grade hyperscaler signed up for 600 megawatts and committed more than $200 million up front. He said that if Fermi converts its pipeline of prospective customers into leases, it would completely fill its 2.2 gigawatts of current capacity. Fermi said the customer is making financial and development commitments ahead of finalizing a lease because it wants access to power within its delivery timeline. Fermi said the customer is making commitments "ahead of finalizing a lease."

McIntire's remarks were in the release. The TensorWave lease was for 222 MW of total facility power, about $6.5 billion of contracted revenue over an initial 15-year term, and expansion rights that could take the relationship above 650 MW. In October, AMD signed a credit support agreement backing that 222 MW phase-one lease, which Fermi called "a key milestone toward securing project financing," and the two set a framework for up to 650 MW of expansion. Fermi said at the time that closing the TensorWave lease and AMD's obligations were subject to conditions.

The hyperscaler's 600 MW is larger than the TensorWave first phase, but it comes with a prepayment and a construction agreement rather than a signed lease, so Fermi still has no binding long-term revenue contract on the campus. Texas Tech University System, Fermi's landlord, remains committed to the project, and the two continue to work on the land-lease conditions that must be met before vertical construction, chancellor Brandon Creighton said Texas Tech "remains firmly committed to the success of Project Matador." Third-quarter net loss was $141.6 million, or $0.22 a share, and G&A of $142.2 million included $65.8 million of stock compensation and $21.5 million of advisory fees paid in stock. The year-earlier loss of $346.8 million included $309.0 million of other expense.

Capital spending was $133.4 million in the quarter and $759.5 million over nine months, taking net property, plant and equipment to about $1.67 billion. Debt, net, rose to $958.4 million after a $463.0 million net increase in borrowings under its convertible notes and equipment financing facilities, while cash and restricted cash fell to $315.5 million from $408.5 million of cash at the end of 2025. The deck lists $1.2 billion of financing commitments, including a $500 million turbine warehouse facility with about $445 million drawn and $431 million of 5% convertible notes due 2031. Fermi puts its maximum 2027 power at 925 MW if all contracted turbines and equipment are delivered, rising to 1,332 MW in 2028 and 2,000 MW of Fermi-owned generation in 2029, plus up to 200 MW from Xcel Energy.

The deck pitches a "Powered Land+" model, in which Fermi supplies power, land, water and fiber and the tenant builds the data halls, at an illustrative $3.9 million to $5.1 million of capital per megawatt of gross power versus $12.1 million to $15.0 million for a turnkey facility. Fermi has no revenue. Fermi ended September with $316 million of cash and restricted cash and $958 million of net debt. The release gives no reason for the termination.

Articles.Title: Fermi gets $200 million hyperscaler prepayment for 600 MW and ends TensorWave lease - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: ESDS, E2E Networks rise up to 5% as AI stocks stage sharp comeback globally
stories.Summary:
Shares of ESDS Software Solution, E2E Networks and other artificial intelligence-related companies in India extended their gains on Thursday, following a sharp recovery in global technology stocks after a recent selloff on Wall Street. The Nasdaq 100 rose 2.5 percent in the previous session, and Nvidia shares gained 4 percent. Among domestic names, ESDS Software Solution was the top gainer, climbing as much as 4.67 percent, while E2E Networks advanced 3.27 percent. Netweb Technologies India traded 0.11 percent higher at Rs 4,157.50, MTAR Technologies gained nearly 2 percent, and Black Box rose close to 1 percent. Anant Raj also climbed 4 percent.

The rally extended beyond India, with CoreWeave Inc. surging 24 percent after issuing an upbeat outlook. Investor interest in AI-related stocks picked up again across markets, according to the report. OpenAI reported quarterly revenue of USD 10 billion, which the article cites as a sign of strong demand for AI services. Anthropic PBC's proposed initial public offering was also reported to be multiple times oversubscribed. Anant Raj has expanded into AI-ready digital infrastructure and data centres through its subsidiary, Anant Raj Cloud.

The article attributes the moves to market sentiment rather than to any single company decision, and it notes that the views and investment tips quoted from experts are their own and not those of the website. It advises readers to check with certified experts before making investment decisions. The article does not name any regulator or official response, and it does not describe any policy, filing or structural change tied to the gains. It also gives no forecast for how long the rebound will last.

Articles.Title: ESDS, E2E Networks rise up to 5% as AI stocks stage sharp comeback globally - TradingView

stories.Headline: E2E Networks Expands Data Centre Capacity For AI Computing Demand
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks announced on 12 November 2026 that it is expanding its data centre capacity to meet rising demand for AI computing and cloud workloads. The company is adding 12.8 MW of capacity, according to a source alert that the article says was not independently verified. The addition would raise its total data centre capacity to 27.4 MW. Sahi Markets published the report on 12 November 2026 at 02:23 PM IST, and it was last updated at the same time. The report was reviewed by Arpit Seth and runs about two minutes of reading.

The expansion follows the launch of Blaze, a pay-per-token AI inference platform, in November 2026. In October 2026 the company announced a 5.4 MW expansion in NVIDIA Blackwell AI capacity. In September 2025 E2E Networks secured a ₹177 crore order under the IndiaAI Mission. Q2 FY27 revenue reached ₹223.8 crore, up 411% year-on-year, with EBITDA margin expanding to 76.6%. Q2 FY27 net profit reached ₹72.7 crore, up 32.5% from ₹58.6 crore profit before tax in Q1 FY27.

The article attributes the capacity figures to a source alert and states they were not independently verified. It says the additional capacity targets increasing enterprise workloads across AI model training and cloud services. It describes E2E Networks as actively positioning itself as a key domestic infrastructure partner for India's AI mission. It says the company addresses compute availability constraints while leveraging high operational margins from scaled GPU infrastructure. It says expanding the compute footprint allows E2E Networks to capture incremental market share in high-margin enterprise AI inference and LLM deployment.

The article lists high capital expenditure intensity for advanced GPU cluster deployment as a key risk. It also lists potential supply chain constraints or procurement delays for high-end accelerator chips as a risk. It says demand for localized cloud GPUs and data centre capacity in India is accelerating due to sovereign AI mandates and growing enterprise adoption of generative AI workloads. It says the revenue growth was supported by high GPU cluster utilization. It gives a medium-term time horizon of 3 to 12 months and names cloud infrastructure, AI compute and data centres as overweight.

The article says the capacity addition aligns with strong financial momentum reported in Q2 FY27. It cites utilization rates of newly commissioned megawatt capacity and enterprise adoption of inference platforms like Blaze as trigger factors. It says continuous infrastructure capacity scaling strengthens E2E Networks' strategic positioning within India's hyperscale ecosystem. It says the news section may include AI-generated or AI-assisted content subject to human review. It advises readers to independently verify information before relying on it.

The article does not state a completion date for the 12.8 MW addition or a cost for the expansion. It does not name the source behind the capacity alert beyond calling it a source alert. It does not give the date of the Q2 FY27 results or the venue of any announcement. It does not say how the Blaze platform or the IndiaAI Mission order will affect future revenue. It leaves open whether the 27.4 MW total will be reached as stated.

Articles.Title: E2E Networks Expands Data Centre Capacity For AI Computing Demand - Sahi

stories.Headline: Siri AI Still Not Enabled on HomePod Mini 2 With Latest Software Update
stories.Summary:
Apple released HomePod software version 27.2.1 on Friday, November 13, 2026, according to MacRumors, but the update does not enable Siri AI on the HomePod mini 2. The report was published by Joe Rossignol at 12:18 pm PST that day. Apple also released tvOS 27.2.1 the same day. That update enables Siri AI on the Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) and the Apple TV 4K (3rd generation). The HomePod mini 2 still lacks the feature after the new software.

Apple's website continues to say Siri AI is "coming in a future software update," but Apple has not provided a timeframe. The HomePod mini 2 has only 2GB of RAM, well below the minimum 8GB of RAM required for dedicated Siri AI. Because of that limit, personal context requests on the HomePod mini 2 will require a paired Apple Intelligence, enabled iPhone or iPad with Siri AI turned on. Siri AI is an opt-in feature on the Apple TV 4K models, so after installing tvOS 27.2.1 you must open the Settings app and tap General, then Siri, then Siri AI (Beta). That step initiates a download with support.

If you update to tvOS 27.2.1 and take no further action, Siri Classic remains enabled by default. The MacRumors article carries a related roundup for the HomePod mini 2 and tags for the Siri Guide and Siri AI. It also links a buyer's guide for the HomePod Mini with a Buy Now option. The article points readers to a related forum for HomePod, HomeView and CarPlay under Home & Auto Tech. The page shows 38 comments on the story.

Commenters on the article questioned the rollout, with one calling the Siri AI rollout inconsistent and another writing that the release "made zero sense." One commenter wrote that the feature is "coming on Febutober the eleventeenth." Another said it would be good if a senior Apple executive were asked about this sort of thing in an interview rather than a promotional piece. One commenter said Apple was already subject of a class action lawsuit about Apple Intelligence and that selling hardware on vague or delayed promises of functionality wastes your brand. Another commenter said turning the feature on would improve sales of Google Home speakers.

MacRumors also reported that HomePod Software 27.2 adds a Sound Glow feature to the HomePod, HomePod mini and HomePod mini 2. Apple introduced Sound Glow as a HomePod mini 2 feature, but it is available for the second-generation HomePod and the original HomePod mini too. HomePod Software 27.2 was available as a release candidate update for developers and public beta testers. MacRumors also reported that iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2, released on Monday, October 26, 2026, expanded Siri AI to new languages. The site's upcoming calendar lists Apple HomeView and Apple TV, both with Siri AI support, as launching November 13.

The MacRumors article does not say when, or whether, Siri AI will arrive on the HomePod mini 2. It gives no date for the "future software update" Apple's website mentions. It does not state how personal context requests will work on the HomePod mini 2 without a paired device. It does not say whether Siri AI on the HomePod mini 2 will also be opt-in. The article does not report any Apple comment on the missing feature beyond the website wording.

Articles.Title: Siri AI Still Not Enabled on HomePod Mini 2 With Latest Software Update

stories.Headline: Why So Many AI Prototypes Never Make It Past the Database
stories.Summary:
Dave Page, CTO at pgEdge and a Postgres Core Team member, wrote in SD Times on 12 November 2026 that AI coding agents and app builders often provision a database on default settings wherever a demo runs quickest. Page began using PostgreSQL around 1997 at a UK social housing provider where he was head of IT. That project used Postgres version 6.3.2 so tenants could see their rent accounts online without per-user licensing costs for the internal system. Page said coding agents can produce a working application with a database far faster than any developer can. He said these databases are often created without thorough review from experienced DBAs.

Page said someone must check what access a database grants, how it fails over, where backups live and what happens when something breaks. He said Postgres features have been added continually for three decades, and every release brings major changes DBAs must know. He said experienced DBAs were hard to find well before agents came along, so databases awaiting review can outnumber the people able to review them. He said prototypes often fail in production because the database was never built for the push to prod. He said hosted platforms ask you to pick a region when you create a project, but where server logs are shipped can be overlooked.

Page said Postgres by default logs any statement that triggers an error, and a unique constraint violation includes the duplicate value in the error detail. He said logs can therefore contain sensitive information that cannot be disclosed and can be sent to wherever the model is hosted, outside the range you defined. He said these issues do not matter to a proof of concept containing test data, but a regulated business will have to pay attention. He said problems often surface only when a compliance team looks at something already in production, making it a production problem that is much harder to deal with. He said poorly designed queries are instant against a few hundred rows but painfully slow against the millions of rows a busy application builds up.

Page said many issues are never seen until the application is tested in a real-world environment. He said solving these problems comes down to the same discipline that makes coding agents useful. He said it is important to spend a lot of time before any code exists going back and forth with the model on the design until there is a spec and an implementation plan. He said production requirements must be clearly defined alongside features, giving examples such as customer data, including backups and logs, staying in particular regions, or losing no more than five minutes of writes.

He said those requirements should remain front and center for testing and auditing before the prototype reaches production. Page said someone who knows the database can more effectively audit what has been implemented and ensure essential company requirements are met. He said not every prototype needs expert review, and plenty of demos will only ever hold test data, so they can stay as created, but you should prepare before loading sensitive data. He said AI agents are incredibly useful tools that make it simple to create a demo, but they have made it just as easy to go a long way before anyone thinks about how the database is designed.

He said you should make database decisions on purpose while the application is still small enough to move. He said you should follow the same practices you use with code and have someone who has run that database technology in production review it thoroughly before pushing to production. Page has over 28 years of Postgres development experience and created pgAdmin. He said he originally began using PostgreSQL around 1997 at a UK social housing provider.

He said the database in that project was a decision somebody made for a reason. He said it is now quite possible to build an application, AI features and all, without an actual person making that decision. He said a prototype database may be a helpful start that lets teams visualize and work through potential problems and move faster. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why So Many AI Prototypes Never Make It Past the Database - SD Times

stories.Headline: Google outlines no-downtime AlloyDB AI embedding upgrade
stories.Summary:
Google has published guidance on upgrading the vector embedding models used in AlloyDB AI without taking production databases offline. The approach is aimed at teams running semantic search and other vector workloads on live systems, and it describes moving from one embedding model to another while still serving user queries. It relies on in-database model access, automated embedding generation, PostgreSQL functions and concurrent index creation. The guidance was reported on November 12, 2026. Because embeddings from different models cannot be compared directly, switching models normally means re-embedding existing data, rebuilding indexes and changing query logic.

In the example Google gives, a production table of product reviews moves from text-embedding-005, which produces 768-dimensional vectors, to gemini-embedding-001, which produces 3,072-dimensional vectors. The process starts by adding a new vector column sized for the replacement model, then enabling auto-embeddings so the database backfills vectors in the background. AlloyDB AI can generate embeddings at up to 3,000 per second and tracks changes to source rows. Teams can choose transactional mode, which updates embeddings as data changes but adds write latency, or manual mode, which marks changed rows for scheduled batch refreshes. The migration example uses manual mode.

In one benchmark on a 10,000-row table, lowering max_parallel_requests from 400 to 20 cut the longest concurrent writer wait from 5.1 seconds to 0.39 seconds, while raising total backfill time from 5.2 seconds to 7.6 seconds. Google recommends checking for missing embeddings and validating new vectors against fresh model calls before switching traffic. It also says teams should test application behaviour, since retrieval results can shift sharply between models. In Google's internal tests, the top-10 nearest-neighbour results from the two models overlapped by only 31%, so ranking, filtering and evaluation logic may need review.

The process also builds a new ScaNN index on the replacement column concurrently to avoid blocking writes. Google says ScaNN builds were up to 10 times faster than HNSW on open-source PostgreSQL, and in tests on 100,000 rows a 3,072-dimensional ScaNN index took about 50 seconds while an HNSW index using halfvec took seven to 13 minutes. For the final switch, Google outlines two patterns. One uses an atomic column rename and a query function so applications need no code changes, which supports blue-green deployment but not per-query canary testing.

The other uses PostgreSQL session variables and a set-returning function, which allows canary releases and traffic splitting and quick reversion. The atomic rename pattern does not work with transactional auto-embeddings because managed triggers refer to fixed column names. Google also warns of storage and latency costs: single-row update median latency rose from about 37.5 milliseconds to roughly 191.0 milliseconds during migration, then settled near 172.0 milliseconds after cutover, and storage per row grew from about 4.5KB to about 13.3KB, implying roughly 133GB for a 10-million-row table's new column plus about 6GB for its index. After cutover, teams can clear and drop the retired column, which in Google's 100,000-row tests reclaimed 381MB of TOAST space for later upgrades.

Articles.Title: Google outlines no-downtime AlloyDB AI embedding upgrade - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: V2 AI appoints Arseny Chernov to lead Singapore push
stories.Summary:
V2 AI, a data and AI consultancy, has appointed Arseny Chernov as Director, Forward Deployed Engineering - Applied AI, to strengthen its leadership team in Singapore. The appointment was reported on 12 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia. The move comes as the firm expands across Asia-Pacific and builds out its regional hub in the city-state. Chernov will support operations in Singapore and South-East Asia, working with customers and internal technical teams.

His work will cover AI architecture, forward deployed engineering, and secure multi-agent workflows. The role is aimed at helping companies move AI projects out of pilot stages and into live business use. The articles note that many organisations struggle with data, governance, and infrastructure when they try to scale systems across larger operations. Chernov's focus will be on the security, governance, and operational constraints that tend to emerge at that point.

Chernov previously served as Regional Director for ASEAN, Korea, and Greater China at HashiCorp, where he led regional technical teams and worked on AI-native security and governance. Before that, he spent more than five years at Google in senior technical and engineering roles across Asia-Pacific and the US, including work on Google Payments and early generative AI projects. He also led Partner Solutions Architecture for Asia-Pacific and Japan at Databricks. At Databricks, he was the company's first hire in Singapore and built a regional network of more than 50 strategic technology partners.

In a statement, Chernov said organisations are moving past AI experimentation but need strong data foundations, robust architecture, and co-design with security and governance teams to reach reliable enterprise solutions. V2 AI's leadership, speaking through a company representative named Williams, said the appointment reflects the technical and operational demands shaping the regional AI market. Williams said Chernov's experience would strengthen the Singapore team and its ability to help organisations move from AI ambition to implementation. V2 AI was founded in 2023 and operates across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, Singapore, and Kuala Lumpur.

Articles.Title: V2 AI appoints Arseny Chernov to lead Singapore push - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: The AI licences are live. Why hasn't the work changed?
stories.Summary:
Glen Maguire, founder of Matrix AI Consulting, wrote in IT Brief Australia on 13 November 2026 that most calls he takes now come from organisations that already have AI, with licences live for Copilot, ChatGPT or Claude. He said IT has approved the platform and there has been a webinar, sometimes several. A few months later, someone senior asks why it isn't being used more and why the work hasn't changed, he wrote. He said the easy diagnosis is resistance, but in many of his engagements that isn't the first barrier. When he asks teams why they aren't using AI, the most common answer is "I don't know what I'd use it for," and workshop polls point the same way.

He wrote that unclear rules, unsuitable tools, competing priorities and limited time to practise can all contribute, and that relevance, permission and practice tend to fail together. CPA Australia's recent survey of 1,679 accounting and finance professionals across six markets found 88% of Australian and New Zealand respondents' businesses using AI, but only 11% with it deeply embedded. Australia and New Zealand ranked last of the six for broad integration, he wrote. He said licences, logins and webinar attendance tell you whether people can use AI, not whether it has changed how work gets done. As a Prosci-certified practitioner, he uses the ADKAR model, covering Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement, to diagnose stalled AI rollouts.

He wrote that many rollout programmes concentrate on announcing the change and explaining the tool, leaving motivation, practical capability and reinforcement to chance. He said people need a task worth changing, because generic examples such as summarising an email rarely motivate a site engineer or a payroll officer. Employment Hero found 37% of New Zealand workers feel guilty using AI at work, he wrote, adding that this doesn't prove guilt causes underuse but suggests workplace attitudes and expectations matter. He said unclear rules cut both ways, with some people holding back while others use AI quietly outside approved tools. He wrote that what lifts uptake most clearly is in-person workshops built on the organisation's own workflows, where people bring a real task such as a tender response or a monthly report and build the AI-assisted version in the room using approved tools and suitably sanitised material.

He described a clinician whose administrator had watched several generic AI videos and left her more confused and more wary than before. After one personal session built around her own tasks, she built and deployed two Copilot agents that have lifted her productivity, he wrote. He said the technology hadn't changed, but she could see where it fitted her job and felt safe to try. MyHR reported that just 5.7% of AI-using employers in its research had an AI policy, he wrote, and where policies exist they're often too vague to act on. He said employees need guidance they can actually use, ideally on one page covering which tools are approved, what information can and can't go in, which outputs need a human check, that it's fine to say you used AI, and who to ask when something goes wrong.

He wrote that behind that page leaders need to have decided which tools and use cases are approved and who approves new ones, how data is classified and where it may go, where human review is required and who is accountable for the output, and how incidents are reported and escalated and when a pilot is good enough to scale. He said drafting a routine internal summary is different from using AI to assess an employee, advise a customer or inform a consequential decision. He wrote that the CIO owns technical assurance and enablement, and that if the approved tool is slower than the workaround, people will use the workaround. He said HR helps people build capability and confidence, including manager expectations, role impacts and consultation, but business leaders must own the changes to workflows and the results. He wrote that managers should identify suitable tasks, give people time to experiment, set quality expectations and be clear where AI adds risk or little value.

He wrote that Australian work health and safety rules now require employers to manage the psychosocial risks that poorly managed change can create. He said an organisation can increase active users while producing more rework, exposing sensitive information or applying AI to decisions it shouldn't touch. He wrote that the aim is valuable, well-governed use, so organisations should measure which workflows now use AI routinely, output quality and rework, time saved on specific tasks, staff confidence, and incidents or near misses. He suggested teams share one real example in an existing meeting and managers recognise better work rather than prompt counts. He wrote that AI adoption isn't simply a training problem but a leadership and operating-model problem, and proposed a test for the next leadership meeting: name three workflows where AI is genuinely improving outcomes, explain the rules for using it safely, and identify the business leader accountable for the result.

Articles.Title: The AI licences are live. Why hasn't the work changed? - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Virtana launches AI agent war room for IT incidents
stories.Summary:
Virtana has launched Agentic Observability Enterprise Management, a system that coordinates AI agents from different enterprise platforms during IT incidents, according to an IT Brief Australia report published on November 12, 2026. The product is designed to bring together agents that would otherwise work in isolation. It arrives as companies run growing numbers of AI agents across IT service management, cloud, security and software development systems. Those agents are increasingly expected to connect when an incident spans several areas.

The system uses the Model Context Protocol and the open Agent2Agent protocol to bring agents from third-party platforms into what Virtana calls an agentic war room. Virtana says the platform draws on more than 25,000 operational signals across applications, infrastructure, cloud and AI environments. It combines those signals with its System Dependency Graph to map relationships between systems, trace root causes and assess business impact. Companies can start with a recommendation model, move to approval-based remediation and later allow agents to act alone on defined classes of incidents.

Every action stays subject to enterprise policy controls and is auditable, including records of agent activity, token consumption and operating cost. Paul Appleby, Chief Executive Officer of Virtana, described the launch as part of a wider shift toward autonomous IT operations. He said the future belongs to enterprises whose agents understand the whole business and can work together on problems no single agent could solve. Amitkumar Rathi, Chief Product Officer of Virtana, contrasted traditional war rooms, which can take hours to assemble teams and coordinate fixes, with agent-based rooms that assemble, share intelligence and disband in milliseconds.

He said the two protocols give agents enterprise-wide intelligence and let them discover and act together as a governed workforce. The release responds to a fragmentation problem that the article ties to research from Salesforce, which found that the average enterprise runs 12 AI agents and that half operate in silos. Virtana is relying on open protocols rather than asking companies to replace existing tools, so enterprises can bring in agents from platforms they already use. The product is available now to select customers, and general availability is planned for the first quarter of 2027.

Articles.Title: Virtana launches AI agent war room for IT incidents - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Five-Tier K-12 Framework Proposes Age-Gated Limits for Classroom Generative Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A perspective study published in AI, Brain and Child on November 14, 2026, introduces a five-tiered framework for generative artificial intelligence exposure for students aged 3 through 18. The study was authored by researcher Sisi Tao. The model links specific artificial intelligence permissions, quantitative cut-off times, and mandatory independence ratios to neurodevelopmental and cognitive milestones. It moves past polarized debates between absolute classroom prohibition and unrestricted adoption. The blueprint establishes an evidence-based continuum grounded in developmental psychology.

Tier 0 covers ages 3 to 5 and mandates zero direct student interaction, with all technology use adult-mediated and back-stage. Tier 1 covers ages 6 to 7 with a cap of 15 minutes per day and an independent work ratio of at least 95 percent. Tier 2 covers ages 8 to 10 at approximately 30 minutes daily with an independence ratio of 90 percent or higher. Tier 3 spans ages 11 to 13 with a daily limit of 60 minutes and an 80 percent independence threshold. Tier 4 governs ages 14 to 18 with a daily ceiling of 120 minutes and a minimum 70 percent independence ratio, requiring a formal Artificial Intelligence Usage Statement with each assignment.

Educational policymakers must enforce regulation by design, requiring software vendors to incorporate age-gated usage locks matching tiered daily exposure limits as a prerequisite for procurement in public school districts. Technology developers are urged to end direct preschool engagement tools and instead engineer transparent, privacy-preserving teacher resources that operate across varied network bandwidths. Educators are tasked with developing process-oriented curricula emphasizing explicit bias detection checklists, student agency, and oral evaluations. Parents serve as home gatekeepers by aligning domestic device habits with school cut-offs, monitoring family conversational assistants, and curbing uncritical trust or personal disclosure patterns. The author emphasizes that the proposed quantitative thresholds represent theory-driven hypotheses and testable heuristic baselines rather than definitive physiological constants.

In the United States, a presidential executive order promotes system-wide artificial intelligence integration in K-12 schooling despite an absence of age-specific bans. Approximately 40 percent of national education systems restricted smartphone use in schools by 2024, while UNESCO guidance recommends a minimum age threshold of 13 for classroom artificial intelligence tools. An electroencephalography study showed declining neural functional connectivity and post-exposure cognitive debt when individuals write with continuous artificial intelligence assistance. Generative models frequently present factual inaccuracies, fabricated scholarly citations, and systemic societal stereotypes as authoritative output. The framework synthesizes five classical developmental psychology frameworks: Piaget's cognitive stage theory, Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, Erikson's psychosocial theory, Kohlberg's stages of moral reasoning, and Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory.

The author utilized an adapted best-fit framework synthesis methodology, integrating empirical literature from PsycINFO and ERIC using targeted Boolean strings covering generative technology, digital media, and developmental neuroscience in cohorts aged 3 to 18. Four evidence streams were triangulated to set boundaries: Piagetian representational transitions, longitudinal magnetic resonance neuroimaging showing cortical volume peaks and synaptic pruning in frontal and parietal regions, empirical attention spans and executive function trajectories, and practical K-12 grade bands. A four-tier model was rejected because it would artificially collapse the transition around ages 6 to 7 from preoperational to concrete operational thought. A six-tier structure would introduce artificial breaks within adolescence that lack neuroscientific warrant, given that longitudinal neuroimaging demonstrates executive function development follows a protracted, continuous trajectory from age 13 to 18. Historical parallels include the introduction of portable electronic calculators and internet search engines, when observers feared the erosion of fundamental arithmetic and inquiry skills.

Key limitations include the framework's foundation in Western developmental psychology, necessitating future cross-cultural research to explore adaptations within non-Western and collectivist educational settings. Because the model reflects current text-based systems, rapid transitions toward autonomous agentic and multimodal platforms will require regular recalibration. Long-term empirical studies remain essential to test the ecological validity of the suggested cut-off values, track cross-device exposure, and design inherently artificial-intelligence-resistant pedagogies such as collaborative problem solving, embodied physical experiments, and process portfolios. The article states that students must retain intellectual agency as educational technology evolves. The articles do not state any implementation date or adopting institution for the framework.

Articles.Title: Five-Tier K-12 Framework Proposes Age-Gated Limits for Classroom Generative Artificial Intelligence - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: Your AI agents are ready for business. Is your business ready to own them? - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
As AI agents take on more decision-making inside companies, a Nov 12, 2026 ETCIO opinion piece by Manu Swami argues that businesses need stronger governance over them. The article says that McKinsey research found 80% of organizations have encountered risky behaviour from AI agents. It notes that enterprise architecture has long kept applications executing, people deciding and governance setting boundaries, but agents are changing that balance. Agents can interpret objectives, access enterprise systems, execute transactions and adapt their actions. The article says companies are therefore delegating elements of business judgment to software rather than merely automating tasks.

The author says businesses should define the extent of autonomy given to AI agents, with routine low-risk actions handled within predefined limits. Higher-stakes decisions involving financial exposure, regulatory obligations or irreversible consequences should require stronger safeguards or human approval. The piece gives a procurement agent resolving an invoice discrepancy as an example, where access to information does not confer authority to approve a price variance. It describes a customer service agent recommending a refund amount that must be checked against approved limits before processing. The article also says that even correctly configured agents must be continuously validated, since models evolve, tools change and business policies are updated.

Responsibility, the article says, must stay with the business, while IT, security and responsible AI teams build and maintain the controls. Using its examples, it says customer service should set boundaries for acceptable dispute resolutions, and Finance should determine what an agent can approve in financial exceptions. The author summarizes this division as the business owning decisions, technology enabling controls and governance providing oversight. Manu Swami is identified as Chief Technology Officer at Sonata Software, and the article notes that its views are the author's and that ETCIO does not necessarily subscribe to them.

The article states that agents are no longer merely automating tasks but taking on delegated judgment, which affects enterprises that deploy them and the teams that own their outcomes. It says enterprises must establish intended authority at deployment and validate exercised authority at runtime. Monitoring should show what an agent is doing, whether it stays within its authority and what impact its actions have. Important decisions should be traceable and, where stakes are high, independently reviewed, and an agent should not check its own work. Continuous assurance should test failure scenarios, adversarial behavior and edge cases, with mechanisms to restrict permissions, require human intervention or suspend execution.

The background the article gives is the traditional division of enterprise architecture described above, and the fragmented governance in which identity systems manage access, security platforms enforce controls, observability tools monitor execution and business functions remain accountable for outcomes. The article says the missing piece is the connection between these controls and the business authority an agent exercises. It frames AI maturity as how much business-critical work an enterprise can safely delegate while keeping control and accountability, rather than how many agents are deployed. The article says governance must be able to intervene, not just monitor, as AI begins to act rather than advise.

The article does not say what specific governance rules any company has adopted, nor what regulators or standards bodies will require. It also leaves open how the reversal or rollback of agent actions would work in practice across different systems. It gives no timeline for when businesses should implement these controls. The piece ends by stating that the advantage will come from building enough trust and control to extend greater autonomy where it makes sense, without saying how that threshold should be set.

Articles.Title: Your AI agents are ready for business. Is your business ready to own them? - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Space Tech Startup Astrome Bags ₹64 Cr RDI Fund for AI Satellite Network
stories.Summary:
The Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), has signed an agreement to provide ₹64.05 crore to Bengaluru-based space technology startup Astrome Technologies under the Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund. The money will support the development of an indigenous artificial intelligence-powered electronic intelligence (AI-ELINT) satellite constellation. The project is estimated to cost ₹128.11 crore, and TDB's assistance is structured as optionally convertible debt. The report was published by Analytics India Magazine on November 12, 2026.

The constellation will consist of microsatellites weighing about 50 kg each, operating in low Earth orbit. Each satellite will carry an ELINT payload designed to detect and analyse signals across a broad frequency range, along with inter-satellite communication links that let the satellites exchange information. AI-based ground processing software will handle the collected data. The network is meant to provide wider geographic coverage and more frequent observations of areas of interest as more satellites are added. The project also aims to raise the underlying technologies from Technology Readiness Level 4 to Level 9 through engineering, integration, testing and validation.

The TDB Secretary, Rajesh Kumar Pathak, said that through the RDI Fund the board supports Indian enterprises working on frontier technologies that can strengthen the country's strategic technology capabilities. An authorised representative of Astrome Technologies told DD News that the funding would accelerate the integration of technologies for the programme. The article places the award within India's growing private space sector, citing Bengaluru-based GalaxEye, which has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system, and Digantara, which has partnered with Singapore's DSTA on satellite tracking tools using AI-driven analytics. The article does not say when the satellites will launch or what the next milestones are.

stories.Headline: LTM Integrates AI Tool to Fix Quantum Computing Errors on IBM
stories.Summary:
LTM, a technology services company, has added its AI-powered Quantum Error Mitigation capability, called AI-QEM, to IBM's Quantum Functions Catalog. The company said it was the first global systems integrator to publish a function in that catalogue. According to the company, users with eligible IBM Quantum access plans can apply AI-QEM directly within their Qiskit workflows. The announcement was reported on November 12, 2026. The company's own description of the tool is the basis for the details below.

The capability uses AI models to learn error patterns specific to each device and to estimate corrections through classical post-processing. LTM says this improves result accuracy without requiring additional quantum processing unit time, repeated circuit executions or extra qubits, which some conventional error mitigation techniques need. The company tested the tool on IBM Quantum computers across circuits of different sizes and complexities, including experiments involving more than 100 qubits. It did not disclose how much accuracy improved or offer comparisons with other error mitigation methods. IBM's listing describes the function as using circuit, backend and observable characteristics to learn correction factors and to mitigate noisy quantum expectation values.

Scott Crowder, Vice President of IBM Quantum Adoption and Business Development, said in a statement that the AI-QEM function will let users mitigate errors faster and with fewer resources as they develop algorithms and applications. LTM, which was formerly known as LTIMindtree, had earlier joined the IBM Quantum Network as its first Indian global systems integrator. Other providers in IBM's catalogue offer related tools, including Q-CTRL's AI-driven error suppression, Qedma's QESEM function and Algorithmiq's tensor-network approach. The articles present LTM's function as distinctive mainly for its efficiency, a claim the company made without published accuracy figures.

Articles.Title: LTM Integrates AI Tool to Fix Quantum Computing Errors on IBM - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: How Enterprises Are Matching AI Workloads With The Right Models And Infra
stories.Summary:
The Inc42 article, published on 12 November 2026, reports on a leadership roundtable titled Powering AI Workloads at Scale, which Inc42 hosted in partnership with Oracle. The session was moderated by Sameer Dhanrajani, CEO of 3AI & AIQRATE, and brought together five speakers from Indian technology companies. The speakers were Jagadesh Babu Thangavelu, VP of engineering at Data Sutram, and Palanivel Saravanan, head of infrastructure cloud engineering at Oracle. The list also included Raghav Aggarwal, cofounder and MD of Fluid AI, Rohin Parkar, cofounder and CEO of Spintly, and Supreeth Ravi, head of engineering at PhroneticAI (AvenuesAI). The conversation explored how enterprises can move from experimentation to production, match workloads with the right models and infrastructure, manage AI economics and build adaptable systems.

The article says enterprises are moving beyond pilots and embedding AI into customer-facing applications, internal workflows and business decisions. It says the challenge is not simply about having more compute, and that no single model or GPU fits every workload. Enterprises are evaluating different GPUs for inference rather than treating any one option as the default, and open-weight models are gaining traction as rising token consumption pushes companies to seek greater control over AI economics. The approach is to identify which use cases genuinely need frontier models, while other workloads can run on open-weight models or dedicated AI clusters. Data sovereignty is another consideration, pushing larger organisations towards dedicated GPU environments where models can run within controlled data boundaries.

Ravi of PhroneticAI described the transition as a two-phase shift, with the first phase about choosing the right intelligence and the next about putting that intelligence to work at scale. He said enterprises first need to define the business outcome and then find the right balance between performance, reliability, latency and cost. Thangavelu of Data Sutram said the enterprise focus is moving beyond simply getting an answer to ensuring the answer can be delivered sustainably and economically. He said the apportioning of tokens is not just a function of getting the right quality output but also of figuring out whether the right models were used to derive the right outputs. Aggarwal of Fluid AI said a larger opportunity lies in using AI to reinvent products and customer experiences.

Aggarwal pointed to Fluid AI's work with Forbes on an AI avatar of Warren Buffett, an interactive experience where readers could have personalised conversations with the avatar. He said it was initially meant to run for two weeks but stayed on Forbes for three years. Saravanan of Oracle said the challenge cuts across industries, with BFSI, government, manufacturing and IT/ITeS companies looking to scale AI adoption. Parkar of Spintly said the company deploys models on smaller hardware for facial recognition, QR code detection and anomaly detection, and these applications need low latency while operating on relatively low-cost devices. He pointed to the shortage of neural processing units, along with challenges around data centre capacity, cooling and power.

Aggarwal of Fluid AI said some organisations have invested heavily in AI models only to find newer models making those investments less relevant within a short period. He said the answer is to build AI architectures that can adapt rather than locking enterprises into a particular model or technology, and he called for building anti-fragile architecture because the technology is going to change so rapidly. The article says that flexibility also needs to extend to the AI plumbing, so enterprises should be able to switch between frontier, open-weight and smaller models without rebuilding their architecture. Ravi of PhroneticAI said enterprises need to understand what is happening across increasingly complex AI workflows, asking which agent is making what decision and what data is being consumed. He said enterprises are concerned about which model has been exposed and which MCP is available outside.

Thangavelu of Data Sutram argued that enterprises should build a repeatable harness around individual use cases rather than letting every use case be handled differently. The article states that the question is no longer just whether AI can work but whether it can deliver the right business outcome, reliably, sustainably and at the right cost. It says enterprises have never had greater access to artificial intelligence or faced more questions about how to deploy it effectively. The article notes that as increasingly capable models become accessible, companies are moving beyond pilots, and that as enterprise AI use cases scale, so do the challenges. The article does not say what any enterprise plans to do next, and it gives no further dates, figures or decisions beyond those above.

Articles.Title: How Enterprises Are Matching AI Workloads With The Right Models And Infra - Inc42
