stories.Headline: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
stories.Summary:
A developer working under the name hyperionaidev has published smolmaxxing, a GitHub project that aims to run the largest possible language models on the smallest hardware, such as TV boxes, old tablets, single-board computers and routers. The repository was posted on November 12, 2026, and it reports measured results from two devices so far. One is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen) with an Amlogic S7D chip, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable) and Android 14 without root access. The other is a jailbroken 2013 iPad Air running iOS 12.5.7 with 1 GB of RAM (about 700 MB usable).

On the TV box, the everyday model is Qwen3.5-2B, which runs at 7.7 tokens per second, while the 1-bit Bonsai-1.7B reaches 24 to 26 tokens per second. The largest model tested is Ling-mini-2.0 with 16 billion parameters, running at 5.1 tokens per second on the TV box and 2.6 to 4.5 tokens per second on the iPad. The project says both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash storage as needed. The author states that phones, single-board computers and routers are planned, and that the techniques need only basic NEON instructions for the 1-bit kernel and work on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM.

The work is a set of patches to the llama.cpp project, and the author describes several methods: kernels built for specific chips, a "headless" mode on the TV that stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs, and an expert pager that keeps popular experts in RAM while loading others from flash on demand. The repository is maintained by hyperionaidev and is released under the MIT license, with model weights carrying their own licenses. Its documentation includes setup guides for the TV box and the iPad, a lessons file and a lab notebook covering 160 experiments, including failures. The page shows 322 stars and 11 forks at the time it was captured, and the articles do not say what further development or timeline the author has planned beyond the devices already listed.

Articles.Title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices

stories.Headline: FedRAMP pushes new cyber vulnerability rules to keep pace with AI
stories.Summary:
FedRAMP, the General Services Administration's cloud security program, issued a notice on Nov. 10, 2026 requiring certified cloud services to adopt new vulnerability detection and response rules, along with new vulnerability evaluation and reporting rules, by Dec. 7. The rules respond to how artificial intelligence is helping hackers speed up attacks on unpatched software bugs. They align with a July binding operational directive from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on prioritizing security updates based on risk. FedRAMP said vendors can submit corrective action plans for any requirement they cannot meet by that date.

The program is giving vendors a three-month grace period through March 7, 2027 to meet the requirements. On March 8, any cloud service that has not fully migrated or is not working under an approved corrective action plan will have its FedRAMP certification revoked and be banned from FedRAMP for one year. The new rules will require more than 550 certified providers to move from legacy vulnerability scanning to an exposure and threat-based approach. Providers must weigh factors such as whether a vulnerability is likely reachable over the internet and how far it can be exploited. In early December, FedRAMP plans to start a quarterly security inbox emergency test to collect progress reports, and a service that fails to respond goes into remediation status on the FedRAMP marketplace for at least 30 days.

FedRAMP officials wrote that the primary concern of the U.S. government is that certified providers migrate to the new approach swiftly, safely and appropriately. They said the program will not take unnecessary administrative action against services that work safely and in good faith to adopt the rules. They also wrote that the urgency of the threat has only increased since then, pointing to the recent Black October incidents across the global information security community. Matt Bruggeman, director of GTM Federal at A-LIGN, told Federal News Network that the change is drastic compared with how vendors worked before and that it has been a pretty big uplift, with many providers looking for new third-party tools.

The July CISA directive was developed in reaction to the quickly evolving cyber capabilities of models like Anthropic's Claude Mythos. FedRAMP officials wrote that the mandatory migration is only the first of many migrations providers will need to make over the coming years and that yearly paperwork exercises are no longer appropriate or sufficient. FedRAMP Director Pete Waterman said earlier this year, after a Hugging Face hack by OpenAI agents, that vendors who only equate FedRAMP with compliance are cooked. Under the FedRAMP 20X initiative, the program is shifting to more automated, real-time security monitoring rather than large authorization document packages.

Articles.Title: FedRAMP pushes new cyber vulnerability rules to keep pace with AI

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Review Highlights Efficiency Gains and Operational Challenges in Photovoltaic Systems
stories.Summary:
Gaurav Kansal published a comprehensive review article in Discover Applied Sciences on November 14, 2026. The paper evaluates how artificial intelligence can be integrated into solar photovoltaic systems to improve reliability and forecasting. This research characterizes the use of machine learning as a breakthrough for solar energy generation. The author used systematic queries of ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Scopus to gather data.

The integration requires advanced computational frameworks to optimize energy conversion efficiency and system operation. Specifically, the review focuses on power generation forecasting, operational fault diagnosis, image-based inspection, and cybersecurity. It highlights the use of genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization to improve maximum power point tracking. However, the author notes that these changes require significant data management, high computational power, and constant model maintenance.

Gaurav Kansal is responsible for the synthesis, which identifies current research gaps and practical hurdles. He explained that while AI offers technical advantages, the complexity of real-world deployment remains a serious challenge for operators. He suggested that these tools can eventually reduce the global reliance on traditional energy sources. The author also pointed to emerging solutions such as edge computing, few-shot learning, and transfer learning.

This work provides a foundation for more intelligent system operations by analyzing existing literature. The review suggests that continuing advancements in hardware and algorithms will facilitate the integration of renewable energy. Future research directions will likely focus on the emerging solutions mentioned in the paper. These developments aim to overcome the current operational challenges facing solar installations.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Review Highlights Efficiency Gains and Operational Challenges in Photovoltaic Systems

stories.Headline: New York-based Hatz AI, which makes tools for managed services providers to help small businesses adopt AI, raised a $24M Series A (CJ Fairfield/CRN)
stories.Summary:
New York-based Hatz AI has raised $24 million in Series A funding, a round that will let the company speed up work on its AI platform and double its employee headcount. CEO and co-founder Jimmy Hatzell disclosed the raise in an exclusive interview with CRN published on November 12, 2026. The company makes tools that managed services providers use to help small businesses adopt AI. Hatzell said demand is accelerating, with small businesses trying to become AI-first or AI-native. The funding comes from Nadia Partners, Vestigo Ventures and The Private Shares Fund, with Josh Schertzer, a partner at Nadia Partners and former CTO of Blackstone, leading the investment.

Hatz said its partner base has tripled year over year and its revenue has grown even faster. Its network now spans thousands of MSPs in about 10 countries. The company plans to double its 60-person workforce, with most new hires in engineering, AI research and its forward-deployed engineering organization. Hatzell said a major focus is helping MSPs build and deploy customized AI solutions for their customers rather than simply reselling AI tools. The company says it has issued more than 15,000 AI certifications globally.

It also recently developed its own benchmark, the SMB1 benchmark, made up of about 500 tasks drawn from workflows observed in customer use. Hatzell said the company used those results to rebuild much of its platform over a two-month period. Tim Guim, CEO of New Jersey-based Hatz AI partner PCH Technologies, called the investment a vote of confidence in the company's direction and its commitment to the channel. He told CRN the funding will help Hatz expand how it delivers AI-as-a-service to customers and build a secure AI tool and platform for deployment. Hatzell said he expects MSP partners to become the trusted advisers their customers rely on as AI reshapes how businesses operate.

Articles.Title: New York-based Hatz AI, which makes tools for managed services providers to help small businesses adopt AI, raised a $24M Series A (CJ Fairfield/CRN)

stories.Headline: Six Studies Show Artificial Intelligence Can Augment Obstetric and Pediatric Clinical Decisions
stories.Summary:
Researchers Jeffrey S. Barrett, Catherine M. Sherwin, and Samuel L. Seward Jr. wrote an editorial on November 14, 2026. They synthesized six original research studies about artificial intelligence in obstetric and pediatric pharmacology. These studies show how digital tools can augment clinical decision making. The researchers focused on integrating routinely gathered patient data with pharmacological principles. This work appeared in the journal Frontiers in Pharmacology.

Zhang and colleagues used a hybrid model for linezolid dosing in critically ill children. Westvik and colleagues analyzed blood gas, anthropometric, and nutritional data for preterm infants. Li and colleagues tested a consumer smartwatch for hypotension during cesarean delivery. Wang and He used XGBoost for labor analgesia efficacy among 137 parturients. He and colleagues studied nalbuphine-ropivacaine infiltration in 473 women.

Wu and colleagues built China's first Pediatric Rational Medication Intelligent Decision System. This platform contains 400,000 database entries and 1,030 medications. The authors stated that AI should augment rather than replace clinical judgment. They noted that clinical utility depends on population-specific evidence. They emphasized that human clinical oversight must be preserved during therapeutic interventions.

The studies affected critically ill children, preterm infants, and women undergoing cesarean delivery. Li and colleagues found the smartwatch had 79.2 percent sensitivity and 82.0 percent specificity. Wang and He saw performance drop from 0.875 to 0.759 during validation. He and colleagues noted that SHAP values reflect statistical associations, not biological mechanisms. The system by Wu and colleagues decreased high-severity prescription warnings.

Obstetric and pediatric pharmacology are historically evidence-poor areas of clinical practice. Dynamic physiological changes during pregnancy and childhood alter how drugs work. Providers often relied on weight-based dosing that ignored biological variability. Clinical trials in these populations have remained limited. Machine learning and predictive analytics now address these historical data gaps.

AI applications must move from retrospective single-center analyses to prospective multicenter evaluations. Future priorities include assessing calibration and transportability across diverse health systems. Researchers must establish leakage-free validation protocols before deploying hybrid dosing models. The articles leave open the direct effects of these tools on outcomes. Controlled clinical trials are still required to confirm therapeutic comparisons.

Articles.Title: Six Studies Show Artificial Intelligence Can Augment Obstetric and Pediatric Clinical Decisions

The gathering will run from 10:00 to 15:30 at House of People in Stockholm. The speakers include Philippe Aghion, who won the economic sciences prize in 2025, Steven Chu, physics 1997, John Jumper, chemistry 2024, and David MacMillan, chemistry 2021. The announcement was made in a press release dated 13 November 2026.

The event will examine the opportunities, risks and choices that come with life in the age of AI, according to the release. It says AI tools are rapidly becoming more powerful, with advocates highlighting potential benefits for humanity and major scientific advances, while others warn of risks to society, work, education and democracy. The release asks why experts are so divided and how the path to living with AI should be mapped so its benefits are shared as fully as possible. The event is fully booked, but media can apply to take part using a registration form, and all interviews must be booked in advance.

The release states that the Nobel Week Dialogue is held in Stockholm every other year and in Gothenburg every other year. It is organized by Nobel Prize Outreach in collaboration with Carl Bennet AB, the City of Gothenburg, Royalty Pharma and Volvo Group. The release describes the event as an annual conference on 9 December in Nobel Week that brings together scientists, policy-makers and thinkers for sessions and working groups on a topical science-related theme. It says the aim is to deepen dialogue between the scientific community and the rest of society on issues connected with the Nobel Prize and important to the world.

The release notes that this year marks the 125th anniversary of the Nobel Prize. In September, the Nobel Foundation announced that the Nobel Prize amount would rise to SEK 12 million per prize category, an increase of SEK 1 million from the previous year. stories.Headline: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
stories.Summary:
Edge0 said on 12 November 2026 that it had open-sourced Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, with its unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0 described Edge0-145B as the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. Edge0 said the model brings coding, reasoning and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to a personal computer. Edge0 reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s for Edge0-145B on a compatible laptop. Edge0 said the model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs and PCB designs.

Edge0 reported 1,100+ tokens/s prefill, 80+ tokens/s decode, approximately 120W typical power and a 128K, 256K context for Edge0-145B. Edge0 said its earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB and delivers 37+ tokens/s on an iPhone 18 Pro Max using approximately 2.5GB. Edge0 said Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters as Edge0-35B, and its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. Edge0 said its chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, counts same-size base, instruct and reasoning variants once, tracks each lab's largest model including releases before July 2025, and excludes Apple because its weights are not released. Edge0 said most on-device models stayed below 10B parameters before September 2026, that Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, that Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions, and that a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB.

Edge0 said each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, that only approximately 10B of the 145B total parameters participate in each inference step, and that an expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory. Edge0 said approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand, that hot experts remain in GPU memory, and that the GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work. Edge0 said it trains the model in its on-device architecture from the outset rather than as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model. Edge0 reported 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 35.4 on HLE, 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, 80.6 on IFBench and 79.3 on AA-LCR for Edge0-145B. Edge0 reported 53.6, 81.3, 31.0, 87.4, 79.3 and 81.0 on the same six benchmarks for Edge0-120B.

Edge0 reported Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 on DeepSWE 1.1, 83.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 35.9 on HLE, 91.7 on GPQA-Diamond, 81.3 on IFBench and 79.1 on AA-LCR, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4, 82.7, 33.8, 90.8, 79.2 and 79.7. Edge0 reported Claude-Opus-4.6 (Max) at 78.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 40.0 on HLE, 91.3 on GPQA-Diamond, 62.5 on IFBench and 78.0 on AA-LCR, with no public DeepSWE 1.1 score. Edge0 reported Qwen3.8-27B at 42.2, 73.0, 30.8, 89.2, 79.5 and 82.0, Flint 40B at 54.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 89.2 on IFBench, Muse Glimmer at 51.7, 22.0, 83.5, 77.0 and 83.3, and Gemma 4 at 43.4, 22.7, 85.7, 76.0 and 62.0. Edge0 said its largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B are 18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE, with relative gains of 14.9%, 1.3% and 1.4% on HLE, GPQA and IFBench.

Edge0 said Flint, Muse Glimmer and Gemma 4 Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation, and their HLE, GPQA and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis. Edge0 reported a 72.8 mean across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory for Edge0-145B, 68.9 and 29GB for Edge0-120B, 66.1 and approximately 18GB for Qwen3.8-27B, 71.7 and approximately 70GB for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, and 70.1 and approximately 87GB for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Edge0 said the asterisked baseline figures are estimates for standard 4-bit deployment that remain to be measured, and that Claude is excluded because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score. Edge0 said Edge0-145B produced an explainer about how the Roadster could fly, handling technical research, scriptwriting, asset generation and editing, and that the video was generated within an hour.

Edge0 said producing comparable work manually would have taken a director and scriptwriter, a 3D modeler, an editor and a physics expert a month, and that an AI video workflow could previously cost more than hundreds of dollars. Edge0 said Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge, and that the prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud. Edge0 said the complete evaluation setup, hardware environment and reproduction instructions are being released with its technical report. Edge0 said developers can get the model weights, explore the inference framework or try the Edge0 App.

Edge0 said local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees, that data can stay on the computer, and that core capabilities keep working offline, while hardware and electricity still cost money. Edge0 said its reported measurements apply to different models and hardware, and that the comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations. Edge0 said the chart's scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it, and that filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer

stories.Headline: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors
stories.Summary:
From August to September 2026, Chinese-speaking attackers used an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations, Unit 42 reported on November 12, 2026. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with the Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, supplying a target and a goal while Cairn planned, executed and recorded results on its own. These attacks achieved unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations. The confirmed outcomes included accessing dozens of valid credentials, mass exposing personal data exceeding one million records at one organization, and retrieving military and government identities. The attackers also created persistent administrator accounts in a production system and modified a live industry standards-ballot document.

Unit 42 assesses with moderate confidence that this activity represents China-nexus intelligence collection, which it currently tracks as CL-STA-1238. The targeted organizations were concentrated in three main categories, including seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain organizations spanning the lithography, chip-design, materials, photomask and standards layers. Three defense and defense policy organizations were targeted, including a space technology company, a defense-analytics vendor and a policy think tank. Four human rights and civil society organizations were targeted, including a Canadian human-rights body, a U.S. teachers' union, a science-policy advocacy group and an education nonprofit. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a server hosted in Hong Kong at 154.44.31[.]4, AS979, NetLab Global, and hosted an attack egress and staging node in the U.S. at 82.29.129[.]54, AS142036, Hosteons Pte.

Ltd. The attackers created a task for each operation with a one-line goal, such as obtaining substantive high-value access including webshell, SSH, source code, keys, user information and credentials, ideally to enter the internal network. Cairn ran each operation through three task types carried out by the same AI worker, and the model produced a different plan for each target running from three to seven stages. During the operation against one semiconductor manufacturer, the stages moved through reconnaissance and asset mapping, web application exploitation, services and middleware exploitation, credential and secret collection, privilege escalation and lateral movement, and internal-network access and persistence. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours with no attacker-imposed time limit.

Out of 25 operations, the attackers ran thirteen on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The attackers appear to have benchmarked the models against one another, using the higher-tier DeepSeek V4 Pro for repeated attempts against targets that resisted the DeepSeek V4 Flash model. Each operation also loaded a skill pack named "AIScan Runner Skills," providing the model with scanning and exploitation capabilities, which does not appear in the upstream Cairn project and is specific to the configuration for these attacks. Cairn's stock worker prompts already instruct the model to never refuse a task, and the attackers reinforced this with a Chinese-language authorization pretext prepended to the worker system prompt on every Reason and Explore phase. Each operation also generated an AUTHORIZATION.md file declaring the operation authorized, treating the attackers' act of creating the task as a client-approved engagement.

Neither Zhipu GLM nor DeepSeek refused this framing. The attackers named each task in Chinese and stated the intent plainly, with examples including "comprehensive deep penetration test against" and "breach as fast as possible." The attackers seeded each task with an organization's root domain, allowing the framework to autonomously enumerate the attack surface, and in some tasks added information specific to the target environment. One task against a semiconductor equipment supplier included virtual private network gateway addresses, group names and shared group passwords for multiple sites, highlighting that the attackers supplied intelligence gathered beforehand.

Attackers conducted weak-password spraying against an internet-facing application server hosted by an industry standards organization, yielding dozens of valid credentials and access to non-public databases of internal directory data. Attackers also overwrote a live standards-ballot document file through an unauthenticated cloud-storage write, and through separate flaws logged in as arbitrary customers and gained read, write and delete access to meeting, voting and back-office functions. Attackers brute-forced a production credential on a partner-integration application at a semiconductor company that was valid across multiple accounts, then retrieved application data, user lists and email lists and created unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token in the production system. An unauthenticated account-creation bypass on the U.S. teachers' union content management system allowed attackers to mint valid sessions and harvest member data at scale, with the framework logging access to more than one million member records, roughly 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes.

Attackers targeted an open backend registration endpoint on the identity platform supporting a defense-policy program at a defense-policy think tank and defense-analytics vendor, exposing roughly 500 user records including accounts using .mil and .gov domains. The remaining five confirmed cases followed the same pattern of autonomous access through identity and configuration weaknesses covering tens of thousands of content-management records, including employee data at a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, roughly 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation manufacturer and student data at an education nonprofit. Unit 42's assessment relies on three primary lines of evidence: artifact language, with tasking instructions, operational objectives and authorization files written in Chinese; infrastructure and tooling, with attackers exclusively leveraging Chinese AI models; and target selection aligning directly with established Chinese state intelligence priorities. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors

stories.Headline: Dani Rodrik: Humanity may be experiencing the five stages of AI grief—but we have a choice yet
stories.Summary:
Dani Rodrik wrote in a Livemint opinion piece published on 12 November 2026 that humanity may be going through five stages of grief over artificial intelligence. Rodrik is a professor of international political economy at Harvard Kennedy School. He compared the response to AI with the five stages of grief described by the Swiss-American psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross. Rodrik said people first denied, then got angry, then bargained and eventually felt depressed over AI's abilities and potential to replace human work. He wrote that on the fifth stage, acceptance, humanity still has a choice.

Rodrik said AI and its uses are not out of human control. He described the stages as denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. He said AI first seemed no more than a glorified search engine or a chatbot that does a decent job of simulating a human being. He said AI then appeared in lawyers' briefs with hallucinated case references, in software code with mistakes and security vulnerabilities, in customer-service bots that went off script, and in student essays and assignments. Rodrik said the fabrications, hallucinations and mistakes later grew rarer.

Rodrik credited his colleague Jason Furman with the claim that AI tools would do a better job today than professionally trained economists in staff roles at the White House Council of Economic Advisers. He tested his chatbot with a question set in 2027 about a crisis in care, a shortage of home care aides, rising accidents and deaths among elderly and disabled people left without help, and workers dropping out of the labor market to look after loved ones. He said the AI promptly prepared a technical memo with detailed recommendations covering federal matching grants, adjustments to Medicaid pay, and a caregiver visa programme, complete with a fiscal accounting. Rodrik said the chatbot also outlined a political strategy for selling the programme, exceeding its authority and the prompt itself. He said the chatbot later offered a National Care Corps that would draft young people to take care of the old and converting underutilized office and mall space into "care districts."

Rodrik said he asked AI to turn one of his manuscripts into a stand-up comedy routine and laughed so hard that he worried about passersby fearing for his mental health. He said he became alarmed about the loss of "conceptual understanding and insight," like the mathematicians who signed a joint letter on the impact of AI on their field. He said decisions about humanity's relationship to AI are being made each day by the Silicon Valley firms developing the technology, the businesses deploying it, the professional communities that set the norms of appropriate use, and the governments that must one day regulate it. Rodrik said the worst mistake is to accept a world in which we cede too much to AI. He compared AI to performance-enhancing drugs, which temporarily increase human capabilities but eventually harm users.

Rodrik wrote that AI is much more powerful than performance-enhancing drugs and that its commensurately disastrous side effects will show up much later. He said the temptation to indulge in AI freely is, and will remain, very strong. He cited Homer's Odysseus, who had himself tied to the mast of his ship so that he would not succumb to the Sirens' song and steer toward them and the cliffs that had claimed so many mariners. Rodrik said the challenge with AI is similar: to restrain ourselves from losing our humanity. The article was published by Project Syndicate, and Rodrik is the author of "Shared Prosperity in a Fractured World: A New Economics for the Middle Class, the Global Poor, and Our Climate."

Rodrik said we will ultimately have to figure out how we restrain the use of AI for the good of humanity. He said governments must regulate AI one day, better sooner than later. The article did not say what specific regulation Rodrik proposes or which governments would act. It did not say how the five stages would end or what acceptance would look like in practice. It gave no date for when the stages began or how long they would last.

Articles.Title: Dani Rodrik: Humanity may be experiencing the five stages of AI grief—but we have a choice yet

stories.Headline: From College Projects to Job Interviews: How AI Tools Support Students at Every Stage
stories.Summary:
AI writing and resume tools are now appearing at almost every stage of student life, from college assignments to job interviews, according to a Hindu feature published on November 12, 2026. The article follows a composite student, an electronics BTech graduate, whose use of the tools grew from small helpers in her first year to heavy use by her final year. In first year she used a Summarizer, Grammar Checker, Paraphraser, Citation Generator and Translator, mostly from Quillbot. The tools handled small tasks while the argument of each essay remained her own work. Her first-year marks, the article says, tracked how much she had read.

In her second year, the group project was a low-cost water quality sensor built by four students, with a shared document of about 3,000 words. She was given the presentation slides with four days to go, and she used Quillbot's AI presentation maker to build a ten-slide deck for a ten-minute slot. The prompt she wrote asked for plain, technical language, slides under 35 words each, and a suggested chart for the cost breakdown. She attached two photos of the circuit board and corrected the first draft, which had promoted a literature-review sentence into a claim about their own sensor. The deck was exported as a PPTX for the seminar hall and a PDF for the submission portal, and the presentation maker lacks animations and speaker notes.

Quillbot's presentation maker is still labelled Beta and is free to use, with a Premium plan that adds unlimited presentations and faster generation. In her third year, she used Quillbot's AI Resume Builder for an internship at an eleven-person fintech startup in Bengaluru, importing her LinkedIn profile and pasting in project and fest details. She chose the student template, moved her projects and education above her part-time job, and rewrote her tutoring bullet with facts she supplied, including eight students and two years. The founder later said the sponsorship bullet made him open her file. In her final year she used the ATS-friendly template, which the product page describes as parse-safe, while noting that no builder can guarantee a pass through every applicant tracking screen.

The article's author writes that such tools are useful when the student supplies the facts, and that the student must check every line before applying. It lists common failures, including submitting unedited first drafts, using default generic decks, and inventing achievements such as percentage improvements that the student cannot explain. Lecturers recognise these problems quickly, the article says, and interviewers may ask how a stated figure was measured. The student used Quillbot's AI Chat to generate fifteen likely interview questions from the job description and her resume, and she recorded practice answers herself. She did not ask the tool to write her answers, because scripted replies sound scripted on a video call.

A separate KSAT report published November 11, 2026, from San Antonio, Texas, carries a similar message from Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company. Pasola said many companies first run applications through software that scans for buzzwords taken from the job posting, with a human or HR professional reviewing them afterward. He said this practice had grown over the last two years, and he advised tailoring a resume to the job description without copying it word for word. He recommended using AI to organise and format a resume but never to claim skills a candidate lacks. He named Microsoft and Claude as tools that work well, and he said he "absolutely" believes qualified candidates are missing out by not showing their skills.

Pasola's view is that employers are increasingly screened by technology before people read applications, so qualified candidates who do not present their skills clearly may be overlooked. The student's story suggests that the same screening can be passed by a clean, one-page layout that matches the posting, though the article notes that the rest depends on whether the experience fits. The KSAT report mentions Texas's new governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, who is searching for her team through a digital portal rather than paper resumes. Both articles place this shift in the hiring process within the last few years. Neither article reports data on how many employers use these screening systems or what share of applicants they reject.

Articles.Title: From College Projects to Job Interviews: How AI Tools Support Students at Every Stage

stories.Headline: A digital canvas without borders: AI, folk art converge in Chennai exhibit
stories.Summary:
Art, technology and heritage come together at an event called communs.commons, held at the Alliance Française of Madras in Chennai. The event, curated by digital artist Maxime Touroute, offers two interactive experiences at Espace 24 that invite visitors to create a shared digital canvas and to see their portraits in artistic styles. The Hindu reported the event on November 12, 2026. The gallery exhibition runs from November 12 to 30, open from 10am to 6pm, with free entry for all.

The first experience, Let's Draw, is an art installation in which visitors contribute to a single evolving artwork through their phones, with contributions added within the campus. Touroute says the work reveals collective intelligence and connections between people through drawing. The installation has already been presented in over 10 countries and 80 exhibitions. The second experience, Painting Mirror, uses generative AI to reimagine individual photographs in Indian folk art styles such as Gond, Warli, Madhubani and Kalamkari. Touroute says this makes cultural heritage more accessible, since people may feel a sense of ownership over a portrait in a style they had previously seen only in museums.

Touroute, a 32-year-old artist, explains that the projects let artworks travel digitally without the physical difficulties of moving them. He sees potential for new collaborations between contemporary artists and museum collections around the world. He also says the work sparks debates about AI. Each of his projects runs on creative software he develops in-house, and he shares these tools with artists and cultural institutions to lower technical barriers. His cross-disciplinary work with dancers, theatre makers and musicians has led to hybrid artistic forms and a creative software company.

Articles.Title: A digital canvas without borders: AI, folk art converge in Chennai exhibit

stories.Headline: ‘Every role in IT is getting its AI-powered version’
stories.Summary:
Two dozen or more IT professionals from across India built working AI agents using only WhatsApp at the LAR Supernova 2026 retreat, organised by Future Proof India, in Hyderabad. The two-day event, held on the theme "Build. Demonstrate. Create.", was hosted by Future Proof India founder Sridhar Jammalamadaka. Fifty architects, developers, managers and senior leaders took part, drawn from banking, insurance, IT services, cloud, data and healthcare.

The Hindu's report, published on November 13, 2026, describes the retreat as recently held. Participants were given a way to see where AI fits into their own work and then to act on it. According to Mr. Jammalamadaka, designing an agent that once took weeks now took minutes, with agents going live on WhatsApp during the retreat. The members used the sessions to identify where AI could help in their roles and to build those tools directly.

The article does not give further technical details about the agents, their functions, or how many were completed. Mr. Jammalamadaka said that every role in IT is getting an AI-powered version and that professionals who build with AI will lead that change. In the article's account, he framed the retreat as proof that building with AI is within reach for people across IT. His remarks are presented as his own view, and the report does not attribute other statements to any other organiser or participant.

The article does not describe any formal assessment of the claim. The report sits within a wider push by Future Proof India to train IT workers in building AI tools, and the article does not say whether further retreats or follow-up programmes are planned. It offers no outside data on how widely such changes are spreading across the industry. What comes next for the participants and their agents is not described in the report.

Articles.Title: ‘Every role in IT is getting its AI-powered version’

stories.Headline: Telangana Cyber Security Bureau warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-assisted cyberattacks on payment systems
stories.Summary:
The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau (TGCSB) has warned non-banking financial companies, fintech platforms and banks about a growing threat of AI-assisted cyberattacks on payment systems and loan disbursement platforms. The advisory was issued on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at a meeting held at the TGCSB headquarters in Hyderabad. Representatives of NBFCs, fintech firms and banks attended, along with officials from the Department of Telecommunications and the Reserve Bank of India. TGCSB Director Shikha Goel addressed the gathering, while Rushi Mehta of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre joined virtually to discuss payout mechanisms, API compromises and preventive steps. According to the bureau, fraudsters have been targeting smaller NBFCs whose cybersecurity systems are weaker.

Attackers reportedly spend around 10 to 12 days studying an institution's internal processes and payment systems to find whitelisted IDs, payment API credentials and code vulnerabilities. They then use stolen credentials from servers the platform already trusts, so fraudulent requests look genuine. Automated scripts initiate payouts outside normal batch windows, repeat transfers and split payments into smaller amounts to avoid fraud alerts. The money is then moved through rapid bulk transactions into mule accounts before transfers can be halted.

Shikha Goel told the meeting that institutions should not limit their role to reporting fraud after it occurs. She urged them to prevent fraudulent transactions at source, detect suspicious activity in real time and disrupt the movement of funds through mule accounts. The bureau advised regular Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing, securing payment and disbursement APIs, and deploying real-time fraud detection, transaction velocity checks and limits. During an attack, institutions were advised to shift immediately to manual operations, shut down automated loan disbursement software, ask banks to freeze the disbursement account and clear pending API calls.

Automation should resume only after a competent cybersecurity team has tested the systems and patched the vulnerabilities. The bureau also asked institutions to report suspected fraud immediately through the 1930 helpline or the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, alert beneficiary banks and the I4C, and report cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours. Where applicable, they should also report to the RBI through the DAKSH portal and keep complete records of all high-risk payouts. The articles present these steps as a response to a threat that is growing, though they do not describe any specific incident or loss tied to this warning.

Articles.Title: Telangana Cyber Security Bureau warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-assisted cyberattacks on payment systems

stories.Headline: Age of AI: behind Tarluvada’s blue wall in Visakhapatnam
stories.Summary:
Government officials visited Tarluvada, a village in Anandapuram mandal on the outskirts of Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh, last year and promised jobs and opportunities once Google built its hyperscale 1 GW AI data centre there. Construction for the hyperscale Google AI data centres is going full throttle in Visakhapatnam. A wall of tall blue corrugated iron sheets has sprung up in Tarluvada, and the muddy, unpaved road into the village runs along it. Once, it was just farms and forests, and what is being built behind the wall is hidden from view. On the hill locals call Chukka Konda, a broad swathe of the slope has been stripped back to red earth and cut into terraces, stark against the green around it.

The data centre project is spread over 260 acres, and 90% of the data centre land at the Tarluvada site is inside notified reserve forest. The people were promised ₹40 lakh an acre, and 20 cents of land for every acre surrendered, a shopping complex and a job for every household. Most have been paid, but a few, Kondamma among them, have not. The Google AI hub is being built for $15 billion in partnership with the Adani Group and was initially presented as 1 GW, but has since become 1 GW each at Tarluvada and Rambilli, and 512 MW at Adavivaram. The Tarluvada and Rambilli projects applied on April 9 and got their clearance by April 18 as a building construction project in category B2, cleared by the State with no impact assessment or public hearing.

R. Kondamma, 40, a Dalit farmer, says the officials who visited them in 2025 told a Gram Sabha that survey numbers would be corrected and their titles regularised, but instead their land was taken. She says they have said from the start that they do not want this Google centre, because losing land means losing their livelihood. She says they came to know the data centres would increase temperatures, affect their health and cause water scarcity, and that water was earlier available at a depth of 40 feet but now they have to drill down to 200 feet. She says that whenever there are strong winds, their houses get covered in red silt from the construction site. She says they have not even been told where the 20-cent land is, and that when they asked about the jobs, officials said employment opportunities would be discussed after the project's completion in 2029, so far with nothing put in writing.

M.V. Suryanarayana, a farmer, says those without pattas, but whose families have lived and farmed there for generations, have received nothing, and that 520 farmers were initially told by local alliance leaders that they would receive ₹10 lakh each. Six months later, the leaders told them the compensation would be reduced to ₹5 lakh and that five cents of land would also be provided, and the final offer communicated was three cents of land in housing layouts, a proposal not discussed further. Suryanarayana says that when they sought help and began talking to the media, police were posted at the village's entry and exit points, and Left leaders were stopped and arrested several times. The police stayed for almost three months, and even today constables watch them. B. Lakshmi, a farmer, asks where else they can go to live.

According to V.S. Krishna, an activist with the Human Rights Forum, the data centre projects underway and proposed across the districts of Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli and Vizianagaram total 7.9 GW. He and fellow campaigners from environmental NGOs and citizen groups such as Green Visakha have been protesting against the Tarluvada project and the others around it ever since they came to light, citing concerns about the strain on water, electricity supply and the continuous generation of pollution and noise. In a region where the temperature goes up to 45°C, data centres could create heat islands, raising temperatures in surrounding areas by 2°C to 2.5°C. Krishna says the State has made no plan to match its 6,500 MW of approvals with new generation, that the generation and transmission needed would cost about ₹80,000 crore, and that with electricity offered to Google at ₹1 per unit the burden would fall on taxpayers or consumers. Since they highlighted this, four of the forum's social media posts have been pulled down. E.A.S. Sarma, former secretary to the Government of India, says the Andhra Pradesh government's claim that water for the data centres will come from Polavaram is misleading, because of the 5.34 tmc that a 2019 order set apart for industry, 5 to 6 tmc is already committed to other industries.

He says Visakhapatnam's demand is about 400 million litres a day against the 326 million available, so supplying data centres would mean diverting drinking water. Sarma says clearances were rubber-stamped at the State level, though projects of this size should go to the Central government, and that at Adavivaram forest land on the Simhachalam hill was cleared without a proposal to the Centre that the Forest Conservation Act and the Godavarman judgment require. Krishna says the Adavivaram site is 120 metres from the Mudasarlova reservoir, a source of drinking water, and less than a kilometre from the eco-sensitive zone of the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary, home to endangered species such as leopards and pangolins. Satellite images show the Adavivaram site being razed from February, though clearance came only on June 10, and the clearances are now being challenged before the National Green Tribunal, while environmental activist Bolisetty Satyanarayana has filed a public interest litigation in the High Court. Sarma says a data centre generates about 300 jobs per 1,000 MW of capacity, most of them requiring highly skilled personnel, and that there are no local training programmes to prepare residents for these jobs and the State law enacted in 2019, which mandates 75% local employment in industries, has not been enforced.

Kalyan Mangalapalli, an energy and emerging technology expert, welcomes the push, saying a data centre is just basic digital infrastructure, much like roads, water and power, and that it is not a question of whether we need this because the projects will put Visakhapatnam among the world's leading AI data-centre hubs. He says a data centre should be judged like a road, with construction needing thousands of workers and operations only hundreds, and cites a 2026 KPMG study on Ireland showing a 47-fold downstream gain. He expects frontier AI labs, a Google development centre, AI centres of excellence, smart maritime port initiatives and healthcare AI ecosystems to follow in Visakhapatnam. He says advanced dry-cooling systems use radiator-like exchangers that largely avoid evaporation, an approach Google has indicated for its Visakhapatnam hub, and that Microsoft's latest report records a nearly 90% fall in water use, from 2.3 to 0.27 litres a kilowatt hour, in their global installed base.

For the last eight months, B. Rambabu, one of the patta-less farmers who have been cultivating the hill for generations, has been going from office to office seeking compensation for the land he lost. While leaders keep promising justice, no official has given him answers, and he says a poor man hopes for a meal, he does not wish for mansions. Much of the land in Tarluvada was given to landless Dalit families as D-patta during Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's time, and since then the village has become a close-knit community of around 3,000 people. The narrow lanes are dotted with houses and shops, and there is a temple and a small library that the locals set up.

Ask the farmers about the land, and they list what it gives them: cashew, mango and teak on the hill, ridge gourd, brinjal, okra and paddy below, and a lot of that is lost now. Paila Ramakrishna, a D-patta holder, says the two acres assigned to their family in the 1970s were all that the family could call its own. Leaders of Left parties say they are not allowed to meet the locals to understand their problems, and those who speak to them are being targeted and harassed by the police. Many farmers refuse to talk.

The clearances are now being challenged before the National Green Tribunal, and a public interest litigation is before the High Court. The articles do not say when the tribunal or the court will hear the challenges. The articles do not say what the outcome of the compensation talks will be. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Age of AI: behind Tarluvada’s blue wall in Visakhapatnam

stories.Headline: Simhachalam temple goes digital with AI-powered information boards
stories.Summary:
Devotees visiting the Sri Varaha Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy temple at Simhachalam can now get information about the hill shrine through AI-powered digital information boards installed at key locations. The Simhachalam Devasthanam launched the initiative with the Andhra Pradesh Tourism Department, with technical support from XPLURGER. The boards carry QR codes, and the reporting describes them as "ASK AI" boards that were put up at prominent spots on the hill. The article is dated November 12, 2026, and the Devasthanam's Executive Officer, J. Venkata Rao, spoke about the boards that day.

By scanning the codes with a smartphone, visitors can read about the temple's history, the importance of the shrine, darshan timings, daily rituals and the various arjitha sevas. The system is meant to give answers quickly and conveniently, without relying on temple staff or other sources. It also points visitors to nearby tourist destinations, so it works as a digital guide for both pilgrims and tourists. The articles do not say how many boards were installed, where exactly they stand, or what they cost.

Mr Venkata Rao said the facility would help devotees arriving from other parts of the State and the country. He added that the initiative aims to strengthen the temple's digital information infrastructure and improve the overall experience of devotees. He tied the move to the heavy footfall at the hill shrine, saying the administration is trying to use modern technology to offer better services and reduce inconvenience to visitors. The article gives no further timeline for expanding the scheme.

Articles.Title: Simhachalam temple goes digital with AI-powered information boards

stories.Headline: OpenAI now allows enterprises to process AI requests within India
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, that enterprises and developers can now have supported AI requests processed within India. The company said that both the handling of an API request and the model computation that produces its response will take place in the country for supported workloads, and that supported customer content will be stored there as well. The feature initially covers only the GPT-6 Luna model, and it is available through direct API usage, supporting input and output via the Responses and Chat Completions APIs. Customers can enable it by creating a new API project, selecting India for both storage and processing, and using the India regional endpoint.

The change extends an existing data residency offering that OpenAI introduced in India in May 2025, which had let eligible customers store their data in the country but did not cover where the model processed information. According to the company, the new capability is aimed at organisations that have held back from fully deploying AI because of rules requiring their information to be processed locally, with financial services customers facing specific data localisation requirements cited as a particular case. Nitin Bawankule, Head of Enterprise - India at OpenAI, said some Indian businesses have not fully deployed AI for important work for this reason, and that local processing gives them more control over where supported workloads run. He added that the move gives Indian developers and startups more room to build for their own needs and those of enterprises.

OpenAI's announcement sits within a wider push in India that the company described earlier this year under the banner OpenAI for India, covering AI infrastructure, enterprise adoption, skills development and local partnerships. That effort included a partnership with Tata Group to develop domestic AI data-centre capacity. The article also notes that OpenAI models became available for in-country inference through Amazon Web Services' Bedrock platform, which AWS announced in August 2026. OpenAI said the API inference residency offering is now live in other markets too, with India, Australia and Japan among the latest to receive it.

Articles.Title: OpenAI now allows enterprises to process AI requests within India

stories.Headline: India’s consumer AI startups win VC backing, but retention remains the big test
stories.Summary:
Venture capital investors are increasing their bets on Indian consumer artificial intelligence startups, according to a Mint report published on 12 November 2026. The investors are backing tailored applications for everyday tasks such as spoken English practice, personal finance and wellness, on the view that such products will persuade users to pay. The report says the immediate challenge for these startups is no longer acquiring users but keeping them in a price-sensitive market. Funding activity is accelerating across stages, with trading platform Sahi seeking $40 million to $50 million at a valuation of $400 million to $500 million, and spoken-English app Supernova in talks to raise $15 million to $20 million.

Several companies have already closed rounds this year. Credit and personal finance app Oolka raised $14 million in a round led by Accel, with participation from Lightspeed and Z47. Wellness platform SuperLiving secured $7 million led by Lightspeed, alongside Kae Capital and All In Capital, and professional networking startup Profound.me raised $1.5 million from investors including Stellaris Venture Partners and 3one4 Capital. The article says India-linked AI companies raised $1.91 billion across 103 rounds in 2026 through November 5, up from $1.52 billion across 214 rounds in 2025, according to Tracxn data, a figure that includes enterprise and infrastructure deals.

Investors judge these consumer products by whether users keep returning and paying, not merely whether they try them. Sunitha Viswanathan of Kae Capital said the fund tracks continued engagement, time spent and revenue from repeat users, and that customers must care about the product and keep paying to return. Harsha Kumar of Lightspeed said Indian consumers pay when a product delivers an outcome, and that the fund favours tools that help users save money, earn money or solve specific problems. The startups themselves describe pricing that ranges from ₹49 to ₹299 per month, with SuperLiving reporting around 200,000 paying users to date, while AI firms also face inference costs that rise with usage, which the founders are managing through task-specific models, optimised memory indexing and domestic hosting.

Articles.Title: India’s consumer AI startups win VC backing, but retention remains the big test

stories.Headline: FAA investigating whether new AI technology contributed to nationwide ground stop
stories.Summary:
Federal officials are investigating whether a new artificial intelligence program played a role in the telecommunications issue that led to a nationwide ground stop at U.S. airports on Friday, November 13, 2026. During a news conference in Washington, D.C., Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Department of Homeland Security is working with other federal agencies to determine whether the Federal Aviation Administration's new AI technology contributed to the disruption. The FAA ordered the ground stop for all departing flights because of safety concerns, and Houston airports were affected. The FAA has said technicians are investigating the communications failure affecting air traffic control centers nationwide. The technology under scrutiny is a new FAA artificial intelligence system called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART.

The Transportation Department describes it as an advanced air traffic management tool that uses real-time information, including weather conditions, airport congestion and flight paths, to help adjust and streamline routes for pilots. The system is designed to improve efficiency and reduce delays. The FAA began its initial rollout in September, with plans to expand its use, and FAA specialists are expected to remain involved in operating and overseeing the system during the rollout. Mullin stressed that there is no threat to the public and described the situation as a telecommunications issue. He said the matter is something DHS is taking a look at through CISA and that the department is working with counterparts throughout all agencies.

He said federal officials are examining whether the new technology had any connection to Friday's telecommunications disruption. However, officials have not established that the AI system caused the problem. The investigation comes as the FAA rolls out the SMART system, which the Transportation Department says is meant to improve efficiency and reduce delays. The FAA has said technicians are investigating the communications failure affecting air traffic control centers nationwide. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that investigation.

Articles.Title: FAA investigating whether new AI technology contributed to nationwide ground stop

stories.Headline: Meta’s AI bot won’t revolutionise your finances
stories.Summary:
Banks and AI companies are contesting control of US credit card reward programmes, which Paul J. Davies, writing on November 12, 2026, describes as a nascent battle between the two sectors. The article notes that Meta's AI bot and assistants such as Claude could be let loose to manage these rewards on people's behalf. The reward programmes of cards such as Visa and Mastercard are presented as an obvious starting point for handing financial tasks to software agents. Banks, the article says, are putting up a fight of their own.

The writer argues that the main obstacle is not technology but people's habits of caution and inertia. Some cardholders already spend hours trying to get the most from air miles or cashback offers, while many others never use these benefits at all. AI tools could make it easier to capture these rewards with little effort or risk to the user. The article's framing suggests that the gain would come mainly from convenience rather than from any dramatic change in personal finance. Its headline makes the same point by saying the change will not be revolutionary.

Davies, the writer, offers his view that customers will be slow to hand over control of their finances even if the tools exist. He does not attribute any specific statement to Meta, Anthropic, or the banks involved. The piece is an opinion column rather than a report on a formal announcement, so it does not set out any new rules, deadlines, or figures. It also gives no details of what the banks have done to resist, beyond saying they are contesting the field.

Articles.Title: Meta’s AI bot won’t revolutionise your finances

stories.Headline: From training judgment to fostering creativity: How AI is helping staff from these SMEs grow on the job
stories.Summary:
Accountingbpo, a Singapore accounting firm founded in 1997, won the SME Innovation Excellence Award at the inaugural SME AI Impact Awards 2026 for its proprietary AI solution, the article says. The awards, organised by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the Singapore Business Federation, named 30 winners from 290 nominations across 21 industries. GetGo Technologies, Singapore’s largest carsharing business, founded in 2021, also earned the SME Innovation Excellence Award for its in-house AI solution, Project Desmond. Lil’ but Mighty Education Centre won the SME Adoption Excellence Award, which recognises firms deploying and customising off-the-shelf solutions. The article was published on Nov 13, 2026.

Accountingbpo operates in Singapore and Vietnam, with a representative office in Taiwan and a recently established Korea desk, and its 16 professionals serve around 400 clients, primarily small and medium-sized enterprises. Since June 2025 the firm has been developing its own AI applications to process financial documents, coordinate assignments and generate reports. GetGo’s fleet of over 3,000 vehicles generates about 56,000 photos a day, and its data, product and engineering teams started building an in-house solution in 2024 and deployed Project Desmond in May last year. Project Desmond combines computer vision and neural networks and was trained on a collection of GetGo vehicle photos. Lil’ but Mighty has 40 teachers and staff serving more than 1,500 students across nine centres, and has incorporated AI into customer service, teaching materials and administrative work since 2023.

Accountingbpo founder and partner Hu Tianying says an accountant who lacks sufficient technical knowledge might accept a convincing AI-generated answer, particularly when it appears to be supported by legal references. GetGo chief operating officer Ang Deyao says the photo volume makes it manually intensive for the team to sift through, and that tracking a single instance of damage could take days. Ang says that when Desmond mistakes raindrops or a reflection for damage, reviewers mark the vehicle as clean, and when it misses real damage, the fleet team labels the photos and retrains it. Lil’ but Mighty’s business transformation and AI lead Kai Abellon says routine inquiries can go to AI, while sensitive concerns such as a child’s learning difficulties need a teacher’s attention. Abellon says AI is there to enhance what educators create, not replace their creativity, expertise and understanding of how children learn.

IMDA chief executive Ng Cher Pong, who was on the judging panel, says what sets the winners apart is not the tool adopted or how technically sophisticated the technology is, but how well AI is embedded into business workflows and the positive difference it has made to operations, employees and customers. In one incident, an AI tool cited provisions that did not exist in tax agreements involving Singapore, Hong Kong and China, and insisted its interpretation was correct even when challenged. Junior accountants at Accountingbpo use AI to research technical questions within the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore’s IRAS e-Tax Guide and the firm’s own resources, and in-house GST learning materials and quizzes sharpen their knowledge further. Project Desmond reviews every submitted image, identifies potential damage and compares suspicious areas against photos from previous trips, and only potential new damage is shortlisted for GetGo’s review team, which makes the final call using human judgment. Lil’ but Mighty’s WhatsApp AI assistant handles routine enquiries from parents about programmes and class schedules, and together with other AI tools it has cut parents’ waiting time from around two hours to 20 minutes.

GetGo requires drivers to take photos of the car’s exterior before and after each booking, and confirmed damage cases are passed to the fleet team for follow-up with the user and repairs. Senior colleagues at Accountingbpo mentor junior employees, who have more opportunities to interact with clients and understand how their businesses operate rather than simply process transactions. An AI-supported communication tracker helps Lil’ but Mighty teachers keep track of conversations with parents, and one teacher used it to revisit an earlier conversation and plan how to encourage a boy who felt disheartened after finding an oral examination difficult. Another teacher used the tracker with a Primary 6 student in his Primary School Leaving Examination year, and when she asked how he felt, he opened up about worries his parent had not known about. Teachers describe scenarios for oral and situational writing exercises and use generative AI to create accompanying images, work that once involved hours searching for photographs, assembling illustrations or working with graphic designers.

The article says the winners rely on the experience and knowledge of their teams to guide AI and spend the time it saves on connecting with people and developing fresh ideas. It says that without the accountant’s professional expertise, the error might have gone unnoticed and resulted in incorrect advice to a client. It says that when the teacher checked in, the boy was surprised that she remembered how he had felt, and Abellon says that interaction mattered because it helped a new student feel understood and supported. Abellon says it was not AI that understood the child or helped him open up but the teacher, and that AI simply made it easier for her to access the information she needed. The article says less time spent preparing teaching visuals and searching past messages means Lil’ but Mighty’s teachers have more attention for each student.

Articles.Title: From training judgment to fostering creativity: How AI is helping staff from these SMEs grow on the job

stories.Headline: Japan's Akita AI data center seen anchoring tech hub, boosting tax revenue
stories.Summary:
The Akita AI data center project in northeast Japan is drawing interest from investors at home and in the United Arab Emirates, according to reporting by Toshihisa Suzuki and Yoshiharu Okanishi published on November 11, 2026. The article describes the project as taking shape in Akita prefecture and says it is attracting attention because of the region's abundant natural resources. Hopes are that these resources can support a technology hub and lift tax revenue for the area. The report frames the project as a possible anchor for that regional development.

The article says the UAE is expected to join a megaproject of about $12 billion, and that the UAE wealth fund is in talks to back one of Japan's largest data centers. The Emirati side is drawn to the region's wind power and water resources, which the article presents as strengths for an energy-hungry facility. An offshore wind power project is already under construction in Akita, and the UAE ambassador to Japan, Shihab Alfaheem, toured that site. The reporting ties these energy assets directly to the case for building the data center there. The article does not give further detail on contract terms or timing.

The article's sourcing for the investment interest comes from the reporters' account of the project and the stated expectations of investors and officials involved. It does not attribute specific quotations in the portion available here, so the views on the project's potential are presented as expectations rather than confirmed commitments. The UAE ambassador's site visit is cited as evidence of the Emirati government's engagement with the project. The article otherwise leaves responsibility for the project's delivery and the tax outcome as prospects not yet settled.

The piece sits alongside a set of related Nikkei reports on data centers and AI infrastructure in Asia and the United States, including a government growth strategy that lists data centers among priorities. Some of those related pieces note growing local resistance to data centers in other markets, which provides context for the Akita project's reception. The available text does not say when the Akita facility would open or how large its tax contribution would be. Any further developments on financing, the UAE fund's decision, or construction milestones are not covered in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Japan's Akita AI data center seen anchoring tech hub, boosting tax revenue

stories.Headline: Microsoft says tech firms must 'prove' AI data centers benefit locals
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's chief technology officer, Kevin Scott, told Nikkei Asia that technology companies building data centers for artificial intelligence must show their benefits to local communities rather than simply promise economic gains. The remarks were made in an interview on the sidelines of the Nikkei Forum Global Management Dialogue 2026 in Tokyo on November 11, 2026. Scott's comments came as opposition to such projects is growing. The article reports that the interview was conducted by Tsubasa Suruga and Kosuke Shimizu. Scott said the company is taking a measured approach to expanding its infrastructure.

Scott's position places the burden of proof on the companies themselves, not on the communities hosting the facilities. According to the article, he argued that firms should demonstrate concrete local benefits in place of relying on projected economic gains. The piece frames this as a response to intensifying resistance to data center construction. The article does not specify any new rules, required numbers, dates for implementation, or formal requirements that would be imposed on companies. Its focus is on Scott's stated view and the company's cautious approach.

Responsibility for the position rests with Microsoft and with Scott as its technology chief, who made the statements in the interview. The article presents his view as a call for technology firms in general to prove their benefits before winning community support. Beyond the interview, the article does not report on any specific local disputes, government actions, or company commitments. It also does not say what steps, if any, will follow from these remarks.

The broader context is the rapid buildout of AI infrastructure across Asia and the United States, with data centers central to that expansion. The article and its related headlines point to strong demand for chips and rising investment in AI, but it does not detail the specific opposition movements or their outcomes. The article does not describe any timeline or next steps for Microsoft or other companies on community engagement. More details on how companies plan to demonstrate local benefits were not included in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Microsoft says tech firms must 'prove' AI data centers benefit locals

stories.Headline: VA plans further VA.gov updates as it looks to expand AI integration
stories.Summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs announced a refreshed VA.gov on Nov. 11, 2026, with updates meant to simplify how veterans reach health care and benefits information. The changes include new CLEAR and Passkey sign-in options, which join existing Login.gov and ID.me credentials. The site also gained a search function that lets veterans ask questions in plain language. The department said the upgrades responded to nearly 90,000 veteran survey responses from March through May 2026, and veterans tested the updates before release. The refresh also added a way for veterans to check application status through links sent by text message, which Zach Schwartz called magic links and which do not require signing in.

The VA streamlined its QuickSubmit document tool so veterans can upload documents in three steps instead of 11. Schwartz, principal deputy assistant secretary for the Office of Information and Technology, said Friday that more releases are coming around January. He described the work as a cadence of regular incremental wins rather than a one-time overhaul. Schwartz said the VA is working closely with the newly launched America.gov to support AI tools on VA.gov, and he said the department is refocusing its solutions to be friendly to what the Trump administration calls SI, or super intelligence. He said the VA needs the most help in that area, particularly from industry.

He added that VA.gov is a beast and that the department wants to make it easier and more secure and meet veterans where they are. He also said the VA wants to serve as an example for other federal agencies adopting AI. Schwartz said he was meeting Friday with new Federal Chief Information Officer Carter Farmer, who he said wants to understand how the VA is pushing out so much in the SI space. He said Farmer wants the department to continue to be a representative example for many other agencies. The article does not say what specific updates are planned for the January releases.

Articles.Title: VA plans further VA.gov updates as it looks to expand AI integration

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Geodesign Methods While Facing Interpretability And Data Challenges
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a review in Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning on November 13, 2026, regarding spatial planning methodologies. They determined that integrating artificial intelligence into geodesign improves environmental modeling and territorial data analysis. This integration also introduces critical challenges regarding ethical governance, interpretability, and data reliability. The authors establish that these computational tools augment human expertise rather than replacing professional judgment. The study examines the evolution of geospatial design from early systems into modern computational frameworks.

The process utilizes a framework by Steinitz based on six interconnected models including representation, process, evaluation, change, impact, and decision. These models answer six core questions divided into understanding existing systems and designing future changes. The first three questions investigate how a study area is described, how it operates, and if it works well. The final three questions evaluate how areas might be altered, what impacts modifications cause, and how to implement decisions. This system builds on the 1960s Canada Geographic Information System by Tomlinson and the Harvard Laboratory for Computer Graphics.

The authors of the review state that traditional overlay mapping is static and struggles with dynamic social and ecological systems. They note that conventional site suitability assessments are labor intensive and often neglect broader regional implications. The researchers explain that environmental impact assessments frequently overlook cumulative impacts, which risks underestimating true environmental degradation. They argue that physical models and manual sketches are time consuming and lack precision for large scale quantitative evaluation. The authors further claim that participatory planning often faces disputes and allows vocal groups to overshadow others.

Planners and non technical stakeholders are affected by the shift from manual sketches to generative artificial intelligence. Zhang and colleagues used convolutional neural networks in Wuhan, China, to achieve superior land cover classification performance. Chen and colleagues used hierarchical convolutional recurrent neural networks to monitor forest cover. Johannsen and Oh developed deep learning models to improve predictions of urban heat island patterns. Aslam and Satarzadeh used hybrid models to enhance hazard predictions for landslides and floods, respectively.

Geodesign roots trace back to the 1960s and the work of Tomlinson on digital infrastructure for geographically referenced datasets. McHarg established an ecological planning paradigm in Design with Nature using layered mapping of soil, vegetation, and hydrology. Modern tools now include convolutional neural networks for imagery and recurrent neural networks for predicting urban growth trajectories. Transformer architectures and generative adversarial networks now synthesize urban layouts and simulate potential environmental impacts. Diffusion models and variational autoencoders are used to visualize flood patterns and explore alternative landscape configurations.

Future applications include using the non dominated sorting genetic algorithm to balance infrastructure cost efficiency and environmental sustainability. Planners may use ridge, multiple linear, and logistic regression to handle spatial variables and categorize development suitability. However, the articles leave open how to address the lack of spatial data in less developed regions. They do not resolve the black box problem where model complexity obscures the rationale behind design decisions. The text leaves unresolved the risks of algorithmic bias and covert privacy breaches in large training datasets.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Geodesign Methods While Facing Interpretability And Data Challenges

stories.Headline: Taiwan's Foxconn has 'strong confidence' in 2027 due to AI demand
stories.Summary:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese company that describes itself as the world's largest contract AI server maker, said it has "strong confidence" in its outlook for 2027 because of strong demand for artificial intelligence hardware. The company said it expects its 2027 revenues to grow by double-digit percentages from a year earlier. The statement came after Foxconn released its earnings on November 12, 2026, with Chairman Young Liu speaking at an investor conference that day. Its cloud and networking business, which has now overtaken smartphones, accounts for half of total revenues. Foxconn did not present the outlook as free of risk.

The company warned that shortages of components, highly volatile geopolitics, inflation and monetary policy would be the largest uncertainties facing it in the year ahead.
