Those pressures could affect how smoothly it can meet the demand it is seeing. The articles do not give further figures on the shortages or the cost pressures. Liu, who is Foxconn's chairman, made the remarks to investors in Taipei. The reporting presents his comments as the company's own view of its prospects rather than a forecast by outside analysts.

The article itself is the source for the figures and warnings described here. The article places the company's results within a broader supply chain where AI demand is a central driver. The related coverage it links to discusses concerns about an AI slowdown and questions about rising competition among server makers, but the source article itself does not say how those debates will resolve. Based on the available reporting, the company's next major update on its outlook has not been detailed.

Articles.Title: Taiwan's Foxconn has 'strong confidence' in 2027 due to AI demand

stories.Headline: Why city is losing ground in AI data centre race as Malaysia, Singapore advance
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong is currently losing its competitive edge in the race to build AI data centres. This decline became evident in a recent report published on November 13, 2026. Regional competitors like Singapore and Malaysia are now advancing more quickly. The city was once seen as a prime location for this digital infrastructure. However, it has now fallen behind its neighbors in the Asia-Pacific region.

The shift in rankings shows a significant drop for the city. In 2023, Cushman & Wakefield ranked Hong Kong as the fourth-best data centre market in the world. This year, the same consultancy did not even place the city among the top 10 Asia-Pacific markets. Other locations such as Shanghai, Sydney, and the Malaysian state of Johor are now standing out. These changes highlight a growing gap in computing power.

Experts are now considering how to overcome the constraints on the local digital infrastructure. They note that the demand for computing power is currently outstripping the local supply. Data centres are spreading into various areas, from Kwai Chung to Tseung Kwan O. These facilities occupy everything from compact industrial buildings to large factory premises. The goal is to restore the city's status as a tech hub.

The government previously branded the city as a prime location for these facilities. Despite this official support, the reality of the market has been less kind. The city must now find ways to compete with the rapid growth seen in other Asian markets. Future success depends on solving the current supply and infrastructure issues. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why city is losing ground in AI data centre race as Malaysia, Singapore advance

stories.Headline: Utah Invites Public to Vote for Nine Pro-Human AI Finalists
stories.Summary:
Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce announced nine finalists for the inaugural Pro-Human AI Elevation Awards and opened public voting to Utah residents, according to a November 13, 2026 announcement reported by TechBuzz News. Voting runs through November 20. Winners will be announced December 8 at the 2026 Utah Pro-Human AI Summit at the Grand America. The awards recognize Utah-connected companies using artificial intelligence to empower workers, strengthen communities, and build human-centered principles into technology.

The nine finalists are grouped into three categories. Workforce Elevation, for companies using AI to help employees do more, learn faster, and develop new skills, includes ARUP Laboratories, Techcyte, Inc., and XL PR. Community Advancement, for companies using AI to address needs in areas such as healthcare, education, public safety, and government, includes Leland Makombo, Skill Struck, and Pro-Human Breakthrough, which covers companies building AI products with accountability as part of their design, includes Autonomous Solutions Inc. (ASI), Elnora, and Glacis Technologies, Inc. Each Utah resident must affirm residency and may submit only one ballot, selecting one finalist per category and separately nominating one of the nine for the overall grand prize. The public vote determines the winners in all three categories and contributes to selection of the grand prize recipient.

Gov. Spencer J. Cox said artificial intelligence should make people's lives better and help workers succeed, and that the companies are showing what that can look like in practice. He said the state wants to recognize their work and challenge more businesses to put people at the center of how they build and use the technology. Jefferson Moss, commissioner of the Governor's Office of Economic Development, said Utah has built a strong innovation economy and that a wave of companies are developing and using AI in ways that put people first. He said the awards recognize those companies, share what they are doing, and encourage more of this kind of innovation, and that the state wants an economic environment and a Summit that make clear human-centric AI is how Utah does business.

The awards are organized by Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce and spotlight companies that emphasize human agency, dignity, and accountability rather than simply automating tasks or replacing people. The effort builds on the 2025 Utah AI Summit at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City, which advanced the state's push to shape AI around human agency, workforce empowerment, and responsible innovation. Residents can review the finalists through their videos and cast ballots through the official online voting form. Winners will be recognized at the December 8 summit, and more information is available at aisummit.utah.gov.

Articles.Title: Utah Invites Public to Vote for Nine Pro-Human AI Finalists

stories.Headline: LG CNS brings global robotics experts together to advance physical AI
stories.Summary:
LG CNS gathered more than 100 researchers and industry professionals at its 2026 Robotics & Physical AI Forum, held at its Future Robotics Lab in Magok, Seoul. The event drew faculty members, graduate students and company employees from the University of Toronto, Sogang University, Chung-Ang University and Korea University. Discussions covered how physical artificial intelligence could move from laboratories into factories, warehouses and other industrial settings. The company reported the forum in a article published on November 12, 2026. Participants talked about robot foundation models, data, intelligent robotic hardware and simulation, along with the technical problems of running these systems in real operations.

LG CNS pointed to more than two decades of experience and over 1,000 smart factory and smart logistics projects as the basis for its approach. It also introduced two platforms launched this year, PhysicalWorks Forge, a robot-learning platform, and PhysicalWorks Baton, an agentic AI platform for managing robot operations. Participants also exchanged views on manufacturing and logistics applications, the capabilities companies and universities will need, and how human roles may change. Professor Lee Chi-geun of the University of Toronto presented research on building robot foundation models and the technology needed to deploy them on physical robots. He described combining data from different robot types, along with flow matching and action chunking, methods meant to produce smoother, more continuous robot movements.

According to the presentation, differences in robot movement, latency and data availability remain obstacles to the technology. LG CNS executive vice president Lee Jun-ho, who heads its Smart Logistics & City Business Division, said the company hopes ongoing work with academia will strengthen its technological competitiveness and help research lead to innovation in actual industrial settings. The article notes that the company's engagement with universities is meant to turn research into practical industrial results, though it gives no timeline or specific next steps. The piece was published with the help of generative AI and edited by The Korea Times.

Articles.Title: LG CNS brings global robotics experts together to advance physical AI

stories.Headline: KBS returns after three years with the epic period drama ‘Munmu’… Will its AI battle scenes surpass ‘Goryeo Khitan War’?
stories.Summary:
KBS is returning after three years with a new epic period drama, "Munmu," which is scheduled for its first broadcast on KBS 2TV at 9:20 p.m. on the 14th. The production presentation was held on the 12th at a hotel in Guro-gu, Seoul, where KBS President Park Jang-beom, CP Lee Ho, and several cast members attended. The drama centers on Silla King Munmu, played by Lee Hyun-wook, and covers the Silla-Tang War that followed the unification of the Three Kingdoms. It is the first epic period drama KBS has aired since "Goryeo Khitan War."

The series stands out for its large-scale war sequences, which use artificial intelligence to recreate the Battle of Jupilsan, the Battle of Maesoseong, and the Battle of Gibeolpo. CP Lee Ho said the production took about a year and a half from planning through filming, and that the team used the technology for dangerous scenes or for parts that were hard to achieve with conventional methods. He noted that the Gibeolpo sequence, set against mudflats and the sea, suited AI video technology, and that the tools had advanced further during production. Jang Hyuk plays Yeon Gaesomun, Kim Kang-woo plays Kim Chun-chu, and Choi Ye-bin plays Empress Wu Zetian.

Lee Ho explained that the team chose King Munmu as the focus because he is less familiar to viewers than figures such as Yeon Gaesomun, Kim Chun-chu, and King Uija. He said the story of how Silla repelled the Tang offered fun, meaning, and emotion that many viewers may not know. Lee Hyun-wook described King Munmu as a master of restraint, and said he worked on showing the king's gradual decision to protect the nation, while Kim Kang-woo spoke about the challenge of portraying a real historical figure who persuaded rivals with words rather than a sword. Choi Ye-bin said she approached Wu Zetian as someone who made careful choices to survive within the imperial court. The cast and crew also said the project relied on historical records and expert consultation, a response to the historical distortion controversy that surrounded "Goryeo Khitan War."

Articles.Title: KBS returns after three years with the epic period drama ‘Munmu’… Will its AI battle scenes surpass ‘Goryeo Khitan War’?

stories.Headline: In broadcasting battle, ‘Sword & Silence’ aims to reign supreme with assist from AI
stories.Summary:
KBS is reviving the historical epic with its new 28-episode series "Sword & Silence," which uses AI extensively, chief producer Lee Ho said at a press conference at the Link Seoul hotel in Guro District, western Seoul, on Nov. 12. The series follows Kim Beop-min, who becomes King Munmu of Silla and leads the kingdom through the final stages of unifying Korea's Three Kingdoms in the seventh century. After the fall of Baekje and Goguryeo, he joins forces with people from the defeated kingdoms to drive out China's Tang dynasty and secure Silla's independence. The Battle of Mount Jupil relied largely on conventional visual effects, while the Battle of Maesoseong, fought between the forces of Silla and Tang, made greater use of AI. The technology played an even greater role in recreating Silla's decisive naval victory over the Tang at Gibeolpo, a sequence still in postproduction at the time of the press conference, Lee added.

Lee said AI had advanced considerably over the year and a half the team worked on the series, and that whenever new technology became available, they tried to incorporate it. He said AI was used to recreate dangerous scenes and moments that needed to look realistic, including shots no longer filmed individually using conventional methods. Actor Jang Hyuk, who plays Goguryeo military leader Yeon Gaesomun, said acting against an AI-enhanced backdrop was challenging, if necessary. One scene filmed in Mongolia required him to deliver a speech before some 450 horses, even though the scene was meant to depict him addressing an army of 150,000. Jang said he does not think AI is perfect yet, particularly when it comes to conveying emotion, and that actors still have to be at the center of it, bringing the emotions to life while the technology fills in what is around them.

"Sword & Silence" marks KBS's return to historical epics three years after "Korea, Khitan War" aired in 2023, with the most recent forays by rival terrestrial broadcasters MBC and SBS coming in 2012 and 2007, respectively. The budget for "Sword & Silence" has reportedly reached 30 billion won ($22.6 million), surpassing KBS's previous record of 27 billion won for "Korea, Khitan War." Without confirming the figure, Lee said the scale of the series, which spans multiple kingdoms and empires, required substantial investment to recreate the period's architecture and warfare. Lee said producers took "extensive effort" to avoid historical-accuracy controversies, such as basing the story on historical records and working closely with academic advisers to review important details.

Such controversies have affected not only historical epics like "Korea, Khitan War," but also modern fictional dramas such as MBC's "Perfect Crown" this year. KBS pledged in October of last year to produce a historical epic every year, following the reinstatement of a system that collects television license fees with electricity bills. President Park Jang-beom said Thursday that the change had helped stabilize the broadcaster's finances. Park also emphasized the series' central theme of unity, drawing parallels between divisions in modern Korean society, including conflicts over gender and political ideology, and the struggles to unite the ancient kingdoms fictionalized in the drama.

Park said he hopes politicians will watch the drama too, and that they can learn something from the leadership of ancestors who overcame conflict and division to achieve unity. While Silla's unification of the Three Kingdoms has long been a popular subject in Korean historical dramas, King Munmu himself has rarely taken center stage, overshadowed by figures such as his father, Kim Chun-chu, and Yeon Gaesomun. For Lee Hyun-wook, who plays the titular role, the lack of previous portrayals offered more creative freedom, and he said he was excited by how much room there was to explore the character rather than feeling pressured. Lee described Munmu as a master of restraint and said the challenge was figuring out how to convey his ability to embrace his people and his country without making him overly emotional.

"Sword & Silence" premieres on KBS on Saturday and will stream globally on Netflix. The series was reported by Kim Ju-yeon, lifestyle and entertainment reporter, and published on November 12, 2026. Jang Hyuk, Lee Hyun-wook and Kim Kang-woo posed for photos at the press conference on Nov. 12. More to follow.

Articles.Title: In broadcasting battle, ‘Sword & Silence’ aims to reign supreme with assist from AI

stories.Headline: Huang's exit puts Nvidia leadership, AI policy in focus
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as the president, chief executive, and board member of Nvidia on Thursday, November 13, 2026. His immediate departure followed his admission of an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman and reports of two other affairs with company employees. This sudden leadership change caused Nvidia shares to drop as much as 14 percent, eventually closing at $166.19. The company ended the day with a market value of $4.01 trillion.

The company now requires a permanent replacement for Huang, while Colette Kress, the chief financial officer and executive vice-president, will serve as the interim chief executive. The board is currently reviewing both internal and external candidates for the role. This transition occurs as the stock has fallen about 30 percent from its peak in October. Meanwhile, the company faces intense scrutiny from Congress and the FBI regarding national security and chip sales.

House Speaker Mike Johnson stated that there is a growing consensus in Congress to limit the export of semiconductor chips to China. Analysts from SemiAnalysis, including founder Dylan Patel, suggested that restrictions on China will likely accelerate now that Huang, a primary defender of market access, is gone. Ker Gibbs, a former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, noted that Nvidia lost its most effective advocate for the Chinese market. He believes the company will become more cautious and spend less time lobbying against export controls.

The situation may shift the balance of influence in Washington, as Huang had unique access to the White House. Lawmakers are considering whether Huang should provide congressional testimony this month to determine if national security was compromised. Observers will now monitor next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation. Future developments depend on the selection of a permanent leader and the results of ongoing government investigations.

Articles.Title: Huang's exit puts Nvidia leadership, AI policy in focus - China Daily

stories.Headline: President Lee, Samsung break ground on massive AI chip hub in Chungcheong region
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung and Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong broke ground on a high-tech industrial hub in the Chungcheong region on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The ceremony took place at Samsung's semiconductor packaging plant in Asan, South Chungcheong, and launched the government's megaproject initiative to grow the AI industry. The groundbreaking was for the site's fifth production line, a three-story high bandwidth memory facility with a 31,000-square-meter cleanroom. The Onyang campus project aims to begin operations by June 2028 and will expand the site from 270,000 to 420,000 square meters. Samsung plans to invest a total of 144 trillion won in the Chungcheong region, including 46 trillion won to build five HBM production lines.

The project is expected to create some 700 related jobs at Onyang, which will become a hub for advanced packaging technology essential for AI computing. Samsung's Onyang campus will also see a new packaging fab costing 6 trillion won, followed by an additional 40 trillion won in advanced equipment. The government's megaproject initiative covers semiconductor development, physical AI technologies and AI data centers outside the Seoul metropolitan area, with a total of 4.7 quadrillion won ($3.5 trillion). In July, Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and other leading companies had unveiled plans to invest some 392 trillion won in the Chungcheong region. Beyond that original figure, 112 companies in sectors such as semiconductors and biotechnology are set to invest an additional 23.6 trillion won.

President Lee said the government will concentrate its policy efforts so that the megaproject becomes a growth opportunity that improves local residents' lives and achieves balanced national development. Samsung Executive Chairman Lee said the Asan site, which previously focused on simple assembly and testing of standard semiconductors, will be transformed into a cutting-edge HBM hub at the heart of AI semiconductors. President Lee thanked Lee Jae-yong and the company's employees for their bold investment decisions and swift execution. He also credited local governments, including South Chungcheong Province and Asan, for speeding up construction by expediting the permit process. Lee added that preparations for other key facilities, including a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data center in Dangjin, and a biopharmaceutical facility in Osong, are proceeding on schedule.

Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan, local government heads, Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman and CEO Jun Young-hyun and Daeduck Electronics Chairman Kim Young-jae attended the ceremony, along with some 100 officials and business executives. During a closed-door session of a fourth public-private meeting held after the ceremony, President Lee instructed his aides to pursue policy-based financing for small- and medium-sized enterprises more boldly. According to presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan, the president said financial support is essential for sustainable, region-led growth. A university student from Chungnam National University in Daejeon, So Ju-won, spoke at the ceremony about job prospects and said he had an interview at Samsung Electronics next week. The articles do not report how business leaders or local residents outside these events responded to the project.

Samsung's Onyang campus has long served as a center for chip assembly and testing, and the articles describe the site's shift toward advanced packaging and HBM. The articles do not give further background on the earlier 392 trillion won plan beyond its July announcement. President Lee said economic growth is essential to bring hope to the people and pledged proactive measures for challenges faced by business leaders. The articles do not say how the new fab's 700 jobs will be filled or what the financing arrangements for smaller firms will involve. They also do not specify when the other planned facilities in Cheongju, Dangjin and Osong will break ground or open.

Articles.Title: President Lee, Samsung break ground on massive AI chip hub in Chungcheong region

stories.Headline: Nvidia loses its 'Godfather of AI' and now faces first big test without him
stories.Summary:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the company on Thursday, after reports of two extramarital affairs and a board investigation that followed. One of the relationships was with a Chinese businesswoman whom United States authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia announced that Colette Kress, its veteran chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive. The news roiled the company's stock as investors and analysts weighed the path ahead for the artificial intelligence chip giant. Earlier reports had said the board was preparing to oust Huang, and the stock had already fallen on those reports.

Nvidia shares fell roughly 14% from Wednesday's closing price, reaching an intraday low of $148.80 per share before paring those losses. By early afternoon the stock was down only 4.3%, and the latest quote showed it at $166.19, a fall of $7.54. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it to the forefront of the artificial intelligence trade. Nvidia reports its earnings next week, and investors will examine the results closely for a fresh read on demand. The company is also expected to face continued scrutiny over its business dealings with China and any loopholes in export controls.

Nvidia's board of directors is the body that investigated the affairs and now steers the company through the transition. Kress, as interim chief executive, takes responsibility for running the company while it works out its future leadership. The articles quote no direct statement from Huang, from Kress or from the board beyond the announcement of her interim role. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said the resignation lets the board remove the problem quickly and take Nvidia into its next chapter without Huang. Ives added that the company already has a strategic roadmap built around its next family of chips, which Nvidia hopes will keep powering the artificial intelligence boom.

Bret Kenwell, an investment analyst at eToro, said Huang was more than a chief executive and was part of the investment thesis, which will bring greater scrutiny to next week's earnings report. Kenwell added that leadership questions do not erase Nvidia's position as a best-in-class technology company during a transformational period for the sector. James McCann, a senior economist at Edward Jones, pointed to the lack of a clear succession plan and to the financial role Nvidia has played in backing other parts of the artificial intelligence sector. McCann said the corporate fundamentals are unchanged, and the firm advises investors to avoid over-concentration in technology companies and to hold well-diversified exposure across large and midcap American stocks. Inc42 reported that the scandal adds uncertainty for India's neocloud providers, firms that rent out graphics processing units and depend on Nvidia's ecosystem.

Investors had already been selling shares of American neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN suffering sharp corrections that intensified through October and into November. McCann noted that the Nasdaq had delivered gains or losses greater than 1% in seven of the past 10 trading days. Ives said Nvidia remains the clear leader in graphics chips for the artificial intelligence revolution, roughly two to three years ahead of the nearest competitor. His firm holds a price target of $225 a share and an outperform rating on the stock. Inc42 said Nvidia's influence now extends beyond chip supply to financing and strategic partnerships, and that India's neoclouds rely on international customers, government-backed demand and evolving financing arrangements.

The most immediate event is next week's earnings report, when shareholders will look to Nvidia for stability, a fresh read on demand and a reason to regain confidence. The articles do not say who will become the permanent chief executive, and Kress serves only on an interim basis. McCann said it remains to be seen whether a change at the top will materially affect strategy and execution. Ives said the outlook assumes continued headwinds from China-related scrutiny, which he considers already factored into the stock at current valuation. Inc42 left open whether Indian neoclouds will keep the financial backing and customer commitments needed to withstand a global market correction, including CoreWeave's plan to be sole tenant of a 240 megawatt AdaniConneX data centre campus in India.

Articles.Title: Nvidia loses its 'Godfather of AI' and now faces first big test without him

stories.Headline: Meta AI Predicts DOGE Vs. PEPE: Which Goes Higher in 2027?
stories.Summary:
Meta AI predicted which of Dogecoin (DOGE) and Pepe (PEPE) will go higher in 2027, in an article by Ahmed Barakat published by Cryptonews on November 12, 2026. The article was fact checked by the CryptoNews Editorial Team and last updated on November 12, 2026. As 2026 winds down, DOGE and PEPE remain two of the most closely watched meme coins, and both have suffered significant drawdowns from prior cycle highs. Meta AI concluded that Dogecoin appears better positioned for more meaningful, relatively sustained gains than Pepe, though both will likely move with the broader crypto market.

Dogecoin was trading around $0.066 to $0.067 in mid-November 2026, down roughly 20% over the past month, with support near $0.065 to $0.066 and resistance around $0.070 to $0.072. A more meaningful barrier sits near $0.08, and a sustained reclaim of $0.08 to $0.10 would be needed to signal a more constructive trend reversal. Pepe was trading near $0.0000044, far below its late-2024 all-time high, with support tested in the $0.0000042 to $0.0000044 region and resistance layered near $0.0000050 to $0.0000055. The article's ticker showed DOGE at $0.065, down 2.69%, and PEPE at $0.0000045, down 0.28%.

Meta AI said the key differentiator is structural development, since Dogecoin has been making tangible progress beyond pure meme status. It pointed to the near-term launch of DogeOS, an Ethereum-compatible Layer 2 app layer designed to bring smart contracts, DeFi features and additional utility to the Dogecoin ecosystem. Meta AI said reports indicate the project is close to mainnet after completing version 1 and audits, with over 100 developers already building. It said integrations with wallets, oracles and potential zero-knowledge upgrades support the idea that DOGE could gradually shift from a pure tipping and meme asset to something with broader use cases.

Meta AI said Pepe remains a pure-play meme coin driven almost entirely by social sentiment, influencer commentary and speculative rotation. It said PEPE's relatively lower market capitalization gives it higher explosive potential in a strong risk-on environment, but that same pure-meme character makes its upside more fragile and dependent on continuous attention. Meta AI said PEPE's 2027 gains are more likely to be episodic than structurally supported, and that PEPE may deliver bigger short-term percentage spikes during meme-season rotations. It said Dogecoin's brand recognition, liquidity and emerging utility give it a higher probability of stronger, more durable relative performance over a full-year horizon.

The article said Dogecoin's momentum indicators have cooled and volume has remained moderate during the decline, and that on higher timeframes the chart shows a series of lower highs. It said longer-term holders still view the $0.06 area as a potential accumulation zone if broader market conditions improve. The article said PEPE has seen double-digit percentage swings in recent sessions, that volume has occasionally spiked during social-media-driven moves, and that throughout 2026 these spikes have failed to generate sustained demand. It said ecosystem initiatives such as Dogecoin Labs signal an attempt to professionalize development and reduce reliance on pure social hype.

The article said a potential broader market recovery is possible in 2027, and that in a recovering or bullish crypto market both coins should rise. It said the tokens that add real, even if modest, utility while retaining cultural relevance have historically held up better across full cycles than those relying solely on memes. The article did not give a specific price target for either coin in 2027. It also did not say when DogeOS will reach mainnet beyond describing the launch as near-term.

Articles.Title: Meta AI Predicts DOGE Vs. PEPE: Which Goes Higher in 2027?

stories.Headline: Alphabet Climbs 3% as NVIDIA’s Leadership Shake-Up Puts Google’s AI Chips in the Spotlight; Microsoft Gains 2%, Amazon Ticks Up
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA announced on November 12, 2026, that Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The announcement came in a company statement that day, and NVIDIA stock fell 6% in Thursday's trading. Alphabet stock rose 3% to $301.97 in Thursday's trading, and Broadcom stock rose 5%. Microsoft stock rose 2% to $528.98, and Amazon stock rose 1% to $269.49. The buying in Alphabet reflected investor speculation about where future AI chip spending could flow.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while keeping her finance role. NVIDIA's board is weighing internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. NVIDIA's products and existing contracts remain in place through the leadership change. Harvey Jones was named the board's first-ever chair. NVIDIA plans to report its Q3 FY2027 results on November 17.

Harvey Jones said the board expects the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Sundar Pichai, Alphabet's CEO, said on October 28 that the company was also seeing strong demand for its TPU systems across a wide range of customers. Andy Jassy, Amazon's chief executive, said on the company's latest earnings call that the number of companies with a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two. Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, called his company's mix of NVIDIA hardware and its own Maia systems inside Azure a "fungible fleet" that moves capacity to the highest-value work. Google sells TPU systems to a wide range of customers through Google Cloud.

Google Cloud revenue rose 103% year over year to $30.71 billion in Q3 2026, results Alphabet reported on October 28. Azure revenue at Microsoft grew 48% in the quarter ended in September. AWS revenue rose 39% over the same stretch, both well behind Google Cloud's pace. Broadcom helps Google design its TPUs. Amazon runs most of its Bedrock AI service on in-house Trainium chips and is preparing to sell those chips outside AWS.

Alphabet's capital expenditures reached $51.36 billion in Q3, and its free cash flow came in at negative $9.07 billion. Alphabet is funding part of its infrastructure push with debt and at-the-market share sales. Microsoft and Amazon both develop their own AI chips while buying heavily from NVIDIA. Their data centers lean on NVIDIA hardware even as their in-house chips mature. Alphabet has a longer track record in custom AI chips than Microsoft and Amazon.

Alphabet will soon see if TPU demand keeps building as NVIDIA works through its leadership transition. NVIDIA's November 17 release could show whether its customer relationships are holding steady. A quick rebound in NVIDIA stock could cool the speculation lifting Alphabet. The articles say caution could make sense until NVIDIA's search for a permanent CEO concludes. The articles leave open who the board will pick as permanent CEO and whether TPU demand will keep building.

Articles.Title: Alphabet Climbs 3% as NVIDIA’s Leadership Shake-Up Puts Google’s AI Chips in the Spotlight; Microsoft Gains 2%, Amazon Ticks Up

stories.Headline: Yahoo Finance company of the year: Anthropic's AI dominance
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's revenue reached $17 billion in the last quarter alone, jumping 12 times year over year, Yahoo Finance reported on November 12, 2026. The company was founded in 2021 by Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah, all former OpenAI employees. Yahoo Finance named Anthropic its Company of the Year for 2026 during its annual Invest Conference in New York City. Anthropic is set to launch its initial public offering late next week. For the nine months that ended Sept. 30, Anthropic's sales eclipsed $33 billion.

Anthropic brought in $2.5 billion in all of 2025 and just $41 million in 2023. Its number of customers spending more than $100,000 increased from roughly 1,500 in December 2025 to more than 11,900 as of Sept. 30. In its S-1 investor prospectus, Anthropic lists the myriad ways its AI could cause harm if not properly monitored. In September, Amodei penned an essay calling for AI labs to slow the pace of frontier AI development. According to the model-picking platform OpenRouter, open-weight models accounted for 8 of the top 10 models by token usage over the last month.

CEO Dario Amodei has become one of the key figures of the AI explosion alongside rival OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy, who led the company's investment in Anthropic, said Amodei brought over a great team of founders from OpenAI. Murphy said that reduces some risk in any startup when a group of founders really wanted to work together and had work experience and trust with each other. Santa Clara University Leavey School of Business professor Ram Bala said Anthropic made an early bet on focusing on the enterprise as the primary use case. Bala said that paid off for them incredibly well.

NYU Stern School of Business professor Arun Sundararajan told Yahoo Finance there is no real historical analogy for a company that has been this successful this fast. University of Pennsylvania Wharton School professor David Hsu said the revenues are eye-popping in terms of growth and that it remains to be seen how durable that is. Hsu said Anthropic is only five years old itself and it is not like a mature business. Bala said 80% of the usage of models is going to be pretty much open weights.

Bala said Anthropic will probably be a relatively small percentage in terms of token use but probably the dominant figure in terms of dollar use. Anthropic's Claude Code, an agentic coding tool, was a catalyst for the company's growth. That has since expanded to Anthropic's Claude Cowork, which Anthropic says customers are adopting faster than they did when Claude Code was initially released. The midterm election results, in which Democrats took control of the House and Senate, have been interpreted in part as pushback against the AI data center build-out and AI generally.

Anthropic is still contending with the fallout from the Trump administration's decision to label it a supply chain risk after the company said it wouldn't allow the Department of Defense to use its models to develop autonomous weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans. OpenAI has dramatically expanded its enterprise offerings as it seeks to better compete with the company, and Google and Meta are also gaining ground in overall model capabilities and expanding their enterprise platforms. The age of so-called tokenmaxxing, during which companies allowed workers to burn through their AI allotment to find the best use cases, is over. Enterprise companies are increasingly looking for ways to save on AI, opting to use less expensive models from Anthropic and its ilk, or cheaper open-weight models depending on their needs.

Anthropic's computing efficiency has also jumped, meaning it's seeing more revenue per dollar spent on computing infrastructure. Proving it can stay ahead of the pack will be Anthropic's biggest challenge, and investors will be watching closely as it prepares for its public market debut. The articles leave open how the IPO will be priced and whether data center construction will be slowed. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Yahoo Finance company of the year: Anthropic's AI dominance

stories.Headline: How a new AI model could help crushed rock fight climate change
stories.Summary:
Terradot and Microsoft created TerraNova, a new AI model, to make enhanced rock weathering cheaper and easier to measure, the companies announced on November 12, 2026. Terradot co-founder Sasankh Munukutla worked with experts from the Microsoft Climate Innovation Fund, the AI for Good Lab and Microsoft Research to adapt Microsoft's Aurora model. The model predicts chemical changes in soil using data from fields where Terradot works with farmers. The findings will be described in a forthcoming preprint ahead of peer review. Earlier versions were accepted for a climate-focused workshop at NeurIPS 2026 and presented at a workshop on AI for science at ICLR 2026.

TerraNova builds on Aurora, Microsoft's foundation AI model for predicting global weather and other environmental conditions, introduced in 2024 and trained on more than a million hours of atmospheric data. The model analyzes soil composition, minerals in crushed rock from nearby quarries, regional humidity, rainfall, temperatures and global weather patterns such as La Niña. Training TerraNova on data from fields in Brazil enabled it to make predictions for fields in Mississippi, says Felipe Oviedo, a principal research scientist at Microsoft's AI for Good Lab. In simulations using data from agricultural fields, researchers found the model could reduce the number of samples needed at the largest sites by 75% while maintaining the same level of accuracy. Measuring and verifying carbon removal can account for a third to more than half the cost of enhanced rock weathering.

James Kanoff, Terradot co-founder and CEO, said the world needs to remove nearly 10 billion tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere every single year to avoid the worst effects of climate change. He said the big problem is that there are not many solutions that can operate at those scales today, let alone at a price the world could really afford to pay. He said building confidence in enhanced rock weathering around the world will require intensive studies, from taking many samples in the soil to drilling wells down to the bedrock to track where the water goes. He said the work must be done a couple times to learn from the data and then done with the academic community to apply what is learned more broadly. Munukutla said every sample taken helps improve the model, which means it can be used in more fields and eventually make carbon removal more affordable as it expands.

Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft's chief sustainability officer, said TerraNova is an exciting example of how AI can accelerate climate progress by addressing a real barrier to scaling carbon removal. She said it shows what is possible when Microsoft brings together its technology, investment and partnerships to help promising solutions mature and build the markets needed for a more sustainable future. Erika Basham, director of natural capital investments with the Microsoft Climate Innovation Fund, said the Fund went for a moonshot together and wanted to do more than invest in and purchase from Terradot. She said the Fund wanted to help solve a problem holding back Terradot's growth and, by extension, the industry's growth. Oviedo said the measurements are very complex and account for a substantial share of the cost.

Terradot was founded in 2022 by Munukutla and Kanoff, who met at Stanford University. Terradot's team of about two dozen PhD-level scientists has collected tens of thousands of soil samples from fields in Brazil and the U.S. over the past few years, measuring rock weathering rates, drilling wells to see where the water goes and taking geochemical measurements. While visiting a chocolate maker on Hawaii's Big Island in 2024, Munukutla came across a display explaining how tropical soils are fast-forwards of soils elsewhere because the warm, wet climate accelerates natural weathering. That brought to mind Aurora, and he said his intuition was that Aurora could develop new abilities as it learns from more data. Enhanced rock weathering speeds up a natural process that ordinarily takes thousands of years by crushing rocks into powder, exposing more surface area to humidity.

Terradot says rock powder it has spread over fields in Brazil and the U.S. is expected to remove up to 100,000 tons of carbon dioxide over time, and the company is aiming to remove one million tons annually by 2035. Munukutla said continued development and extensive validation are needed to use AI models like TerraNova responsibly, and Terradot will continue building on the approach while working with the broader scientific community. He said what really lights him up is seeing novel capabilities emerge from models like Aurora. He said there are so many problems to solve at a planetary scale and that the world is just beginning to see what AI could help do. The article does not say when the preprint will be published or whether peer review has begun.

Articles.Title: How a new AI model could help crushed rock fight climate change

stories.Headline: AI networking adds security: Nvidia unveils Scale-In
stories.Summary:
Nvidia Corp. unveiled Scale-In, a new pillar of its AI networking infrastructure, according to a SiliconANGLE article published on November 12, 2026. The article said Scale-In brings purpose-built acceleration to secure, manage and operate agentic AI factories. Nvidia introduced Scale-In in August, the article said. Gilad Shainer, senior vice president of networking at Nvidia, discussed Scale-In with theCUBE's Dave Vellante. Shainer spoke for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories ,  Data Centers of the Future interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio.

Scale-In is designed to deliver secure access, high-performance data movement, tenant isolation, simpler operations and more predictable performance, the article said. Scale-In is powered by Nvidia BlueField-4 and Nvidia DOCA and connected over Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet. BlueField-4 is Nvidia's fourth-generation data processing unit, a networking platform built for agentic AI factories and large-scale infrastructure needs. In September, Nvidia introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform, combining OpenShell with Nvidia Sentry for out-of-band monitoring and hardware-based security enforcement. An October announcement added the OpenShell Reference Architecture, integrating Vera Rubin infrastructure, Vera CPUs and BlueField-4 to support secure agent execution across enterprise systems.

Shainer said agentic AI is a completely different use case because many agents need to run on the infrastructure. He said security must increase because agents must be contained in their sandbox and not do the wrong things. He said the infrastructure must ensure security all around, in memory and on storage, which is why Nvidia brought an infrastructure enabling security across everything. Shainer said BlueField-4 can be thought of as a device with in-silicon security engines working out of band and collecting telemetry from memory, storage, GPUs and CPUs. He said that out-of-band monitoring lets BlueField understand exactly what agents are doing.

Shainer said the DPU brings in-silicon security engines and storage accelerations, and DOCA is the framework, software and APIs that enable access to those engines. He said Nvidia wanted another device completely separated and isolated from the agents that can monitor everything out-of-band. He said Nvidia is bringing all the security elements together with OpenShell and BlueField-4 to create a secure infrastructure for agents. According to Nvidia, Sentry runs on BlueField-4 using DOCA software and continuously monitors agent behavior. Nvidia said Sentry can quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their defined software boundaries.

The article said Nvidia has expanded its agent security strategy since the August introduction. The article said Nvidia combined OpenShell with BlueField-4 because it wanted a device that could collect information outside the GPU and monitor an environment no agent could influence. The article said the OpenShell Reference Architecture builds on that approach with Nvidia Sentry. The article said the combination extends OpenShell's runtime controls with an independent enforcement layer. The article said OpenShell is an open-source runtime offering designed to govern agent execution, access and inference routing.

The article did not say what Scale-In costs or when it becomes available. The article did not say which customers have adopted Scale-In. The article did not give further details on the August introduction beyond the month. The article did not say how Sentry quarantine works in practice. The article did not say what results Nvidia has measured from Scale-In deployments.

Articles.Title: AI networking adds security: Nvidia unveils Scale-In

stories.Headline: Microsoft (MSFT) Expands AI Ties With Ohio State, Is The Stock Fully Priced?
stories.Summary:
The Ohio State University's Wexner Medical Center has agreed to a five-year artificial intelligence and cloud partnership with Microsoft, announced on November 12, 2026. The collaboration is aimed at clinical care, research workloads and training for the healthcare workforce. The article describes it as one of several recent AI alliances Microsoft has struck, arriving at a time when the share market has been softer. The article reports that Microsoft's share price fell 4.11% over the previous 30 days, yet it still shows a 5.19% gain over 90 days and a 10.19% gain year to date. Total shareholder return is 4.40% over one year, 41.49% over three years and 58.82% over five years.

The writer reads this as short-term momentum cooling while the longer-term growth story remains intact. Bulls cite the AI deals and recent earnings, while bears point to rising capital spending, political risk and new competitors. The article's valuation discussion turns on what the stock is worth now, and it presents two views. One Simply Wall St community narrative, written by an investor identified as CubanEros, sets fair value at $419.91 against a recent close of $521.13, which it describes as about 24% overvalued. That narrative argues the decline in the multiple looks more like worry over capital spending than damage to the business, and it warns the view could change if AI investment fails to earn strong returns or if regulatory pressure affects cloud and OpenAI exposure.

A second, ratio-based view puts Microsoft's price-to-earnings ratio at 27.1 times, below the US software industry at 31.2 times and above its peer group at 24.3 times, with a fair ratio of 56 times. The article does not report any reaction from Microsoft or the Ohio State University to the valuation debate, and it contains no statement from either party about the terms or financial value of the partnership. It is written as general market commentary, with the article noting that it is produced with AI assistance and is not financial advice. The article does not say when the partnership's first deliverables are due or how the valuation questions will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Microsoft (MSFT) Expands AI Ties With Ohio State, Is The Stock Fully Priced?

stories.Headline: Nvidia's leadership change could unravel AI financing, says NYU Professor Gary Marcus
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned, according to a CNBC report published on November 12, 2026, and the company's finance chief, Colette Kress, has been named interim chief executive. The announcement drew attention from analysts who said the company had no clear succession plan. Commentators on CNBC's programming described the moment as a difficult one for the chipmaker. The articles do not give further details on the timing of the resignation beyond the report date.

Gary Marcus, an NYU professor emeritus, told CNBC's Fast Money that the leadership change could have a ripple effect on the broader artificial intelligence trade. He focused on Nvidia's circular financing, the arrangement in which the company's investments and sales are tied to the businesses that buy its chips. In his view, turmoil at the company could put pressure on that financing. The article presents this as his assessment and does not describe any specific transaction or figure to support it.

Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said that the lack of a succession plan made the day "a dark day for Nvidia." Jim Cramer, also on CNBC, praised Kress and said she was absolutely the person the company needed right now. A separate CNBC segment referenced President Trump's remark that only one man could take Huang's place, naming Apple's Tim Cook. The articles also mention reporting on Alice Huang, whose stakes in Chinese businesses that benefited Huawei during an affair with Jensen Huang were covered in a separate CNBC video.

The articles include no financial figures, share price movements, or statements from Nvidia itself about the reasons for the change. They offer no details on how long Kress will serve as interim chief executive or on any permanent successor. The coverage is largely commentary from analysts and a professor rather than confirmed reporting on the effects of the change. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's leadership change could unravel AI financing, says NYU Professor Gary Marcus

stories.Headline: Thailand expects AI industry to reach 12.2 bln USD by 2030 - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The National Board of Digital Economy and Society Office announced on Friday, November 13, 2026, that Thailand's artificial intelligence industry is poised for significant growth. The agency expects the sector to reach a value of 412 billion baht, or roughly 12.2 billion U.S. dollars, by 2030. This represents a substantial increase from the 187 billion baht, or 5.5 billion dollars, estimated for the current year. The growth is fueled by government support, foreign data center investments, and the nation's role as a global exporter of AI hardware.

This expansion requires a compound annual growth rate of 20.5 percent between 2025 and 2030, starting from an estimated 162 billion baht in 2025. Currently, hardware and infrastructure account for 72 percent of the industry's value and 86.6 percent of the 31.1 billion baht, or 921 million dollars, invested last year. Data from the National Electronics and Computer Technology Center shows that 53.7 percent of Thai organizations use AI this year, compared to 17.8 percent in 2024. Meanwhile, software and data services are growing the fastest at 26.3 percent annually.

The BDE is responsible for these projections and clarified that the figures measure the AI value chain rather than the gross domestic product. The agency noted that while demand for high-performance computing will drive investment, several risks exist. These challenges include a lack of AI talent, a dependence on imported graphics processing units, and energy supply issues for data centers. The agency believes that as AI spreads to the broader economy, more investment will flow into software, data platforms, and model development.

Articles.Title: Thailand expects AI industry to reach 12.2 bln USD by 2030 - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Artificial Intelligence Overcounts Pulmonary B-Lines Compared to Clinical Experts
stories.Summary:
A prospective clinical investigation at Skåne University Hospital in Sweden found that an automated artificial intelligence tool in a commercial point-of-care ultrasound system substantially overcounts pulmonary B-lines compared with visual reviews by expert physicians. The single-center evaluation covered fifty-five hospitalized patients with acute respiratory symptoms, primarily acutely decompensated heart failure. Investigators found poor statistical agreement between the algorithm and experienced human evaluators, driven largely by overestimation across multiple anatomical thoracic zones. The software tested was the automated B-line application embedded in the Venue GO point-of-care ultrasound platform made by General Electric Healthcare. The tool highlights and quantifies B-lines in real time across captured video loops and logs the frame with the maximum artifact count to assign a score for each scanned lung zone.

Examinations were done at the bedside by an internal medicine resident in point-of-care ultrasound training, using a curved low-frequency transducer at a standard depth of sixteen centimeters. A standardized twelve-zone thoracic protocol was used: four anterolateral zones on each side with the patient supine at forty-five degrees, then two dorsal zones on each side with the patient sitting upright. Each sector was captured for four to five seconds in the sagittal plane between adjacent ribs, and a single operator acquired every video loop across all fifty-five subjects. The tool assigned each zone a category of zero, one, two, three, four, or greater than five B-lines, recording 672 thoracic zone clips. Two independent physician experts, a cardiologist and an internal medicine consultant who directs a regional point-of-care ultrasound training academy, classified B-lines into brackets of zero, one to two, three to four, and five or more while blinded to the software.

Of the 672 clips, 574, or eighty-five percent, were eligible for statistical analysis. Ninety-eight clips were excluded: eleven for insufficient image quality, twenty-six for no identifiable pleural line, and fifty-one for pleural effusions. Twenty-two of the twenty-six clips lacking a clear pleural reflection occurred in the second left anterior zone, where cardiac motion obscured the pulmonary field. Pleural effusions were found mostly in the dependent posterior inferior zones, sixty-three percent of effusion findings, with twenty-nine percent in the lateral chest regions. The median B-line count by the artificial intelligence platform was 23.5 per patient versus 2.8 per patient by visual reviewers, a statistically significant difference.

The automated platform classified thirty-eight percent of assessed zones into the highest category of more than five B-lines, while experts assigned only four percent to that category. The software showed a bimodal distribution, with forty-eight percent of readings at zero and thirty-eight percent at greater than five, and only thirteen percent between one and four B-lines. The intraclass correlation coefficient between software and experts reached only 0.28 for the total patient B-line sum and 0.37 zone by zone, while interrater reliability between the two human experts was excellent at 0.92 and 0.91. Bland-Altman analysis showed a systematic positive bias of 1.86 with a standard deviation of 2.15 and ninety-five percent limits of agreement from negative 2.35 to positive 6.07. Among the 574 analyzed zones, fourteen percent of algorithmic errors came from the software tracking acoustic data in adjacent rib spaces rather than the central intercostal target.

In one percent of zones the software mistook subpleural consolidations with irregular acoustic shred lines, also called C-lines, for true vertical B-lines, and in another one percent it counted normal rib shadowing as pathologic vertical artifacts. Correlation was poorest in anterior zone two and posterior superior zone five, where overcounting was most pronounced, and better in the lateral and posterior inferior sectors. Reviewers recorded significantly higher total B-line sums in hypervolemic patients than in euvolemic individuals, averaging 4.6 versus 0.75 artifacts. The authors noted recruitment from a single medical center, reliance on a single image operator, and software capping granular counting at five artifacts per sector. To align categorization schemes, researchers assigned software values of one or two to 1.5 and values of three or four to 3.5 to mirror expert score ranges.

An initial evaluation by Short and colleagues cited in platform marketing materials documented an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.79 using the same software, but that study evaluated only four patients. Later assessments found lower concordance, such as an evaluation by Russell and colleagues reporting 0.56 between automated scoring and expert review. An investigation by Damodaran and colleagues in patients with viral respiratory infections recorded intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.52 to 0.53, borderline moderate agreement closer to the Swedish cohort. The Swedish study used an upright twelve-zone method including dorsal regions, whereas recent heart failure research suggests a simplified two-zone anterior-superior protocol can yield comparable diagnostic utility to an eight-zone exam. Current commercial point-of-care tools rely mainly on prespecified image-processing rules that struggle with rib margins or tissue consolidations.

The researchers concluded that automated B-line quantification in current commercial point-of-care hardware requires further algorithmic refinement before it can be safely relied upon for autonomous clinical decision-making. They noted that future improvements likely depend on deep-learning neural networks trained on extensive imaging datasets coupled with expert human visual validation. True cardiogenic B-lines generate smooth pleural reflections in a diffuse pattern, whereas comet-tail artifacts from other pulmonary disorders feature irregular, fragmented pleural reflections with narrow heads and wide tails, and the platform may struggle to differentiate these presentations. The articles do not state whether the software's manufacturer has responded to the findings or whether regulatory action followed. They also do not say whether a follow-up study or software update is planned.

Articles.Title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Artificial Intelligence Overcounts Pulmonary B-Lines Compared to Clinical Experts

stories.Headline: Kiwanis Rough Risers to hold presentation on artificial intelligence - Waterloo-Cedar Falls Courier
stories.Summary:
The Cedar Falls Kiwanis Rough Risers invited the community to a special presentation on artificial intelligence at 6:30 a.m. Wednesday at First Christian Church, 1302 W. 11th St. The event is titled “Let’s Talk AI,” according to the Courier. The presentation asks what exactly AI is, how people can use it, and what the future might hold. Artificial intelligence is changing the world, the article states.

Visitors are welcome to enjoy breakfast at the event, the article says. The article gives the start time as 6:30 a.m. and the day as Wednesday. The address given is 1302 W. 11th St. in Cedar Falls. The article names First Christian Church as the location.

stories.Headline: Historic turning point in human-machine ties with AI
stories.Summary:
Mahmut Özer published a column in the Daily Sabah on Nov 14, 2026, at 12:05 am GMT+3, arguing that artificial intelligence marks a historic turning point in human-machine relations. He wrote that AI is transforming societies at an unprecedented pace and differs fundamentally from previous technological breakthroughs. He said an entirely new technological ecosystem centered on artificial intelligence is emerging as fields from education and health care to industry, the economy, biotechnology and defense are transformed. He noted that this rapid transformation generates excitement and expectations across all segments of society while also intensifying concerns and anxieties. He observed that perhaps no previous technological development has evoked these two contrasting emotions simultaneously and with such intensity.

Özer wrote that humanity has used machines first to expand physical capabilities, then to automate repetitive tasks, and finally to begin transferring certain cognitive activities to machines. He said artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI, is entering a broader domain encompassing not only what humans do but also how they think, interpret information, solve problems and generate new content. He said AI can in some cases directly substitute for human thinking and creative processes, and that for the first time humans face the possibility of routinely delegating their own cognitive activities to machines on a widespread scale. He cited recent experimental studies suggesting certain cognitive processes associated with critical thinking, independent problem-solving and memory may be adversely affected, particularly when AI tools are used as substitutes for individuals' own thinking. He said these effects vary depending on how AI tools are used.

Özer said AI technology is increasingly reshaping social stratification, introducing new divisions based on skill levels alongside traditional distinctions of class and social status. He warned that a new divide may emerge between those who can use AI technologies effectively and those who become dependent on the ready-made outputs these technologies provide. He said significant differences in skills and capabilities may develop even among individuals who use the very same technology, and that what ultimately matters is not simply access but the nature of the relationship individuals establish with the tools. He described a potentially dangerous cycle of cognitive dependence in which delegating thinking, analysis and problem-solving to AI reduces mental effort, weakens the ability to perform these tasks independently, and increases the need for the tools. He said this cycle may also cause people to feel inadequate when they cannot access AI tools.

Özer said AI tools can reproduce biases embedded in their training data and present information with no basis in reality in an extremely convincing manner, making it essential to evaluate the accuracy of AI-generated content before using it as is. He warned that when cognitive processes are increasingly delegated to machines and dependence grows, the very capacity to verify such information may be undermined, magnifying the scale of potential harm. He raised the question of agency in content production, asking who is the actual agent behind a product when virtually any type of content can be produced rapidly and at negligible cost. He said research suggests that when agency shifts from humans to machines, individuals may become alienated from the products they generate and may struggle to recall even basic details of content produced only a short time earlier, indicating a weakening of memory. He said a substantial decline in the diversity and richness of arguments has been observed, particularly in written texts.

Özer cited TurkStat's 2026 statistics on artificial intelligence, which indicate that use of AI for professional purposes remains considerably more limited than for personal purposes. He said approximately 86.4% of individuals using these technologies in 2026, compared with 80% in 2025, reported using them for personal purposes, while only 37.3%, compared with 33.8% in 2025, reported using them for professional purposes. He said these figures suggest that although AI adoption is rapidly expanding in Türkiye, this expansion has not been reflected to the same extent in professional applications and consequently in professional productivity. He said the difference in purposes of AI use does not by itself reveal the level of awareness or skill with which individuals use these tools, and that there is a need to measure not only the prevalence of AI use but also the quality of that use. He said the extent to which individuals remain actively engaged in cognitive processes, how thoroughly they verify AI-generated content, whether they preserve independent problem-solving abilities, and whether they can translate AI use into professional productivity have become fundamental questions requiring systematic investigation.

Özer said a pedagogical framework for human-machine relations is needed that does not diminish human participation in cognitive processes, continuously maintains awareness of the need to evaluate the accuracy of generated content, and ensures that agency over the final product remains with humans. He said the central issue in the age of artificial intelligence is not how widely these technologies are adopted but where human beings stand within this new relationship. He asked whether we can preserve our abilities to think, question, verify and create while using artificial intelligence, or whether we are gradually delegating these abilities to machines and becoming increasingly dependent on the capabilities they provide. He suggested the defining distinction between societies in the future may not be who has greater access to AI technologies but who is better able to preserve human cognitive autonomy while using them. He said the most important educational challenge of the AI age is not merely to raise individuals who know how to use these technologies but to cultivate individuals who can strengthen, rather than surrender, their ability to think, question and create.

Articles.Title: Historic turning point in human-machine ties with AI

stories.Headline: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation
stories.Summary:
Yuxuan Wang and ten other authors introduced a new multi-agent system called DoGNAVY-Exploit on November 13, 2026. This tool uses open-weight models to turn known software vulnerabilities into working exploits. The researchers developed this system to overcome the high costs and access restrictions associated with frontier large language model agents. It aims to help open-weight models maintain progress across long exploitation chains.

The system requires a hierarchical architecture that separates strategic planning from parallel execution. It uses stage-aware decomposition to break long tasks into short, verifiable milestones, providing only the relevant expert knowledge for each step. Using GLM-5.2, the tool achieved a 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and a 100% one-day and 97.5% zero-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, GLM-5.3 solved 157 tasks, while GLM-5.2 solved 79, both outperforming Claude Code baselines.

The authors are responsible for the design, which includes a controller that accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. They stated that a shared structured memory allows agents to consolidate verified facts and failed routes across different branches. This design ensures that validated knowledge is carried into subsequent milestones. The researchers noted that these specific memory and orchestration designs substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.

Articles.Title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation

stories.Headline: Ghana Faces Governance Readiness Gap as Artificial Intelligence Deployment Outpaces Oversight
stories.Summary:
Ghana’s artificial intelligence deployment across finance, healthcare, agriculture, digital services and public administration is expanding faster than the institutions meant to supervise its risks, according to a qualitative investigation of the country’s National Innovation System. Researchers Benedict Afful Jr. and Kassim Alabani evaluated Ghana’s institutional environment to determine whether it has the operational capacity, cross-agency coordination and statutory authority to enforce responsible artificial intelligence standards. Their empirical findings show an uneven, system-wide governance readiness gap rather than a total absence of governance mechanisms. Ghana launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025, 2035 on April 24, 2026, and participated in UNESCO’s AI Readiness Assessment Methodology. Formal policy ambition has developed ahead of the technical competence, routine advisory channels and enforcement capabilities of implementing state bodies.

The researchers combined National Innovation Systems theory with Technological Innovation Systems functional analysis and normative governance benchmarks set by UNESCO and the African Union. They collected qualitative evidence from 32 purposively selected institutional leaders across Ghana’s innovation landscape. The sample included eight participants from universities and research institutes, six from commercial technology firms and industry, six from government regulatory and policy agencies, four from financial institutions, four from intermediary bodies such as technology hubs and incubators, and four boundary-spanning actors. Data collection used a three-part qualitative protocol of vignette-based scenarios, triadic elicitation and the Critical Incident Technique, with each semi-structured session lasting 60 to 90 minutes. Data were evaluated through reflexive thematic analysis using NVivo software.

The authors termed their central theoretical contribution the Governance Readiness Paradox, a structural condition in which commercial deployment and high-level strategy accelerate faster than the institutional capacity required to convert technical evidence into enforceable, accountable and legally sound public oversight. They built a systemic failure typology of four mutually reinforcing mechanisms: capability failures, connectivity failures, legitimacy failures and resource failures. They triangulated documents against publicly available policy frameworks such as the Data Protection Act 2012 and the National AI Strategy 2025, 2035. They maintained analytic reflexivity and conducted member checking with selected informants to verify findings while protecting participants from deductive identification. They developed the Ghana AI Governance Readiness Matrix, which cross-tabulates innovation system components against the four international governance pillars of safety and security, transparency, accountability and inclusion.

Academic respondents reported severe barriers when transmitting technical insights into public policymaking, and a completed study evaluating automated credit-screening discrimination in domestic financial technology had no formal institutional pipeline to translate findings into regulatory briefs or actionable policy interventions. Academic research agendas were found to be predominantly driven by international donor funding, which rewarded technical performance metrics such as processing velocity and model sophistication while giving negligible incentives for governance-oriented inquiry, ethical evaluation or local policy relevance. Industry participants said corporate legal counsel routinely advises silence to minimize corporate liability in the absence of explicit statutory disclosure duties. A documented critical incident from the financial sector involved an internal corporate audit that revealed an automated credit-scoring model assigning systematically depressed scores to applicants from three northern regions despite repayment records comparable to other applicants, and the firm recalibrated the model entirely internally, omitting regulatory notification, affected customer disclosures or independent remediation. Regulatory officials acknowledged that internal personnel lacked the specialized technical expertise to draft credible assessments independently for a vignette requiring a 48-hour parliamentary briefing on an emerging artificial intelligence incident, while possessing no formal procedures to commission academic assistance on short notice.

Although statutory bodies such as the Data Protection Commission and the National Information Technology Agency maintain defined mandates, cross-agency coordination remains fragmented. Critical incident accounts showed that successful knowledge transfer from researchers to state bodies occurred almost exclusively through informal personal connections, temporary academic secondments or prior individual relationships rather than durable administrative routines. When key personnel resigned, retired or concluded donor-funded contracts, institutional memory and advisory channels collapsed. Commercial banks and investment actors routinely evaluated technology through conventional operational and reputational risk categories, completely lacking dedicated criteria to assess artificial intelligence safety, data provenance or algorithmic fairness. Intermediary bodies, including technology hubs, accelerators and university technology transfer offices, operated effectively as commercial bridges connecting startups to private capital and markets, but their potential role as regulatory bridges remained entirely unactivated, and entrepreneurship training curricula omitted instruction on regulatory compliance, legal liability and ethical deployment.

Chronic resource shortages acted as a systemic multiplier, with domestic funding lines dedicated to public sector artificial intelligence research, regulatory monitoring and expert technical staffing virtually nonexistent, leaving institutions reliant on fragmented, temporary external assistance. Component ratings on the Ghana AI Governance Readiness Matrix ranged from very low to moderate across dimensions, illustrating fragmented integration rather than absolute institutional absence. Systemic failures propagated through self-reinforcing cycles: missing diffusion pipelines left regulators without technical evidence, low regulatory capability created ambiguous market oversight, ambiguous expectations discouraged private firms and financiers from investing in auditing routines, and an absence of domestic governance demand incentivized universities to prioritize externally funded technical projects over public policy translation. The matrix identified relative institutional assets that can serve as foundations for reform, including existing academic expertise, emerging policy frameworks, boundary-spanning professionals and international market linkages. The authors formulated eight sequenced policy recommendations distributed across three distinct implementation phases spanning five years.

Phase I focuses on low-cost structural alignment, establishing a national cross-agency coordination mechanism, creating an interim expert roster to channel university research into regulatory processes, and integrating civil society into National AI Strategy implementation. Phase II establishes dedicated artificial intelligence units within sectoral regulatory bodies, launches structured institutional secondments between universities and public agencies, pilots proportionate impact assessments, and institutes a domestic research funding window to mitigate external donor dependency. Phase III consolidates professional certifications, according to the article, which ends there. The articles leave open what Phase III’s remaining measures are and whether any of the eight recommendations have been adopted.

Articles.Title: Ghana Faces Governance Readiness Gap as Artificial Intelligence Deployment Outpaces Oversight

stories.Headline: Genomic Machine Learning Shows High Accuracy but Limited Validation in Global Surveillance
stories.Summary:
A scoping review examined artificial intelligence and genomic technologies for bacterial antimicrobial resistance surveillance. The study was published in Discover Public Health on November 14, 2026. Researchers synthesized findings from 27 peer-reviewed investigations published between January 2020 and March 2026. The review evaluated how predictive algorithms infer phenotypic resistance from raw genomic sequence data. It focused on the reliability of these models in resource-limited environments.

The review analyzed 1,150 records from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, Google Scholar, bioRxiv, and medRxiv. It identified 22 studies relevant to low- and middle-income countries, including Pakistan, Vietnam, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, and Nigeria. Predictive performance measures for various bacterial pathogens ranged between 78% and 98% accuracy. Only 30% of the examined studies performed external validation using independent or cross-regional cohorts. The authors used World Bank income classifications and Joanna Briggs Institute frameworks.

The authors stated that current computational architectures often capture dataset-specific artifacts rather than biologically robust determinants. They noted that existing literature is overwhelmingly skewed toward models designed and calibrated in wealthy regions. The researchers argued that resource-constrained settings often serve as peripheral sources of validation data. They emphasized that genomic feature engineering influences final model performance more than the selection of architectures. The authors advocated for a transition toward data-centric systems design.

The review found that antimicrobial resistance caused 1.27 million deaths and contributed to 4.95 million fatalities in 2019. This global health crisis disproportionately impacts low- and middle-income countries where traditional diagnostic systems face resource constraints. Conventional phenotypic testing is essential but slow, which may delay the detection of complex resistance mechanisms. The most studied organisms were Mycobacterium tuberculosis in seven studies and Escherichia coli in six studies. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was assessed across three investigations, while eleven studies analyzed other Gram-negative organisms.

The research identified four dominant encoding paradigms used to convert nucleotide sequences into numeric matrices. Tree-based ensemble models like Random Forest and XGBoost showed the most consistent performance across heterogeneous datasets. Neural networks achieved predictive metrics from 86% to 94% but were less frequently applied in limited settings. Only nine of 27 studies met One Health criteria by incorporating isolates from two or more reservoirs. Most studies used multi-reservoir data as pooled inputs rather than modeling interactions between compartments.

The authors called for mandatory external validation across independent, cross-country datasets as a standard benchmark for publication. They suggested using federated learning frameworks to facilitate cross-border training while safeguarding national biological data sovereignty.
