Future reporting should include sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1-scores, and calibration metrics. The articles leave open the quantifiable boost that multi-reservoir data integration might provide to accuracy. There is an almost total absence of prospective clinical implementation trials or cost-effectiveness studies.

Articles.Title: Genomic Machine Learning Shows High Accuracy but Limited Validation in Global Surveillance

stories.Headline: Legal Departments Have Room to Grow Regarding Engagement With AI Governance, Survey Shows
stories.Summary:
A new survey suggests that legal departments are not as actively involved in AI governance and deployment as they could be. The article, published by Law.com on November 12, 2026, reports on findings that raise doubts about the depth of legal teams' engagement with how their organizations adopt and oversee artificial intelligence. The piece is written by Chris O'Malley and was posted at 10:43 AM that day. The coverage is limited to the article's summary, so the survey's sample size, methodology, and specific figures are not available here.

The survey's central point, as the article presents it, is that legal departments have room to grow in their role. A representative of Diligent, Kira Ciccarelli, is quoted as arguing that legal does not need to control every operational aspect of AI but should have a clearly defined role in governance. She argues that legal should be involved early enough to shape important decisions rather than only reviewing risks once a system has already been deployed. The article frames this as the main gap the survey identifies. No dates, deadlines, or required actions beyond this recommendation are given in the material provided.

Ciccarelli is the source responsible for the recommendation, and the article attributes the view to her and to the survey's findings. The article does not describe any formal rule or regulatory change arising from the survey. Its context is a broader trend in which companies are adopting AI, and the article itself is one of several on Law.com about AI and in-house counsel. A related piece from the same period quotes Raman Rai, an AI deployment adviser, who told general counsel at a Law.com conference that companies are investing heavily in AI without always defining which problems the technology should solve. The available material does not say what steps, if any, will follow the survey.

Articles.Title: Legal Departments Have Room to Grow Regarding Engagement With AI Governance, Survey Shows

stories.Headline: Even When Everyone Knows It’s AI, Video Can Sway a Judge
stories.Summary:
An AI-generated video of a murder victim, Christopher Pelkey, was shown in an Arizona courtroom and helped lead to a reduced sentence for the man who killed him. The article's central point is that the video influenced a judge even though everyone in the room knew it was artificial. The piece was published by Law.com on November 12, 2026, under a byline from Laura Lorek, and it places the episode in the wider context of courts struggling with deepfakes. The article describes the video as an AI avatar of Pelkey, and it notes that the sentence was undone after the avatar was presented. The coverage is aimed at lawyers and legal professionals who follow how new technology enters the courtroom.

The article indicates that the problem is twofold, since courts must both detect fabricated material and reckon with how such material shapes decisions. Even when participants understand that a video is synthetic, the emotional force of seeing a lifelike figure can still affect how a judge weighs a case. The article frames this as a challenge that goes beyond simply spotting fakes. Its authors treat the influence of such evidence as a matter the legal system has not yet settled. The headline's core claim is that awareness of artificiality does not by itself neutralize the persuasive effect.

Responsibility for the video and its presentation rests with the parties who introduced it in the Arizona proceeding, and the article attributes the choice to use the avatar to them. The article quotes or paraphrases the people involved in describing the statement as a tool meant to convey the victim's voice to the court. Judges and commentators interviewed for related coverage in Law.com's surrounding reporting have expressed a nuanced view of AI's growing role in courts, acknowledging both promise and risk. Those accounts suggest that the legal community is still deciding how much weight such material deserves.

The article sits within a broader debate over deepfakes and synthetic media that is reaching courtrooms across the country. Related Law.com pieces note that appellate lawyers are experimenting with AI for oral argument preparation while stopping short of replacing human moot courts. The article does not report any formal rule changes or court orders arising from this specific case. What happens next, according to the available coverage, remains open as courts continue to work through how to admit, label and limit AI-generated evidence.

Articles.Title: Even When Everyone Knows It’s AI, Video Can Sway a Judge

stories.Headline: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
Cyberattackers are using artificial intelligence to increase the speed and scale of their operations. These actors have not changed their core objectives or the techniques they employ. Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques used in these attacks. AI tools make these attacks easier to mount and cheaper for unskilled attackers. Security experts reported these trends in a feature published on November 13, 2026.

Chinese state-sponsored actors abused Claude Code for a cyber-espionage campaign in September 2025 called GTG-1002. The JadePuffer ransomware campaign was disclosed in July 2026 and used an LLM-driven agent. It exploited CVE-2025-3248, a missing-authentication flaw in the open-source framework Langflow. Attackers used Chinese models GLM and Kimi 3 because they have fewer content restrictions. These tools target end-user devices, API calls, and ungoverned AI agents.

Ronald Lewis of Black Duck says AI increases the volume and velocity of attack processes. Darren Meyer from Checkmarx notes that adversaries gain development velocity and operational speed from AI. Nazar Tymoshyk of UnderDefense describes agentic APTs as combining multiple specialist roles into one. Crystal Morin from Sysdig says AI agents shorten the detection windows for defenders. Nathan Smolenski of Qualys states that frontier AI tools shrink the window for exploitation.

Enterprises with years of technical debt are affected because AI finds flaws faster than patching. Many security leaders say their teams struggle to meet business needs according to recent reports. Human attackers are being replaced by agentic threat actors who compose plans live. These AI agents are often catchable because they are noisy and frequently hallucinate. This shift empowers single individuals to deploy threats that previously required coordinated specialist teams.

Attackers traditionally identify targets, perform reconnaissance, establish footholds, move laterally, and cover their tracks. The current baseline consists of AI-orchestrated operations that surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted attacks toward fully autonomous operations. Human attackers previously built playbooks per campaign, but agentic actors now use inference budgets. Software flaws are rising as a root cause of breaches due to AI discovery.

Organizations must shift from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defenses to counter these threats. Security teams should implement agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails to automate lower-level triage. Defenders can no longer rely on traditional 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets. Foundational security defenses like patching and authentication controls remain necessary for all defending organizations. The articles leave open how to accurately attribute attacks to specific AI models.

Articles.Title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Geospatial Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Geographic Methods and Theory, Researchers Conclude
stories.Summary:
Researchers Cláudia M. Viana and Jorge Rocha, from the Centre of Geographic Studies, Institute of Geography and Spatial Planning, and the Associate Laboratory TERRA at the University of Lisbon, published an opinion article in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence analyzing the emergence of Geospatial Artificial Intelligence, known as GeoAI. The article traces the origins of this field to 1986, when Helen Couclelis, a pioneer of Geographic Information Science, first pointed out links between geography and artificial intelligence. Her early work examined the logical and mathematical aspects of early computing and their consequences for modeling, prediction and scientific processes. Four decades of technological change have since transformed geographic analysis, which now relies heavily on advanced machine learning. These algorithms process large, varied, high-dimensional spatio-temporal datasets, often described as Big Data.

The authors explain that GeoAI draws on several overlapping fields, including geomatics, geocomputation, GIScience and digital geographies, rather than emerging on its own. Geomatics covers the acquisition, management, analysis and mapping of geographically referenced information, including geographic information systems, photogrammetry, remote sensing, digital geodesy and surveying. The authors favor the term geospatial because it refers specifically to data and phenomena tied to locations on Earth, while spatial can describe non-geographical topologies. Geocomputation contributes computational simulation, spatial modeling and automated processing, providing the algorithms needed to parse massive territorial archives. The authors present GeoAI as a unified methodological platform built on these precursors for addressing sustainability, ecological risks and societal challenges.

The article distinguishes conventional spatial analysis from GeoAI by noting who specifies the analytical structure. Classical methods such as spatial econometrics, geostatistics, Markov models and supervised classifications require researchers to predefine variables, rules, parameters and functional forms. GeoAI shifts much of that specification to algorithms that learn latent representations and nonlinear boundaries directly from data, which the authors describe as a fundamental paradigm shift rather than simply faster computing. They argue that GeoAI does not make conventional spatial statistics obsolete, since spatial analysis, geocomputation and artificial intelligence form cumulative layers, and data-driven findings must remain grounded in established geographic hypotheses. The authors place this argument within a broader discussion of how the discipline is changing.

The transformation is already visible in physical geography, particularly in Earth observation, topographic mapping and environmental risk analysis, where national mapping agencies are adopting scalable algorithms. In remote sensing, deep learning now extracts spatial, textural and spectral features from raw satellite imagery instead of relying on analysts to choose bands and craft classifier boundaries by hand. In hazard assessment, models such as Random Forest, gradient boosting and deep neural networks capture nonlinear interactions among factors like elevation, slope, lithology, precipitation and proximity to drainage networks. These tools have improved automated landslide detection through transfer learning and support predictive flood-risk modeling and wildfire tracking. In human geography, urban planning, transport analysis and health geography are adopting GeoAI, which draws on mobile device data, location-based social networks, urban sensors and street-level imagery alongside traditional censuses and surveys.

The authors note that qualitative and interpretive traditions in human geography remain hesitant about GeoAI, citing concerns about transparency, reproducibility and the reduction of lived social space to numbers. They connect this hesitation to a long-standing tension between macrogeography, which seeks general laws, and microgeography, which emphasizes local context and description. They observe that complexity research shows how interactions among individual components produce emergent collective behavior, and that modern geographic information science addresses this tension by encoding macrogeographic principles into algorithms while supplying microgeographic specificity through fine-grained empirical data. The article also links GeoAI to digital geographies, which examine the cultural, political and socio-economic effects of digital technologies on how people perceive and move through space. The authors warn that GeoAI trained on unrepresentative or biased data will reproduce spatial injustices, and that access to high-performance computing and authoritative geospatial databases remains heavily skewed toward well-resourced institutions and away from developing countries.

Beyond data bias, the authors identify persistent methodological problems that GeoAI inherits, including spatial dependence, spatial heterogeneity, edge effects, uneven sampling and the modifiable areal unit problem. Models calibrated in one climatic, topographic or urban setting may fail when transferred to another landscape. The pervasive collection of mobile telemetry and street imagery also raises concerns about geoprivacy, state and corporate surveillance and algorithmic accountability. The researchers argue these challenges require rigorous spatial validation, methodological transparency and attention to the institutional frameworks that govern data generation and use. They also identify the black-box problem, in which deep neural networks process inputs through millions of latent parameters that obscure how decisions are made, a barrier to adoption in high-stakes public policy.

Articles.Title: Geospatial Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Geographic Methods and Theory, Researchers Conclude

stories.Headline: Letters to the Editor: ‘There is no rogue AI, only rogue program directors’
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Times published a reader letter on November 12, 2026, under the headline "Letters to the Editor: 'There is no rogue AI, only rogue program directors.'" The letter was written by Julie May of Los Angeles and responds to an earlier column by Michael Hiltzik about whether AI systems can become conscious. The page also shows a photo of Pope Leo XIV presenting, in May, an encyclical warning against treating AI systems as conscious or human. The letter is a response to a published opinion piece, not a report of an incident, so there is no event, date of harm, or agency action to describe.

May thanks Hiltzik for his column, which ran on November 3, and says the debate about AI consciousness misses the basic point that AI is a human invention controlled by humans. She draws on her own experience, recalling that in the mid-1950s she worked for a UCLA astronomy professor whose small group tracked the orbits of two minor planets and two moons of Jupiter. The group used a mainframe computer called SWAC, and the postdoc who ran the office wrote the code they needed. She recalls that the guiding principle then was "garbage in, garbage out," and she argues that the same principle applies to AI. Her conclusion is that people, not the machines, shape what AI produces.

May places responsibility squarely on tech executives, saying they direct how AI is programmed and used and are therefore accountable for its output. In her view, there is no rogue AI, only rogue program directors. The letter does not propose any new rule, law, or policy, and it names no specific company or executive. The surrounding page carries other letters on unrelated topics, including child punishment, rail transit, and California politics, which are not connected to the AI piece. The articles do not indicate any follow-up, response from Hiltzik or tech companies, or further coverage of this exchange.

Articles.Title: Letters to the Editor: ‘There is no rogue AI, only rogue program directors’

stories.Headline: Conversational Artificial Intelligence Framework Enhances Wireless Sensor Network Security and Longevity
stories.Summary:
Researchers Sauvik Bal and Lopa Mandal published a study in Discover Networks showing that a conversational artificial intelligence framework placed at the network sink layer can extend the life and improve the security of wireless sensor networks. The work targets resource-constrained deployments used in smart agri-ecology and remote environmental monitoring, where hardware endurance and defensive resilience often conflict. The framework places a conversational orchestration engine at a cloud-assisted edge server or local gateway sink, removing complex mathematical modeling from low-power sensor nodes. In simulation tests across established benchmark scenarios, the framework improved network lifetime by approximately thirty percent and cut energy consumption per operational round by twenty percent. The researchers present the approach as a viable path to adaptive, lightweight sensor coordination under challenging field conditions.

Sensor nodes in the architecture only gather physical telemetry and run basic transmission routines using lightweight protocols, with no local model training. Cluster heads aggregate local measurements and send compressed summaries of operational status, traffic volume and residual power to the sink. The sink, hosted on an edge server or gateway with intermittent cloud connectivity, handles all conversational reasoning and reinforcement learning. Because model parameters and gradient data never cross wireless links, the field sensors remain lightweight. The sink converts network summaries into structured natural language prompts that produce deterministic, machine-parseable control directives.

The reward function penalizes energy consumption, security vulnerability and conversational query cost, so the conversational module is activated only on a coarse timeframe. The article attributes the study to Sauvik Bal and Lopa Mandal, who describe the framework and report its simulation results. The article does not provide direct quotations from either researcher. It notes that the framework is described in a study published in Discover Networks. The article gives no statements from institutions, sponsors or other parties involved in the research.

Its description of the framework's objectives and outcomes comes from the study itself, as reported by the publication. Wireless sensor networks are widely used in precision agriculture, industrial sensing and disaster response, where nodes operate on strictly limited batteries over long periods in remote settings. Conventional protocols named in the article include Directed Diffusion, LEACH, HEED, SEP and TEEN, which rely on static heuristics and fixed probabilistic calculations. The article says traditional cryptographic protections and node-level intrusion detection add heavy sensing loads and transmission overhead that accelerate battery depletion. Field operators, remote monitoring projects and the sensor clusters they run are the parties the article identifies as affected by these trade-offs.

The article presents the improvements as relevant to deployments facing persistent energy and security constraints. The framework comprises two cooperative components, ACOS for energy-efficient clustering and duty cycling, and SCReS for defense against intrusion. In the simulations, one hundred static sensor nodes were placed randomly across a two-hundred-meter by two-hundred-meter area, using a first-order radio model. Telemetry from the Intel Berkeley Research Lab dataset and attack profiles from the UNSW-NB15 dataset were used to drive the tests.

ACOS delayed First Node Depletion by twenty-nine percent, and total network lifetime rose by twenty-seven to thirty percent against LEACH and HEED baselines. Control overhead fell by approximately forty to fifty percent, and SCReS reached a True Positive Rate of ninety-three percent with a False Positive Rate of seven percent. Average reconfiguration latency was two point five seconds. The article does not state whether the framework has been tested on physical hardware or in real field deployments, as all reported results come from simulation.

It also does not report what happens to network performance beyond the simulated scenarios, or whether the approach will be adopted or extended by others. The article ends partway through its discussion of detection results, so later findings and any stated limitations are not available. It gives no timeline for further testing, publication of follow-up work, or commercial use. Questions about real-world reliability, cost of the edge or gateway hardware, and performance at larger scales remain unaddressed in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Conversational Artificial Intelligence Framework Enhances Wireless Sensor Network Security and Longevity

stories.Headline: Training Artificial Intelligence on Top Physicians May Reduce Intensive Care Bias
stories.Summary:
Researchers Daniel Ostrovsky, Daniel Talmor, and Victor Novack published a perspective in Intensive Care Medicine proposing that clinical artificial intelligence models be trained only on the practice patterns of top-performing physicians. Their argument is that such training could eliminate decision noise while stopping algorithms from absorbing systemic biases found in routine clinical data. The authors suggest that, instead of learning from every case across a whole clinical staff, critical care algorithms should selectively mimic clinicians identified locally as following best practice. The perspective was published on November 12, 2026, and was reported by bioengineer.org. The authors frame the proposal as a response to widespread variation in critical care decisions that the articles describe.

Medicine is described as a noisy decision-making environment, with noise defined by Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein as undesirable variability in judgments about the same problem. Unwarranted variation appears most often in discretionary decisions where evidence does not point to a single correct action. The articles cite intensive care unit admissions, which vary substantially even after adjustment for patient case mix and measured hospital factors. Similar discrepancies appear in antibiotic prescribing, in the timing and threshold for invasive mechanical ventilation in hypoxaemic respiratory failure, and in the use of renal replacement therapy and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. The articles state that an algorithm applied uniformly removes noise, but whether it also removes bias depends on its training data.

The articles say that algorithms trained on operational endpoints, such as intensive care transfers or clinical deterioration, reflect clinician practice patterns and local system constraints. Standard models therefore reproduce the average of observed practice rather than an optimal standard of care. In a hypothetical intensive care unit, clinician admission rates range from 0 percent to 24 percent, with a mean of 12 percent. If best-practice clinicians admit at 8 percent with non-inferior outcomes, an algorithm trained across all clinicians would perpetuate a four-percentage-point over-admission bias. To avoid this, the authors suggest filtering training data so that the algorithm learns only from best-practice clinicians, identified in advance using objective metrics such as low complication rates or reduced intensive care utilization with non-inferior outcomes.

Other identifiers mentioned include peer rankings, patient assessments, experience, and knowledge tests. The authors caution that apparently superior performance may stem from non-random case mix rather than better decisions, so developers must apply rigorous retrospective risk-adjusted comparisons. The articles note that models trained on top clinicians cannot serve as universal standards without local calibration, because ward capabilities, staffing, geography, and unit capacity vary. Restricting training to fewer clinicians reduces sample size and may degrade accuracy in rare patient subgroups. The articles recommend federated data access across multiple intensive care units, formal fairness audits, prospective evaluations, and safeguards against automation bias.

They also state that clinical workflows change in response to algorithms, so continuous validation and drift monitoring are required. Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein's definition of noise underpins the authors' critique of current machine learning methods in critical care. The articles say that in digital pathology and image-based diagnosis, models are trained on definitive diagnostic labels, which reduces both noise and diagnostic bias. When such labels are absent, algorithms are routinely trained on recorded clinical decisions or on endpoints such as patient deterioration or death.

The articles describe this reliance on historical practice as creating vulnerabilities in discretionary critical care decisions. Variation also occurs within individual physicians over time, as one clinician may admit a patient on one day and refuse an identical patient on another. Triage models trained on such records therefore reproduce inconsistent judgments rather than identifying patients who would truly deteriorate without intensive care. The articles do not report any reaction from other clinicians, hospitals, or patients, and they do not describe any deployed system adopting the approach.

They state that the proposal applies to critical care environments and that patients admitted or not admitted under these models would be the people affected. The articles also say that restricting training data risks degraded accuracy for rare patient subgroups, which would affect those patients most. Beyond the perspective itself, the articles do not describe any trial, regulatory action, or institutional response. The available reporting is limited to the authors' proposal and the methodological hurdles they list.

Articles.Title: Training Artificial Intelligence on Top Physicians May Reduce Intensive Care Bias

stories.Headline: IAB Launches New Framework to Track When AI Influences or Completes Purchases
stories.Summary:
The Interactive Advertising Bureau released a new framework on Thursday, November 12, 2026, to account for the role artificial intelligence plays in purchases, according to a press release. The framework is called the AI-Era Attribution Blueprint. It gives the industry a way to classify AI's role in a conversion and to evaluate which parties can claim credit for it. The release was reported by PYMNTS on November 13, 2026.

The blueprint asks who or what created the intent, made the decision and completed the purchase. It classifies each conversion as Human-Owned, AI-Assisted or AI-Executed. It also provides a pathway to determine which parties are eligible for a decision claim or a contributory claim, and what evidence each claim requires. The framework works alongside existing attribution systems.

Caroline Giegerich, vice president of AI at IAB, said the clicks and referrals used for attribution are thinning out or disappearing. She said AI-influenced sales are sometimes reported as search or direct traffic, so companies may send their next marketing investment to the wrong channel. She said the blueprint defines the additional credit claims AI creates and the evidence each one requires. IAB CEO David Cohen said AI has added a new dimension to the challenge of determining how influence becomes an outcome.

He said the blueprint is honest about what the industry cannot yet substantiate, and he invited everyone in the ecosystem to apply it. A PYMNTS Intelligence report from October found that nearly 61 million consumers in the United States, or 23%, now name AI as their main starting point when researching retail purchases online. The report said a consumer who welcomes AI's advice can keep control of checkout, return to a trusted marketplace or delegate the purchase. It said AI is displacing established research habits faster than it is displacing established buying relationships.

Articles.Title: IAB Launches New Framework to Track When AI Influences or Completes Purchases

stories.Headline: Review Assesses Artificial Intelligence Applications in Thyroid Cancer Diagnosis and Management
stories.Summary:
A review led by researchers at The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University has synthesized evidence on artificial intelligence in thyroid cancer diagnosis, risk assessment, and treatment. The review was published in November 2026 and covers its roles across the full course of the disease. Thyroid cancer is among the most common endocrine malignancies worldwide, with GLOBOCAN 2022 recording more than 821,000 new cases in 2022 alone. Standard diagnosis relies on palpation, neck ultrasonography, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy, but clinicians face interobserver variability, indeterminate cytology in over 15 percent of biopsied nodules, and tumor heterogeneity. The authors note that high accuracy on technical metrics does not by itself show better clinical decisions or patient outcomes.

The investigators ran a structured PubMed search on September 29, 2026, covering English-language papers published from June 10, 2021, to September 29, 2026. The search identified 1,674 records, from which the authors selected 36 original clinical studies using human-derived data. They did not carry out a pooled quantitative meta-analysis. Instead, they built a five-domain framework to assess technical feasibility, diagnostic validity, transportability, clinical decision value, and patient benefit. The framework was applied across ultrasound, cross-sectional imaging, digital pathology, genomics, and management pipelines.

Ultrasonography is the main frontline tool for nodules, which are common and carry malignancy rates of about 5 percent. One dual-view detection pipeline combining YOLOv5 with XGBoost reached an area under the curve of 0.840 in a held-out test cohort. A fusion model of B-mode ultrasound and strain elastography for TI-RADS 4 nodules reached 0.927 on external validation. The BETNET framework reached 0.951 internally and 0.970 externally. In one reader study, assistance from the ThyGPT language model raised mean radiologist area under the curve from 0.805 to 0.908, with a p-value below 0.001.

In a simulated setting, the proposed algorithm cut the share of nodules sent for biopsy from 64.2 percent to 23.3 percent. The authors caution that such retrospective simulations do not prove that biopsies can safely be avoided in practice. For staging and surgical planning, CT and MRI models were also reviewed. A prospective CT study combining an ensemble three-dimensional network with clinical factors reached 0.829 for predicting lateral cervical lymph node metastasis.

An MRI model called AMMCNet reached 0.891 for central lymph node metastasis in papillary thyroid carcinoma. In pathology, an EfficientNet model showed 94.7 percent sensitivity but only 14.4 percent specificity in the atypia of undetermined significance subgroup. A patch-based U-Net achieved 0.946 on 1,374 frozen-section slides, falling from 0.986 when only common lesions were assessed. The reviewers stress that such performance imbalances can hide excessive false positives.

Among the molecular and prognostic studies, an immune-related long non-coding RNA signature from The Cancer Genome Atlas reached one-, three-, and five-year areas under the curve of 0.929, 0.956, and 0.951 in training. A radiomics model across 1,076 papillary thyroid carcinoma patients predicted TERT promoter mutations with 0.802, rising to 0.897 when clinical variables were added. The authors emphasize that such predictive correlations cannot replace definitive laboratory molecular sequencing. A CatBoost recurrence model achieved 0.990 using SHAP explanations, but the authors caution that high concordance indices do not ensure reliable absolute risk calibration.

They also note that binary recurrence models often ignore variable follow-up and censoring. The review does not state whether any of these tools has been adopted in routine clinical practice, nor whether prospective trials have confirmed the simulated biopsy reductions. It also leaves open how the models perform across different populations and hospital settings beyond those studied. The source material is cut off before its discussion of therapeutic management, including surgical navigation, radiotherapy delivery, and systemic response forecasting, so the authors' conclusions on those applications are not available here.

Articles.Title: Review Assesses Artificial Intelligence Applications in Thyroid Cancer Diagnosis and Management

stories.Headline: Explainable Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Predicts Renal Sinus Fat Invasion in Kidney Cancer
stories.Summary:
A multicenter retrospective study of 875 patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a common kidney cancer, tested an explainable artificial intelligence system for predicting whether the tumor has invaded the renal sinus fat before surgery. The integrated multimodal system combined clinical, radiomics, and deep learning models, and the study reports that it achieved higher numerical predictive performance than any of those models alone. It reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.791 in the first test set and 0.777 in the second, with 95% confidence intervals of 0.7213 to 0.8607 and 0.6894 to 0.8655 respectively. The study was published in Cancer Imaging and reported by Scienmag and bioengineer.org on November 12, 2026.

The cohort was drawn from four independent medical institutions and split into a training set of 445 patients, an internal validation set of 111 patients, and two external multicenter evaluation sets of 181 and 138 patients. For the radiomics component, researchers extracted features from the tumor itself and from expanded regions dilated by 1 mm, 3 mm, and 5 mm, with the peri-3 mm ExtraTrees model performing best among radiomics approaches. In the deep learning component, a 2.5-dimensional model built on the ResNet34 network using a 5 mm peritumoral region showed the most consistent results across both test cohorts. A standalone clinical model reached area under the curve values of 0.735 and 0.736 across the two test sets. The representative models from each modality were combined through a support vector machine stacking ensemble, and SHAP analysis indicated that features from the 2.5D deep learning model contributed most to the final prediction.

The study authors, led by Lv, D. with co-authors including Zhou, H., Wang, Q., and Shuang, W., concluded that the system may offer adjunctive quantitative information for preoperative risk stratification in patients with suspicious computed tomography findings. They emphasized, according to the article, that prospective evaluation against existing expert assessment is needed before the system could be adopted clinically. The article does not describe any regulatory review or clinical deployment plans. It reports only the retrospective findings and the authors' stated next step of prospective testing.

Articles.Title: Explainable Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Predicts Renal Sinus Fat Invasion in Kidney Cancer

stories.Headline: Primary Care Patients Report Cautious Perceptions Toward Portal Artificial Intelligence Chatbots
stories.Summary:
Researchers surveyed active primary care patient portal users at an academic health system about a hypothetical artificial intelligence chatbot before any rollout, and the findings were published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine on November 12, 2026. The chatbot was described as based on Epic's Emmie system, and patients rated it cautiously on safety and accuracy. The study team, led by P. Haessner along with C. L. Romero, O. Ike-Okpe, N. C. Hammer and M. E. Gregory, wanted to learn how portal users felt about a chatbot connected to their medical records. Little was previously known about this, even as health systems weighed putting conversational tools into patient portals.

The authors collected responses from 2,955 portal users, a response rate of 16.1 percent, and 2,678 completed responses were included in the final analysis. Participants rated four areas on standardized 5-point scales: general acceptability, trust in receiving accurate health information, perceived patient safety, and their personal willingness to talk to the chatbot. The overall mean for acceptability was 3.30, while trust in accuracy averaged 2.59, perceived safety 2.51, and willingness to talk 2.79. The researchers used multivariable linear and ordinal logistic regression models that adjusted for age, gender, race, retirement status, portal task counts, portal use frequency and levels of technophobia. Results showed that older age and Nonwhite race were linked to higher acceptability, while female gender was linked to lower acceptability, and these patterns held across the other domains.

The authors reported that greater portal task counts were associated with higher acceptability and greater willingness to talk to the chatbot, whereas technophobia was associated with lower acceptability, with stronger effects at moderate or high levels. Retired status was linked to lower acceptability and lower perceived safety. The authors concluded that patients were more open in some groups but widely cautious about clinical safety and factual accuracy. They said these findings support a careful approach to deploying portal-embedded chatbots, one that accounts for patient perceptions along with the known limitations of large language models. The article does not describe any planned rollout or next steps beyond that recommendation.

Articles.Title: Primary Care Patients Report Cautious Perceptions Toward Portal Artificial Intelligence Chatbots

stories.Headline: Chinese company unveils AI-powered laser mosquito zapper - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A Chinese company recently launched a new laser device designed to kill mosquitoes. This technology uses artificial intelligence to track the insects while they are flying. Once a target is identified, the machine burns the wings of the mosquito. The product was unveiled on November 13, 2026.

The system relies on autonomous technology to operate effectively. This specific design ensures that the laser remains safe for humans. It also prevents the device from harming pets in the home. The company intends for this to be a modern solution for pest control.

The developers of the device are responsible for its safety features. They claim the AI can distinguish between pests and other objects. This allows the laser to fire only at the intended targets. They believe this represents the future of eliminating insects.

The company introduced this tool as a high-tech alternative to traditional zappers. It aims to provide a more precise way to handle infestations. The device is now available for use in various environments. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Chinese company unveils AI-powered laser mosquito zapper - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Expands Epidemiological Reasoning but Demands Rigorous Human Evaluation
stories.Summary:
Researchers writing in the European Journal of Epidemiology, through an essay by Ulrich Mansmann, examine whether artificial intelligence can broaden the conceptual space in which epidemiological reasoning takes place. The analysis traces the idea of automated deduction back more than three centuries to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Leibniz proposed a formal language, the characteristica universalis, and a calculus ratiocinator for resolving relations between scientific concepts. Faced with disagreement, he imagined disputants saying "Calculemus," meaning let us calculate. Modern generative systems reverse that direction, since large language models learn from the historical record of human discourse rather than from an external system of rational truth.

The essay argues that generative artificial intelligence can move researchers from ordinary cognitive tasks toward systematic meta-reasoning. Because training corpora include scientific claims together with criticism and debate, such systems can compare arguments across domains, juxtapose competing hypotheses, and detect incompatible assumptions. They can also propose alternative explanations and test whether conclusions follow from stated premises. Human epidemiologists work within limited disciplinary horizons, so these systems can help investigators look beyond narrow traditions. However, the essay stresses that generated propositions must connect back to empirical evidence, formal logic, computation, and reproducible analysis.

Breadth of concepts does not guarantee completeness, and textual consistency does not establish truth. The essay draws on empirical research by Zhou and colleagues, who found that larger and more instructable language models do not simply become more reliable. Instead of avoiding difficult queries, more capable models often give sensible-looking answers that are factually wrong, and human supervisors frequently fail to detect these errors. The authors conclude that the capacity to broaden a reasoning space is distinct from the capacity to evaluate it accurately.

The essay also notes that epidemiological inference rarely moves directly from observations to definitive conclusions, relying instead on a chain running from study design through statistical analysis and causal interpretation. Artificial intelligence could test whether each link in that chain holds together. To illustrate the approach, the essay reviews colorectal cancer screening within Germany's FARKOR programme, which evaluated screening for people aged 25 to 50 with a familial risk of colorectal cancer. Conventional German screening was predominantly age-based and excluded individuals under 50.

Persons with a positive family history develop colorectal cancer more often and at younger ages, with relative risks reported as roughly two- to four-fold higher depending on family constellation. The essay describes the key shift as moving from asking at what age screening should begin to asking at what level of risk it should begin. Among FARKOR participants undergoing colonoscopy, detection rates for adenoma and advanced adenoma were roughly the same magnitude as those in older populations already eligible for conventional screening. The essay concludes that artificial intelligence's value lies in revealing when an apparently coherent age-based policy argument rests on an incomplete picture of the health problem, not in autonomously declaring a screening age.

The World Health Organization has described prospective roles for artificial intelligence across evidence-informed health policy, including problem identification, evidence synthesis, policy design, scenario simulation, implementation and monitoring. The WHO frames such tools as augmenting rather than replacing human judgement, with multidisciplinary deliberation and sustained human oversight. The essay separates three domains: evidence, consistency and values. Artificial intelligence can survey evidence and test consistency, but the values that society should prioritize cannot be derived from epidemiological data alone.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Expands Epidemiological Reasoning but Demands Rigorous Human Evaluation

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence applied to marketing: 67% use it to create advertising content
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is spreading through retail marketing and advertising departments, where companies use it to generate content, recommend products, place ads, and tailor campaigns to individual consumers. According to a report called State of AI in Retail and Consumer Packaged Goods: 2026 Trends, published by NVIDIA and covered by Merca2.0 on November 12, 2026, content creation is the leading AI use case in digital commerce, cited by 67% of respondents. The same report found that 58% use recommendation systems and 54% apply AI to marketing and advertising placement. Another 52% use adaptive advertising, and 50% employ customer service assistants. The findings describe a shift in which AI covers several stages of the relationship between brands and consumers.

The report also points to AI agents as a trend gaining traction. These are systems able to reason, plan, and carry out specific actions with more autonomy than traditional tools. Among organizations implementing them, 48% use AI agents for personalized marketing and advertising. Personalization also reaches product discovery, where 42% use catalog enrichment to improve and localize product information through text, images, and video. Shopping assistants account for 31% and guide consumers through discovery and purchase.

Taken together, these uses let companies adjust messages and recommendations to each customer's context. NVIDIA is the source of the data, and the article attributes the findings to its report rather than to independent verification. The report says 91% of retail and consumer packaged goods companies are already using or evaluating AI, while 58% say they have actively deployed it. Among the technologies being used or evaluated, data analytics and generative AI and large language models each reached 66%, and agentic AI stood at 47%.

Respondents also said AI has had a positive effect on their business, with 89% reporting a positive impact on revenue and 95% reporting that it helps reduce annual costs. The article presents these figures as evidence that marketing is entering a new phase, in which AI is no longer used only to speed up the creation of advertising materials. It now plays a role in audience selection, product recommendations, ad placement, message personalization, and customer service. The article does not describe specific regulatory requirements or changes that companies must make, and it does not indicate what further developments are expected next.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence applied to marketing: 67% use it to create advertising content

stories.Headline: STALLARD: Artificial intelligence can't replace the real kind
stories.Summary:
Gary Stallard wrote a column published by The Lufkin Daily News on November 13, 2026, about artificial intelligence. He described using a form of AI to restore old family photos. One restored photo showed his mother and grandmother together, the only picture he has of the two of them. The original was a hazy, faded black-and-white image with white spots from age and time in a photo album. The restored result was crystal clear, with faces just as he remembered them down to the smallest detail.

Stallard also ran a color photo of himself, his brothers and their dad through the AI, and the restored picture showed people he did not recognize. He tried clearing up a recent sports photo he had shot that was slightly out of focus. The AI gave the kid a third ear, and the lettering on his jersey looked like hieroglyphics. He once read an AI-generated recap of a sporting event that had numerous errors, including the wrong final score and the wrong winning team. He said his biggest issue with artificial intelligence is accuracy.

Stallard wrote that AI is here to stay and has its value. He recalled listening to a panel of business and state leaders who fielded questions on the future of artificial intelligence. Some examples related how technicians in certain fields can use prompts to get quick answers from AI, saving countless hours of analysis. The business owners acknowledged that blind trust in AI is not realistic and that a human element must ensure information is accurate and useful. Stallard boiled the ethical use of AI down to using it as a tool for one's own work, such as a student checking spelling and grammar or a photographer sharpening an image.

He wrote that using AI to create work is risky and unethical, and that he could have prompted AI to write the whole column and then put his name on it. He said he would not have been able to guarantee the information was factual. He noted that some AI content flooding social media is made for fun, but other content is created with the sole intention of deceiving. He said people who recognize it call it "AI Slop," and that not everyone has those recognition factors. He admitted to falling for a fake image at first, only realizing he was being duped after closer inspection.

Stallard wrote that he understands fears of society getting overrun by AI agents taking all jobs and doing all thinking and decision making. He said that from what he is seeing and learning so far, AI is not yet ready for a full-on takeover. He wrote that plenty of real intelligence is still needed to handle all the artificial stuff. He is a regular contributor to the Opinion page of The Lufkin Daily News, and his email address is garylstallard@gmail.com.

Articles.Title: STALLARD: Artificial intelligence can't replace the real kind

stories.Headline: Nurses’ Clinical Reasoning Competency Linked to Higher Artificial Intelligence Literacy in China
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a cross-sectional study in China that concluded on November 13, 2026. The investigation found that registered nurses with stronger clinical reasoning skills also possess higher artificial intelligence literacy. This link suggests that basic reasoning abilities help healthcare workers better understand and use digital tools. The study was published in the journal BMC Nursing.

The project involved 306 registered nurses from healthcare institutions in Guangdong Province. Participants used the SO JUMP platform to provide data via the Nurse Clinical Reasoning Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. The nurses earned a median literacy score of 90.00, with a range between 79.00 and 97.00. Statistical tests showed a positive correlation between reasoning and literacy, with coefficients from r = 0.289 to r = 0.551.

The research team, including authors such as Yang, Lu, and Peng, managed the data analysis. They used multiple linear regression and the Mann-Whitney U test to evaluate the results. The authors stated that clinical reasoning is a vital cognitive trait for managing intelligent systems. They argued that training programs should teach reasoning skills alongside technical instruction.

The study used Cognitive Load Theory to explain how clinicians handle the high demands of automated systems. It posits that advanced reasoning helps nurses organize complex digital information during patient care. The findings highlight a need for updated nursing curricula to integrate these cognitive skills. This approach aims to improve how professionals employ machine intelligence in routine workflows.

Articles.Title: Nurses’ Clinical Reasoning Competency Linked to Higher Artificial Intelligence Literacy in China

stories.Headline: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
stories.Summary:
Developers can get AI coding assistants with minimal setup by using a large language model gateway and LiteLLM to reach foundation models on Amazon Bedrock, according to an AWS blog post published on 12 November 2026. The post shows how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate. The pattern puts Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API so developers reach foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key. The post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models as examples. The gateway gives platform teams latency and error monitoring, finance teams cost attribution to teams and projects, and security teams consistent access controls.

A developer's OpenAI-compatible client reaches the gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront and an Application Load Balancer, then authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL for virtual-key and spend state, Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM invokes the Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management task role, and Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute and tokens per minute metrics and the quota alarm. LiteLLM documents the AI Gateway as free for up to five users with a license required beyond that, and the self-service key issuance described in the post requires the Enterprise version. The example configuration sets a max_budget of 250 with a 7d rolling window, max_parallel_requests of 10, max_retries of 3 and a timeout of 900 for extended thinking on Sonnet, and a timeout of 120 on Haiku.

The post says operations engineers set the spend policy in the LiteLLM portal while developers self-provision API keys within those parameters, and the portal can integrate with corporate single sign-on. It warns not to hardcode the master key or database credentials in config.yaml, because LiteLLM resolves os.environ references at load time from variables set on the Fargate task and sourced from AWS Secrets Manager. It says that when the model is a raw inference-profile ARN, LiteLLM cannot find it in its built-in cost map and defaults the cost to $0, so per-key spend stays 0 and budgets never enforce, and per-token costs must be set explicitly. It recommends Global cross-Region inference when the selected models support it and organizational policies permit processing across supported AWS commercial Regions worldwide, while Geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a defined geography. It says the copyFrom ARN for Global CRIS must reference the system-defined inference profile prefixed with global., not the foundation-model ARN directly, and that scoping only to the application-inference-profile ARN returns a not authorized error at invoke time.

The post says developers can configure tools such as Claude Code, Continue and Cursor with a single base URL and API key, and can swap models, add fallbacks or migrate model providers without touching developer configurations. It says LiteLLM Enterprise is a scalable, production-minded licensed version that includes the open source gateway plus single sign-on, audit logs, delegated admin roles and support. It says Langfuse provides open source LLM observability for prompt-level telemetry, latency tracking and debugging, complementing the infrastructure-level metrics of Amazon CloudWatch with application-level insight. It says the post does not cover adding Amazon Bedrock Guardrails such as content filtering and grounding, but that appropriate responsible AI controls would normally be included before deploying to production. It says the free tier supports virtual keys, and that the LiteLLM AI Gateway component is open source and suitable for a small pilot with some limitations.

The post gives prerequisites of an AWS account, Amazon Bedrock model access, appropriate IAM permissions and LiteLLM. It says each model such as Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku gets its own inference profile managed with the AWS Cloud Development Kit, giving per-model quota isolation and a clean abstraction layer between LiteLLM's configuration and Amazon Bedrock model versioning. It says Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference avoids the overhead of implementing cross-Region request routing yourself, with benefits including access to a broader pool of Regional capacity, automatic routing to a supported Region with available capacity, and broader model selection because some models are available only through an inference profile. It says Global cross-Region inference provides access to a broader pool of Regional capacity with potential pricing benefits compared with Geographic cross-Region inference. It says model availability, applicable service quotas and model-specific pricing can be verified through current AWS documentation and AWS pricing pages.

The post says the inference profile handles model resolution and cross-Region routing transparently without additional configuration, and that Amazon Bedrock routes to available capacity across configured AWS Regions and returns the response. It says LiteLLM integrates with Langfuse through logging callbacks, giving visibility into model invocations without changes to developer tool configurations. It says the portal can be opened at http://localhost:4000/ui during local testing. It says readers will understand the pattern well enough to build their own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS CDK constructs. It says the IAM policy is scoped least-privilege, naming the exact models in use rather than bedrock:* or *, and for Global CRIS it must include the inference profile, the regional foundation model and the global foundation model resources.

Articles.Title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM | Amazon Web Services

stories.Headline: Atman, Brahman, and the machine: An Upanishadic reading of artificial intelligence, in six questions
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a story with the paragraph and sentence structure you've set, because the article is an opinion essay, not news. It argues a philosophical position about the Upanishads and artificial intelligence, and the excerpt cuts off mid-argument, so it contains no reported events, dates of a news development, named responsible parties or their statements, or affected groups. The "what happened, who did it and when" framing doesn't fit, and forcing the essay into that shape would mean inventing facts or padding. What I can do accurately is summarize the essay's own argument in the requested style, which means sticking to what the author actually claims: The essay, published by The South First on November 13, 2026, takes the Upanishads' distinction between what a person knows and produces and what a person fundamentally is, and applies it to artificial intelligence.

The author argues that individual human knowledge has always been limited by bounded capacity, bounded time and a slow, lossy transmission process, so each generation largely re-derives its inheritance. The author notes that storing knowledge outside the mind is not new, citing writing, which Plato's Phaedrus warned would breed forgetfulness, along with libraries, the printing press and the internet. What is new, the author argues, is the scope and speed of retrieval, which has begun to make the human search for information look like drawing water from a well when a tap is available. On the philosophical side, the essay explains the Upanishadic method of neti neti and the concept of Atman as a witness that is not identical with anything it perceives.

It sets out how Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita differ on how close the individual self stands to Brahman. The essay then argues that a superintelligent AI, however capable, has a beginning, is an object of knowledge and can be switched off, so it does not fit the Upanishadic description of Brahman as unconditioned and without beginning. The author says some technologists are projecting Brahman onto the machine, and the excerpt ends before the author finishes developing that critique. If you have a news article about a specific AI event, such as a regulation, a release or a company announcement, send it and I will write it in the six-paragraph format.

Articles.Title: Atman, Brahman, and the machine: An Upanishadic reading of artificial intelligence, in six questions

stories.Headline: Union County moms say daughters are victims of AI child porn created by classmates
stories.Summary:
Two Union County mothers told WBTV that their daughters, who were in eighth grade at Marvin Ridge Middle School, were victims of AI-generated child pornography created and shared by classmates. The mothers said two of the girls' classmates created the photo using an app or website and passed it around the school. The daughters were 13 and 14 years old at the time of the incident. The mothers spoke on the record with WBTV, which is not identifying them because their children are underage. The photo was a happy moment from the end of the softball season, the mothers said.

According to the Union County Sheriff's Office, the two boys have been charged with second-degree sexual exploitation of a minor. The sheriff's office said the charges were filed by the school resource officer and that there have been no additional reports or incidents related to this matter. The Union County District Attorney's Office is prosecuting the case in juvenile court, according to the mothers. The school resource officer told the moms that one of the boys deleted the photo. The Union County Public Schools student code of conduct published online says discipline for possession of pornographic, profane, and/or violent material could lead to a three-to five-day suspension for middle or high school students.

The mothers said they are the ones being made to feel like they have done something wrong. "We don't want another parent or child to be in the same shoes we're in," one mother said. "If we stay quiet, what are we doing?" One mother said she went into her daughter's room and found her crying, saying there was a naked picture of her and her friends passed around school. The other mother said she felt tremendous guilt having to ask her daughter if she was nude in a picture, and her daughter was horrified and said she would never do that.

The moms said the girls' bodies in the photo are artificial intelligence, but their faces are all too real. The mothers said their daughters have faced mental and emotional trauma and have lost friends. One mother said the girls have been uninvited to things because parents saw the invite list, saw the girls' names, and uninvited them. The mothers said families have contacted them separately advocating for the boys' families to essentially say "boys will be boys." One mother said the boys can sit as close as they want to the girls as long as they don't contact them, and that it is very uncomfortable for the girls.

The mothers said simply deleting the photo off a phone after it had been distributed does not give them any peace of mind. FBI Charlotte Special Agent in Charge Reid Davis said AI-generated child pornography is just as bad as the real deal. Davis said there are mechanisms for perpetrators to take a photograph of a clothed individual and de-clothe them, using the images for gratification, exchange in dark web networks, or sextortion. Davis said the tools are available across all platforms and can be found for free in the app store on your phone.

Davis said an adult child psychiatrist in Charlotte was charged and sentenced to prison for AI child porn after FBI agents in Charlotte investigated, using childhood photographs of colleagues and de-clothing them. The FBI does not investigate cases with juvenile suspects, leaving it to state and local authorities to charge and prosecute teenage offenders. The Union County Public Schools district said it can't release information about student matters but said violations of the student code of conduct are "immediately addressed by school-level staff." The district said if an incident may violate Title IX regulations, possible complainants can file a formal Title IX complaint for the district to investigate, which would require a pause on disciplinary action pending completion of the investigation.

The district said Policy 4-23 addresses student criminal behavior, but any district action based on that policy is limited to circumstances where a student has been convicted or charged with a violent crime as outlined in the statute. It was not immediately known whether a Title IX complaint was filed in this case. Davis said parents should explore applications to put locks and filters on what their kids can see and do on the internet. The mothers said they are due back in court for a hearing in late November regarding their case.

One mother said it is so easy to do and will be wildfire, and that if schools, the state, or the country doesn't get ahead of trying to create accountability, another mom is going to be sitting right there. The other mother said any parent should know this is this easy with AI and that it is destructive to the person who creates it, who should be held accountable. Davis said super intelligence is everywhere and will only gain more of a foothold in everything done with the internet. The mothers said the image was out on the internet, the vast wide web, and that the girls have been victimized all over again as if they were the problem.

Articles.Title: Union County moms say daughters are victims of AI child porn created by classmates

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s leadership crisis puts enterprise AI’s dependence on one company under scrutiny
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Thursday that president and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned, effective immediately, Network World reported on Nov 12, 2026. Earlier that week, news broke that Huang had had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report. EVP and CFO Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO, and Nvidia’s board began searching for a permanent replacement. The revelations and Huang’s swift departure sparked a US national security crisis, the article said. They also raised questions about over-reliance on one tech vendor and about supply chain and compute constraints.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993, initially targeting the gaming market, and the company later pivoted to meet the intensive compute demands of AI. Nvidia’s GPUs became the standard for graphics rendering, and companies building AI came to depend on them for training and running large language models and increasingly sophisticated AI agents. Nvidia has inked deals and established partnerships with Anthropic, Meta, Dell, HPE, Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Accenture, Marvell Technology, Hugging Face and many others. The company has hovered around 90% market share for a long time, according to analyst Carmi Levy. Nvidia’s board initiated an independent investigation into Huang’s actions earlier that week.

Levy, a technology analyst, said the scandal opens a hornet’s nest of security concerns Nvidia won’t be in a position to answer for months, if ever. He said it throws into doubt the company’s leadership and security practices and ignites questions around board-level governance and oversight. He said Nvidia has been the default choice for AI infrastructure buyers for as long as there has been an AI infrastructure market. He said this chapter should serve as a wakeup call to corporate boards, which are responsible for mitigating risk on behalf of their organization and its stakeholders. He said boards “can’t afford to look the other way when human-factored risks hit their radar.”

Asa Hiken, senior analyst at Emarketer, said AI technology has become critical to US national security, making even the personal relationships of industry leaders a potential vulnerability. Levy said IT buyers may take a pause, and that enterprises now face the stark reality that the Nvidia of the future may not be the default choice the Nvidia of the past has always been. He said a hobbled Nvidia could in the near term result in supply chain issues, component shortages and project delays. Jack E. Gold, president and principal analyst at J.Gold Associates, said there is some real risk that Huang’s leaving could hamper new technology deployments and create a bottleneck in R&D. Stephanie Balaouras, a Forrester VP, advised that tech leaders shouldn’t overreact but should treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers and investment plans.

Levy said that longer term the stage is set for improvements as customers shift focus to other suppliers and competitors reposition themselves. He said a more diversified vendor landscape means customers may finally wean themselves off this overly dominant provider. He added that this comes with near-term costs enterprises should account for before planning their post-Jensen-Huang Nvidia relationship. He said development could foreshadow a more robust AI ecosystem where chipmakers compete more aggressively and one dominant player doesn’t set the tone. He said that when a market is as dependent on a single player as the Nvidia-led space has been, it is reasonable to conclude it was never sustainable to begin with.

Gold said Nvidia had been able to define a very fast moving field through sheer tech prowess under Huang’s leadership. He raised the questions of whether its ability to define the tech space will be affected and whether Huang’s leaving will give rivals an ability to catch up and perhaps exceed Nvidia, lessening its dominance. He said that wouldn’t happen immediately but could over time. Levy said changing vendors could mean major shifts in how customers choose to build out their architectures, how they pay for them and how they maintain them. The articles leave open who will become permanent CEO and what the board’s independent investigation will find.

Articles.Title: Nvidia’s leadership crisis puts enterprise AI’s dependence on one company under scrutiny

stories.Headline: SDSU researcher puts artificial intelligence to work in wheat fields
stories.Summary:
Subash Thapa, a doctoral student at South Dakota State University, is drawing growing attention from the science and agriculture industries for research that combines wheat breeding with plant disease work. According to The Dakota Scout, the article was published on November 12, 2026, and it highlights a string of recent recognitions for his work. Those recognitions include a $20,400 Global Wheat Health Alliance Seed Grant, which he received in recent months. He also took part in an international plant research program in Ghana and won an Innovation Sprint quiz competition. Additionally, he received a $1,000 Phi Kappa Phi Love of Learning Award.

The article notes that Thapa was the only U.S. student selected for the Ghana training program. The Scout describes the trip and his awards as adding to a growing list of accomplishments. The piece also states that his work involves using artificial intelligence in wheat fields, with a focus on how crops are bred and how they resist disease. The article does not provide details on the specific methods of the AI tools or the results of his experiments. It also does not describe what the grant or award money will be spent on.

The story is based on the reporting of The Dakota Scout, and the article is written as a profile of Thapa's accomplishments rather than as a formal announcement from the university. Thapa himself is quoted in the piece, but the article is not clear on every detail of his research timeline. The coverage is presented as part of a broader look at graduate research at the state's land-grant institution. The article also features a courtesy photo of Thapa standing in a wheat field at the Dakota Lakes Research Farm near Pierre. The Scout does not state whether any follow-up research, publications, or further funding are planned.

Articles.Title: SDSU researcher puts artificial intelligence to work in wheat fields

stories.Headline: Medical Artificial Intelligence Procurement in China Concentrates Heavily in Tertiary Hospitals
stories.Summary:
A national analysis of public procurement data from Chinese public hospitals between 2020 and 2024 has found that the spread of medical artificial intelligence across regions hides a growing concentration of diagnostic equipment in top-tier tertiary hospitals. Researchers Panpan Jiang and Lisha Cheng tracked where capital-intensive, AI-enabled diagnostic and screening devices were bought and installed across the country. They wanted to know whether these real-world deployments matched goals of equitable healthcare access. The study was published in BMC Health Services Research under the title "Geographic convergence masks institutional stratification in the scale-up of medical AI in China."

The researchers applied Theil-T indices, spatial agglomeration metrics and location quotients to separate two trends that pointed in opposite directions. At the regional level, national device volume rose from 8 units in 2020 to 298 units in 2024, a 37.25-fold increase. Over the same period the population-based Theil-T index fell from 0.425 to 0.047 and the hospital-based index fell from 0.591 to 0.070. Regions with zero adoption were eliminated by 2022. Within hospitals, however, tertiary facilities held a location quotient of 2.154 in 2024, while secondary hospitals' quotient slipped from 0.361 in 2020 to 0.320.

The authors state that the within-region, tier-based share of total inequality grew from 47.3 percent in 2020 to 84.5 percent in 2024. They conclude that regional equity metrics alone understate institutional inequality in how medical AI spreads. They argue that policy frameworks and deployment monitoring should incorporate hospital tier classifications rather than relying only on aggregate device counts or regional distributions. The article does not report any planned policy changes or government responses to the findings. Its authors are the study's only stated sources on these conclusions.

Articles.Title: Medical Artificial Intelligence Procurement in China Concentrates Heavily in Tertiary Hospitals

stories.Headline: Massachusetts Invests $3.3M to Find New Challenges for AI
stories.Summary:
The Healey-Driscoll administration and the Massachusetts AI Hub have awarded $3,295,792 in state money to five projects that apply artificial intelligence to practical problems. The awards were reported on November 12, 2026, by Ashley Silver of Government Technology. The projects span Boston, Cambridge, Fall River, Marshfield and Lincoln, and they address public health, coastal protection, workforce training, manufacturing and defense. The latest round raises the Hub's total investment in applied AI projects to about $6.1 million, and the five recipients will add more than $1.1 million in matching support from their partners. The money comes through the MA Applied AI Models Innovation Challenge, which began in January 2025 and funds smaller, specialized AI models built for specific industries.

Grants can pay for everything from collecting data to testing a model in real conditions, and each project can receive up to $1 million. The largest award, $958,550, went to the Atlantic Resiliency Innovation Institute, which is building a system to predict flood risk at specific coastal locations, especially around energy infrastructure. Boston University received $298,394 for PandemIQ Llama, also called the BEACON Platform, which scans global health information to flag possible disease outbreaks. Bristol Community College received $727,270 for an AI tool that assesses workers' skills from examples of their completed work and compares them with industry standards. Harvard's Kempner Institute received $811,578 for Large Video Planner-Industrial, a project to teach robots tasks by having them watch videos of people, and the UMass Lowell Applied Research Corporation received $500,000 for a platform that coordinates sensors during counter-drone operations.

Economic Development Secretary Eric Paley, speaking in an emailed news release, said the state wants the investments to help industries meet their challenges while keeping responsible AI development in focus. He said the program supports projects that can strengthen the economy and keep Massachusetts a leader in applied AI. Sabrina Mansur, director of the AI Hub, said in a statement that the Challenge helps researchers build, test and refine domain-specific models so that new technologies move closer to practical use across the state and beyond. The article presents these statements as the official rationale for the grants.

The awards sit within a wider state effort to put AI to work in government and public services. Massachusetts has introduced an AI virtual assistant on mass.gov that has handled an estimated 700,000 to 800,000 conversations across multiple agencies, according to Chief Digital Officer Devyn Paros. In June the state launched a Constituent Experience Center of Excellence to help agencies improve their online services. The article does not say what the next round of funding or the next phase of these projects will involve.

Articles.Title: Massachusetts Invests $3.3M to Find New Challenges for AI

stories.Headline: Review Assesses Artificial Intelligence as Investigational Support for Cutaneous Lupus Care
stories.Summary:
A narrative review published in Frontiers in Medicine concludes that artificial intelligence shows early promise for helping diagnose and monitor cutaneous lupus erythematosus, but the technologies remain investigational and need substantial validation before clinical use. Researchers led by Heying Wang evaluated computational algorithms designed to assess lupus-related skin lesions, extract severity indicators from medical records, and interpret biological signatures. Cutaneous lupus is difficult to diagnose because its lesions range from acute inflammatory eruptions to scarring chronic plaques that closely resemble eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, and lichen planus. The review found that algorithmic sophistication has outpaced rigorous, disease-specific clinical validation across diverse patient groups. The authors mapped published studies by clinical task, data type, disease relevance, and validation maturity.

The authors separated studies that examined cutaneous lupus patients from those that studied systemic lupus or general dermatology datasets. Image-based systems have shown preliminary feasibility for lesion recognition and subtype classification in cutaneous lupus. A multicenter study led by Li and colleagues used a multimodal deep learning platform trained on 800 clinical photographs and 3,786 multicolor immunohistochemistry images from 25 institutions in China. That platform covered 446 total cases across 13 diagnostic categories, and it reached a sensitivity of 0.8288 and a specificity of 0.9852. With the system's help, dermatologists' diagnostic accuracy rose from 66.88 percent to 81.25 percent.

The review noted that the 446 cases spanned multiple diagnostic categories rather than cutaneous lupus alone. Current severity-assessment evidence relies on natural language processing of text rather than computer vision of photographs. In a proof-of-concept study by Nezafati and colleagues, a rule-based pipeline and fine-tuned BERT model parsed 124 clinical notes from 50 patients at a single medical center. The text-based model classified disease activity with 0.91 accuracy and damage with 0.89 accuracy on a test cohort of 26 patients.

Its estimated scores correlated with clinician-recorded scores at r = 0.64 for activity and r = 0.88 for damage. The review stressed that this shows feasibility for extracting clinical documentation, not automated scoring of photographs, which remains unvalidated. The review also described molecular and cellular studies, which offer biological insight but not validated patient-level decision tools.
